Maurice Coquet presents a 2025 proceedings paper, on behalf of a large collider collaboration, on telling apart two kinds of a heavy particle in nuclear collisions. The particle, a bound charm pair state, comes in prompt form, made at the crash site, and a delayed form, born later from beauty particles. The split reveals how each fares in the hot medium the collisions create.

The team measured both forms in lead on lead collisions at a set energy, at central angles. The delayed form also opens a window on how beauty quarks lose energy in the medium. A new forward tracker extends the same split to forward angles in the latest run.
arxiv-2501-01378:
Domokos Szász reviews random walks and Lorentz processes in a 2025 paper. Both serve as basic models of Brownian motion, the jittery movement seen in particles. Random walks belong to probability theory, while Lorentz processes, where a particle bounces among fixed obstacles, belong to the theory of chaotic dynamical systems, and the two fields rarely meet.

Szász recounts how probability methods cracked questions about the Lorentz process, starting from a 1981 question by Sinai on limit laws for locally disturbed versions. In the plane, small local changes to a random walk leave its limit laws untouched, whether jumps are bounded or not. Related results cover the Lorentz gas with finite horizon, and they yield a fresh proof of its recurrence. An infinite-horizon case stays open.
arxiv-2501-01578:
Nikki Arendse and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on two exploding stars whose light was bent by a galaxy in front of them. Only two such lensed type Ia supernovae behind a lone galaxy are known. Their split images shine with brightness ratios that a smooth lens model cannot explain. Tiny lumps in the lens galaxy, even single stars, may be bending the light further.

By matching the images to simulated maps of that fine bending, the team measure how steeply the lens galaxy's mass is packed and how much of it could be dark compact objects. They found no sign of such a dark population, with an upper limit of about a quarter of the mass. The result uses the stars' known brightness as a rare clean yardstick.
arxiv-2501-01678: Shengyu Li and Zhigang Wang study a geometric flow for circle patterns in a 2025 math paper. Circle patterns tile a surface with circles in set arrangements, and finding patterns with prescribed curvatures is a core task in discrete geometry. Their combinatorial Calabi flow deforms a pattern toward the target shape. The authors prove the flow runs for all time in both hyperbolic and Euclidean settings and settles exponentially fast on the ideal pattern whenever the target curvatures can be attained.
arxiv-2501-02078:
Fernando Dobarro and Carolina Rey wrote a 2025 math paper on warped product spaces that solve the Einstein equation. Warped products build a large space from smaller ones with scale factors. The authors focus on products with many warped parts and on a broad class named after Kasner, here built on a base with many dimensions.

The paper gives conditions for when such Einstein spaces exist and when they cannot exist. It also gives bounds on the Einstein constant, the number that sets the curve of the space, and shows how those bounds limit which forms are possible. Readers get a clear map of the space of allowed shapes for this family, stated as firm rules rather than examples alone. The work is pure theory, aimed at geometers who study curved spaces.
arxiv-2501-02178:
Peiyang Yu and co-authors survey language models in recommendation systems in a 2025 paper. Classic filters struggle with new users, sparse data, and narrow inputs. Language models can read reviews and social text for richer signals.

Systems like GPT-4 can reason over unstructured user content. That ability can ease the cold-start problem for new items. Diversity of suggestions may also improve beyond past clicks. The survey organizes applications by task and method. Open problems in cost, bias, and evaluation are discussed. Readers get a map of where language models genuinely change recommendation practice.
arxiv-2501-02278:
Chen, Böhlen, and Helmer present a study from twenty twenty-five comparing tree data structures for connectivity queries on changing graphs. Graphs with frequent edge insertions and deletions need fast connectivity answers. Many structures have been proposed over decades for that task. Few were ever implemented, let alone tested head-to-head. The team build reference implementations for the main proposals. They benchmark them across a wide range of graph types. No current solution is ready for direct deployment, they find.

Each structure shows critical practical weaknesses in their tests. Balanced structures carry heavy space and time overhead. Lean structures degrade badly in worst cases. Maintenance costs burden the balanced options further. The authors close with guidance for building robust versions.
arxiv-2501-02378:
Fatih Dinc and co-authors give an analytic model of abrupt learning in recurrent neural networks, the sudden jumps in skill seen on working memory tasks. Networks in such cases pass through slow regions of state space that stretch their time scales. The cause of the jumps, and their role in learning, had stayed unclear.

Their ghost mechanism names the cause: a brief slowdown near the remnant of a saddle-node bifurcation. A one-dimensional form captures learning through a single scale parameter. It predicts a critical learning rate that falls as the time scale grows, and two failure modes past that rate, tied to vanishing and oscillating gradients. Tests in low-rank and full-rank networks matched the theory.
arxiv-2501-02478:
Chenxi Bai and Zhaoxin Liang report an anomaly in a core rule of topological physics in a 2025 paper. Bulk-edge correspondence says the deep properties of a material's interior dictate the states on its edge. The rule is a design foundation for topological devices.

Their testbed is a nonlinear Rice-Mele model, a chain with alternating bonds and site energies. Recent work handled nonlinearity in eigenvalues by adding auxiliary values to restore the correspondence. The authors find a case where the correspondence still breaks in an anomalous way. Pinpointing where the rule fails protects device designs that bank on it, and it refines the theory for nonlinear systems, a growing frontier.
arxiv-2501-02678:
Liedokto wrote this 2025 mathematics paper introducing a new algebraic structure called the (m,n)-seminearring. Algebra builds number-like systems from sets with operations that follow set rules. The new structure widens an older notion, the (m,n)-semiring, by loosening some of its demands.

The paper develops the basic theory of the structure step by step. It defines substructures and ideals, and treats the case where the system has a unity element. Maps between two such systems that respect their operations are studied as homomorphisms. A factor construction built from a congruence relation is also given, along with several properties of these objects. The method is to adapt the established theory of (m,n)-semirings to the wider setting. The work is foundational rather than applied.
arxiv-2501-02778:
Predicting how long a cancer patient will survive works better when more kinds of data are combined. Binyu Zhang and co-authors present a network, ICFNet, that fuses four data types in this 2025 paper: tissue slide images, gene activity profiles, patient details, and treatment records. Special encoders first turn each type into features on its own terms.

A fusion module then merges those features, helped by a step that strips out redundant parts. A custom loss keeps training fair across patients whose outcomes differ widely. On five public cancer data sets, covering bladder, breast, brain, lung, and womb cancers, the network beat prior methods. The authors offer it as support for treatment planning and precision care.
arxiv-2501-02878:
Nyergesy and four co-authors wrote a 2025 physics paper on heat and quantum gravity. They study a view called Asymptotically Safe gravity, where gravity stays well behaved at very small scales. Their tool is a thermal form of the renormalization group, which tracks how rules change with scale.

The team ties the heat value to the running scale, so heat acts like a second cutoff beside the quantum one. They track how the gravity strength and the cosmic constant shift as heat grows. At very high heat, the fixed point for gravity strength fades and the cosmic constant turns negative. As the cosmos cools through a phase change, their account has the constant run to the positive value seen today.
arxiv-2501-02978:
Conti and Ortiz present a rigorous method to infer the elastic law of a material from measures taken only at its boundary, in a paper from 2025. The head gives the authors by surname only in the part shown. No full field imaging of the inside is needed, since total energy can be read from work done at the edge.

Their cost measure compares the total energy of a trial law with the measured energy across many boundary pushes. They prove that best laws exist in their framework, and that whether a law can be identified rests on how well boundary data separate laws. The frame points to a class of neural networks built from piecewise linear parts. Those networks can approximate any energy law as they grow.
arxiv-2501-03078:
Théophane Vallaeys and co-authors improve a method for squeezing data vectors into compact codes, in this 2025 paper. Such codes power fast search through huge image and text collections. A popular scheme encodes each vector in steps, fixing the error left by the step before. Its flaw is that each step ignores what the others chose, which wastes accuracy.

An earlier design fixed that flaw by letting a neural network set each step's codebook from the partial rebuild so far. This paper's version, Qinco2, refines that idea for sharper results at high accuracy settings. The gain is a better trade between code size and rebuild error. Faster, tighter codes mean search engines can hold more data in memory and answer queries sooner.
arxiv-2501-03178:
Miljenko Čemeljić and co-authors simulate gas falling onto a naked singularity in a 2025 astrophysics paper. A Reissner-Nordström singularity is a charged point mass with no horizon hiding it. Using a pseudo-Newtonian potential tuned to match its true orbital frequencies, they ran the first thin-disk simulations around one. Orbital speed around such an object vanishes at a zero-gravity radius and peaks just beyond it.

Viscosity can only push gas inward outside that peak, so inflow stalls and piles into a glowing torus near the zero-gravity sphere. The ring matches shapes predicted by exact relativity calculations. A bright ring with no hole behind it could one day be a telescope signature of these exotic objects.
arxiv-2501-03378:
Jalal Jalali and co-authors tune indoor light networks that bounce signals off smart mirrors. Optical intelligent reflecting surfaces can steer light around a room, letting a cell-free wireless network shape its own channels. The team jointly optimized transmitter power, receiver tilt, mirror element assignment, and mirror placement.

Two goals pull against each other: spectral efficiency, how much data the light carries, and energy efficiency, how cheaply it carries it. The authors fold the pair into one problem with a constraint method and solve it by successive approximation. Simulations show the mirrors lifting both measures under quality guarantees, evidence that programmable light paths can upgrade indoor optical networks.
arxiv-2501-03678:
Valentin Brunn presents a 2025 thesis on young stars and their planet-forming discs. T Tauri stars flare with X-rays when their magnetic fields snap and reconnect. Those events hurl fast particles outward, and some may strike the disc where planets form.

The thesis builds a framework that joins disc observations with chemical and motion models of the particles. It reviews how charge in the disc shapes its flow, counting standard sources such as starlight and cosmic rays. A model based on solar flares then tests flare particles as an added charge source. Results suggest they can charge the inner disc strongly. Time-varying tests show gains in flow, heat, and chemical richness as well.
arxiv-2501-03878:
Denys Timoshyn and co-authors survey Ukraine's role in particle physics, past and future, in a 2025 paper. Many famed scientists in the field were born in Ukraine or began their careers there. The authors set out to reclaim that legacy for readers at home and abroad. They also report on the state of labs and teams two years after the full-scale invasion began.

The survey traces past work by Ukrainian scientists and their schools. It then describes present projects and the damage and strain the war has brought. Expected future work with CERN, the European particle physics lab, gets its own section. The authors hope the account will spur the next wave of Ukrainian scientists. It also serves as a record of a research community working under wartime pressure.
arxiv-2501-03978:
Andrew Renninger and Carmen Cabrera use mobile phone data to watch extreme heat empty Spanish cities of motion, in a 2025 study. Heat research on daily movement has leaned on small samples, leaving whole-population patterns unknown.

Network records covering thirteen million people, over a quarter of Spain, were split by age, sex, income, and activity. Movement fell by up to ten percent on hot days, and twenty percent on hot afternoons. Older adults cut work and other trips most. Lower earners could not skip work as easily, and social mixing shrank as centers emptied. The authors warn that cities lose economic and social sparkle when heat keeps people home.
arxiv-2501-05078:
Language models memorize chunks of their training text, leaking private and copyrighted material, and Tarun Ram Menta, Susmit Agrawal, and Chirag Agarwal hunt the cause inside the architecture in this 2025 paper. Their tool is attribution: switch off the attention modules of one block at a time, leave the rest untouched, and watch what the model forgets.

The pattern splits cleanly by depth. Attention in the deep blocks carries the memorization; attention in the early blocks carries generalization and reasoning instead. Theorems bound what each bypass does to the outputs, and experiments across two model families and five data sets confirm the split. The practical payoff is a surgical fix: damp the deep attention and the model memorizes less, while its smarts, housed up front, survive.
arxiv-2501-05178:
Nicodemus and co-authors present a 2025 paper on KLAP, a method that nudges a non-passive engineering system into passivity with the least possible change. Passive systems never create energy, a safety trait controllers prize. The fix is framed as plain optimization: shrink the distance to the original system under a frequency-weighted measure. A classic lemma from control theory supplies the math, and gradients stay cheap even for big systems.

Every best answer lands on the same passive system, they prove. Without a direct feedthrough path, any local best is automatically the global best. Starting tricks and restarts handle the trickier feedthrough cases. The authors target large models where older passivation tools crawl.
arxiv-2501-05278:
Testing a new bidding or allocation policy online is slow and costly, so Ritam Guha and Nilavra Pathak study how to judge policies from data that an older policy already logged. This approach, called off-policy evaluation, uses estimators that reconstruct what would have happened under a different set of choices. The pair focus on dynamic auction settings, where rivals react fast and slow testing can mean losing ground.

The authors examine whether these estimators can predict the outcome of resource allocation strategies well enough to guide which policies deserve a live test. Using them as a screening step could cut the time and cost of experiments and raise confidence in the policies finally chosen. On the strength of their early findings, they sketch an analytics system that would assess new strategies continuously as fresh logged data arrives.
arxiv-2501-05478:
Robot guides that follow spoken directions mostly train in English, and Arabic speakers are left untested. Malak Mansour, Ahmed Aly, Bahey Tharwat, Sarim Hashmi, Dong An, and Ian Reid run that test in a 2025 paper. Four language models, one built for Arabic among them, steered a navigation agent step by step. Instructions came in English and Arabic from a standard route dataset.

Top models planned well in both languages, the team reports. Some smaller models stumbled in Arabic through parsing slips and weaker reasoning. No training runs were used; each step was a fresh prediction. The authors call for stronger multilingual planning in navigation models. The work is billed as the first Arabic study of its kind.
arxiv-2501-06278:
Zenon Lamprou and co-authors compare brain scans with language models to see how each handles punctuation, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Punctuation seems minor, yet it shapes how readers chunk meaning. The team lined up four modern transformer models against records of human brain activity while people read, using a matching method from past work.

One model, RoBERTa, tracked brain activity most closely, beating an older benchmark model. The team then stripped punctuation from the text and watched what changed. Oddly, the older model's match with brain data got better without the marks. The study adds to work on how machines and brains each build meaning from text, and on what small marks contribute to that work.
arxiv-2501-06978:
Davide Martinenghi writes in a 2025 paper about making a classic database rule easier to see and check. Two-phase locking is the standard policy databases use to keep concurrent transactions from corrupting each other's work. The policy itself is well understood, in both its plain and strict forms.

What is not easy is turning a given schedule of operations into a clear table or picture that shows whether the locking rule holds. The paper walks through the technical hurdles in building such a tool and how they were handled. The goal is an analysis that a person can read at a glance, rather than a verdict delivered by opaque machinery.
arxiv-2501-07178:
Simon Martin, Hans-Theo Normann, Paul Püplichhuisen, and Tobias Werner wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It studies how pricing algorithms split the gains when they collude in a two-firm market, and how the split shifts when the firms are unequal.

The team ran repeated Cournot duopoly games with self-run algorithms. Both buyers and firms can gain from some asymmetry: matched firms saw sharper rivalry, while lopsided pairs saw softer play. The plain Nash benchmark missed on counts and gains but hit total welfare well. The best fit was the equal relative gains rule, with algorithm deals landing on or near the best joint front. The old view that matched firms collude most may not hold.
arxiv-2501-07278:
Junhao Zheng and co-authors wrote a 2025 roadmap for lifelong learning in language model agents. Most agents are frozen after training and cannot adapt. Real settings change, so agents must keep learning without forgetting. The survey is the first to map this space in full.

The authors split an agent into three parts: perception, memory, and action. Each part gains its own set of lifelong techniques. Sight and sound input, stored knowledge, and grounded acts all evolve. The pillars work together to keep the agent current. The map points builders toward AGI-grade, ever-learning systems.
arxiv-2501-07378:
Zhipeng Deng, Zhe Xu, Tsuyoshi Isshiki, and Yefeng Zheng present, in a 2025 paper, a learning setup for outlining organs and tumors in medical scans when labels are scarce. Hospitals cannot share raw data, so federated learning trains across sites in private. Semi-supervised learning then exploits the many unlabelled scans. A snag the field had skipped is domain shift: each hospital's scans look a bit different, and the model must still work at new sites.

Their framework attacks the problem at two levels. Globally, it weights each site's model by how well that model generalises. Locally, two teachers refine the guessed labels for unlabelled scans. A consistency rule also keeps features steady under small changes. Tests span four scan tasks, from heart MRI to bladder cancer.
arxiv-2501-07478:
Lewis Stuart and Michael Pound present a converter, in a 2025 preprint, that turns Gaussian splatting scenes into ordinary point clouds and meshes. Splatting builds rich 3D scenes from fuzzy blobs, but needs special viewers. Point clouds work in nearly all 3D software. Their tool samples points from each blob as if it were a small cloud of density. A distance rule trims wild outliers. Color is the tricky part, since a blob's color shifts with viewing angle.

To fix colors, the tool renders the scene and credits each blob with the pixel it influenced most. Every sampled point then takes its blob's settled color. A mesh option runs surface reconstruction over points drawn from surface blobs. No retraining is needed. The package is built to slot into existing splatting pipelines. Artists and engineers can carry splat scenes into standard tools.
arxiv-2501-07678:
Yusui Chen and Kaiqi Xiong study two-time correlation functions for light-press systems in a 2025 paper. Such a system pairs a light cage with a tiny moving mirror; its joint stats over two times drive fine sense tools. The team use a chance wave path to trace those stats. Two cases face the lens: a long-time settled state and a state that shifts as time runs. Sim runs carry the proof.

Settled states split by world kind: memory-free and memory-full baths leave unlike marks. The split shows in the two-time stats at once. Time-shift stats tell more of the bath than the old spectrum path does. The authors pitch the stats as a bath probe for sense work.
arxiv-2501-08178:
A jet of light fluid can pulse on its own, and outside sound can pull that pulsing into step. Abhijit Kushwaha and five co-authors study the road to that lock-in in a 2025 paper. Before full sync, the jet passes through a half-synced state whose shape depends on the route taken, and those shapes are hard to tell apart by eye.

The team forced a low-density jet with sound at varied pitch and strength, then recorded how its speed rose and fell over time. From those traces they built recurrence plots, maps that mark when the jet returns to a past state. Measures drawn from the maps separated the different routes to lock-in cleanly. The authors offer the method as a general tool for spotting sync paths in fluid systems that excite themselves.
arxiv-2501-08278:
Nicholas Kamp, Carlos Argüelles, Albrecht Karle, Jennifer Thomas, and Tianlu Yuan propose two neutrino detectors near the Large Hadron Collider, in a 2025 paper. Neutrinos made in collider crashes fly forward in huge numbers and are rarely studied. One design places panels on the surface above a collision point. The other sinks a water detector into Lake Geneva to watch a second collision point.

Simulations predict millions of neutrino events during the collider's high-output era. The surface detector would catch muon neutrinos, while the lake detector sees all flavors. The data could pin down how often neutrinos interact and how charm particles are made in crashes. The authors pitch both as cheap partners to a planned forward physics facility.
arxiv-2501-08378:
Louisa Canepa and four co-authors train a machine learning model to measure the faint glow between galaxies in a cluster, in a 2025 paper. That intracluster light traces a cluster's history of mergers, but it is very dim and past measures needed heavy hand work. Big new surveys will multiply the images to process.

The model learned from fifty thousand images with fake light profiles injected. It was then fine tuned on 101 real clusters whose light share was measured by hand. After that short tuning, it handled real survey images directly, with no manual preparation. It can process hundreds of images in seconds on one graphics card. The authors release the model and training code. They note it can be retuned for other surveys and other measurement styles.
arxiv-2501-08678:
Tobias Rohe and five co-authors test whether quantum-classical hybrid generators can fake shipping route data well enough to train and test other software. Their 2025 study uses hybrid quantum generative adversarial networks, called QuGANs, fed with real shipping data turned into graphs of sea routes. The question is whether these small quantum systems learn the shape of the data with fewer parameters than classical rivals.

The QuGANs learned the underlying patterns and geometric features of the routes quickly, the team reports. Their weakness was variety: the samples they produced varied less than the real data. Still, some hybrid models matched the quality of much larger classical networks while using far fewer parameters. The authors present the shipping case as a concrete sign of where quantum generation may pay off, and where it still falls short.
arxiv-2501-08778:
Guilherme Varela, Alberto Sardinha, and Francisco Melo study teamwork among networked agents that cannot see the full state, in a 2025 paper. Earlier cooperative learning methods assumed complete information or shared observations, which real systems rarely have. Privacy limits and lost messages make the problem harder still.

The authors frame the setting as a networked dynamic partially observable Markov game, where agents talk over a changing communication network. Their method, DNA-MARL, pairs local consensus messages with local gradient descent, so agents build a shared team value estimate and learn to cooperate. Across benchmark scenarios, it beats prior methods. The approach suits real domains where agents must coordinate while seeing only part of the world.
arxiv-2501-08978:
Gamma-ray bursts are the brightest explosions in the universe, and Oindrila Ghosh and co-authors show they can double as detectors for heavy axion-like particles. In the hot fireball that launches a burst, such particles would be born in large numbers and stream straight out, carrying enormous energy away with them. When they later decay into photons, those photons stay too dilute to rebuild the fireball through pair production.

The burst therefore dims or fails. By adding the particle interactions to standard fireball models, the team bounds the axion-photon coupling tightly across masses from 200 megaelectronvolts to 5 gigaelectronvolts. Bright observed bursts, they argue, leave little room for such particles.
arxiv-2501-09078:
Lorenzo Fioroni and Vincenzo Savona offer a 2025 paper on hard choice problems that need the best pick from many options. Exact answers are often out of reach, so people use fast rules of thumb drawn from physics. The authors build a new rule of thumb that borrows ideas from quantum annealing, a method that lets a system settle into a low-energy state.

Their method uses smooth quantum states that can hold entanglement, the link that makes quantum systems hard to copy. Energy and slopes can be worked out with modest math, so problems with thousands of spins can be tried. Tests on a glass-like magnet model show speed and quality close to well-known rival methods.
arxiv-2501-09378:
Van der Sijpt and co-authors ask where the turbulence inside giant stars comes from, in a 2025 astrophysics paper. The outer layers and winds of the hottest, heaviest stars show a restless small-scale structure that widens their spectral lines. Sub-surface boiling has long been blamed, but the claim had not been tested closely.

The team attacked the question from two sides. A stability analysis of thick stellar envelopes named two candidate instabilities, one convective and one acoustic, with formulas for how fast each should grow. Computer simulations of two star types, O stars and Wolf-Rayet stars, were then measured for how their density patterns grew over time. Matching the two sides lets the authors judge which instability truly seeds the structure, a step toward explaining why these stars look so turbulent.
arxiv-2501-09478:
Yuchen Meng and five co-authors find a new fingerprint of quantum scars in twenty twenty-five. Some interacting quantum systems avoid thermalizing, against expectations. Quantum many-body scars are eigenstates that evade heat death and sustain long oscillations. Symmetry and algebra views explain some scars, but no universal diagnostic existed.

The authors propose Fisher zeros as that diagnostic. These are zeros of the partition function extended into the complex temperature plane. In scarred systems, they conjecture, a continuous line of zeros appears off the usual axis. That line splits the plane into regions with distinct thermalization behavior. Readers get a complex-plane signature to hunt scars with, in systems where other tests stay silent.
arxiv-2501-09578:
Federica Galluzzi and Bert van Geemen classify special shrinking maps on a class of four-dimensional shapes, in a paper from 2025. The shapes are Hyper-Kähler, a rich kind of geometric space tied to K3 surfaces. A shrinking map on such a shape has an exceptional part shaped like a bundle of conics over a K3 surface.

A lattice count shows five types of such bundles can occur. When a shape has the smallest rich rank and two distinct shrinking maps, the authors pin down which bundle types pair up. Just seven pairings occur. For a famed family from cubic shapes, only four pairings occur, and the authors give examples of each. The work adds to the map of these shapes'forms.
arxiv-2501-09778:
Patrick Llerena and co-authors wrote this 2025 paper on a hidden bargain inside firms: idle time wastes output, yet it also breeds ideas. Their agent-based model breaks a factory into funds and flows, letting inefficiency appear on its own from frictions rather than being assumed. Workers learn, forget, and, when idle, create.

In the model, a firm that keeps idle workers and routes them into innovation does better than one that treats labor as a simple dial. Results hinge on how the firm is organized, how fast skills grow and decay, and how quickly new methods arrive. Idleness cuts both ways, eroding skill while feeding the creativity that powers process gains. The authors close by questioning layoffs as a default fix and sketching paths for further work.
arxiv-2501-10478:
András Grabarits, Federico Balducci, and Adolfo del Campo solve how defects form when a quantum magnet is driven through its phase change at any speed, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The model is the transverse-field Ising chain, a basic quantum system. Defects here are kinks, and their count follows rules tied to the drive speed.

Standard transforms split the problem into modes, each solved with special functions. At slow drives, a famous scaling law and fresh universal rules for higher counts hold. At fast drives, the counts turn non-universal and non-monotonic. The counts stay narrower than random noise at every speed, the team shows.
arxiv-2501-10778:
Charly Robinson La Rocca, Jean-François Cordeau, and Emma Frejinger teach a search heuristic which variables to change. Their twenty twenty-five paper improves large neighbourhood search for mixed-integer programs. Such programs model scheduling, routing, and planning decisions. The destroy step choice strongly shapes solution quality.

A machine learning model guides the destroy operator after light offline training. The team built a modular test bench for fair comparisons. Tests on a standard problem library beat strong commercial solvers in places. Noisy prediction checks showed how accuracy affects final quality. Tweaks to loss functions and sampling improved the learner further. Random search stayed competitive, but supervised learning led overall.
arxiv-2501-11078:
Stishov and co-authors published a 2025 note on a puzzling change of state in a magnetic material called MnSi. Below a certain temperature, the material's tiny magnets line up in a slow spiral. Warm it, and the spiral melts into a disordered state. Decades of study show this melting is unlike most such changes.

Just above the melting point, many of the material's properties swing to extremes: heat, expansion, and flow measures all peak or dip. Such behavior looks more like what happens in flat, two-dimensional systems than in a solid crystal. The authors describe the change as happening in two steps. First comes a sharp jump of the usual kind. Then the leftover swirls of magnetism, vortex-like knots in the spiral pattern, break down. The note gathers this odd evidence and offers that two-step picture as a tentative account.
arxiv-2501-11178:
Kristin Blesch and co-authors propose a method called cARFi for measuring how much one feature matters for a model's predictions once other features are already known. Such conditional checks need fresh feature values that respect the joint pattern of the data, which is hard to make by hand. Adversarial random forests can generate such on-manifold values for mixed table data with little tuning.

The method samples replacement values from those learned conditional distributions and watches how model performance moves. It needs little tuning for steady scores, can switch between conditional and marginal views, and can condition on sets of features. Statistical tests for the scores are also built in.
arxiv-2501-11378:
Mateusz Barański and co-authors study fake speech from silence in the Whisper recognizer in a 2025 paper. Speech models can hallucinate words, and this team asks what non speech sounds trigger Whisper to invent text. Sounds of many kinds were fed to the model at test time to provoke false transcripts.

A set of stock hallucinations showed up again and again across sounds. Mixing such sounds into real speech bred more of the same fakes. The team then built a bag of known hallucinations that can scrub transcripts after the fact. That cleanup cut word error rates and guards users from the worst false lines.
arxiv-2501-11678:
Seiji Fujimoto and a large team report a candidate galaxy lit only by the first generation of stars, in a 2025 paper. Population III stars, born from pristine gas, have eluded every search so far. The team built a new selection method for the James Webb telescope's near-infrared camera and validated it with simulations.

Searching about five hundred square arcminutes of legacy fields, including the deepest lensed imaging yet, they found one strong candidate, GLIMPSE-16043. Its spectrum shows fierce hydrogen emission, a Balmer jump, no dust, and no detectable metal lines, capping its metal content below half a percent of solar. The galaxy is young, under five million years, and tiny, around a hundred thousand solar masses. Its abundance also gives the first observational constraint on how many such galaxies exist at that era. The measured density matches theory well, strengthening the candidate's case.
arxiv-2501-12378:
Alexander Schmidhuber and co-authors open, in 2025, the study of quantum algorithms for a powerful knot invariant. Khovanov homology sorts knots far more finely than older polynomial invariants, but its computing cost was largely unknown. The team first shows that even rough estimates of its ranks are hard for classical and some quantum models.

For two useful accuracy levels, they give a quantum algorithm that is fast when a related operator settles quickly and keeps a wide spectral gap. A pre-cooling trick lets it work even when the answer is tiny compared with the search space. Links to graph theory supply evidence for the needed gap.
arxiv-2501-12678:
Ryan Robinett, Lorenzo Orecchia, and Samantha Riesenfeld build a graph stand-in for curved data shapes in a 2025 paper. Shapes like these sit inside many learning tasks, but their curve math is slow to run. The stand-in lays a web of small map patches over the shape, much like an atlas.

On a known shape, the web speeds up a classic search task past prior tools. On photo patch data, the web can be learned straight from the points and keeps the true shape. A curved take on a margin sorter then runs on the learned web. Noisy, wide settings are the next test.
arxiv-2501-12878:
Nils Japke and co-authors presented a tool in 2025 to cut the running time of tiny performance tests for software. Such tests, called microbenchmarks, catch slowdowns early, but suites can take hours because each test is repeated many times for accuracy.

Their tool uses the results of one full run to set the smallest repeat count for each test that still gives stable readings. It works from static settings, not live tuning. On fourteen open source projects in two languages, it cut the measuring phase by up to about ninety-five percent. The best stability metric varied by project, and warm up phases mattered for one language. It still caught real slowdowns.
arxiv-2501-13078:
Senbagaraman Sudarsanam studies a math model of how views spread in markets. His 2025 paper uses an Ising model, a grid of agents that flip between two stances under peer pull and noise. Such models can mimic real market swings, where calm spells bunch with wild ones.

The author lifts the model into a larger system with a trick called bailout embedding. That move splits off the bubbling behavior that sparks bursts of wild swings. A single dial in the trick can push the model through set grades of stability. Under the right settings, the model shows bursts that look like real price swings. He reads the dial as a gauge of how slow traders are to change course.
arxiv-2501-13478:
Tianbai Xiao builds a flow solver that can learn from its own runs in this 2025 paper. Predicting flows that span smooth continuum motion and thin, rarefied gas motion is notoriously hard. Models and numerical schemes carry knobs that experts tune by trial and error.

Differentiable programming changes the game: the whole simulation is written so a computer can take its derivatives end to end. Xiao presents the first such solver covering both flow regimes. Mechanical models with neural parts can be trained on the fly, using gradients passed backward through the simulation itself. Tests on forward and inverse problems for fluid and kinetic equations show the method working, and the code is open source.
arxiv-2501-13878:
Ethan Wilson and colleagues proposed in 2025 that an AI assistant should watch where you look, not just listen to what you say. Multimodal agents increasingly collaborate with users on tasks in the physical and digital world. Today they depend on explicit communication: typed or spoken instructions. The authors hypothesize that gaze, an implicit signal, can convey a user's interests and intent continuously, without demanding attention to formulate commands.

Presented at an eye-tracking research symposium in Tokyo, the work explores how systems can consume gaze as an attention channel. When an assistant knows which object a user is considering, it can offer help earlier and ask fewer clarifying questions. The risks are real too, since gaze reveals more than users may intend. Framing gaze as a first-class input gives designers a shared problem to solve: reading attention helpfully without reading minds intrusively.
arxiv-2501-13978:
Sangyeop Yeo and co-authors propose a prompting method for code generation that embeds clear functional objectives in the prompt, published in 2025. Language models are now widely used to write code. Many methods add context or guidance to prompts, often by mimicking step-by-step human reasoning in a fixed sequence.

Such sequences, the authors argue, can constrain flexibility, since code has a structured nature that does not always fit a step list. Their method, Chain of Grounded Objectives, instead states the grounded goals a program must meet, without spelling out a procedure. This lets the model use its own path to meet the goals. Tests showed the method improves code generation over prior approaches, addressing the limits of sequential reasoning prompts.
arxiv-2501-14078:
Laurian Suciu and Andra-Maria Stoica study liftings that act almost like isometries in a 2025 math paper. Liftings raise an operator to a bigger space where it behaves more simply, a classic move for contractions on Hilbert spaces. The pair ask when such lifts can be quasi-isometric and still invertible from the left.

They prove such liftings exist and test them on set classes like quasicontractions. Operators with left invertible minimal lifts get a full account inside the frame of A-contractions. The matrix shape of those lifts is worked out as well. The results echo the known isometric lifts of plain contractions.
arxiv-2501-14278:
Jaehyun Park, Dongmin Park, and Jae-Gil Lee tackle a cost problem in AI that must keep learning new tasks, in a 2025 paper. Labeling data by hand is pricey, so systems pick the most useful samples to label. Standard picking looks only at the new task, which makes the model forget old ones.

Their method, AccuACL, picks samples using a math tool that tracks how much each sample teaches the model, summed across old and new tasks. That balance guards old skills while still speeding up new learning. In tests across many setups, the method raised average accuracy by about 24 percent and cut forgetting by about 17 percent against standard picking. It offers a practical way to keep long-lived models both fresh and stable.
arxiv-2501-14378:
Carmine Autieri and co-authors hunt for an unusual magnetic order hiding in a famous superconductor in this 2025 paper. The material is strontium ruthenate, long studied for its odd superconductivity. Its crystal cages tilt easily, and that tilt may switch on altermagnetism, a new kind of order that splits electron energies without net magnetization.

Computer calculations on a single layer with tilted cages found exactly that phase, selective to certain electron orbitals. A stripped-down model showed the order grows from longer-range links between a few orbitals, while one orbital needs much longer links to join in. The same model, with one orbital swapped, mirrors the copper oxide superconductors. In the bulk crystal the phase survives as the ground state for a range of tilts, with a changed symmetry between layers. The authors discuss which pairing styles the order would favor for superconductivity.
arxiv-2501-14478:
Arend Moerman and co-authors describe how they aligned and verified a wide-band spectrometer on a telescope in the Atacama, in work from 2025. The instrument, DESHIMA 2.0, observes across a broad microwave band. Its warm optics sit on a motor-driven hexapod that can tilt and shift them into exact position.

The key tool is a sky chopper with small apertures that couple the beam to the cold sky. By scanning the beam across the aperture and minimising the warm-cabin signal on the detectors, the team finds the best alignment. They characterised the procedure in the lab with a liquid nitrogen cold source, then applied it at the telescope. Aperture efficiency improved clearly over earlier reported values, confirming the method works on site.
arxiv-2501-14578:
Harry Richardson, Josh Dunn, and Andrew McCluskey tackled a quiet numeric trap in 2025. The trap is finding the center of mass of a group of particles inside a box that repeats periodically, as model cells do. A particle near one face may belong with partners imaged through the opposite face, so a naive average lands in the wrong place. A popular fix projects places onto a circle and averages there.

The authors show that popular method averages the particles in a way that is not physically meaningful and makes inaccurate centers. The correct built-in weighted average exists but is costly and hard to compute analytically. They therefore propose a more lean route to that built-in mean. Built to suit the majority of chemical systems, so simulators can locate molecular centers correctly without paying the full careful cost.
arxiv-2501-14978:
Alireza Nikzamir and co-authors design a radiating array that locks into a steady hum at a special operating point, in a 2025 paper. The device is a waveguide studded at regular intervals with elements that amplify the signal and radiate it into the air. At a condition called an exceptional point of degeneracy, the system's behavior simplifies and stabilizes.

Once the signal grows strong enough to saturate the amplifiers, that special point fixes the oscillation frequency for the array. Every element settles to the same gain and radiates the same power, even if the starting gain was uneven. Unlike ordinary cavity designs, the frequency does not depend on how long the array is. A test board matched the simulations, saturating at the special point with a low-noise tone. The authors propose the scheme for high-power antenna arrays with amplifiers spread along their length.
arxiv-2501-15378:
Manzong Huang and co-authors patch a leak in how language models use knowledge graphs. Turning text into tidy triples drops the context that gives facts their sense. Their framework rebuilds the lost wording behind each triple. It also lets each user question feed back, pulling missing facts into the graph on the fly.

Across five question answering benchmarks, the method beat rival graph aided systems by wide margins on exact answers and overlap scores. The gains held across varied datasets. The authors argue no real graph is ever complete, so retrieval systems should repair loss as they go.
arxiv-2501-15778:
Alexandra Utiralova studies how representations of the general linear groups are labeled in a special category that works in positive characteristic. The work follows an earlier paper by Venkatesh on these Verlinde categories. Her 2025 paper answers how to translate between highest weight labelings tied to different choices of a Borel subgroup.

The general case is reduced to a smaller one, built from two simple blocks, using a method called odd reflections. On that smaller category, she sets up a highest weight structure and an action of a related algebra through translation functors. That frame explains projective and injective objects, a reciprocity rule, duality, and lowest weights for simple modules.
arxiv-2501-15878:
Adil Kaan Akan and Yucel Yemez adapt image generators in a 2025 paper on object-based learning. Their method, SlotAdapt, joins slot attention, which splits a scene into object slots, with a pretrained diffusion model that builds images step by step. Extra adapter layers let the slots guide generation, steering clear of the model's usual bias toward text prompts.

A guidance loss lines up the adapter's focus maps with the slot maps, with no outside labels needed. Tests on several datasets, including real photos, beat leading methods at finding objects and at generating images. On complex real scenes the method composed new images from parts far better than rival slot-based systems. The work points to generators that understand scenes as objects, not just textures.
arxiv-2501-15978:
Vincent Delecroix and Clément Legrand-Duchesne play a reshaping game with surfaces built from squares, in this 2025 mathematics paper. A square-tiled surface is exactly what it sounds like: a surface paved by unit squares, long used as a concrete handle on abstract geometry. Their allowed move is a shear inside one cylinder of the tiling, realized as a careful sequence of diagonal flips that keeps the surface square-tiled.

The big question is connectivity: which surfaces can be morphed into which by such moves? The authors conjecture the answer mirrors the connected pieces of the moduli space of quadratic differentials, the deep object these tilings discretize. They prove the conjecture for the hyperelliptic components of Abelian square-tiled surfaces. There, any two surfaces of genus g can be joined by on the order of g cylinder shears, a strikingly short path.
arxiv-2501-16078:
Ching-Yi Chen and co-authors added a language model proofreader to a news writing system in a 2025 paper. The base system drafts sports news on its own in three languages. Drafts made by machine can carry spelling and grammar slips that hurt trust, so a check step is key before any text goes out to readers.

They wired a large language model in as the checker, set to fix spelling and grammar only. Tests ran on sports drafts still in progress in all three tongues. The team reports the fixes came out at a level fit for use. The paper shows how a general model can serve as a quality gate inside a working text pipeline.
arxiv-2501-16178:
Wenxuan Xie and Fanpu Cao present a 2025 paper on a light model for long-range forecasting of time series. Big sequence models forecast well but are too heavy for small devices at the edge. Light models exist, yet they stumble on series that shift and drift over time, which are common in real use.

Their model splits a series with a wavelet method that loses no information, then joins the bands with a learnable filter. A single shared layer, or a shallow small network, maps each sub-series to its forecast. Across many data sets, the model matched or beat the best known results while staying cheap to run.
arxiv-2501-16278:
The superconductor YBCO loses its magic as oxygen leaves its crystal, and Acha and co-authors use electric current as a probe of that loss in a 2025 paper. They built contacts between platinum and YBCO samples with four levels of oxygen depletion, then measured current against voltage across a range of temperatures.

A classic conduction model, Poole-Frenkel emission, fit the behavior well. In that picture, each missing oxygen leaves a potential well that traps charge carriers. The traps grew deeper as depletion increased, matching a peak seen earlier in optical measurements. The authors read this agreement as support for tying the vacancies to an impurity band's ionization energy. The study shows how plain transport measurements can expose microscopic structure in a complex oxide.
arxiv-2501-16378:
Qing Li and five co-authors present a safety fix for vision-language models that works by editing their inner activations mid-answer, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Adding images to a language model weakens its safety training: pictures shift the model's internal state, and even simple jailbreaks then succeed. Their method nudges those activations back toward safe territory while the model writes.

The steering acts at two scales, whole layers and single attention heads, using vectors drawn from safe and unsafe example pairs. Across four safety test sets, attack success fell by roughly a third to a half, while helpfulness barely moved. The authors stress that no model weights were retrained to gain the improvement.
arxiv-2501-16578:
Joel Tropp, a lone author, proves new results about the smallest eigenvalue of sums of random matrices. The paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five and sits in pure and applied mathematics. It deals with matrices whose entries are random but whose values stay at or above zero in a set sense. Such sums show up often in modern work with data in many dimensions.

Tropp shows that the smallest eigenvalue of the sum is ruled by that of a matched Gaussian random matrix. That link matters because Gaussian matrices come with a large stock of known tools. He then gives short, clear proofs of old and new results in high-dimensional statistics. The paper also settles an open question about very sparse random matrices.
arxiv-2501-16678:
Ao Sun, Zhihan Wang, and Jinxin Xue study what happens when a shrinking surface flows through a kink point, in a paper from 2025. Mean curvature flow moves a surface inward at a speed set by how curved it is. Such flows often form singularities, spots where the surface pinches or folds. The paper looks at the mild, cylinder-like kind of pinch.

They prove these pinch points stand alone in space and time. They then give a full account of how the surface's shape and topology change as it passes through. The change matches the jump seen when a landscape function crosses a saddle point. In plain terms, the flow performs a clean surgery on itself. A new distance formula drives the proof. It tracks a quantity like the frequency tools used in other fields.
arxiv-2501-16778:
Arvin Tashakori and four co-authors built a light system for generating human motion that respects physics in a 2025 paper. Animation, virtual reality, and robotics all need motion that is cheap to make, true to the body, and easy to steer. Past methods traded one of those goals against the others.

Their model diffuses motion in a compressed space, so no physics simulator is needed and training stays fast. A pretrained transformer reads joint spots, contact forces, muscle drives, and joint effort together, keeping results physically sound. A plug-in module adds steering over those same channels. Tests on extended data sets showed gains in realism, physical fit, and control. The authors set the work as a new bar for motion synthesis.
arxiv-2501-16978:
David Jaklitsch and Harshit Yadav studied in 2025 a special class of maps between tensor categories. They call a tensor functor tensor-Frobenius when its left and right adjoints agree as bimodule functors. The paper gives several ways to recognize this property. The sharpest test links it to whether a certain centralizer category is unimodular.

With those tests in hand, the authors track how module categories behave when pulled back along such a functor. For perfect functors, exactness survives the pullback. When the functor is tensor-Frobenius, pivotality, unimodularity, and sphericality survive too. Applications reach maps between Hopf algebras and the algebra structure of internal natural transformations. The results settle questions raised by other researchers in the area. Category theorists working with fusion categories are the main audience.
arxiv-2501-17178:
David Salinas, Omar Swelam, and Frank Hutter cut the cost of tuning the models that judge other models. Their 2025 paper explains that large language models are now used as judges, comparing two models' answers to rank them without human labels. Papers differ in the judge model, prompt, and settings all at once, so fair comparisons are hard.

The team tunes judge settings in a systematic search. To afford it, they use a method that tests many settings cheaply at low effort and promotes the best to fuller tests, balancing accuracy against cost across several aims. The search cut costs to about a thousandth of the naive price. It found judges that beat existing benchmarks in both accuracy and cost, using open weight models that anyone can rerun.
arxiv-2501-17278:
Gonçalves and four co-authors review how programming is taught in Brazil, in this two thousand twenty-five systematic literature review. Programming is valuable for careers and for keeping minds sharp, yet Brazil struggles to standardize how it is taught in universities and high schools.

The team gathered the research literature on Brazilian programming education and sorted its gaps, common techniques, and teaching approaches. Their findings point to where curricula and teacher preparation fall short and where chances for improvement lie. They close with recommendations for policymakers and educators toward updated national policies. Reviews like this help a country align scattered classroom experiments into a coherent strategy for digital skills.
arxiv-2501-17478:
Antonio Baeza and co-authors present, in a 2025 paper, approximate Taylor methods for solving ordinary differential equations. Classic Taylor schemes reach very high accuracy orders but demand derivatives of the equation's functions, which is laborious. Runge-Kutta methods avoid derivatives yet make arbitrary high orders awkward to build.

The new approach mimics Taylor expansions using only the functions themselves, like Runge-Kutta, at the price of more function evaluations per order. In exchange, schemes of any order become easy to produce, and the total cost can undercut exact-derivative Taylor methods. Tests show results as good as the exact procedure with less effort.
arxiv-2501-17578:
Marco Pasini, Stefan Lattner, and George Fazekas present an audio autoencoder that squeezes music into a compact code, in work from 2025. Compact codes serve music generation and search tasks. Past autoencoders struggle to shrink audio a lot while keeping sound quality and staying useful for later tasks.

Their system encodes a clip as a set of summary embeddings, where each part of the set captures a global feature of the sound rather than a moment in time. That unordered design reaches better quality at the same squeeze ratio. A staged decoding model rebuilds clips of any length, working on chunks in sequence. A two-step decoding trick then polishes the output at no extra training cost. Tests beat rival continuous autoencoders on quality and downstream tasks.
arxiv-2501-17678:
Pablo Valle sets out a doctoral research plan for automatically repairing the software of cyber-physical systems in 2025. These systems mix code with physical machinery, from robots to satellites, and checking their software by hand consumes much of the development budget.

Automated program repair is mature for ordinary software but barely tried here, where fault localisation is hard, tests run slowly and fitness scoring is weak. Valle proposes combining spectrum-based fault localisation with patch generation and modern AI methods. The plan will be tested on open and industrial code bases. The goal is repair tools that scale to the long, expensive test cycles of embedded systems.
arxiv-2501-17978:
Mateusz Nowak, Wojciech Jarosz, and Peter Chin improve a fast method for building three-dimensional scenes from photos, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The base method fills a scene with soft blobs, but it mixes up objects with the shiny light on their surfaces. Highlights and reflections then look wrong from new angles.

Their fix lets each blob's opacity depend on the viewing angle. Blobs that carry glare can fade when seen from the wrong side. Tests on four standard sets gave top scores, with speed kept above sixty frames per second. Memory use rose only a little, the authors report.
arxiv-2501-18178:
Sattwik Basu and co-authors untangle overlapping chirps, signals whose pitch sweeps over time, in a 2025 paper. Radar, sonar, and wireless systems all need the numbers behind a noisy chirp mixture. Simple chirps have good tools; higher-order ones, whose sweeps bend, break them. The team cast the estimation as a non-convex optimization problem, a landscape full of false valleys.

Their sampler walks that landscape guided by its average curvature, a twist on Langevin Monte Carlo. The curvature sense steers the walk out of traps toward the true minimum. Tests show the method holds up even when noise nearly drowns the signal. The authors pitch it for real sensing jobs with messy returns.
arxiv-2501-18278:
Amitay Sicherman and Kira Radinsky present a module in a 2025 paper that unifies protein and molecule representations. Top models embed proteins in one space and small molecules in another, which blocks joint reasoning about body processes. Reactions, though, tie the two worlds together, since partners in one reaction share a functional role.

Their plug in module aligns ready made embeddings from protein and molecule models into one shared space. A weighted reaction graph and a tailored sampling plan supply the training signal, so no costly retraining is needed. The joined embeddings perform strongly on cross domain benchmarks. Code and the reaction database are open for public use. The approach suits drug and enzyme research.
arxiv-2501-18378:
Ye Tian and co-authors redesign antenna arrays so terahertz systems can find signal directions fast. Future 6G links at terahertz frequencies will steer huge antenna arrays, and knowing each signal's direction of arrival is step one. Giant arrays break classic estimators and two-dimensional searches cost too much. Their hybrid dynamic subarray layout splits elements into groups arranged so each group's phase pattern speaks of one direction coordinate only.

On that layout they build a corrected MUSIC estimator that fixes large-array bias, plus a faster variant exploiting the sparsity of terahertz channels for quick first guesses. Theory bounds and simulations together claim top accuracy at far lower compute than standard methods.
arxiv-2501-18478: Daniel Bermuth and co-authors present a pose estimation system that uses depth as well as color to track several people at once. Their 2025 paper, SimpleDepthPose, targets multi-view settings where reliability matters more than squeezing the last point of benchmark accuracy. Single-camera systems falter under occlusion and viewpoint change; depth data gives bodies a geometry that flat images lack.
arxiv-2501-18978:
Shiva Konakanchi and co-authors study fast flickers of magnetic order in a special class of magnets, in a 2025 paper. The magnets are chiral antiferromagnets, where spins form patterns with no net pull. Their order can be summed up by a quantity called an octupole. How fast that quantity settles after a push sets the speed limit for devices built on it.

Simulations show the octupole settles in two ways: by hopping over an energy hill, or by spinning out of phase. It settles far faster than the order in normal magnets, in about a trillionth of a second. The team derives formulas for the timing and draws a close match with a known type of magnet. They also propose using an injected spin current to tune the timing with electricity. That control could suit future devices that compute with chance.
arxiv-2501-19078:
Dominik Benkovič and Mateja Grašič widen the notion of a Jordan derivation on algebras that have an identity element, in this 2025 paper. The new concept covers both Jordan derivations and Jordan centralizers at once. Their setting excludes only fields of characteristic two.

A map counts as a generalized Jordan derivation when two partner maps make a set identity hold for all pairs. The authors show any such map splits into parts named quasi Jordan centralizers and quasi Jordan derivations. They also give a clean characterization of the maps. The work unifies two literatures that grew side by side.
arxiv-2501-19278:
Anirudh Chari and co-authors borrow the foraging logic of ants to help language models reason better. Models that think step by step still struggle to find good reasoning paths for hard problems, since the space of possible steps is huge. Their method fields a team of specially tuned model 'ants' that walk a shared tree of possible reasoning steps. Each ant weighs the scent trails left by earlier ants against its own bent of expertise.

A panel of expert scorers grades complete paths, and strong paths gain more scent, drawing later ants toward them. Across iterations, the colony concentrates on the most productive routes through the problem. On three hard test sets, covering grade-school math, science questions, and competition math, the method beat earlier approaches for improving chain-of-thought reasoning. The authors suggest that collective search, copied from biology, can sharpen machine reasoning at run time.
arxiv-2501-19378:
Lang Cao and Hanbing Liu present, in a 2025 paper, a recipe for helping language models handle tables. Tables are a basic way to store linked facts, yet models trained mostly on prose stumble over them. The pair name four snags: finding the right cells, grasping what the table means, slip-ups in number work, and rigid logic.

Their framework, TableMaster, first pulls out the relevant part of a table and restates it in words with added context. It then reasons in a flexible way, switching between plain text steps and symbolic steps to fit each question. On a standard table benchmark, the setup reached about seventy-eight percent accuracy with a mid-size model, ahead of earlier methods. The authors offer it as a practical step toward trustier table reading.
arxiv-2502-00278:
Tyler Parsotan and co-authors present a 2025 arXiv paper on BatAnalysis, an open Python pipeline for data from the Swift satellite's Burst Alert Telescope. The telescope watches for gamma-ray flashes and saves its finest event data on triggers, but standard products use fixed time and energy windows. The new tools let researchers download and process that raw event stream freely.

Users can build spectra, light curves, and sky images on their own settings, and mix the tools with other Python packages. Case studies cover a gamma-ray burst, a fast radio burst trigger, a faint X-ray binary catch, and a burst seen while the satellite slewed. The authors aim at the time-domain community.
arxiv-2502-00478:
A family of symmetric polynomials extends the classic Macdonald family with spin and inhomogeneity. Matteo Mucciconi proves these spin q-Whittaker polynomials are orthogonal. The inner product uses a variant of the Sklyanin measure on the multi-dimensional torus. That trait makes the family a basis for such forms in any number of variables. The proof leans on eigenrelations that partly generalize the Macdonald ones.

Special cases get their own treatment. They include variants of symmetric Grothendieck forms and spin Whittaker functions. The result places the newer family on the same firm footing as its famous relatives. Mucciconi works with the case where the Macdonald parameter t equals zero.
arxiv-2502-00578:
The Gross-Pitaevskii equation describes waves in superfluids and condensates, and its spinor version handles multi-part systems. Fabrizio Canfora and Pablo Pais analyze a generalized form in two dimensions in a 2025 paper. They find an endless family of self-interaction rules for which the equation admits energy bounds of Bogomol'nyi-Prasad-Sommerfield type, together with simpler first-order equations whose solutions automatically solve the full problem.

The simplest nontrivial solutions of those first-order systems carry fractional vorticity, with the fraction set by the strength of the nonlinearity. The authors examine the sixth-order case in depth, a setting tied to the quantum Hall effect and to supersolids. They also extend the method to mixtures and discuss where it meets, and departs from, supersymmetry.
arxiv-2502-00678:
Hyeong Kyu Choi, Yixuan Li and their co-authors propose the Kernel Divergence Score to measure benchmark contamination in large language models in 2025. When test data leak into training data, scores rise and no longer show true skill on new data.

Their score compares how similar sample embeddings are before and after fine-tuning on the benchmark in question. The logic is that tuning shifts unseen samples more than ones the model has already seen. In controlled tests, the score tracked contamination levels almost perfectly and beat prior methods. Extra checks confirmed which design choices made the score reliable.
arxiv-2502-00778:
Hiroaki Nishikawa, writing solo, presents a 2025 algorithm for fluid flow simulations on triangular and tetrahedral grids. A common method, called edge based discretization, needs a dual control volume around each grid node. Building those volumes takes steps that join edge midpoints and cell centers. It also takes time, above all on three dimensional grids. Nishikawa asks whether the needed values can be computed without ever building the dual volumes.

He shows they can. The lumped area vectors at each edge, and the dual volumes themselves, follow from simpler local sums. The new code is simpler to write and faster to run, though the total saving in a full simulation is modest. The bigger prize, he argues, is the path it opens toward four dimensional and space time grids, where forming dual volumes is far harder.
arxiv-2502-01678:
Yihe Wang and co-authors build, in a 2025 paper, a foundation model that reads brain wave recordings to detect Alzheimer's disease. Brain wave tests are cheap, safe, and widely available, yet past methods lacked big data and failed across new patients. The team gathered the largest such data set yet, with more than two thousand subjects.

Their model uses a gated design that handles recordings of varied length, channel layout, and sample rate. Pre-training spanned thirteen data sets of brain disorders, with a contrast method that teaches by comparison. Fine-tuning and tests ran on five other Alzheimer's data sets. The model topped all twenty checks against rivals, including other foundation models for brain waves.
arxiv-2502-01778:
Four researchers wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five on a smarter decision transformer for shifting environments. Reinforcement learning struggles when state and action spaces change, rewards are rare, and problems grow large. Decision transformers learn from past trajectories instead of live trial and error.

Their model, GNN-DT, adds graph neural network encoders and a new shortcut link between input and output tokens. On the test problem of scheduling electric vehicle charging, it beat existing transformer and offline methods while needing far fewer training trajectories. It also held up in unseen settings and with larger action spaces.
arxiv-2502-01978:
Jeong Hwan Lee and co-authors weigh how model choice skews galaxy mass estimates in a 2025 paper. The coming SPHEREx mission will map the sky in infrared light and yield mass maps for nearby galaxies. Turning that light into stellar mass depends on synthetic models of star populations, and the models disagree.

Nineteen nearby spiral galaxies from a major survey served as the test bed, with their masses taken as the reference. Four population models were compared at the key infrared wavelength. Two of them gave mass-to-light ratios notably lower than the other pair, and ratios tracked stellar age closely. Young populations thus bend mass readings in a systematic way. The authors pick a best band for mass work and show that adding color data cuts the scatter sharply across all models.
arxiv-2502-02478:
Tiny flaws in diamond can sense magnetic fields with quantum precision, even at room temperature. Yanzhao Guo and co-authors pack those flaws into a chip in a 2025 paper. A laser writes a light guide inside the diamond, so more flaws can be probed at once through a fiber.

The flaws in the guide kept spin traits as clean as those in plain diamond. Sensing through the guide reached fine levels for both steady and changing fields. That is at least ten times better than a standard lens setup, the team reports. A small, fiber-linked chip like this could bring quantum sensing to labs and field gear.
arxiv-2502-02778:
Jorge Martinez-Montejano, Hector Mendez, and Yajaida Velazquez-Inzunza prove results about limit sets in a 2025 math paper. They work with a space whose points are closed sets, measured by a standard distance. For a map on that space, they study the set of all long-run limit sets.

One result says this set has empty interior when the base space has no isolated points. For a class of branched spaces, a transitive map makes the limit set split into separate pieces. Yet for one large such space, they build a map where the limit set holds a whole arc. The contrast shows how much the base space matters.
arxiv-2502-02978:
David Schmoll and six co-authors showed in 2025 how patterning a magnetic film can remove a broadening of its resonance signal caused by the crystal beneath it. The film, a garnet prized for hosting quantum waves of magnetism, sits on a substrate that turns magnetic at low temperatures. That substrate's stray field widens the signal and shortens wave lifetimes, a problem for quantum uses. The team studied films of several shapes with resonance tests across temperatures.

Cutting the film into microstructures erased the uneven broadening from the substrate's field. The tests also showed the linewidth behaving in a nonstandard way at low temperatures, separate from the substrate effect. The authors present patterning as a practical fix for quantum devices built on this platform.
arxiv-2502-03078:
Nina Freise and co-authors reviewed in 2025 how machines can tune their own prompts to coax better synthetic data out of large language models. Fake data matters where real data is locked away, as in healthcare. Six peer-reviewed studies from 2020 to 2024, screened by standard review rules, form the evidence base.

Three families of methods emerged: those that learn from feedback, those that learn from their own errors, and those borrowed from control theory. All showed promise at refining prompts without human fuss. None, the authors say, is complete alone. They propose a combined, looping framework that stacks the strengths. The goal is synthetic data good enough to train on, made with minimal manual work. Sensitive fields stand to gain most.
arxiv-2502-03278:
Mehdi Heydari Shahna, Pauli Mustalahti, and Jouni Mattila present a control system that keeps heavy work robots moving when parts fail, in a 2025 paper. Their machines are wheeled robots of several tons, driven by hydraulics, with each wheel steered and powered on its own. A sensor or motor fault can throw such a robot off course, risking harm and costly damage.

Their design first writes the robot's motion with fault modes built in. A layered controller then spots each fault and shifts power among the valve-run wheels to hold the planned speeds and steering angles. Tests on a 6,500-kilogram robot over rough ground, under varied faults, showed the system held its course.
arxiv-2502-03378:
Haya Schulmann and Shujie Zhao tackle false alarms in internet routing security in a 2025 paper. The RPKI system checks that networks announce only routes they own. Past errors often make valid routes look invalid, so networks that filter them lose real traffic and income.

Their mechanism, LOV, learns which conflicts are harmless and builds a whitelist at internet scale. Networks can then keep filtering true threats without dropping good routes. Over half a year of live routing data, the system whitelisted more than 52,000 routes with benign origin errors. The authors argue this removes a main block to wider use of route filtering.
arxiv-2502-03678:
Zeyu Tang, Zhenhao Chen, Xiangchen Song, Loka Li, Yunlong Deng, Yifan Shen, Guangyi Chen, Peter Spirtes, and Kun Zhang wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. Its title page calls it a supplement, and its text presents Reflection-Window Decoding, a way to let text models fix their own words as they write.

Plain left-to-right writing cannot revise, so early slips drag the rest down. The authors gauge how far such text can stray from the best full-length text, and tie the risk to spikes of doubt in the run. Their method slides a reflection window over fresh text and pauses by a set rule, so fixes and new words take turns. Broad tests show the balance of speed and quality pays off.
arxiv-2502-04078:
Zheming Yang and co-authors match video jobs to the right servers across edge and cloud, in a 2025 paper. Edge-cloud systems drown in varied tasks and shifting resources, wasting both. Their framework, CDIO, first reads each task's spatial complexity and processing needs to predict what kind of resource it prefers. A cross-domain algorithm then assigns tasks to ideal servers on that basis.

On public data sets, the system met accuracy and delay demands while cutting computing and bandwidth use by twenty to forty percent against leading rivals. Energy use fell by over forty percent. The savings come from fit, not from bigger hardware.
arxiv-2502-04178:
Cotfas studies how the coherence of a quantum state depends on the measurement frame used to look at it. Coherence measures how wavy, rather than particle-like, a quantum state behaves. Standard measures tie the answer to one fixed basis of states.

Cotfas works with tight frames, a broader kind of measurement made of rank-one operators. He defines frame-based coherence directly, without the detour through a larger space that older definitions need. Using several bases at once gives a finer picture of the state's coherence. He also gives a frame-free version for single and multiple qubits. The work aims at sharper tools for quantum information tasks.
arxiv-2502-04678:
Ruiyuan Huang and Zengfeng Huang study choice problems where each pick also teaches about linked picks, in a 2025 paper. A case in point is a first price auction, where one bid can hint at results for like bids. Past work left open if a key rate could be kept as cases grew.

The pair gives a method that meets that rate, even when losses are set by a foe and some arms give no direct news. The trick is to set one hard arm aside in each round and fix its drift. Tests on made up data back the claim, and the proof is checked in full by a proof tool.
arxiv-2502-04878:
Patrick Leask and his seven co-authors, publishing in 2025, challenge a hopeful belief about a popular tool for interpreting AI models. Sparse autoencoders tease a network's inner activity into separate features that humans can name. Many hoped they would reveal the one true list of atomic concepts a model uses. The team tests that hope with two new techniques, and both tests fail it.

First, they stitch features from a large autoencoder into a smaller one. Some transplanted features add genuinely new information, which means the smaller tool was incomplete. Second, they train an autoencoder on the first one's own wiring. Its features split into combos of simpler ones, Einstein dissolving into scientist, Germany, and famous person, so they were never atomic. The authors still call the tools useful. They advise picking a size to fit the task instead of chasing a canonical list.
arxiv-2502-05078:
Tushar Pandey, Ara Ghukasyan, Oktay Goktas, and Santosh Kumar Radha grow reasoning graphs on the fly for language models in a 2025 paper. Fixed chains and trees waste effort on easy subproblems. Their framework, Adaptive Graph of Thoughts, spends compute where needed. It works at test time with no extra training.

Hard queries split recursively into linked subproblems. The result is a directed graph of reasoning steps. Only tangled nodes expand further under the scheme. Chain, tree, and graph styles merge in one system. Science questions gained up to about 46 percent in accuracy. Multi-hop retrieval and maths tasks also improved. The gains rival costly reinforcement learning runs.
arxiv-2502-05178:
Yue Zhao and co-authors present QLIP, an image tokenizer that understands as well as it draws, in a 2025 paper. Turning pictures into tokens lets one model both read and generate images. Past tokenizers forced a trade: sharp reconstruction or strong language alignment, not both.

QLIP trains its quantizer on both goals at once, balancing the two losses as training proceeds. A two-stage schedule handles the clash between the big batches alignment wants and the memory reconstruction demands. Plugged into two known systems, it matched or beat their original vision parts on understanding and on text-driven generation. A single mixed model then handled both jobs, a step toward unified multimodal systems.
arxiv-2502-05278:
Leonie Kayser asks how hard it is, in computing terms, to test whether a given polynomial belongs to a set built from other polynomials. Her 2025 paper studies polynomial subalgebras, a topic close to the older study of ideals and their Gröbner bases. Interest in fast methods for these sets has grown in recent years.
