Kayser pins down the cost of the membership test and of bounds on polynomial degree. The general problem turns out to fill a very high cost class, while the uniform-degree case sits one level lower. She draws out where the subalgebra setting matches the ideal setting and where it parts ways. Special families, such as sets built from single-term polynomials, get separate treatment in the paper.
arxiv-2502-05578:
Oleksii Galganov and Andrii Ilienko present a probability paper, published in 2025, on a classic random process named after a restaurant seating puzzle. In the Chinese restaurant process, guests join tables one by one, building a random split of a growing group into blocks. The authors study the small blocks in that split and how their pattern looks when the group grows very large.

They show the small block pattern settles toward a limit built from Poisson measures, a standard model for scattered random points, arranged across cones of rising dimension. That limit then yields classic and stronger path wise limit results for features of the process. Readers get a unified route to facts that once needed separate proofs.
arxiv-2502-05678:
Stacey Staples, a solo author, studies a graph matrix built in an unusual algebra in a 2025 paper. For any finite simple graph, this zeon Laplacian is a square matrix whose entries live in that algebra. She asks what its special values reveal about the graph. The algebra has a nilpotent part, which normally vanishes under repeated multiplication.

She shows that when a graph has a single vertex of a given degree, the matrix has a matching special value. The nilpotent part of that value counts the cycles that start at that vertex. A generalized version counts all cycles in the graph. Viewed as an operator, the matrix acts like a random variable whose values expose cycle structure.
arxiv-2502-05778:
Ananya Goon Tuli and co-authors give the first detailed study of the layer between the Milky Way's disk and its halo below one spiral arm, published in 2025. This interface, under the Perseus arm, mediates the exchange of mass and energy between the thin disk and the halo above it. Little was known about its vertical structure in this region.

The team combined space telescope spectra toward stars and distant active galaxies behind a narrow slice of the arm. They measured several gases and ions from near the mid-plane up to a few thousand light years below it. Neutral gas fell sharply with height, then more slowly. High ions stayed near constant. Matching motions and a uniform ion ratio point to turbulent mixing layers between warm and hot gas.
arxiv-2502-05978:
Sarthak Choudhary presents, in a 2025 paper for the DarkSide-20k collaboration, quality checks on plastic sheets that shift light for a dark matter detector's neutron veto. The detector hunts dark matter in liquid argon, which glows in deep ultraviolet. Big detectors need a shifter that can cover huge areas, and common coatings are costly to lay down.

The veto will use nearly two hundred square meters of a polymer foil as its shifter. Samples from the production batch are tested at very low temperatures in a new argon gas setup. Argon glow excites the foils, letting the team measure how well each sheet shifts the light. First results from that cold testing are reported here.
arxiv-2502-06378:
Alan Joy and Joseph O'Hagan explore in 2025 a social question raised by augmented reality: when anyone can pin digital content to real places, what should be allowed, and where? A protest note on a government wall, an ad on a war memorial, and art on a cathedral raise very different feelings.

The pair built a phone app that let people post and view location-tied content themselves. Afterward they surveyed attitudes toward artistic, protest, social, informative, and commercial posts across cultural sites, religious sites, and ordinary streets. The early findings sketch where the public draws lines around an augmented world.
arxiv-2502-06778:
Victoria Bollo and nine co-authors published a study in 2025 on how the universe's supply of cold gas has changed over cosmic time. Cold molecular gas is the raw fuel of star birth, and carbon monoxide glow is its main tracer. Earlier surveys were small and hostage to luck in where they pointed, so the team mined calibration data from a major telescope array for an unbiased sample.

They charted the brightness spread of carbon monoxide sources and the total gas density out to when the universe was young. Gas density rose to a peak when the cosmos was a few billion years old, then fell slowly. The pattern fits a picture of galaxies steadily refilled with gas. Splitting surveys across many small fields, they stress, beats staring at one patch.
arxiv-2502-06878:
Sukumar Kishanthan and Asela Hevapathige fuse oversampling with deep learning itself in a 2025 paper. Class imbalance, where rare cases drown in common ones, still defeats many classifiers. The standard fix, generating synthetic minority examples, usually runs as a separate pre-step blind to the model being trained.

Their framework rebuilds oversampling as a chain of discrete decisions made during learning, so synthetic data serve the model's own representation needs. Experiments on imbalanced tasks beat leading algorithms. Fraud, disease, and defect detection all live or die on rare classes; making the sampler part of the learner is a structural answer.
arxiv-2502-07078:
Hyett and colleagues built a machine learning model in twenty twenty-five for the smallest swirls of turbulent flow, a key target in fluid physics. Simulating turbulence at real-world intensity is still beyond any computer, so modelers must capture the statistics of the tiny scales instead of the full motion.

Their model follows the velocity gradient, the quantity that tracks how flow stretches and spins at a point. It uses an attention design, which lets the model weigh the most telling moments in a fluid parcel's past. The approach beat current physics-informed methods on both early checks and full run-throughs. Reading the trained model's attention turned up a surprise: the history of the stretching pattern links closely to the pressure forces that shape the flow. The authors say the tool both predicts better and teaches something new about turbulence.
arxiv-2502-07178:
Alex Tong and co-authors blend road-path calls from many guess tools on the fly. The work dates to 2025. Path calls guide safe self-drive cars, and many call tools exist. Each tool's skill swings with the place it runs in, though.

Their take treats each tool as a guide hand and keeps a weight mix cross them. Fresh true moves at each next step shape a loss score. That score's slope steers the mix toward the best blend of hands. The team blends tools taught on split cities in one big set. The blend matched or beat each lone tool, even on a fresh town's set.
arxiv-2502-07278:
Aditya Vora and co-authors bend one part of a still 3D object on text command, in a 2025 paper. Datasets rarely label how parts move, so older methods generalize poorly. Their approach borrows a video diffusion model's sense of motion: a few reference frames teach it a motion tag for the target part, tuned to the given object.

The tuned model renders the part's plausible motion from many views, and a rendering based loss pulls that motion back into the object's own 3D frame. On two part motion datasets, the method produced truer, more realistic articulations than rivals, the authors report.
arxiv-2502-07378:
Each clean maths space can wear a wide coat of loose maps, and that coat is key to a frame that reads waves and signals. Nikolas Hauschka, Peter Balazs, and Lukas Köhldorfer firm up that coat in a 2025 study. Past work left gaps in how the coat and its weighed forms are built.

The team sets out the coat in a wide frame and proves it is a full, firm space in its own right. They weigh two ways to read its shape: a weak star view and a strict span view. Weighed coats, tuned by a weight rule, get the same firm base. The work closes holes that users of the frame had to step round.
arxiv-2502-07478:
Wojciech Żuławiński and co-authors improve a signal method used to find early damage in rolling bearings. Their 2025 paper deals with vibration signals that repeat in cycles but also carry sharp, random impulses. Classic tools assume smoother noise, so the fault pattern can drown in the mess.

The team swaps the standard averaging step inside spectral coherence for robust versions that resist outliers. The improved method picked out periodic fault patterns more accurately in tests. It was checked on simulated signals with three kinds of harsh noise and on real vibration data from bearings in a crushing machine. The results support robust statistics as a practical upgrade for machine monitoring.
arxiv-2502-07678:
Callum Samuels and six co-authors simulate air entering square channels at an angle, a layout common in car exhaust treatment and heat exchangers. Straight entry is well charted, but slanted entry adds unknown pressure loss and may trip the flow turbulent at the mouth. Large eddy and averaged turbulence models were both run against experiments. The eddy-resolving runs showed a shear layer at the entrance shedding eddies that persist downstream near Reynolds number 2000.

Pressure losses mostly matched measurements, and rounding the entrance edge, as real parts have, closed the remaining gap. The averaged model stayed within 5% except in transitional cases, where error hit 40%.
arxiv-2502-07778:
Anirudh Sundara Rajan and Yong Jae Lee argue that fake-image detectors should ignore what real images look like and hunt only for generator artifacts. Detectors often latch onto spurious cues such as compression patterns tied to real photos. Those shortcuts fail when images are processed or come from new sources.

Their algorithm, Stay Positive, constrains training so the detector's evidence comes from traces left by generative models. Detectors trained this way resisted spurious correlations better and generalized more robustly through post-processing. They also caught inpainted real images more reliably, a case where real-image cues mislead. The paper reframes detection as a search for positive evidence of generation only.
arxiv-2502-07878:
Innes Bigaran and Richard Ruiz refine, in a 2025 paper, how weak bosons are counted inside fast-moving particles. At high energy, a W or Z boson can act as if it were a component, or parton, of the particle that emits it. A known shortcut, the Effective W Approximation, encodes that view, but its finer corrections carry flaws that were long conjectured and not proven.

The pair derive those finer terms for weak bosons from massless fermions, in two gauge choices. They set new kinematical consistency conditions that keep the bad traits in check. When the conditions hold, the approximation matches full calculations well for complex processes. That match suggests a clean factorization of the process holds at tree level. The authors say the approximation can be tested at the Large Hadron Collider with same-sign WW scattering data.
arxiv-2502-07978: Moeini and six colleagues survey in-context reinforcement learning in twenty twenty-five. Reinforcement learning agents usually update their network weights to improve. That process needs costly backward passes through the network. Some agents instead solve new tasks with no weight updates at all. They condition on context, such as their past actions and observations. The survey collects and organizes work on this behaviour. It covers how agents learn from context within a single run of experience. The authors frame the area as a strand of reinforcement learning research.
arxiv-2502-08478: Abraham Loeb shows that a dedicated space telescope could find many small interstellar objects. Such objects drift between stars and pass through our solar system unseen. A meter-wide scope could spot ten-meter objects that pass near the Sun. Splitting their heat glow from reflected sunlight would give their surface heat, area, and shine. Vapor from them, at an expected heat near six hundred kelvin, could be read for clues to their makeup and birth places.
arxiv-2502-08678:
Haitian Wang and co-authors present a study of weed detection in farm lands in Western Australia, published in 2025. Drones with multispectral cameras flew over two test areas near Kondinin. The team built a dataset from four years of flights. Ground crews used GPS gear to mark which plants were weeds and which were crops.

The authors then built a full pipeline that cleans and aligns the images before sorting each patch of land. The system mixes plant health indices with the camera channels and feeds them to deep learning models. A ResNet model did best, finding weeds with about 92 percent accuracy. The work gives farmers a tested dataset and a working method for spotting weeds from the air.
arxiv-2502-08778:
Ivan Rapoport and four co-authors model the glow of hydrogen alpha light from galaxies, mapped place by place. Near infrared surveys hunt far off galaxies that give off strong lines of light. To draw tight limits, the clumps of these galaxies must be well grasped. A clear model of the glow helps link galaxies to the dark halos they sit in.

Their plain model tracks how light moves through gas. It adds glow from the warm, thin gas spread between stars. The counts of atoms at each level hold steady, worked out with the coronal shortcut. Run on IllustrisTNG sims at redshifts one to two, hits between atoms give about 40 percent of all the line light. Counts of galaxies by glow match surveys if a mild, even veil of dust is used. Counts per halo match the Euclid Flagship mock, apart from gaps from gas feedback.
arxiv-2502-08878:
Justin Chen and co-authors tackle in 2025 a privacy puzzle. Many users each hold a set of items. The group wants to publish as much of the combined list as possible, without leaking who held what. This partition selection problem underlies private vocabulary building, category statistics, and learning on user supplied items. All of it sits under the shield of differential privacy.

Their algorithm, MaxAdaptiveDegree, shifts weight around cleverly. Items far above the safety threshold give up spare weight, and items with little support gain it, raising the odds that rare items make the cut. They prove the method beats the standard parallel approach in a strong stochastic sense. A two round variant uses round one's results to bias round two. In tests the methods led rival parallel algorithms and scaled to data sets with hundreds of billions of items, far beyond earlier sequential work.
arxiv-2502-08978:
Calvin McCarter probed in 2025 what a celebrated table-prediction model has actually learned. The model, TabPFN, was trained to solve fresh table tasks from examples in context, with no retraining. McCarter treats it as a black box that generates fit functions and studies those functions across many data sets.

The learned habits swing between brilliant and baffling: sharp instincts on some patterns, odd blind spots on others. Mapping those instincts shows where the model can be trusted and where it will mislead. The essay closes with lessons for building and judging this whole family of pre-fitted networks.
arxiv-2502-09378:
Hadar Sharvit, Raz Karl, and Tsevi Beatus taught a neural network to plan a robotic wing's flapping in a 2025 paper. Controlling a flapping wing is an inverse problem: choose the wing motion that produces a desired aerodynamic force. For propellers the input-output map is simple, but flapping flight involves intricate fluid motion, making real-time inversion computationally impractical by classical means. The authors instead learn the inverse map directly from experiment.

Their rig flaps a wing while measuring its aerodynamic force and filming its three-dimensional motion with high-speed cameras, generating the training data. A sequence-to-sequence model, fitted with a novel adaptive-spectrum layer that learns in the frequency domain, then predicts the kinematics needed for a target force. Data-driven inversion could give flapping robots the responsive control fixed-wing craft take for granted.
arxiv-2502-09478:
Chi-Kin Tam and co-authors give a method to work back from how pairs of particles move together to the shape of the source that made them. That link is set by a known equation, but noise in the data can lead a plain fit astray.

The team adapt a deblurring method first used for images, with guards that keep the result smooth and rightly scaled. One guard favors low disorder in the source, a new twist they set out in full. Tests on made up data and on real pairs, protons and a deuteron with an alpha particle, show the method works well.
arxiv-2502-09778:
Micha Elsner and David Liu use large language models to help document endangered languages, in a 2025 paper. Interlinear glossed text, where each word gets a translation and grammar label, is basic infrastructure for linguistics. Making it by hand is slow. The authors argue that language models, good at following plain instructions, can make the process more accessible.

Their system prompts the model word by word, with retrieved examples as guidance, across the seven languages of a shared benchmark. It beat the previous best automated baseline on morpheme-level scores for every language. A simple oracle picking among three guesses beat the challenge winner on word-level scores in five languages. In a case study on Tsez, the model even wrote and followed its own instructions, cutting errors on a tricky grammar feature. The authors see interactive glossing help as the prize.
arxiv-2502-09978:
Yachao Yuan and co-authors built a road hazard sentinel in 2025 that learns from many roadside sensors at once without gathering their private data in one place. Crashes often start with a hazard nobody flagged in time, and cameras plus other sensors see more together than alone.

Their system trains a shared detector across edge devices, each keeping its raw data. A privacy layer scrambles local data in a way tuned for high dimensional, mixed media streams, and the training chatter is squeezed to a thousandth of rival systems' cost. On real world and public crisis data sets it hit about ninety-six percent accuracy with answers in a blink. The design targets live city networks.
arxiv-2502-10178:
Marco Bondaschi and seven co-authors study how the Mamba model learns from examples placed in its input. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Mamba is a fast rival to the transformer models behind most chat tools. The team tested it on Markov chains, simple step-by-step random processes. Even a single-layer Mamba learned a classic smoothing rule for guessing the next step.

The team shows that this smoothing rule is the best possible guess in two formal senses. They explain the result through the way Mamba mixes nearby steps, a step called convolution. Tests matched the theory. The authors say this is the first formal link between Mamba and a best-known statistical method. They close by pointing to new research paths the result opens.
arxiv-2502-10278:
Julian Wykowski wrote a 2025 math paper that opens the study of profinite rigidity for modules. The question is how far a module over a Noetherian domain is fixed by its finite images alone. Group theory has classic results of this kind, and Wykowski builds the module parallel.

He sets out three profinite invariants for modules over any such domain. Free modules prove rigid when the domain meets a homology condition. Over a Dedekind domain he maps the full genus of each module, and over a principal ideal domain all finitely generated modules prove rigid. As a use, he proves a family of solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups is rigid in the absolute sense, a first for its kind.
arxiv-2502-10378:
Learners reading in a second language stall on words they do not know. Seven authors present EyeLingo, a system that watches a reader's eyes and reads the text at the same time. It then predicts which words are likely unknown, so help can appear at the right moment. A transformer model combines gaze patterns with language features to make the call in real time.

In a study with twenty readers, the system reached 97.6 percent accuracy, with an F1 score of 71.1 percent. The team built a working reading assistant on top of it. Users rated the prototype more useful. They also said they would be more willing to use it than baseline methods. The authors present gaze as a practical signal for vocabulary support that fits the reading flow instead of interrupting it.
arxiv-2502-10578:
Stark and Steinberger compare in twenty twenty-five two ways of keeping high-dimensional fitting honest: penalising complexity outright, or stopping training early. They study gradient descent on a squared-error task with a penalty term, in settings where data points and features are both plentiful. Their analysis tracks how test error evolves as steps accumulate.

With the penalty tuned well, test error glides down toward the best benchmark as steps grow. Plain training stopped early hits that benchmark only in rare special cases. So explicit penalty proves nearly efficient, while early stopping is not. They add a data-driven way to pick the penalty strength that costs less than cross-checking. New covariance results support the theory.
arxiv-2502-10778:
Zhen-Fan Wang, Yu Tu, Kai Zhang, Dai Zhou, and Onur Bilgen improved wind farm layout search in 2025 with a Bayesian method that swaps its own strategy. Placing turbines to maximise yearly energy is costly to simulate at high fidelity. Their framework alternates two acquisition rules, balancing exploring new layouts against refining known good ones.

A Kriging surrogate is retrained on the best layouts found so far, sharpening predictions as it goes. On standard test functions the switch beat either rule alone. On three wind farm cases with wake models it reached near-optimal energy with far fewer calculations than classic heuristics. Coupled with fluid dynamics simulation, it still found higher-energy layouts, pointing to cheaper high-fidelity design.
arxiv-2502-10878:
Chao Tian and Shlomo Shamai give a concrete meaning to a puzzling information measure, in a 2025 paper. Partial information decomposition splits what several signals jointly reveal about a target. One piece, the synergy, captures what only the signals together can tell. The idea caught on in biology and machine learning, yet its exact meaning stayed informal.

The authors tie synergy to the classic broadcast channel, where one sender serves two receivers. Synergy, they prove, equals the cooperative gain of that channel, or at least a firm lower bound on it. Receivers helping each other gain exactly what the abstract synergy promised. The result gives users of the decomposition a firm operational footing.
arxiv-2502-11178:
Enes Doruk and Hasan Ates present a detector that keeps working when the world it watches changes, in this 2025 paper. Object detectors trained in one setting often stumble in another, a gap called domain shift. Transformer detectors handle wide context well but cost too much computing, while older networks miss long-range links.

Their model, DA-Mamba, mixes the Mamba sequence architecture, which scales gently, with attention modules that align features across domains. Scanning runs along both space and channels in a domain-aware way. A distillation step driven by uncertainty cleans the noisy features that mixing can create, and a gating step with random nudges guards against overfitting. The design aims at one-stage detection that adapts as it runs. The authors present it as the first Mamba-based detector built for this adaptation task.
arxiv-2502-11478:
Yunsik Kim, Yonghun Song, and Yoonyoung Chung release a paired speech data set for cleaning up throat microphone recordings. Their 2025 paper explains the trade off. Throat mics shrug off noise in factories, subways, and busy streets. But sound passing through skin and tissue loses its high frequencies, so speech turns muffled. Learning based fixes lacked a standard training set.

Their TAPS data set pairs throat and acoustic recordings of the same speech from sixty native Korean speakers. An alignment method was built to fix the timing and level mismatch between the two channels. Three baseline models were benchmarked on the set. Mapping based approaches did best at restoring quality and content. The authors offer TAPS as a shared yardstick for the field.
arxiv-2502-11578:
Birger Moell and Johan Boye test whether grading text complexity can cheaply signal a language model's general skill, in a 2025 paper. Models stumble on exact calculation and structure tasks. Swedish school and university essays supplied the test material. Models computed a standard readability score for each essay. They also measured average dependency distance, a parsing task.

One compact model performed most consistently on both jobs. It led on score accuracy and on parsing alike. Model accuracy on the readability task tracked a famous general benchmark closely. The correlation was strong across the six models checked. The authors call complexity grading a noisy but handy proxy. It needs no big benchmark suite to run. Quick proxy checks could screen models before costly full evaluations.
arxiv-2502-11878:
Daniele Girolimetto and Tommaso Di Fonzo forecast Italian electricity output in twenty twenty-five. The data is daily and split by region and by energy source. Forecasts made piece by piece often clash with each other. The parts must add up to the national total, and independent forecasts rarely respect that.

Their approach combines forecasts from multiple experts while enforcing coherence. The combination is balanced and multi-task, and it uses unbiased base forecasts. Applied to Italian generation data, the method beat single-task forecasts. It also beat combined forecasts and a leading single-expert reconciliation method. Readers who forecast hierarchical time series get a way to gain accuracy and consistency at once.
arxiv-2502-12078:
Dheeraj Pasham and three co-authors propose hunting a new cosmic burp by its infrared echo. Their 2025 paper concerns quasi-periodic eruptions, repeating soft X-ray flares from galaxy centers, of which only about ten are known. The problem is finding more: they seem to shine only in X-rays, which few telescopes watch full-time.

Their clue comes from one known source, where a surrounding dust shell has been glowing brighter in the infrared, steadily, for about a thousand days. The authors argue the original stellar disruption cannot power that long rise, but dust reprocessing the repeated eruption light can. The model makes testable promises: faint infrared flickers at the eruption rhythm, and a matching slow fade if the eruptions stop. One other event shows the same behavior and may hide eruptions. The authors pitch wide-field infrared surveys, and a coming space telescope, as the net.
arxiv-2502-12878:
Jon Vehovar, Miha Rot, and Gregor Kosec study, in a 2025 paper, how accuracy choices affect simulation speed when a problem is split across many computers. Their method estimates derivatives at scattered points from neighbors' values, with no grid. Using more neighbors gives sharper answers but forces more data exchange between machines. On one computer, sharper always wins. Across a cluster, the exchange cost may change the answer.

The team solves a standard test equation on a uniform CPU cluster. Machines share work by region, using one tool for talk between machines and another within each. They scan settings to find which mix of sharpness and chatter reaches a target accuracy fastest. The paper maps the trade-off rather than declaring one winner, giving simulation engineers a way to tune meshless codes for distributed systems.
arxiv-2502-13578:
Santiago Oviedo-Casado, Daniel Cohen, and Javier Cerrillo model noise in tiny-scale magnetic scans in this 2025 paper. Such scans can read liquid samples at the nanoscale, but wandering molecules blur the signal. Trapping the sample in a small space should cut that blur.

Once wandering is tamed, slower noise sources long hidden beneath it come into view. The team studies two of them in depth for the first time: how molecules stick and rub at the trap walls, and how pores in the trap shape the signal. Both effects can spoil the gains of trapping, they show. Yet each also carries news about the sample and its surroundings, which skilled users could exploit.
arxiv-2502-13678:
Thijs Kamma and Antoon Pelsser reformulated a classic savings problem in 2025. An agent chooses how much to consume over time, but satisfaction depends on consumption relative to an internal habit built from past consumption, and here the habit enters multiplicatively, as a ratio. That ratio form destroys the problem's concavity and makes the present depend unavoidably on the whole path, so the usual Lagrangian route to a dual problem fails.

Using a duality theorem of Fenchel, the authors identify a candidate dual formulation and prove strong duality, meaning the two problems share the same optimal value. From that they derive relations converting optimal choices in one problem into optimal choices in the other. The dual view also yields an analytical way to bound how accurate any approximate solution to the original problem really is.
arxiv-2502-13778:
Jiaqi Li and co-authors present a poster on a cyber range that builds itself in a 2025 paper. Factories going digital face tangled security needs, and test ranges often lack fresh scenarios or take long to craft. Their platform, SpiderSim, aims at fast and light scenario making for industry security research.

Three parts drive it: a shared frame for scenario modeling and a team of agents that write scenarios on their own. Plug in blocks of atomic security skills allow mix and match builds. Trials span settings like marine ranch monitoring rigs. The open source tool rests on a theory base for wide reuse.
arxiv-2502-13978:
Allen Lobo and Saravanan Arumugam treated random trials as dynamic systems in this paper from twenty twenty-five. They grow out of Bernoulli's law of large numbers, the classic rule on how rates settle with many trials. The pair ask how the felt randomness of a trial shifts as trials pile up. A coin toss and a dice roll serve as their worked cases.

By hand and by number runs, they show that the randomness of each outcome can rise by chance. That rise hangs on how fast the felt rates grow. Trial runs and sims check the math. Readers in probability get a flow view of how chance itself seems to move as a trial repeats.
arxiv-2502-14978: Konrad Deka and Bo Peng construct a family of symbolic systems with striking properties. Their short paper appeared in 2025. The systems are generalized Oxtoby subshifts, rules that generate endless symbol strings. Each allows a set of stable statistical patterns, called invariant measures, and those sets always form a shape known as a Choquet simplex. The authors show their family can realize every such shape. They also show that telling whether two systems in the family match is tame: the sameness relation is hyperfinite, the simplest kind of infinite complexity.
arxiv-2502-15378:
Yi-Jun Chang and co-authors settle the cost of a backup-route problem in distributed computing. Given the shortest path between two nodes, the replacement paths problem asks, for every link on that path, the best detour if that link fails. Nodes in the network must compute the answers by passing small messages, and the question is how many rounds it truly takes. Their 2025 paper pins the answer down exactly for unweighted directed graphs.

The tight bound grows as the two-thirds power of the network size, plus its diameter. Their method also gives near-exact answers for weighted graphs. Even the easier question, finding just the single smallest detour, cannot beat the same bound. The result improves a 2024 bound from both sides at once, closing the gap between algorithm and impossibility for this classic problem.
arxiv-2502-15578:
Jayeeta Chaudhuri and colleagues demonstrated a hardware attack called FLARE in 2025 against shared FPGA chips. Cloud FPGAs increasingly host several tenants at once, each uploading circuit designs, called bitstreams, that a manager loads into reconfigurable regions. FLARE strikes during that upload, not while the victim's circuit runs, which separates it from classic fault attacks and hides it from runtime defenses.

By briefly activating power-wasting circuits during reconfiguration, the attacker corrupts the configuration address inside the incoming bitstream, redirecting the upload into a neighboring tenant's region and overwriting their pre-loaded module. On a commercial development board the team compromised multiple user bitstreams this way. The attack shows that the reconfiguration pathway itself, meant to make multi-tenancy flexible, is a security boundary that current countermeasures largely ignore.
arxiv-2502-15678:
Luca Schulze Buschoff and five co-authors test if fine-tuning can make vision-language models see the world more like people do. Their twenty twenty-five paper notes that even strong pre-trained models lag behind human visual thought. The team gathered images and human judgments across many kinds of visual tasks.

They then fine-tuned models on true answers for two domains: intuitive physics and causal reasoning. Scores rose in the tuned domain, and the models also matched human answers more closely there. But the gains did not carry to new looks or new domains. The verdict is that narrow tuning helps locally, yet broad human-like sight needs more.
arxiv-2502-15778:
Hui Wang, Fafa Zhang, and Chaoxu Mu test whether large language models can handle multi-criteria decision making at expert level, in a 2025 paper. Such choices weigh many factors at once, and older methods strain when the factor count grows. The team built a general framework that hands these problems to language models and scores them against human expert answers on three real tasks.

Off the shelf, open and commercial models reached only about sixty percent accuracy. Prompt tricks like step-by-step reasoning lifted scores to near seventy percent. A light fine-tuning method called LoRA did far better, pushing accuracy to about ninety-five percent across tasks. The gap between models nearly vanished after tuning, which the authors read as a stable edge.
arxiv-2502-15878:
Pietro Baratella and co-authors simplify a hard calculation needed to pin down how fast false vacuums decay in this 2025 paper. A false vacuum is a space state that looks stable but can collapse. Its decay rate sets how long such a state survives. Precision rates need a correction factor from field fluctuations. That factor, a functional determinant, is notoriously messy to tame. The team handles particles of three spin types at once.

Their route uses standard diagram tools and a double expansion. The end result is a simple recipe of single integrals. It works for any scalar landscape and any mix of fields. Ghost fields tied to gauge bosons are covered too. A worked example shows the method in action. The paper serves particle theory and early-universe studies.
arxiv-2502-16078:
Xuding Zhu surveys a famous graph puzzle and its fall in a 2025 paper. In 1966 Hedetniemi guessed a clean rule about coloring the combined graph of two networks. If neither network alone can be colored with a given number of colors, their product cannot be colored either. The guess drew fifty years of work.

Shitov disproved it in 2019 for large color counts, and later papers shrank the counterexamples until the guess was known to fail for every count from four upward. It still holds at three and below. Zhu's survey gathers the line of results, explains the ideas behind the counterexamples, and lists the related questions still open. The paper serves as a map of a closed problem and its open neighborhood.
arxiv-2502-16178:
Sitong Pan and co-authors build TutorUp, a system that lets new online tutors rehearse with simulated students, in a 2025 paper. Online teaching is booming, yet novice tutors get little practice at keeping remote students engaged. Real practice classes are scarce and feedback is slow.

TutorUp uses a large language model to play the student in scripted trouble spots drawn from surveys of 86 and 102 respondents on engagement problems. Tutors try their moves in live dialogue, then get instant and later feedback tied to proven teaching tactics. In a test with 16 users, tutors rated TutorUp well above a plain baseline on both usefulness and ease of use. The system offers a safe gym where tutors can fail, adjust, and grow before facing real classes.
arxiv-2502-16778:
Sanaz Hasanzadeh Fard and Emily Dolson tested how missing data distort summaries of species interaction networks in two thousand twenty-five. Such networks map who interacts with whom in nature, like pollinators and plants. Field work often misses some links, which could skew the graph measures ecologists rely on.

They studied one hundred forty-eight real networks across four interaction types, from pollination to seed dispersal. For each, they tracked six structural measures as extra links were added back. Some measures changed slowly and seemed robust, while others shifted fast. Community-finding methods also differed, with two far steadier than two rivals. Robustness varied by interaction type for some measures, which guides careful metric choice.
arxiv-2502-16878:
Rezaie and Azizi study Z boson production in proton-lead collisions in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Such collisions, run at high energy, probe how quarks and gluons are spread inside heavy nuclei. The authors use a family of distribution functions that track partons' sideways motion. They test three versions of the approach: two orders of one model family and a parton branching scheme.

They set the predictions against data from the CMS experiment. Both model orders mostly match the data well. The lower order overshoots in some regions, while the higher order, with a stricter ordering rule, agrees better there. The paper shows how fine choices in parton modeling shape collider predictions. Nuclear physicists who model proton-nucleus runs are the readers.
arxiv-2502-16978:
Spin liquids are magnetic states that never settle, their moments rippling under strict local rules that mimic electric field laws. Naïmo Davier and co-authors design a family of such states in this 2025 paper where the telltale scattering signature stretches from a point into a line.

They build the states by stacking layers of two-dimensional algebraic spin liquids, and simulations confirm several worked examples. Along the line, the character of the emergent field can slide continuously, a feature tied to exotic fracton physics. The team also reads the line as the interference of two emergent electric fields and tests the idea on other lattices.
arxiv-2502-17078:
Junseo Lee and co-authors (2025) ask what happens when modern image synthesis runs on the graphics hardware built for games instead of on general-purpose cores. Radiance field methods, above all 3D Gaussian splatting, render photorealistic views quickly, but studies so far ran them as software on programmable shaders. The fixed-function units in a GPU, fast but rigid, sat mostly idle. The team implemented Gaussian splatting through graphics APIs and measured it on synthetic and real scenes.

The measurements exposed where the hardware pipeline strains under volume rendering. Their answer, VR-Pipe, folds two changes into the pipeline to streamline it for this workload. The paper's contribution is architectural: as neural rendering moves toward products, letting the dedicated graphics path carry it promises speed and efficiency that shader-only implementations leave on the table. Chip designers get concrete bottlenecks, with numbers, to design against.
arxiv-2502-17278:
Andraž Repar, Nada Lavrač, and Senja Pollak improved term extraction in two thousand twenty-five for specialist Slovenian texts. Picking the true terms of a field out of its papers is a core step for glossaries and search. Their method joins classic features from older extractors with fresh context features from contextual word embeddings.

Working from a newly annotated Slovenian corpus, they derived rules for candidate terms, then trained a support vector machine on statistical, linguistic, and context features. Across four fields, from biomechanics to veterinary science, their scores beat the prior best for Slovenian by a clear margin. Context embeddings, they conclude, are a real asset for this task.
arxiv-2502-17378:
João Helis Bernardo and co-authors survey developers about continuous integration in machine learning projects, in a 2025 paper. Continuous integration, the habit of merging and testing code often, works well for normal software but strains in ML projects, which show longer builds and thinner test coverage. The team asked 155 practitioners from 47 projects why.

Eight key differences surfaced, from test complexity to infrastructure needs. Model training, heavy data handling, and thirst for compute stretch build times, while the randomness inside ML systems makes tests flaky and hard to trust. The authors propose ML-specific tweaks to standard practice. Their message: keep the core principles, but adapt the plumbing.
arxiv-2502-17778:
Quantum sensors promise measurements of extraordinary sharpness, but most research polishes the sensor hardware rather than the system around it. Anastashia Jebraeilli and co-authors present STQS, an architecture that weaves sensing, memory, communication, and computation into one design. Within a gate-based framework, users can explore sensing schemes and probe how noise creeps in at each step of a workflow.

A new distance-based score rates how far a sensing state sits from its reference, giving a confidence readout. The team demonstrates the design on quantum radar and dark matter hunting with qubits. Parts of the system already run on today's IBM and IonQ machines.
arxiv-2502-18678:
Esteban Cárdenas and co-authors prove a predicted effect in mixed quantum gases in this 2025 paper. Experiments with ultracold boson and fermion atoms showed the fermions pulling bosons together, plus a flip between stable and unstable states. No math proof of that flip existed.

The team studies the low-energy spectrum of the mixed system's governing operator. They show its values converge to those of a simpler boson-only model that includes the fermion effect. For small coupling, the bosons hold steady; past a strength, they do not. The proof grounds a striking lab finding in firm theory. It also gives modelers a cleaner equation to use.
arxiv-2502-18778:
Qingpei Guo and co-authors present an open-source model that takes in and produces any mix of text, image, audio, and video, in a paper from 2025. Such omni models promise a single assistant that can watch, listen, read, and reply in kind. Training one is hard because data amounts and learning speeds differ wildly across the senses.

Their model, M2-omni, treats every input and output as one interleaved sequence. A step balance plan during early training evens out the data gaps between senses. During instruction tuning, an adaptive plan keeps the senses progressing together. Pure text skill is guarded throughout. The authors report performance rivaling a leading closed model, with real-time interactive use as the goal.
arxiv-2502-19278:
Anderson Tomaz, Rafael Mattos, and Mario Barbatti review the quantum measurement problem, a puzzle at the heart of physics for nearly a century. Left alone, a quantum state evolves smoothly and can hold many outcomes at once, like a coin that is both heads and tails. A measurement, though, always lands on one outcome.

The review sorts out what is well understood from what is still open. It walks through the main lines of thought, including decoherence, many-worlds, collapse theories, hidden variables, and views that treat the quantum state as knowledge. The authors also point readers to curated online material that explains the core ideas in plain terms. Their aim is a clear map of a debate that is narrower than it once was.
arxiv-2502-19478:
Sowmiya Balan and four co-authors link two big facts in one model: a hum of gravity waves caught by pulsar clocks, and a light form of dark matter. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Strong first-order shifts in a dark sector can make that low hum. The team asks if the same shift can give mass to a stable dark particle that fills the dark matter count. Their dark sector has a hidden force with a dark photon that talks to our world by a slight mix. The shift sits at a low heat, so the dark particle is light. It gains its count by wiping out into electrons and dark Higgs states. The plan can be tested in labs.
arxiv-2502-19578:
Alec Dektor, Peter DelMastro, Erika Ye, Roel Van Beeumen, and Chao Yang present a math method for very large eigenvalue problems in a 2025 paper. Such problems arise when data has many axes, yet the answer can be stored in a compact low-rank form. Each step of the solve tends to swell that form, so steps must squeeze it back down.

Their method builds its search space from rough guesses at the answer itself. A rival method builds a set that is hard to keep exact in compact form. In tests, the new method shrugs off squeeze errors far better and keeps going where a third method stalls. It also works for a wider class of matrices.
arxiv-2502-19878:
Alexander Medvedev, Anton Proskurnikov and Zhanybai Zhusubaliyev warn that pulse-based drug dosing can behave chaotically, in their 2025 arXiv paper. Many dosing systems deliver discrete pulses rather than a continuous infusion, mimicking manual administration over longer periods. That makes the control loop hybrid: drug dynamics run continuously while the controller acts in steps, and hybrid loops are strongly nonlinear.

Studying anesthesia dosing of a muscle-blocking agent, they find the intended regular rhythm coexists with unwanted periodic patterns, multiple stable regimes and even deterministic chaos. Their conclusion is practical: dosing algorithms built this way need thorough bifurcation analysis before they can be trusted with patient safety.
arxiv-2502-20178:
Zhaoxuan Wang and co-authors designed a stealthy attack on the satellite navigation that guides delivery and survey drones. Spoofing fake GPS signals is a known threat, but its success depends on how the drone is moving, a factor security studies often ignore. The team first showed that turning and other nonlinear motion makes position spoofing work better and makes speed-based detection less likely to fire.

Building on that, their attack, called SSD, waits for the right motion state before striking, acting as a state-triggered backdoor. In tests it greatly increased position errors and mission failure risk while staying invisible to three current detectors. The work warns that drone route planners must judge navigation security state by state, not on average.
arxiv-2502-20278:
Lior Gishboliner, Eoin Hurley, and Yuval Wigderson prove new results in a 2025 paper on graph homomorphisms, maps between graphs that keep linked nodes linked. Many classic results say, in rough terms, that a triangle-free graph with set traits can be mapped into a small triangle-free graph. Threshold results give this when the graph is dense enough, and an approximate version gives it for all graphs when the map is allowed some slack.

The authors study uneven versions, where the traits demanded of the source and the target need not match. For one case, a graph with no short odd cycles and a set density maps into a small triangle-free graph whose size rests only on that density. The cycle demand can be loosened when the graph has bounded complexity of a set kind. The work also sharpens a known proof.
arxiv-2502-20478:
Hou and Wang survey doctors on which explanation styles they prefer when an AI model predicts a patient's outcome. Clear explanations are meant to help clinicians trust and use such predictions. Their 2025 study builds a model that reads intensive care admission notes to forecast death in hospital, then explains its calls in four ways.

The four styles are word-importance scores, highlighted text spans, similar past patients, and free-text reasons written by a language model. Thirty-two practicing clinicians rated and compared the styles. The authors distill their feedback into guidance on when each style fits, where each falls short, and how each could improve. The work targets designers of clinical AI tools.
arxiv-2502-20678:
Aaryan Garg, Akash Kumar, and Yogesh S Rawat tackle video grounding without box labels in a twenty twenty-five computer science paper. Their task locates a described subject in space and time inside a video. Only a text query is given for training. Recent vision-language models offer a starting point, but simple use of them falls short.

The team first links text queries to short video segments called tubelets. Then their STPro system learns in stages. One module builds up complex actions step by step. Another module raises scene difficulty in a guided way. Tests on three benchmark datasets show gains over earlier methods, including on crowded scenes.
arxiv-2502-20978:
Richard Gerlach, Antonio Naimoli, and Giuseppe Storti develop a method for forecasting financial tail risk several steps ahead. Their targets are Value-at-Risk and Expected Shortfall, the standard measures of extreme losses. The approach is quantile-based and semi-parametric: returns are scaled by an estimated quantile series, then resampled to build forecast distributions at multiple horizons.

The method works whenever the relation between the two risk measures is stable over time. It extends to models incorporating realized volatility measures, in the spirit of realized GARCH and CAViaR frameworks. Simulations check finite-sample behavior, and a forecasting study compares one-day and ten-day forecasts at the one and two-and-a-half percent levels against competitors.
arxiv-2502-21078:
Titus Pinta (2025) builds a framework for analyzing Newton-type optimization methods when the problem is not smooth and the curvature information is random. In many applications the Hessian, the matrix of second derivatives that guides Newton's method, can only be estimated noisily. Pinta derives bounds, in expectation and in probability, on how many iterations such methods need before they reach an approximately optimal point.

The analysis uses a variant of Chernoff bounds adapted to random stopping times. Unusually, the results do not require the curvature estimate to be unbiased or to have finite variance, two assumptions earlier work leaned on. Pinta then demonstrates the theory on two applications: a stochastic quasi-Newton method for orbital tomography with X-ray free-electron lasers, and a sketched Newton method for image denoising.
arxiv-2502-21278:
Kulin Shah and co-authors ask whether image-making AI must memorize its training pictures to stay creative, in this 2025 paper. Top diffusion models often copy training images, above all when the training set is small. Past fixes for that copying tend to dull image quality. The team looks for a way to keep quality high and copying low at once.

Their theory shows copying is only forced at low noise levels, the stage that adds fine detail. So they train the model on noisy data at large noise scales instead. The change cuts memorization a lot without hurting image quality. It works for text-guided and unguided models, and across varied data supply. The paper offers a principled route to more original generative models.
arxiv-2503-00178:
Raghu Raj, Ryan O'Dowd, Owen Huber, and Hrushikesh Mhaskar lay groundwork, in a paper published in 2025, for a broader theory of sparse recovery. Sparse methods rebuild a signal from few measures by assuming most of its parts are zero. They power compressive sensing, which samples far less than older rules demand. A newer family based on mixed bell-shaped noise priors often beats them in practice, but lacked a theory.

The authors define a wider notion of sparsity that can hold both families. Within it, they state a key condition on the sensing setup and adapt two classic algorithms, basis pursuit and a reweighted squares method. They show a subset of the newer priors fits the frame. The work aims to explain why the newer methods win.
arxiv-2503-00278:
Vedant Khandelwal and a team of co-authors built a search system for systematic reviews in medicine. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with a slow step in such reviews: finding the right papers. Large language models help, but they lack niche terms and deep domain logic, and they can invent facts. Old tools lean on plain text methods and share the same gaps. The team mixed a domain tuned model with structured knowledge.

Their system, NeuroLit Navigator, draws on medical subject headings and a large medical language bank. That mix grounds search in set terms, not just raw text. Readers who run evidence reviews get a tool that aims for care and speed. Good search cuts the risk of missed or false claims in a review.
arxiv-2503-00378:
Rickard Brännvall proposes a privacy-friendly fix for uneven data in federated learning, in a 2025 paper. In federated learning, many clients train one model together without sharing their data. When each client's data looks different, the shared model can wobble and converge poorly.

His fix lets each client compute summary statistics of its own data, such as averages and spreads, and keep them private. During training, the model learns to adjust itself based on those local summaries. At use time, the same summaries steer each client's predictions. Experiments show the approach handles uneven data well and scales better than methods that hunt for similar peers. No extra information leaves the client, so privacy holds while accuracy improves.
arxiv-2503-00478:
Bao-Xi Sun asks whether a known particle is really two overlapping ones. The f1(1420) shows up in particle data tables as a single state. Sun models it as a bound pair of a kaon and its vector partner, held by pion exchange. Solving the wave equation yields a second bound state besides the known f1(1285), sitting just below threshold.

With outgoing wave rules, each bound state spawns a resonance near the same mass. Both land where the f1(1420) sits. Sun proposes the listed particle may be the blend of these two resonances from different couplings. The study is a compact piece of hadron theory.
arxiv-2503-00578:
Tuğrul Hasan Karabulut and İnci Baytaş proposed in 2025 a graph neural network that pays heed channel by channel. Graph networks learn from linked data by passing notes between nodes, but deep stacks blur every node's voice into the same hum, a flaw called over-smoothing. Their model, CHAT-GNN, learns which neighbor channels to lift or mute at each pass, so unlike voices survive the trip.

On standard test graphs, the model resisted the blur better than rivals. It also topped scores on graphs where linked nodes tend to differ, the hard case for note passing. The pair frame channel-wise heed as a general guard for deep graph learning. Code is shared in public.
arxiv-2503-00778:
Yingbo Tang and co-authors present AffordGrasp, a framework that lets robots grasp objects for a task, in clutter, in a 2025 paper. A good grasp depends on what the object is for: you hold a mug by its handle to pour, not by its rim. Older methods needed heavy training on fixed tasks and objects, so they stumbled on new scenes.

AffordGrasp leans on the reasoning power of vision-language models. It infers the task from loose, everyday instructions rather than strict commands, finds the task-relevant object, and grounds the right part to hold. Grasp poses are then generated inside that affordance region. The result is manipulation that respects both function and context, easing natural human-robot teamwork.
arxiv-2503-01078:
Uksang Yoo and co-authors teach soft robot hands by guiding them with human hands. Soft hands bend and grip with care, a boon for safety, but that bend makes them hard to steer and hard to teach. Past tools lean on camera views that hands block, or on stiff state codes that miss soft shape. Their 2025 frame, KineSoft, reads shape from strain sensors built into the hand.

Shape maps feed a learned plan that ends in fine shape control at the low level. A teacher can grab and move the hand, and the hand logs how its shape shifts. Tests on real hands show sharper shape reads than rival tools and cleaner shape tracking. Task wins also beat a past teach-by-showing method, the team reports.
arxiv-2503-01278:
Zi-wei Ou and co-authors search for gamma rays from a nova called V1405 Cas in a 2025 astronomy paper. Novae can emit high-energy gamma rays that reveal shocks accelerating particles near white dwarfs. This nova was reported to show a weak gamma-ray signal after its optical peak, at low significance.

In a continuous search of Fermi-LAT data, the team found no gamma rays. The flux limit sits below that of other well-studied Fermi novae. Radio data show the nova is bright and wrapped in low-density ionized gas, which may explain its quiet high-energy behavior.
arxiv-2503-01478:
Dai and co-authors propose a better yardstick for the retrieval half of retrieval-augmented generation, the technique that feeds a language model with searched documents. Today's tests either grade search and writing together, hiding the search's true contribution, or use ranking scores borrowed from web search that say little about usefulness to the model. Their metric, SePer, measures how much a retrieved passage lowers the model's semantic perplexity — its internal uncertainty about meaning.

The logic is simple: good retrieval should make the model more sure of the right content. Across varied test settings, SePer lined up closely with human judgments of retrieval quality, more precisely and cheaply than rivals. The authors present it as an automatic way to compare retrievers inside real generation systems. For teams tuning such systems, a metric that prices information gain in the model's own terms can steer design choices that ranking scores miss.
arxiv-2503-01978:
Riechert and co-authors run a qubit on a single molecule. Their 2025 paper builds a gatemon, a tunable transmon whose weak link is a quantum conductor. Past gatemons used wide semiconductors or graphene sheets. Here the link is one carbon nanotube, set on a clean boron nitride base inside a circuit quantum electrodynamics frame.

A gate voltage tunes the qubit's tone, echoing the nanotube's quantum dot nature. Coherence hit two hundred nanoseconds, a record for nanotube qubits. Extra tests finger charge noise as the main spoiler, with a strong gate link. The authors say nanotubes now contend for quantum hardware, and the device opens a window on single-electron processes in tiny conductors.
arxiv-2503-02078:
Jonathan Jacobi and Gal Niv present a 2025 arXiv technique for making language models explain their own inner workings. An earlier method, Patchscopes, transplants a model's internal activations into fresh prompts so the model describes what it was representing. Many features, though, ride on top of each other in superposition and come out too faint to read.

Superscopes turns up the volume: it systematically amplifies those superposed features in hidden states before the transplant. The trick borrows from guidance methods in image generation, and needs no extra training. Amplified features yielded interpretations where the older method drew blanks. The authors say the clearer readings reveal how models build context and stack complex concepts. For interpretability research, which tries to audit what these systems actually compute, a brighter flashlight on hidden features is a practical advance.
arxiv-2503-02678:
Simulating a chemical reaction on a computer requires templates that describe each molecule before and after it reacts. Building those templates by hand is slow and error-prone. Julian Konrad and Robert Meißner present a Python tool that builds them automatically for a widely used simulation package. The method treats molecules as mathematical graphs, then matches patterns between the starting and ending structures to find which atoms stay put, which ones react, and how atoms map across the change.

The authors tested the tool on three reaction families: poly-addition, poly-condensation, and chain polymerization. It handled tricky cases such as symmetric reactants and atoms that look identical. The templates keep only the parts of each molecule that matter for the reaction, which keeps large simulation batches fast. The team plans extensions to mixed organic and mineral systems.
arxiv-2503-02878:
Mendes and Ritter show language models can self-improve at state-value estimation for better search, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Ground-truth rewards for multi-step reasoning are costly, above all in web tasks. Their Self-Taught Lookahead framework needs no labeled rewards at all. The value model learns by simulating one lookahead step in language.

Training predicts next action, resulting state, and rationale for its value. That chain-of-thought value iteration refines estimates self-supervisedly. Sharper values let lightweight search expand fewer states at equal strength. Web agent success rises by thirty-nine percent with mid-size open models. Gains generalize to multi-hop questions and math puzzles.
arxiv-2503-03078:
Federico Fogantini and co-authors find a hidden rhythm in X-ray light from the black hole system Cygnus X-1, in a 2025 paper. The system has been watched since 1964, and its flicker is a key probe of how matter falls inward. Its flicker spectra usually look smooth, with no narrow beats of the kind seen in sister systems. The team hunted for beats that hide outside the plain spectra.

Data from the NICER telescope, split into soft and hard X-ray bands, held the clue. A narrow dip in a coherence measure, plus a sharp jump in time lags, marked the same shifting frequency. A faint beat component with a large lag explains both signs. Its traits match a known beat type, the authors argue, making this its first sighting in Cygnus X-1. Similar signs in two other systems support the reading.
arxiv-2503-03178:
Nick Winovich and three co-authors present a 2025 paper on fast solvers for partial differential equations that also own up to their doubt. Neural operators can spit out solutions in a flash, but users need to know how far to trust each answer. Older doubt gauges cost a lot to train and run.

Their light method is built for a popular solver type and ports to kin solvers too. On linear and curved test equations, its doubt bands were fair and held up on new kinds of inputs. The authors show the bands can steer tasks like Bayesian search that full solvers make too pricey.
arxiv-2503-03578:
Samuels sets out a design for fault tolerant quantum memory built in a doped crystal in twenty twenty-five. The memory stores units called qudits, which hold more than the two states of a qubit. Errors must be caught without wrecking the stored state. His plan for a europium doped crystal weaves three tools together.

Echo pulses draw out error clues without a direct read of the data. A Fourier method in a tweaked form names the error with fewer steps. A group based scheme then splits big fix steps into small ones, which keeps errors from spreading. The design skips the costly stacking used in qubit memory. It aims at long lived, large scale storage.
arxiv-2503-03778:
Wang and seven co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on making new brain scans by warping a learned template. Fake brain images must look plausible and match traits like age or disease. Direct image synthesis can miss fine shape details. Their method learns a template brain, then deforms it with a generated warp field. A diffusion model produces the warp rather than the image itself. An encoder blends image and template into a code that drives the warp. Alignment loss trains the whole system end to end.

Their method beats generative baselines on diversity and trait match. Shape measures on the fake brains also track real ones better. The code is posted in public for reuse. The authors aim at richer synthetic data for brain research.
arxiv-2503-04778: Jingxu Wu and Yuwen Yin read the unpublished thought notes of Lev Landau for the root of his shape-first physics. Landau held that laws fall out of symmetry breaks in bound state spaces, as sure things. His scorn for interpretation debates in quantum work and his lean-course fame grow, in this reading, from one root: a faith that truth must show through spare form. Economy of size is his test of a law. The 2025 note traces that faith through his notes and books.
arxiv-2503-04878:
Jeremy Booher and Rachel Pries sort curves by a rare trait in a 2025 math paper. They study curves that admit a cover of the line branched at three points, a tight and rich class. The trait in view is being supersingular once the curve is read in positive characteristic, a stark form of reduction.

Their tool is the Shimura and Taniyama method, which links such curves to abelian data. With it they give a full sorting for all curves of genus up to ten in this class. They also count how often primes yield a supersingular curve this way. The share of such primes turns out larger than first guesses would suggest.
arxiv-2503-04978:
Jake McNaughton, Abbas, and Ivan Maksymov present a 2025 paper on using a tunnel diode's physics as the activation function inside neural networks. The head title stresses full-precision and ternarised networks; the catalog title frames the same work as neuromorphic quantum networks. Activation functions shape how each unit in a network responds, and standard choices are pure math.

A tunnel diode has a bent current-voltage curve born of quantum tunneling. Used as the activation, that curve beat standard functions in deep networks, giving lower loss and higher accuracy in training and testing. The authors also argue the device suits future hardware for lean, energy-saving AI chips. The work links semiconductor electronics, quantum physics, and machine learning in one component.
arxiv-2503-05078:
Hangli Ge and co-authors build a traffic evacuation model for railway disruption in a 2025 paper on resilience in the Greater Tokyo rail network. When stations or lines fail, crowds must move to nearby stations without swamping them.

The model joins lines across operators with local geography in one frame. An optimized plan is solved with nonlinear math on matrices, weighing station capacity and travel cost. It can simulate failure at any number of stations or lines. Trials on Tokyo, Shinjuku, and Shibuya stations kept flows within neighbor capacity and recovery time. Average travel time also improved. Transit planners get a tested tool for crisis routing in dense rail cities.
arxiv-2503-05178:
Helena Bergold and co-authors ask how few triangles it takes to fence off one color of points from another, in a 2025 paper. Picture red and blue dots scattered on a page. A separator is a set of triangles that covers all points of one color while never enclosing a point of the other. Fewer triangles means a simpler fence. The team studies several flavors of the problem, with overlapping triangles allowed or not.

Their headline result is a warning: finding the smallest separator is NP-hard, a class of problems with no known fast exact method. They also bound how bad the worst case can be for a set of a given size. The paper is pure math and computing theory. It tells algorithm designers not to hunt for a perfect shortcut here, and it maps the terrain for smarter near-best methods.
arxiv-2503-05378:
Iva Kertusha and co-authors survey a decade of research on testing web applications, in a 2025 review. Testing keeps web systems reliable, secure, and fast, and the field has shifted hard toward automation and artificial intelligence. The team analyzed 259 papers from 2014 to 2025, charting methods, tools, venues, and how studies were run, with special attention to links with industry.

Work clustered on new techniques for black-box automated testing, with one conference leading and Selenium the most used tool. Human studies and real industrial use lagged behind, and many tools were never released openly. The survey maps where the field is strong and where practice still trails research.
arxiv-2503-05478:
Yu Rong and co-authors measure how the spin of galaxy groups lines up with the cosmic filaments they sit in. Filaments are the long strands of the cosmic web, and groups of galaxies gather along them. A natural guess is that a group's spin comes from its filament's spin. Their 2025 observational study, placed in an astrophysics letters journal, tests that guess.

Group spin axes turned out to sit at right angles to the filament spines, a clear perpendicular trend. The signal grew stronger in richer groups with more member galaxies. The team credits the orbital motion of galaxies falling in along the filament, not filament spin. Cosmologists get an observational clue to where group rotation really comes from.
arxiv-2503-05778:
Tapasvi Panchagnula published a paper in 2025 on a deep learning system that reads dream reports for themes and feelings. Dreams offer a direct record of the sleeping mind, yet they are usually studied by slow hand coding. The author's framework, DreamNet, scores the meaning and emotion in dream texts, with an option to add brain wave data from the dream stage of sleep.

On fifteen hundred anonymized dream reports the text-only version sorted emotions with about ninety-two percent accuracy. Adding the brain signals lifted accuracy to about ninety-nine percent. Some links were striking, such as falling dreams tracking anxiety closely. The author also releases the enriched data set, aiming DreamNet at mental health screening and sleep science.
arxiv-2503-05878:
Talebi and Li add long-run risk limits to a classic control problem, in a 2025 paper. Controllers are usually judged on average performance, but rare large disturbances can matter as much. Their new criterion captures cumulative risk over time using limit theorems from probability, and it stays well behaved even for heavy-tailed noise, as long as the noise has a finite fourth moment.

They fold this risk measure into the linear quadratic regulator as a constraint, then solve the problem with a primal-dual method that optimizes average performance while respecting the risk cap. Simulations show the resulting controller also tames the long-run variance, shrugging off sporadic large shocks.
arxiv-2503-05978:
Talking-head videos made from a photo, a script, and a voice usually stall at short clips and stiff faces. Hongwei Yi and co-authors present MagicInfinite, a diffusion transformer built to run without a length limit. It animates realistic people, full-body figures, and anime characters, even from back-facing poses, and can drive several characters at once, with masks naming who speaks.

Three ideas carry the design. Full three-dimensional attention with a sliding-window denoising scheme gives endless, coherent footage. A two-stage curriculum ties lip motion to audio, expression to text, and identity to a reference image. Region masks with adaptive losses balance global text control against local voice cues. Distillation speeds generation twentyfold, producing ten seconds of video in ten seconds at the smaller size. On the team's new benchmark, the system led in lip sync, identity keeping, and natural motion.
arxiv-2503-06178:
Usman Sanusi, Sona John, Johannes Mueller, and Aurélien Tellier study how parasite rest states affect the time until an epidemic dies out, in a research paper from 2025. Some parasites go inactive for a time, losing infectiousness, then wake again. Hosts with a resting parasite cannot recover, yet they also cannot spread it.

Their model splits hosts into susceptible, infected, resting, and again susceptible states. Resting does not change the basic reproduction number. For wide settings, the model acts like a simpler epidemic model on a slower clock. That clock is set by the share of time spent active. Resting thus works as a hedge against random die-out.
arxiv-2503-06278:
Bojan Lukić gives a hands-on tour of building neural networks that forecast values over time. His 2025 paper first traces the history and core ideas of machine learning, then moves into network designs for time series data. The worked example predicts temperature from weather records with several variables at once.

The main model is a deep recurrent network with LSTM cells, a design built to remember long patterns. Work was done in Python with TensorFlow and Keras tools. Results show the network can forecast weather well over short spans. Lukić closes by naming the limits of such forecasts and where they break down. Newcomers get both theory and a full applied case.
arxiv-2503-06378:
Zhou and colleagues proposed a new way in twenty twenty-five to evaluate artificial intelligence systems, built on general scales rather than fixed test scores. Benchmarks drive progress, but a score on one test says little about what a system can do on a fresh task.

Their method rates every test item by the demands it places on eighteen general ability scales, from knowledge to reasoning. Fifteen large language models were profiled across sixty-three tasks. The profiles explained what each benchmark truly measures and exposed how skills shift with model size and thinking style. Better still, demand ratings predicted a model's success on brand-new items, beating standard black-box predictors, above all on unfamiliar tasks. The authors call it a step toward evaluation that explains and forecasts, not just ranks.
arxiv-2503-06778:
Feng Gu and co-authors test large language models as annotators in a 2025 paper. Labeling events in news data matters for tracking markets and trends, but expert coding is slow and costly. Their test covers a full workflow: dropping irrelevant documents, merging reports of the same event, and labeling what remains.

Fully automated model labels beat older text methods but still fell short of human experts. The picture changed when models assisted the experts instead. Help with grouping events cut time and mental effort, and experts agreed more with model-extracted details than with fully automated labels. The authors favor models as assistants, not replacements, for careful annotation work.
arxiv-2503-06878:
Xiaoyou Chen and Lewis prove two results in the character theory of finite groups. Codegrees are numbers tied to a group's irreducible representations. M-groups are groups whose characters all arise by induction from linear ones, a tidy class. The first theorem is crisp: if a group has exactly three codegrees, it must be an M-group.

The second result moves to modular characters, the Brauer characters at a prime p. If every such character has prime degree, then any normal subgroup splits the difference. Either the subgroup or the quotient over it is an Mp-group. The proofs add clean entries to the dictionary between arithmetic data and group structure.
arxiv-2503-07278:
Teams of robots can explore caves, disaster zones, and other unknown places faster than one robot alone, but coordinating them is a research field of its own. Chuqi Wang and co-authors survey the state of the art in a 2025 review. They organize the field into modules: mapping and localization, cooperative motion, and communication under tight limits.

Within motion, they separate learning-based methods from staged planning that generates targets, assigns them, and plans paths. Communication gets its own treatment, since real sites restrict range and bandwidth. The review also covers systems built for the DARPA Subterranean Challenge, a major underground robotics contest. It closes with open challenges and likely directions, aiming to serve as a reference for builders and researchers.
arxiv-2503-07378:
Yusuke Hashimoto and co-authors build maps that join lab data and computed data on materials, in a 2025 paper. Data science promises faster discovery of new materials, but lab and computed sets are hard to merge. The team first trained a model on lab data and applied it to a computed database.

They then use a graph-based deep learning frame to draw maps linking material traits to structure. A statistical check shows the frame pulls out features that reflect how complex a structure is. Oddly, that strength did not always mean better trait forecasts. The authors link this to the model's strong learning, which can shape how points sit on the map. The maps aim to help lab researchers choose what to try next.
arxiv-2503-07578:
Tianyu Chen and five co-authors present a 2025 method for training image makers from dirty data. Image models learn from clean photos, yet in science clean data can be scarce or pricey. Noise in training photos can teach a model the wrong patterns. The team asks whether a flawed teacher can still yield a clean maker.

First they train a spread model on noisy photos alone. Then they distill it into a maker that gives a clean image in one step. Tests across noise levels and data sets showed steady gains. Theory for a simple case shows the method finds the clean data's main axes. That view casts distillation as a quality tool, not just a speed tool.
arxiv-2503-07878:
Rahul Nair and co-authors build in 2025 a yardstick for when image captioning models do not just copy bias but make it worse. A captioning model trained on skewed photos may describe a woman with a knife as if the knife defined her, sharpening stereotypes at output time. Older bias measures were built for sorting tasks and cannot read caption wording.

One newer measure reads language but cannot say which side of a pairing the bias leans toward. Their new metric, directional bias amplification in captioning, fixes that: it tells whether captions bind a trait to one group over another. It also holds steadier when the sentence encoder behind it changes, and it estimates the effect more faithfully. Tested on gender and race in a standard photo caption set, theirs was the only measure the authors found reliable. Caption audits can now name the direction of a model's lean.
arxiv-2503-07978:
Jiahao Xu and co-authors propose a defense for federated learning, where many devices train one shared model without sharing raw data. That open design invites backdoor attacks, in which poisoned updates bend the shared model on chosen tasks. Their 2025 method, AlignIns, screens each update by direction before it joins the model.

AlignIns checks how well each update lines up with the overall update direction. It also compares the signs of key parameters in an update against the main sign pattern across all updates. Updates that line up in an odd way are treated as hostile and dropped. Tests on both uniform and uneven data splits show stronger protection than rival defenses, and the authors supply proofs of robustness plus the code.
arxiv-2503-08578:
Hui Huang, Hicham Kouhkouh, and Lukang Sun prove that a rescaled swarm-style search method reliably finds the best answer, in a 2025 paper. Consensus-based optimization lets many candidate points drift toward a weighted average, mimicking how groups settle on a choice.

The twist here is shrinking that average point by a small fixed factor.
