Under mild conditions on the goal function and starting points, the authors prove the method settles on the global minimum without fail. The proof covers the joint limit of long time and sharp weighting. It also extends to problems with many best answers, or whole sets of them. The work gives the popular heuristic a firm theoretical base.
arxiv-2503-08678:
Yuanhao Wang and co-authors present a tool for making three-dimensional clothes from one photo in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Non-expert users can design garments in flat images, but turning a single view into a full garment that can be edited is hard. Views made by older methods often fail to match each other.

Their system, called GarmentCrafter, builds new views step by step. It first predicts depth and warps the image to guess new angles. A diffusion model then fills in hidden areas, guided by the changing camera view. By inferring color and depth together, the method keeps views consistent. Tests showed better detail and coherence than leading rival methods.
arxiv-2503-09278:
Zhou and co-authors review a fresh way to understand metallic glasses, built on networks rather than on single atoms. Metallic glass-forming liquids freeze into solids without forming crystals, and why their particles slow down so unevenly has long resisted simple explanation. The review pulls together work on aging, slow relaxation, glass-forming ability, and how these materials answer stress.

Its central claim links how a particle relaxes to the shape of the whole network its neighbors form around it. Particles sit in shifting local structures, and the global pattern of those structures tracks the wide spread of relaxation behavior. Thinking in terms of topology, the authors argue, can expose effects that older local measures miss. They present this graph-and-dynamics view as a route to new questions about glassy matter, not just a new label for old results.
arxiv-2503-09678:
Mitman and co-authors improve how the ringing tones of a merged black hole are pulled from simulations. After two black holes merge, the remnant rings with quasi-normal modes. Those tones can test Einstein's theory, if they are measured cleanly. Knowing when the tones truly describe the wave is part of the challenge. Their algorithm fits the wave over the whole sphere at once. It also searches backward in time with a sturdier fitting routine.

The fit yields a fuller model of the strain signal. Amplitudes of each tone come out with the timing. Cleaner extraction sharpens any test of gravity built on ringdown. The method extends earlier tools in three stated ways.
arxiv-2503-10378:
The calcium lines in a star's spectrum are workhorse tools for measuring its makeup and motion, but the standard shortcuts for reading them are crude. Cis Lagae, Anish M Amarsi, and Karin Lind compute these lines in full three-dimensional model atmospheres of metal-poor stars. They drop the usual assumption of local thermodynamic equilibrium and compare every simpler combination of assumptions.

Correcting from the standard one-dimensional equilibrium recipe shifts calcium abundances by up to a full order of magnitude for strong lines in giant stars. Radial velocities shift by up to 1.5 kilometers per second. Which assumption you make changes the line shapes themselves. The team releases grids of synthetic spectra so observers can analyze real stars more accurately. The paper appears in 2025.
arxiv-2503-10478:
Liyan Luo, Songyan Tian, and Lei Wu fuse two simulation worlds that rarely meet: turbulent gas flow and rarefied gas flow. Thin, fast gases near spacecraft behave by particle rules, while turbulence follows fluid equations. Real problems, like a jet punching into thin upper air, mix both at once.

Their method couples a particle simulation with synthetic fluid equations and a standard turbulence model. Particle data feed the fluid solve; the fluid answer then resets the particles. Tests show the blend slides smoothly into whichever single method fits the local regime. Applied to an opposing jet in hypersonic thin gas, it exposed strong swings in surface behavior from the interplay.
arxiv-2503-10978:
Ayoub Laayoun and Badr Missaoui prove an existence result in a 2025 probability paper. Their system is a stochastic equation with reflection, which keeps the solution inside a boundary, steered by a control the user picks. The question is whether a best control exists at all, in both strict and relaxed senses.

Using weak convergence methods in a strong topology, plus a representation theorem, the authors show that optimal controls of both kinds do exist. The paper is brief and technical, aimed at specialists in stochastic control. Its value is foundational: before anyone can compute a best control for such reflected systems, existence must be secured, and that is what the proof delivers.
arxiv-2503-11278:
Ana Silva and Efi Efrati study geometric phases in chaotic systems in a 2025 physics paper. A geometric phase is a shift a system gains from its own past path, and it shows up in settings from quantum effects to swimming at tiny scales. Since the phase records the history of the motion, it can serve as a fine probe of chaos.

The authors build a small toy model with a flat inner state space and a single phase, then track how that phase spreads over time. Plain loop counts for random walks predict the phase would speed up without bound. By bounding the space, or adding a pull toward the center, they recover the slower spread seen in real systems. The work ties phase spread to the shape of the space a system moves in.
arxiv-2503-11478:
Zubair Iftikhar and co-authors run an experiment testing a classic formula of physics in an extreme setting. The Kubo formula links the noise a conductor makes to how it responds to signals. It is usually checked near equilibrium, where systems sit at rest. The team drove a tiny tunnel junction far from rest with a steady voltage.

Their device joins two superconductors through a thin insulating layer. Following an old proposal, they measured the power the junction trades with a quiet detection circuit. From that power flow they extracted the noise the junction emits and the noise it absorbs. The gap between the two matched the junction's measured response, confirming the formula within experimental accuracy. The authors show the math still works when the detector pushes back strongly on the device. The result supports using noise as a probe of quantum electronics far from equilibrium.
arxiv-2503-11578:
Engl and colleagues wrote in twenty twenty-five about unwanted effects in fresh ferroelectric hafnia devices and how to remove them. Ferroelectric hafnia stores charge states for memory devices. Fresh devices show imprint and split switching peaks, flaws that fade with cycling. The team inserted niobium oxide layers at varied positions in device stacks. Spectroscopy and electron microscopy probed how the added layer changes the hafnia. Charged vacancies from the niobium oxide likely create an internal bias field.

That field skews the starting polarization state of domains. Opposing bias fields in up and down domains likely cause the split peaks. One stack design placed the layer between ferroelectric and insulator. It produced a device free of both splitting and imprint from the start. Charge trapping near the new interfaces explains the fix, they argue. The result could simplify making reliable ferroelectric memory.
arxiv-2503-11778:
James Sunseri, Adrian Bayer, and Jia Liu study the information content of the cosmic web in a 2025 cosmology paper. The web splits into nodes, filaments, walls, and voids. Using large simulations and a modified structure finder, they ask whether treating each type separately sharpens estimates of cosmological parameters.

Splitting the density field by structure type and combining spectra gave much tighter constraints than a single spectrum. Gains were largest for neutrino mass, improving by large factors at some smoothing scales for the matter field. Gains were smaller for a field including baryons. A public software package accompanies the work.
arxiv-2503-12578:
Ismar Volić and Leah Valentiner view voting games through the lens of topology, and find the two subjects were secretly studying each other. A simple game, the abstract skeleton of any voting system, is defined by which coalitions win. Flip the picture: the losing coalitions form a simplicial complex, a geometric object topologists know how to interrogate.

Classic constructions, cones, joins, Alexander duality, translate into familiar game operations. Better, homology, the algebra of holes, yields new results about weighted voting games. The paper is an invitation, introductory and self-contained, arguing that an entire dictionary between fields waits to be written, with theorems smuggled across the border in both directions.
arxiv-2503-12778:
Sorting breast cancer into subtypes from tissue images is hard: classes look alike, some are rare, and images vary by lab. Gul Sheeraz and co-authors build MultiRisk, a framework that first predicts where the classifier may go wrong. A risk model uses features from several neural networks to rank each case by its chance of misclassification.

That ranking steers a second stage, where the prediction model is fine-tuned with extra weight on risky cases and tuned to each dataset. On three collections, the risk analysis scored AUROCs of seventy-eight point one, seventy-five point six, and seventy-six point three percent. After adaptive training, subtype F1-scores rose to sixty-one point one five, sixty-five point nine eight, and eighty point five three percent. The authors say it holds across resolutions and domain shifts, and could make diagnosis steadier when labeled data are scarce.
arxiv-2503-13078:
Tobias Østmo Hermansen, Manuela Zucknick, and Zhi Zhao propose a Bayesian survival model that uses biological network knowledge to select cancer biomarkers. A central goal in cancer research is predicting a patient's survival from a small panel of genes or proteins. Purely data-driven models can produce results that are hard to interpret biologically.

Their penalized Bayesian Cox model uses graph-structured selection priors: a Markov random field prior built on a biologically meaningful graph of relationships between multi-omics features. Because the graph shapes prior probabilities rather than imposing hard constraints, the model can confirm known information and still flag novel biomarkers. Simulations show more trustworthy and stable variable selection than methods that treat covariates independently, with no loss in survival prediction. Performance also held up when the graph was only partially correct. That robustness matters, since real biological networks are never fully known.
arxiv-2503-13178:
Jin, Duan, and Hang built a lean game agent in twenty twenty-five for Gomoku, a five-in-a-row board game, that beats big net agents on small gear. Big net agents need vast compute to play at top strength. Their agent uses a small net with a book of board pat-terns drawn from big nets.

A step-by-step update trick cuts work when just a few stones change per move. That trick also speeds deep search by a large share. With tuned scores and search it beat the top open AlphaZero-like Gomoku agent sans fast chips. It ranked first in a large bot pool and won a known cup.
arxiv-2503-13278:
Jérôme Lodewyck and Tetsuya Ido examine a candidate way to redefine the second using several optical atomic transitions at once, in a 2025 paper. The current definition rests on a cesium transition and is expected to give way to an optical one within a decade. One option builds the unit from a weighted geometric mean of several transitions rather than a single line.

The authors review what that choice implies and add two tools. One is a quantitative recipe for setting the weights. The other is a picture of the unit that separates its definition from how labs realize it. The goal is a definition that stays robust as clocks improve.
arxiv-2503-13678:
Roberto Biondo, Davide Castelnovo, and Fabio Gadducci published this study in 2025. It gives e-graphs a formal home in category theory. E-graphs are a data structure for program optimization: instead of rewriting code, they add equal versions and mark them the same. That equality saturation hunt finds cheaper programs efficiently. The authors describe e-graphs using adhesive categories, a setting where graph rewriting rules behave well.

The formal dress is not mere tidiness. It makes the structure's properties exact and provable. Adding an equal program piece becomes a standard graph transformation step. That opens the door to results about parallel updates and clashing edits, borrowed from the adhesive theory shelf. The paper serves formal-methods readers who want e-graph reasoning on solid ground.
arxiv-2503-14278:
Dan Goreac and co-authors sort controllability for mean field stochastic systems in a 2025 paper. Mean field dynamics steer crowds of agents by shared rules. The noise term here need not have full rank, a twist past work.

Classical exact control, they show, forces rank rules on the noise. When those fail, rank rules on the drift can take over. That swap asks less smooth controls to reach the goal. When both fail, a new target form is set: normal laws at the end. A set valued backward equation class grows from that form. The sort widens which crowd systems can be steered at all.
arxiv-2503-14578:
Richard Pincak and co-authors present a 2025 paper that sets out a new geometric flow and reads physics off it. The flow extends the Ricci flow, which smooths the shape of a space over time, to seven dimensional spaces with a special structure and twist. The team studies how lone wave solutions evolve under the flow.

Their model proposes that the masses of the W and Z bosons come from the twist of the space itself, not from an outside scalar field as in the Higgs story. That twist drives a form of spontaneous symmetry breaking in gauge theories. The paper also probes a link between extra dimension geometry and the curvature of our spacetime, with a bearing on the positive cosmological constant seen in data.
arxiv-2503-15078:
Simulating soft, stretchy materials in real time, with contact and friction, is one of the hard problems of computer graphics. Zeng and co-authors present a simulator that handles hyperelastic objects at interactive speeds without giving up accuracy.

Their framework runs on the GPU and folds the rules of non-penetration and friction into a local-global solver as complementarity conditions, which brings rapid convergence. A sparse way of handling the system inverse keeps the math parallel-friendly, and a splitting trick for the non-smooth parts sharpens the friction model. Tests ranged from large scenes and extreme stretching to precise friction, across soft and stiff materials alike. The authors stress that the method stays simple, resting on standard matrix operations.
arxiv-2503-15178:
Alireza Akbari and Peter Thalmeier show how a surface probe can photograph a spiral of trapped magnetic moments in this 2025 paper. A scanning tunneling microscope reads the wandering electrons at a surface, not the fixed ones. Yet experiments on a gadolinium compound showed the fixed moments' spiral order in the spectrum anyway, and the authors explain why.

The wandering electrons exchange energy with the fixed moments, which rebuilds their bands. That rebuilding stamps satellite peaks into the tunneling spectrum at the spiral's wave vector, even on a clean surface. The authors then work out how dirt on the surface scatters the rebuilt electrons, giving an interference pattern that carries more detail about the order. Bound states near impurities also shift under the coupling. The theory turns a surface tool into a camera for hidden magnetic textures.
arxiv-2503-15278:
Christopher Albert and four co-authors give plasma simulators a way to track charged particles for very long times without the numbers drifting, in this 2025 paper. In a fusion device, a particle spirals tightly around magnetic field lines while its guiding center drifts slowly through the doughnut-shaped field. Following the fast spiral directly wastes computer time, so codes follow the guiding center instead.

The trouble is keeping the simulation faithful over millions of steps. The authors transform the equations into canonical coordinates, using part of the magnetic potential itself as a coordinate, which works for fields of any topology and skips the usual flux-coordinate machinery. In those coordinates, symplectic integrators, schemes that preserve the physics' geometric structure, keep energy-like quantities honest. Tested on a tokamak field with islands and chaotic zones, the classic midpoint scheme beat ordinary methods on accuracy per cost.
arxiv-2503-15378:
Jacobs and Paolone work out how a local power grid can sell its spare flexibility. Rooftop solar, batteries, and flexible loads scattered through a distribution network could offer support services to the wider grid. That works only if their combined capability at the connection point is known and reliable. Their method uses an optimal power flow calculation on a linear network model.

The approach prices each device's effort and picks the cheapest mix. It then wraps the answer in uncertainty sets that promise a chosen coverage level, matching new Nordic market practice. A feeder-splitting trick keeps the math manageable on large networks. Case studies show the method works and that ignoring network limits would overstate what the grid can offer.
arxiv-2503-15478:
Yifei Zhou and six co-authors presented SWEET-RL in twenty twenty-five, a method for training AI agents that work with a human partner over many turns. Such agents must judge which of their many steps helped or hurt, a hard credit problem. To study it, the team built ColBench, a test suite where an agent and a person solve real coding and design tasks together.

SWEET-RL trains a critic that sees extra facts available only during training. The critic scores each step, giving the agent fine-grained feedback. On ColBench it beat rival methods by six points in success and win rates. It let a modest open model match or beat a top commercial model on joint content creation. The work points to better training for partner-style AI tools.
arxiv-2503-16078:
Two swirl patterns in magnets were long seen as unlike states, and Haobing Zhang, Xintao Fan, and Weiwei Wang show they can merge into one, in work from twenty twenty-five. A vortex swirls in a ring with a core that points up or down. A skyrmion is a tight knot that needs a twist force to hold.

Computer runs found a merged state: skyrmions nested inside a vortex. The charge of the merged state is the sum of the parts, scaled by how many skyrmions sit inside. Like plain vortices, the merged states can flip ring sense and core sense on their own, and states with the same charge share the same energy. The find widens the menu of magnet states for future memory parts.
arxiv-2503-16378:
Self-driving research trains on sunny city streets, leaving muddy farm tracks in the rain nearly unmapped. Tzu-Yun Tseng and co-authors release Panoptic-CUDAL, a dataset recorded in rural Australia during rainy weather to fill that gap. High-resolution laser scans, camera images, and vehicle poses were captured together, targeting the task of labelling every point in a three-dimensional scan by object and instance.

Rain spatters sensors with noise and phantom reflections, exactly the stress test the dataset supplies. The team analyses the recordings and reports baseline scores for panoptic and semantic segmentation plus three-dimensional occupancy prediction. They offer the data so perception systems can learn the countryside's wet, unstructured reality before meeting it on the road.
arxiv-2503-16578:
Yang Chen and nine co-authors present SeniorTalk, a Chinese speech data set for very old adults in two thousand twenty-five. Voice tools serve more old users, but they lag for this group. Old voices have traits like weak tone and local speech forms that training sets miss. Data on those past age seventy-five is scarce.

SeniorTalk holds many hours of talk from over a hundred chats. Speakers are balanced by sex, region, and age. Rich tags span many traits of each clip. Tests cover speaker checks, speaker splits, speech to text, and speech edits. Results give a base for tools built for the oldest users.
arxiv-2503-16678:
Afrah Farea, Saiful Khan, and Mustafa Serdar Celebi shrink the cost of solving physics equations with neural networks by adding a quantum part. Physics-informed networks learn to solve partial differential equations by baking the laws into training. They work, but they need many parameters for hard problems. The team's hybrid design hands part of the job to a quantum circuit.

They tested two circuit layouts across five benchmark equations, hunting for the best arrangement. The hybrid matched the classical networks on accuracy and settled just as steadily. It did so with only ten to thirty percent of the trainable parameters. On three of the five equations, the final error fell noticeably, by margins from a few percent to nearly two-thirds. The authors pitch the design as a leaner route into physics-based machine learning.
arxiv-2503-17078:
Saika Wong and three co-authors review body-signal methods for teamwork between construction workers and robots, in a 2025 paper. Signals like brain waves and heart patterns could let robots sense worker states. Better mutual awareness may improve safety and coordination on site. The review uses a concept-method-value lens. It surveys what has been tried in construction settings.

Brain activity recording was the most common method found. Most studies remain proofs of concept with thin evidence. Three future directions are proposed. First, combine several signal types at once. Second, run experiments in richer, more realistic settings. Third, adopt skin-friendly or contactless sensors for harsh sites. The authors aim to guide later practical work. Robots that read worker strain could time their help better, they suggest.
arxiv-2503-17178:
Carlos Vargas studies the rare points where two eigenvalues of a matrix family collide, events called exceptional points. His families blend a fixed random matrix from the Ginibre ensemble with a rotating diagonal matrix whose entries travel along circles or other curves. By tracking the eigenvalues as the parameters loop, he can spot when they swap places, which betrays a collision inside the loop. Software to compute and visualize them accompanies the paper.

The counts show a regularity: for circular paths the number of collisions came out as the matrix dimension times itself minus one, under fairly general conditions. Elliptical and other curves produced even more. The pattern links random matrix theory to the topology of eigenvalue motion. Exceptional points matter in physics, where they mark sharp changes in a system's behavior. Vargas offers both a counting phenomenon to explain and tools to explore it.
arxiv-2503-17478:
Newman and a large team weigh a dormant black hole in a distant galaxy in twenty twenty-five. Black holes and their host galaxies grow together over cosmic time. Their masses follow linked patterns in nearby galaxies. To see if those patterns held long ago, astronomers need precise masses for distant black holes.

The target galaxy lies at redshift near two and is magnified by a foreground gravitational lens. The team used the James Webb Space Telescope to map how stars move near its centre. Fitting dynamical models gave a black hole mass of about six billion solar masses. That mass is high for the galaxy's bulge mass, by local patterns. It does match the local pattern that uses stellar velocity spread.
arxiv-2503-17578:
Sharon Lin and co-authors present a 2025 computing paper showing that a backdoored language model can recite long secret strings word for word. Backdoor research mostly studied image classifiers flipping labels. For language models, the dangerous trick is different: a trigger that makes the model print an exact planted sequence, such as a hard-coded encryption key.

The team poisoned fine-tuning data with trigger-response pairs buried in benign text. Triggered, the model reproduced random keys up to a hundred characters exactly, even under light low-rank tuning. The attack worked on models the size of a phone-class system. A round of clean fine-tuning afterward disabled the planted behavior in their tests. The paper flags supply-chain risk in borrowed fine-tunes.
arxiv-2503-17778:
Matteo Milazzo and co-authors open the full stock registers of Finland to study how concentrated household portfolios really are. The data cover single Finnish legal entities trading on the Helsinki venue from 2001 to 2021. Concentration is read with the Herfindahl-Hirschman index, a standard sum-of-squares gauge.

Foreign investors held the most concentrated combined portfolio, ahead of Finnish institutions and households. Looked at one by one, more than half of retail investors held highly concentrated portfolios. Many household accounts hold just a stock or two, despite two decades of cheap diversification. The long panel lets the authors watch concentration evolve, not just snapshot it. Finance researchers get rare whole-market proof of how undiversified the typical saver stays.
arxiv-2503-17878:
Raj Kumar Das and Arpan Krishna Mitra offer a new driver of cosmic expansion in a 2025 paper. Their fluid is non-commutative, a twist expressed through a deformed bracket in the dynamics. That twist adds a fresh parameter to the Hubble law drawn from Newtonian cosmology.

The added term acts like slow matter creation, since the fluid is no longer conserved. With it, the model matches the observed speeding-up of the universe on its own. No dark energy or cosmological constant is invoked at all. Fresh survey data from DESI and other sources then bound the new parameter. A single number doing the work of dark energy is a bold, testable claim.
arxiv-2503-18478:
Watching an hour-long video is still hard for AI models, since thousands of frames swamp their memory. Xiangrui Liu and co-authors present Video-XL-Pro in this 2025 paper, a system built to compress video tokens in a way that keeps their meaning. Its core module learns, without labels, to rebuild masked video content from compact tokens.

Two parts drive the learning: a synthesizer that fakes video tokens from still image tokens, and a masking scheme that hides the most redundant pieces. A query-aware selector then finds the tokens a question needs, and a pruning strategy trims training cost. With three billion parameters, the system beat most larger rivals and handled over eight thousand frames on one graphics card.
arxiv-2503-18578:
Tianyu Chen and co-authors present Galaxy Walker in a 2025 paper, a geometry aware vision language model for astronomy at galaxy scale. Standard models embed images in flat Euclidean space. Astronomy needs spherical geometry for orbits and hyperbolic geometry for black holes, and backbones that handle such curved spaces.

Their geometry prompt creates geometry tokens from random walks across a multi scale physical graph spanning diverse spaces. A geometry adapter then compresses and reshapes the spatial anisotropy with a mixture of experts. The model set top scores on galaxy property estimation and morphology classification, beating both specialist and general models.
arxiv-2503-18978:
Tobias Timofeyev and Alice Patania link group synchronization in networks to graph spectra in a 2025 paper. Oscillators on a network often lock into clusters rather than one chorus. Fair partitions of the network, where each node sees the same mix of groups, were known to underlie such clustering. The authors build a general spectral framework around that link.

Eigenvectors tied to those partitions span a subspace of the graph's Laplacian spectrum that rules cluster behavior. Clustered states reduce to motion on a smaller quotient graph. The framework explains passing hierarchies and multi-frequency locking, tying them to symmetry and community shape. Real networks are imperfect, so the authors relax the partition idea with a tolerance level. The relaxed version keeps the useful traits under noise. They aim the results at systems from neural circuits to power grids.
arxiv-2503-19078:
Backhaus and co-authors present a new infrared survey of deep space with the James Webb telescope, in a 2025 paper. The MEGA survey images the Extended Groth Strip, a well-studied sky field, in four mid-infrared bands across twenty-five pointings. It overlaps most of an existing near-infrared survey of the same field. Mid-infrared light reveals the obscured universe: dust-hidden star formation and feeding black holes that shorter wavelengths miss.

The paper covers the survey's design, its data reduction beyond the standard pipeline, and the first public catalog. Warm pixel masking and custom background subtraction were added to clean the images. A shared, deep infrared map of a benchmark field becomes infrastructure for hundreds of later studies of how galaxies assembled their mass.
arxiv-2503-19478:
Saverio Cavasin and co-authors build a forensic tool that creates extra mugshot style images to aid identification in 2025, using team framing since the head byline order differs from the catalog list. Police often hold few or old photos of a person of interest. Poor images hurt photo based identification. Their framework makes more high grade images from what exists.

The method uses tunable augmentation while keeping face traits true to the source. Trials show gains in accuracy and robustness across forensic settings. The tool aims to be trustworthy for law work. It guards the biometric sameness of the person shown. Index terms in the head tie it to re identification and vision language models.
arxiv-2503-19578:
João Olívia and Rui Dilão build a minimal electric model of the whole human heart, in a paper from 2025. The model tracks how the heart signal spreads and can print a basic three lead heart trace.

Its traces matched real traces from a Norwegian athlete set with strong closeness. The team then broke the signal paths in set ways to mimic illness. Fast chamber rhythms, loop rhythms at the node, extra paths, and starved tissue all gave traces that fit clinic forms. The authors offer the lean model as a fast digital twin of the heart.
arxiv-2503-19678: Yuetong Fang, in a short mathematics paper from twenty twenty-five, proves a result about a special class of functions on compact Hermitian manifolds. These spaces are a broad form of the curved spaces used in complex geometry. Fang shows that all functions of this kind can be raised to a power and still have a finite total size on the space. The bound on the power depends on the size of the space and on a second number tied to the function class.
arxiv-2503-19878:
Nengbo Wang and four co-authors add causal maps to the way language models look up facts, in a 2025 paper. Standard retrieval chops texts into chunks and grabs the chunks that read most alike, which can shred context and fetch near-miss passages. Their system, CausalRAG, instead builds a graph of cause and effect from the source texts.

At query time, the system traces paths through that graph to gather evidence that hangs together as a story, not just as similar words. Tests against plain retrieval and graph-based rivals show gains on several accuracy scores. Answers also become easier to audit, since each claim can be traced along a causal chain. The authors pitch causal grounding as a fix for a core weakness of lookup-based AI.
arxiv-2503-20178:
Axel Ureña-López and co-authors update limits on axion dark energy in this 2025 paper. Dark energy drives the late expansion of the universe, and an ultralight axion field could play that role. New survey data from DESI sharpen the test.

The team fit the model using its full cosmic history and its true potential shape. The data pin the axion mass to a narrow ultralight range. Its energy scale lands close to the reduced Planck scale. Results lean toward dark energy that changes over time. A simpler changing model still wins on formal evidence scores. The authors note that more DESI data could settle the contest.
arxiv-2503-20378:
Adaptive controllers tune themselves while running, which raises a fair question: how close to optimal are they when the world keeps pushing back? Alexander Fradkov takes up that question alone in 2025 for nonlinear systems under bounded disturbances.

Fradkov works with controllers built by the speed-gradient approach and defines what estimated optimality should mean for them under a stated class of uncertainty. He gives sufficient conditions for a controller to count as near-optimal in that sense, for versions hardened by negative parametric feedback. A worked case on passification-based control of a standard linear system shows the machinery in action. The paper gives designers a way to claim, with proof, that an adaptive scheme is nearly as good as possible.
arxiv-2503-20578:
Alif Al Hasan, Subarna Saha, Mia Mohammad Imran, and Tarannum Shaila Zaman test whether large language models can extract failure-inducing inputs from bug reports, in a two thousand twenty-five software engineering paper. Developers need those inputs to reproduce and fix bugs, but reports are written in prose.

Their technique, LLPut, benchmarks three open-source generative models: LLaMA, Qwen, and Qwen-Coder. The evaluation runs over a dataset of two hundred six bug reports and measures the accuracy and effectiveness of the extracted inputs. Findings map where current generative models help automated bug diagnosis and where they still fall short, guiding both tool builders and practitioners.
arxiv-2503-20678:
Gabriel Palma, Mariusz Skoczen, and Phil Maguire test a recipe for predicting hourly price moves in a 2025 finance study. Their pipeline first splits price series into simpler waves with empirical mode decomposition. Features from a linear model and classic indicators are then computed inside a rolling window of recent hours, and a Gaussian mixture model sorts market conditions into clusters.

Trading tests cover a meme stock, an electric car maker, and a cryptocurrency, over samples of different lengths. The mix of decomposition, clustering, and machine learning aims to sharpen the decision to buy or sell. Cluster filtering is meant to skip hours when signals disagree.
arxiv-2503-20878:
Alexander Beckett and a large team of co-authors described in 2025 the design of a space telescope survey hunting galaxies that leak ionizing light. The catalog title carries stray facility and software notes, while the hosted text gives the clean title. Their survey images thirty-seven separate fields in three or four color bands. Galaxies seen as they were when the universe was young may have reionized it, and leaks are the clue.

Colors pick candidate galaxies at the target distances, with about ninety percent purity in tests on fake samples. The team expects roughly 1,400 candidates, including dozens of likely leakers whose light can be stacked for an average leak rate. Using many fields apart reduces bias from gas between galaxies. A first spectrum from a ground telescope confirms the method can pin distances.
arxiv-2503-20978:
Yiqiao Jin, Stefano Petrangeli, Yu Shen, and Gang Wu built a compact way to record what a user does on screen, in a 2025 paper. Software agents that act inside apps need to learn from user behavior, but training data are sparse and user intent is subtle. A lean record of actions over time could make that learning scale.

Their record form, called a stateful screen schema, tracks key actions and aims as they unfold. On top of it they trained ScreenLLM, a family of multimodal models tuned for screen understanding and next-action guessing. Tests on open and private models showed the models track behavior well and predict actions with care. The authors present the schema and models as groundwork for stronger app agents.
arxiv-2503-21078:
Nedialko S Nedialkov and John D Pryce present a simpler way to build Taylor series solvers for differential equations, in this 2025 paper. Such solvers expand the solution as a power series at each step, which allows very accurate, large steps. The catch is that every function inside the equation normally needs its own hand derived recurrence, which makes the software heavy to build.

Their trick, the sub-ODE method, replaces each special function with the small differential equation that the function itself obeys. That turns a few lines of code per function into a place in a shared library. The change formally turns the system into a mixed form, so the authors prove the resulting recurrences stay sound no matter how many such swaps are made. Their Matlab solver compares well with standard tools.
arxiv-2503-21478: Tomasz Kobos and Konrad Swanepoel prove that the space of flat symmetric convex shapes, measured by Banach-Mazur distance, holds equilateral sets of any size. An equilateral set is a family where every pair sits at the same distance. Their construction reaches sizes that match, in growth rate, the best possible separated sets known since Bronstein's 1978 bounds, so the result is essentially optimal for this geometric setting.
arxiv-2503-21678:
Zsolt Páles and Tomasz Szostok examined a family of inequalities in a 2025 analysis paper. At the center is a blend of two points, weighted by a signed measure, fed into an unknown smooth function. They ask when the weighted average of the function over all blends stays at or above zero for every pair of points.

The answer turns on stronger forms of monotonicity, where not just the function but its higher rates of change keep one sign. From that they build rules for comparing random outcomes across whole classes of such functions at once. One necessary condition for a mixed ordering is also given. The results extend several classic facts about how risk and order compare.
arxiv-2503-21878:
Audrey Huang and co-authors ask whether picking the best of many model answers is really the best use of extra computing, in a 2025 paper. Best-of-N sampling draws many responses and keeps the top-scored one, but when N grows, scores can be gamed and quality drops, a failure called reward hacking. The team formalizes the task as inference-time alignment against an imperfect reward model.

They show best-of-N can be optimal only under strict coverage of good answers by the base model, and that it provably degrades for large N otherwise. Their new algorithm bakes in pessimism through rejection sampling, stays optimal, and never degrades as N grows. Experiments across tasks and models back the theory.
arxiv-2503-22078:
Santiago Palumbo, Pablo Cornaglia, and Jorge Facio study in 2025 the band structure of a trigonal crystal known as a Weyl semimetal. The material shows a superconducting phase tied to its surface states. Knowing its normal phase is key to grasping that odd behavior.

Their calculations trace the semimetal state to a crystal distortion of a parent structure. The distortion breaks mirror symmetry of the lattice and also cuts its translation symmetry. That break, they find, is the dominant energy scale, larger than spin-orbit coupling. Even without spin effects, the distortion alone creates the Weyl nodes near the Fermi level.
arxiv-2503-22178:
Merging several fine-tuned models into one multitask model saves memory and compute, but the ingredients can clash. Chanhyuk Lee and co-authors study where the clashes live. Each task's update to a model can be split into directional components. The biggest components, they show, often cause the interference that drags other tasks down.

Their method, AdaRank, prunes those components adaptively instead of by a fixed rule. During a test-time tuning step it trims ranks by watching an entropy signal. Across many backbones and task counts, AdaRank topped earlier merging methods. It closed the gap to separately fine-tuned models to about one percent. The authors frame rank choice as the key decision in model merging.
arxiv-2503-22478:
Max Hennick and Stijn De Baerdemacker link the workhorse training method of machine learning to Bayesian statistics, in a 2025 paper. The method, stochastic gradient descent, nudges model weights down a loss slope in noisy steps. Why its wandering works so well has long been a puzzle.

The pair show the wandering acts like diffusion across a fractal landscape, whose rough dimension fits a Bayesian frame. In that light, the method is a tweaked Bayesian sampler, one that respects how the fractal shape blocks or opens paths. Tests on real training runs match the picture, with weights spreading as the frame predicts. The authors offer the view as a grip on what drives learning.
arxiv-2503-22778: Francisc Bozgan, writing alone, studies a fifth-order wave equation known as the modified KP-I equation, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The equation is critical in the energy sense, which makes its long-term behavior delicate. Bozgan proves solutions exist for all time when the starting wave's mass stays below the ground state's. He also finds a region with short-time control, where sharply localized data can still blow up in finite time. On a half-periodic domain, small data give global solutions.
arxiv-2503-22878:
William Peria and colleagues build a capacitance probe that keeps working inside pulsed magnetic fields, where fields spike and vanish in milliseconds. Capacitance reveals how a material polarizes, but ordinary meters drown in cable artifacts when the field sweeps fast. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team uses an auto-balancing bridge with a high-bandwidth amplifier to cancel the parasitic signals from the coaxial leads. They test the rig on a magnetoelectric crystal whose magnetization they measured alongside.

The capacitance showed a clear hysteresis loop matching the magnetization, and the energy-loss peak sharpened at faster sweep rates, exactly the dynamics slower methods smear out. In steady fields the new readings agreed closely with a standard meter. The authors offer the technique for multiferroics and other correlated materials that only reveal themselves under extreme fields.
arxiv-2503-22978:
Muhammad Talal Khalid and Ann-Perry Witmer study how to guide language models in sorting text themes in this 2025 paper. Sorting themes by hand from interviews or open text takes much time and money. Models can help, but many teams use them in ad hoc ways that are hard to check or repeat.

The authors review past work on model help for this task, with a focus on how prompts are written. From that review they set out four key steps for sound prompt design. They also discuss newer prompt methods that can help at each step. Their aim is more open, steady, and trusted use of models in theme sorting.
arxiv-2503-23078:
Zhengyi Zhao and co-authors give in a 2025 study chatbots an event map of the conversation, so replies respect what the talk is actually about. Language models tend to read turns one by one and lose the plot. EventWeave builds a living graph that separates core events, the main goals, from supporting ones, and links them in three distinct ways.

An attention step picks which events matter for the current turn, sparing the cost of rereading everything. On three dialogue data sets, answers came out more natural and better fitted, across short and long talks alike. Ablations credit the event links themselves, not extra data.
arxiv-2503-23178:
Pengyu Chen and co-authors build a vision-guided bear deterrent for the Tibetan Plateau in a 2025 paper. Brown bears raiding homes and herds endanger people and, when they are killed in response, the bears too. Guards cannot watch remote villages around the clock.

A low-power camera system runs a detection model on an edge board, solar-fed and independent of networks. Trained on over a thousand wildlife images, it spotted bears reliably day and night in validation. In staged approach tests it fired bear spray within a fraction of a second, almost always correctly. Automated, non-lethal deterrence could cool a conflict that harms both sides.
arxiv-2503-23378:
Yuqin Yin and co-authors build a theory for bound states of two mesons where at least one partner is itself unstable, in a 2025 paper. Such molecular states are exotic particles that decay quickly, and their fleeting parts make standard tools awkward. The team extends the Bethe-Salpeter framework, a relativistic method for bound states, to handle the unstable case.

They first derive the propagator for an unstable meson made of a quark and antiquark, then feed it into the molecular problem. The scheme yields the mass and width of the combined state, including the effect of the unstable partner. The authors offer it as a workable route for a class of exotic particles that theory had struggled to treat cleanly.
arxiv-2503-23478:
Ivan Anokhin and co-authors tackle delay in real-time reinforcement learning, where a learning agent must act on a fixed clock, in this 2025 arXiv paper. While the network computes, the world keeps moving, so each action rests on stale sight. Deeper networks see more but lag more, since every layer adds its own delay.

The team's fix joins two ideas: connections that skip forward in time, and observations enriched with recent history. Agents built this way stayed strong across neuron speeds, learning methods, and test worlds, from simulated robot bodies to classic arcade-style games. Running neurons in parallel also sped up decisions by six to three hundred fifty percent on ordinary hardware. The authors frame the work as groundwork for real-time agents.
arxiv-2503-23678:
Xiao-Ping Zheng and four colleagues use the Crab pulsar's largest glitch to test whether starquakes cause its long-term spin changes. After a glitch, the pulsar's spin-down rate stays elevated for years, which was taken as evidence of quake-driven changes in the external torque. The team analyzed seventeen hundred ten days of radio data after the 2017 glitch.

The persistent spin-down increase was extreme, letting them test the relation between glitch size and persistent shift predicted by starquake models. Their analysis does not support external torque variation from quakes. They suggest an internal mechanism instead, involving superfluidity inside the star. The absence of flux or profile changes around glitches fits that reading.
arxiv-2503-23878:
Schurmann and twelve co-authors forecast groups of evolved massive binary stars in the Small Magellanic Cloud from a rapid binary evolution code. Massive star paths hold large unknowns, and most such stars are born in close pairs that sway each other. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The code builds mock post contact pairs at a set mass transfer yield, with a merger rule that adjusts to that yield. One yield alone fails to match the seen groups. A high yield fits the Be star counts, while a low yield fits Wolf-Rayet counts better. A mixed picture follows.
arxiv-2503-23978:
Yazhuang Miao and co-authors study in 2025 a bent chain model with spin linked gauge fields that do not commute. The base chain is a known two site toy for edge states in one dim matter. Their form adds a loss and gain twist, so the math no longer mirrors in the plain way.

Rich phases turn up, with braid like energy forms and a skin pull that can be tuned. A zone math frame maps where bulk and edge calls still match. Gauge fields boost the chain's self heal under a move hit, a lot. Lab paths in light, atoms, and cold wires are named.
arxiv-2504-00078:
Sebastian Harris, Yasuaki Hikida, Volker Schomerus, and Takashi Tsuda build a fresh family of interfaces in symmetric product orbifolds. Their paper from twenty twenty-five works in holography, where such two-dimensional theories mirror higher-dimensional gauge setups. Interfaces act like line operators and have drawn wide interest. Their family plays a dual role, akin to Wilson lines and to Karch-Randall walls at once.

The build starts from boundary choices in the seed theory. A folding trick turns those into boundary states for the interfaces. Overlaps of the states yield the spectrum of interface-changing operators through a modular swap. A worked case uses the supersymmetric four-torus as seed. There the interfaces match AdS2 branes in a tensionless string limit. The paper gives holographers a new set of walls to test duality with.
arxiv-2504-00178:
Craig Schmidt, Varshini Reddy, Chris Tanner, and Yuval Pinter present BoundlessBPE in two thousand twenty-five. Byte Pair Encoding is a core way to split text into tokens. A first step, pre-tokenization, cuts text on spaces and marks. That step skews token counts toward common full words.

Skew blunts the gain from larger vocabularies in the model. BoundlessBPE relaxes the boundary rule that causes the skew. It merges whole pretokens into units the team calls superwords. Counts across the corpus turn far more even as a result. Text also packs tighter, with more bytes per token.
arxiv-2504-00278:
Jonathan Conroy and Arnold Filtser settle a long open question about splitting networks into safe clusters in this 2025 paper. A padded decomposition cuts a space into clusters of bounded size so that small balls around points usually survive uncut. The padding parameter measures how safe the balls are, and it drives many algorithms.

For graphs that avoid a fixed minor, a forbidden pattern, the best padding was unknown. The pair proves it grows only logarithmically with the size of the forbidden pattern, and that this is tight. On the way they build sparse covers for such graphs with sharper parameters than known, plus a general bridge from covers to padded decompositions. The old bound falls by an exponential margin.
arxiv-2504-00778: Slawomir Rams and Matthias Schutt study Miyaoka's bound, a cap on how many conics can lie on a K3 surface of degree 2h. Their 2025 paper shows the bound is actually reached when h is large, so the cap cannot be tightened in that range. The same result is shown for smooth rational curves of higher even degree. The work settles the sharpness of a classic bound in the geometry of K3 surfaces.
arxiv-2504-01078:
Arhum Ansari, Arka Banerjee, Sachin Jain, and Sahil Lalsodagar push a cosmology shortcut past its old limit in a 2025 paper. The shortcut builds the clumping of matter in the universe from symmetry rules. It had worked to third order for both matter and the objects that trace it.

Time effects that reach across steps start to bend the tracer rules at fifth order. The team extend the shortcut to fifth order in both of its two frames. The two frames agree, and the time effects are fully caught. A new trick skips a hard hunt for false poles in one frame. The match firms trust in the method.
arxiv-2504-01278:
Si Chen and co-authors build an agent that attacks language models over several conversation turns, in a 2025 paper. Safety testing, called red teaming, usually probes a model with single prompts, but real attackers chat back and forth, adapting as the model answers. Their agent learns on two levels. Globally, it gathers tactic knowledge across attempts and generalises it to new goals. Locally, it refines the wording for one goal when early tries fail.

Unlike earlier methods with a fixed playbook, the agent can discover fresh jailbreak tactics, pick tactics by goal, and polish the chosen wording. On a benchmark, it broke past ninety percent attack success against two models within five turns, beating the best baselines. The authors present it as a warning and a tool: defences must be tested against attackers that learn, not against static prompt lists.
arxiv-2504-01478:
Haoyang Liu, Cuihua Du, Thomas Donlon, and Mingji Deng study the chemistry of two dense star clouds in the Milky Way in a 2025 paper. Both clouds were long thought to be debris from one past merger with a dwarf galaxy, called Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus. The team used element data for 1.26 million giant stars from a large survey catalog.

Each cloud held two distinct chemical groups, not one. One group was poor in metals and rich in alpha elements, and the other was the reverse. The groups match two recently named debris parts, Nereus and the Virgo Radial Merger. The mix suggests more than one merger fed these clouds, and the star motions of the two parts overlap so much that they look alike.
arxiv-2504-01678:
Takumi Fujiyama and Yoshihiro Kanno design trusses under distribution doubt in two thousand twenty-five. Loads on a truss are unsure, and past data on them are scarce. Scarce data can spoil designs tuned to a guessed distribution. Past confidence based methods strain on cost and accuracy for hard constraints.

Their method pairs two goals for the worst case of compliance. One is the mean, the other a tail risk gauge. Kernel density estimates stand in for a fitted distribution. The problem cuts down to a second order cone program for two kernel types. Tests trace the Pareto front of the two goals.
arxiv-2504-01878:
Ian Xul Belaustegui, Alessio Franci, and Naomi Ehrich Leonard extend a spiking opinion model into a tunable controller in a 2025 paper. The model borrows from neurons: views are held as spikes in continuous time, letting a system switch choices fast when conditions change. The design goal is agile group decisions.

The authors find when steady spiking begins, giving conditions for the threshold that triggers it. They show how base sensitivity tunes that threshold and how spike rate above it encodes input strength. The balance between staying firm and reacting fast can thus be set by design. They close by casting the model as a neuromorphic control block for wider networks.
arxiv-2504-02278:
Seeing a three dimensional object through a fog like medium, whether tissue or air, blurs every view. Suguru Shimomura and two co-authors propose in 2025 a digital twin method that rebuilds the hidden object in a virtual copy of the scene. They model the object as a cloud of soft dots and simulate how the medium smears light.

By fitting the twin to the blurred images, they recovered a clear, high contrast copy of the object behind the scatter. The method joins measurement with simulation instead of treating them apart. The authors aim it at fields such as medicine and astronomy, where looking through murk is routine. They present the twin as a way to test what a scene holds before trusting a raw image.
arxiv-2504-02578:
Andrew Allan and Aline Vidotto model gas loss from distant planets in this 2025 paper. Planets baked by their stars shed air into space, and a helium glow in transit can betray that loss. Past work by the pair found the glow strongest when a planet is young, for one test planet.

Yet surveys found weak glows for several young planets, which clashed with that trend. The team now models those very systems in detail. Their glow forecasts match the survey data far better. For one planet, youth still means stronger loss. Across many planets, though, other traits swamp the age trend. Deep transits, they note, give the best shot at a clear signal.
arxiv-2504-02678:
David Mayrhofer and Andrey Chubukov map the electron seas of two-layer graphene as charge and electric field change, in a 2025 physics paper. Bernal bilayer graphene stacks two carbon sheets in a set pattern, and its electrons can line up by spin or by valley, two labels of motion. Earlier math without a warping term found stark states where some electron seas empty out fully.

Adding the warping term, which bends the energy landscape into threefold shapes, softens the picture. At low charge, states emerge with strong but incomplete lining-up, and both majority and minority carriers stay present. That matches what experiments actually see. The team check cases where the two kinds of interaction pull equally and where they do not. The work gives a firmer map for a material prized in tiny electronics research.
arxiv-2504-02778:
Vincent Gbouna Zakka, Luis J. Manso, and Zhuangzhuang Dai present a radar-based activity recognition system in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Cameras raise privacy concerns and fail in darkness, so the authors use millimetre-wave radar, which yields privacy-preserving point clouds. Those clouds are sparse and noisy, and graph methods usually apply one fixed kernel everywhere. The team argues kernels should adapt to each local neighbourhood's geometry.

Their Multi-Head Adaptive Kernel module generates several dynamic kernels inside a graph convolution network, each capturing a different aspect of local structure. Features refine progressively while global spatial context is preserved. On benchmark datasets the method reached state-of-the-art accuracy for recognizing human activities. The target application is domestic service robots that monitor elderly or vulnerable residents safely.
arxiv-2504-02978:
Adrian van Kan, Alexandros Alexakis, and Edgar Knobloch simulate giant swirls in two-dimensional turbulence. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, removes bottom drag from the flow. In flat turbulence, energy can pile into a few huge vortices called condensates. Whether tidy theory predicts that state has been an open question.

Huge simulations of the flow equations map the steady state. Condensates appear once the flow strength passes a sharp threshold. Near that point, energy growth follows a clean power law. The big-scale spectrum matches a classic balance prediction there. At higher strength the spectrum steepens, and most energy loss happens inside the giant swirls themselves.
arxiv-2504-03278:
Guido Barducci and co-authors present a model that predicts how mutations shift protein stability, in this 2025 paper. Small letter swaps can steady or wreck a protein, and the energy shift is the key number. Their model reads sequence alone, drawing on embeddings from a protein language model.

An attention design compares the normal and mutant forms from both directions at once. Built-in rules force the physics to behave: swapping the swap must flip the sign, and chains of swaps must add up. Results matched or beat structure-based rivals on single and multi-letter changes. The authors see the tool aiding protein design and disease work.
arxiv-2504-03478:
Satellite labels lie often enough to mislead the models trained on them, and Spyros Kondylatos and five co-authors make the models admit their doubts in a 2025 paper. Labels in Earth observation come from photo interpreters, old maps, and crowds, each with its own errors, and ordinary models swallow the errors whole.

The team's probabilistic models instead learn how noise depends on the input and report uncertainty beside each prediction. They trained such models across a spread of high-stakes tasks, flood and crop mapping among them, with varied sensors and setups, and built a pipeline to grade both accuracy and honesty. The uncertainty-aware models beat standard ones on most datasets and measures, and their stated doubts checked out under scrutiny. The authors argue trust, not just accuracy, is the deliverable for Earth observation.
arxiv-2504-03778:
Stefano Cirillo and four co-authors test AI enrichment of anonymized data in twenty twenty-five. Data archives hold sensitive, identifying details about people. Anonymization techniques such as k-anonymity protect subjects, but they also thin the data. Thinner data weakens the predictive processes that use it.

The authors ask whether large language models can enrich anonymized sources. The enrichment must add value without breaking anonymity. They designed custom prompt templates for that delicate task. Feasibility and limits are both explored in the study. Readers in data governance get a careful look at a tempting idea: using generative AI to restore utility that privacy protection removed, without restoring the risk.
arxiv-2504-03978:
Francesco De Santis and co-authors tackle explainable AI in a 2025 paper on concept-based models. Such models first name human ideas found in the input, then decide from those ideas, so users can step in and fix a wrong idea. One model type is easy to fix but less exact; a second type is more exact but harder to fix once data shifts.

Their new model, V-CEM, uses a form of reasoning under uncertainty to make fixes work better. Tests on text and image data check plain accuracy, how well fixes help at home and on shifted data, and a new score for how clean the idea codes are. V-CEM kept the high accuracy of the second type while matching the first type on fixes for shifted data.
arxiv-2504-04078:
Sumito Hasegawa, Kazuki Kanai, and Yasuhiro Oki study a question in algebra about shapes called multinorm one tori in a 2025 paper. The question asks when such a shape can be described by simple formulas, a property called rationality.

For a large class of these tori, the authors prove that two forms of the rationality property amount to the same thing. They also give a test for when those properties hold. Their result extends a 2011 theorem about the simpler case of norm one tori. To get there, they widen a tool called the character group and build general ways to reduce harder cases to easier ones. They close with a new case where a known principle holds.
arxiv-2504-04578:
Cornelio and co-authors improve robot planning by language models in a 2025 paper. Such planners falter on long tasks in niche settings where facts are scarce. The team joins three aids: layered planning, a knowledge graph that feeds facts on demand, and a symbolic checker. Big tasks split into subtasks, then into single steps a robot can run.

The checker lines up the expected world state with the seen state, so it doubles as a failure alarm. Across tasks of varied hardness and several language models, the joined method beat base methods by clear margins. The authors also offer their test setup and scores as a tool for gauging planning skill in future models.
arxiv-2504-05078:
Piotr Kica and co-authors run a heavy gene aligner the serverless way in a 2025 paper. The STAR aligner maps RNA reads with high accuracy but eats memory, a poor fit for serverless slots made for light, short jobs. The team still built a STAR pipeline on a cloud container service.

They tuned the setup in several ways and ran it on a large body of sequence data. Set beside plain rented machines, the serverless route held up well for small scale batch work. Where sheer throughput rules at big scale, rented machines stayed the wiser pick. The tests map where the trade pays off.
arxiv-2504-05278:
Zahra Atf and co-authors tackle how language models in medicine should state their uncertainty, in a 2025 paper. A model that sounds sure while wrong can harm patients. Honest odds help doctors weigh machine advice against their own judgment.

The authors blend math tools, from Bayesian methods to group voting and dropout tricks, with text based gauges of meaning spread. Extra parts handle closed model access, mixed data sources, and steady recalibration as models learn. Maps of doubt and clear scores aim to earn clinician trust. They argue for owning a degree of doubt rather than chasing false certainty, since medical knowledge itself shifts.
arxiv-2504-05378:
Mitrajyoti Ghosh and co-authors propose catching neutrinos in an atomic identity swap. Whether neutrinos are their own antiparticles, the Majorana possibility, or distinct from them, the Dirac one, remains unsettled, and the flagship test, a rare nuclear decay, can only ever confirm one side. Their 2025 paper examines muonium, an electron orbiting a positive muon, flipping into its antimatter twin, a process a planned experiment called MACE will chase.

The team recomputes the flip rate in the standard model extended with heavy neutrinos of either kind, taking care with the infrared scales earlier work mishandled. A symmetry cancellation crushes the pure Dirac rate. Loosening the mixing matrix's unitarity, they show, cannot rescue it without muddying the very property under test. A hybrid case, mostly Dirac with a whisper of Majorana mass, can lift the rate strongly, especially in one mass ordering.
arxiv-2504-06078:
Leoni Winschermann and three co-authors tackle the charging of electric buses in a 2025 paper. Towns are swapping diesel fleets for electric ones, but fleets draw huge power at once when they plug in. That surge can strain the grid, and charging at peak hours can carry a high carbon cost.

The team weighs plans that trade off three goals: low carbon, low cost, and room on the grid. They test the plans on data from a real bus charging site in the Netherlands. Smart plans cut peak draw and fumes next to plug-in-and-go charging, and the paper shows the gains of each mix.
arxiv-2504-06478:
Hatef Nouri, George Sklivanitis, Dimitris Pados, and Elizabeth Serena Bentley shape a shared band link in space and time in 2025. A new data link must join a full band with a many-antenna pair while it spares the links in place. Beam weights and pulse codes are tuned as one to cut send cost per bit.

A set grade bar holds at the join filter while send cost drops in the tune. Test runs in light and dense band crowds beat plain and part-tuned links. The flex link spares in-place links by not sending spare waves.
arxiv-2504-06578:
Rahul Singh Maharjan, Marta Romeo, and Angelo Cangelosi build a network in 2025 that reads feeling from images. Pictures stir emotions through many cues at once, and the gap between raw pixels and felt emotion is wide. Most past models read the whole image and skipped the cues that drive the feeling.

Their network, A4Net, tracks four cues: brightness, color richness, scene context, and facial expression. It learns the cues and the emotion call together, each helping the other. Tests across several emotion data sets matched top methods. Heat maps from the network show which regions drove its calls, aiding trust in the results.
arxiv-2504-07178:
Gabriela Barenboim, Julien Froustey, Cyril Pitrou, and Hector Sanchis test whether the early universe's neutrino background could be strongly distorted, in a 2025 paper. Standard cosmology assumes a smooth neutrino spectrum. Their gray model bends that spectrum with a single parameter, allowing large changes.

They ran the distorted spectra through a code for the formation of light elements and combined the results with microwave background data. The combined data rule out replacing more than about half the neutrino energy with dark radiation. Still, some large distortions with extra radiation fit the data as well as or better than the standard case. The authors urge renewed study of neutrino decoupling.
arxiv-2504-07578:
Federico Mazzone and co-authors cluster shared data without exposing it in a 2025 paper. In vertical settings, each party holds different features of the same records, so distances needed for clustering cannot be computed openly. Older secure methods cost too much chatter as data grow. Noise based privacy methods, meanwhile, blur results badly.

Their method outsources features once under homomorphic encryption, so a server clusters them while blind. Privacy noise touches only the cluster centers, sparing accuracy. Communication cost drops sharply compared with past designs. One test sorts one hundred thousand points into five clusters. The design targets real multi-party data work.
arxiv-2504-07678:
Luis Torres-Figueroa and co-authors test secrecy built into the 5G signal itself at millimeter waves. Their twenty twenty-five study runs during the cell search step, when a phone first finds the tower. An eavesdropper nearby records raw channel samples without touching the link.

Messages ride the broadcast channel with physical layer encoding meant to keep meaning from the listener. The team lowers transmit power step by step to map where secrecy holds. Error bounds grade how well the spy can tell messages apart. Beamforming, the tight aiming of these waves, becomes a secrecy tool. Proof on real airwaves moves such schemes toward standard practice.
arxiv-2504-07778:
Julian Giraldo-Barreto and Viktor Holubec propose a flocking model where agents align with where neighbors will be, not just where they are. Their 2025 study tackles a classic flaw in active matter models: alignment alone rarely keeps a group together under noise. Past fixes add walls or pull forces by hand.

Predictive alignment needs no extra parameters yet yields robust, noise-proof cohesion. In the stable regime, flock size grows in a straight line with interaction range. The group stays near immune to noise and speed changes. It can also follow a leader through noise. The authors frame prediction as a cognitive-like twist that opens a new class of flock models.
arxiv-2504-07878:
Jianshu She and six co-authors present a system that lets small language models on edge devices call on a large cloud model only when needed in a 2025 paper. Small models run fast and cheap but answer worse and invent facts more often. Large models answer better but are costly to run for every word.

Their system routes at the level of single tokens, the chunks that make up text. The small model writes most tokens on the device and sends only key ones to the cloud model. In a test on a laptop, a tiny model gained sixty percent in score while sending under seven percent of tokens to the cloud.
arxiv-2504-07978:
Nikita Kalinin extends in 2025 a classic prime sum theorem to the ring of Gaussian integers. Those are whole numbers with an added square root of minus one part. The classic claim ties sums of prime inverses to neat split rules.

For primes past seven, a sum of inverses over a grid of such numbers is shown to vanish to a high power of the prime. Kalinin then lifts the claim to higher power sums, which show set split forms as well. Guesses link the new claim to binom style counts. Small prime quirks up to one thousand are worked out in full.
arxiv-2504-08178:
Zhang and three co-authors wrote a theory paper in twenty twenty-five about stochastic gradient descent, the step-by-step method that trains many learning systems. They study cases where the loss curve is steep near the best point but flattens out far away, a shape that shows up in robust fitting and in quantile regression.

The authors build a new piecewise tool, called a Lyapunov function, that tracks how the method settles down over time. With it they prove bounds on the error for shrinking and fixed step sizes, plus results on long-run behavior and bias. They then apply the theory to two tasks: fitting a line when some data are corrupted, and estimating quantiles from streaming data. The results match earlier rates reached under stricter assumptions, and they relax a common condition past work needed.
arxiv-2504-08278:
Ming Xu, Stephen Gould and Iman Shames present FilterDDP, an algorithm for optimal control problems with nonlinear equality constraints. Past methods lean on merit functions or augmented Lagrangian ideas. FilterDDP instead uses a step filter with a line search to handle the constraints.

Two design choices drive its strong numeric results. The step test uses the Lagrangian rather than the cost, and the backward pass perturbs the value function Hessian. The second choice comes with a formal proof of local quadratic convergence. The authors add a primal-dual interior point form for both equality and inequality constraints, and test the method on three contact-based trajectory problems from robotics.
arxiv-2504-08378:
Phones cannot hold a big language model's full weights in fast memory, which caps how smart on-device AI can be. Fucheng Jia and nine co-authors present ActiveFlow in 2025, a framework that swaps the weights a model actually needs between flash storage and fast memory as it runs.

Only a slice of weights wakes up for each chunk of text. The system predicts which weights later layers will need, using signals from the current layer, so loading overlaps with computing. A self-distillation step keeps the trimmed model faithful to the full one. A scheduling pipeline then divides memory among cached, preloaded, and working weights. The authors report the best speed-cost balance among the methods they compared.
arxiv-2504-08778:
Bo Xiong and Steffen Staab ask how language models build a lattice of concepts from raw text tokens in 2025. Masked language models learn rich concept knowledge in training. Concepts in them form a web that looks like a lattice. The team uses a math frame that builds concept lattices from object and trait links.

They show the training goal makes the model learn just such a link table in secret. From that table, a concept lattice can be rebuilt by the classic method. Their frame needs no human set concepts. It can find latent concepts past human labels. Three new data sets test the claim. Results back their account of where the lattice comes from.
arxiv-2504-08978:
Abdelmalek Boumali and Sarra Garrah extend a classic relativistic model to richer gauge fields in a 2025 paper. The Dirac oscillator blends quantum relativity with a spring-like pull and can be solved exactly, which makes it a prized test bed. The authors set the model in a background of non-Abelian gauge fields, the kind that act on an inner two-state charge called isospin.

Starting from the gauge-aware Dirac equation, they add the oscillator through its standard non-minimal swap. The field strength then gains a commutator term with no counterpart in the simpler Abelian case. That term yields couplings that mix spin and isospin as matrices. With the fields switched off, the model falls back to the classic solved case, which anchors the new theory.
arxiv-2504-09078:
D Bhanu Prakash and D K K Vamsi wrote a 2025 math paper on prey and predator models where extra food is given to predators. Their model has predators that also compete with each other. The feeding response is of a type where too much prey can slow the predator down.

They prove the model has one global valid path for any start. They map its rest points and check which are stable. They also trace sudden shifts in behaviour as food and rivalry vary. Then they ask how best to set food quality and amount over time. The results may guide pest control, where extra food can steer predators in useful ways.
arxiv-2504-09378:
Kartik Ravisankar and co-authors published this paper in 2025. It asks how large language models manage to answer questions in many languages when most of their training text is English. The authors test whether the model first maps other languages onto English inside its own layers.

They built a score that measures this inner mapping for single examples, across twenty-four languages and three kinds of task. Wrong answers came with weak mapping, above all in the model's middle layers. The team then swapped in the matching English activations at those layers, and many wrong answers turned right. That swap test shows the mapping is not just linked to success; it helps cause it. The work gives builders a clearer target for improving weaker languages.
arxiv-2504-09478:
Jun-Gill Kang, Dohyeon Lee, and Soohee Han built this 2025 drone modeled on the flying squirrel. Ordinary rotor drones push in one direction only, which limits agility in tight spaces. A squirrel glides and brakes with skin wings. The team's drone folds and unfolds silicone wings mid-flight to widen its range of poses and forces.

Reinforcement learning, trained on human demonstrations, steers the wings. Learning was needed because the wing forces defy tidy math models. In flight tests, the drone deliberately raised drag to gain a pushing force even when its motors were maxed out. Tracking stayed stable through the maneuvers. The work shows how animal design plus machine learning can yield small aircraft that dart through confined spaces.
arxiv-2504-09778:
Kevin Farias and a large student team describe their entry for the 2025 RoboCup Rescue Robot League, in a paper from 2025. The league sends robots into mock disaster zones to find victims, stand in work for real search and rescue machines. For this team, UruBots, the event marks a first appearance at the world competition.

Their paper presents the vehicle and the full approach to locating victims in wrecked environments. Standard robotics tools fill the design: an open robot software framework, mapping while moving, human robot interaction, and image segmentation for perception. The team builds on lessons from earlier regional contests and research projects. True to league custom, the whole approach is released as open source for rivals to learn from.
arxiv-2504-09878:
Yunpeng Tan, Junlin Hao, and colleagues speed up training for neural scene rendering in a 2025 study. Neural radiance fields render new views with high quality, yet even fast variants need minutes of training. Multimedia uses such as telemedicine want results in real time, and wasteful sampling is a major bottleneck.

Simple regions of a scene need less sampling than detailed ones, but older methods sample both at full fineness. Their method uses a tree search strategy to vary resolution by block, spending effort where texture is complex. Rays aimed at easy regions cost less. The payoff is faster training without giving up view quality where it counts.
arxiv-2504-10078:
Wanyun Zhou and co-authors mine social media for stock signals in a 2025 paper. Price and company data are the usual inputs for predicting stock moves. Posts on platforms like StockTwits add a live stream of opinion, but most posts are noise and public mood alone predicts little. The team's claim is that a few posters do know something, and they can be found.

Their algorithm traces posters over time and keeps those whose calls are consistently right, plus a surprising group whose calls are consistently wrong in a usable way, the inverse experts. Filtering out the rest sharpened trend prediction over older expert-finding methods. The authors also note a limit shared by the whole approach: turning expert calls into a precise return forecast stays hard. The work shows signal hides in social noise.
arxiv-2504-10178:
Reasoning traces that teach code models can be built for a dozen programming languages at once, in a 2025 paper by Naizhu Jin and co-authors. Most chain-of-thought work feeds Python only, leaving multilingual code generation, the everyday reality of software teams, underserved.

The team first built a structured reasoning data set covering twelve languages, using several cooperating agents to draft solutions. Their method, MSCoT, then teaches models to reason in that structured way across languages. Large experiments compared its generalization against existing chain-of-thought generators and helped the study clarify where structured reasoning transfers. The goal is code assistants whose thinking habits survive a switch from Python to Java or C++ without retraining.
arxiv-2504-10278:
Jinyue Zhang and co-authors present, in 2025, a new method for spotting moving objects in satellite imagery. The targets are tiny, the images grainy, and older deep learning methods reason about probabilities in ways that limit how objects and frames inform each other. Their method works with points marking object centers instead.

Borrowing from diffusion models, the system denoises scattered points step by step until true centers emerge. Added modules let points exchange spatial and semantic information and carry memory across frames.
