A staged matching strategy sets the learning target at each denoising level, and an extra loss stops points from clumping onto only the brightest objects.
arxiv-2504-10378:
Qinyuan Zhang, Tian-Qi Huang, and Zhuo Li ask whether flashes of neutrinos born from cosmic ray collisions could appear as point sources in the sky. Their paper appeared in 2025. Ultra-high energy cosmic rays hitting background light make these cosmogenic neutrinos. If the cosmic ray sources are brief events like gamma-ray bursts, the neutrino glow should arrive as tight, time-limited spots. The team computed the spots' spectra and shapes over time.

Intergalactic magnetic fields steer the parent rays and so set the spot sizes, generally under a degree. Early on, a spot's flux can outshine the whole diffuse background within its patch. A recent record neutrino event fits a nearby transient source better than the diffuse glow. The authors say hunting such spots could finally reveal the cosmic ray sources.
arxiv-2504-10478:
Xingyu Dang and four co-authors report a simple fix for a training flaw in reasoning models in this two thousand twenty-five paper. As fine-tuning proceeds, a model's answers grow more alike. Its first guess keeps improving, but its chance of solving a problem in many tries falls. That loss hurts test-time strategies like majority voting. The authors blend the weights of the final model with an early checkpoint, a trick called WiSE-FT.

The blend nearly restores the lost diversity while keeping the first-guess gains. It also improves voting scores and later reinforcement learning results. Extra gains appear that decoding tricks alone cannot give. The team frames the effect as a bias-variance trade-off. The recipe is cheap and easy for model builders to adopt.
arxiv-2504-10778:
Christian Iliadis looks at why marks of spin and flip for core tiers so often muddle readers. These marks are key for work on core form and on how cores act. Yet rules for marks shift from source to source. Iliadis weighs the rules of a file of core data that has been judged next to work by Endt and his team.

He finds stock roots of muddle. One is vague use of strong and weak points. One more is new test finds merged with past bounds with no clear mark. His tips call for clear rules for marks. They call for clean splits of point strengths and for more teach in the group. They also call for new finds told on their own. The aim is core data that staff and judges can use with no wrong read.
arxiv-2504-10978:
Pu Wang and five co-authors build an agent that cleans up colonoscopy images before an AI outlines polyps in them. Their 2025 paper starts from messy reality: scope images often suffer dim light, blur, and glare, which throw off the outlining step. Missed polyps can mean missed early cancers.

An image judge, guided by a vision-language model, first names what is wrong with a picture in words. A reinforcement learning agent then picks fixes like denoising and contrast boosts, step by step. A feedback loop checks quality and refocuses both cleaning and outlining. The frame is modular, so other cleaning tools and outlining networks can plug in. The authors aim the design at real endoscopy hardware.
arxiv-2504-11178:
The center of the Milky Way hides behind dust that blocks visible light, but radio waves pass through. William Cotton and co-authors surveyed the Galactic bulge with South Africa's MeerKAT telescope at 1.3 gigahertz. The maps cover about 173 square degrees around the center plus scattered fields farther out. They resolve details a few arcseconds wide.

Most sources are distant galaxies shining through our own. Polarization measurements pick out compact Galactic objects and reveal fine-scale magnetic twisting across the region. Hunting for giant radio galaxies, the team catalogued seventeen spanning more than 700 kiloparsecs. The survey releases full polarization images and source lists for other astronomers.
arxiv-2504-11278:
Tanja Auge and co-authors work toward a unified framework for workflow and data provenance in a 2025 paper. Provenance records where data and results came from, which is essential for tracing studies and trusting their findings. Two kinds matter: how the workflow ran, and how the data themselves evolved.

Their framework adds dimensions and granularity to both kinds, letting users answer a standard set of provenance questions. A biomedical use case demonstrates the approach, designed to transfer to other fields. Unifying the concepts, the authors argue, supports credibility and reproducibility of research findings.
arxiv-2504-11378:
Horndeski theory is the broadest healthy extension of Einstein's gravity with a scalar field. Hatice Özer and Özgür Delice ask what gravitational waves look like in a massive version of it that carries a general potential. Earlier work often ignored the potential's lowest point; here it takes center stage.

That lowest value acts like an effective cosmological constant, curving the background the waves cross. Solving the weak-field equations step by step, the authors get the background shape, then the wave solutions on top of it. The scalar-caused curvature shifts the frequency and spacing of the tensor waves in a way that sets them apart from the scalar wave. How the constant is introduced also changes the scalar wave's speed and polarization. The comparison clarifies what future detectors could test.
arxiv-2504-11478:
Hao Kang and co-authors coax a stock image generator into subject-driven creation with no training at all. Keeping a chosen subject's identity across new scenes normally takes fine-tuning or extra data. Their insight is that the Flux model already knows how, if the task is framed as filling a grid.

Their 2025 paper tiles the subject photo into a mosaic and asks the model to complete it, waking strong identity-keeping behavior for free. A cascade attention design and meta prompting sharpen fidelity and range. Benchmarks and human judges favor the trick over trained baselines on key scores, with some trade-offs. Logo placement, virtual try-on, and subject swaps all run through the same untrained door.
arxiv-2504-11878:
Shaima Abidrabbu and Hüseyin Arslan secure a shared wireless stream in a 2025 communications letter. Rate-splitting networks send every user a common stream plus a private one, and the common part is an eavesdropping target because everyone is meant to decode it.

Their defense interleaves each user's common bits using a pattern derived from that user's own private bits. Only a receiver who correctly decodes its private stream can reconstruct the pattern and unscramble the common part; a listener without it faces a moving target. A selection method refreshes the patterns while balancing safety against efficiency. Simulations showed real security gains with system reliability intact.
arxiv-2504-12378:
V Markov and co-authors present a 2025 astronomy paper on how dust dims and reddens the light of early galaxies seen by the James Webb Space Telescope. Dust curves vary a lot between young galaxies, and astronomers disagree on what drives the variety: the dust itself, how much there is, or how it is arranged around the stars. The team quantifies each curve by its ultraviolet slope and a bump feature.

They analysed 173 dusty galaxies from when the universe was young, spanning redshifts two to about eleven and a half. Correlating curve shape with galaxy traits aims to name the physical levers behind the variation, which matters because dust corrections shape every measurement of early galaxy growth.
arxiv-2504-12678:
Jerome, Klimchik, Maloletov, and Kulathunga planned vehicle paths over rough ground in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Car-like robots on uneven land face slopes that shift from patch to patch. The terrain is modeled as a mesh of triangles. Their planner, GAKD, searches with a genetic algorithm that breeds and mutates candidate routes.

The search works over a fixed look-ahead window and keeps controls within safe bounds. A heuristic mutation step steers the breeding toward workable routes. Against two sampling-based rivals, GAKD cut the cost of crossing terrain by up to twenty percent. Path length stayed about the same. The authors offer the method for robots that must cross broken, sloped ground.
arxiv-2504-12778:
Yuxuan Zong and Benjamin Piwowarski shrink the storage of top search models in 2025 without dulling their aim. Late-interaction models score a query against every word-piece of every document, which ranks well but eats memory for all those stored pieces. Past pruning cut pieces by rules of thumb, with no promise the score would survive.

Their fix starts from a clean rule for when a piece can go with zero score change. Three added training goals push the model toward shapes where most pieces are safe to cut, and two cutting plans apply the rule. In tests at home and abroad, the model kept its ranking quality while storing only thirty percent of its pieces, they report. Memory savings that size decide whether such search runs on one machine or a rack.
arxiv-2504-12878:
Dmytro Yaremchuk and six co-authors study a frustrated quantum magnet built from two kagome layers in this 2025 paper. The spin-half Heisenberg model on this bilayer, with strong coupling between layers, resists exact solution. The authors map it onto a gas of rhombi living on the kagome lattice.

That classical lattice-gas picture captures the low-temperature behavior, and finite-size numerics back its validity. Two findings stand out. First, no order-disorder phase transition appears. Second, just below the saturation field, the low-temperature specific heat stays sensitive to the sample's shape even in the large-system limit. The work shows how a hard quantum problem can borrow a classical shadow. It also warns that shape effects need not vanish with size.
arxiv-2504-13078:
Riza Velioglu, Petra Bevandic, Robin Chan, and Barbara Hammer teach a diffusion model to strip outfits from photos of dressed people. Their 2025 paper extends virtual try-off, the inverse of try-on tools. Try-off yields clean garment images from a person photo, a harder task when several garments appear at once.

Their model handles tops, bottoms, and dresses in one frame. A latent diffusion design reads garment shape, texture, and pattern from image conditions. Class-specific embeddings help the model sort garment types apart. Scores lead the field on one benchmark and rival the best on a dress-heavy set. Paired with try-on models, the tool cuts unwanted trait transfer, such as skin tone bleed, in person-to-person tests. Code and models are public.
arxiv-2504-13578:
Zhou, Ye, and Yu describe a contact-free way to push spin currents through a magnetic film in one locked direction, in this 2025 physics paper. Magnons, the waves of a magnet's internal compass needles, can carry spin information without moving charge. A nearby metal layer holding an excess of one electron spin can drive them through long-range dipolar coupling alone, no contact exchange needed. The induced magnon flow always runs perpendicular to the spin excess.

That fixed right-angle relation, a chiral locking, holds universally in their analysis. It even works when the spin excess points along the magnetization, a geometry where contact transfer fails. Direction-locked, contact-free spin injection is a tempting building block for low-heat computing hardware.
arxiv-2504-14178:
Yijie Li and co-authors split sky from cloud at the speed of sight in a 2025 paper. Ground shots of the sky feed weather lore and sun craft, but past nets trade truth for speed and stall on small gear.

Their net first drafts a rough map, then splits it in two: a sky face and a cloud face, each weighed on its own terms. The split lets fine rims stay sharp while the whole stays light. The large form, with a few mil parts, matched the best nets with near a third less bulk. The lite form, a sliver of that size, ran past a thou frames a blink on lean gear. A warm-up train trick lifts the score with no big bank of past shots.
arxiv-2504-14578:
Biao Dong and co-authors study, in 2025, a quantum phase that is at once a crystal, a superfluid, and a patterned spin texture. They create this chiral supersolid in a cloud of ultracold magnetic atoms with spin-orbit coupling. By tuning interactions, they map out how the system changes form.

Two kinds of transition appear: an abrupt jump to a triangular pattern and a smooth shift to a square one. The phases differ in lattice shape, spin texture, and how freely they rotate. Under a balanced gain-and-loss setup, current swings fade at rates tied to the superfluid share. The work points to cold atoms as a platform for designer quantum matter.
arxiv-2504-14878:
Ranran Guo and co-authors study how a magnet-like model settles after a sudden change in a 2025 paper. The model is the three-dimensional kinetic Ising model, a grid of interacting spins used to study phase changes. The team trace the free energy landscape along the whole line where the system jumps between phases.

Near the change point, the landscape matches classic Landau-Ginzburg theory. Far below it, the landscape grows fine traps that catch random starting states and delay settling badly, an effect the authors name ultra-slow relaxation. They propose a signature for it: the spread of settling times blows up on its own. They offer that signature as a new hallmark of first-order transitions.
arxiv-2504-14978:
Rafael Bicudo Ribeiro and Henrique Musseli Cezar release clusttraj, a tool that groups molecular snapshots while respecting solvent identity, in a 2025 paper. Molecular simulations produce floods of configurations, and clustering sorts them into families. When identical molecules swap places, naive distance measures inflate and blur the families.

The program first finds the best pairing between configurations, then applies the Kabsch alignment to minimize positional distance before clustering. Built-in metrics help users pick the cutoff and compare grouping schemes automatically. Tests ran from pure water clusters to a solvated protein and a small solute in varied solvents. The authors studied how system size and pairing method change the results. They also checked whether cluster centers represent optical traits well. The Python library targets generic ensembles, not just solute-solvent systems, and is offered for general modeling use.
arxiv-2504-15478:
Edoardo Provenzi revisited in 2025 a classic result on the geometry of color perception. A 1974 theorem by Resnikoff says our perceived color space can carry only two possible curved geometries, once a few natural rules and a sameness condition hold. Provenzi restates that model in modern color science terms and gives a much simpler proof of the main result.

He then shows the favored geometry clashes with a known effect where colors sharpen against pale backgrounds. Experiments are needed to test one key assumption. The mismatch tells designers that current color distance formulas rest on shaky ground.
arxiv-2504-15578:
Six authors build a live experiment design for cell chem models in 2025, driven by reward learning. Set test plans for such models eat time and miss shifts in live use. Their frame bends the charge flow fed to a lithium cell so model terms stand out most, round by round in real time. A rig with real gear in the loop hosts the runs.

The learned plan beat stock plans on check test error in the rig runs. It also cut the time the fit test took by a firm span. Live tailoring is the core gain the team claims for cell work. Fit grade rose while test span fell in the same trials.
arxiv-2504-15878:
Glasses break the rules of ordinary solids: their heat capacity humps where theory says it should not, and their heat flow stalls at the same temperature. Elijah Flenner and Grzegorz Szamel revisit the suspect behind both anomalies in a 2025 paper. The suspect is defects, spots in the disordered material that scatter sound.

The authors test which proposed defects truly damp sound strongly, and tie some of them to quasi-localized vibrations, the extra modes beyond Debye's count that pile up at the boson peak. They then derive a cleaned-up relation between sound damping, sound speed, and the excess modes, dropping an approximation earlier authors used. The new relation matches the measured density of states well except near the peak itself. It nails the peak in two-dimensional glasses but underestimates it in three, a clue the authors leave pointed at the defect picture.
arxiv-2504-16078:
Thomas Schmied and co-authors diagnose why language model agents make poor choices. Their twenty twenty-five paper names three failure modes: greediness, frequency bias, and the knowing-doing gap. An agent may know the right move, state it in reasoning, and still not take it.

Tests span simple bandit games, context bandits, and tic-tac-toe. The proposed fix fine-tunes the model with reinforcement learning on its own chain-of-thought traces. Decision skill improved across the test suite after that tuning. The work matters as language agents move into shopping, planning, and tool use, where a greedy streak can waste real resources.
arxiv-2504-16278:
Message passing is the workhorse method for reading properties of networks, from epidemic spread to the size of the largest connected cluster. Peter Mann and Simon Dobson present a different route to the same answers for bond percolation. Like the standard method, theirs is exact on tree-shaped networks and approximate on the rest.

The new framing stretches further with less strain. It handles sequential percolation and non-binary versions of the process in a natural way. It can also describe the local surroundings of a single node at equilibrium, information the classic approach cannot reach. The 2025 paper offers network scientists a more flexible lens on percolation.
arxiv-2504-16978:
Yu Shi presents a 2025 paper on the scientific spirit of Chien-Shiung Wu, the great experimental physicist. In 1950 Wu and her student published a coincidence experiment on entangled photon pairs from electron-positron annihilation. It verified quantum electrodynamics precisely. It was also the first tightly controlled entangled state of separated particles, though Wu did not know that then. In 1956 she led the Wu experiment, which found that parity is not conserved. That result ranks among the century's greatest experiments.

The paper traces her career through the twin themes of precision and accuracy. It is the text of a speech for the 110th anniversary symposium of her birth. Physics readers get a career read as a lesson in experimental craft. Yang's remark that her experiments were famed for precision frames the talk. History of science gains a practitioner's view of how care in measurement changes what a field can know.
arxiv-2504-17278:
Raza and four co-authors set a cap in twenty twenty-five on how many look-alike graphs a directed graph can have. Two such graphs are mates if a set of score lists from their link tables match in full. Mates that are not the same graph can confuse work that tries to name a graph by its scores.

The team ties the cap to a count from a walk table built from the graph. As a side case, they give a test for when the sole mate is the graph flipped end to end. The tests link to how well a web of linked parts can be steered.
arxiv-2504-17578:
Hongshu Guo and co-authors teach a grand hunt tool to pick its own split in a 2025 paper. The tool hunts best forms in wide fields by a herd that learns the land's shape, and a split of the field in parts makes vast hunts tractable.

A hand split needs a deep adept. Their frame swaps the hand for a small net that reads the hunt's state and calls the split, step by step. Prize-and-blame train taught the net on a set of sample tasks. On wide tests the frame beat the best set ways in score and in cost. It held its form on tasks it had not met in school. The authors cast learned splits as a way to free vast hunts from adept hands.
arxiv-2504-17678:
Qiuyan Xiang and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on MindFlow, a model that spots odd traffic on networks of smart devices. Factories and homes now link huge numbers of devices, and attacks hide in the flood. Their model is built on a Chinese AI framework and mixes two network types.

One part reads local patterns in the traffic stream. The other reads the stream both ways to catch long range cues. Tested on a known botnet data set, the model scored near perfect on accuracy and on balance measures. The authors say the pairing stays robust against varied and stealthy attacks. Such tools matter as device networks grow harder to watch by hand.
arxiv-2504-17778:
Paul Leask studies how a knotted light-like texture in a liquid crystal transforms in a paper from 2025. Hopfions and torons are three-dimensional topological solitons in chiral liquid crystals. Bending the molecular alignment creates strain, which generates electric polarization through the flexoelectric effect. That polarization makes its own field, which pushes back on the alignment. Computing this self-interaction is the hard part.

Leask adapts a method built for magnetic skyrmions to the liquid crystal case. Unlike their magnetic cousins, these textures feel the back-reaction strongly. As the flexoelectric strength rises, the hopfion converts into a toron. The transition is shown in confined three-dimensional systems. The results guide soft-matter soliton design.
arxiv-2504-17978:
Aurora Aguayo and a large team confirm a ring in the disk around the young star MP Mus, in their 2025 arXiv paper. Protoplanetary disks are planet birthplaces, and rings and gaps in them may mark planet formation. This nearby disk had shown a ring in scattered light at wide radius, but millimeter images looked different.

New ALMA observations at a shorter wavelength reveal a dust ring at about fifty astronomical units after the smooth disk profile is subtracted. The team measures the disk's dust mass at two wavelengths and maps how the spectral index climbs from the inner disk outward. Gas extends much farther than the compact dust, a contrast that informs how disks clear and evolve.
arxiv-2504-18078:
Xiaolu Chen, Chenghao Huang, Yanru Zhang, and Hao Wang estimate hidden rooftop solar output without pooling private data. Their 2025 paper tackles photovoltaic disaggregation: splitting net load into solar generation and true demand. Behind-the-meter panels hide their output from grid operators, tangling supply balance.

Federated learning trains models across data centers without moving raw records. A personal twist handles the spread of climates and habits across sites. Each site runs a transformer that embeds local solar conditions; an adaptive step borrows only the global knowledge that helps locally. A central server merges uploads into shared learning. Real-world tests beat benchmark methods on accuracy and robustness, the authors report. The frame suits a grid that must see solar fleets it cannot meter.
arxiv-2504-18178:
Jiaqi Zheng and Tiow-Seng Tan unified two classic ball problems in a 2025 geometry paper. Given a set of compact convex objects, the smallest intersecting ball is the tiniest ball touching them all, while the smallest enclosing ball is the tiniest ball containing them all. Versions of these problems recur across computational geometry and machine learning, from facility placement to classifier margins.

Zheng and Tan show both problems can be written as zero-sum games, where two players' opposing goals encode the geometry. For the intersecting version they give an approximation algorithm, the first results of its kind in high dimensions for inputs like polytopes, balls, and ellipsoids. The game view may unlock algorithms for related covering problems.
arxiv-2504-18378:
David Holec and four co-authors model from first principles how alloying shifts phase change effects in beta titanium alloys, known by the short names TWIP and TRIP. These effects shape how the metal bends without breaking. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The team used density based theory on pure titanium and on mixes with nine other elements. Some elements steadied the beta phase, yet the most stable phase sat between beta and alpha, a martensite form. Twin borders of one type face a positive energy wall that alloying raises. The other twin type shows no wall save for two elements, since its mid state looks like the alpha phase. Twin border energies round out design hints.
arxiv-2504-18678:
Francesco Giancaterini, Alain Hecq, Joann Jasiak, and Aryan Manafi Neyazi extend a covariance estimator for high-dimensional data, in a 2025 paper. The base method fits models by matching generalized covariances. In high dimensions, a key matrix flip becomes unstable. That blocks its use on rich data or many transforms.

Their fix adds a ridge-style penalty to steady the flip. They prove the estimator stays consistent and follows a normal limit. Conditions for top efficiency are given, along with a way to pick the penalty size. A diagonal shortcut eases computing. Two classic tests are extended to the new setting. Simulations show the estimator and tests behave well in practice.
arxiv-2504-18778:
Infinite-layer nickelates superconduct like cuprates but with one clear difference: their Fermi surface is three-dimensional, varying along the stacking direction. Xia, Zhou, and Chen ask what that difference does to the superconductivity itself.

Using a combined method that pairs a random-phase treatment with dynamical mean-field theory, they solve the linearized gap equation. Against a flat two-dimensional Fermi surface, the three-dimensional one carries van Hove singularities, points where the density of states spikes. Those points push the system closer to an antiferromagnetic instability, strengthening spin fluctuations, and the pairing grows much stronger as a result. The paper argues that subtle Fermi surface shape can decide how strong unconventional superconductivity becomes.
arxiv-2504-18878:
Robert Leppich and co-authors introduce in 2025 a light architecture for forecasting and filling gaps in multivariate time series. Their model builds representation layers based on convolutions, each tasked with learning a different temporal pattern. An attention layer then extracts features and a merge layer combines them, in a layout inspired by the transformer encoder with self attention at its core.

Across seven established benchmark data sets, the model beat leading approaches on most tasks for both forecasting and gap filling. It also used far fewer learnable parameters than those rivals. Source code is released. Readers who work with sensor, finance, or other time series data get a cheaper model to try.
arxiv-2504-19478:
Weitao Feng and co-authors present CasaGPT, a method to build indoor scenes, in a 2025 paper. Past tools place full objects from bounding boxes, which can cause clashes in the room. Their method breaks each object into simple cuboid blocks and learns to arrange those blocks one by one.

A step by step model builds scenes that stay physically plausible. A filter step in fine tuning throws out scenes where objects collide, which cuts clashes further. The team also cleaned a known scene data set of much of its noise. Tests on both the old and cleaned sets beat leading methods on realism. The work offers a compact path to scene design for interiors.
arxiv-2504-19578:
Machine-learned atomic models promise one potential energy surface for all of chemistry, but promise is not proof. Anyang Peng and co-authors build the proving ground. LAMBench tests large atomistic models on how well they generalize, adapt, and apply across problems. Ten leading models, all released before August 2025, face the benchmark.

The verdict is humbling. A significant gap separates today's models from the ideal universal surface. The authors name what is missing: training data across domains, support for mixed fidelity, and models that respect basic physical constraints like energy conservation. The platform is built to evolve as models improve. Benchmarks like this one turn a marketing word, 'universal,' into a measurable claim.
arxiv-2504-19678:
Mohamed Amine Ferrag, Norbert Tihanyi, and Merouane Debbah survey the fast-merging worlds of language model reasoning and autonomous agents, in a 2025 review. Benchmarks, frameworks, and protocols have multiplied without a shared map. The authors set out to consolidate the sprawl.

They compare benchmarks from 2019 to 2025 side by side and sort roughly sixty of them into a taxonomy. The classes run from knowledge, math, and code to retrieval, domain tests, multimodal and embodied tasks, orchestration, and interactive evaluation. Agent frameworks from 2023 onward get the same treatment, followed by real applications from materials science to finance. Three collaboration protocols, ACP, MCP, and A2A, are surveyed as emerging standards for agents talking to agents. The review closes with research directions: failure modes in multi-agent systems, automated discovery, and protocol security. It is pitched as a field guide for newcomers and a checklist for builders.
arxiv-2504-20078:
Kalyan Cherukuri and Aarav Lala present a smarter way to compress neural networks, in this 2025 paper. Big networks are heavy to store and slow to run. A classic trick replaces weight tables with low-rank versions, but picking one rank for every layer wastes capacity in some and starves others.

Their method reads the spread of each layer's singular values, a measure of how much real information it holds. Layers with rich content keep higher ranks, while redundant ones shrink hard. The result is layer-wise compression with better performance and lower space and time costs than fixed-rank cuts. The pair frame rank choice as an information budget problem.
arxiv-2504-20578:
Carpine and three co-authors test how the build and mix of space dust grains bend their light marks, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Dust models decode how grains cool gas, grow in disks, and seed planets. Most models are tuned to thin space gas and treat grown grains as plain balls.

The team grew one micron grains from a known small grain set and used a dipole sum to work out their light acts. They varied the grain's stuff, its holes, and its clump shape. In the heat and long wave bands where scopes read dust, all three choices moved the marks. Clumps could not be faked by smooth balls, and the long wave slope could shift at fixed grain size. The pilot warns model makers off easy cuts.
arxiv-2504-20678:
Yaroslav Getman and co-authors present NOCASA in 2025, a data competition on grading children's speech. The task is to score single-word pronunciations by young learners of a second language, inside a game-like training app. Training data are scarce, and scores are heavily unbalanced across levels.

The organizers release a pseudo-anonymized set with over ten thousand recordings from forty-four speakers. Each child tried Norwegian words and was rated from one to five stars by humans. Two baseline systems are shared, one based on classic sound features and one on a modern speech model. The stronger baseline sets the bar entrants must beat.
arxiv-2504-20778:
Arup Sarkar and Alessandro Lunghi compute the excited states of two molecular magnets eyed as quantum bits, in this 2025 paper. The molecules carry vanadyl or copper centers inside flat porphyrin rings. Excited states steer how the spins behave, yet they stayed poorly mapped.

Using heavy multiconfigurational methods with four active spaces of rising size, the pair sorted the low states by type. The biggest calculations show the lowest excitations come from the ring's own electrons jumping within quartet states. The picture matches lab observations. Knowing which states sit lowest should help explain spin motion and guide qubit design.
arxiv-2504-20878:
Painos Chitanga, Bas Lemmens, and Roger Nussbaum study dimension spectra for continued fractions in a 2025 math paper. A continued fraction writes a number as a stack of fractions. The spectrum measures how large the set of such numbers can be when the entries are drawn from a set list.

For lists made of powers of one number, they prove the spectrum is full, settling an open question. Adding one extra entry opens many gaps in the spectrum. For lists made of powers like squares and cubes, the spectrum stays full up to the fifth power, then splits into a few neat intervals as the power grows.
arxiv-2504-20978:
Shamil Asgarli, Sara Krehbiel, and Howard Levinson ask whether a graph's coloring web can name the graph itself, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Points of the web are legal colorings, and edges join colorings one vertex apart. Unlike graphs can share a web in the tight case.

With spare colors beyond the least needed, the web becomes a full fingerprint. Same web then forces same graph and same color count. No tight-case web can pose as a spare-case one. A build-it proof even tells which case a web came from, though slowly. Readers get a neat line where extra colors buy identity.
arxiv-2504-21478:
Zherui Zhang and six co-authors present CAE-DFKD in two thousand twenty-five. The method transfers knowledge from a teacher net to a student net with no real data. Past methods chase image scores on the source task. They neglect how well the learned codes travel to new tasks.

The new method works at the level of embeddings, not just images. Category aware codes shape what the student learns. A change in how the generator trains brings big speed gains. Tests show scores on par with the best data free methods. Codes learned this way moved to downstream tasks with rare strength.
arxiv-2504-21578:
Kamila Barylska, Franck Delaplace, Anna Gogolińska, and Ewa Pańkowska model glucagon and insulin production in pancreatic cells in a 2025 paper. They use Petri nets and Boolean networks, two formal tools for mapping how parts of a system switch and flow.

The models cover insulin release from beta cells and glucagon release from alpha cells. The two hormones pull in opposite ways: insulin guards against high blood sugar, and glucagon guards against low blood sugar. A joint model lets both run at once by blood sugar level. The work builds toward a full model of glucose control and diabetes.
arxiv-2504-21678:
Davide Ferri ties mirror laws to twists for set-based wave maps in a 2025 paper. Two famed laws from physics can be set in any web of joined goods. In plain join webs, each fix of the mirror law yields a twist of a wave law fix, he proves.

Twists count since two wave fixes link by one just when their braid acts match. Set fixes each own a group with a braid form of its own. Group mirrors then yield the twists in a clean path, the work shows.
arxiv-2504-21778:
Ayman Ameen, Thomas Richter, and André Kaup cut the computing cost of learned image compression. Their twenty twenty-five paper presents a design called LoC-LIC. Learned codecs can beat classic formats on file size. Their heavy maths blocks use on modest devices, though.

The design extracts features in a hierarchy across scales. Wide early maps use few channels to stay cheap. Narrow deep maps can then afford many channels. That split keeps compression strength while slashing operations. Computing per pixel fell to a fraction of the earlier level. Phones and small devices could plausibly run such codecs. The work points toward learned compression that fits everyday hardware.
arxiv-2505-00078:
Ordinary matter particles come in twos and threes of quarks, but nothing in the theory of the strong force forbids four-quark states, and recent experiments keep finding candidates. Bhabani Sankar Tripathy, Nilmani Mathur, and Padmanath attack the question computationally, using lattice QCD. They simulate the strong force on a spacetime grid and watch how pairs of mesons containing bottom quarks interact.

Their study explores the channels where doubly heavy tetraquarks, bound states of two bottom quarks and two lighter antiquarks, might live. The work uses established supercomputing ensembles of gauge configurations shared by the MILC collaboration. Understanding whether such states bind, and how, probes the non-perturbative side of quantum chromodynamics that no formula can reach. The paper presents the lattice setup and its exploration of these heavy four-quark systems.
arxiv-2505-00278:
Lo Pang-Yun Ting and four co-authors build an AI system for chip testing work, in a 2025 paper. In chip factories, failed circuits must be matched to the right engineers for analysis, and poor matching wastes time and money. Earlier software focused on finding or sorting defects, not on who should handle them.

Their system, DeCo, first builds a graph that links defects which fail together, giving each defect a fuller fingerprint even when examples are few. It then builds matching profiles for engineers and tasks, shaped by the graph's local and global patterns. A contrasting step pairs tasks with engineers by skill and current workload, keeping the load fair. On real factory data the system reached the highest success rates in its tests, above eighty percent, and it sometimes spotted engineers who could handle defects new to them.
arxiv-2505-00478:
Subhaditya Bhattacharya and co-authors hunt dark matter through an axion-like middleman in a 2025 paper. Axion-like particles could bridge the dark sector and ordinary matter. Their model couples such a particle to light and to a fermion dark matter candidate.

The team maps where the setup yields the right cosmic abundance of dark matter. Early kinetic decoupling, often ignored, matters in the resonant corner of the map. Indirect searches are weighed for what they can already say. At future electron-positron colliders, the signature is one photon plus missing energy. That variable splits signal from background sharply, they show, because the same light coupling sets the relic count. Sensitivity curves follow.
arxiv-2505-00778:
Chris Bispels and six co-authors asked in 2025 whether two famous families of never-prime multipliers hide numbers built from repeated digits. A Sierpinski number keeps one expression composite for every exponent, and a Riesel number does the same for its twin expression. Repdigits repeat one digit in a chosen base, like 777 in base ten.

The team hunts for such patterned members inside both families and sorts out which bases and lengths can occur. Repeated-digit numbers are rare and rigid, so finding them, or ruling them out, sharpens what is known about these stubborn multiplier sets.
arxiv-2505-00878:
Karan Srivastava and Jonathan Lenchner present SynPAT, a 2025 tool that forges fake physics theories for testing discovery software. Programs that hunt for laws of nature need practice cases, but true theories are few. SynPAT fills the gap by building made-up worlds with known rules.

Each case ships with a set of axioms, a target result that follows from them, and noisy data that fits the result. The tool can also build flawed worlds, where the data clash with the axioms and the solver must fix its base claims. Tests with law-hunting programs show the cases sort strong tools from weak ones fairly.
arxiv-2505-01478: Thomas Chene and co-authors tune a smart radio surface in a 2025 paper. Such a surface holds many small elements that can be angled to steer radio waves, fighting fade and interference. Finding the best setting for all elements by trial would take far too many tests. Their approach learns the setting without any channel knowledge, using a trial and error learning method framed as a shortest path problem. It aims to reach a near best setup in few tests, lifting data rates for the links the surface serves.
arxiv-2505-01778:
Afan Ali, Abdelali Arous, and Hüseyin Arslan published a telecommunications paper in 2025 on signal design for future networks. Two chirp-based schemes are candidates for sixth-generation mobile systems. Both suffer from high peak-to-average power ratios. Large peaks waste energy and strain amplifiers.

The authors propose spreading the data before modulation to smooth peaks. They compare four spreading transforms under one shared approach. The method needs no extra side information for the receiver. It also adds little computing cost, unlike older peak-cutting schemes. Tuning the chirp settings improved resistance to difficult channels. Smoothing the spread signal also cut interference. The paper frames spreading as a cheap, general fix.
arxiv-2505-01878:
Misyura studies gravitational waves past the first, linear approximation in a twenty twenty-five paper. Real waves are weak, so most work treats space-time as flat plus a small ripple. At second order, the ripples themselves act as a source, and new effects can appear.

The author builds a general metric for this case and tracks bundles of paths for both massive and light travelers. For massive paths, the bundle spreads and shears but does not rotate. For light, all three effects vanish. A numeric run in a split space-time scheme finds one more trait: test particles drift slightly along the wave's own direction of travel, a second-order effect only.
arxiv-2505-02478:
Baptiste Coquinot and co-authors show that the walls of tiny fluid channels help carry electric current, in work from 2025. Studies of nanofluidic transport usually apply steady voltage or pressure, missing what happens under alternating drive.

Under oscillating voltage, electrons in the channel wall couple to the ions in the liquid through a capacitive electrochemical link. Past a critical frequency and length, this electron path dominates conduction. The coupling also reshapes electric-field-driven flows, and momentum passing between liquid and wall electrons leaves distinct signatures that depend on the charge carrier's sign. The team builds a combined transport framework, and suggests using alternating drive to probe surfaces and design new channel functions.
arxiv-2505-02578: Oliver Schnetz proves a new identity for Feynman periods in a short 2025 maths paper. Feynman periods are numbers that arise from the diagrams used to compute particle interactions. The new identity acts on cuts that pass through five vertices of completed, primitive diagrams in a standard theory. Schnetz shows the five-twist identity stands apart from the known tools of its kind, since it does not follow from the twist, the Fourier identity, or the Fourier split.
arxiv-2505-02778:
Andrzejewski studies, in a 2025 paper, how the entanglement of quantum fields grows with the size of the region examined. For ordinary matter in flat space, entanglement entropy follows an area law: it scales with the boundary, not the volume. A companion measure tracks how that entropy fluctuates.

The author checks the fluctuation measure on two shapes, a sphere and a strip, finding the same area law. The work then turns to quenches, sudden changes that set the field ringing. Expanding and curved cosmological spaces join the analysis. Comparing surface and volume terms through the ringing tests stories told about how information spreads after a jolt.
arxiv-2505-02978:
Anushka Sharma, Anamitra Pal, Rajasekhar Anguluri, and Tamojit Chakraborty wrote this research paper, published in 2025. It gives power grid operators a practical way to estimate grid inertia, the stored spinning energy that keeps frequency steady when something fails, from ordinary sensor data.

As wind and solar replace spinning generators, inertia shrinks and must be watched live. The method uses ambient readings from phasor units scattered on the grid, plus a split form of the swing equation that governs machine motion. It allows for bounded errors in network data and in the readings themselves. A key trick is spotting stretches when mechanical power input truly stays constant, using knowledge of how plants run. Tests on two standard simulated grids, including versions with renewables, showed accurate estimates of inertia, damping, and power input.
arxiv-2505-03378:
Tasnim Ahmed and co-authors published this paper in 2025. It stress-tests hybrid quantum neural networks, which pair a small quantum circuit with a classical network. Today's quantum hardware is noisy, and the authors ask how two leading designs hold up as noise grows.

They fed five kinds of noise into the circuits, at levels from light to total, and watched image sorting accuracy. One design, QuanNN, stayed strong at low noise but buckled under two noise types at high levels. The other, QCNN, oddly improved under some noise at high levels, beating its own clean score. Other noise types wore it down step by step. The mixed picture shows noise is not simply bad. The authors say these maps should guide error-fixing work for near-term quantum machines.
arxiv-2505-03678:
Show a language model a drawing of a network and its answers depend on how the network was drawn. Walter Didimo, Fabrizio Montecchiani, and Tommaso Piselli measured those dependencies in this 2025 paper. Models increasingly get graphs as pictures rather than as lists. Layout style, drawing neatness, and the wording of the question were varied in turn.

Three research questions organized the experiments. Choosing the right layout family mattered a great deal. Drawings optimized for human readability also helped the model. Picking the best prompting style proved tricky but decisive. The lesson cuts against treating the picture as neutral: presentation is part of the input. Graph tools for AI should design drawings for machine eyes too.
arxiv-2505-03878:
Five authors present a 2025 method for running real-time scattering tests on quantum computers. Their work uses Hamiltonian Truncation, a way to shrink a large field model by keeping only the low-energy states of a simpler base model. The test case is a scalar field in one space dimension plus time.

Wave-like packets are first built by slowly turning the weak free field into the stronger mixed field. The team tried this step on an IonQ trapped-ion device and checked it in simulations. Results show packet motion, overlap effects, and new particles after a hit, with far fewer qubits than grid methods but with deep circuits as a cost.
arxiv-2505-04278:
Weiwei Ye, Zhuopeng Xu, and Ning Gui build NsDiff, a 2025 diffusion forecaster whose uncertainty can breathe over time. Standard diffusion forecasters assume a fixed noise level, but real series, driven by physics and outside shocks, get more or less predictable as conditions change.

Their framework swaps the fixed noise model for a location-scale one and pre-trains an estimator of the mean and spread at each step. An uncertainty-aware noise schedule then matches noise to the moment's true uncertainty. Across nine real and synthetic data sets, NsDiff beat existing probabilistic forecasters. Code is public.
arxiv-2505-04478:
Pairs that fleet through a cold film can be herded one way by a wave field, if the film's own melt mark is bent in space. Parafilo, Kovalev, and Savenko draw that herd in a 2025 study of a thin film at the cold edge. The flow they birth runs square to the wave's push, a hall drift of fleet pairs.

The drift is a twin order ware: it needs both the field and the bent melt mark. Round wave light steers the drift's aim. Near the melt edge, the drift's growth with heat span runs steep, far past the known fleet ware's. That steep run makes the drift swell hard at the edge. The team pitch it as a new cold tool.
arxiv-2505-04778:
Ali Taani and co-authors review how pairs of neutron stars form and what their orbits reveal. A neutron star is the dense core left when a huge star explodes. In a pair, the second star's birth blast shapes the orbit the pair keeps. Their 2025 analysis sorts pairs by orbit traits to tell apart two kinds of blast.

Gentle blasts, fed by electron capture, tend to leave tight, near-round orbits and small kicks. Core-collapse blasts more often leave wide, stretched orbits. The authors find a mass line near which the gentle kind gives way to the stronger kind. They also weigh how mass loss and the galaxy's pull shape each pair. The chart they build may help read the past of new pairs found by surveys.
arxiv-2505-05078:
Silvan Peter, Patricia Hu, and Gerhard Widmer present in 2025 a music tracking system that follows a live piano performance in a score by working in symbols, not just sound. Older systems warp the audio against an audio form of the score and had hit a plateau. Their system first transcribes the live audio into notes in real time, then tracks those notes against the score with a new symbol level tracker.

Compared with a like audio only system, the mixed approach gave smaller tracking errors and succeeded more often. The authors argue that turning sound into symbols early, even with imperfect transcription, makes the tracking task cleaner. The method may help tools for practice, teaching, and live accompaniment.
arxiv-2505-05278:
David Johansson, Janne Nurminen, and Mikko Salo tackle an inverse task for a class of curved equations in two thousand twenty-five. The task is to learn the hidden rule inside the equation from tests made only at the edge of a region. The rule here can depend on both place and the unknown value itself.

They show the rule is fixed, apart from one known kind of freedom, by those edge tests near a known solution. The advance lies in how rough the rule and the solution may be. Past results needed smooth data, while real tests are often rough. Their proof gives the same claim under much weaker terms.
arxiv-2505-05578:
Lorenzo Malanga and six co-authors show a trap in how we read the life of discs of gas and dust around young stars, where planets form. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Two main views of how such discs fade have not yet been split by what we see. The team built fake groups of discs and let them age under one view, where drag and light from the star wear them down. Light discs vanish fast. The discs left then look, on the whole, heavier, even though each one lost mass. This seeming rise is a bias of who survives. The trap holds with or without links to the star's mass.
arxiv-2505-06078:
Yuta Murotani, Tomohiro Fujimoto, and Ryusuke Matsunaga unify theories of a light-driven Hall effect in a 2025 physics study. When light and a bias field act on a material, a sideways photocurrent can appear. Two mechanisms compete to explain it: Berry curvature created by the light itself, tied to topological change, and an asymmetry in how light-born carriers move, tied to the field.

Earlier work separated the two except in numerical studies. The authors build one theory covering both field-induced and light-induced curvature effects. A unified account helps experimentalists assign measured currents to the right cause when engineering optical responses.
arxiv-2505-06278:
Tongfei Bian, Mathieu Chollet, and Tanaya Guha address how robots read social scenes in a 2025 paper. A robot needs to read body, face, and gaze cues from its own view. Past models are often too heavy for real time and fail when some cues are missing.

The authors train a large teacher model on many cue types at once. They then pass what it learns to a small student model that uses body pose alone. On two public data sets, the student beat rival methods by a clear margin. It stayed strong even when much of its input was spoiled, and it ran much faster.
arxiv-2505-06678:
Zijun Zhan and co-authors design robust contracts for edge AI content services used in teleoperation, published in 2025. Remote operation needs AI-generated content delivered with very low delay, so services run at the network edge. But service quality is uncertain, and operators cannot see how much capacity each provider really has left.

Contract theory handles the hidden information side, while distributionally robust optimization handles the quality uncertainty. Joining the two is the paper's main extension of contract theory. The hard joint problem is reshaped into an equivalent two-level form that can actually be solved. A block coordinate descent method then derives reward schemes that stay robust. Simulations on a teleoperation platform test the schemes, aiming at incentives that keep working even when conditions shift.
arxiv-2505-07178:
Yuri Nakao asks who answers for the outputs of text-and-image machines in a 2025 paper. These systems are so tangled that even experts cannot trace why a given output came out. The paper sorts past work on openness and answerability, and argues that openness alone does not give answerability, though it can help.

If full openness proves out of reach, the tech acts like a made nature: a force we live with but cannot steer. The paper then borrows the play-it-safe rule used for such risks. A forum where the public takes part is the last piece the author calls for.
arxiv-2505-07278:
Maksymilian Wojnar and co-authors published a 2025 paper on scheduling Wi-Fi transmissions when many access points share the air. As Wi-Fi grows denser, letting every device grab the channel at random no longer gives fast, steady service. A coming Wi-Fi standard lets access points coordinate. In the variant studied here, several devices send at once on the same channel, with power tuned to limit interference.

The hard part is choosing which devices send together, and at what settings. The authors first build an exact model that finds the best possible schedule, for speed or for fairness. That model is too slow for live use, so they add a learning method that probes the network and adapts. In simulations and on real hardware, the learning method raised total throughput by about eighty percent over legacy Wi-Fi. It did so without cutting any station's chances to send.
arxiv-2505-07378:
Yaqiao Li, working solo, proves that some questions in additive combinatorics can never be settled by any algorithm, in a 2025 paper. Many deep results in the field reduce to polynomial inequalities about how dense a set of numbers is and how much its sums overlap. Graph theorists had already shown the parallel question for graph patterns to be undecidable.

Adapting those methods, plus algebra and Fourier tools, Li proves two undecidability theorems for subset densities and additive energies. No general procedure can certify every such inequality, however long it runs. The result redraws the border of the field: some truths there can only be reached case by case, never by a universal machine.
arxiv-2505-07878:
Eteri Samsonadze proves, with elementary methods alone, that certain power-sum equations cannot be solved in whole numbers, in this 2025 paper. The catalog's title and author line are in Russian; the head gives the title in English and governs. The equations ask for nonnegative integers whose n-th powers sum to a prescribed value, a family in the tradition of Fermat's problem.

Samsonadze's conditions turn on the prime makeup of one coefficient. When its prime power factors satisfy a divisibility condition involving Euler's totient function, the equation has no solution at all. A sharper result follows when the coefficient also sits between two natural bounds. A second theorem handles a like shape whose right side is built from primes obeying similar totient conditions, for exponents of three or more. The paper adds clean sufficient tests to the ancient question of which Diophantine equations are impossible.
arxiv-2505-07978:
Anchal Gupta and nine co-authors demonstrate control of plasma detachment in the KSTAR fusion device after its upgrade to a tungsten divertor. The divertor takes the exhaust heat, and even tungsten can sputter and contaminate the core if heat flux runs too high. Detachment, lifting the hot plasma off the plates, is the standard remedy.

One method steered detachment using an attachment fraction estimated from Langmuir probe currents in the divertor. The second used DivControlNN, a neural surrogate of two-dimensional simulations, running live to estimate heat flux and adjust impurity gas. Both approaches worked in experiment. The paper also shares controller tuning lessons aimed at future burning plasma devices.
arxiv-2505-08078:
Perry Dong, Suvir Mirchandani, Dorsa Sadigh, and Chelsea Finn ask what helps robots learn from batches of self-collected data, in a paper from 2025. Robots that gather their own practice data could improve with little human help. In practice, many methods fail to gain much from such data or stall at weak performance.

The team varied three choices in a broad set of tests: method type, how actions are picked from a policy, and how flexible the policy is. Methods guided by value scores beat those based on copying alone. Picking the best sampled action proved key, and flexible policies beat stiff ones. Their proposed method builds on all three lessons.
arxiv-2505-08278:
Álvaro Martín-Cortinas and co-authors present work from two thousand twenty-five on voice conversion using self-supervised features. Voice conversion changes who a recording seems to come from while keeping the words. Trained systems often need costly matched recordings, and separating content from speaker traits is hard, since pitch patterns can leak or be lost.

The team feeds combined features from self-supervised speech models, plus a speaker embedding, into a sound generator trained to rebuild the input. In zero-shot tests, where speakers are new, the method kept the source speaker's content and rhythm of speech. It matched the speaker likeness of a system based on phonetic features. The approach suits uses from anonymization to personal speech synthesis.
arxiv-2505-08578:
Olivier Pasche, Henry Lam, and Sebastian Engelke sharpen forecast intervals for rare disasters in a 2025 paper. Conformal prediction wraps any black-box model in intervals with a stated coverage promise. When regulators demand very high confidence, as for floods or market crashes, the usual method returns useless, endless intervals if calibration data are scarce.

Their fix marries conformal methods with extreme value statistics, the math of rare events. The new intervals stay finite and honest at high confidence, and can ride on any good extreme quantile model. A weighted version handles data that drift over time. Simulations and a flood risk case show the gains, offering officials intervals they can actually use.
arxiv-2505-08678:
Precup and Stan pin down where critical points sit in Banach spaces, and show that more than one can exist, with the Nehari manifold, in work from twenty twenty-five. To find many answers inside ring-shaped parts of a cone once took heavy warping proofs. Their route pairs Nehari tools with the cone form of the Birkhoff-Kellogg invariant-direction theorem. The pair gives a much more plain path to both points.

The points are placed in plain terms, inside annular parts of a cone. A worked case on p-Laplacian boundary value problems shows the route in use. It does without Ekeland's rule and without squeeze-and-stretch gear at all. The one must-have part is a variational build, an energy-like score. Other classes of problems with that build should gain in the same way.
arxiv-2505-08778:
Guichard and four co-authors grew solutions to reasoning puzzles in this paper from twenty twenty-five. The ARC benchmark asks for the rule behind a few example grids, a task people find easy and AI finds hard. Their approach uses neural cellular automata, grids of cells that update by local rules. Growth-like dynamics echo how living systems develop.

One version adds hidden memory cells to the basic automaton. The developmental style is meant to build answers rather than recall them. Early results, the authors report, rival a leading chatbot on some tasks at a fraction of the cost. The paper frames the work as a proof of concept. It argues development is a promising path toward flexible reasoning.
arxiv-2505-08878:
Dor Tsur and colleagues analyzed text watermarking for large language models in 2025. Watermarks hide a detectable signal in machine-written text so the text can later be identified as machine-made, ideally without hurting its quality. The authors study the simplest one-shot setting, where a single piece of text must carry the signal.

Framing the problem as hypothesis testing with side information, they work out the basic trade-off between how reliably a watermark can be detected and how much the text must be distorted. A central choice is how the secret side information pairs with a random split of the model's vocabulary. They identify the best pairing strategy, give a formula for its detection rate, and compare the scheme with the theoretical best in numerical tests.
arxiv-2505-09278:
Rick van Essen and co-authors present a 2025 paper on a farm drone that learns to hunt scattered objects over fields. Drones gather crop data well but drain their packs fast, and full sweeps waste flight when finds are patchy. Their planner learns by trial to find the most objects on the shortest path, guided by a rough map from a high first pass.

Training ran in a simulator with plant layouts, flight moves, and flawed sight built in. In sim tests the path shrank by more than half against full sweeps, with a mild recall cost. Real flights found fewer, and map quality drove the gap.
arxiv-2505-09478:
Eduard Kuric, Peter Demcak, and Matus Krajcovic built a tool that simulates card sorting with language models, in this 2025 study. Designers use card sorting to learn how users group content in their heads, but human rounds are slow. Their simulator asks a model to sort the cards and gives quick, automated feedback while a study is still being shaped.

The team checked the mimicry against twenty-eight real studies with 1,399 sorters in all. Agreement scores were good overall, though the model's grouping maps differed from human ones in places, a gap they tie to its top-down style. More cards and tanglier labels also dulled the match. The authors back model sorting as a useful first pass, not a replacement.
arxiv-2505-09778:
Mohammad Khalafi and Digvijay Boob present a first-order algorithm for two-level inequality problems with random data, in a 2025 methods paper. The problem class, called bilevel variational inequality, covers many tasks where one optimization sits inside another. Their method, R-OpEx, blends a smoothing trick with an extrapolation step borrowed from operator methods. It runs in a single loop and needs just one look at each operator per round.

The team proves cost bounds for the method across smooth and rough cases. Batching tricks cut the cost at the outer level when the inner level is smooth. Stronger assumptions cut the cost further. Computer tests back the theory. The authors claim the first study of the rough, random case with guarantees this strong.
arxiv-2505-10378:
Ashkenazi-Golan, Mergoni Cecchelli, and Plumb study what happens when all players in a game update their choices at once, each picking a best reply to the last round. Their 2025 paper works with potential games, a class where one shared function tracks every player's gains, with payoffs drawn at random.

For two players with many actions, the joint play quickly settles into a two-step cycle. That cycle sits near two distinct stable outcomes without landing on either. With three or more players, simulations show fast arrival at a stable outcome in most runs. The pattern survives when payoffs are merely close to a shared function. Against gradient-based learning, the best-reply rule reached outcomes of like payoff much faster.
arxiv-2505-10578:
Yunji Feng and co-authors build a drone system that maps rooms in 3D from plain photos in a 2025 computing paper. Lidar gear does this job well but costs and weighs too much for small drones. Their framework, ExploreGS, flies, photographs, and rebuilds the scene on board in real time. A word-bag model of image features keeps the processing light enough for the drone's own computer.

The scene is stored as a field of soft 3D blobs, a format that renders fast and trains quickly. Tests in simulation and in real rooms matched the quality of heavier rivals. Low overhead matters most where the drone must explore and map in one flight, such as disaster zones.
arxiv-2505-10678:
A controller that steers a machine and learns its physics at the same time is the goal of this 2025 paper by Rebecca Hart and co-authors. Neural networks often steer well but never truly learn the system, unless the motion keeps exciting every mode. The authors remove that requirement with a concurrent learning scheme that replays stored data alongside live data.

New update rules adjust every layer of the network at once, and a stability proof keeps tracking and learning errors near zero under a milder excitation condition. In simulations, the method improved its model of the system by forty to seventy percent over the baseline. Tracking quality and effort stayed about the same. Off-path test points showed even larger learning gains.
arxiv-2505-10778:
Rafael Costa and Ginaldo Sá study regularity for dead-core problems in this 2025 mathematics paper. The equations are fully nonlinear and elliptic, with a Hamiltonian term that can degenerate or blow up as the gradient nears zero. Non-negative solutions may vanish on whole regions, called plateau or dead-core zones. The free boundary, where the solution lifts off zero, is the focus. The authors prove that solutions grow away from that boundary in a regular way.

Under stated conditions on the exponents, the growth rate they find is optimal. A non-degeneracy result supports the sharpness claim. Two uses follow: solutions stay positive where expected, and the boundary of the coincidence set has controlled size in the Hausdorff sense. The work extends free boundary theory to operators with singular gradient terms.
arxiv-2505-11178:
Yixin Wan and Kai-Wei Chang present a benchmark and feedback method for compositional text-to-image generation, in their 2025 arXiv paper. Image models render single subjects well but stumble on prompts with several objects, attributes and spatial relations. Their benchmark, CompAlign, holds nine hundred complex prompts stressing number counts and 3D spatial layouts.

Their evaluation framework, CompQuest, breaks each prompt into atomic sub-questions and has a multimodal model answer each one about a generated image, giving fine-grained feedback. That feedback then serves as preference signals to train diffusion models. Testing nine image models showed compositional tasks, especially 3D spatial ones, remain hard, and open models trail closed ones.
arxiv-2505-11278:
Fabian Falck and co-authors look at image-making models in 2025 from a new angle: how they treat fine detail versus broad shapes. These diffusion models learn by adding noise to data and then removing it. In the frequency view the team uses, fine detail sits in high bands and broad shapes in low bands, and real data fade fast toward the high bands.

Standard training noise corrupts fine detail much sooner than broad shapes, so models build broad shapes first. The team shows this skew breaks a key math assumption and hurts fine detail quality. Their alternate process noises all bands at the same rate. It did far better where fine detail matters most and matched standard results on common image tests.
arxiv-2505-11378:
Alexander Kim and Charlotte Botha classify singing registers in male pop recordings with machine learning, in a 2025 paper. Singers struggle to place their voice around the break between chest and head registers. Pop styles blur that boundary with mixed textures. Their methods read texture features from spectrogram images. Two classifier types were trained and compared.

Both a support vector machine and a neural network classified registers consistently. Results held across the tested recordings. The team also built a companion analysis tool for singers. It aims to give feedback during practice and study. Broader voice types and genres are future targets. Reliable register labels could aid teachers and students alike. The paper argues texture alone carries strong register clues. Automated ears may soon coach technique at scale.
arxiv-2505-11478:
Mingxuan Li, Junzhe Zhang, and Elias Bareinboim built a learning method in two thousand twenty-five that stays safe when past data are biased by hidden factors. Agents often learn from old logs, but unseen confounders can skew those logs and mislead standard methods such as deep Q-learning. Their method hunts for a policy that stays safe in the worst case that still fits the data.

Built on a celebrated deep Q-network, the method shapes rewards on its own from the confounded data. Tested on twelve rigged Atari games, it beat the standard method in every game where hidden bias and input mismatch were present. The work aids learning from real-world records.
arxiv-2505-11678:
Yan Chen, Zheng Tan, Jose Blanchet, and Hanzhang Qin build a statistical test for judging whether an algorithm is fair enough without being useless, in a 2025 paper. Fairness rules in lending, marketing, and healthcare often cost accuracy, and strict parity demands may be more than a situation requires. Their framework tests approximate fairness and utility together: outcomes must stay close to a demographic parity standard while overall benefit stays above a chosen floor.

The test statistic comes from a Wasserstein projection, a way of measuring the smallest change to the data that would meet the standard. This lets auditors tell whether a fairness-utility trade-off is built into the algorithm or is just noise in the sample. The authors show the test is computable and readable, apply it to several real datasets, and note it extends to broader settings. The paper reframes fairness auditing as hypothesis testing.
arxiv-2505-12178:
Ayush Khaitan, Ishan Mata, and Bhargav Narayanan prove a surprising inequality in this 2025 arXiv paper in combinatorics. The setting joins two classic objects: elementary symmetric polynomials, which average products of numbers, and random permutations, the shuffles of a list. The fixed point measure weights each shuffle by the numbers sitting in the spots the shuffle leaves unmoved.

Under that weighting, the authors show the average product over fixed points beats a certain average over all pairs of spots. The bound cannot be improved, since cases exist where equality nearly holds. To prove it, they build a set of differential operators that drive a steady flow, pushing the quantities until the inequality becomes clear. Such exact results are rare in this corner of probability, and the flow method may serve other problems.
arxiv-2505-12278:
Zhengyi Luo and co-authors train simulated human-like robots that learn to see, search, and handle objects with no inside tips. Their 2025 paper gives the robots only first-person vision to define each task. No exact object places or shapes are fed in. One learned policy must reach, grasp, place, and work jointed objects around a home. Training runs from scratch with reward-based learning in a simulated world.

Search moves arose on their own, as the robots learned to look around for what they need. Hand and eye work also lined up in a human-like way. The authors argue that vision-led control plus rich tasks can close the loop between seeing and acting.
arxiv-2505-12678:
Anson Chen forecasts a new way to test whether the universe looks the same in every direction, in a 2025 paper. Measurements of the cosmic dipole, a slight one-sided pattern in the sky, clash between early- and late-universe data. Part of the pattern comes from our own motion, but an inbuilt tilt of the universe could add to it and even mimic dark energy.

Chen looks to golden dark sirens: nearby mergers of compact objects whose ripple signals pin down their home galaxies. Ten years of watching with today's detectors would catch too few of them. A network with more than one next-generation detector, though, could pin the dipole down hard.
arxiv-2505-12778:
Cho and co-authors propose a way to build quantum bits using MRI methods. Their 2025 paper reviews past NMR routes to quantum computing, then sets out a new one. Their qubits come from water protons, shaped by magnetic gradients like those in a scanner. Local reverse gradients carve out small zones, each with a steady field and its own frequency.

The setup runs at room temperature apart from the main magnet, which matches a standard scanner. Fifty years of scanner pulse methods can be reused for control and signal work. One use is spin purification, a cleanup step for quantum states. The authors frame MRI hardware as a ready platform for a fresh kind of quantum machine, distinct from spectroscopy routes.
arxiv-2505-13178:
Gas in the sky cools by light and crash, and the cool curve can tip the gas to break up or to hold. Amanda Stricklan, Tim Waters, and James Klimchuk map where that tip lives in a 2025 study. Their map is built on a famed cool bar, set by a past rule for the ill's edge, and stretched to count heat spread.

No full map of the ill's space for off balance gas had been made. Their map gives one, and shows a twin ill, the crash cool ill, can rule where the old ill is held by heat spread. Loop sims of sky rain bear it out: rain loops sit in the crash ill's zone, not the old one's. The map is a guide for all thin gas sims.
arxiv-2505-13278:
Daniel Weiner and Raj Korpan present a task assignment system for building robots in a 2025 paper. Modular construction makes parts off site and assembles them on site, a process that needs tight coordination. Robots with different skills must be matched to tasks well for the work to run smoothly.

Their framework rates each robot against each task in a suitability table, using profiles of what each robot can do. Six voting methods, aided by a large language model, then pick the best robot for each task. A search method plans paths so robots do not collide during assembly. The design aims at faster, more exact building. The authors note that tests across varied simulated building scenes are still under way.
arxiv-2505-13378:
The SXS Collaboration presents its third catalog of binary black hole simulations in a 2025 paper, with Mark Scheel and many co-authors listed. Computer runs of two black holes circling and merging help scientists read real signals from space. The group uses fast spectral methods in a code built for extreme space time settings. This update nearly doubles the size of the older catalog.

The catalog now holds three thousand seven hundred fifty six configurations, up from two thousand eighteen. It covers spinning pairs that precess, with mass ratios up to eight and strong spins, at near zero orbital stretch. It also adds runs at higher mass ratios with moderate spin. More than two hundred fifty runs cover pairs on stretched, eccentric orbits, a part of the space that was sparse before.
arxiv-2505-13478:
Turning data structures into text so they can be stored or sent is a daily act in computing, and the format chosen has lasting effects. A twenty-one author team surveys the main text formats, JSON, XML, YAML, and CSV, comparing their structure, readability, size, and fit for different jobs. The survey also covers how reading and writing actually work, including parsing methods and the role of schemas that define a document's shape.

To make the trade-offs concrete, the team presents example performance tables that compare the formats on writing and reading speed and on the size of the output. The discussion weighs verbosity against clarity and machine speed against human ease. The authors aim to give developers a single reference for picking a format with open eyes, rather than by habit, when building systems that exchange data as text.
arxiv-2505-13778:
Guoheng Sun, Ziyao Wang, and their co-authors tackle a billing trust problem in commercial AI services. Their 2025 paper explains that top language models now reason in hidden steps before answering. Providers hide those steps, show only the final answer, and charge for the unseen tokens, which often form most of the bill.

Users have no way to check the count, and a provider could pad it with cheap fake tokens. Their framework, CoIn, audits both the count and the sense of hidden tokens. A hash tree built from token fingerprints verifies how many tokens ran. A matching step checks that the hidden steps stay relevant to the task. The work aims to make opaque AI services accountable for what they charge.
arxiv-2505-14178:
Xiang Zhang and co-authors argue that how a language model chops text into tokens can cap its reasoning, in a 2025 paper. Tokenization is the first step a model takes, long before it thinks through a problem. Common schemes merge chunks of text into single tokens. That can blur the small units a math or logic task turns on.

The authors coin the term Token Awareness for how well a token split lines up with those units. They test models on sums and symbol tasks with varied token splits. Even with step-by-step prompts, poor splits led to failure. Clean, atom-by-atom formats let a small model beat a far larger one. The lesson is that reasoning skill rests on token design, not just model size.
arxiv-2505-14278:
Xuan Mao, Meng Liu, and Yuxiang Li pinned down in 2025 the exact mass at which a colony of moving cells collapses into a spike. In chemotaxis models, cells chase a chemical they release, and past a threshold mass they pile up in finite time. An older model on a disk had a known threshold that the team confirms with a cleaner comparison method.

They then apply the method to a newer three-part model in four dimensions. Below a set mass, solutions stay smooth forever. Above it, some starting states collapse into a sharp spike in finite time. Sharp thresholds tell biologists when crowding turns dangerous.
arxiv-2505-14378:
The hot gas between galaxies in a cluster, called the intracluster medium, churns with turbulence that is hard to measure. Alexeï Molin and co-authors prepared in 2025 for a future X-ray telescope, NewAthena, whose spectrometer will map that gas in fine detail. This fourth paper in a series tests whether simulation-based inference can recover the traits of that churning hidden in the data.

The method trains neural networks on simulated data so they can infer the gas velocity spectrum directly. Tests on mock data recovered the key values well. The authors also show that simpler methods make results look more certain than they are, because sample variance is severe. Advanced modeling is needed to read the coming data honestly.
arxiv-2505-14478:
Geirnaert, Kappel, and Kidmose compare three ways to record brain waves for hearing aids that follow attention in twenty twenty-five. In a noisy room, a listener must pick one voice out of many. Future aids could read brain waves to learn which voice that is. Scalp sensors work best but are bulky and hard to wear all day.

The team recorded scalp, around ear, and in ear signals at the same time from the same people. A simple decoder named the right speaker most often from scalp data. Ear based sets scored lower, but still well above chance. Adding just a few scalp sensors lifted ear scores a lot. Comfort and accuracy trade off, they conclude.
arxiv-2505-14678: Gareth Speight and Scott Zimmerman prove results about curves in special curved spaces called Carnot groups, in a 2025 paper. They show that if a curve bends only within allowed directions, that freedom still lets two classic tools work. One extends a curve smoothly beyond its patch, and the other swaps it for a smooth curve that stays close on most of its length. As a use case, any level curve in the Engel group must share positive length with a smooth level curve.
