arxiv-2505-14778:
Allison Lin, Maria Charisi, and Zoltán Haiman published this astronomy paper in 2025. Pairs of supermassive black holes should betray themselves by making their host quasars brighten and dim on a regular cycle. Searches usually rely on the Lomb-Scargle periodogram, a standard tool tuned to smooth sine-wave signals. Simulations, though, predict spikier, sawtooth-shaped pulses. The team tested how badly that mismatch hurts detection.

They built fake quasar light curves with realistic noise and injected both sine and sawtooth signals. They mimicked an older survey's data and the coming Rubin Observatory survey. Even sine signals were recovered less than half the time. Sawtooth recovery collapsed to about nine percent in survey-like data and near one percent in the cleaner sets. The authors conclude past searches missed most binaries, and future surveys need better tools than the standard periodogram.
arxiv-2505-14878:
Tatsuo Kobayashi, Hiroshi Okada, and Hajime Otsuka build neutrino mass models from an unusual symmetry rule, in a 2025 paper. Neutrinos have tiny masses that standard theory does not explain. One route generates those masses through quantum loop effects. The authors impose selection rules from a fusion algebra instead. Fields in the model are labeled by algebra elements.

The rules hold only at the basic interaction level. Loop corrections then break them softly, which is exactly what tiny masses need. A leftover symmetry from the algebra guards dark matter stability. That guard is usually added by hand in such models. Assigning fields in a family-dependent way yields interesting mass patterns. The paper ties three puzzles together: neutrino mass, dark matter, and family structure. Each follows from the same algebraic choice.
arxiv-2505-15278:
Fernando Ballesta-Yagüe eases a rule for weights on curves in a 2025 math note. The weights sit on a Lipschitz curve, a curve with bounded slope. Past work showed such a weight can stretch to the region above the curve as an analytic map.

A past class of good stretches added a Smirnov type extra rule. The note proves that rule is the same as a simple size rule on the stretch. So the extra rule can be dropped from the class. With the leaner class, the author proves new facts about weighted Hardy spaces. Those spaces help solve a classic edge value task in the region.
arxiv-2505-15478:
Six researchers wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five on spotting when a wireless link has a clear path. High-frequency links fail easily when buildings or objects block the line of sight. Knowing the state of the path in real time helps keep links reliable, but measuring it everywhere is costly.

The team trained AI models on data made by a network digital twin, a software copy of the network that can simulate radio waves. They compare training strategies for one general model. Their approach beat the best prior model, above all when the signal was weak. It also shrank the input the model needs while keeping its accuracy.
arxiv-2505-15778:
Zhen Zhang and seven co-authors present a new way for large language models to reason through hard problems. Today's models think in single words or word pieces, picking one at each step. That forces thought down one narrow path at a time. The authors instead let the model think in soft concept tokens, blends of many word meanings at once, which better match how people mull over fluid ideas.

Their method needs no extra training and can be added to existing models. Each soft token holds several meanings together, so the model in effect weighs many reasoning paths at once before settling. On math and coding tests, the method raised accuracy by up to about two and a half points while using up to a fifth fewer tokens. The outputs stayed readable, too. The authors argue the approach lifts a built-in limit of word-by-word thought.
arxiv-2505-15978:
Zeynab Kaseb, Matthias Möller, Pedro P. Vergara, and Peter Palensky wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on running power grids with quantum-style machines. Power flow studies work out how electricity moves through a grid, and the optimal form also picks the cheapest safe settings. The authors recast both tasks as puzzle-like problems that annealers can solve.

The paper builds on their earlier quantum power flow method and adds a new one for the optimal case, written as binary problems with no extra constraints. They test both on grids from four buses up to 1,354 buses, using a D-Wave quantum machine, a hybrid solver, and two Fujitsu systems. The methods found valid answers and scaled in a hopeful way, though hard, ill-posed cases still need care.
arxiv-2505-16578: Hikaru Kawai and Nobuyoshi Ohta revisit a dispute about whether basic constants of nature change with energy scale, a behavior called running. Some claimed the standard beta function gives the wrong running in certain theories. Others claimed the cosmological constant and Newton's coupling do not run at all. Their 2025 note argues the trouble comes from tying the scale choice to momentum in a fixed way. A better choice of scale restores the correct running. Running can also be discussed on curved spacetime, answering the claim about the two constants.
arxiv-2505-16678:
Jimin Bai, Peter Keim, and Matteo Baggioli tracked shear waves freezing out of a two-dimensional colloid in a 2025 paper. Theory from Maxwell and Frenkel says liquids lose their shear waves at short wavelengths when they melt, opening a gap in the wave spectrum. Simulations agreed, but experiments across a gradual glass transition were missing.

The team measured the wave spectrum directly as their colloidal monolayer turned glassy. The gap opened continuously, right where the static stiffness vanished and the glass transition began. Shear relaxation times extracted from the data followed the classic super-Arrhenius law of glass formers. The authors present the result as direct experimental proof of the Maxwell-Frenkel picture.
arxiv-2505-16878:
Michael Levine presents a 2025 algorithm for mixture models whose parts lean on each other. A mixture reads a crowd as a blend of hidden groups. When the traits in each group move together, a copula, a link device, must join them. Past solvers either lacked a sure climb or worked by chance. The new MM method climbs a smoothed, penalized fit score at every step, never down.

Proof covers both the score's climb and the path of the guesses it makes. Runs on fake and real data match the best past solver. Monotone climbs make runs easier to trust and to stop. Such mixtures serve risk, gene, and market work where parts refuse to move alone.
arxiv-2505-16978:
Tang and co-authors test whether large language models can write formal grammars from just a few examples. Grammars underpin parsing and structured output, yet model skill at inferring them was unmeasured. Their 2025 paper builds a set of 540 grammar challenges, each with a small set of fitting and non fitting examples, and scores eight models with six metrics.

Current models proved weak at the task. The team then adds HyGenar, a hybrid genetic algorithm steered by a language model, which breeds and mutates candidate grammars toward the examples. The method substantially improved both the form and the meaning match of generated grammars across the models tested. The authors offer the dataset and method as tools for structured generation research.
arxiv-2505-17278:
Elisa G Vergamini and co-authors describe a test bench built to judge how robot joints handle physical contact, in a 2025 paper. A catalog record lists the work under a project code, but the head gives the plain title and author list used here. Robots that work beside people need to control not force or speed alone, but the relation between them, called impedance.

The bench mixes straight and rotating motion, and accepts electric or hydraulic drives, with loads the user defines. It was built to be free of play and highly reliable, so teams can validate models of joint behavior and compare controllers fairly. The paper details the mechanical, electrical, and hydraulic choices behind it. Similar benches exist in many labs, but the authors stress this one's mix of versatility and trustworthiness.
arxiv-2505-17378:
Can a material's core state be changed just by the light cage it sits in, with no light shone in? Itai Keren and co-authors test that thought in 2025 with a flat crystal that traps light waves in a tight space. They lay that crystal on a molecular superconductor whose key stretch mode matches the cage's trapped tones.

Fine light maps backed sims that show the cage tones and the stretch mode do link up. Force scans then found the flow with no loss ran far weak near the join than deep in the stuff. Cage swaps that miss the tone match showed no such fade. The team reads the fade as a cage made shift in the ground state. Dark cages may be a new dial for quantum stuff.
arxiv-2505-17778:
Yu Xie, Jielei Zhang, and others generate realistic text inside scene images without any optical character recognition crutch in a 2025 computer vision study. Posters, signs, and packaging in synthetic images often carry garbled lettering, and current generators lean on extra conditioning modules fed by large annotated corpora, notably for multiple languages. Their diffusion transformer takes a leaner route.

Dropping the auxiliary modules while keeping glyph accuracy is the central claim under test. High-fidelity scene text matters for advertising mock-ups, film props, and training data for reading systems, where one wrong character ruins the illusion.
arxiv-2505-17878:
Matthias Grätsch studies families of functions with bounded generalized Schwarzian derivatives in this 2025 math paper. The Schwarzian derivative measures how far a function bends away from the simplest fractional maps. Bounding a generalized form of it turns out to control how wildly a whole family of functions can behave.

Grätsch shows such families are quasi-normal, meaning they stay close to the tidy behavior of normal families. Related families built from derivatives and their logarithms get similar results. A new formula for the generalized derivative yields extra findings for locally one-to-one functions and for entire functions. The classical case sits inside the framework as one special choice.
arxiv-2505-18178:
Min Namgung, Yijun Lin, JangHyeon Lee, and Yao-Yi Chiang present a method to learn compact descriptions of geographic regions from many data types, in work from 2025. Region learning helps analysts read complex traits of a place. Past methods use contrast between two data types and keep only what they share.

That shared only view drops details unique to each data type, which can matter for a task. The authors factor the data into shared and unique parts. Extending that split past two data types explodes the number of goals. Their method injects cross modal knowledge to keep the split workable. Paired views of a region teach the model.
arxiv-2505-18278:
Rabab Alkhalifa and co-authors review ways to solve the Traveling Salesman Problem with many processors at once, in a 2025 survey. The problem asks for the shortest tour through a set of stops, and it grows hard very fast as stops are added. The review sorts methods into exact ones, quick rule-based ones, broad search methods, and mixed ones that blend ideas.

The authors also add scores tied to each task type, so mixed and adaptive solvers can be judged on fair terms. They close by naming gaps: deep learning links, quantum-inspired ideas, and shared test setups that others can repeat. The survey serves readers who plan routes in shipping, transport, and smart systems.
arxiv-2505-18478:
Lucas Tecot, Di Luo, and Cho-Jui Hsieh write a 2025 paper on quantum computing. Quantum circuit classifiers sort data using circuits whose settings can be tuned by training. Noise in those settings is a chief barrier to trust in near-term quantum machines.

The team gives a training theory and method with proof that the result resists noise in the settings. The method links to evolution strategies, a classic search approach from computing. It needs only small changes to common training tools and fits many circuit types. Tests on sorting quantum phases show the approach works in practice. The authors frame it as a step toward quantum tools that stay sound on real, noisy hardware.
arxiv-2505-18578:
Celia González-Sánchez and co-authors present a 2025 physics paper on layered devices that mix superconductivity with a magnetic crystal. Such stacks are a hunting ground for new quantum phases, since the two orders usually fight each other. The team built junctions by sandwiching a magnetic layer between two superconducting flakes.

Single junctions behaved like interference devices, the kind normally made by looping two junctions together. The authors trace that surprise to the way the magnetic layer's spin texture plays against the superconductors on both sides. Their reading rests on how the current through the device responds, and it points to edge states inside the stack.
arxiv-2505-18878:
Kung-Hsiang Huang and co-authors published a benchmark paper in 2025 testing how well AI agents handle real business software work. Customer relationship platforms run sales and service for most companies, yet realistic public test data is rare, so earlier benchmarks felt artificial. The team expanded an existing CRM testbed into a broader, more faithful suite.

Their benchmark holds nineteen expert-checked tasks spanning sales, service, and price quoting, in both business-to-business and consumer settings. Conversations run over multiple turns with varied personas, and keeping secrets is graded too. Top agents passed only about fifty-eight percent of single-turn tasks and thirty-five percent of multi-turn ones. Workflow execution scored highest, while confidentiality awareness sat near zero without special prompting. Enterprise readiness, the authors conclude, is not here yet.
arxiv-2505-19178:
Akhila Yaragoppa and Siddharth published a research paper in 2025 on predicting how viewers will feel about a video from where their eyes are drawn. Emotion tech usually leans on self-reports, faces, or body sensors. Their approach instead measures the video's salient areas, the spots that grab attention, using a deep saliency model plus face-action software.

Two simple features did the work: how much of the frame is salient, and how many salient spots compete. Videos with many spots tended to spark pleasant, calm feelings. One dominant spot leaned toward unpleasant, charged feelings. Self-reports often clashed with face-based readings, a caution for the field.
arxiv-2505-19778:
A textbook zero turns out to be large, in a 2025 arXiv paper by Cañas, Yassine, and Ambacher on built in electric polarization in common semiconductors. The zincblende family was long assumed to carry no spontaneous polarization. Its wurtzite cousins are famous for it.

The authors first argue that the flat layered crystal, not zincblende, is the honest zero point for wurtzite measures. Turning the same logic on zincblende itself, they find a polarization about three times the wurtzite size. The result rests on how a ferroelectric flips. It also separates the bulk property from the charge that gathers at interfaces.
arxiv-2505-20178:
Pranav Mani and three co-authors give a non asymptotic analysis of prediction powered inference and find no free lunch. The method combines gold standard labels with possibly noisy machine pseudo labels for statistical estimation. Adaptive versions were shown to beat gold only estimation asymptotically, whatever the pseudo label quality, which sounded too good.

An exact finite sample analysis of mean estimation demystifies the claim. The adaptive method wins only when correlation between pseudo and gold labels passes a threshold set by the labeled sample size. For Gaussian data the bar is one over the square root of n minus two. Exact variance formulas under sample splitting let practitioners judge the benefit in their own setting.
arxiv-2505-20278:
Language models often solve tasks by matching patterns, yet that habit can fail on tasks built from parts. Hoyeon Chang and co-authors pin down what pattern matching can and cannot do in a 2025 paper. They define it in a strict way: two input parts count as a match when swapping them never changes the result. Test tasks were built to isolate that one skill.

Success on each test case was well predicted by how many settings showed the same match. The team also proved a tight bound on how much data a two-step structure needs for full learning. Tests on two model types matched the theory across a wide size range. A flaw called path ambiguity was named as a hard structural bar.
arxiv-2505-20378:
Martin Guillemaud, Vera Dinkelacker, and Mario Chavez present a way to place the nodes of a multi-layer network into curved space, in a 2025 paper. Multi-layer networks model systems with several kinds of links and linked parts. Placing nodes in a low-dimensional space helps analysis, but layers are often handled apart.

Their method supports unlike node sets across layers and links between layers. It gives each layer its own placement for close study, while also keeping the whole structure together in the same curved space. Tests on made-up networks with known group structure support the approach. The authors offer the frame for work on complex systems in many fields.
arxiv-2505-20478:
Jongmin Mun, Paromita Dubey, and Yingying Fan cluster high-dimensional data while picking the few traits that matter. Sparse clustering must assign groups and choose traits at once, a tightly linked pair. Their base is a semidefinite relaxation of K-means, which they show resists picking too many traits. On top sits a loop that swaps between clustering and trait choice.

Trait choice is cast as a bandit game solved by Thompson sampling. Rewards come from clustering runs and tough shuffle tests. Past picks feed a memory that steers which traits get explored next. The team proves exact group recovery for the adaptively picked trait sets. Fake and document data runs beat top sparse rivals.
arxiv-2505-20778:
Groups of smooth transformations, acting locally on a space, leave fingerprints that topologists read as characteristic classes. Yaroslav Bazaikin and co-authors compute two such classes for diffeomorphism pseudogroups, following Losik's program. The classes live in the cohomology of frame bundles over the quotient space, built from the classic Gelfand-Fuchs generators.

The team gives explicit formulas for both, one named for Godbillon and Vey, the other a first Chern-type class. By trimming the bundles, the first class becomes a volume form on a space of dimension two n plus one. The second becomes a symplectic form in dimension two n. Worked examples in dimension two close the 2025 paper.
arxiv-2505-20978:
Duan and co-authors compute rare decays of heavy baryons carrying two strange quarks in a 2025 paper. Such decays, where a heavy quark turns into a light one and sheds a lepton pair, test the standard model's weak force rules.

A sum rule method on the light cone yields the shape factors for two such decays. Fed into spin aware rate formulas, the factors give branching shares. Two versions of the method clash hard: one matches other groups' results, the other lands orders of magnitude away. The clash flags an open puzzle in how the method's inputs are built.
arxiv-2505-21078:
Enrico Bernardi and Tatsuo Nishitani study a class of wave-type equations in a 2025 paper. The operators they treat lose their standard strong form at points where they vanish to second order.

In part of the region, the structure tied to the main symbol changes type, which makes the analysis delicate. The authors find special coordinates that put the problem in a normal form. They then study the linked system of paths that the symbol defines. A factorization result breaks the operator into simpler pieces. Together, these steps prepare the ground for a later energy estimate, the tool that would prove the equations behave well.
arxiv-2505-21478:
Uri Gadot and co-authors present a 2025 method for building text to image pipelines. Such pipelines now chain many parts, such as tuned image makers, adapters, and steps that enlarge or edit the image.

Designing a good chain by hand takes deep skill, and past tools that used language models cost too much or just copied chains seen in training. The new method first trains reward models that guess image quality from a prompt and a chain plan, with no image made. It then trains in two phases to steer toward high reward chains. The result is more varied chains with better image quality than past methods.
arxiv-2505-21678:
Heat-based radiation sensors are prized for long-wavelength light, but they usually stop responding well above a low cutoff rate. Chang Zhang and co-authors show in 2025 that this limit can be beaten when a sensor runs at its deepest physical noise floor. Their device is a tiny mechanical resonator whose tone steadiness is limited only by random temperature flicker.

That steadiness held across a band thirty times wider than the thermal cutoff, keeping sensitivity within a factor of three of its peak. The team also derived a formula for the largest possible bandwidth gain in such resonators and confirmed it in tests. The result points to faster heat sensors for far-infrared work without giving up sensitivity.
arxiv-2505-22078:
Pauline Vidal, Emily Bourne, Virginie Grandgirard, Michel Mehrenberger, and Eric Sonnendrücker present a numerical method for solving Vlasov-type equations on grids made of several joined patches. Such equations track how huge numbers of particles move, and they sit at the heart of plasma simulation. Patch edges, though, make smooth tracking hard.

Their approach fills in values between grid points with local cubic splines, one patch at a time, with special care at the borders. They adapt the method to patches whose points are unevenly spaced or do not line up neatly. They also study when a small shared system must be solved to make the patches agree. Tests on a two-dimensional guiding-center model check that the scheme behaves as hoped.
arxiv-2505-22278:
Afroja Parvin, Giovanni Samaey, and Julian Koellermeier published an applied mathematics paper in 2025 on a shallow water model for water carrying sediment. Their model joins bedload and suspended load transport with changing mixture density. It extends a moment framework by adding a sediment concentration equation, density coupling in the momentum balance, and erosion and deposition terms.

The team derived when the regularized model stays hyperbolic, finding strict behavior for even moment orders and weaker behavior for odd ones. Energy balance relations were derived for low orders. Numerical tests with a path-conservative scheme confirmed balance at rest, convergence, and agreement with lab dam-break data. The results show how moment detail and erosion coupling shape surface, bed, and sediment.
arxiv-2505-22878:
Shams Tarek and co-authors fine-tune a language model to hunt security bugs in chip designs. Checking system-on-chip hardware for vulnerabilities is manual, slow, and hard to scale, and flaws at the design level are costly to catch late. Their framework, BugWhisperer, trains an open model on hardware security knowledge so it can read register-transfer-level code and flag weaknesses. The fine-tuning also aims at knowledge transfer, so lessons from one design help on others.

The team reports that the tailored model made verification faster and more flexible than standard practice. They also built a broad database of hardware vulnerabilities to support the training and share it with the community. The work treats hardware security as a language task: the same reading skill that models apply to software can, with the right training, be pointed at the blueprints of chips themselves.
arxiv-2505-23178:
Tonglin Liao and Youming Li solve a queueing model exactly in this 2025 mathematics paper. The model describes customers who arrive in patterned batches and are served by an endless pool of servers, so no one waits for a free one. Time runs in discrete steps rather than as a smooth flow.

The authors build a Markov-style description of the system that can be handled in closed form. From it they derive the exact distribution of the number of customers present at any time, along with its averages. Computer simulations matched the formulas. As a check, they worked out the classic case of random arrivals and random service times. They then compared that step-by-step result with the well-known smooth-time version of the same queue. Exact results like these give engineers a firm base for planning systems with ample service capacity.
arxiv-2505-23578:
When two fluids of unlike density meet and the boundary shakes, two kinds of instability compete to stir them. Tianyi Chu and co-authors study that contest in a 2025 paper on vibrated fluid layers.

One instability grows from the push of gravity on the heavier fluid; the other comes from the shaking itself, in short waves. The team found a new mixed pattern that appears when both act at once. Math analysis shows the shaking drives shifts between the two forms rather than simple boosting. Computer simulations confirm the analysis and follow the boundary as it breaks into fine, tangled flow. Even a fast-growing shaking pattern can be suppressed by the gravity-driven form.
arxiv-2505-23678:
Gabriel Sarch and co-authors published this study in 2025. It trains vision-language models to reason with their eyes on the evidence. Text-only reasoning chains have boosted math and coding skills. Visual tasks add a demand: the model must look at the right place at each step. Their system, ViGoRL, learns to tie each reasoning step to exact image coordinates. When fine detail matters, it zooms into the spot it named and reasons again.

Across spatial reasoning, visual search, and screen-grounding tests, the grounded model beat plain fine-tuning and standard reinforcement learning. It scored 86.4 percent on a hard visual search bench. Grounding also bred other good habits, like checking regions and setting visual subgoals. Human raters found the model's pointers accurate and helpful for following its logic.
arxiv-2505-23778: Vittorio Lippi, a solo author, proposes a test for posture experiments in a 2025 paper. A frequency response function sums up how body sway reacts to an outside push, as complex values across a set of frequencies. Comparing average outcomes between groups needs a sound method, so Lippi offers an unpaired test based on bootstrap resampling that compares group averages without pairing subjects.
arxiv-2505-23878:
Jing Ma, Chenhao Dang, and Mingjie Liao present AC-ODM in 2025, a method that adjusts the training data mix for language models while training runs. The blend of data sources strongly shapes what a model learns, and fixed blends ignore how needs change over time.

The method borrows an actor-critic setup from reinforcement learning to steer the mix. The authors prove the policy acts like a moving stand-in that helps gradients from different sources reinforce each other. A policy learned on a small model can transfer to a larger one. On one test model it reached top scores with up to two thirds fewer steps, at a tiny cost in time and memory.
arxiv-2505-23978:
Giulio Malavolta and Tamer Mour design tests that let a plain computer check whether a small device truly uses quantum power, in a 2025 paper. Such a proof should be cheap to verify, while no classic machine could pass it. Past proofs leaned on assumptions about what the cheating machine cannot compute.

Their new approach assumes only a cap on the memory of the prover, with no limit on its time. One simple protocol gives a modest gap between the memory an honest prover needs and the cap set for a cheater, resting on a known classic lower bound for matrix inversion. A second protocol widens that gap hugely, using tools from bounded-storage cryptography. Both can be checked efficiently by the verifier.
arxiv-2505-24078:
Zihan Zhang and Jan Hannig apply modern cause-and-effect methods to the pay gap between men and women in higher education. Their 2025 paper uses salary records for more than twelve thousand tenure-track faculty in the University of North Carolina system, matched with data on field, rank, and writing output.

The authors matched similar faculty and used a forest-based method to adjust for rank, subject area, output, and years on the job. After those adjustments, women still earned about six percent less than men with like profiles. The size of the gap shifted with career stage and output level. The study shows how such tools can give fairer readings of pay gaps in large records.
arxiv-2505-24878:
Yaxin Luo and co-authors launch, in a 2025 paper, a public testing ground for how well AI agents handle CAPTCHA puzzles on the web. These puzzles block automated agents from finishing online tasks, yet the multi-step reasoning they demand had never been benchmarked properly.

Their platform covers twenty modern puzzle types and 225 challenges in total. A new score counts the thinking and clicking steps each puzzle needs. Humans scored near perfectly, while the best AI agent solved at most forty percent. The gap shows how far multimodal agents still lag on small, interactive visual tasks, and gives builders a clear target for improvement.
arxiv-2506-00178:
Anirudh Nair and four co-authors let prompts for language models compete in debates and evolve toward better wording. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Writing a good prompt takes skill, trial, and time. The pain is worst for tasks judged by taste, where no clean score exists to chase.

Their framework, DEEVO, pits prompts against each other in set debates. Winners and losers both feed lessons into the next round's wording. Ratings borrowed from chess rank the field and keep weak but diverse prompts alive. Smart crossbreeding mixes the strong parts of rivals rather than splicing at random. Tests beat both hand-written prompts and rival auto-tuners on open and closed tasks. No true answers were used as feedback. The method suits teams that need strong prompts but lack the hours to handcraft them.
arxiv-2506-01878:
Gold dust can turn radiation therapy into a local hammer, and Pedro Teles and seven co-authors simulated exactly how, in a 2025 paper. Using the PENELOPE Monte Carlo code, they fired radiation at gold nanoparticles in water and breast tissue models and tracked every secondary particle.

Bigger particles delivered bigger boosts, with dose enhancement ratios passing a hundredfold next to the gold. A phase-space census around each particle showed 80 percent of the emitted electrons came from photoelectric absorption, spawning Auger cascades that dump energy within nanometers. The team linked secondary counts directly to particle volume and used a local effect model to draw cell survival curves by particle size and gold concentration. The results give radiotherapy planners a physical map of where the extra dose actually lands.
arxiv-2506-02278:
Juhi Jang and Trevor Leslie prove that separable motions exist for a body of elastic matter that pulls on itself by gravity, in a paper from 2025. The matter is hyperelastic, meaning its stored energy follows set rules from how it is strained. Separable motions split the movement into parts that vary with space and time apart.

Their proof rests on fitting assumptions about the strain-energy function. The family they build includes motions that expand forever in time. It also includes motions that collapse to a point in finite time. Other authors had built expanding cases in like settings. The collapsing cases, the authors note, are fully new.
arxiv-2506-02378:
Ukyo Honda and Tatsushi Oka lift in-context learning by probing explanations for each answer that could be picked, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. In-context learning lets a language model do tasks from a few shown examples. It often fails when the data at hand is not like those few.

A past variant adds notes on why the right label is right. The team takes it one step on: their frame writes out such notes for all candidate labels. To weigh rival notes side by side should make each call more full and more robust. Tests on a range of natural language understanding datasets back the idea. The work held up far better on data far from the norm than the old ways did, by a clear margin. To see why wrong picks tempt the model seems to help it hold firm.
arxiv-2506-02678:
Zhong-Zhi Li and a large team of co-authors present a 2025 training plan that trims long chains of thought from language models. Long thought chains lift scores but cost much time and compute at use. Heavy data labels or model blending can trim them, yet both add work. The team instead shifts the training mix as training runs.

Their plan steadily reweights fast, gut-style data against slow, step-by-step data. Redundant thought steps fade while core skill stays. Tests on two distilled models across tests of mixed hardness cut output length by near forty percent. Accuracy held steady at the same time. The authors plan to share code and data soon.
arxiv-2506-02978:
Mohamed Djilani and a team of colleagues test how easily tabular foundation models can be attacked, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. Models such as TabPFN and TabICL predict from examples in context, without retraining. Their strength raises a security question the field had largely left unexplored.

Across benchmarks in finance, cybersecurity, and healthcare, small structured changes to test inputs sharply cut accuracy. The training context stayed fixed during these attacks. The models could also be misused to craft evasions that transfer to random forests and XGBoost. As a defense, the authors propose adversarial training inside the context itself. Their strategy swaps in perturbed examples gradually to harden predictions.
arxiv-2506-03178:
Writing chest X-ray reports eats radiologist time, and a tuned language model may draft them with clinical sense. Md Zihad Bin Jahangir, Muhammad Ashad Kabir, Sumaiya Akter, Israt Jahan, and Minh Chau present LLaMA-XR in a 2025 paper. Their system pairs a vision encoder with the LLaMA 3.1 model. A memory-light tuning method, QLoRA, adapts the model without full retraining. A public Indiana X-ray set judged the drafts.

Scores on two standard text measures set new marks for the task, the team reports. Coherence and clinical accuracy both improved over rival systems. The tuning strategy cuts memory needs, speeding generation. The authors pitch the tool for easing reporting loads in busy departments.
arxiv-2506-03278:
Christodoulos Constantinides and co-authors set a test set in a 2025 paper for speech models on plant gear. Plants run on sensors, and when one fails, the rest tell the tale in their reads. To fix fast, a mind must know which sensors kin which, and how fails spread.

Their set poses picked-answer asks on gear kinds across plant worlds: what a sensor reads, what it kin, and how it breaks. Old ask sets score plain facts, not this web of ties. The aim is a shift to lore-led calls next to count-led tools. Plant teams gain a yardstick for models that claim to know their gear.
arxiv-2506-03378:
Chetia Phukan and co-authors present in 2025 a system that flags harmful content for children in videos by listening as well as watching. Unsafe scenes hidden in a few frames can slip past visual checks, and sound cues have been little used. Their framework aligns audio and video features through a staged transformer design, first handling each stream on its own, then blending them step by step.

The system beat single stream methods and standard fusion baselines, setting a new best result on fine grained detection. The authors argue that audio adds real signal for spotting violence or explicit material aimed at or shown to children. Platform moderators get a stronger tool for a fast growing audience.
arxiv-2506-03478:
Capturing a face well enough for film-quality digital doubles usually takes a studio rig of lights and cameras. Seven researchers close that gap at home in 2025 with a phone and its flashlight in a dim room. Their trick is a prior: a diffusion model trained on studio scans learns what real skin reflectance looks like, one small patch at a time. Patch training stretches a small dataset further and steadies the learning.

During capture, the system samples full-face reflectance maps patch by patch, steering each one to match the phone video. The seam-free maps come out close to studio quality in tests. The authors say everyday users could soon clone their own faces into the digital world with gear they already own.
arxiv-2506-03578:
Ashesh Giri, Chandra Shahi, and Adrienn Ruzsinszky test a newer class of density functionals on cerium's odd phase change, in a 2025 paper. Cerium flips between two crystal forms with the same structure but different electron behavior, one with roaming f electrons and one with localized ones. The change is driven purely by electron correlation, which simpler functionals capture poorly. The authors examine meta-GGA functionals, which use extra orbital information, against this hard test case.

One recent functional, LAK, breaks from the usual semilocal mold and scores striking accuracy on the transition. The paper argues that functionals in this family could open new ground for quantum materials with localized electrons. Cerium serves as the proving ground.
arxiv-2506-03678:
Minseong Kwon and five colleagues present a 2025 astronomy catalog hunting galaxies made mostly of dark matter. The Arecibo radio survey found hundreds of hydrogen clouds with no visible stars; some may be genuine dark galaxies, others tidal debris. The team winnowed three hundred forty-four such sources, removing known tidal clouds, sources with faint optical matches, and anything suspiciously near other gas or galaxies.

Deep optical, ultraviolet, and infrared images confirmed no starlight or dust for the survivors: one hundred forty-two dark galaxy candidates. Compared with normal galaxies they carry smaller total masses, more hydrogen per unit mass, and lonelier neighborhoods, matching what simulations predict. The authors offer the list as a testbed for theories of galaxy birth.
arxiv-2506-03978:
Hieu Trung Nguyen, Bao Nguyen, and Viet Anh Nguyen report a surprise: cutting parts of a language model can make it reason better. Their two thousand twenty-five paper focuses on attention heads in transformer models. Pruning is usually done to save compute. Here, removing certain heads raised scores on hard problems. The team set out to find which heads to cut, and when.

Their method, SPRINT, learns to pick the best head and layer to prune during use. It matches question embeddings with head embeddings to guide the choice. Tests used best-of-N sampling, which draws many answers and keeps the best. SPRINT beat both plain best-of-N and random head choice. The gains showed on the MATH500 and GSM8K math datasets.
arxiv-2506-04078:
Ming Zhang and a large team of co-authors present a 2025 benchmark for testing medical language models. Medicine allows little room for error, so models need hard, fair tests. Current tests lean on exam style multiple choice questions. They rarely use real patient cases, and they judge complex reasoning poorly. The team built a new test from real health records and expert written cases.

The benchmark holds nearly three thousand questions across five core areas of medicine. Scoring is automated but guided by expert checklists. Doctors checked the machine scores against their own, and the checklists were refined from their feedback. The team ran thirteen models through the test, spanning medical specialist models, open models, and closed models. They share the data in public and offer the results as guidance for safe use of these models in care.
arxiv-2506-04178:
Etash Guha and a large team of co-authors describe open data sets for training reasoning models, in a 2025 paper. Top reasoning models often train on private data, leaving open questions about the best recipes. The OpenThoughts project aims to make such data public. An earlier set from the project trained a model that matched a leading rival on standard tests.

The team then ran more than a thousand controlled tests on each step of their data pipeline. The improved set holds well over a million examples. A model trained on it set new marks for its size on math, code, and science tests. Gains over a key rival ranged from fifteen to twenty points. All data sets and models are public, the authors note, so others can build on them.
arxiv-2506-04278: Yumiko Nishiyama proposes a way to sort functions by the structures they build, in a 2025 paper. The idea, called Construction Defining Functionality, treats a function as a generator of structures through repetition, recursion, and logical steps. Nishiyama sets out the spaces that such generation creates and builds a framework to classify their traits. The framework aims to capture what functions do, by looking at the generated structures rather than at input-output pairs alone. It offers a fresh lens for sorting functions in logic.
arxiv-2506-04778:
Zhao Su, Zhiyuan Li, and Zongnan Li simulate the feeding of Andromeda's black hole in this 2025 paper. The galaxy's central black hole is huge yet strangely dim. It must feed at a trickle. The team tests whether winds from nearby old stars supply that trickle. A disk of aging stars circles the hole on tilted orbits.

Their three-dimensional simulation lets one hundred giant stars shed slow winds. Over millions of years a cool gas disk a few parsecs wide takes shape. It feeds the hole at a rate matching the dim glow seen by telescopes. The predicted X-ray brightness also fits observations. Sleepy giant black holes elsewhere may feed the same way.
arxiv-2506-04978:
Gabriele Digregorio, Elisabetta Cainazzo, Stefano Longari, Michele Carminati, and Stefano Zanero study security inside modern vehicles in a 2025 study. Cars exchange data over an internal network, and machine learning tools can spot intrusions on that network. Training such tools centrally, though, raises privacy and data movement concerns.

The authors build a federated version of a known intrusion detector based on recurrent autoencoders. In federated learning, models train locally and share updates rather than raw data. They compare detection quality and communication cost against the central version. Their evaluation presents the federated setup as a workable option for vehicle networks.
arxiv-2506-05178:
Joshua Hess and Quaid Morris prove that generative diffusion models and associative memories are two views of one machine, meeting where the noise dies. Diffusion models build data by slowly removing noise. Associative memories settle into stored patterns. Their 2025 paper shows the first converges to the second as noise vanishes, and it characterizes stability, robustness, and capacity for both.

A class of smooth dynamical systems turns out to approximate any associative memory. Diffusion is then that system plus a whisper of white noise. As noise fades, the system's shifts between creating and remembering happen at isolated, countable tipping points. The math gives both fields a shared language. Learning theorists get a bridge with load-bearing proofs, not metaphors.
arxiv-2506-05478:
Konstantinos-Rafail Revis and co-authors complete the map of entanglement classes for graph states built from qutrits. Graph states are workhorse quantum states drawn as networks, and states reachable from each other by local rules form one class. For ordinary qubits those classes were charted up to twelve particles. Their 2025 paper extends the chart to three-level systems, up to seven qutrits.

Each class becomes an orbit under local complementation and local scaling moves. The team studies the orbits as graphs in their own right. Their connectivity tracks the states' entanglement, and links to the Schmidt measure hint at which states are cheap to prepare and which resist errors. A public code repository accompanies the census. Quantum information readers get the full qutrit atlas.
arxiv-2506-05578:
Babu Ram and co-authors describe two new boron-oxygen carbon sheets in a 2025 study based on computer modeling. Adding boron and oxygen to graphene layers makes a buckled sheet called BO-graphane. Stacking makes BO-diamane, a thin diamond-like film between boron monoxide layers. Both were tested with density functional calculations.

The sheets prove very stiff, stiffer than fluor or hydrogen versions. Both act as wide band gap semiconductors up to three layers thick. Vibration and heat runs show they stay intact even at high heat. Their heat conduction beats a known ceramic by a wide margin. Such sheets could serve in tough electronics and heat spreaders.
arxiv-2506-05678:
Haotian Jiang, Zeyu Bao, Shida Wang, and Qianxiao Li build a test bed for models that read sequences. Their 2025 paper spans the main model families, from older recurrent nets to Transformers and state-space designs. Each family claims strength at holding memory over time, but fair tests are scarce.

Their bench makes fake targets with a dial that sets how strong the memory must be. Four shapes of memory are used, from fast decay to long-range spikes and sparse bursts. Trials on many models confirm some known theory and reveal fresh trade-offs. The authors argue that such dialled targets are the right way to judge new designs against the same clear yardstick.
arxiv-2506-05878:
Andreas Bergmeister and co-authors propose a new way to train neural networks, in a paper published in 2025. Standard training follows slopes downhill to cut error, which needs smooth math at every step. Their method instead treats training as a hunt for settings that meet many local rules, one rule per small operation in the network.

Training then means projecting the settings onto those rules again and again, a local act that can run in parallel across the network. Their software, PJAX, builds these projection steps on its own, much as other tools build slopes. It runs on fast chips and feels like common array software. Tests trained several network types on standard tasks. The authors argue the method suits problems where slopes do not exist or parallelism matters most.
arxiv-2506-06078:
Mario Bravetti, Luca Padovani, and Gianluigi Zavattaro close an open problem about safe substitution in communication protocols described by session types. Session types let programmers check that message-passing processes follow an agreed pattern. A fair refinement rule allows a process to send outputs early, ahead of many inputs, which matches common asynchronous practice.

Until now, a test-based definition of this refinement had only a one-sided description: methods could confirm it but might miss valid cases. The authors give a description that is both sound and complete. They connect it to known results for synchronous types through a new transition system that embeds asynchronous behavior.
arxiv-2506-06178:
Policy gradient methods teach software agents by trial and error, but they usually throw away each run of experience after one use. Alessandro Montenegro, Federico Mansutti, Marco Mussi, Matteo Papini, and Alberto Maria Metelli ask whether reusing old runs can speed up learning. Their algorithm, RT-PG, mixes fresh runs with recent past ones and corrects for the mismatch with a special weighting.

The team proves that this reuse cuts the number of runs needed to reach a given accuracy. When all past runs are recycled, the rate they prove is the best known for this family of methods. Experiments back the theory, with RT-PG beating rivals that hold the previous best rates. The work gives a firm base for a trick practitioners already suspected was sound.
arxiv-2506-06278:
Lee and a large team of colleagues make model unlearn stick by pouring it into a fresh net in this twenty twenty-five paper. Unlearn drills strip a fact from a model, yet a short re-drill can bring it back. That flaw shows the fact's skill stays hid in the net's deep parts.

Inside, a fresh blank net is trained just on the unlearned model's words. The blank net picks up its acts yet leaves the hid skill behind in the move. Their full route adds noise to the copy step to widen that shed gap. At top strength it matched a from-scratch retrain for firm unlearn, at less cost. The route also held on a grave-harm test set that labs use for such checks.
arxiv-2506-06378:
Charalampos Tsirmpas and co-authors split a skin signal into its fast and slow parts, in a 2025 paper. The signal, electrodermal activity, tracks sweat gland response and hints at stress and feeling. Wearable gear now records it in daily life, where noise runs high. Splitting it cleanly is key to reading what the body is doing.

The split parts are a fast phasic stream, tied to brief events, and a slow tonic drift beneath it. The authors compare older rule-based and math tools with learning-based ones. They add a new model, the Feel Transformer, which splits the signal with no labeled examples. It pools data and strips trends so the parts stay true to body behavior. Tests show it holds up well on messy real-world data, a step toward live stress tracking.
arxiv-2506-06478:
Sowmiya Dhandapani wrote a 2025 paper on keeping software pipelines safe from attack. Modern teams build and ship code through automated pipelines, and a breach anywhere in that chain can poison the final product. The study applies a structured threat-spotting method to a typical pipeline.

The model pipeline uses common tools for code hosting, building, packaging, and deployment. Each stage is scanned for six classes of threat, from fake identities to raised privileges. Found threats are matched with defenses drawn from national standards and industry checklists. The defenses are also graded against a maturity scale for supply chain trust. To make the plan real, the paper lays out how to wire the checks into the pipeline as code. The result is a practical roadmap that teams can follow to harden their delivery process.
arxiv-2506-06678:
Xin Li and Zhang-Qi Yin detect quantum phase changes from circuit settings in a 2025 paper. Phase transitions mark where matter reorganizes, and spotting them in quantum systems usually needs hard measurements. Circuit parameters themselves may secretly encode which phase a state belongs to.

Their framework feeds those parameters into an autoencoder with an attention mechanism borrowed from language models. Hidden correlations among the settings reveal phase structure without any labeled examples. The trained model doubles as a compact classical stand-in for the quantum states. It can also generate states belonging to chosen phases. Tests across several systems worked broadly, with the strongest results on topological transitions. The trick sidesteps measurement cost by reading the recipe instead of the dish.
arxiv-2506-06978:
Zitian Li and Wang Chi Cheung study a pure test task for choice machines. The work dates to 2025. A user asks if any choice pays at least a set level, or if none does. The machine must be right with high chance while using few pulls.

Past work fixed the long-run cost of this task but left the short-run cost unclear. The authors give a new method and prove its cost is close to the best possible cost. The gap is only a small log factor. Tests on data also show the method beats older methods. The result helps users who must test options with care and low waste.
arxiv-2506-07178:
Yong Zhang and Peng Ru study how a change in particle mass inside matter distorts a classic size measurement in a 2025 physics study. The Hanbury Brown and Twiss method infers the size of a particle-emitting source from correlations between identical particles. When a particle's mass shifts inside the medium, a squeezing effect reshapes those correlations.

The authors compute the effect on the three-dimensional radii for three particle pairs. Squeezing blunts the influence of outward flow on the sideways size while widening the source along the beam and in rapidity. Their result warns that naive size readings can mislead heavy-ion analyses.
arxiv-2506-07278:
Santos and co-authors present IDEIA, a 2025 AI system that helps newsrooms find story ideas in real time. Built with a large Brazilian media group, it watches trending topics and drafts headline and summary suggestions for editors.

The system pairs a trends feed with a generative model through a modular web stack. Early results show the time and mental effort of editorial planning dropping sharply, with gains up to 70 percent at the idea stage. The paper weighs gains against risks: dependence on outside models, ethics of automated news judgment, and how far the design can scale. The team suggests uses beyond journalism as well.
arxiv-2506-07378:
Yuen Chen and co-authors unify ideas for models that must work in new settings in a 2025 paper. A model trained in one hospital or camera set often fails in another. Past fixes aligned gradients or curvature across settings, but they were slow and poorly understood. The authors build a theory that ties them together.

Their moment alignment view shows all three older methods as parts of one rule under a transfer measure. They then design a closed-form algorithm that aligns gradients and curvature without repeated backpropagation. Tests with light and full tuning beat standard training and rival methods. Readers get both insight and a faster tool.
arxiv-2506-08278:
Kyung-Eun Choi and co-authors find magnetic kinks parked at the edges of small flux ropes in the young solar wind. Their 2025 letter uses data from the Parker Solar Probe, which flies closer to the Sun than any craft before. Kinks, called switchbacks, flip the field direction in bursts, while flux ropes are twisted tubes of field.

Edge kinks show a tidy pattern: their axes line up with the rope axis, and their polarity flips in step. That link beats chance and beats links to nearer stray kinks. Some kinks may be born at rope borders, the team argues, or thrive in rope-shaped fields. Geometry tests back the pairing.
arxiv-2506-08378:
The Euclid Collaboration reports the on-ground performance and calibration of the spectroscopy channel of NISP, the near-infrared instrument aboard the Euclid space telescope. Before launch, instruments of this scale must be tested and calibrated on the ground with great care. The paper documents that work for the channel that splits light into spectra, one of the mission's core tools for mapping the universe.

The huge author list reflects the scale of the Euclid project, with institutes across Europe and beyond contributing to the instrument. Ground campaigns of this kind verify that the hardware meets its design values and supply the calibration data that later science analysis depends on. The paper serves as the reference record for the channel's pre-flight state. Companion Euclid preparation papers cover the mission's other instruments and systems.
arxiv-2506-08478:
Avinash Bhardwaj and Animesh Bhandari write a 2025 short note on a special class of signal frames that can recover a signal's phase. Fusion frames split a signal across many subspaces, a scheme valued in spread out processing, sensor networks, and packet coding for its backup copies and toughness. Weaving fusion frames mix two such splits strand by strand.

Phase retrieval asks whether a signal can be rebuilt from strength readings alone, with its phase lost. The note studies which weaving fusion frames keep that power, giving key traits that deepen the picture of their structure and behavior. A closing use case treats random loss of data, the erasure problem, to show the frames at work. Results of this kind guide the design of sensing systems that must rebuild signals after parts go missing.
arxiv-2506-08678:
Vision-language models such as CLIP can name a broad range of visual concepts, but they falter at fine detail in small regions of an image. Yeo and co-authors propose ATAS, a self-distillation method that sharpens this region-level skill without extra labeled data.

The method teaches the model from its own representations across all levels, aiming at two goals at once: keeping meaning coherent across a scene and aligning words with fine visual detail. Rival approaches often buy detail at the cost of coherence, or need added modules and supervised fine-tuning. ATAS uses only unlabeled images and works inside the model's vision encoder. On open-vocabulary detection and segmentation tests it scored well above the base CLIP models.
arxiv-2506-08778:
Mengying Qiu and co-authors use a nuclear response measure to pin down the energy of neutron-rich matter at low density, in a paper from 2025. The measure is the inverse electric dipole polarizability of three nuclei: calcium-48, nickel-68, and lead-208. How stiff neutron matter is at one-third of normal density guides models of stars and collisions.

The team ran a set of relativistic mean-field models plus Skyrme models. The inverse measure tracked both the symmetry energy and the pure neutron matter energy in tight lines. For lead-208, the second link was nearly model-free. A Bayesian fit to measured values gave 17.8 MeV for the symmetry energy and 9.1 MeV for neutron matter. The second value sits above most direct theory results.
arxiv-2506-08978:
Anna Langedijk, Jaap Jumelet, and Willem Zuidema probe in 2025 how well three network types generalize on a logic task. Models must find value sets that satisfy logic formulas, a clean test of rule learning. A balanced data set removes shallow patterns and adds unseen operator mixes.

All three types do well on training-like cases, yet unseen patterns trip them in clear ways. Negation poses the top hurdle, above all for transformer models. Adding built-in structure helps transformers apply negation in steps. The finds point to a need for stronger built-in bias when true rule use is the goal.
arxiv-2506-09178:
Denis Zhidkikh, Ville Isomöttönen, and Toni Taipalus decode how programming students at risk of dropping out actually study, in a 2025 paper. The catalog title carries stray subject-classification text; the printed title is clean. Introductory programming sheds students at a notorious rate.

Trace logs from the course platform, a dropout predictor, and student self-reports were combined for 47 students. Low-risk students used three tidy strategies, varying how they balanced tasks and reading. High-risk students showed nine patterns. Some were temporary detours students recovered from; others marked the slide out of the course. Weekly strategy types made the invisible visible. Support, the authors argue, can now be timed to the pattern, not just the grade.
arxiv-2506-09278:
Yuchen Zhang and co-authors unify two classic image-matching jobs into one model, in a 2025 paper. Dense correspondence means finding, for every pixel in one photo, its mate in another. Optical flow handles small shifts between frames, while wide-baseline matching handles big viewpoint changes. The two fields grew up apart despite sharing that goal.

Their model, UFM, trains on both kinds of data with a plain transformer design. It predicts the flow directly, skipping the costly comparison volumes older methods rely on. UFM beat the best flow methods on accuracy and crushed wide-baseline matchers on both error and speed. Unified training outperformed specialists in both arenas, a first. Fast, general matching could serve robotics, mapping, and tracking alike.
arxiv-2506-09678:
Zae Young Kim and Jae-Weon Lee wrote a 2025 paper that links black hole physics with quantum machine learning. The head of the text lists Kim first among the authors. The black hole information paradox asks how facts about what fell in can ever be read back from its glow.

Rebuilding operators from that glow can be cast as a linear inverse task on the joined black hole and glow system. In learning, a like shape shows up as double descent, where error dips twice as models grow. A key time in the black hole story, when both halves match in size, lines up with the learning threshold. A classic law for random matrix spectra lets them score the rebuild weights. Spread of those weights spikes near that point.
arxiv-2506-09878:
Ryan Barker lays out the science and strategy of virtual radio access networks in a 2025 paper. Software defined mobile networks promise cheaper 5G spread. Talks on them split spectrum, cloud, and culture into apart boxes.

Barker joins those threads across four pillars in one view. A United States case study shows mid band runs with millimeter wave boosts. Math bounds cap capacity and lag for split base station builds. Full encryption costs a throughput toll that he weighs. Twin driven automation keeps call retries in a tight time budget. Culture drag can still slow the cycle, he warns.
arxiv-2506-10078:
Zenan Liu and co-authors study, in a 2025 physics paper, what the entanglement spectrum reveals at a quantum phase change. The spectrum reads out how deeply two halves of a system are linked, and it is a sharp tool for exotic phases of matter. Its behavior in smooth, gapless states was unclear. The team used quantum Monte Carlo methods on a magnet model laid out on a square-octagon lattice.

At the critical point and in the ordered phase, the spectrum showed an M-shaped wave mode with a curved, slower-than-linear spread. That shape matches a one-dimensional chain with long-range links. In other words, hidden long-range forces emerge inside the entanglement description. The authors trace the effect to lines in a path picture becoming unbound. Gapless modes, they show, can reshape entanglement itself.
arxiv-2506-10178:
Bill Psomas and eight co-workers wrote a 2025 paper on a cheap way to test image models. Fine-tuning big models is costly, so testers often freeze the model and train a small head instead. Plain heads can understate models trained on local patches. A focus-based head can pool patch traits with more care.

Past focus heads were heavy and slow, though. The team ran the first broad study of such heads and their design choices. Their new head uses fewer, shared parts and weighs less to train. Across tests, it beat plain and older focus heads. Its focus maps also showed new, paired patterns worth study.
arxiv-2506-10478: Yihan Chen, Jialin He, and Tianying Xie present a 2025 arXiv paper on covering a graph's four-cliques. A classic 1966 result bounds how many cliques cover all edges of a graph. Later work did the same for triangles, ending in a guess: for larger clique sizes, the Turán graph is the worst case. The authors settle the guess for cliques of size four. Their proof mixes induction, a greedy partition method, local adjustments, and older clique-counting lemmas.
arxiv-2506-10578:
Shikun Cui and co-authors find the exact mass line that separates calm from collapse in a model of cells swimming in flowing fluid. The model couples cell aggregation, the force that makes bacteria swarm into clusters, with fluid motion. Without flow, three-dimensional clusters can blow up no matter how little mass starts out. A simple shear flow, sliding faster on one side, changes that verdict.

With strong enough shear, solutions starting below a sharp mass threshold live forever. The threshold the team proves appears to be the best possible. Above it, for any flow strength, they construct smooth starting states whose solutions still collapse in finite time. The proof leans on an exact simplification: one part of the system behaves like the classic two-dimensional aggregation model, where an energy argument forces the blow-up.
arxiv-2506-10978:
Donghoon Ahn and co-authors pinpoint where to perturb attention inside image generators in a 2025 paper. Guidance by perturbation steers diffusion models when no classifier signal exists: weaken the model in a smart way and push generation away from the weak version. Older methods blur whole layers without asking which parts matter.

The team found that single attention heads govern distinct visual ideas like structure, style, and texture. Their HeadHunter framework picks heads that match a user's goal, one by one. A soft interpolation knob then tunes each chosen head's strength and curbs artifacts. On two large text to image models, the approach beat layer level perturbation for both general quality and targeted styles.
arxiv-2506-11378:
Bernardo Schaeffer and co-authors analyze how random noise affects sampling in diffusion models, in work from 2025. Such models build images by reversing a slow blurring process. Users can add noise during reversal or follow a smooth path with none.

The authors track a standard gap measure between model output and true data. With a perfect score guide, noise shrinks that gap over time. With a flawed guide, noise can fix old errors but can also boost fresh ones. Which effect wins depends on when in the process the guide errs most. Tests on toy and standard data sets matched the theory. The results guide tuning of future samplers.
arxiv-2506-11478:
Aman Sinha and co-authors ask whether language models grasp what oncologists see in paper abstracts in a 2025 study. Biomedical models are spreading into daily research use. The team tested models against expert clinicians at spotting hallmarks of immunotherapy in breast cancer abstracts.

Their results carry a surprise for the current moment. Smaller pretrained domain models beat large general models at finding very specific, low-level concepts. Broad fluency did not equal fine clinical grounding in this task. The authors frame the gap as a warning for medical text work: model size and chat skill can mask weak concept roots. Expert-checked benchmarks remain vital before clinical use.
arxiv-2506-11578:
Byeongchan Lee and co-authors let small and large language models collaborate through planning to cut inference costs. Big models reason well but charge heavily per use. Small models are cheap yet stumble on hard tasks.

Their COPE framework splits work into planning and doing. A planner model first sketches a lightweight plan. An executor model then carries the plan out. Models swap the two roles across several stages. Plans pass back and forth as the task advances. Tests covered math, code, open tasks, and agent work. Performance nearly matched the big model alone. Costs fell because the big model ran less often. The scheme suits teams watching their AI budgets.
arxiv-2506-11678:
MingZe Tang and Madiha Kazi benchmark action recognition on deliberately small data and crown an upset winner. Using a three-action slice of the COCO image collection, they run everything from plain feed-forward networks to vision transformers. Their 2025 study asks what survives when training data is scarce, as it usually is outside tech giants.

A binary vision transformer hit about ninety percent test accuracy. Convolutional models managed only about a third, and CLIP-based ones about three fifths. Explanation tools then showed why: the transformer stared at limbs and posture, the exact cues that define an action, while weak models read background texture. The study is as much about diagnosis as score. Vision practitioners get evidence that architecture and attention maps beat dataset size excuses.
arxiv-2506-11778:
Jingrui Sun, Jiaqiang Wen, Jie Xiong, and Wen Xu wrote this 2025 math paper on steering a noisy system when the controller sees only part of the state. The setting is a linear system with quadratic costs, a classic control problem, but with three twists. The control feeds the noise term. The control and the record of what is seen shape each other in a loop. And the observed signal drifts without bound.

The team first shrinks the set of allowed controls, which lets a change-of-measure trick break the loop. A non-standard variation method then solves the smaller problem. Taking the limit of a chain of such solutions gives a near-optimal control for the full problem. The authors present the result as a firm handle on a case that had resisted the usual methods.
arxiv-2506-11878:
Spinning magnets can pump two kinds of angular momentum into a neighbor: spin and orbital motion. Hanchen Wang and seven co-authors report in 2025 the first clear detection of pure orbital currents pumped from a magnetic insulator, a bismuth doped garnet. They compared devices capped with several metals to separate the two currents.

Oxidized copper, which barely converts spin, let the orbital signal stand alone, and its strength tracked the garnet's inner orbital motion. In chromium, the spin effect still ruled the signal. Better contact between layers boosted both currents. The authors say orbital flow is real but often the junior partner, a fact device builders must weigh.
arxiv-2506-12678:
Pranay Gupta, Henny Admoni, and Andrea Bajcsy help robot policies cope with unfamiliar sights by analogy, in a research paper from 2025. A policy trained by copying demonstrations often fails when objects or rooms change. Collecting fresh demonstrations for every new look is slow and costly.

Their insight is that old behaviors often fit new scenes that work the same way, like a pencil for a pen. An expert simply tells the system which familiar scene the new one matches, instead of demonstrating again. The method first checks whether a scene is truly unfamiliar and whether look-alike training scenes disagree. Tests on a real robot arm show clear gains from this light feedback.
arxiv-2506-13278:
Salim Msaad, Murray Harraway, and Robert McAllister present a 2025 control scheme for autonomous greenhouses. Good control lifts crop yield while it trims energy bills. Past work used learning based control or predictive control alone, or used the predictive part as the learner brain.

Their scheme trains a learning policy first, then uses it to set the end cost and end zone for a predictive controller. That blend pairs the learner ease with uncertainty and the controller live optimization. Sims ran in a fixed world and in a world with noise. In both, the blend beat each parent method and worked with shorter forecast spans.
arxiv-2506-13378:
Pronay Biswas, Amartya Goswami, and Sujit Kumar Sardar wrote a 2025 math paper that frames ideal theory for semirings in functor terms. Semirings drop the subtraction rule of rings, which spawns several kinds of ideals: plain, subtractive, and strong. The head gives the work a longer title on radical ideal functors and quantale completion.

The authors sort those ideal kinds into one functor frame, with radical growth as a left adjoint to contraction. Prime spectra for the three kinds nest inside each other as spectral functors. A support bifibration gathers finite supports, and a completion step lands in a known class of quantales. Uses reach to positive cones of special rings.
arxiv-2506-14578:
The SMARTHEP Network reviews machine learning in real-time analysis at the Large Hadron Collider in this 2025 whitepaper. The collider's four big experiments must judge each collision in a flash, keeping the interesting ones and dropping the rest. Learning algorithms now sit inside that split-second filter.

The paper samples real uses across the experiments, from spotting particle tracks to tagging jets. It stresses teamwork between physics labs and industry, where similar real-time problems arise. Examples from outside physics show shared tools and mutual gains. The authors frame the document as a high-level tour rather than a full catalog, meant to spark wider exchange.
arxiv-2506-14878:
Alan Zhou, Scott Dodelson, and Daniel Scolnic test in 2025 whether cosmic growth runs at the same rate in all directions, early and late. Even growth is a base claim of standard cosmology, but past tests split by era. The team merges three probes into full-sky maps for the first time.

Maps draw on exploding stars, galaxy plane data, and heat left from the early universe. No sign of uneven growth or link between early and late maps turns up. Upper bounds on unevenness sit below one percent in each probe. One galaxy map quirk looks like a data flaw, since it tracks density patterns and no other probe.
arxiv-2506-14978:
Aayush Mishra and Anqi Liu improve how to guess a model's error rate on data from a new domain, in this 2025 paper. Safe systems need that guess before deployment, when no labels exist. A leading method pits classifiers against each other to bound the error. The authors spot a flaw: the fight wastes itself in the region where old and new data overlap, where disagreement should stay low.

Their fix, called ODD, only counts disagreement outside the overlap. Domain classifiers estimate how much the two data worlds share. The new bound then tracks true performance better than the older one while staying a valid bound. Tests across many benchmarks show smaller estimation error. Code and results are posted openly for reuse.
arxiv-2506-15078:
Fang and co-authors improve in 2025 vector quantization, the step that turns smooth features into codebook entries for sequence models. Two faults plague the method: training wobbles from a gradient shortcut, and codebook collapse, where most entries go unused. The team traces both faults to a mismatch between the spread of features and the spread of code entries.

They align the two spreads with a classic transport distance. That fix drove codebook use near one hundred percent and cut the error from quantization sharply. Both theory and experiments back the approach. Cleaner codes mean less information lost when data is compressed into tokens, which should help the models built on top.
arxiv-2506-15178: Makoko and De Propris used exploding stars to set limits on present-day star formation in galaxies that already had their great burst, in a study published in 2025. They searched a wide transient survey for the kind of supernova that only young, massive stars produce, within the visible edges of nearby post-starburst galaxies. None were found. From that silence they derived an upper limit: at 95 percent confidence, these galaxies form stars at less than eight-tenths of a solar mass per year.
arxiv-2506-15278:
Reuben Binns and co-authors audited Uber's pay algorithm with drivers in a 2025 study of work on ride platforms. Uber markets driving as flexible, yet drivers must guess when and where the algorithm will offer work and at what pay. That guessing game sits at the heart of the paper.

Working with drivers and union organizers, the team analyzed one and a half million trips from a few hundred drivers in the United Kingdom. They compared pay before and after Uber rolled out dynamic pricing, which sets pay case by case. The long view shows how the change shifted driver earnings and risk. The study models a worker-led audit method that other platform workforces could copy.
arxiv-2506-15378:
Frank, Ripken, Lied, Müller, Unke, and Chmiela adapt in twenty twenty-five a powerful image generation method to sample the three-dimensional shapes of molecules. A molecule can fold into many shapes, and drug design needs realistic samples of them. The method, built on diffusion transformers, was not designed for molecules, which mix a fixed bond graph with smooth spatial geometry.

Their framework splits the work: one part handles spatial positions, another handles bond information. Two graph-based strategies feed bond data into the model, each paired with attention styles that either respect spatial symmetry or not. That choice trades accuracy against speed. On standard benchmarks their method reached top precision and physical soundness.
arxiv-2506-15678:
A vertex operator algebra hides inside four-dimensional N=4 super Yang-Mills theory, and Federico Bonetti and Carlo Meneghelli argue it comes from one universal structure. Using bootstrap methods, they assemble evidence for a nonlinear W-algebra holding an endless tower of extra generators, arranged in short supersymmetry multiplets, with a single free parameter, its central charge.

At one special value of that charge, depending on the gauge group's size, the algebra's simple quotient matches the one tied to the physical theory. They also define a filtration on the algebra that mirrors a known filtration used to extract physical data. Explicit formulas for the wedge algebra's brackets complete the case. The paper appears in 2025.
arxiv-2506-15778:
Supersymmetric cousins of quantum chromodynamics, called SQCD-like theories, can be rolled up on a circle to drop from four dimensions to three. Niall Macpherson and co-authors build the holographic duals of that roll-up: curved spacetime backgrounds that encode the same physics as the field theory. The circle shrinks smoothly while twisting with the theory's R-symmetry.

The construction only works when the flavor count is exactly twice the color count. That is the same condition the field theory needs to cancel its anomaly, a satisfying match. The authors compute several observables, including the central charge and Wilson loops. The rolled-up theory lands in a gapped three-dimensional phase described by a Chern-Simons theory. The work shows geometry enforcing a field theory's own consistency rules.
arxiv-2506-15878:
How tangled is the strong force's own quantum state? Twagirayezu tackles that question in a 2025 paper using a holographic model that maps the strong force onto a gravity-like picture. The twist is flavor: light and heavy quarks get their own fields, and the count of flavors is allowed to rival the count of colors.

Entanglement measures come out separately for space regions and flavor groups, tracked against heat and density. The sharpest flavor contrasts appear near the boundary where quarks break free of confinement. Checked against lattice simulations, the results link to patterns seen when heavy nuclei collide, offering testable signs of the tangling.
arxiv-2506-15978:
Toan Nguyen and three co-authors built a Vietnamese dataset for text segmentation and reading tests, in a paper published in 2025. The language ranks twentieth in the world, with more than a hundred million speakers, yet its tool data are thin. Their set pulls nearly 16,000 wiki texts for segmentation tasks. Machine-made multiple choice questions, checked by hand, add a similar count for reading tests.

A multilingual model beat monolingual models on both tasks. It hit high marks on the reading test and a mid-level score on segmentation. The team reads the gap as a hint that mixed training helps thin-resource languages most. The set is free on a known hub. They aim it at tools for similarly starved languages.
arxiv-2506-16078:
Tianle Gu and co-authors probe a soft spot in AI safety training: small hidden nudges can undo it, in a 2025 paper. Safety alignment teaches chat models to refuse harmful requests. Yet the team observe that tiny shifts inside the model's hidden layers can still wake unsafe answers, as if the refusal were only skin deep.

Their diagnostic measures how likely the model's own original answer remains after a small latent shift, using a standard likelihood score. A sharp drop flags shallow alignment near that input. Mapping these weak spots shows where safety training changed surface behavior more than inner workings. Developers could use such probes to harden models before release, rather than trusting refusal tests alone.
arxiv-2506-16178:
Alexander Sobolev bounded the eigenvalues of two matrices tied to an atom's quantum state in twenty twenty-five.
