For a bound state of an N-electron atom, the one-particle density matrix and its kinetic energy counterpart summarize what single electrons do. How fast their eigenvalues decay governs how well the state can be compressed or approximated.

He proves decay rates with constants that depend explicitly on the wave function, sharpening his own earlier results with more direct proofs. When the wave function vanishes where particles meet — as antisymmetric states do — extra smoothness speeds the decay further, and he proves the faster rates too. The arguments rest on derivative estimates that track distance to those meeting points. The results feed approximation theory for many-electron problems.
arxiv-2506-16378:
Erdoğan and co-authors settle the reach of wave operators in a 2025 mathematical physics paper. Wave operators compare a particle's motion under a potential with its free flight, and whether they act boundedly on each function space decides how scattering theory handles higher-order Schrödinger operators.

The tricky case is a threshold eigenvalue, a bound state sitting exactly at the edge of the continuous spectrum. Extending earlier work into lower dimensions, the authors prove boundedness across the natural range of exponents when no resonances interfere. Extra orthogonality conditions on the zero-energy states widen the range further, and the classical case gets a cleaner proof.
arxiv-2506-16478:
Seth Lloyd and Michele Reilly count the information processing done by life itself. Their 2025 note starts from a simple claim: every physical system holds information, and its changes process that data. Living things gather free energy and spend it on chemistry, and each reaction can be read as a tiny logic step.

They call such steps bio-ops and tally them for the whole Earth. All life now runs some 10 to the 33rd to 10 to the 35th bio-ops each second. One human body runs about as many as all human computers combined. Only a few percent of human bio-ops occur in the brain. The tally over Earth's history is far larger still.
arxiv-2506-16678:
Ananth Agarwal and co-authors test whether probing a language model explains its grammar skill in a 2025 paper. Large models handle sentence structure well, which hints they store that structure inside. Probing is a method that reads such structure from a model's inner activity. The question was whether probe scores predict how a model does on targeted grammar tests.

The team checked thirty two open models across many English grammar cases. Probe scores for grammar features failed to predict test outcomes again and again. That gap suggests what a probe can find inside a model may not drive what the model actually does. Readers learn a caution for research that treats inner readings as proof of how a model works.
arxiv-2506-16978:
Yanchen Wu, Martin Bazant, Allan Myerson, and Richard Braatz developed in 2025 a generalized theory of nucleation at surface edges that includes line tension. Crystals and droplets often start at edges, where uneven capillary forces create this extra tension, but its role was poorly understood. Their treatment extends classic nucleation theory to nanoscale confinement.

Working through droplet formation in defined nanopores, they derive a closed formula for edge-pinned line tension based on pressure, pore shape, and wettability. Line tension can reshape the energy barrier to nucleation, with effects that hinge on contact angle and pore form. That gives a tunable, geometry-based lever for controlling phase change, with uses from nanofluidics to crystallization.
arxiv-2506-17178:
Kevin Gomez and Ken Ono study the Hecke polynomials attached to a mock modular form born from Ramanujan's Delta function. The form has weight minus 10 and its nonholomorphic part is the period integral of the Delta function. A Hecke operator acts on it through Ramanujan's tau values and a monic polynomial in the j-invariant. The question is where that polynomial's zeros fall.

Every zero, including the special points 0 and 1728, turns out distinct and inside the interval from 0 to 1728. As the index grows, the zeros spread evenly through that interval. The result mirrors classic findings for the j-function itself.
arxiv-2506-17378:
Abhishek Phadke, Shakib Mahmud Dipto, and Pratip Rana present a workflow for making synthetic LiDAR datasets in simulation in a 2025 paper. Self-driving and robotics research needs large labeled laser-scan datasets, which are costly to gather in the real world. A simulator can generate them with perfect ground truth attached.

Built on the CoppeliaSim platform, their pipeline mounts several sensor types on a virtual vehicle in an urban scene. It automates capture, storage, and annotation in multiple formats, with pose truth included. The team validate it by producing large point clouds with matching color and depth images. They also probe security holes, such as fake point injection, and show how synthetic data can test defenses. Limits in realism and scale are discussed.
arxiv-2506-17678:
Mehmet Kaan Erol and Eyüp Emre Ülkü build a working radio link that lets drones in a flying network share their locations. They use software defined radio, in which radio parts that were once hardware are written as software, making the system flexible and long-lived. Much prior work in this area was tested only in simulation.

The team set up multi-channel communication between two radios using a token circulation scheme for channel access. The software was built on the GNU Radio platform. They ran the system in a realistic test setting rather than a simulator, noting that real tests expose cost, hardware, and environmental effects that simulations miss. To help others repeat the work, they published their block diagrams and code openly. The paper supports location sharing as a base service for multi-drone systems.
arxiv-2506-17878:
Tam Trinh, Manh Nguyen, and Truong-Son Hy build a team of AI agents that fact-check claims together. Their 2025 paper responds to the flood of online misinformation, which human checkers cannot match in volume. Language-model checkers exist, but they often stumble on complex claims and murky sources.

Four agents split the work. One breaks a claim into parts, one writes targeted search queries, one gathers evidence from trusted sources, and one delivers a verdict with a plain explanation. On three benchmark sets the system beat rival methods by about twelve percent on the main score. The authors stress transparency, since each verdict can be traced to its evidence.
arxiv-2506-17978:
Salim Meddahi wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five as the sole author. It sets out a high-order numerical method for thermo-poroelastic systems, where heat, fluid, and solid strain act on each other in waves.

The laws are cast as a first-order system with solid and fluid speeds, heat flux, stress, pore pressure, and heat as the state. The author proves the base problem is well set with semigroup tools. The hybridizable discontinuous Galerkin scheme then keeps energy true for the joined system while staying local and cheap to condense. A joint accuracy proof in mesh size and order is given, and tests in mixed media match the forecast rates.
arxiv-2506-18678:
Tianchen Deng and co-authors present the first shared mapping system that lets several robots build one neural map together. Their 2025 paper works in dense visual SLAM, where a moving camera builds a map while tracking itself. Past neural versions serve one robot and strain on big scenes or long runs. Sending full maps between robots also floods the link. Their design splits work across robots and fuses part-maps with care.

A new scene form joins grid and plane traits to sharpen rebuilds. A loop method ties spots within one robot's run and across robots, which keeps the joint map consistent. A teaching step merges part-maps without hauling all data to one place. The team also builds a real-world test set with exact ground truth for maps and paths. Scenes range from small rooms to large outdoor sites.
arxiv-2506-18878:
Roni Con and Ray Li construct error-correcting codes for a middle kind of noise, where symbols are deleted but the damage is not aimed at the code. In this oblivious model, the errors are hostile in effect yet blind to the random choices made while encoding. DNA storage motivates the setting, since its noise comes from hard-to-model physical processes rather than an attacker.

Their first construction matches the best known redundancy bound for fully hostile deletions. They then show that any good list-decodable code can be turned into an oblivious deletion code with nearly the same cost. A randomized version does better still, and the same idea improves codes built for hostile deletions too. The shared trick shrinks the hash by working modulo a prime picked from a small set, with the prime itself tucked into the encoding.
arxiv-2506-18978:
Ruairidh Sutcliffe and co-authors study how a hidden kind of magnetic order splits sound-like waves in crystals in a 2025 paper. Some magnets hide eight-pole order that plain probes miss. The team links such order to paired wave modes in a crystal where the pairs would else share one pitch.

Both the eight-pole order and a four-pole cousin break the pair apart. The eight-pole case favors waves with a twist, and the split is big enough for light-scattering tests to catch. The team names two real compounds where such tests could expose the hidden order. The idea widens twisted-wave physics to a broad class of such magnets.
arxiv-2506-19078:
Dipankar Paul, Harekrushna Behera, and Sukhendu Ghosh analyzed in 2025 the stability of a soapy film sliding down a slippery slope under wind shear. Gravity pulls the film down while soap-like chemicals ride in the flow and gather at the surface, changing its pull. Earlier work left out the slippery bottom and the outside shear.

The team set up the full flow and chemical equations, including soap soaking into and out of the surface. They solved the stability system with a long-wave method. Results show how slip and shear each calm or excite waves on the film, knowledge that guides coating and cleaning flows.
arxiv-2506-19478:
Leif Doring and co-authors present ADDQ, a method to curb overestimation in value based learning in a 2025 paper. Learning agents that grade actions by a value score often grade too high, which slows learning. Many top methods owe part of their success to curbing that bias, directly or not. The team builds on methods that learn a full spread of values, not just a mean.

Their tweak adapts the curb to local conditions and takes only a few lines of code to add to existing methods. Theory backs the design, and a double value method shows how to fold it in. Tests span table tasks, Atari games, and simulated robot control.
arxiv-2506-19778:
Alexis Ralli, Tim Weaving, and Peter Love set out firm properties of a special class of quantum Hamiltonians, in two thousand twenty-five. A Hamiltonian sums up the energy rules of a quantum system. This class, built from Pauli operators, avoids a deep quantum trait called contextuality, which makes it easier to simulate.

The team prove these Hamiltonians can hold more operators than simple diagonal ones. That means they can describe more physical interactions while staying tractable. They show the energy spaces have a neat classical description. For each energy, some state can be described with effort that grows only in step with the number of qubits. They also pin down where repeated energies can arise.
arxiv-2506-19978:
Gianni Dal Maso and Davide Donati build a new measure for rough deformation fields in this two thousand twenty-five math paper. Their setting is the space of functions of generalized bounded deformation, used to model materials that can crack or slip. For smoother fields, a symmetric gradient measure already exists. The authors extend that idea to the rougher space. They attach to each field a measure whose values are symmetric matrices.

They prove this measure splits into three parts: a smooth part, a diffuse Cantor part, and a jump part. The split mirrors the known case for simpler fields. Using it, they characterize a subspace that was defined only through slicing. The paper serves analysts who model fracture and plasticity.
arxiv-2506-20278:
Cox and co-authors characterize, in a 2025 paper, when the pure embeddings between presheaf categories can be generated from a small set of basic ones. Presheaves are a general home for structures acted on by a category. Whether their pure monomorphisms form a cofibrantly generated class turns out to hinge on the base category's own shape.

For actions of a monoid, the answer is a neat arithmetic test on its elements. The proof travels through model theory: the generation question equals the existence of a stable independence relation, which equals the generation property itself. A corollary shows the property fails for actions of the natural numbers under multiplication. The work links homotopy-style generation questions to plain semigroup arithmetic, with a bridge built from stability theory.
arxiv-2506-20478:
Nikita Guseynov, Xiajie Huang, and Nana Liu present a quantum framework for linear PDEs with Robin boundary conditions, widening what quantum methods can handle. They blend value and slope constraints at edges, and source terms and varying constants join too. A finite-difference grid first puts the equation on a grid.

A Schrodingerisation step turns the system into unitary evolution. The Hamiltonian is block-encoded with polylogarithmic cost in grid size, and quantum signal processing can then apply the evolution. No oracle queries are needed in the method, and costs are counted in basic gates like CNOTs. PDEs across physics become solvable this way. This extends earlier quantum PDE work.
arxiv-2506-20678:
Mira Welner, Andre Hazbun, and Thomas Beechem wrote this 2025 paper on a simpler way to detect gases with infrared light. Normal tools scan more than a thousand points of the spectrum, which makes the hardware costly and complex. The team asked how few points a sensor truly needs to name a gas.

Their method, called sparse infrared spectroscopy, picks a small set of filters based on a large gas database. Tests in a virtual setup found target gases at one to ten parts per million with just 20 to 50 samples. The method held up under noise and in gas mixtures. It points toward smaller, cheaper sensors that still do the job.
arxiv-2506-20878:
Junpei Harada wrote a 2025 paper giving an exact vacuum solution of Einstein's equations built on the Hopf fibration, a classic way of filling a sphere with linked circles. The metric is written in Kerr-Schild form around a twisting set of light rays. Two parameters shape the result.

Oddly for such solutions, the space has no singular points at all. Its curvature measures stay finite everywhere, and both key scalars are nonzero. Hidden symmetries appear as extra conserved structures. The derivation is short and self contained. Harada offers it as a clean, geometry led route to new exact solutions in relativity.
arxiv-2506-21178: Johnata Brayan and co-authors present UAIbot in 2025, a free web-based simulator for learning and research in robotics. Standard simulators often demand heavy installation and setup, which blocks beginners. UAIbot runs in the browser with Python and JavaScript interfaces. Users can explore core math and physics ideas hands-on, from robot arm motion to pedestrian flow. The authors aim to deepen student understanding, speed up trials, and help share research results.
arxiv-2506-21378:
Adamu Issifu, Débora Menezes, and Tobias Frederico wrote a 2025 astrophysics paper on how dark matter mixed into a newborn neutron star changes its cooling story. In their single fluid picture, dark matter seeps through ordinary matter via the Higgs portal and shares its temperature. The star is studied during its first cooling phase, when trapped neutrinos still help hold it up.

The simulations show dark matter soaking up heat without radiating it away efficiently, rewriting the star's thermal history and neutrino glow. Trapped neutrinos also block dark matter from piling up early on. To stay consistent with the heaviest observed neutron stars and with supernova remnant data, the authors cap the dark matter particle's mass at a low value. A contrasting limit is drawn for colder, older stars.
arxiv-2506-21578:
Andrew Maranhao Ventura D'addario built a large Portuguese-language test of health knowledge for language models, in a 2025 paper. Most health tests for these models center on doctors and on English. That slant, the author argues, flatters the models and ignores team care. The new test holds more than five thousand six hundred questions from Brazil's national licensing and residency exams. It spans medicine plus nursing, dentistry, psychology, social work, and more.

Over twenty leading models took the test cold, with no tuning. The best scored near eighty-seven percent overall. That headline hid sharp dips: near-perfect marks in eye care, but barely passing marks in brain surgery and social work. Every model showed the same spiky profile. The author releases the test and tools in public, urging audits that read the whole profile, not one score.
arxiv-2506-21678:
Raffaele Di Donna and Lorenzo Tortora de Falco study a check for valid proofs in linear logic in a 2025 paper. Linear logic tracks resources as they are used, and its proof sketches must pass a graph test to count as real proofs. A known trait of the graphs is that they stay free of loops.

That trait alone is not enough to rebuild a full proof in the full system. The authors add a shape condition that makes it enough in set fragments of the logic. In one fragment, the check matches the freedom to swap rule order. In another, it matches the rule of having one output, and rebuilds proofs when no axioms are used.
arxiv-2506-21778: Stefan Hoffelner constructs a set-theoretic universe with a rare mix of properties in a 2025 paper. The universe obeys the continuum hypothesis, a statement about the size of the set of real numbers. It also has a well-ordering of the reals definable by a formula of modest complexity, plus a uniformization property. The method lifts to richer inner models, giving the same mix at any finite level.
arxiv-2506-21878:
Fan Wang and four co-authors build in 2025 tools for spotting the moments when a layered, changing network reorganizes itself. Their data are multilayer networks observed over time, where the same actors connect through several kinds of ties, and the pattern holds steady until, suddenly, it does not.

Their two-stage algorithm first hunts candidate change points with a seeded segmentation search, then refines them with low-rank tensor estimates of the network's hidden positions. The authors prove the method finds the true number and timing of changes, and they derive the uncertainty of the estimates. Network surveillance, from finance to neuroscience, needs exactly this kind of alarm with error bars.
arxiv-2506-22278:
Diego Conti and Alejandro Gil-García classify a family of geometric structures on Lie algebras in a 2025 math paper. The algebras they study are almost abelian, built from an abelian part plus one extra direction. On such spaces they consider pseudo-Kähler structures, which blend a complex structure with a metric of mixed sign. One case has no match in the usual positive-definite setting: the abelian part itself can be degenerate.

The pair sort all cases up to a natural notion of sameness, in every dimension. They show that every nilpotent example with a complex structure also admits a fit metric, but that this fails for the wider class. They list exactly which algebras have a complex and a symplectic structure yet no fit metric. They also study the curvature of their metrics and build Einstein examples in higher dimensions.
arxiv-2506-22478:
Liu proposes an odd mechanism behind an entropy puzzle in Bose gases. The 2025 paper studies an ideal Bose system held at fixed energy, where only particles in excited states add to the count of microstates. Particles in the ground state, on this view, add no entropy at all.

When two such isolated gases merge into one, the total entropy ends up below the sum of the two parts. Liu shows numerically that this drop comes from an anomalous exchange among excited particles. The mean number of excited particles after merging is smaller than the two starting numbers added together. A ratio of factorials built from those means falls below one, marking the effect.
arxiv-2506-22578:
Xufei Lv and five co-authors found a hidden link in two thousand twenty-five between two ways of training language models. One way, RLHF, learns from human feedback at high cost. A simpler way, DPO, learns from chosen and rejected answers. Both are widely used to align models with human values.

The authors show both methods can be read as a form of contrastive learning that raises shared information between good answers and the prompt. That view helps explain why RLHF may not add reasoning skill beyond the base model. They propose a new method, MIO, that fixes a late drop in chosen-answer likelihood seen in DPO and scores well on reasoning tests.
arxiv-2506-22678:
Nicolas Caytuiro and Ivan Sipiran survey deep learning methods that generate three-dimensional shapes in a 2025 review. Generative models can now synthesize objects that are complex, varied, and semantically sensible, from chairs to characters. The survey organizes the field around three components: how shapes are represented, how generation is modeled, and how results are evaluated.

Representations split into explicit forms like meshes, implicit forms like signed distance fields, and hybrids. Each choice trades detail, memory, and editability. For newcomers and tool builders alike, the map shows which representation suits which job and where evaluation still lags behind generation quality.
arxiv-2506-22778:
Yuto Fujie, Hiroki Shibata, Yuto Nakashima, and Shunsuke Inenaga pin down how much a single edit can change measures of string repetitiveness, in a 2025 paper. Such measures say how compressible a string is, and they matter for indexing huge texts. The question is sensitivity: if one character is edited, how much can the measure jump in the worst case?

The team prove an upper bound that grows with the square root of string length for two measures, the smallest string attractor and the smallest bidirectional scheme. That matches known lower bounds, so those results are tight. For the Lempel-Ziv family of compressors, they give matching upper and lower bounds that differ by scheme. Two variants grow as the two-thirds power of length, while LZ78 can change by the full length. The work closes open gaps on how stable these measures are under small edits.
arxiv-2506-22978:
Language models that read grammar trees along with words may generalize better, but their design space is a maze. Yida Zhao, Hao Xve, Xiang Hu, and Kewei Tu map that maze in a 2025 study. Their focus is models that build phrase meanings bottom-up from constituency trees. A single framework holds older designs and new variants side by side.

Every variant was tested on language modeling, grammar probes, summarizing, dialogue, and speed. Clear design advice comes out of the sweep. Code was released for others to rerun the comparisons. The authors aim to settle which grammar tricks earn their cost. ShanghaiTech and Ant Group supported the work.
arxiv-2506-23378:
Srinivasan Aiyappan, Aditi Chattaraj, and Irina Pettersson study a wave problem on a very thin cylinder whose weight function changes sign along its length. Sign change means the spectrum holds endless positive and negative values, and what happens as the cylinder shrinks toward a line depends on the average sign of that weight. The team focuses on the case where the local average is negative.

They derive a simple one-dimensional stand-in, a harmonic oscillator on the whole line, and prove the true spectrum settles onto it. A side result secures a positive leading value for a related problem on one repeating cell. Such sign-changing problems arise naturally in population genetics.
arxiv-2506-23478:
Pedro Alonso, Tianrui Li, and Chongshou Li propose GeoCD, a new way to measure how well a generated 3D shape matches its target, in a 2025 paper. The standard measure, Chamfer distance, compares points by straight-line distance, which can miss the true surface geometry of a shape. GeoCD instead approximates distance along the surface, and it stays smooth enough to train models with.

The team took several models already trained with the standard measure and fine-tuned them with GeoCD. A single extra round of training brought clear gains across many quality metrics and datasets. The authors present the method as a drop-in improvement for point cloud learning that respects a shape's own structure.
arxiv-2506-23578:
Łukasz Kamiński and Sławomir Lasota study a reachability puzzle in a 2025 math paper. Their systems hold a state plus a row of counters that steps can raise or lower, and the ask is whether one set state can ever be reached.

In the plain case that ask is known to be very hard. The twist here is that the steps stay the same when the counters are shuffled by a set of swaps. When the swap set is the full set, the team shows the ask can be solved in a bounded span of work space, no matter how many counters there are. They also weigh mid cases, such as even swaps and ring swaps, and a mix linked to a known open case.
arxiv-2506-23678:
Rock Pang and co-authors made AI reasoning visible and editable in two thousand twenty-five. Chain-of-thought text is long and hard to scan. Users cannot correct its hidden detours. Their design draws reasoning as a topic tree. Branches can be pruned, added, or clarified live. A prototype called Hippo hosts the interface.

It targets decisions with uncertain trade-offs. Sixteen people tested the interactive approach. They reviewed and steered model reasoning directly. Control improved trust and output fit. The tree view exposed assumptions worth challenging. Static transcripts offer no such handles. Decision tools may adopt reasoning you can touch.
arxiv-2506-23778:
Smet presents a math paper from twenty twenty-five on special Lie superalgebras in characteristic three. A family is described using products of composition algebras. Named examples from earlier work sit inside this family. For one key algebra, the new view goes past its old construction route. More general forms of it become buildable as well. A semisimplification functor links these algebras to classic large symmetry types. The functor applies broadly across algebras from ternary structures in this setting.

The paper unifies scattered constructions under one method. Characteristic three quirks drive the whole story. It extends a line of work on exceptional symmetries.
arxiv-2506-23978:
Samuele Marro and Philip Torr argue that AI agents will break the walls around closed platforms, in work from 2025. The net's base was built open, but its app layer is ruled by closed services that hoard user data. Open links cost a lot to build, and leaders gain little by sharing. Agents change that math, the pair holds.

Agents can translate data forms and use human-facing screens on their own, which makes any two services able to swap data cheaply. That shift, called universal interoperability, cuts lock-in and frees data. The pair warns of fresh risks in security, upkeep, and law, and urges early guardrails.
arxiv-2506-24078:
Deep-inelastic scattering smashes electrons into protons to probe their innards, and Saurav Goyal and co-authors compute its semi-inclusive version to unusual precision. Working in quantum chromodynamics, they extend the soft and virtual corrections to the cross section out to four loops. The derivation leans on threshold resummation plus recent two-loop results, known form factors, and splitting functions.

They also add the leading corrections that fade as the threshold nears. Numerically, the new four-loop terms shift the cross section only slightly. That smallness signals a stable perturbative series, with lessened dependence on the arbitrary scales theorists must choose.
arxiv-2507-00078:
Xie and co-authors tackle a puzzle about foundation models for time series: why should one model work across many unrelated streams of data? Time series come from distinct systems, so transfer looks unlikely, yet these models succeed widely. The authors study patch-based models, which read time series in short chunks.

They argue the models extend the language model idea, replacing fixed vectors with probability patterns. Their analysis shows chunks of a smooth series can be split into a discrete vocabulary whose statistics resemble those of natural language. That resemblance, they claim, explains the models' strong transfer. The work aims to ground the safety and design of large time series models.
arxiv-2507-00478:
Yan-Hong Yao and Jian-Qi Liu test whether dark matter might be almost, but not quite, cold in a 2025 paper. Standard cosmology treats dark matter as pressureless dust. Their variant gives it a tiny constant equation of state, a whisper of pressure, while dark energy stays a plain cosmological constant. The test case is a known friction point: how clumpy today's universe looks versus how the early universe says it should.

Five data families, from the microwave background to weak lensing, pin the model down. Both data blends prefer a pressure a hair above zero, and the clumpiness tension shrinks from glaring to under one sigma. The variant also edges out the standard model on the full blend. The authors are careful: the preference is marginal, a hint worth chasing with sharper surveys.
arxiv-2507-00578:
Dizhan Du and co-authors study time delays between light and X ray emissions from black hole binaries in a 2025 paper. They used daily multi wavelength data for three well studied systems. A cross correlation method compared X ray emission from hot gas with optical and infrared light. The pattern flipped between the rising and decaying phases of outbursts.

During the rising hard state, X ray emission lagged the optical and infrared by several days. During decay, the optical and infrared lagged the X rays by roughly six to thirty five days. Viscous heating in the accretion disk explains the optical light, and a disk instability model fits both delay patterns, the authors argue. Readers see timing used as a probe of disk physics.
arxiv-2507-00878:
Rajdeep Mazumdar and co-authors rebuild a modified gravity theory around a dark energy idea, in a 2025 paper. The universe's late speedup is usually blamed on a fixed constant. Their route rewrites gravity itself, in the f(Q) family, shaped to mimic New Agegraphic Dark Energy, which ties dark energy to the universe's age and size. A power-law growth history yields a clean formula.

Tested against recent baryon acoustic oscillation data, the rebuilt cosmos tracks the measured expansion closely, edging out the standard model on their scores. The history flips from slowing to speeding at the right era. Diagnostics keep the model in the accepted lane. Geometry, not a constant, does the pushing here.
arxiv-2507-01178:
Alec Helbling and Duen Horng Chau build an interactive tool for learning how diffusion models work in this 2025 paper. Such models drive most image, video, and some text generators. Their math has striking geometric traits that show up well in flat, two-dimensional cases.

Older guides demand heavy theory or dwell on network wiring. Their tool, Diffusion Explorer, lets users train small 2D models right in the browser. Animated sampling shows each step as it unfolds. Motion and play make the ideas land faster than static text. The tool targets students and curious readers who want the geometry, not the algebra first.
arxiv-2507-02178:
Stephan McCandliss and co-authors lay out a survey plan to count the universe's ionizing light sources, in a 2025 paper. Ionizing radiation keeps space mostly ionized, yet its makers across cosmic time are poorly tallied. The team wants counts binned by distance out to a set redshift.

The job needs a vast number of faint targets, far-ultraviolet sensitivity, and a spectrograph that reads many objects at once. Only a proposed instrument on the Habitable Worlds Observatory could carry it out, they argue. The counts would show how much newborn radiation is swallowed by gas and dust on its way out, and how much escapes to ionize space. The paper is a science case for building that capability into the next great observatory.
arxiv-2507-02478:
Phones and laptops hide their hardware addresses by randomizing them, yet Wi-Fi chatter still betrays which device is speaking. Abhishek Mishra and Mathieu Cunche present StateFi in a 2025 paper, a fingerprinting method built on behavior rather than address. Older tricks read fixed fields in probe frames, and those cues fade in crowded spaces or under heavy randomization.

StateFi models each device's frame exchange as a finite-state machine, a map of steps and switches that captures both structure and timing. Those maps shrink into compact vectors that support fast matching and classification. Across five campus networks the full method named devices with 94 to 97 percent accuracy. Using probe frames alone, it re-identified devices behind randomized addresses at up to 97 percent on public data of over a million frames. The results expose a side channel that randomization does not close.
arxiv-2507-02778:
Ken Tsui shows, in a 2025 preprint, that language models often fail to fix their own mistakes even when they can. Telling apart cannot from does not is the hard part of studying self-correction. His benchmark, Self-Correction Bench, plants the same error in two frames. In one, the error is blamed on the user. In the other, the model supposedly wrote it. Fourteen open models were tested. They fixed the outside error far more often than the identical inside one.

The gap, about sixty-five percent, is named the self-correction blind spot. Training data explains much of it: fine-tuning sets rarely show anyone correcting a model. Adding a few thousand correction examples cut the gap by three quarters. Appending the word Wait helped even more, with no training. Tsui finds a direction inside the model tied to speaker role that switches correction on or off.
arxiv-2507-02978:
People mentally fold paper and rotate furniture without touching anything, and Jiahuan Zhang and six co-authors built a test of whether vision-language models can do the same, in a 2025 paper. Their benchmark generates deformation puzzles from two dimensions into three, with data machinery that can mint unlimited fresh problems.

Each puzzle runs both directions: given the operations, predict the final shape; given the final shape, name the operations. A ladder format raises the step count rung by rung to find where a model's ability ends. Almost no model showed plausible deformation reasoning at all. Targeted training and standard reasoning boosters barely moved the result. The authors present the ladder as a measuring stick the field currently fails near the ground floor, evidence that fluent spatial talk is not spatial understanding.
arxiv-2507-03378:
Seunguk Yu and three co-authors test language models on Korean endings in twenty twenty-five. Korean is an agglutinative language with complex sentence endings. Models strong in English may falter on such grammar. The authors built a data set, KoSEnd, to measure exactly that skill.

It holds three thousand sentences drawn from diverse sources. Each is annotated for the naturalness of fifteen sentence ending forms. Eleven language models were evaluated on the set. Analysis covered model size and how consistent each model's judgments were. Telling models that an ending might be missing improved their performance. That hints that explicit attention to a linguistic feature matters. Readers get a fine-grained probe of a low-resource language's hardest corner.
arxiv-2507-03578:
Yana Hasson and a team of co-authors present SciVid, a benchmark that tests video models across science domains. Their twenty twenty-five paper notes that video foundation models are often built for one field and tested only there. Yet many science tasks can be cast as video problems, so a general model might serve them all.

SciVid holds five tasks from three areas: medical vision, animal behavior, and weather forecasting. The team adapts six top video models with small trainable readout parts. The general models matched or beat specialist baselines on several tasks, which shows real transfer. Gaps remain, and the team shares code to spur better general models.
arxiv-2507-03678:
François-Marie Le Régent benchmarks how close experiments have come to fault-tolerant quantum computing. The goal demands two races at once: better physical qubits and working error correction. The review spans the main platforms. Trapped ions, superconducting circuits, neutral atoms, diamond defects and semiconductors all get scored.

Physical measures such as coherence time and entanglement error have climbed by orders of magnitude in twenty years. The author fits those trends and tracks error-correction codes in parallel. Early toy codes have grown into surface and color code runs with real parameters. Hardware gains explain much of the progress. Gaps to a scalable machine remain plain. The data and code behind the review are public.
arxiv-2507-03878:
Qi Chen, Rui Liu, Kangtong Mo, Boli Zhang and Dezhi Yu present DK-RRT, a motion planner that steers robot arms in orbit through fields of moving debris. Planning there is hard because obstacles move in complex ways and forecasts carry error. Their method joins deep learning with Koopman operator theory, which lifts messy motion into a space where it is easier to predict, and feeds those forecasts into a random-tree planner.

Sensor feedback keeps refining the forecasts as the arm moves, so plans adapt in real time. In simulations the planner beat classic random-tree planning and plain Koopman planning on adaptability, strength and speed. The authors pitch it for self-running space servicing work.
arxiv-2507-04378:
Chihao Li and co-authors pin down the origin of extra electron pockets in a nickel-based material that mimics copper superconductors. Their 2025 study uses light-based spectroscopy on NdNiO2, an infinite-layer nickelate. The material shares a key band shape with the cuprates but hosts added pockets whose orbital roots had sparked rival theories.

Measurements with varied light show the pocket comes mostly from electrons sitting in the gaps between atoms, in so-called interstitial s states, not from the rare-earth atoms' own orbitals. Even spread of those electrons through the film shows up as clean quantum well states. A comparison with the lanthanum cousin sharpens the picture of how the rare-earth choice matters.
arxiv-2507-04478:
Sathesh Sivashanmugam tests whether private data can be pulled out of a large language model, in a 2025 paper. Language models sometimes memorize chunks of their training data. The author probed Llama 3.2, a multilingual model built by Meta, with carefully shaped prompts meant to trigger such recall.

The reported attacks drew out private items such as passwords, email addresses, and account numbers. Even a smaller model proved open to this kind of extraction. The author reviews defenses, including training with noise-based privacy guards and scrubbing data before training. The paper closes with a call for more work on privacy-keeping machine learning. For builders and users alike, the message is that memorized data is a live risk, not a theory.
arxiv-2507-04578:
Noam Horowicz and Tsvi Kopelowitz published this study in 2025. It settles costs for two linked data problems about closeness. One, the snippets problem, asks for the two closest occurrences of two patterns in a text. The other builds a color distance oracle: given two colors, find the nearest pair of points wearing them. Past work left gaps between the best algorithms and the proven limits.

Using fast matrix multiplication, the authors give near-optimal algorithms for approximate versions of both problems. Their tradeoffs between preparation time and query time match the lower bounds closely. For the exact oracle problem, they prove the older algorithm is essentially unbeatable, under a standard hardness assumption. So approximation is strictly easier here than exactness. The result draws a clean line that algorithm designers can plan around.
arxiv-2507-04778:
Artur Michalak and co-authors describe a hardware stand-in for the quantum behaviour of a single electron in a semiconductor nanowire. Instead of solving the wave function directly, they emulate it with classical analog electronics built on the Kron model, a circuit framework that mirrors the mathematics. Wires shaped as lines or closed rings can be mapped onto the model, matching the layouts used in position-based qubits.

The team compares measurements from the emulator with theory across several of these geometries, focusing on how signals are analysed spectrally. They also show how a two-dimensional wave function can be represented in the same framework. The authors present the method as a practical test bench for single-electron devices, and point to further experiments the setup makes possible.
arxiv-2507-05078:
Radio telescopes have found a new kind of object that flashes on a slow beat, far slower than known pulsars. Sanne Bloot and co-authors report one such source in 2025, found in a sky survey with a Dutch radio array. They recorded nineteen pulses, each lasting at most ten seconds and repeating on a cycle of about fourteen minutes.

Every pulse was fully polarized, but the type of polarization flipped from pulse to pulse, which is unusual. Faint ultraviolet light hints that the system holds a white dwarf, the dense core of a dead star. The pulse pattern suggests a partner star tugs on the dwarf, making it beam radio waves toward Earth in a steady rhythm.
arxiv-2507-05278:
The TUCAN collaboration, a large international physics team, reports progress on a neutron experiment in a 2025 paper. The neutron may carry a tiny electric dipole, a slight separation of charge that would reveal new physics. The team is building an intense source of ultracold neutrons at a Canadian lab to hunt for it with record sensitivity.

Their source chills neutrons until they creep, so they can be held and watched for long stretches. The final setup should give a hundred times the data of the best past experiment. The paper describes how the source was brought into operation in 2024, step by step, and how the measuring device is coming together. Substantial parts of the full system have now run together. The collaboration aims at a sensitivity goal that would test theories far beyond current reach.
arxiv-2507-05378:
Francesco Spezzati, Marco Marinucci, and Marko Simonovic compare two ways of extracting cosmic information from galaxy maps, in a 2025 paper. One way uses summary counts of point patterns at several orders. The other, called field-level inference, works with the whole field at once and is claimed to capture more.

In a simple setup with dark matter halos and one free cosmic value, the team compute the pattern counts and run a joint analysis up to fourth order. Adding the fourth order cut the error on the value by only a fifth to a third. Their joint results match recent field-level results in the same setup. Error bars also shrink with scale in the same way in both approaches. The authors conclude that, on large scales, field-level methods gain little beyond standard kernels and counts, and they discuss a clash with some recent work.
arxiv-2507-05478:
Andrew Jacobsen, Alessandro Rudi, Francesco Orabona, and Nicolò Cesa-Bianchi recast a learning problem in a 2025 paper. In online learning, dynamic regret scores a learner against a moving target path. Static regret scores it against one fixed rival, which is simpler to handle.

The team show a moving path can be seen as one fixed function of time. Placed in a rich function space, the dynamic task turns into a static one. That swap restores a known best rate for straight losses and adds fresh scale-free bounds. It also works for loss types past methods barred. Though the space is endless, the math stays workable in practice.
arxiv-2507-05978:
Yun Du and co-authors present FineGrasp, a robot grasping method tuned for small and delicate objects, in a paper from 2025. Modern manipulation stacks can find and name almost any object part, yet the grasp itself often fails on the tiny or fragile ones, sinking the whole task. The fixes come in three parts.

First, network changes sharpen sensitivity to delicate regions. Second, a new label normalization tackles the imbalance between easy and hard grasp spots in training data. Third, a fresh simulated dataset, mixed with real data in training, lifts performance further. Tests showed clear gains, above all on small objects, and the system held up in language-guided semantic grasping trials.
arxiv-2507-06178:
Arvind Mishra asks whether feeding pulsars can betray dark matter through their orbits in a 2025 paper. Pulsars in pairs lose energy and spiral inward at a rate clocks can track with great care. If dark matter piles onto each star, the pair grows heavier and the decay should shift.

Near Earth, the author finds, the inflow is far too weak to leave a mark that data could catch. The galactic center is another story, since dark matter crowds thick there. Future watches of merging pairs in that zone could probe dark matter traits through timing shifts. The paper maps where the test turns from hopeless to hopeful.
arxiv-2507-06278:
Kemboi Cheruiyot and co-authors survey multi-agent reinforcement learning across federated, cooperative, and competitive settings, in a 2025 paper. Fleets of AI agents increasingly learn together in shared worlds. Their interaction can be centrally coordinated or fully decentralized. Some settings align incentives, while others pit agents against each other. Each regime has grown its own literature and jargon.

The survey unifies the three under one formal frame. Structural likenesses and real differences are drawn out. Methods are compared on coordination, communication, and trust needs. Open problems common to all regimes close the review. New researchers gain one map instead of three. System designers can spot ideas that transfer between regimes.
arxiv-2507-06878:
Lucile Favero and co-authors wrote a position paper from 2025 asking whether AI tutors free learners or make them dependent. AI tools are spreading fast through schools and universities. The authors grant that such tools can support study. Their worry is the unchecked pattern: students leaning on AI for every step. That habit, they argue, can dull the very thinking skills school exists to build.

Drawing on cognitive science and teaching research, they trace several harms. Over-reliance can erode effortful learning and foster conformity. It can sap students' belief in their own skill, blur honesty lines, and put well-being at risk. Privacy practices of the tools raise further flags. The paper also centers what students themselves say about the tools. It closes with concrete strategies for teachers and schools: use AI on purpose, in the open, and with a critical eye.
arxiv-2507-07278:
Alvaro Gonzalez-Hernandez published a 2025 mathematics paper on the symmetries of genus-two curves. Every such curve has a Jacobian, a related geometric object whose internal type can be classified. The moduli space, the master map of all genus-two curves, is carved into strata: regions sharing an automorphism group, and regions whose Jacobians share a type, pulled back from another classification.

The author first lists which symmetry groups a genus-two curve can have in positive characteristic, and parametrizes each family. An algorithm then computes the curves of each Jacobian type. Finally he computes the intersections of the two stratifications: their dimensions and how many pieces each intersection has. Two curves can look alike by symmetry yet differ in Jacobian type, and this paper tallies exactly where the two classifications cross. Such explicit geography of moduli spaces feeds arithmetic geometry, where curves over finite fields are counted and used.
arxiv-2507-07378:
Shoji Yokura, writing alone in two thousand twenty-five, constructs a co-working bivariant theory from cohomology operations in algebraic topology. Bivariant theories sort out how cohomology and homology interact across maps between spaces.

Fulton and MacPherson's working bivariant theory has a dual, co-working version. Starting from a contravariant functor, Yokura defines a generalized cohomology operation for maps that never break and have sections. The operation connects to Quillen's classic Steenrod power operations. From it he builds a certain co-working bivariant theory, shown to sit inside the general co-working theory tied to the functor. The paper is a basic building work for specialists rather than an application.
arxiv-2507-07778:
Wooseong Jeong, Jegyeong Cho, Youngho Yoon, and Kuk-Jin Yoon set out a test-time training way that keeps a model's many tasks in step as its world shifts. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Test-time training uses a side self-taught task to shrink the gap between the source world and the new one. But when a model must do many tasks at once, the steps that help one task can clash with the next. The team finds the tasks drift out of sync. Their way, S4T, rests on a claim: to keep tasks in step, the model must foretell how task links shift with the world. They show the way on known multi-task sets.
arxiv-2507-07878:
Jiayi Wu and a team of co-authors restore underwater photos in a single diffusion step instead of hundreds. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Murk steals color and contrast, yet marine science, farming, and archaeology all depend on clear images.

Their network, SLURPP, pairs a pretrained latent diffusion model with an explicit split of the scene. That split lets the model account for light fading and scattering with depth, the failure mode of earlier methods on complex scenes. Training data came from a physics-based pipeline that drowned ordinary photos realistically, with full annotations. On synthetic tests the method ran over two hundred times faster than diffusion rivals and scored about three decibels cleaner. Real-world images improved convincingly too.
arxiv-2507-08578:
Verstraete and a large team of co-authors report five years of new features in Abinit, a workhorse code for materials physics. The code predicts the traits of solids and tiny structures from first principles. Demand has shifted with new hardware, mass screening runs, and machine learning fed by its results. The paper tours what the code gained in that span.

New tools cover ground states with fixed charge, spin, or heat. Others extend response theory to bent charge effects and roaming charges. Excited state methods grew inside many body frames as well. The authors frame the release as a base for high throughput and data driven materials work.
arxiv-2507-08678:
Hossam Taha and two co-authors hunt for a dark particle at a future electron-positron collider. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. The target is a dark gauge boson from a model rooted in Einstein-Cartan theory. Such a particle is a dark matter candidate. The International Linear Collider would smash electrons and positrons at high energy. Simulations stand in for the real machine.

The WHIZARD package generates both signal and background events. The study follows the boson's decay into muons. Several classifiers, from Fisher discriminants to boosted trees and neural nets, sort signal from noise. Most benchmark points prove reachable within current limits. The work maps discovery chances for this dark sector idea.
arxiv-2507-08878:
Xinyu Huang and co-authors present a 2025 paper on a smart home assistant that keeps household data in the house. Today's assistants ship voice commands, profiles, and home layouts to cloud servers, which worries users. Their system, HomeLLaMA, runs a small language model on local hardware, tutored by big cloud models before deployment.

Once installed, the local model keeps learning from the household and refreshing its user profiles. For hard questions, an optional shield decides which queries are safe to send out and which must stay home. The team built a benchmark to grade service quality across these modes. The design tries to keep personalization without the surveillance trade-off. Proactive help, they argue, should not require surrendering the front door's data.
arxiv-2507-08978:
Katherine Limes, Nathan Malkin, and Kelsey Fulton survey what United States schools are told to teach about security and privacy. States and national groups publish teaching standards that shape lessons for grades from kindergarten to high school. No one had yet checked how those standards line up with what experts think students should learn.

The team read nearly twelve thousand standards and marked about thirty-eight hundred as security or privacy related, sorted into just over a hundred topics. Topics ran from encryption and network safety to laws, ethics, and online conduct. Talks with eleven professionals showed broad overlap with the standards, though the experts stressed threat thinking and a security mindset far more.
arxiv-2507-09178:
Liang Ding, Simon Mak, and Jeff Wu wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It gives a Gaussian process model that can take in boundary facts on odd-shaped domains, for use as a cheap stand-in for costly simulators.

Gaussian processes learn from few runs, since each run of the true simulator costs much. Boundary facts from science can add free knowledge, but past models mostly fit box-shaped domains and gave no smoothness control or error bounds. The new BdryMatérn frame takes Dirichlet, Neumann, and Robin bounds on a broad class of shapes. Its paths meet the bounds with set smoothness, and a finite element shortcut comes with a full error proof. Tests show the gains.
arxiv-2507-09378:
Mohammadsaleh Refahi, Mahdi Abavisani, Bahrad Sokhansanj, James Brown, and Gail Rosen built a new training method for models that read DNA code. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Such models are good at short spans of code but often miss links across long spans.

Their method, called CARMANIA, adds a loss term that teaches the model how one code letter tends to follow the next. This helps it learn the shape of whole genomes. In tests on many gene tasks, the model beat the best long-span rival by at least seven percent. It also ran about two and a half times faster, which makes large jobs more practical.
arxiv-2507-09478:
Cliff Sun and two co-authors design a superconducting diode that lets current flow freely one way and not at all the other, in this 2025 physics paper. Fast superconducting computers need such one way devices, the analogue of the semiconductor diode. Their design is a quantum interference device woven from several superconducting nanowires.

The model predicts a large critical current in the forward direction and exactly zero in reverse, a perfect efficiency of one hundred percent. The perfection survives small wobbles in the applied magnetic field, which matters for real hardware. Under broad conditions the same device becomes a range controller: supercurrent flows without voltage only inside a narrow, adjustable window that excludes zero. Both functions, the authors argue, suit the logic of future superconducting machines.
arxiv-2507-09578:
The glowing disks around giant black holes may be oval rather than round, and a 2025 paper by Hongping Deng builds that case. Such eccentric flows can form when gas streams in from around the nucleus or when a star is torn apart by the black hole.

In Deng's model, the ovalness fades with distance, running from above 0.8 near the center to 0.2 farther out. The uneven heat pattern of the flow explains lopsided dust fronts and the separate parts seen in broad emission lines. Tight inner streams make soft X-rays at their closest pass, while slow turning of the whole flow grinds out hard X-rays and drives the flicker seen in light curves. The model ties several puzzles into one shape.
arxiv-2507-09678:
Balinsky, Krzemiński, and Balinsky tested in twenty twenty-five if fair odds tools still work on locked data, for private smart learning. They lock a known digit set with a fixed key so like pics lock to like codes. Odds tools give sets of calls with a stated trust rate.

Tools trained on locked pics still found real form, far past guess rates. One odds kind held true labels in its sets in most test cases, though its sets were wide. A second kind gave tight sets but missed more true labels. The trade twixt tight sets and trust is the key point.
arxiv-2507-10178:
Wonung Kim and ten colleagues design a memory-side accelerator for the new wave of language model designs, in a 2025 paper. Post-transformer models promise cheaper long-context serving, but they shuffle state so heavily that memory bandwidth, not arithmetic, becomes the wall.

Their chip, Pimba, parks processing units inside memory, each shared between two banks for interleaved access. The units handle both attention and the state updates the new models need, using a low-precision number format the authors found best balances accuracy and area. Against GPU systems, with and without memory-side help, Pimba generated tokens up to four times and two times faster. The design aims to serve both model generations in one framework.
arxiv-2507-10478:
Andrew Powell and co-authors predict how sound travels high in Saturn's atmosphere in a 2025 paper. The catalog record mixes an affiliation line into the author list, and the byline misspells one name; the team framing here follows the paper itself. Future probes may listen to Saturn's winds and waves acoustically, so knowing sound's speed and fading matters.

The model covers pressures from one millibar to one bar, assuming still, cloudless air of hydrogen and helium. Hydrogen's two spin forms vary with height, and their mix shifts the gas properties. A linearized fluid model folds in viscosity, heat flow, and molecular relaxation to get sound speed and fading across frequencies. The predictions give mission planners a first acoustic map of the upper air.
arxiv-2507-10978:
Ayush Gupta and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on recognizing people by their walk when part of the body is blocked from view. Gait identification works at a distance, but fences, crowds, and furniture routinely hide limbs, and methods trained on paired blocked and full clips are impractical to gather. Their idea treats the blocked signature as a small deviation from the whole one.

A network learns that residual gap and blends it in adaptively, repairing blocked sequences without dulling accuracy on clean ones. On three demanding data sets the method improved blocked-gait recognition while keeping whole-body performance. The authors release the code, aiming at real surveillance and search scenarios.
arxiv-2507-11178:
Meiliang Liu and co-authors present a gradient-based framework for finding cause and effect in time series data in a 2025 paper. Neural network versions of Granger causality have improved results, but most build a separate model for each series. That design makes them slow and costly on complex data.

The team uses gradient regularization, which reads causal strength from gradients, to avoid the one-model-per-series cost. They apply the method to complex industrial processes, where knowing which signals drive others guides control and fault finding. The catalog title differs from the text's own title, and the description follows the text.
arxiv-2507-11278:
Arnab Dhani, Jonathan Gair, and Alessandra Buonanno present a 2025 paper on catching model errors in cosmic distance measurements made with gravitational waves. Merging black holes act as standard sirens: their signals carry a distance, and matching them to galaxies yields the universe's expansion rate. The catch is that distances come from fitting waveform models, and a flawed model skews every answer.

Working inside a population analysis, the authors test whether the spread of single-event results is self-consistent, which exposes modelling error without knowing the true rate in advance. They use top-grade waveform models to size the effect for present and future detectors, and show where better waveforms matter most.
arxiv-2507-11378:
Guangyao Li, Richard Zhipeng Wang, and Natalia Berloff present a 2025 paper on solving a class of hard math problems with light-based hardware. The problems ask for point positions that best match a set of measured distances. The cost is a weighted sum of gaps between the measured distances and the gaps the placed points imply.

By writing the point positions as complex numbers, the team maps the task onto optical fields. They solve it two ways: a transform method and a gain-based split method. Two tweaks, staggered updates and a steeper slope, sharpen the first method. Both methods suit many kinds of optical hardware, and the authors see promise for fast work on large, high-dimensional tasks.
arxiv-2507-11478:
Alessio Cela and Alberto Landi compute the integral Chow rings of certain moduli stacks that classify hyperelliptic Prym pairs, geometric objects tied to double covers of curves. This paper is the second in a series on these rings, which encode how algebraic cycles intersect on the stacks. For each genus, the stack splits into several components.

The authors focus on one family of components for odd genus and give explicit presentations of their rings. As a payoff, they also obtain the rings for all components of the stack of hyperelliptic spin curves of odd genus. A side result computes the ring for a stack of unordered pairs of divisors on the projective line.
arxiv-2507-11778:
Why does anything that starts to exist have a cause, and what would break if it did not? Daniel Linford takes up that puzzle alone in a 2025 philosophy paper. He sets a classic causal rule next to an older claim tied to Hobbes, Edwards, and Prior: without the rule, things would pop up at any time, place, or kind.

He then turns to a view, drawn from physics, that holds cause is absent at the base level of nature. Fans of that view can still reject the older claim, he argues. So the claim should carry no force against them in debate. The paper sorts out which tools each side may fairly use.
arxiv-2507-11878:
Jiachen Zhao, Jing Huang, and colleagues show that language models keep two safety concepts apart inside in a 2025 study. Models learn to refuse harmful requests, and earlier work found a single internal direction controlling refusal. The authors ask whether the model also represents how harmful a request is, separately from whether it will refuse.

A distinct harmfulness direction exists in the model's activations, apart from the refusal direction. Steering along it changes model behavior in causal tests, showing the representation does real work. Separating the two notions matters because a model might refuse by rote while misjudging harm, or the reverse.
arxiv-2507-12878:
Yaniv Shulman, in a solo paper from twenty twenty-five, framed a Bayesian way to model systems that change over time. The task is to read a linear time varying system from its in and out data. That task is ill posed: many systems fit the same reads. Shulman treats the system's impulse response as a chance process. It splits into a mean part and a random wobble part.

That split gives a clean read of doubt, both from the channel's own swings and from lack of knowledge. It also names a new class: systems that are time invariant in expectation. For the math, he uses Bayesian neural nets and Gaussian processes with scaled inference. Tests on worked cases show the frame in action.
arxiv-2507-13178:
Testing software needs input sequences with tangled internal logic, and the logic language Prolog is a natural generator for them. Marcus Gelderie, Maximilian Luff, and Maximilian Peltzer study how to randomize that generation in a 2025 paper. Random choice keeps the generator from drowning in an endless space of possible tests.

The authors propose two strategies. One layers randomness over standard Prolog behavior. The other changes the rule by which Prolog picks its next step. Both are analyzed with Markov chain models that predict how long a target test takes to appear and how many tests are produced on the way. Experiments compare the two strategies in practice. The goal is test generation that is both structured and fast to reach rare cases.
arxiv-2507-13278:
Xiying Zhang, Pol Bordas, Samar Safi-Harb, and Kazushi Iwasawa map the X-ray glow around a speeding pulsar inside a supernova wreck, in a 2025 paper. The pulsar, a spinning stellar cinder, blows a wind of particles that lights a nebula. Three space telescopes supplied the data. The pulsar sits at the southern edge of the remnant W44 and drags an elongated tail behind it, as earlier work found.

New analysis adds a surprise: an outflow feature ahead of the pulsar, about a light-year long, plus a faint halo wrapping the whole nebula. The outflow's spectrum is harder, meaning richer in high-energy photons, than the pulsar's or the tail's. The authors argue that both the outflow and the halo come from the fastest particles escaping the nebula. Similar halos are now seen around other such systems, hinting at a general escape route for cosmic particles.
arxiv-2507-13478: Nick Lindemulder and co-authors study the Laplace operator on rough domains in a 2025 math paper. They show it admits a bounded functional calculus on weighted Sobolev spaces whose weights are powers of the distance to the boundary. The domains need mild smoothness, with fixed-value or zero-flux edge terms. A trade-off drives the result: rougher edges can be offset by a larger weight power. The payoff is maximal regularity for the linked heat equation, extending well-posedness where classic methods fail.
arxiv-2507-13878:
Timothy Chan, Linfeng Jiang, and Dominik Krug build a predictive model for bubble-particle collisions in turbulent flow, a key step in froth flotation efficiency. Bubbles are typically much larger than particles, and no earlier model handled finite bubble size and particle inertia together consistently. Building on a frozen turbulence approach, they now predict collision rates a priori from bubble, particle, and turbulence properties.

Comparisons with simulations show good agreement for modest Froude numbers across a range of bubble and particle inertia values. The authors give a criterion for the model's validity beyond the tested range. At typical flotation parameters, particle inertia and settling usually matter, and smaller bubbles, larger particles, and stronger turbulence raise collision rates.
arxiv-2507-14278:
Minjeong Song and Arthur Parzygnat ask when the results of quantum tests admit a plain cause-and-effect story, in a 2025 study. For two linked quantum systems, test results can hint at how the systems sat in space and time. A system pair may fit a story where one side directly sways the other. The authors prove a first key claim about separable states, those with no entanglement.

They show every separable state fits the direct-cause story for a wide class of tests. So any state that fails the test must be entangled. They also give a working sense of the two time paths that fit such data. Last, they state exact rules for when any pair state fits, a time-based twin of a known space test.
arxiv-2507-14378:
Shrunal Pothagoni and Benjamin Schweinhart add shape sense to tissue slide classification in a 2025 paper. Neural networks read tissue slides well but can lose the topology of what they see. In tissue, how cells are arranged often signals disease.

Earlier topology tools summed up a whole slide's shape, erasing where features sit. Their new convolution operator makes local shape summaries that move as the image moves. Persistent homology supplies the shape language behind them. Models trained with the new layer beat standard networks on slide tests. Several ways of showing slides to the model were matched head to head. Local shape gives the network what pathologists themselves rely on: not just texture, but arrangement.
arxiv-2507-14678:
Tom Mestdag and Kenzo Yasaka extend a branch of geometry used to describe systems of equations, in a 2025 mathematics paper. Exterior differential systems are usually built on smooth spaces and their tangent bundles. The pair rebuild the theory on Lie algebroids, a broader setting that blends space and symmetry in one object.

They define what counts as a solution surface, called an integral manifold, in this wider setting. Worked examples support the theory at each step. One example treats moving systems that carry a symmetry group. Another applies the frame to the inverse problem of the calculus of variations, which asks when a set of equations comes from an energy principle. The paper gives dynamicists a larger toolbox.
arxiv-2507-14978:
Shabat, Sokolov, and Tsiganov study the Novikov equations for rings of differential operators that commute. The rings are built from ones of orders three, four, and five. Their 2025 paper sits in the theory of integrable systems. Such pairs are rare and rigid, and their equations encode that rigidity. The authors present them in explicit Hamiltonian form. That form turns them into a flow with conserved structure.

Compatible Poisson brackets then do the heavy lifting. With them, the authors separate the variables. The split takes place on a hyperelliptic curve of genus two. Separation turns a tangled system into independent motions in one dimension. That split is the classic mark of integrability. These forms serve specialists who classify commuting operators and their soliton equations.
arxiv-2507-15178:
Pei-Xi Liu and co-authors sketch a planet-wide quantum network held up by balloons in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Sharing quantum links across the globe is blocked by signal loss in air and fiber. Satellites help, but loss stays high.

Their backbone uses chains of balloon relays in the high air. Tuning beam shape and adding adaptive optics nearly wiped out air disturbance losses, beating satellite relays by a wide margin over ten thousand kilometers in their tests. Ground repeaters handle local links, and clients join by fiber for fast switching. Simulations with current quantum memories gave slow but real link rates across that distance. The authors call it a near-term path.
arxiv-2507-15278:
Zhizheng Pan, Xianzhong Zheng, and Xu Kong measured in 2025 how concentrated the hydrogen-alpha glow is in nearby star-forming galaxies, and what that says about how galaxy structure forms. That red glow traces newborn stars. Their index compares the glow inside a small radius with the glow inside a larger one, both set by the galaxy's own size scale.

The sample held 3,098 low-redshift galaxies from a large sky survey's integral field data. The index tracked strongly with the age gradient of the stars, weighted by light. It also responded to environment: low-mass satellite galaxies below the star-forming trend tended to have higher concentration. For central galaxies, the pattern split by mass and disk type. The catalog title appends software credits; the clean title governs. Readers get a simple index that reads a galaxy's recent history.
arxiv-2507-15578:
Gabriele Inzerillo, Diego Valsesia, Aniello Fiengo, and Enrico Magli move change detection from the ground station onto the satellite itself. Spotting what changed between two Earth photos usually waits hours or days for download and map correction. Their single neural system does three jobs in sequence. It compresses each photo to save storage, and it aligns photo pairs that were never map-corrected. It then flags the changes with a model built to ignore lighting and season shifts.

The design respects the tight power budget of orbit. On low-power hardware it processed 0.7 million pixels per second on a 15 watt accelerator. Change scores stayed strong as compression tightened. The authors call it the first end-to-end onboard system of its kind and a step toward near-real-time alerts from space.
arxiv-2507-15678:
Amine Aboussalah and Abdessalam Ed-dib present a learning method that respects the geometry of physics in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Physical laws rest on symmetry and conservation. Standard neural networks often ignore that structure. Their forecasts can drift and break basic principles over long runs. The authors build networks around Hamiltonian mechanics, the frame that governs energy-based motion.

Their design hard-wires two geometric facts. It treats inertia with its natural curved geometry, and it keeps the phase space structure that Hamiltonian systems require. A constrained autoencoder enforces the second of these. The result is a model that learns motion while keeping physical law intact. Such models could stay stable on chaotic, high-dimensional problems where plain networks fail.
arxiv-2507-15978:
Algebra has its own notion of sobriety, borrowed from topology, and Saeid Jafari and Ernesto Lax study the rings that have it in a 2025 note. A commutative ring is sober, in their sense, when every prime ideal that is not maximal fails to be exactly the overlap of the strictly larger prime ideals above it.

The note establishes the class's basic structural properties. Sobriety survives two standard constructions: passing to a quotient ring and localizing at a chosen set of elements. The authors also examine what happens when polynomial variables are added, where the property is less automatic. Connections with other known families of rings are drawn along the way. The paper is a compact map of a young definition, aimed at algebraists who work with prime spectra.
arxiv-2507-16078:
Enrique Ide, an economist, asks in 2025 what happens when machines take over the junior tasks where young workers learn. His paper studies tacit knowledge, the practical skill that people pick up by working beside experts rather than from books. He builds a model where generations overlap and novices learn on the job from seasoned staff.

In the model, growth comes because the most skilled experts run production and pass their know-how to many novices. Better entry-level automation can raise output at first yet slow growth and welfare over time. The harm arises when novices are moved away from top experts, while tools that link more novices to those experts help growth.
arxiv-2507-16278:
Yash Kumar probes small neural networks in a 2025 study of how they learn and hold up. Big models rule modern deep learning, yet tiny models expose basic trade-offs more clearly. Kumar builds tasks from the MNIST digit set with rising visual difficulty. Pairs range from easy digits to hard, look-alike ones.

Three findings stand out. First, the least size that learns well grows in step with task difficulty. Second, trained nets survive pruning of most weights and still work well, so sparse subnetworks hide inside them. Third, extra size buys real strength against corrupted inputs. Saliency maps show sparse nets keep the core logic of the full nets.
arxiv-2507-16378:
Roger Clay and Tadeusz Wibig ask if a near dwarf galaxy could be the source of the most energetic cosmic rays. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. A large observatory logged the top hundred events over many years, at extreme energies. The authors study the sky directions of those events.

The most energetic events bunch in one small patch of sky in a way that is not random. A long-suspected source, Centaurus A, lies near that patch. But the Large Magellanic Cloud, a dwarf galaxy that orbits our own, lies even closer in angle. They weigh the case that this cloud, not just the far galaxy, sends some of these rays our way.
arxiv-2507-16678:
Scan a body by weak currents and you can map its inner flow traits, and each drive tone shows a new slice of that map. Giovanni Alberti, Damiana Lazzaro, Serena Morigi, Luca Ratti, and Matteo Santacesaria join such tones in a 2025 study. Pure sums can stall on the twist in the task.

Their net is built by unroll: each layer of the net is one step of a sound sum loop. A graph net rides each step and learns how the tones talk to each other. The mesh of the body stays whole through the run, not squared off. Mixed zones in the flesh, the hard case, come out whole. The team banks on sums' clarity with the net's speed.
arxiv-2507-16978:
Mohammad Refahi and co-authors benchmark two vector search engines on gene data in a 2025 paper. DNA data now grows faster than classic alignment tools like BLAST can handle, above all for odd, distant sequences. Embedding methods turn sequences into number vectors that capture deeper traits, then search by vector closeness.

The team compared FAISS and ScaNN, two leading vector search libraries, on biologically meaningful gene embeddings. Their checks stress the hunt for novel sequences, including genes from unstudied species or with no known relatives. Both engines saved memory and time versus alignment-heavy routes. Retrieval quality also improved on the test tasks. The authors present embedding search as a strong partner, or stand-in, for classic tools.
arxiv-2507-17078:
Gert-Martin Greuel and Gerhard Pfister give a fresh proof of the splitting lemma, a basic tool in singularity theory also known as the generalized Morse lemma. The lemma says that, near a singular point, a power series can be split into a simple quadratic part plus a smaller residual part that carries the real complexity. Older proofs covered fields of most characteristics, but the uniqueness of the residual part in characteristic two had resisted proof.

Their argument is short and works over any field for formal power series. They also extend the result beyond the formal setting, to algebraic power series and to convergent real and complex analytic ones. The proofs are new even for non-isolated singularities, where the singular set is not a single point. The paper tidies a corner of algebra that many other results quietly rely on.
arxiv-2507-17578:
Brian DeRenzi, Anna Dixon, Mohamed Aymane Farhi, and Christian Resch test whether fake voice data can teach speech tools for African tongues. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Most of the more than two thousand tongues in Africa have no speech tech at all. Real voice data is dear, so the team asks if made-up voice data can fill the gap.

Their flow makes text with a language model, speaks it with a voice tool, then tunes a speech model on it. They made vast hours of fake voice at a tiny share of real cost. For Hausa, a mix of real and fake data matched a much larger real-only run. Gains for two low-data tongues were mixed.
arxiv-2507-17878:
Benjamin Bedert and co-authors introduced in 2025 a stronger way to shrink hard logic problems before solving them. Classic sparsification deletes constraints. Their strong version instead merges variables, which can compress a problem further. The test case is 1-in-3-SAT, where each clause needs exactly one true variable out of three.
