The algorithm's proof rests on a new bound for sets of binary vectors, kept below quadratic size. That bound leans on the recent Polynomial Freiman-Ruzsa Theorem from additive combinatorics. As a payoff, the team improved the best algorithm for approximating ordered colorings of three-uniform hypergraphs. They also probe which other constraint problems admit the same trick. The work links logic, combinatorics, and algorithm design in one argument. An extended abstract was set for a major theory conference.
arxiv-2507-17978:
Paulo Mendes and co-authors merge scattered public collections into one large corpus for training phishing detectors. Their 2025 paper presents MeAJOR, a dataset of nearly 136,000 emails spanning many phishing tactics and legitimate mail, each described by a broad engineered feature set. Machine learning detectors are only as good as this raw material.

Four standard classifiers were trained across feature configurations to test the corpus. The best, a gradient boosting model using the full feature blend, reached an F1 score near ninety-eight percent. The authors emphasize the dataset's housekeeping virtues: class balance handled, labels consistent, splits reproducible. Fragmented, aging corpora have quietly capped progress in email security research. MeAJOR's pitch is unglamorous but real: one maintained, diverse, reusable resource instead of every lab scraping together its own. The paper reports both the resource and the baseline scores future work must beat.
arxiv-2507-18078:
Qian and co-authors show that the x-ray flash from a laser-blasted plasma carries a hidden signature: its light is strongly polarized. Next-generation lasers aim to create plasmas ruled by strong-field quantum effects, like those near pulsars. A bright x-ray flash is the expected sign of reaching that regime, but ordinary processes also make hard x-rays, muddying the claim.

The team's analysis shows flash photons above a set energy are more than sixty-five percent polarized for a stated laser intensity hitting an aluminum target, while the background stays unpolarized. Polarization thus works as a fingerprint proving the quantum regime was truly entered. The result gives experimenters at multi-petawatt facilities a practical diagnostic for their headline goal.
arxiv-2507-18378:
Jasper Wijnands and co-authors compare two designs for machine-learning regional weather forecasts, in a 2025 paper. Graph neural networks now beat traditional models on regional forecasts at a fraction of the cost. Builders split into two camps: limited-area models fed at their borders by a global model, and stretched-grid models that carry a coarse global view inside.

To isolate the design choice, the team built both types from one shared architecture inside the Anemoi framework, trained on near-identical global and regional reanalysis data. Forecast runs over Europe then probed where each design shines and where it strains. Both proved competitive and broadly comparable, so the choice turns on use case rather than accuracy alone.
arxiv-2507-19078:
Digital tools carry an ecological cost that organizations rarely question. Valentin Girard, Antoine Martin, Maud Rio, and Romain Couillet propose a protocol for ecological redirection of digital practice. Rather than chasing efficiency, the approach asks which uses to give up. First, a survey maps how attached staff are to their tools. Next, training builds the knowledge needed for a real debate. A structured discussion then arbitrates which practices to close or transform.

The protocol will be tested in live organizations. The planned study measures how smoothly participants run it and whether it meets its redirection goal. Social and technical barriers are part of the scorecard.
arxiv-2507-19378:
Alessandro Benfenati, a solo author, extends a popular image-restoration strategy to a harder noise model in this 2025 paper. Plug and play methods restore images by alternating a deblurring step with an off-the-shelf denoiser, and they shine when the noise is Gaussian. Poisson noise, common in photon-limited imaging, breaks the theory: the fit term has no closed-form step and its slope is not tame.

Benfenati's method, PnPSplit+, rebuilds the scheme around the alternating direction method of multipliers. That change yields a closed-form deblurring step, so no inner iterative solver is needed. Convergence is guaranteed as long as the denoiser used is firmly non-expansive, a mild stability property. On a range of Poisson restoration problems, the method performed strongly even with heavy noise and severe blur. The author presents it as a practical route to plug and play restoration beyond the Gaussian world.
arxiv-2507-19478:
Xuehui Wang and colleagues released a benchmark in 2025 that grades computer-using agents the way a patient examiner would, level by level. Their framework, MMBench-GUI, spans Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS, Android, and the web. It has four levels: understanding what is on screen, locating the right element, automating a task, and collaborating across tasks. Each level isolates a skill that real automation needs.

The team also proposes an efficiency-quality area metric, which scores how well an agent balances speed against success in live automation. Their evaluations identified accurate visual grounding, pinpointing the right screen element, as a critical bottleneck for current agents. As software agents move from demos to daily tools, hierarchical benchmarks like this show developers exactly which floor of the building is unfinished.
arxiv-2507-19678:
Pusep and co-authors report a sharp change in light emission from an electron-hole plasma in a 2025 paper. The plasma sits in a narrow gallium arsenide channel under a strong magnetic field. Without current, its glow comes from jumps between Landau levels in two bands.

Past a critical current, the glow changed radically, with light holes taking the lead role. The current drags light holes into local piles, the authors show, which strengthens coupling and forms bound pairs called excitons and trions. The finding reveals a current switch for optical behavior in small devices. Such switches interest builders of light-based electronics.
arxiv-2507-19978:
Junhyung Chang and Joshua Cape study how statisticians can recover structure from a noisy table of numbers. The setting is matrix denoising: a clean signal table is buried under random Gaussian noise, and the goal is to recover its leading directions. Most earlier work measured error in average ways. This paper asks about the worst row instead, using a two-to-infinity norm that captures the largest row-wise miss.

They prove that, after centering and scaling, that error follows a Gumbel curve, the law of extremes, as the table grows. From the limit they build a hypothesis test for low-rank structure, along with corrected estimates of the signal strengths it needs. In trials, the new test beat the average-based distance at spotting alternatives that differ in only a few entries or rows. It held up when the noise was not Gaussian.
arxiv-2507-20478:
Kishikawa, Muto, and Kotsuki use conditional diffusion models to fill gaps in global rainfall maps in a 2025 paper. Satellite rainfall products miss large regions because microwave sensors pass only at certain times. Current filling methods often leave spatial breaks in the maps.

The task is framed as video inpainting. A 3D network with a condition encoder rebuilds full maps using infrared images, location grids, and time inputs. Training used hourly reanalysis data, with fake satellite masks applied to mimic real gaps. On a held-out year, the method produced maps that were more consistent in space and time than standard methods. The authors see promise for global rainfall monitoring.
arxiv-2507-20778:
Iuliu Cuceu, Marie Anne Bizouard, Nelson Christensen and Mairi Sakellariadou test the origin of gravitational-wave event GW231123, in work from 2025. The LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA team had read the signal as a merger of two black holes. The signal is short, with only about five cycles seen by the two LIGO detectors, so other sources deserve a check.

The authors run a Bayesian model comparison between a binary black hole merger and signals from cusps or kinks on a cosmic string. They find significant evidence for the black hole merger origin. Readers get a direct test of an unusual alternative, carried out on one of the most striking events reported so far.
arxiv-2507-22178:
Martin Costabel and Monique Dauge studied how math solutions blow up near sharp corners. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with harmonic functions on domains with corners. At a true corner, the rates of change of a solution can grow without bound, even for smooth data. When the corner is rounded off, the solution stays tame but its norms can still surge as the rounding shrinks.

The pair checked two cases: a rounded corner in any dimension, and a flat corner split into smaller angles. They used an inner expansion from recent work on power series forms. From it they proved plain bounds for the norms and the singular parts. Readers in numeric math get clear rates for this blow up.
arxiv-2507-22378:
Yueh-Po Peng, Vincent Cheung, and Li Su present a brain decoding model in a 2025 paper. Reading mental states from brain scans is a core goal of neuroscience, but scan data are noisy, huge, and scarce for any single person. The team borrows a trick from image AI: learn general patterns from a very large scan library first, then adapt to small tasks.

Their model, a transformer design, learned from scans of 995 people in a major public project. It splits attention between space and time, which keeps the computing cost in check. After this broad training, the model read task-driven brain activity far better than models trained from scratch, across tasks of sensing and thinking. Gains also came from wide spatial views and from training data that matched the task at hand.
arxiv-2507-22478:
Lei Sheng and Shuai-Shuai Xu show that small language models can turn plain questions into database queries in a 2025 paper. Big models ace this text-to-SQL task, but small ones, with under two billion parameters, lag on logic. Their speed and fit for edge devices still make them worth pushing.

Starting from a large open dataset, the team built two training sets: one for writing SQL, one for merging and fixing drafts. Supervised fine-tuning came first, then reinforcement learning, then a self-checking step at run time that corrects its own output. On a standard benchmark, five small models gained about thirty-one points on average. The smallest reached about fifty-seven percent exact-run accuracy, and the largest about sixty-seven percent. Code, data, and models are released in public for others to build on.
arxiv-2507-22578: Morozov derives, in a 2025 mathematics paper, a family of nonlocal conservation laws for the two-dimensional Euler equation written in vorticity form. The laws govern how an ideal fluid's motion preserves certain quantities. His route joins two tools: the canonical conservation law construction and the nonlocal cosymmetry idea. Blending them yields the new collection. For ease of computation and presentation, the work performs a complex rotation of the independent variables. Each added law deepens the map of what this classic flow model keeps fixed beneath its swirling surface.
arxiv-2507-22878:
Ethan Frakes, Yinghui Wu, Roger French, and Mengjie Li build a linked data graph for power outages, in a 2025 paper. Outage reports by county are fine in time but coarse in space. Night light photos from satellites show place in fine detail, but only once a day.

Their graph joins both sources with high detail outage maps under a shared scheme. It holds more than ten million outage records, hundreds of thousands of night photos, and thousands of maps, spanning about a decade. Joining the sources should sharpen how outages are found, mapped, and forecast. That can aid grid risk work and storm response planning.
arxiv-2507-23078:
Niladri Dutta, Elham Abolfazli, and Themistoklis Charalambous built a test platform in 2025 for cars that drive in close convoys. Their system links cruise control with car-to-car radio talk, so each car can react to the group, not just the car ahead. Most past work on such convoys stayed in computer models.

The team reviewed known control designs and ran both models and real tests on robot car setups. Several convoy layouts were tried to check how steady the group stays. Both model and field results showed clear gains from the linked control method. Steady spacing held up well in the tests. The work gives engineers a working rig for trying convoy control ideas in the real world.
arxiv-2507-23178:
Siyuan Liu, Zhice Yang, and Huangxun Chen present AutoBridge, a tool that writes code to link smart devices to a central platform. Their twenty twenty-five paper notes that each new device now needs hand-written code, a slow task that takes expert skill. AutoBridge aims to generate that code on its own.

The tool splits the job in two: first the device control logic, built by fetching device facts step by step, then platform-ready code. A debug stage tests the code on virtual devices, then on real ones with just yes or no feedback from the user. On thirty-four devices it hit high success and coverage rates with no human help.
arxiv-2507-23378:
Takaaki Ishii, Keiju Murata, and Keita Sugawara build new forms of a Kaluza-Klein monopole with scalar hair. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. The base object is a known monopole in five-way gravity. Hair here means a scalar field that grows on it and changes its traits.

They write the field as a set of parts, using Wigner matrices to fit the shape of the base monopole. The plan works for a set of any size. They then solve the cases of a triplet and a quadruplet in full by computer. The range of mass and spin for these hairy forms grows as the set gets larger.
arxiv-2507-23578:
Min-Qi Li and co-authors wrote this 2025 particle physics paper on rare B meson decays. They predict how often the mesons decay into a charmonium plus a light scalar meson, and how lopsided those decays are between matter and antimatter. The light scalars are suspects in the hunt for glueballs, particles made of pure glue, possibly fragmented across several states. The calculations run in an improved perturbative QCD framework with next-to-leading corrections.

Mixing among the four scalar states is built into the flavor basis. One headline rate, for the strange B decaying through the 980 state into two pions, comes out near 2.87 times ten to the minus four, matching measurements within errors. The team also forecast large rates and large CP asymmetries for the 1500 state, squarely testable at LHCb and Belle II. Verdicts there could settle whether that scalar is a true glueball.
arxiv-2507-23778:
Li Siyao and co-authors add physical touch to a digital human model in a 2025 paper. Popular body models capture shape and pose well but only move points in space. They cannot push objects or rest on surfaces, so virtual people often sink into chairs or pass through props.

Their half-physics method turns posed motion into a live physics simulation while keeping control of the pose. The body can then press, lean, and collide in a believable way. The method needs no training, works for any body shape or motion, and runs in real time. Readers in graphics and robotics get a practical bridge between motion data and physical scenes.
arxiv-2508-00278:
Gao and co-authors report a fifty-second pulsing rhythm in the fading X-ray glow of a gamma-ray burst, in this 2025 paper. Long bursts are thought to come from collapsing massive stars feeding black holes. Direct proof of the engine has stayed out of reach.

The slow pulse, near zero point zero two cycles per second, appeared in the early afterglow of burst GRB 220711B. The team read it as a wobbling jet from a greedily feeding black hole. Late X-ray energy input fit the wobble story, while the prompt flash showed no pulse. The split hints the star's core and envelope stored spin differently.
arxiv-2508-00478:
Yuning Jiang and co-authors build a game based engine to help defenders pick which software flaws to patch first. Their 2025 paper models cyber conflict as a game between attacker and defender. Attack unfolds in stages, and defenders must rank fixes under uncertainty. Older game models used fixed assumptions and ignored live threat data. This engine adds language models with retrieval to guide tactic choice and patch ranking.

The contest is framed as a game with partial information, played across the stages of a standard attack chain. Both sides track belief states about the other. The attacker adapts tactics; the defender re-ranks patches as risks shift. In a dynamic patch scheduling test, the engine favored high risk flaws. The design can extend to many agents, such as coordinated attackers or joint defense teams.
arxiv-2508-00578:
Marlen Neubert, Patrick Reiser, Frauke Grater, and Pascal Friederich teach computer models the energy maps of hydrogen atom moves in peptides, in work from 2025. Such moves matter in living systems, for one in how damage spreads in proteins. Mapping them needs quantum level care over large systems, which is costly.

Machine learned models can reach near quantum accuracy at far lower cost. The team built large data sets with fast and with careful methods. They tested three graph based network designs on how well each learned the energy maps. Good maps would let researchers trace radical moves in proteins at scale.
arxiv-2508-00778:
Jiankai Tang and seven colleagues wrote a 2025 paper on a smart ring built for research. Smart rings can track heart rate, motion, and skin heat all day without getting in the way. Most rings on sale are closed systems, which blocks scientists from checking or reusing the data freely.

Their platform, called τ-Ring, is open for research use. The ring packs light-based heart sensors, a motion chip, a heat sensor, tap-to-share tech, and on-board storage, all in sync. Its software lets users set sample rates and power modes fast. The team hopes an open ring speeds up wearable studies. The paper describes both the hardware and the tools that come with it.
arxiv-2508-01178:
Yi Jiang and co-authors introduce a single model for many music tasks in a 2025 paper. Music research has long relied on narrow models, each built for one task. Their model, called MuFun, is meant to grasp music as a whole, handling sound and lyrics together in one design.

Training covered a large set of tasks, from sorting genre and tagging traits to answering questions about songs. The team also built a new test set, called MuCUE, to judge broad music grasp. On those tests, MuFun beat current audio language models by a clear margin. The work points toward one base model for music tools instead of many small ones.
arxiv-2508-01678:
Zhaochen Wang, Yiwei Wang, and Yujun Cai bake the task text into the picture itself and watch model hallucination swing both ways, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Three open vision-language models took the baked-in prompts. One channel must then carry all the facts.

One model gained four points on a truth test and lied less on photo sets. The other two crashed from near eighty-four percent to coin-flip levels. Their vision encoders stared too hard at the baked text and lost the scene. The winner's encoder stayed calm and its two channels drew closer. Readers get a cure for one model and poison for its kin, from one trick.
arxiv-2508-02078:
Patrick Sonnentag, Fabian Michel, and Markus Siegle present a new way to shrink large Markov chains in this 2025 paper. Their method builds on the Arnoldi iteration, a standard tool for cutting down big linear systems. The goal is to estimate how a chain's state chances change over time without tracking every state.

Unlike older grouping methods, their lumped states can each stand for parts of many original states, so the reduced system is no longer a Markov chain. The authors prove results on exactness and smallest size, and they add a rule for when to stop growing the reduced system. Tests on several models compare the method with a lumping-based scheme.
arxiv-2508-02378:
Zhenhua Zhu, Gu Zhang, and Dong E Liu show how to weigh entanglement with wires and currents. Their 2025 paper designs a transport protocol that reads out von Neumann entropy and mutual information. These quantities are normally locked inside a quantum system's full state, in devices where several parts interact and fluctuate.

The key finding is survival: the link between entanglement entropy and simple two-point correlation functions, known in tidy settings, persists with many-body interactions and multiple subsystems. The measurement works for systems interacting at their boundaries and, harder still, for bulk-interacting systems whose couplings are suddenly quenched. The authors offer mutual information as a practical gauge of how entangled a system is with its environment.
arxiv-2508-03278:
Albertus Handoko and Riko Made review, in 2025 work, how smart models that create new designs are changing the hunt for new materials. Fast test tools, learning methods, and open data sets now let teams state the traits they want and search back to a material that fits. That flip is often called inverse design.

The review sets out the main kinds of such models and the ways materials can be coded for them. It then shows uses in catalysts, chips, plastics, and crystals. Hard parts get full space too: scarce data, high cost, hard-to-read models, and bias in data sets. New fixes include models that mix data types, build in physics rules, and link straight to lab tests in a loop.
arxiv-2508-03478:
Kexun Shen, Zhiwen Cheng, and Zhiyong Qiu derive in this 2025 paper the steady spectra of weak kinetic-Alfvénic turbulence, a plasma wave cascade near ion scales. Starting from gyrokinetic theory, they build a wave kinetic equation for how the waves trade energy through three-wave meetings. A classic transform trick then yields exact power-law spectra.

The solutions cover long and short wavelength limits, and waves running both against and with each other. The team identifies which way each cascade flows and confirms the steady states by solving the full equation numerically. They close by tying the spectra to solar wind turbulence and to helical forms of the same cascade.
arxiv-2508-03678:
Yangtian Zi, Harshitha Menon, and Arjun Guha probe how prompt detail shapes code generation in two thousand twenty-five. Top language models score high on general code tests. They lag on niche suites like ParEval, though. The gap could stem from thin domain facts or thin prompts.

Their tool, PartialOrderEval, grows any code test with prompts from bare to full. They run it on HumanEval and on serial and parallel parts of ParEval. Two model families show varied prompt sensitivity by task. Close looks name input output specs, edge cases, and step splits as key drivers. Scores alone thus hide much of what prompts do.
arxiv-2508-03778:
Ai and Zhang give a sharp spectral condition for Hamilton cycles in tough balanced bipartite graphs, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. A Hamilton cycle visits every vertex exactly once and returns. Spectral radius, the largest adjacency eigenvalue, can certify such cycles. Bipartite toughness measures how hard a graph is to split apart.

For balanced bipartite graphs with toughness at least one, they find the exact spectral threshold. Above it, a Hamilton cycle is guaranteed to exist. At the threshold, the extremal structure is pinned down as well. The result settles an open problem posed in prior work. It links eigenvalue bounds and toughness in a tight, complete way.
arxiv-2508-03878:
Matias Cattaneo and Rocío Titiunik introduced the regression discontinuity design for medical researchers in twenty twenty-five. This design exploits cutoffs in treatment assignment. When a measurement crossing a threshold decides treatment, patients just above and just below are nearly alike. Comparing them then reveals the treatment's causal effect. The design is a workhorse in economics and is spreading in medicine.

Their article explains the design's logic with a running medical example. The focus is on causal interpretation — what the comparison does and does not prove — with brief coverage of estimation and inference. The piece is a primer, meant to help medical scientists read and use discontinuity studies soundly, recognizing both their unusual credibility and their local scope.
arxiv-2508-03978:
Amir Shaikhha and co-authors build Raqlet, a translator that carries recursive queries between database worlds that rarely talk to each other. Their 2025 paper addresses a fragmented scene: recursive SQL, graph languages like Cypher and GQL, and the logic language Datalog each run recursion their own way. New standards promise common ground, but vendor support is patchy.

Raqlet routes a query through a chain of intermediate forms, from a graph flavored one to a logic flavored one and finally to recursive SQL. Each step rests on defined semantics, so meaning survives the trip. The chain doubles as a reference build for the standards, and supports tricks like magic set rewriting for speed. The goal is portable recursion anywhere.
arxiv-2508-04378:
Hossein Jond, writing alone in 2025, presents a flocking model that aligns agents using positions alone. Flocking models balance pulling together, keeping apart, and matching neighbors' direction to produce stable collective motion. Classic models need velocities, which are harder to measure than positions in many real systems.

The model approximates velocity differences from initial and current positions and adds a threshold weight to sustain alignment. In simulations with fifty agents in two dimensions, it produced stronger alignment and tighter, more rigid formations than a position-velocity model. Position-only flocking could suit drone swarms tracked by cameras.
arxiv-2508-04478:
Bernardino D'Amico and three co-authors ask who actually saves from insulation in twenty twenty-five. Cutting home energy demand is central to climate and fuel poverty policy. Efficiency upgrades do not save equally for everyone, though. The team applies causal machine learning to nationally representative data on English housing.

They estimate average and subgroup effects of wall insulation on gas use. On average, demand falls by as much as nineteen percent. Households with low energy burdens capture substantial savings. Households with high burdens see little or no reduction. The explanation is behavioral, not wasteful: squeezed families spend the savings on warmth they previously could not afford. Readers in energy policy get a distributional warning: headline savings hide who was cold.
arxiv-2508-04578:
Peter Namdar and co-authors design quantum light operations in thin-film waveguides in this 2025 paper. Modern photonics can control the color and timing shapes of light with great care. That control is key for building larger quantum information systems.

The team target two non-Gaussian steps: taking one photon away and adding one photon. Both steps must act only on a chosen shape of light pulse. They work in the telecom band, where fiber networks already operate. Their design is the first framework for both steps in thin-film lithium niobate. It builds on earlier near-infrared work on photon subtraction. The plan could support future quantum networks and processors.
arxiv-2508-04978:
Sippanon Kitimoon presents in a 2025 dissertation two signal processing methods built on localized kernels, math tools that focus on small slices of a signal. Both methods recover hidden parameters from noisy data without heavy assumptions. The first finds the pitches and strengths inside a mix of pure tones that fade or grow.

That method beat two classic tools when noise ran high, and a projection trick let it handle multi-part signals with few samples. The second method splits apart sliding tones, called chirps, even when they cross or break off, at noise levels far below the signal. Both share fast Fourier-based code and need no sparsity guesses.
arxiv-2508-05578:
Julio Hernandez and co-authors revisited a family of gas equations in 2025 to better forecast how fast air cools with height on other planets. This cooling rate is called the adiabatic lapse rate. Their equations extend the classic van der Waals model with one added dial that tunes how particle attraction shifts with heat. They worked out the model's core traits, from phase borders to entropy.

The team then computed cooling rates for the lower skies of Titan and Venus. Their model matched the observed rates more closely than the classic equation did. Adding the spin and shaking motions of molecules was part of the gain. Better rates help scientists read alien weather from sparse data.
arxiv-2508-05678:
Xinying Tang and Wenqian Zhang give spectral conditions for a graph to contain a k-factor. Their 2025 arXiv paper works with the spectral radius of a graph's adjacency matrix. A k-factor is a spanning subgraph where every vertex has degree exactly k. The question is when a large spectral radius forces such a factor to exist.

The setting fixes a minimum degree of at least k for the graph. The order of the graph must also pass a stated lower bound. Under those terms, the authors give a sharp lower bound on the spectral radius. Any graph meeting the bound is guaranteed to contain a k-factor. Sharpness means the bound cannot be weakened in general. The result adds a spectral test to factor theory.
arxiv-2508-05878:
Martyna Majchrzak and Jacek Mańdziuk ask whether fake music can teach computers to hear chords. Recognizing chord sequences in recordings is a standard task in music technology, but training data is scarce because most recordings are copyrighted. Artificial multitrack music, generated rather than composed, offers a legal substitute.

The team trained two transformer-based models on mixes of three datasets: the artificial set, a dataset of Schubert songs, and a pop chart collection. They scored the models on how well they named chord roots, chord types, and full chord content. Artificial data alone could train a model that reads pop chords respectably when nothing else is available. Mixed with a small human-made set, it strengthened results further. The authors note that generated music is simpler than composed music, so it cannot replace real recordings outright.
arxiv-2508-05978:
Wei Chen and six co-authors present a 2025 method for changing one singing voice into another from a single sample. The task keeps the tune and the words while swapping the tone of the singer. The hard part is copying a new singer's tone without leaking the source tone or spoiling the sound.

Their method swaps the source audio's learned features for the closest matching features from the target sample, which blocks tone leakage. A dual attention block blends the singer traits, the tune, and the word content. A flow matching block then builds clean audio from the blend. In both human and machine tests, the method beat the best prior systems on how close the tone matched and on how natural the result sounded.
arxiv-2508-06178:
Hugo Abonizio and three colleagues compare ways to teach language models new facts when only a little fresh text is available, in a 2025 paper. Big updates are easy; small ones risk teaching little while erasing old skills.

The team used recent news, absent from the models' training, and quizzed the models on it. Plain extra training on the small set helped only modestly. Rewriting the facts in many varied forms helped much more, above all when prompts pushed for variety. A lookup-based method damaged old skills the most. Models could even write their own useful practice data, hinting at self-improving updates.
arxiv-2508-06278:
Petr Novák, Stefan Biffl, Marek Obitko, and Petr Kadera build a knowledge graph to help factories spot and fix unwanted states in flexible production lines. Their 2025 paper notes that robot workcells that switch tasks often break older quality-check methods. Problems can hide in how products, processes, and machines interact.

Their model, PPR-AKG, extends a proven industry framework with a formal ontology that records errors and unwanted conditions directly. Paired with language models, it lets operators ask questions in plain words. A test case on electric vehicle battery remanufacturing shows the graph supports smart resource assignment. It also helps teams find and soften production problems.
arxiv-2508-06478:
Dan Johnson and co-authors study how fast computers can tell whether two algebra systems are the same. Their 2025 paper treats finite groups and near-group systems given by full product tables. Splitting a system into basic blocks turns out to be the lever that makes the task fast.

For groups whose blocks are simple in set ways, a known graph-like test names the group in very few rounds. The team places that task in a low parallel class, a step better than past bounds. For a wider class, they give a fast labeling method and show the split itself can be computed quickly in parallel. One more result speeds up tests for a special near-group class.
arxiv-2508-06578:
The authors rework heat math for black holes bathed in dark matter in a 2025 paper. Their frame uses a sharp energy gauge fit for curved space. Phantom fields form the backdrop. Fresh forms of force, bulk, heat, and waste heat come from that gauge. Small holes shake with heat noise, so the team add fix terms for those shakes.

With the new forms they grade stored heat, free heat, and heat hold of the holes. Graphs of heat hold against hole rim size sort firm holes from frail ones. The dark bath shifts those grades in set ways. The paper serves black hole heat work in dark settings.
arxiv-2508-06678:
Anantha Suresh Babu and co-authors test the turbulence recipes ocean simulators use when the flow meets a coastline. Their 2025 paper extends a quasi-geostrophic solver, running on graphics processors, to handle islands and capes through a penalization method that embeds land inside the fluid grid. Four analytical sub-grid closures are compared: two classic eddy-viscosity formulas and their dynamic variants.

The closures were judged twice: on how well their terms match filtered truth, and on how well the resulting simulations rebuild the real flow's patterns around obstacles. Differences concentrated in phase and feature reconstruction near boundaries, exactly where coastal applications live. Ocean models cannot resolve every eddy, so closures carry the physics; knowing which one fails least near land is operational knowledge. The benchmark suite gives modelers a coastal yardstick that open-ocean tests never provided.
arxiv-2508-07278:
Qing-Han Yang and six colleagues show how slipping extra atoms into the magnet CrI3 could push its magnetism near room temperature, in a 2025 paper. In its plain form this layered material only stays magnetic below 45 kelvin, far too cold for spintronic devices. Using first-principles calculations, the team tested intercalation, which inserts atoms between the layers.

Lithium worked best, lifting the predicted Curie temperature to 286 kelvin, close to an experimental report of 420 kelvin. The boost comes from two exchange effects acting together, plus charge transfer that mixes chromium valence states. Copper and sodium insertions also helped, giving the authors a general recipe for designing warmer magnets.
arxiv-2508-07378:
Paul Mella studies a question in geometry and dynamics in a twenty twenty-five paper. He looks at the geodesic flow on curved surfaces and spaces known as Riemannian manifolds. The question is whether ergodic measures, a special kind of invariant measure, are generic there. Generic here means that almost all such measures have that property.

Mella gives a new condition under which the answer is no. If the metric splits as a product near a certain complete submanifold with a closed geodesic, the ergodic measures fail to fill the whole set. His result answers a question tied to a specific three-dimensional example from Gromov. Readers in dynamics get a clean test for when genericity breaks down.
arxiv-2508-07678:
Kun Xu tests how trustworthy the small dark-matter clumps in cosmic simulations really are. These subhalos host satellite galaxies and anchor many galaxy-formation models, but inside big halos, tides tear at them and simulations may lose them artificially. Xu compares two huge simulations of the Jiutian suite that differ in particle mass, tracking clumps with a dedicated finder.

Counts of surviving clumps settle down only for the heftiest ones. Adding back orphan clumps, lost ones whose galaxies should live on by a merger-clock model, repairs the counts well. With orphans included, positions and speeds of clumps match between the two runs to within five to ten percent down to small scales. The finest scales still resist, and measures that fold in galaxy recession speeds are harder still to recover.
arxiv-2508-07978:
Hamidreza Mazandarani and co-authors present, in a 2025 paper, a joint plan for placing image-generating AI services on edge servers and sharing access to them. Diffusion models make rich images but need many costly steps, which strains real-time mobile use. Their framework splits the cleaning steps of generation across mixed edge machines.

A learning algorithm moves service pieces as demand shifts, while cutting steps when quality allows. A greedy access rule joins a deep learning placement method that weighs reward now and later. Sending the hidden image state between servers adds cost, which the model counts. Simulations beat fixed, single-server plans on scale and delay, the authors report.
arxiv-2508-08178:
Ozhan Suat and co-authors present a 2025 method for building a 3D mesh of a human body from one color-plus-depth view. Depth cameras are cheap and common, yet most mesh work still uses plain color images. Full training sets for the depth task are small and lack pose variety, so the team turned to motion capture data.

They built full meshes from capture models, then cut them to what one view would see. A masked model learned to fill in the hidden parts. At test time, depth points are matched to a template mesh and the model completes it, with low error on two benchmarks.
arxiv-2508-08578:
The authors build a data-driven control frame for grid power converters in a 2025 paper. Converters link solar, storage, and cars to the grid. Stock control stacks tuned PID loops on a crude grid model. Real grids shift and hide their form, so tuned loops can lag or shake. Their DeePC frame reads grid traits from live data and picks control moves for best grade, sans a set model.

Units run this way earn the name DeePConverters. The paper lays out the frame's parts, grades, and built-in grit. Cost and online shift craft get full play. High-fact sims and hardware-loop tests back the claims. The team pitch data as the model the grid keeps hid.
arxiv-2508-08978:
Zhentao Fan, Zongzuo Wang, and Weiwei Zhang present a 2025 paper on speeding up AI video generation without wrecking the picture. Video diffusion models spend many steps cleaning noise from each frame; caching shortcuts reuse earlier calculations but usually skip early steps, which distorts structure and breaks character consistency. The team's method, TaoCache, works at the late steps instead.

Rather than caching leftover differences, it predicts the model's noise output from a fixed-point view, calibrated by how consecutive noise changes align in direction and size. That preserves fine structure while skipping aggressively. The trick needs no retraining and combines with other accelerators. On three video models it beat earlier caching methods on standard quality scores at equal speedups.
arxiv-2508-09378:
Artem Chernodub and four co-authors built a system that writes and improves its own prompts for language models, with no human-drafted starting text. Prompt engineering is usually artisanal trial and error, and existing automatic optimizers still need a seed prompt. Their method, APIO, induces a prompt from the task and refines it against the score that matters.

They aimed it at two editing tasks: fixing grammatical errors and simplifying text. On both, APIO reached the best reported results for purely prompt-based language model methods, beating hand-crafted and seeded approaches. The gains suggest that a model can bootstrap its own instructions better than a person guessing what it wants to hear. The team released the data, code, prompts, and outputs for others to inspect. They frame it as a way to make language model tools less dependent on scarce prompt-crafting expertise.
arxiv-2508-09478:
Moinak Bhattacharya, Gagandeep Singh, Shubham Jain, and Prateek Prasanna present GazeLT, a method that uses radiologist eye gaze to sort chest X-ray diseases, with stress on rare classes. A reader's gaze holds both fine and broad disease clues, and it shifts over the read. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

Experts also glance at minor finds, which make up many rare classes. GazeLT folds gaze in and out over time to mimic that search. Tests on two large public sets for rare class sorting beat the best rare class loss by a clear margin. It also beat a gaze based baseline by a far larger margin, the authors report.
arxiv-2508-09578:
Ai-Jun Ma and Wen-Fei Wang calculate a subtle effect in the decays of B mesons, heavy particles whose breakup patterns test the Standard Model, in this 2025 physics paper. Inside some three body decays, a short lived resonance can act while off its natural mass, and such virtual steps can sway the outcome more than expected. The authors study that effect for one resonance in two decay families.

Working inside a standard calculation framework, they first derive the needed coupling strengths from a known cousin coupling, using flavor symmetry. The predicted rates for the virtual channels come out extremely small, in a range experiments cannot yet reach. One family lands at about half the rate of the other, mostly from space for the products. Data from two running experiments are expected soon.
arxiv-2508-09778:
Nikos Frantzikinakis and Andreas Mountakis prove recurrence results for a class of number based dynamical systems along Pythagorean type triples. Their 2025 paper studies solutions of a generalized equation joining three squares with weights. Recurrence asks whether a system must return near its start along such patterns. The systems here are built from multiplicative functions with a tame, pretentious character.

The main theorem confirms a conjectured ergodic form of a partition regularity claim in this setting. A coloring consequence follows. Take any finite coloring of the whole numbers built from level sets of such functions. Somewhere, a single color class must contain a full generalized Pythagorean triple. The result links number theory, dynamics, and combinatorics. Structured systems, not just arbitrary ones, are shown to force these arithmetic patterns.
arxiv-2508-10078:
Peter Dankelmann, Sonwabile Mafunda, and Sufiyan Mallu study how spread out the points of a flat network can be. Their 2025 paper uses the mean distance from each point to all others. The smallest such mean is called proximity, and the largest is called remoteness. Past work set broad caps on gaps between these values for any linked network.

The authors show much tighter caps for flat networks that use all possible links, and for networks with strong links between parts. Like results hold for four-sided flat networks and for flat networks drawn in a ring. They give sample networks that show their caps are sharp or near sharp.
arxiv-2508-10178:
Jozef Skakala presents a 2025 paper on estimating carbon stores in Europe's shallow shelf seas. These seas matter for both economies and the carbon cycle, yet direct measurements of their carbon pools are sparse and shaky. Full reanalysis runs that blend models with observations are costly, so Skakala tests a cheaper stand-in.

He trains a team of neural networks on a free-running physics and biology model of the North-West European Shelf. Fed with reanalysis inputs, the networks predicted pools such as detritus, zooplankton, and bacteria far closer to the reanalysis than the raw model did, while also reporting their own uncertainty. Driven by raw observations, they worked too, but only where and when observations existed. The approach could fill carbon maps cheaply.
arxiv-2508-10278:
Dark matter may collide with itself, and simulating that process inside dense halos is slow with standard methods. Sarah Schon and co-authors present a hybrid scheme that switches to fluid equations where the gas of particles is dense. A local measure of particle crowding sets where each method runs. The switch targets the deep collapse stage of halo centers, where density climbs steeply.

The hybrid runs reached center densities about a hundred times higher in much less time. Results looked much like those from older methods, though details of the halo shape differed. The authors call this a first step and plan to add non-ideal fluid effects. The method could open collapse studies in varied, changing settings.
arxiv-2508-10378:
Yu Chen and co-authors design a smarter control frame in 2025 for robot arms worn on the human arm. Such exoskeletons help with home care tasks, yet they need to read the wearer's intent and adjust to what is being held. A cup and a tool call for different help, and past systems rarely grasped that.

Their frame lets a large language model read the task's meaning and set the help levels on its own. At the start, the suit runs clear so the wearer's grasp intent can be caught. A diffusion-based watcher tracks the human-robot state and triggers fresh planning when odd signs appear. The aim is help that is both safe and tuned to intent, across more home tasks.
arxiv-2508-10878:
Nora Sherman and a large team describe a supernova survey program in a 2025 paper. Precise measures of Type Ia supernovae at low redshift anchor our knowledge of cosmic expansion. The program, DEBASS, will deliver the largest evenly calibrated set of such supernovae in the southern sky.

It uses the Dark Energy Camera for imaging and a wide-field spectrograph for host galaxy data. Sharing instruments with two major surveys gives a robust calibration base. The paper lays out the motive, design, and first data release. Cosmologists get a firmer low-redshift bedrock against which to test dark energy models and the shape of expansion.
arxiv-2508-10978:
Devon Stockall and Matthew Yu prove a sweeping version of the crystalline equivalence principle, a bridge between two ways of describing quantum field theories with symmetry. On one side stand theories defined on a space whose symmetry acts through the space itself; on the other, theories where it acts internally. The principle says the two descriptions match as categories.

Beyond the main theorem, the paper defines and classifies anomalies, the obstructions that can spoil it, for theories living with spatial symmetry. It then lifts that notion of anomaly to the broader setting of categorical symmetry, where symmetries themselves form a richer structure. The result gives physicists and mathematicians a general dictionary for moving it between geometry and algebra.
arxiv-2508-11078:
Yacine Mokhtari tackles network design problems with tree-shaped backbones in this 2025 paper. Many flow networks must ride on a spanning tree, a choice that explodes combinatorially. The test case limits how many hops each delivery may take across shared goods.

The method relaxes the yes-no choices into smooth values and glues them to a tree answer through a penalty scheme. Each round solves a smooth subproblem, then snaps the result to the cheapest valid tree, a fast classical step. A distributed twin lets agents cooperate by local messages alone. Experiments found near-best designs in many cases. The author frames the approach as a practical heuristic for large, hard design problems.
arxiv-2508-11778:
Matt Gottsacker and co-authors argue that extended reality headsets need a new design center: switching tasks without leaving the world. On a desktop, workers flick between apps with shortcuts, and headsets now allow several flat windows at once. But the XR apps that matter for knowledge work are spatial, and flat windows serve them badly. Today each immersive app runs sealed off, so changing jobs means quitting one world and loading another.

The paper lays out a vision for XR-first context switching, where focus and control glide across rich spatial apps the way they glide across desktop windows. The authors mean the framework as a compass for researchers and builders, naming what such interfaces must do. They frame fast, graceful switching as the missing piece that keeps XR from serving real knowledge work.
arxiv-2508-11978:
Viacheslav Yusupov and co-authors bend geometry to sharpen product tips in a 2025 paper. Tip engines learn user and item codes from past clicks and likes. Curved, hyperbolic space can hold tree like taste patterns that flat space fits poorly.

Their model reworks curved distance to free up more code room. A three way loss weighs a liked item against a shunned one for each user. The curved model beat flat and past curved rivals in tests. It also cut the bias toward hit items, so tips grew more varied and more personal for each user.
arxiv-2508-12078:
When can one promise that a partition function never hits zero? Jan Philipp Neumann derived in 2025 a test that answers this for lattice gases whose particles interact in groups, not just pairs.

The test extends recent results on independence counts for hypergraphs, and covers hard-core cases where particles cannot overlap. Neumann gives two proofs: one builds step by step on an earlier inductive method, and one uses a classic hierarchy of equations. The second proof's covering scheme also sharpens a famous 1968 bound on a key operator. Zero-free regions matter because they guarantee that counting methods and sampling schemes behave well.
arxiv-2508-12378:
Saad Eddine Baddis, Adil Belhaj, and Hajar Belmahi wrote this 2025 arXiv paper using graphics processors to stress-test ideas from string theory against black holes. The swampland program asks which low-energy theories could ever arise from a consistent quantum gravity, and charged black holes in an inflationary potential make a sharp test bed.

Running the heavy numerics on CUDA-parallel hardware, the team mapped how the black hole's horizon roots move as charge, mass, and scalar settings change. They traced a charge-to-mass relation that approaches the extremal limit, the edge where a black hole is as charged as physics allows. Thermodynamic analysis then showed where black holes destabilize into light states, exactly the fate swampland conjectures predict past a critical ratio. The paper is as much a methods note as a physics result: consumer-grade parallel computing can reach questions once reserved for clusters.
arxiv-2508-12878:
Michael Lashkevich and Amir Nesturov compute response values for twisted operators in a classic toy theory of mass, in a 2025 paper. The stage is the sinh-Gordon model, a field theory in one space dimension prized for its exact solvability. They set it on a Riemann surface of stacked planes, joined along cuts that end at branch points. A twist operator sits at each branch point, the tool that lets one count entanglement in the flat model.

Their operators are composite: a plain local field is fused into the branch point by a limit trick. The values sought, form factors, are the operator's overlaps with the theory's standing states. Full sets exist in principle from bootstrap rules, yet matching them to real fields stays hard. The pair build a method for this class in the semiclassical limit, where the field runs heavy and slow.
arxiv-2508-13278:
Fabio La Monaca and co-authors measure the polarization of X-rays from a neutron star system called GX 340+0, a bright member of the Z-source class. Three space telescopes took part, one built to read polarization and two that read spectra. The team studied the source in its normal branch state and compared it with an earlier horizontal branch reading.

The light was clearly polarized in both states. The share fell from about 3.7 percent in the horizontal branch to about 1.4 percent in the normal branch. The angle stayed on the same trend. The glowing gas component blamed for much of the signal was more polarized than plain theory predicts for a boundary layer. The authors suggest a wind or an extended corona above the disk adds to the signal, and they argue polarization data sharpen our picture of how such stars feed.
arxiv-2508-13378:
Yiting Wang and co-authors set out a deployment plan for small language models in medical imaging in a 2025 paper. The head title frames the work as governance-ready models, covering prompting, abstention, and hospital system integration. Small models suit narrow imaging chores where privacy, speed, and cost rule. Their test task is tagging chest X-rays by view direction, a small but real workflow job.

Four compact vision-language models were tried on a public chest X-ray set. Prompts that made the model reflect helped the lighter models most. Stronger models cared less about prompt style. The authors stress measures beyond accuracy: how often the model abstains, how well its confidence matches its hit rate, and how much human oversight it needs. Outputs are mapped to hospital data standards so results slot into record systems. The plan is offered as a playbook, not as clinical proof.
arxiv-2508-13578:
Gourab Pathak and Mrinal Kumar Das build a neutrino model in 2025 that explains several open puzzles at once. Neutrinos have tiny masses and mix as they travel, and a classic mechanism explains the pattern with a broken extra symmetry. Their version gets the same effect from modular symmetry, where set weights play the role of the extra charges.

Using one modular group, the model fits the measured mixing and mass data. It also speaks to two deeper questions: a rare decay that would prove neutrinos are their own antiparticles, and the cosmic surplus of matter over antimatter. The authors show the model can cover all three fronts within one scheme.
arxiv-2508-13678:
Xiao-Wen Yang and a large team survey neuro-symbolic methods for fixing the reasoning of large language models. Fluent models still stumble on logic, planning, and multi-step deduction. Marrying neural learning with symbolic machinery is a leading remedy. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the survey first formalizes what reasoning tasks demand, then introduces the neuro-symbolic paradigm. Methods are sorted by the direction of the marriage. Some feed symbolic structure into the model. Others extract symbolic artifacts from it. A third family runs the two in tight partnership.

The review closes with open challenges and promising directions. A public repository collects the papers and resources. The intended reader is a researcher choosing where symbolic scaffolding can still move the needle on machine reasoning, a milestone on the road the authors link to general intelligence.
arxiv-2508-13778: Jaka Pelaic builds a math model of a famed wave system in a bounded space in a 2025 paper. The system, called the massive sine-Gordon model, is studied in a calm regime below a key threshold. His build uses a scaling method that peels the model layer by layer. The result is a sound measure with tame tails that keeps the space's wrap-around symmetry and a mirror rule the field demands. The work is brief and aimed at experts in math physics.
arxiv-2508-13978:
Hardy and co-authors rebuild the first step of news recommendation, the step that picks which stories a reader may see. News tools quietly carry values: they lift some voices and views and leave others out. Past fixes just reshuffled a list that had already been picked. The 2025 method shapes that candidate pool itself, tagging each story by sentiment, political leaning, topic, and framing.

A small autoencoder sums up each reader's tastes, and a decoder guesses the tag mix that reader will pick next. The tool then flips some of the predicted tags on purpose as it searches, widening the range of views on offer. Settings can slide between personalization and democratic goals, with no need to retrain the tool. Tests found fresh, varied, surprising candidates. The team calls this control, not raw accuracy, the real gain.
arxiv-2508-14178:
Flavio Benevenuto da Silva Junior and Anderson Caproni wrote a study from 2025 on a bright, jetting galaxy core named AO 0235+164. Such cores, called blazars, fire a thin jet of fast matter close to our line of sight. The jet of this one seems to swing slowly, like a wobbling top. The pair studied public radio maps made at two bands.

They tracked thirty-six parts of the jet and measured how each part moved across the sky. A model in which the jet swings in a steady circle fit the motion well. One swing took about eight years, close to a cycle long seen in the light of the core. The pair suggest that two giant black holes at the core may drive the swing, though they note other causes could fit too.
arxiv-2508-14278:
Elena Alegret and co-authors present GALA in this 2025 paper, a method for grasping 3D scenes in words. A user should be able to query a scene with open-ended terms, not just a fixed label set. Past methods struggle to keep fine detail while adding word meaning to a 3D scene built from 2D images.

GALA learns a field of instance features for each scene through self-guided contrast learning. A cross-attention module with two learned codebooks adds word features that do not depend on the view angle. That design keeps features of one object close and saves memory by avoiding a large feature per point. Tests on real data show strong results for both 2D and 3D queries.
arxiv-2508-14478:
Shan-Ming Ruan and Yu-ki Suzuki work toward a sound definition of holographic entanglement entropy in de Sitter space, in a research paper from 2025. De Sitter space describes a universe that expands at an accelerating rate. A popular recipe for this entropy breaks a basic rule that entropy must obey, called strong subadditivity.

Using a replica method with twist operators, they derive an entropy formula for three-dimensional de Sitter space built from its Green's functions. They then demand the formula obey the fundamental entropy inequalities. That demand carves out real constraints on the free parameters of static patch holography. The authors present the inequalities as a sharp test for any future proposal.
arxiv-2508-14778:
Syed Furqan Abbas Hashmi and Sanjay Rebello study how undergraduates solve physics problems with an AI chatbot in a 2025 paper. Giving each student tailored hints at scale is a standing teaching challenge. Their chatbot asks Socratic questions rather than giving answers, and it was used in a large first year mechanics course at a Midwestern public university.

Full chat logs came from 150 first year science majors. Post chat surveys gave the bot solid ratings for knowledge skills and fair ratings overall. Student questions grew far more specific over each chat, from a small share at first to all by the last turn. Specific questions also tracked with higher expected course grades.
arxiv-2508-14978:
Lucas Fernandez-Sarmiento, Riccardo Penco, and Rachel Rosen test in 2025 a guess that links entropy to small tweaks of a low energy theory. The guess says the top tweak that keeps a theory's rules must raise its entropy. Clues come from black hole heat math.

The team shows the guess equals a drop in heat grand value at fixed heat. They then check it on four known cases, from gold stone bits to a bent magnet model. Wide accord with the guess turns up. Cases where it should fail, such as rule breaking tweaks, are marked out as well.
arxiv-2508-15278:
Chang Liu and Adam Miller present, in a 2025 paper, a tool that strips a host galaxy's glow out of a spectrum so a fleeting event inside it can be read cleanly. Classic methods guess the galaxy light by drawing a straight line across the slit near the event. Their method instead builds the galaxy's profile from archive images taken in several colours, which record how the glow varies along the slit.

A Gaussian process turns those images into a smooth prior for the background. A second process models how the real spectrum strays from the prior. On fake data cut from a real galaxy cube, the method beat classic ones whenever the galaxy was resolved. Applied to two real transients, it recovered faint features buried in galaxy light. The code is free under an MIT licence.
arxiv-2508-15478:
Nghiem Thanh Pham and co-authors introduce SLM-Bench, a benchmark that grades small language models on skill, speed, and environmental cost together, in a 2025 paper. Small models promise cheap, reachable AI, yet no shared test had weighed their power use and carbon alongside accuracy. Their bench runs fifteen models on nine tasks drawn from twenty-three data sets across fourteen fields.

Four hardware setups were used to keep comparisons fair, and eleven measures covered correctness, computing, and consumption. Some models led on accuracy while others won on energy, with no single winner. The team released its pipeline openly, aiming to make efficiency a routine part of how small models are judged.
arxiv-2508-15578:
Elsa Danielsson and co-authors built in 2025 a framework for squeezing the best performance from quantum energy devices. Some tiny conductors are fed by nonthermal resources, energy sources that no single temperature can describe. Such sources arise below the thermalization length, from competing environments or from light. The team combined scattering theory with a Lagrange multiplier method to optimize conversion.

The method can target efficiency, precision, or a chosen trade-off between them at a fixed output current. It also reveals which transmission shapes reach that optimum. A worked example covers a refrigerator driven by realistic nonthermal resources. That device beat one fed by a plain thermal source. The authors offer the results as design guidelines for future nanoelectronic energy converters.
arxiv-2508-15678:
Ronald Richman, Salvatore Scognamiglio, and Mario V. Wüthrich propose a new neural network design in this 2025 paper. Their model, called a Tree-like Pairwise Interaction Network, is built for tabular data where pairs of features matter together. Insurance pricing is their main example, since rates there depend on how risk factors combine.

The network copies the shape of decision trees while learning only pairwise effects between features. Because of that design, a user can inspect the interaction effects directly instead of treating the model as a black box. Scores that explain each prediction are also cheap to compute. On a well-known French motor insurance dataset, the model beat both older methods and modern neural networks in accuracy, while still showing how each feature pair shaped the price.
arxiv-2508-16378:
Crypto markets swing on mood as much as on math, and Qizhao Chen builds that mood into portfolio design in this 2025 paper. The strategy mixes two trend gauges, a relative strength index and a moving average, with feeling scores read from news. A language model checked the news scores that a simpler sentiment tool produced.

Those signals reshaped expected returns inside a classic risk-balancing optimizer, under set constraints. In backtests across several coins, the blended strategy beat a momentum plan, a Bitcoin long-short plan, and an equal-weight basket on risk-adjusted return. Mood alone or trend alone did worse than the mix. Deep drawdowns still hit during market panics, so Chen adds that stronger risk brakes are needed.
arxiv-2508-16578:
Mujahid Abbas and two co-authors prove in 2025 that two maps sharing a weak compatibility property must meet at a common fixed point. Fixed point theory underpins many existence proofs in analysis. The maps here obey a generalized condition B, a loosened contractive rule.

The proof extends theorems by Al-Thagafi and Shahzad and by Babu and co-authors, covering their settings as special cases. Weak compatibility asks only that the maps commute where they already agree, a mild demand that makes the result widely usable. Such common fixed points anchor iterative schemes across nonlinear analysis, from equations to optimization.
arxiv-2508-16678:
Konrad Cinkusz, Jaroslaw Chudziak, and Ewa Niewiadomska-Szynkiewicz test language-model agents for agile software project work, in a 2025 paper. The agents are placed inside a scaled agile framework and given roles in simulated projects. A simulation platform recreates real software challenges, such as matching technical work to business goals and handling links between teams.

Across repeated runs, the agents delegated tasks, talked with each other in natural language, and managed project stages. The authors report measurable gains in task completion time, quality of deliverables, and coherence of communication. The agents also scaled across varied and complex settings. The study presents such agents as a way to automate parts of project management, while noting this could shift how human teams collaborate and solve problems together.
arxiv-2508-17178:
Shipeng Li and Hengfei Ding loosen a step-size rule for computing phase separation with long memory, in a 2025 paper. The time-fractional Cahn-Hilliard equation models mixtures unmixing, with a fractional derivative that remembers the past. Its solutions spike near the start, so solvers use uneven time steps, but earlier theory chained step ratios into a narrow band.

With new splitting techniques, the authors relax the cap on consecutive step ratios to a larger constant. On that freer foundation they build a scheme: an L2-type formula in time and a compact fourth-order difference in space. They prove the method always has exactly one solution, conserves volume exactly, and handles energy properly. Freer meshes mean faster, stabler simulations.
arxiv-2508-17378:
Omer Nacar grades an Arabic-focused language model through the chat window its users actually see. The model, ALLaM 34B, was built by Saudi Arabia's data authority and now powers the HUMAIN Chat service. English-trained models often miss Arabic dialect and culture. His 2025 study probes the service with prompts in standard Arabic, five dialects, and mixed speech.

The pack also tests facts, sums, time sense, story writing, and safety traps. Each prompt ran five times, for 115 outputs in all. Three top rival models scored each answer. Writing and code-switching earned near-perfect marks. Dialect fidelity lagged a bit but still scored well. Safety answers held steady. Nacar reads the model as ready for daily use.
arxiv-2508-17478:
Xuhao Shan and nine co-authors, including Changmiao Wang, predict patient outcomes by fusing several kinds of medical data inside a graph neural network. Prognosis improves when imaging, clinical, and molecular data speak to each other, but their structures differ wildly. Modeling those cross-modal relationships, near and far, is the core difficulty.

GraphMMP builds feature graphs using mutual information to decide which features connect. A global fusion module based on the Mamba architecture then mixes information across the whole graph. The two-stage design targets both local interactions and global dependencies. On liver prognosis data and the METABRIC breast cancer study, the model surpassed existing methods, supporting the fusion strategy.
arxiv-2508-17578:
Job Feldbrugge and Ue-Li Pen examine the hidden paths that shape how a quantum particle crosses or bounces off a step in potential energy. In the Feynman path integral picture, allowed motion follows real classical paths, while forbidden motion is carried by complex paths called instantons. The authors study these complex paths in a smooth step and in a sharp one, following their role in the particle's propagator.

The complex paths turn out to have a rich structure: they connect to caustics and can vanish as plain solutions when they strike a singularity of the potential. By widening the definition into equivalence classes, the authors track the paths past such crossings and identify the instanton behind quantum reflection. Most complex contributions are tiny, but some survive at full strength into the classical limit. The authors also give ways to detect these paths from propagation amplitudes.
arxiv-2508-17878:
Honghong Wang, Jing Deng, Fanqin Meng, and Rong Zheng teach a speech model to hear emotion by making it do four jobs at once, in a 2025 paper. The catalog record lists the authors by first names only; the printed byline is used here.

Alongside emotion, the model learns gender, speaker identity, and the words spoken. A co-attention module lets the tasks trade features dynamically, so context flows where it helps. A new loss function leans on hard and rare examples, fighting the imbalance of real emotion data. The system fine-tunes a self-supervised speech model rather than starting cold. On a naturalistic challenge task, the approach improved performance markedly. The authors credit the cross-task conversation.
arxiv-2508-18378:
Delgado-Quesada and Guzmán-Verri model three linked transitions in a family of cooling oxides in a paper from 2025. The compounds, quadruple perovskites with copper and iron, chill sharply under pressure. That barocaloric gift suits solid-state refrigeration. Charge transfer, magnetism, and lattice strain all switch together, which complicates the physics.

Their minimal Landau theory couples four ingredients: ligand-hole imbalance, staggered magnetization, volume strain, and thermal expansion. Across seven rare-earth variants, it matches the measured magnetism, volumes, and phase boundaries. It also predicts strong elastic softening near the boundary. A compact theory that captures the whole family can screen new coolants on paper. Fridges of the future might run on squeezed oxides.
arxiv-2508-18978:
Tattwamasi Amrutam, Yongle Jiang, and Shuoxing Zhou proved a splitting result in two thousand twenty-five in the theory of von Neumann algebras. They study a product of two groups acting on an algebra, with a random walk that splits across the two factors. Between a base algebra and a larger one built from the Poisson boundary, sit intermediate algebras.

They show every such intermediate algebra splits as a product: the base part times a boundary part. That extends a known factor theorem from the measurable setting to this non-commutative one. They also give more splitting examples, and show where extra assumptions are needed because ideals can block the split.
arxiv-2508-19078:
Fahao Chen and co-authors fine-tune giant sparse models across weak devices in a 2025 paper. Mixture-of-experts language models activate only a few expert parts per token. Even so, tuning them usually demands data-center hardware, not consumer cards. Privacy rules also bar pooling everyone's raw data in one place.

Federated tuning spreads work across many owners' machines without pooling raw data. Prior tries leaned on pruning or offloading with shaky assumptions about those systems. Their system, FLUX, profiles expert use cheaply through quantized local runs. It then schedules work to cut time-to-accuracy on modest home and office GPUs. MoE-specific smarts, not generic tricks, drive the speedup.
arxiv-2508-19478:
Maeliss Jallais and co-authors published this 2025 study on reading brain tissue from diffusion MRI scans. Such scans track how water moves in tissue, hinting at cell shapes below. Models that include water exchange between cell parts promise richer maps of gray matter. But their numbers may be shaky, and two rival settings can fit the same scan.

The team tested two recent models on fake and real brain data. They used a Bayesian tool that reports doubt alongside each estimate. Some values, like how fast water moves outside cells, came out firm. Others, like exchange time and cell body size, swung widely and leaned biased. The authors urge the field to report doubt openly and to drop readings the data cannot support.
arxiv-2508-19778:
The ATLAS Collaboration hunts for physics past the Standard Model with anomaly spotting in busy lepton events. The paper is from two thousand twenty-five; the pack row gives no title or year, so the text head is the source. The search takes proton clash data from the full Run 2 at the LHC. It asks for ends with at least four light leptons.

Event kinds are split by shape, and untrained machine learning flags the odd ones out, with no model in mind. No clear excess past the known background shows. Bounds are set in a model-free way for each shape, and on set test models, from kin of known leptons to smuons. One flavour-rich model gets its first bound here.
arxiv-2508-19878:
Brains made of light could compute with far less energy, and disorder may be a feature, not a bug. Matthew Wilson and three co-authors built a tiny learning chip in a 2025 paper whose core is a stadium-shaped cavity where light bounces chaotically. The input is written into the color of laser light entering the cavity, and the scattered speckle pattern at a surrounding wall serves as the readout layer.

Because the cavity's response shifts wildly with tiny color changes, the speckles carry rich information. On four different classification tests the device performed well, and widening the readout area let the team tune it per task. The work shows wave chaos as a practical computing resource.
arxiv-2508-19978:
Fabrizio Sgobba and co-authors demonstrate momentum-resolved two-photon interference with weak coherent states, in a research paper from 2025. Hong-Ou-Mandel interference is a classic quantum optics effect used for precise position sensing. Its range is limited by how alike the two photons are, since distinct photons stop interfering in the usual setup.

Their scheme resolves the transverse momentum of photon pairs with single-photon detector arrays. Fourth-order correlations then recover interference even for independent, partly distinct photons. Results are checked against the best precision bounds from quantum estimation theory. The method extends sensing range and suits high-resolution imaging. It also eases demands in quantum information tasks.
arxiv-2508-20378:
William Detmold, Rohan Kanchana, and Cagin Yunus study the spread of paired reads from grid runs of the strong force, for systems with one to four heavy parts. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Such paired reads are the raw stuff from which masses and traits are drawn. Their true spread is not known for this theory. Past work found tail forms for the spread in simpler theories. The team tests if those forms fit the real data. With many stats tests, they find the simple model's forms fit well at zero momentum, across a wide span of gaps in time. The fit holds most of all at large gaps.
arxiv-2508-20978:
Marianne Defresne and co-authors present a learning system in 2025 that can be taught to solve hard logic and optimization problems without a solver in the training loop. Hybrid systems that join neural nets with exact reasoning are a growing aim, since large language models are weak at such problems. Their system learns both the rules of a problem and its goal.

A new probabilistic loss drives that learning. It lets the net pick up the constraints and the objective at once, which yields a full model that experts can inspect and extend with extra rules. Leaving the exact solver out of training makes the training scale to larger problems. Exact answers can still be drawn at test time. The paper reports how the design scales on known hard problems.
arxiv-2508-21578:
Mosquera and Sanz-Vicario analyze how electrons and nuclei entangle in molecules in a 2025 paper. A molecule can be seen as two linked parts, one electronic and one nuclear. The authors compare several standard ways of writing the joint wave function, using simple models that include the hydrogen molecular ion. A math split method lets them measure entanglement with an entropy score.

Ground state molecules under the classic split look almost separable, with little entanglement, they find. Exciting the nuclear motion raises entanglement step by step. Sharp changes in the electronic wave shape across nuclear positions raise it further. Crossings between energy curves boost it strongly in one picture but far less in another. Readers learn what drives a hidden link inside molecules.
arxiv-2509-00278:
Maria Chudnovsky, David Eppstein, and David Fischer study string graph obstacles in 2025 among graphs of restricted girth and degree. A string graph records which curves in a plane cross each other. An obstacle is a graph that is not a string graph, but becomes one after any single edge contraction or vertex deletion.

Kratochvíl's known obstacles hold huge cliques, so their girth is three and degree is unbounded. The team builds an infinite family of obstacles with girth four that also avoid a set pattern and sit near planar. They prove a subcubic obstacle of girth three exists, and none exist at high girth. Subcubic string graphs are characterized, with a fast recognition method to match.
arxiv-2509-00578:
Abdellah Zakaria Sellam leads six authors in total, with Ilyes Benaissa, Salah Eddine Bekhouche, Abdenour Hadid, Vito Reno, and Cosimo Distante, in improving car damage detection from images. Fine damage is hard to spot reliably, even for human experts, and context can decide whether a mark counts as damage.

Sellam and his co-authors build C-DiffDet+, which extends a diffusion-based detector that refines guesses by denoising, removing noise step by step. Their Context-Aware Fusion uses cross-attention, a way for each object proposal to weigh scene information, to blend global scene context from a separate encoder with local features. Results on the CarDD benchmark beat leading models and set new marks for context-aware detection.
arxiv-2509-00678:
Qintong Xie, with three co-authors, Edward Koh, Xavier Cadet, and Peter Chin, presents a Nash Q-Network for cybersecurity simulation. Defense pits defenders against hackers, so multi-agent reinforcement learning, where several learners adapt at once, fits well, but simultaneous training in complex settings is unstable and non-stationary.

Xie and his co-authors design a policy-based Nash Q-learning method meant to converge directly onto a steady equilibrium, a strategy pair neither side wants to leave. Their network blends ideas from proximal policy optimization, deep Q-networks, and the Nash-Q algorithm. In a two-player zero-sum Markov game, a contest where one side's gain is the other's loss, distributed data collection and tailored architectures yield robust defenses.
arxiv-2509-00778:
Pragun Jaswal, with two co-authors, presents a systolic array for matrix multiplication. Matrix multiplication is the core operation of deep neural networks. A systolic array moves data in rhythm through a grid. Each cell in the grid does a small multiply-and-add step. Their array uses new exact and approximate processing elements.

The elements rest on positive and negative partial product cells. The team calls those cells PPC and NPPC. An eight-by-eight array with eight-bit designs saves clear energy.
