The approximate version saves more than the exact one. In a discrete cosine transform task, output quality stays high. That transform is a standard step in image compression. Edge detection by convolution also keeps good quality. The design suits error-tolerant image work.
arxiv-2509-00878:
Ritu Dey leads a team of seven authors on tungsten emissions for fusion use. Tungsten is used in tokamak walls, the walls of fusion devices. Its spectral lines help diagnose the plasma inside. The study is a simulation study of neutral tungsten. It reports electron-impact excitation data for that species.

The team computes cross-sections and rate coefficients for three transitions. The wavelengths of the transitions are listed in the record. They use the relativistic distorted wave approach in the flexible atomic code. Energy levels in the code were corrected against the NIST database. Cross-sections cover incident electron energies up to a high stated value. Some of these lines are also observed in tokamak plasma. The rate coefficients are provided for fusion applications.
arxiv-2509-00978:
Christiane K M Klein, writing alone, explores quantizing gravity on rotating black holes via the Teukolsky scalar. Quantizing linearized gravity on black hole space-times is a sought-after goal. Building states for that theory is equally difficult. Candidate states must reconcile positivity with gauge invariance. That tension is a main reason for the difficulty.

On Kerr space-times, spin-2 Teukolsky scalars capture the same degrees of freedom as metric perturbations. They do so up to pure gauge and radiative solutions. They also avoid the gauge issue directly. Klein shows the theory can be written with a Green-hyperbolic operator. That allows construction of the algebra of observables. A reconstruction scheme tracks the physical subalgebra. It indicates how to build the Unruh state on subextreme Kerr space-times.
arxiv-2509-01378:
Modular forms are highly symmetric functions central to number theory, and in 1975 Zagier introduced a family of hyperbolic Poincare series that became very influential. Andreas Mono, Larry Rolen, and Johann Stumpenhusen connect the divisor modular form built from those series to a new object, a weak Maass form with shifted weight. Maass forms extend modular forms to a broader, less rigid class.

The team shows the generating function of their new form shares the same modularity traits as the theta kernel of Kohnen and Zagier, the tool that produces Zagier's series. That match yields a new theta lift, a construction that moves forms from one setting to another. Such lifts are prized because they turn hard questions in one world into workable ones in another, linking arithmetic objects across theories.
arxiv-2509-01578:
Heaps and trusses are algebraic structures that generalize groups and rings, and Hom-type versions twist their operations by a chosen map. Tarik Anowar, Ripan Saha, and Sayan Thokdar introduce Hom-heaps, Hom-trusses, and Hom-braces, and map how these new objects relate to each other. Their aim is a unified frame for this growing branch of algebra.

The team shows the retract of a Hom-heap at a point forms a Hom-group exactly when that point is fixed by the twisting map. Translation maps then give isomorphisms between the retracts at different fixed points. Three equivalent notions of Hom-trusses are set out, and three variants of Hom-braces are tied to them, with certain trusses giving braces and the reverse. The authors note possible uses for the Yang-Baxter equation and non-associative geometry.
arxiv-2509-01678:
Raphael Skalidis, Konstantinos Tassis, Aris Tritsis, and Paul F Goldsmith plan a survey of faint streaks at the edges of star forming clouds. These streaks, called striations, run in near parallel lines and align with magnetic fields. Models say magnetic waves help shape them, but direct proof is thin. The team would use the PRIMA space observatory and its polarization tool, which maps field direction from dust glow.

Three nearby clouds with clear streaks form the target list, each about one degree wide on the sky. Maps in two far infrared bands would hunt for the wave pattern in field angles. About fifty-nine hours of viewing should give clear detections when the data are averaged. The survey would test how fields guide the first steps of star birth.
arxiv-2509-02078:
Giulia Meucci leads eight co-authors in tests of nanowire switches that work at deep cold. Such switches use thin wires of indium arsenide, a mix of two elements. They may give fast, low power parts for quantum machines one day. Growth in set zones yields flat wire layouts that fit standard chip making steps.

The team checks on-off rates, switch points, slopes, trap counts, lag, and drift in the cold. The parts work well in circuits that lean on the full on state of the switch. In amp style use at low drive, the parts outrun the cryostat wires for speed. Lag in the gate still makes fine tuning of the amp point hard. Flaws in the crystals and build steps may drive much of that lag.
arxiv-2509-02178:
Andrii Kuibarov leads eleven co-authors in a check that a platinum bismuth mix meets three known marks for high heat superconductivity. Why some stuff conducts with no loss at high heat stays a hard open case. Known marks are dense states near the Fermi level, strong links to a next degree of freedom, and scope to tune the stuff. Light based probes read the surface states of the mix head on.

All three marks are met to a rare degree on the surface of the mix. That surface holds Fermi arcs, open ended states that are a sign of a topological phase. Pair links and scope to tune line up with the classic list at that surface. The finds pave a path to firm up and lift superconductivity in this stuff. Work on the surface may raise its switch point yet more.
arxiv-2509-02778:
István Kovács and Gábor Somlai wrote a 2025 group theory paper completing a classification of dihedral groups with a special rigidity property. A group is called DCI when any two isomorphic Cayley digraphs, graphs built from the group's own multiplication, must already match through a group automorphism.

Earlier work by Dobson, Muzychuk, and Spiga showed that a non-abelian generalised dihedral DCI-group has to be an ordinary dihedral group whose order is square-free, meaning no prime divides it twice. Kovács and Somlai prove the converse: every dihedral group of square-free order is indeed a DCI-group. The two results together close the classification for this family, a tidy endpoint for a problem in algebraic graph theory.
arxiv-2509-02978:
Xiaohan Cai wrote a 2025 mathematics note on a conjecture of Wang about harmonic functions. Harmonic functions satisfy a balance law tied to averaging, and they model steady states in physics. The setting here is a compact curved space with edges, called a manifold with boundary, plus a nonlinear rule at that edge.

Cai proves Liouville type theorems, results saying that only very simple functions can meet all the stated conditions. Positivity, gentle curvature, and a strictly convex boundary drive the argument. For the ball, the simplest such space, he gives a fresh proof of Wang's conjecture using a general method based on a helper quantity called the P-function. The same method then classifies solutions of related equations with edge conditions.
arxiv-2509-03078:
Tobias Rohe and 5 co-authors reviewed the literature in 2025 on how to benchmark quantum computers. Benchmarks are standard tests that show whether hardware and software are improving and where they stall. With so many kinds of machines and users, picking the right test is itself a research problem.

The review is presented as the broadest of its kind so far. It joins automated text clustering with expert reading to build a taxonomy, a structured family tree of benchmark types. Categories split along the quantum stack, from hardware through software to applications, with shared terms defined clearly. The map exposes recurring design patterns and gaps where tests are missing. It also shows which groups each benchmark type actually serves.
arxiv-2509-03878:
O. Saeki and one co-author ask whether a parity survives deformation for a class of fold maps in a 2025 mathematics paper. A fold map folds one manifold onto another along a singular set; it is image simple when singular points never land on the same image point. The parity counts its connected components, modulo two.

In even dimensions, with an orientable target, that parity was known to be a homotopy invariant. The odd-dimensional story goes the other way. For maps from manifolds of dimension three or more onto surfaces that may be non-orientable, the parity can change under homotopy: it is not an invariant. Two constructions establish this, one from open book decompositions with round fold maps, one from allowable moves. Each construction adds one component. A new proof of the even-dimensional invariance is supplied, and an example shows it fails for non-orientable targets.
arxiv-2509-04078:
Jingjing Liu and nine co-authors introduce a harder test for software-fixing language models in a 2025 research paper. Most bug-fixing benchmarks use single small functions. Real projects are whole repositories, meaning many linked files, where errors are messier. Their new data set, RepoDebug, spans eight programming languages and three kinds of debugging work. It also sorts mistakes into twenty-two subtypes, from simple typos to deeper logic faults.

Ten leading language models were tried on the benchmark. Even the strongest one, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, struggled with repository-level repair. The gap shows how far automated debugging still sits from everyday developer work. RepoDebug gives builders a shared yardstick for closing that gap.
arxiv-2509-04478:
Iniakpokeikiye Peter Thompson and two co-authors build a phone system that coaches safer driving in culturally tuned language for Nigeria in a 2025 research paper. The end-to-end system detects trips automatically, analyzes behavior on the device, and writes feedback. Its dual-component language engine mixes legally grounded safety tips with persuasive behavioral reports shaped by theory. A two-step reflection process polishes the wording quality.

A specialized model spots alcohol-influenced driving, flagged as a key local danger. The design copes with patchy connectivity and noisy sensors, both common in low-resource settings. A pilot with ninety drivers showed the approach works and surfaced initial patterns of unsafe behavior. Data-to-text systems for social good gain a working framework.
arxiv-2509-04878:
Path geometries can be turned into almost Grassmann structures by a construction in the style of Fefferman. Zhangwen Guo introduces two such constructions in a solo 2025 geometry paper. The first associates a structure of a stated type to every path geometry of one higher dimension, and Guo proves it is normal.

Two matching conditions characterise which structures arise locally, one using parallel tractors and one using a Weyl connection. A second, related construction links structures of neighbouring sizes. Guo proves that one is non-normal and describes its local image in Cartan geometric terms.
arxiv-2509-04978:
Torsors over finite flat group schemes carry a natural quadratic form built from a trace. Philippe Cassou-Noguès and one co-author study that quadratic structure in a 2025 number theory paper. The setting is a group scheme over the ring of integers of a number field whose generic fibre is constant.

Scaling the trace form gives a non-degenerate invariant form on each principal homogeneous space. For groups of odd order, the authors show the form is locally isomorphic to the standard one and study when global isomorphism holds. Over a local field, they bound the kernel of a scalar extension map between Grothendieck groups.
arxiv-2509-05078:
Judging facial beauty from a photograph depends on features at several scales at once. Djamel Eddine Boukhari proposes a hybrid model for that prediction task in a solo-authored 2025 computer vision paper. Convolutional networks extract features well but usually at a fixed scale, missing links between fine and global traits.

The Scale-Interaction Transformer first applies parallel convolutions at varied receptive fields to capture multi-scale features. A transformer encoder then models interactions among those representations through self-attention. On a widely used benchmark, the model sets a new leading correlation score in the author's experiments, beating previous methods.
arxiv-2509-05178:
Operators that respect a symmetry set by another such map raise a question: which extensions keep that symmetry? Christoph Fischbacher, lead author with two co-authors, study such K-invariant operators in a 2025 analysis paper. They ask when self-adjoint and maximally dissipative extensions of a symmetric one stay K-invariant.

Two classic extensions of a nonnegative one, the Friedrichs and Krein-von Neumann ones, always keep the invariance. The Friedrichs one also works for sectorial cases. Uses cover the Sturm-Liouville case, where the symmetry involves a change of variables linked to Schröder's equation. All invariant self-adjoint ones are described there.
arxiv-2509-05378:
Medical coding, turning doctors' free-text notes into diagnosis and procedure codes, gets an agent-based system from Andreas Motzfeldt and five co-authors in a 2025 paper. Human coders follow official guidelines, and their system is built to do the same with language models.

It is described as the first approach able to cover the full ICD-10 code set, with tens of thousands of labels. On rare diagnosis codes it performs best to date, while tuned classifiers still win on common codes, the only ones they can handle. The authors also analyse where the system systematically undercodes. That blind spot analysis is offered as a guide for future work.
arxiv-2509-05478:
Repeating rhythms hidden inside long data streams are built into a learning method by Jia Wang, Xiao Wang, and Chi Zhang in a 2025 paper on multivariate time series. Such data hold many measurements tracked together over time. Such data are high-dimensional, often short on labels, and change character over time.

Their framework, PLanTS, learns without labels by cutting series into patches at several time scales in a period-aware way. A generalised contrastive loss keeps both whole cases and inner states comparable across those scales. A second task predicts the next state transition, forcing the representation to carry forward-looking information. Across classification, forecasting, tracking, and anomaly tasks it beat earlier self-supervised methods.
arxiv-2509-05678:
Testing whether a data stream depends on its own past, in very high dimensions, is the job of a new statistic from Qihua Zhu and three co-authors in a 2025 statistics paper. Serial independence is a basic assumption in time series work, and real data may be non-numeric or live in curved spaces.

Their test, WISE, aggregates pairwise similarities between observations, weighted by the time lag between them. It detects general forms of dependence, including non-linear links with no correlation. The authors prove normal limits under two null views and consistency in both classical and high-dimension, low-sample regimes, a first for this problem. Simulations show accurate size and strong power, and spatial-temporal data illustrate the method.
arxiv-2509-05978:
Imagining how a patient's brain scan would look under a different disease course is the goal of a 2025 paper by Mohamed Mohamed and three co-authors. Vision-language models generate striking flat images, but three-dimensional medical generation has no such ready base. Their framework produces high-resolution three-dimensional counterfactual scans of made-up patients from free-form language prompts.

The team adapts leading three-dimensional diffusion models with design ideas from Simple Diffusion and stronger text conditioning. On two brain MRI datasets, the system varies lesion load in multiple sclerosis and cognitive state in Alzheimer's disease while preserving each subject's identity. The authors call it the first language-guided native three-dimensional diffusion demonstration in neurological imaging, and a base for prompt-driven studies of disease course.
arxiv-2509-06178:
How slippery can a fluid possibly be? Marilù Chiofalo and three co-authors review the ratio of shear viscosity to entropy density in a 2025 perspective. A famous bound by Kovtun, Son, and Starinets sets a floor for that ratio across strongly coupled fluids, a result born in gravity theory through holography.

The review summarizes the bound, then examines proposed violations and what they would teach, including their ties to fundamental causality conditions. Experimental tests in very different systems, from quark-gluon plasma to ultracold atoms, are surveyed, with an eye to upcoming measurements. The authors present the ratio as a shared diagnostic linking gravity, nuclear physics, and condensed matter.
arxiv-2509-06578:
Scheduling jobs that arrive at random on a moving server is framed as a queueing control problem by Dongnuan Tian and one co-author in a 2025 operations research paper. One server travels around a network, serving jobs of different types that appear at demand points under Poisson arrival patterns. Setups and processing can be interrupted, and the server may change course at any moment.

Costs grow the longer jobs wait, and the goal is keeping the long-run average cost of that waiting as low as possible. The authors prove a stable stationary policy exists when workload stays below a stated condition. They then offer index-based heuristic policies, rules that score jobs and serve the best score, with appealing structural properties. Tweaks keep the rules practical at larger sizes, and extensive numerical experiments show they perform well against suitable benchmarks.
arxiv-2509-06878:
A dissolved substance carried by a noisy flow settles into an effective diffusion law in a 2025 chance-based analysis paper by Federico Butori and two co-authors. Transport noise is a standard way to stand for turbulence, and the Itô-Stratonovich diffusion limit describes how such noise produces a fixed effective equation. Most known cases use simpler noise than real layered turbulence.

Here the noise is a sum of separate vector fields, each living on a small region, matching boundary-layer and Boussinesq settings. Because the noise is uneven by direction, the corrector term becomes a general elliptic operator with varying coefficients. Homogenisation theory is then needed to pin down the limiting effective diffusivity. The authors derive a formula for that matrix and study how it acts as molecular diffusivity vanishes across several regimes. Careful computer work backs the analysis, showing nonlinear behavior in some regimes.
arxiv-2509-07178:
Muhammad Saad Saeed and 2 co-authors test whether face enhancement tools can fool deepfake detectors in a 2025 paper. Enhancement tools clean up and beautify faces in photos and video. Deepfake detectors try to spot faked faces, often by checking fine biometric traits, the measurable features of a face. The authors suspect that polishing a face may also erase the clues detectors rely on.

They apply both simple filters and advanced GAN-based enhancement, where a neural network rebuilds the face, to faked material from three public datasets. Even basic filters cut detection accuracy sharply, and the GAN methods did worse damage still, with attack success up to about three quarters of cases. Training detectors on enhanced fakes helped test whether they could adapt. The findings warn that easy, everyday tools can serve as anti-forensic aids, so detectors need to be built tougher.
arxiv-2509-07278:
Plant diseases and pests spread from plant to plant, so breaking the paths between neighbors can slow an outbreak. E. G. García Prieto, leading 8 co-authors, models that idea with percolation theory in a 2025 research paper. Percolation theory studies how connections form across a grid. Their grid stands for a plantation, and some sites can connect to fewer neighbors, mimicking physical barriers placed between plants.

The authors compute the percolation threshold, the point where spread becomes system-wide, as barriers increase. A simple curve shape describes how the threshold moves. They also link barrier counts to the share of barriers actually placed, which helps estimate strategy costs. One layout, placing two barriers per site in a corner pattern, saved a modest share of cost versus random placement. Farmers could then plant more vulnerable varieties with less risk.
arxiv-2509-07378:
Mohammad Sadegh Sirjani and 4 co-authors tackle task scheduling in fog computing in a 2025 paper. Fog computing places small servers near Internet of Things devices so time-sensitive jobs get quick responses. The challenge is assigning each task to a node without wasting energy or missing deadlines, the latest times by which jobs must finish.

Nodes are split into low-traffic and high-traffic groups. Short-deadline tasks go to quiet nodes under an improved golden eagle optimization method, a search inspired by hunting eagles and tuned with genetic operators. Long-deadline tasks go to busy nodes under reinforcement learning, where an agent learns from rewards. The combined method, RIGEO, cut energy use by up to 29 percent and response time by up to 86 percent in tests against leading methods, with fewer missed deadlines.
arxiv-2509-07678:
X. Pérez-Couto and 4 co-authors trace the past path of the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS through our Galaxy in a 2025 paper. 3I/ATLAS is the third known interstellar object, after 'Oumuamua and Borisov, and its high excess velocity and active cometary nature make it a probe of the Galaxy's icy planetesimal population. Its origin might be written in past close passes by stars.

The team integrates the comet's orbit backward for ten million years alongside Gaia DR3 stars with high-quality measurements, hunting encounters within two parsecs. They find 93 nominal encounters, 62 significant, yet none meaningfully perturbed the orbit. The strongest passerby, at 0.30 parsecs and 35 kilometers per second relative speed, changed the velocity by only a tiny amount. No flyby in the past ten million years within 500 parsecs explains the present trajectory or its origin.
arxiv-2509-07978:
Estimating an object's exact position and orientation from one reference photo is the challenge met by Zheng Geng and 7 co-authors in a 2025 computer vision paper. Robots meet endless unfamiliar objects, and usually no 3D model exists. Single-image reconstructions also lack true scale, and generated models differ from real camera views.

Their pipeline, OnePoseViaGen, first aligns scale and pose in a coarse-to-fine way, combining multi-view feature matching with render-and-compare refinement. A text-guided generative step randomises the training domain so the estimator survives the gap between synthetic and real images. One-shot pose estimation would let warehouse and home robots handle new products and tools without lengthy enrolment for every item.
arxiv-2509-08078:
Hotter systems sometimes cool faster than lukewarm ones, and Cameron Beetar with 2 co-authors find a quantum version of that oddity in a 2025 physics paper. The quantum Mpemba effect describes states farther from equilibrium relaxing sooner than states that start closer. Standard thermalization intuition says the opposite should happen, so a sharp diagnostic is needed.

Krylov complexity, which tracks how a state spreads through a structured basis, turns out to encode the asymmetry behind the effect. New projective complexity measures sharpen the connection further. Remarkably, their values at the very first moment already predict whether a Mpemba-like inversion will occur. A predictor that works at time zero would let experimenters choose preparations that relax fast on purpose.
arxiv-2509-08178:
M. V. Umansky and 4 co-authors model how a radio antenna stirs the edge of a fusion plasma in a 2025 paper. The work uses a slab of plasma with thin plates that stand in for the antenna's side walls. Such antennas heat the core of a tokamak. First, their waves must cross the rough edge plasma.

The plates are given an electric bias. That bias stands in for the sheath voltage the antenna itself creates. Runs that let plasma flow through show profiles and flicker much like real edge data. Swirling cells form near the antenna and carry extra heat and matter out. Edge losses help decide how long reactor walls last, so this effect is worth the care.
arxiv-2509-08278:
A fundamental theorem from Hopf module theory is carried into a newer algebraic setting by Yan Ning and 2 co-authors in a 2025 mathematics paper. Transposed Poisson algebras swap the roles of multiplication and Lie bracket in the rule that defines Poisson algebras. The authors work with modules that are simultaneously compatible with such an algebra and with a Hopf algebra acting on it.

Under stated conditions, including a colinear algebra map into the algebra's transposed Poisson centre, the classical structure theorem generalises to this category. Relative projectivity results follow. Fundamental theorems of this kind are load-bearing: they tell algebraists that objects in the new category decompose as predictably as in the classical one, so whole toolkits transfer across.
arxiv-2509-08678:
Abdallah Daddi-Moussa-Ider and 1 co-author study a point force near a no-slip wall in a Brinkman fluid in a 2025 paper. Brinkman flow models fluid through a porous medium. The force acts perpendicular to the wall, very close compared with the screening length.

A closed form solution is given up to a single integral. It expands cleanly in far field and near field limits. The flow becomes a series of source multipoles, plus a known correction near the wall. Comparisons with numerical integration confirm accuracy. The results also apply to unsteady Stokes flow from a beating cilium, a tiny hair-like structure on a surface.
arxiv-2509-08778:
Minyeong Choe and 3 co-authors ask whether all autoregressive transformers recall facts in the same way in a 2025 paper. Earlier work on GPT style models pointed to early feedforward layers as key for recall. Whether that holds for other designs was unclear.

Models from GPT, LLaMA, Qwen, and DeepSeek families are compared on where and how facts are stored. Qwen models differ: early attention modules matter more than feedforward modules for recall. Other models follow the earlier pattern more closely. The finding shows small design changes can shift recall mechanisms. That matters for interpreting models and for editing facts inside them.
arxiv-2509-08878:
Levi Condren and 1 co-author present a model-agnostic tracker for unexpected non-helical tracks in a 2025 paper. Many new physics theories predict particles that do not follow the usual helical path in a magnetic field. Standard trackers assume helices, so such particles stay invisible.

Their network learns a broad class of smooth tracks from training examples, without a formula for each path. It performs well even on track types outside the training set. Striking tracks that a human eye might notice can now be reconstructed. The study is a proof of principle. It opens a search route in data already collected at colliders.
arxiv-2509-09078:
Teresa Portone and 4 co-authors present scalable extensions to given-data Sobol index estimators in a 2025 paper. Sobol indices measure how much each input drives output variance in a model. Given-data methods reuse existing evaluations, but huge input counts break them.

A general estimator with arbitrary partition is defined, plus a streaming algorithm that processes samples in batches. Memory needs fall sharply, enabling models with over ten thousand inputs like neural networks. Analysis shows the usual equiprobable partition can bias estimates even at large sample sizes. A screening heuristic for small indices is motivated. Tests on neural network problems show comparable accuracy and runtime.
arxiv-2509-09178:
Ayan Biswas and 1 co-author describe implementation of an eight-bit Wallace tree multiplier in a 2025 paper. Wallace tree multipliers do binary long multiplication in parallel, reducing many partial products per stage with adder circuits. That keeps circuit depth growing slowly with input size.

The paper documents design, progress, and method for a course final project in ECE 55900. Schematic and layout are built in Cadence Virtuoso using a forty-five nanometer process library. Earlier design attempts are included alongside the final product. A sixteen bit multiply accumulate unit is also implemented as a combinational design. The report is a student project record rather than a research advance.
arxiv-2509-09278:
Patterns like stripes, spirals, and flocking emerge from simple local rules, but recovering those rules from sparse, noisy footage is hard. Saumitra Dwivedi and 4 co-authors attack that recovery problem in a 2025 research paper. Their framework learns soft artificial life models, agent-based and cellular automaton rules, directly from observations of reaction-diffusion systems. No prior physics knowledge is assumed.

The framework had earlier succeeded on classic test cases like the Game of Life and flocking models. Here the team probes how noise and sparse sampling degrade the learning. The learned models predicted the emergent dynamics accurately and held up under Gaussian noise and time gaps. The team even recovered the structure and parameters of the governing partial differential equations. Such tools could help ecologists and epidemiologists infer hidden rules from the little data nature provides.
arxiv-2509-10278:
Vidit Vidit and 5 co-authors test whether vision-language models can spot tampered text inside images in this 2025 paper. Changing a word on a sign, a label, or an ID card is a simple fraud, yet most forgery research looks at whole-image edits. Text edits in pictures have drawn far less study.

The team benchmarked closed and open models on several text manipulation data sets. Open models are catching up but still trail the strongest closed model. Models built just for general image forgery also struggled, failing to generalize to text edits. Tests covered both everyday scene text and fantasy ID cards, the second standing in for a hard real-world misuse case.
arxiv-2509-10478:
Oluwaseyi Giwa and 3 co-authors sketch a future radio network run by a language model in this 2025 paper. Sixth-generation radio access networks will be too complex for traditional automation. Their proposal, the LLM-RAN Operator, places a large language model inside the control loop to turn high-level human intent into concrete network actions.

Unlike earlier trials, the design comes with a formal framework. An adapter aligned with the Open RAN standard makes the model's guarantees checkable, and slow strategic guidance is separated from fast local reaction. The authors also prove results on what policies the system can express and on settling to stable behavior, and they name open problems in safety, speed, and grounding.
arxiv-2509-10578:
Protiva Sen, Laurent Hébert-Dufresne, Pablo Bose, and Juniper Lovato ask what ethics should govern studies that deliberately expose people to harmful content in this 2025 paper. Computational social science often works this way: showing volunteers conspiracy theories, letting hackers attack a test system, or releasing bots onto social media. The authors name these social challenge studies, after medical challenge trials where volunteers are exposed to a pathogen under controlled conditions.

Medicine has built detailed ethical frameworks for that risky design; social research largely has not, and its exposures happen with far less control. The authors examine the medical frameworks and ask which principles could transfer. Their aim is deliberately modest: open a serious discussion on formal standards for social challenge studies, including long-term tracking of the harms such research might cause.
arxiv-2509-10678:
Type a description, get an animatable character head. Jiahao Luo and ten co-authors present T2Bs in this 2025 graphics paper. Text-to-3D tools sculpt detailed but frozen heads. Video diffusion models produce motion. Their motion wobbles between viewpoints and over time. T2Bs welds the two together. It uses deformable 3D Gaussian splatting. That registers the moving video content onto the static geometry.

A view-dependent deformation network carries the motion. The static model anchors consistency. On accuracy and expressiveness, the result beats older 4D generation methods. Video artifacts are fewer. The head geometries come out smooth and fully registered. Those heads are built to scale into morphable models. Think reusable digital faces with diverse, realistic expressions. Animation and virtual production pipelines consume exactly that kind of asset.
arxiv-2509-10778:
Anirban Kundu computes how two magnetic impurities talk to each other in this solo-authored 2025 paper. A two-dimensional electron gas carries the conversation. The interaction is the RKKY interaction. It decides magnetic configurations in spintronic devices. His electron gas is spin-polarized. Rashba spin-orbit coupling and an altermagnetic dispersion shape its two bands.

Kundu uses Green's function methods. He separates the interaction into three parts: Heisenberg, Ising, and Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya. Two regimes of magnetic order get studied. With strong out-of-plane order, every part oscillates with distance. Each fades as the inverse square. Beating patterns appear, tunable through the coupling strengths. The Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya vector lies in the plane. It grows with the Rashba strength. Under weak in-plane order, the Heisenberg part responds nonlinearly to the exchange coupling. The results give spintronics designers a map of levers.
arxiv-2509-10978:
Abdul Wadud and Nima Afraz model how much power a 5G radio unit really uses in this 2025 telecommunications paper. Their setting is O-RAN, the open radio access network architecture, and their tool is the ns3-oran simulator. Energy models exist, but theirs is the first in this simulator built around the radio unit itself and controllable by an xApp, the small applications that steer an open network.

The model is parameterized by hardware details: transceiver counts, power amplifier efficiency, millimeter-wave overheads, and standby behavior, and it plugs into the simulator's energy tracking. Numerical studies confirm it reproduces realistic, nonlinear power scaling as transmit power varies, and they identify the operating points where a radio unit behaves most efficiently. The audience is practical: researchers designing xApp-driven energy management for real O-RAN deployments.
arxiv-2509-11078:
Yunghwei Lai and three co-authors introduce Patient-Zero in this 2025 paper on medical artificial intelligence. The framework creates fake but realistic patient records and simulated patients for training and testing, without using any real person's medical data.

Records are built from clinical guidelines by mixing patient attributes in a structured way, and a two-part memory system lets each simulated patient stay consistent during long question-and-answer sessions with a doctor. In tests, senior physicians could not reliably tell the synthetic records from real ones, and medical reasoning models trained on the fake data scored much higher on medical question benchmarks. The approach offers a privacy-safe supply of practice data for medical AI.
arxiv-2509-11178:
Chengde Lin and five co-authors present StegOT in this 2025 computer vision paper. It concerns steganography. That is the art of hiding one image inside another of the same size. The secret can later be recovered.

Many hiding models suffer mode collapse. Adversarial and variational designs are both prone to it. Collapse unbalances the combined image. Too little of the cover or the secret survives. Recovery suffers as a result. StegOT is an autoencoder built on optimal transport theory. Its multi-channel module reshapes the feature distribution. Several peaks become a single peak. The two images' information is balanced. Experiments improved both image qualities. The hidden image looked better. The recovered secret looked better too.
arxiv-2509-11278:
Shravan Mohan, writing alone, proposes a conjecture about recovering a signal's spectrum in this 2025 paper. The setup starts with a discrete magnitude spectrum, the strength of each frequency with its phase discarded. A fixed phase pattern, Newman's phase sequence, is attached, the signal is transformed back to the time domain, its absolute value taken, and the result reversed.

Mohan conjectures that, as the number of samples grows without bound, this round trip recovers the original magnitude spectrum. The phase pattern is the same for every input and is unique up to one overall shift. Why the recovery should work is not yet understood, and the author leaves the wider meaning of the effect open for study.
arxiv-2509-11378:
Hadi Zayyani and three co-authors broaden a way of sending data in noise itself. This 2025 engineering letter covers noise modulation. In that scheme, data rides on the shape of a sent random signal. No clean carrier wave is used.

Their broader scheme adds two voltage biases. It lets the noise be non-Gaussian in form. Mixtures of Gaussians count. Laplacian noise counts too. The receiver can now split symbols by mean and by spread. That doubles the data rate. The team derived exact error-rate formulas for two noise families. Computer tests show the broader scheme shines when noise is not Gaussian. Low-power and secure links may gain the most.
arxiv-2509-11478:
Andrew G. Breithaupt and seven co-authors designed a talking agent to help diagnose dementia earlier, in this 2025 health informatics paper. Alzheimer's disease and related dementias are usually caught late, and good diagnosis depends on rich patient narratives that busy clinics struggle to gather.

Their voice-interactive agent, built on a large language model, interviews both patients and informants to draw out relevant symptoms and experiences. Thirty adults with suspected dementia took part in the evaluation, which combined conversation analysis, user surveys, and a comparison against blinded specialist interviews. The symptoms the agent elicited agreed promisingly with the specialists' findings, and users valued its patience and systematic questions, which helped them describe hard-to-express experiences. The authors frame the agent as structured diagnostic support, pending larger validation studies.
arxiv-2509-11578:
Swayamsiddha Maharana and Rama Vadapalli revisit what a physical black hole may look like up close. This 2025 general relativity paper works with round solutions of Einstein's equations. A semiclassical frame is used. Two demands are imposed. A trapped region must form in finite time for far-off watchers. The spacetime must stay regular at the apparent horizon.

Those demands constrain the energy-momentum tensor near the horizon. Past work kept only some tensor classes as viable. Other classes were dropped on shaky grounds. The authors show directly that the dropped classes are indeed unphysical. They also give a new class of static solutions. Those are regular at the horizon. Far-off watchers see horizon crossing in finite time.
arxiv-2509-11678:
Marco Lewis and Benoît Valiron built a tool that designs photonic quantum circuits by solving constraints. This 2025 quantum computing paper treats photonic processors. Optical parts must form circuits that act like quantum gates. Success comes only with some chance. Synthesis must find a circuit that computes right and succeeds often.

Their tool drives dReal, a solver for approximate satisfiability over real numbers. It searches for circuits and tunes their success odds. It certifies that the result is optimal. Known circuits from past work were recreated in demos. Several were extended. New results for Givens rotation gates were produced. The solver route is pitched as more reusable than hand-built constructions per gate.
arxiv-2509-11878:
Sofia Jamil and 4 co-authors let readers reshape images made for poems in a 2025 paper on weighted prompt manipulation. Poetry invites many readings, since readers bring their own feelings, pasts, and cultural roots. A single made image rarely honors that variety.

Their method shifts attention weights and text embeddings inside diffusion models in a planned way. By raising or lowering the weight of specific words, it strengthens or softens their sway on the final image. Large language models and past poetry datasets support the structured method. The result is richer, more fitting visualizations that audiences can adjust to their own reading. The authors present it as the first use of weighted prompt work for poetic imagery in a zero-shot setting.
arxiv-2509-11978: Mark L. Lewis and Emanuele Pacifici wrote a 2025 mathematics paper on Camina pairs, a special setup in group theory, the study of symmetry and structure. Their single question is how the Fitting subgroup, a key subgroup built from well-behaved parts, relates to the Camina kernel. The whole paper is devoted to that one relationship, between the Fitting subgroup and the Camina kernel of a Camina pair.
arxiv-2509-12178:
Maya M. Martirossyan and 9 co-authors warn that common benchmarks for generating crystal structures can mislead, in a 2025 paper. Generative models promise new inorganic materials, materials built from chemical composition alone. Progress depends on datasets that are clean and scores that mean what researchers think they mean.

The team found three problems. One widely used carbon dataset contains only about two fifths unique structures. Random splits of other datasets leak related forms, called polymorphs, between training and test sets. Match rates can also look good without reflecting real structural variety among identical building blocks. The paper examines the carbon-24, perov-5, and MP-20 datasets as examples. It urges stricter dataset building and reporting so model comparisons can be trusted.
arxiv-2509-12378:
Coasting through green lights saves fuel, but advising one car at a time can tangle the whole platoon behind it. Ruining Yang and four co-authors build a platoon-wide speed advisory system in 2025, driven by safe reinforcement learning for connected autonomous vehicles in mixed traffic.

A multi-agent controller tunes speeds for energy use and travel time together. Control barrier functions are folded into the learned policy, giving hard guarantees on the two dangers that matter: rear-ending the vehicle ahead and running a red light. Simulations show the system beating prior methods on both safety and platoon energy consumption.
arxiv-2509-12478:
Kathrin Hovelmanns, Daan Planken and two co-authors review in 2025 how to join quantum key sharing with standard key exchange, the step that sets up secret keys for safe online talk. Each path alone may fail if future quantum machines break current codes.

The review finds gaps in how past work treats the labels that name quantum keys, gaps that allow attacks where one key leans on another. The authors model the quantum link as an oracle that matches a real standard interface. In that model they prove a new mixed protocol safe, the first such proof that keeps the strong safety of the quantum part.
arxiv-2509-12578:
Privacy policies are long, legalistic, and ignored, while bite-sized notices shown at the moment of risk can interrupt and annoy. Shuning Zhang and seven co-authors design Conflect in 2025, a contextual privacy policy for mobile apps built to make users stop and reflect rather than tap through.

Workshops with designers mapped the design space and flagged a core flaw: notices describe a risk but disconnect it from the action at hand. Conflect answers with sidebar alerts tied to the live context, extracting the matching policy text automatically with high accuracy and a few seconds of delay. Users understood more, trusted more, and felt less burdened.
arxiv-2509-12778:
Sumit Das, Shaun Hampton and Sinong Liu study in 2025 string backgrounds where a Liouville wall moves faster than light. In such one-plus-one settings there is no usual scatter picture, so what space feels like for small ripples was not clear.

They use the dual matrix model and watch ripples of its shared field. While the wall stays slower than light, the felt space matches full flat space with a time-like wall. Once the wall turns faster than light, the felt space gains an edge where links blow up. That edge acts like a space-like break in the near theory, and exact effects must be added to grasp it.
arxiv-2509-13178:
Claudio Battiloro, Andrea Cavallo, and Elvin Isufi put forth a new way to learn from signals that live in endless spaces in a 2025 paper. Past work used the covariance of a signal, a gauge of how its parts move as one, to build neural nets with good traits. Those nets were shown to be strong and to transfer well, but only for spaces with a fixed, finite size.

The new work defines filters based on the covariance operator and stacks them, with non-linear steps, into full nets for endless spaces. It gives a clear rule for turning such a net into a finite one a computer can run. It also proves a link to a classic tool for finding the main patterns in data. Tests on both made-up and real time-series tasks sort data well, the authors report.
arxiv-2509-13778:
Sarah Zhao and Emmanuel Candès propose imputation-powered inference in a 2025 statistics paper. Modern datasets often lose whole blocks of features for whole groups of people. That pattern is called blockwise missingness. Throwing away incomplete cases wastes data and can bias results. Fancy corrections are hard to compute. Black-box imputation offers no guarantees when its guesses are wrong.

Their framework pairs flexible black-box filling-in with a bias correction. The correction is built from the fully observed cases. The ideas borrow from prediction-powered inference. The method gives valid, efficient estimates when data are missing completely at random. It also sharpens estimates for subgroups under a weaker condition they formalize. Simulations and a clinical case show real gains. Rival methods lose their promised coverage in the same settings.
arxiv-2509-13878:
Janne Laakkonen, Ivan Kukanov, and Ville Hautamäki harden audio deepfake detection in a 2025 paper. Speech foundation models such as Wav2Vec2 learn strong audio representations. Once fine-tuned on a fixed set of genuine and spoofed clips, they often fail. New forgery methods they never saw during training fool them.

Their fix installs a mixture of low-rank adapter experts inside the model's attention layers. LoRA adapters are small trainable add-ons. A routing mechanism switches on whichever specialists fit the incoming audio. The detector can then adapt to evolving attacks. In tests the approach beat standard fine-tuning both in-domain and out-of-domain. It cut the average out-of-domain equal error rate from roughly eight and a half percent to about six percent.
arxiv-2509-13978:
Renan Souza and seven co-authors put language model agents on top of workflow provenance in a 2025 paper. Modern science runs data workflows across edge devices, clouds, and supercomputers. The provenance records of what ran where are gold. They serve checking hypotheses and reproducing results. At scale, though, those records become too tangled for scripts, queries, and static dashboards.

The team contribute three things: a reference architecture, an evaluation methodology, and an open-source system. In the system, agents translate natural language questions into structured provenance queries. Lightweight metadata carries the answers. Testing covered LLaMA, GPT, Gemini, and Claude models, across query types and a real chemistry workflow. Modular design, prompt tuning, and retrieval augmentation yielded accurate, insightful answers. The answers went beyond what was literally recorded.
arxiv-2509-14278:
Yuntao Du and three co-authors warn in 2025 that privacy risks from large language models go well beyond training data. Much past work guards the data a model learned from. Far less guards what can leak once a model is live inside apps and agent tools.

Du and colleagues map the new risks in a systematic review. Plugged in models can leak data by accident or be tricked into sending it out. Attackers can also use agent abilities, such as browsing and tool use, to mount large privacy attacks. Harms reach past single users to money and public trust. The study sorts these threats and points to defences that must sit at deployment, not only at training time.
arxiv-2509-14378:
Siddharth P. Maharathy and seven co-authors assess in 2025 whether future electron positron colliders could find a charged scalar particle near a mass of one hundred fifty gigaelectronvolts. Hints in collider data near that mass motivate a model with an extra Higgs triplet.

The model adds a neutral and a charged Higgs like particle with close masses, beyond the Standard Model set. The charged member is hard to see at the Large Hadron Collider because it decays mainly into busy final states. At a cleaner electron positron machine, pairs would be made through photon and Z boson exchange. The authors define search regions using the dominant decays and estimate discovery reach. A clean find would reshape Higgs physics.
arxiv-2509-14678:
Hyungjoon Soh and Junghyo Jo set out stochastic clock attention in 2025, a way for attention to act as an alignment model for ordered sequences. Standard attention leans on position codes and masks, but it does not force smooth, in order matches. Frame synced targets need both traits.

Learned clocks that never run backward tick on the source and target sides. Attention is then the chance that the two clocks meet. A path integral route gives a closed form score, shaped much like a Gaussian bump. The score favours causal, smooth, near diagonal matches by build, with no added position fixes. Speech and translation tools rest on in order matches, so a built in bias could cut the scaffolding they now carry.
arxiv-2509-14878:
Zhonghao Liang and Qunying Liao construct new error-correcting codes with special dual properties in a 2025 coding theory paper. Two prized families meet here: maximum distance separable codes, which reach the best possible error correction for their length, and linear complementary dual codes, whose intersection with their dual is trivial. Such codes matter for both reliable storage and certain secure computations.

Earlier work built several classes of these codes from twisted generalized Reed-Solomon constructions. Liang and Liao unify those results by defining a broader twisted code family with two parameter sets. They derive the parity-check matrix of the new family, which certifies the dual properties, and then construct four classes of LCD codes from it. Worked examples close the paper, confirming the parameters the theory predicts.
arxiv-2509-15078:
Lei Yang and six co-authors report superconductivity in a tungsten-rhenium carbide with a chiral crystal structure, in a 2025 condensed matter paper. The compound's atoms arrange without mirror symmetry, a handedness that can intertwine with electronic behavior. Its superconducting transition sits near six kelvin, low in absolute terms but rich in physics.

Measurements and analysis show bulk type-II superconductivity with a full, isotropic energy gap, the classic BCS picture. First-principles calculations trace the electron-phonon coupling, the glue of that pairing, mainly to the heavy metal atoms' electronic states vibrating at low frequencies. Broken inversion symmetry also allows Weyl points, special band crossings, to appear in the electronic structure. The material thus offers one stage where chiral structure, superconductivity, and band topology meet.
arxiv-2509-15178:
Zaiquan Yang, Yuhao Liu, Gerhard Hancke, and Rynson W. H. Lau locate objects in video from text queries using multimodal language models with no task training, in a 2025 computer vision paper. Spatio-temporal video grounding asks for the tube through space and time that a described target traces. Their zero-shot approach leans on what large multimodal models already know.

Two observations steer the design. The models seem to set aside special grounding tokens when localizing a query, and they often ground poorly because they underuse cues like attributes and actions inside the query. Their framework splits the query into attribute and action sub-queries, checks the target's presence across space and time, then assembles the evidence with temporal augmentation. The strategies aim to unlock reasoning the base models possess but do not spontaneously apply to grounding.
arxiv-2509-15578:
Shanghong Li leads a team that spots fake news in short videos. Short video apps spread false claims fast, and the harm can be wide. Past tools struggle with the mix of video, sound, and text moving together. The team build a frame that joins all three and checks the data for trust first.

Their net, HFN, weights each input type on the fly during use. A fusion part keeps it working even when one input type is missing. They also build a new data set of short videos with checked facts. On that set and an older one, the method beats top rivals on a balanced score. The gains are a few points on each set.
arxiv-2509-15778:
Mohammad Bahari leads a team that designs an all electric heavy duty robot arm. Such arms move big loads in industry, and electric drives are taking over from hydraulics. Their drives are linear motors whose traits vary with direction. The team model the motors and the arm together, in both motion and force.

A safe path maker turns end point goals into joint motions within speed and range limits. A genetic search then picks the best motor setup against several goals at once. A neural model inside the search predicts motor efficiency fast. For the chosen design, a physics anchored statistical model learns the motors' quirks from data. That model supports control without force or speed sensors.
arxiv-2509-16178: Kathrin Bringmann, Shane Chern, Johann Franke, and Bernhard Heim count pairs of matrices over finite fields that commute, meaning the order of their product does not matter. They derive formulas that describe how this count grows as the field and matrix size change. Their method uses product expansions of generating functions, which package the counts into a single power series. The short note gives a clean asymptotic picture for a classic counting problem in algebra.
arxiv-2509-16278:
Language models often lose track of facts that appeared far back in a long text. Alok N. Shah and three co-authors add special meta-tokens during training, plus a matching attention tool that teaches the model to use them. These tokens act as trainable landmarks that compress and cache the text before them.

Trained on far less data than usual, their model did well on test tasks after fine-tuning. It also handled texts up to twice its trained length, even with a length extender added. Checks inside the model support the landmark story. The trick offers a cheap path to longer context handling.
arxiv-2509-16478:
Self-driving systems change with every update, and a fix in one place can quietly break behavior elsewhere. Hossein Yousefizadeh and three co-authors present CoCoMagic, a testing method that hunts for such regressions without a perfect answer key. It breeds both test scenes and tweaks to them in a joint search, aiming to widen gaps in how two versions handle the same rules.

On a full driving stack in a virtual simulator, the method found far more severe behavior gaps than baseline searches, while keeping scenes realistic. Built-in explanations help engineers trace why versions diverge. That supports targeted fixes and sharper safety checks.
arxiv-2509-16778:
Eason Chen leads a large team studying an AI tutor for math proofs in a 2025 paper. The system pairs a proof checker that gives live feedback with a chat tool for questions. A trial with well over a hundred students tested it on homework. Students with the tutor did better than a control group.

Interviews with a smaller group praised how easy the tool was to reach. Students also flagged limits and a risk of leaning on it too much. The authors argue that a chat tool alone is not enough for deep learning. Design guided by learning science is needed. The work is a field test, not just a lab demo.
arxiv-2509-16878:
Xuan Zeng and co-authors model hypernuclei with a new force in a 2025 nuclear paper. A hypernucleus holds a lambda particle alongside protons and neutrons. The force between a lambda and a nucleon shapes those systems. The team derive that force from in-medium calculations with a modern chiral approach.

With no adjustable settings, their model matched measured binding energies across light to heavy systems. Some light cases still drift from data. Overall, the match beat other microscopic forces. The work validates the new force at leading order. It also gives modelers a practical interaction set for wider studies of exotic nuclei and dense matter.
arxiv-2509-17178:
Tian Lan, Jinyuan Xu, Xue He, Jenq-Neng Hwang, and Lei Li wrote a 2025 arXiv paper on explaining the choices of large language models. Knowing which input words swayed a model matters for trust, but many explanation tools are slow or blurry. The team wanted a method that is light, cheap, and still faithful to the model.

Their score, called MACS, grades each input token by how steady the model's peak attention stays across its layers. In tests, MACS matched the faithfulness of much heavier tools. It also used notably less video memory and ran with lower delay than those tools. The authors offer it as a practical add-on that can be dropped into decoder-based models with little fuss.
arxiv-2509-17278:
R. Winkler and U. Zülicke address a basic measurement gap in solid-state physics in a 2025 arXiv paper. Ordered crystals carry electric and magnetic multipole densities, from the familiar dipole density of ferroelectrics to the octupole density of altermagnets. Knowing that such order exists is not enough; physics needs its size, and that size has been hard to pin down in a clean way.

The pair give a general method built on projection operators. It yields absolute values for every kind of electric and magnetic order, and the values do not shift with gauge choices. Test cases use variants of lonsdaleite and diamond structures to show the method at work. The authors note the measures can serve as state variables, even as order parameters in Landau theory. The method is built to slot into standard materials software.
arxiv-2509-17878:
Philipp Hacker, Lilian Edwards, and Atoosa Kasirzadeh warn that AI joined with big platforms can fail at whole-system scale. Their 2025 paper builds a frame for that risk from fields such as finance, climate, and cyber safety. New EU laws name the risk but define it in narrow ways.

The authors split AI system risk into four levels. Harms like bias at scale and firm false claims may fall outside the law's focus on top models. They test two EU laws and their own frame on five cases. Reforms they propose would widen how the laws treat such risk.
arxiv-2509-18078:
Emerald Lin and 8 co-authors confirm lens candidates with a spectrograph on a very large telescope. Their 2025 paper reports on dozens of strong lens candidates found by a neural net in survey images. The MUSE unit on the VLT can take spectra across a whole field at once, which suits lens hunts.

From more than two hundred spectra, the team got both lens and source distances for most of the true systems. Some targets gave lens distance only, and a few proved not to be lenses at all. Cases span multi-source setups and group-scale fields. The sample feeds work on dark matter and galaxy shape.
arxiv-2509-18278:
Maya Skarbinski leads a large team that reads how massive galaxies shut down star birth at cosmic noon. Their 2025 paper uses Webb telescope spectra for a set of such galaxies at mid cosmic time. Star birth pasts were rebuilt from the spectra, step by step.

Each galaxy shows a large burst of star birth, then a fast shut-off. Counts of such shut galaxies fit the view that dusty burst galaxies are their parents. The glow of the burst fades on a set time scale, shorter for heavier galaxies. Shut-off times span a wide range, which hints at more than one path. Weak centre activity shows in some.
arxiv-2509-18478:
Straight-chain hydrocarbons called alkanes fold into hairpin shapes once the chain grows long enough. Chen Qu and six co-authors build the most accurate energy model yet for these molecules in this 2025 paper. Alkanes are simple, but the switch from straight to folded shapes is a sharp test of molecular models. Past models missed a key force, the weak pull called dispersion.

The team upgrades existing potentials with a delta machine learning step. High-grade quantum calculations supply the correction at a level near the gold standard. The corrected models predict the energy gap between straight and folded forms well across many chain lengths. They also report vibration spectra for two long chains. The authors call the new potentials the most accurate ones now available for linear alkanes. Chemists can use them to study how long chains fold and pack.
arxiv-2509-18778:
Robots learn manipulation from demonstrations, but the camera encoder behind the policy is often an afterthought. Shijia Ge and six co-authors present VGGT-DP, a control framework built on a strong vision foundation model, in this 2025 paper. The encoder is a pretrained 3D perception transformer. It is paired with the robot's own body-state feedback, as animal vision pairs sight with body sense.

A guided learning step aligns the visual features with the robot's internal states, sharpening spatial grounding. To cut delay, a token reuse trick recomputes features only for the newest frame and recycles the rest. Random token pruning adds robustness and curbs overfitting. On hard MetaWorld tasks, the system beat strong baselines, above all on precise and long tasks. The authors argue encoder structure deserves the same care as policy design.
arxiv-2509-18978:
Sunder Ram Krishnan, writing alone, sharpens a classic limit on how well unknown quantities can be estimated from data. The Cramér-Rao bound sets the lowest possible error for unbiased estimators. When a model family curves through the space of distributions, that plain bound can be too optimistic. Krishnan extends a curvature-corrected version of the bound from one parameter to many.

The correction comes from the bending of the model surface, read through its second fundamental form. For matrix-valued bounds, he gives conditions that can be checked with a computer method based on sums of squares. Two test cases show the point: a curved Gaussian model where bounds pinch to zero along main axes, and a spherical model where curvature is the same in all directions.
arxiv-2509-19078:
Deep Gaussian processes stack layers of flexible random functions, gaining power at the price of hard inference. Jian Xu and three co-authors improve a recent diffusion-based method for that inference. The older method runs a diffusion backward from a plain Gaussian start, but the true answer is complex and far from that start, so paths are wasteful and slow. Their version starts the backward run from a learned, data-dependent distribution instead.

A neural network sets that starting point, improving as training proceeds and narrowing the gap to the true posterior. The network works on inducing inputs, compact summaries of the data that match the variables being inferred. The team derives a training objective under this bridged setup. On regression, classification, and image tasks, their method beat the older diffusion approach and other baselines in accuracy, speed, and posterior quality.
arxiv-2509-19178:
William De Deyn and three co-authors fix a noise problem inside EMC3, a leading Monte Carlo code for plasma at the edge of stellarator fusion devices. The code does not yet handle the electric drift of plasma self-consistently. That drift needs the electric field, which comes from the slope of the electric potential. Plasma fields from Monte Carlo runs are noisy, and taking slopes the usual way amplifies the noise, worse on finer grids.

Their method, extended from a one-dimensional technique, derives an equation for the electric field itself. A Monte Carlo run can then estimate the field directly, with no slope-taking at all. Tests on manufactured solutions show noise growing far more slowly as the grid refines. The authors flag limits near X-points and in island divertors, and call the work a proof of concept.
arxiv-2509-19278:
Mathew D. Penrose and one co-author ask how large a net of random points must grow before it covers a curved surface completely. Points are scattered uniformly at random on a compact Riemannian manifold, possibly with a boundary. Around each point sits a small geodesic ball, and the coverage threshold is the smallest radius at which the balls jointly cover a chosen region. The authors find the exact limiting distribution of that threshold as the number of points grows.

Boundary effects leave clear fingerprints in the formulas: surfaces with edges cover differently from closed ones. A strong law of large numbers pins down the threshold's growth rate as well. The results extend to multiple coverage, where each spot must be covered several times, and to Poisson-distributed samples. They also hold for Euclidean balls in place of geodesic ones. Random covering theory underlies sensor network design and materials sampling.
arxiv-2509-19478:
Blockchains slow down when every node must handle every trade. Sharding splits the work across groups, and Ziwei Wang, Cong Wu, and Paolo Tasca ask whether it fits Hedera. Hedera is a shared ledger that spreads news by gossip between nodes and tolerates faulty ones. The authors survey sharding methods from research and industry, then weigh gains against risks.

Their plan splits Hedera into local groups and a global group that links them. Group membership shifts over time to keep the system safe. The authors report lower storage and message costs, plus room to grow. Fault handling also improves in their design. The study reads as a road map for Hedera rather than a live test, so real gains still need proof on a running network.
arxiv-2509-19778:
The Dice score, a standard grade for medical image outlining, punishes small organs more than large ones for the same slip. Hartmut Häntze and four co-authors show that this quirk bends scores by sex. Women's organs are on average smaller, so an equal outlining error costs women more points. The team tested the effect in a clean setting with no model involved.

They applied identical fake errors to hand-drawn MRI outlines from fifty people. Even a one-millimeter boundary shift produced systematic score gaps between sexes. Small structures showed the largest gaps, while lungs and liver barely differed. A normalized version of the score is also examined. The finding warns benchmark designers: a model may look worse on women purely because the ruler is biased.
arxiv-2509-19878:
Abelian varieties, higher-dimensional cousins of elliptic curves, are sorted by two competing stratifications. Steven R. Groen, Elvira Lupoian, and Mychelle Parker ask where those sorts cross in dimension five. One scheme groups by the isogeny class of a variety's p-divisible group; the other by its p-torsion group scheme. In general, nobody knew which crossings are nonempty.

For dimension five the authors settle the question completely. A payoff is an explicit description of the second stratification restricted to the supersingular locus. Moduli spaces like this one sit under much of modern number theory. Knowing the intersection pattern in the first hard dimension guides conjectures for all dimensions. The work is pure geometry with arithmetic stakes.
arxiv-2509-19978:
Graphene in a strong magnetic field carries current in quantized steps, until the state breaks down. Torsten Röper and six co-authors probe that breakdown with excitation from direct current up to ten gigahertz. Their high-mobility devices use the Corbino geometry, which avoids edge effects. Conductance across the range follows variable range hopping, a tunneling pattern among localized states.

Hopping energies extracted from heat-driven and field-driven runs agree. Thermometry built on that model separates a cold regime, ruled by field-driven hopping, from a hot one ruled by Joule heating. The crossover between them is the breakdown story. Quantum Hall standards underpin electrical metrology, so their failure modes matter. Graphene's wide energy scales make the crossover unusually visible.
arxiv-2509-20178:
Yuanyang Xie, Alexey Krasavin, and Anatoly Zayats wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on light and nanomaterials. Chirality means a structure differs from its mirror image, a trait that matters in chemistry and drug design. Chiral plasmonic nanoparticles can sort molecules and sense tiny samples. The paper shows that some of these particles hide their chirality from standard tests.

The effect appears when a particle's chiral absorption and chiral scattering cancel each other out. Ordinary circular dichroism measurements then report no chiral response at all. The authors call such particles meso-chiral, by analogy with meso compounds in chemistry. Simulations showed the effect across the whole visible range for layered gold particles. Experiments on gold helicoid particles confirmed hidden chiral absorption where standard readings showed none.
arxiv-2509-20478:
Learning to reach any goal from logged experience is the aim of Vivek Myers and three co-authors in a 2025 arXiv paper on offline reinforcement learning. Two traditions structure the learned representation of states. Contrastive methods infer future outcomes, while distance methods tie representation gaps to travel time. Each tradition fails where the other succeeds.

The authors unify them inside a quasimetric representation space, distances that obey a triangle inequality but need not be symmetric. With the right extra constraints, that geometry supports successor representations that yield optimal goal reaching. The method works even when the logged data is suboptimal and the world is stochastic. It keeps the stability and long-horizon strength of contrastive learning. It also gains the stitching ability of distance-based methods, joining fragments of different trajectories into new routes. Benchmarks showed gains exactly where each parent method struggled.
arxiv-2509-20978:
Finding one anomalous graph among many is vital in drug discovery, yet labeled examples are few and skewed. Xiangyu Dong, Xingyi Zhang, and Sibo Wang present FracAug in a 2025 paper on graph-level anomaly detection. Their framework plugs into graph neural networks to ease the label shortage.

Instead of heuristic edits, FracAug learns the semantics inside the given graphs. It synthesizes fractional variants that preserve meaning while varying multi-scale topology. A weighted, distance-aware margin loss guides that synthesis. Predictions on original and augmented graphs then verify each other to produce pseudo-labels. Because generation is learned rather than rule-based, imbalance in the original data hurts less. The authors aim for stronger detection under the limited supervision that real screening programs face.
arxiv-2509-21078:
Young stars grow by pulling in gas, and the energy of that inflow shapes how they and their disks evolve. E Fiorellino and twelve co-authors revisit how astronomers measure accretion luminosity in a 2025 paper accepted by Astronomy and Astrophysics. It is the seventh paper of the PENELLOPE program.

Direct measurement is often blocked by limited spectral coverage and hard ultraviolet modeling. Astronomers therefore rely on empirical relations between accretion luminosity and observable tracer lines. The authors test those relations on sixty-four classical T Tauri stars observed with the VLT/X-Shooter instrument. They check whether the relations hold across different star-forming regions and for other kinds of accreting young objects. Reliable relations underpin most studies of how stars assemble their mass.
arxiv-2509-21178:
Error correcting codes built from lattice polytopes are called toric codes, and their strength is measured here. The 2025 paper is by Amelia Gibbs and 4 co-authors. Toric codes are error correcting codes built from toric varieties. Those varieties match lattice polytopes, which are flat sided shapes on a grid. The paper studies two dimensional polytopes and the codes they define. It focuses on shapes with a period one property.

For period one shapes, the count of grid points scales in a simple way when the shape grows. The authors prove an explicit formula for the minimum distance of codes from one class of such shapes. Minimum distance measures how well a code can spot errors. They also use Vandermonde matrices, following Little and Schwarz, to find the distance for another class.
arxiv-2509-21478:
Lattice data with discrete categories appear in psychology, image analysis, biology, and forestry. Maria Paula Duenas-Herrera and 2 co-authors model such data in a 2025 paper. The Ising and Potts models are standard tools for binary and multinomial lattice data. Both models have known shortcomings. Fitted simulations often fail to look like the observed data.

Phase transitions and ground states complicate inference and interpretation for these models. Intractable normalizing constants block likelihood based methods. The authors develop a tapered version of the Ising and Potts models. Tapering addresses the poor fit and phase transition problems. Efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo maximum likelihood methods are developed for the tapered model.
arxiv-2509-21678:
Removing oxygen from phenol is a step toward turning biomass derived oils into fuels. Isaac Onyango and Qiang Zhu study that reaction on iron based surfaces in a 2025 paper. A Gaussian process regression calculator accelerates nudged elastic band calculations of reaction paths. Test calculations show a large speedup over conventional density functional theory. Energy barrier errors stay very small, preserving hit rate.

Cobalt and nickel modifications are examined in top and subsurface layers of the iron surface. Subsurface substitutions preserve favourable thermodynamics and kinetics for carbon oxygen cleavage and carbon hydrogen formation. Top layer substitutions generally raise the cleavage barrier and make the step endothermic. Reverse reaction barriers also grow sharply there. On the fly surrogate models guide the comparison.
arxiv-2509-22078:
Tony Liimatainen and Janne Nurminen solve an inverse problem for a surface equation in this 2025 mathematics paper. The equation prescribes the mean curvature of a surface, a measure of how it bends at each point. The inverse problem runs the usual direction backward: from measurements at the boundary, recover the source function inside. Their work extends earlier inverse studies of minimal surfaces, and it is the first treatment of an inverse source problem for a quasilinear equation.

The authors prove that in two dimensions the boundary data, packaged as a Dirichlet-to-Neumann map, determines the source uniquely. A subtle feature drives the proof: although the domain is ordinary flat space, linearizing the equation produces a conductivity problem whose coefficients form a curved metric set by the background solution. A uniqueness result for conformal mappings then solves that system and recovers the source.
arxiv-2509-22178:
M. Atzori Corona and four co-authors turn dark matter detectors into neutrino observatories. Huge tanks of liquid xenon, built to catch dark matter particles, also record neutrinos scattering off nuclei and electrons. Two collaborations recently reported the first evidence of solar neutrinos bouncing coherently off whole nuclei in such detectors. Their 2025 paper analyzes the latest recoil data from three experiments: XENONnT, PandaX-4T, and LUX-ZEPLIN.

The rarer signal comes from the Sun's most common neutrinos scattering off atomic electrons. It is faint under the standard theory, but many extensions of that theory would amplify it strongly. The authors use the combined data to test both the standard picture and those extensions. Even so, these detectors are sensitive to the tau flavor share of solar neutrinos, a piece the dedicated experiments see weakly. That makes the dark matter tanks a complementary window on low-energy neutrino physics.
arxiv-2509-22478: Florian Kéruzoré and Lance A. Moreau introduce halox, a Python library for dark matter halo calculations. Halos are the gravity wells that host galaxies and clusters. Their traits and counts help infer basic facts about the universe. Halox computes key halo properties and the halo mass function, which counts halos by mass. Built on JAX, the library runs fast and supports automatic differentiation. That makes it fit gradient-based workflows, such as Hamiltonian Monte Carlo sampling and machine learning.
arxiv-2509-22778:
Benjamin P. Gompertz leads a large team that pinned down the distance to an extraordinary day-long gamma-ray burst. GRB 250702B repeated over a full day, unlike any normal burst. Spectroscopy with the James Webb Space Telescope found narrow hydrogen lines at one consistent redshift, which fixed the distance and thus the energy scale. The gamma-ray energy release is among the largest ever inferred.

No ongoing emission remained at the burst site, and any companion supernova must be fainter than a known comparison event. Rates suggest such bursts are over a thousand times rarer than normal long bursts. The host galaxy is unusually large, dusty, and massive for a burst host, which hints the environment shaped the progenitor.
arxiv-2509-22878:
Robin H. D. Corbet applies a principle of radical mundanity to the Fermi paradox. The paradox asks why no strong evidence of technology-using alien civilizations has turned up. Radical mundanity prefers the dull answer: the galaxy holds a modest number of civilizations, none able or willing to build huge astro-engineering works. On that view, none will colonize a large share of the galaxy, even with robotic probes, and no long-lived high-power beacons exist.

Corbet still sees a reasonable chance of contact on a short historical timescale. That event would be momentous, though perhaps slightly disappointing in its ordinariness. Such a universe is less terrifying than either horn of the famous Clarke dilemma. It also implies many planets host some form of life.
arxiv-2509-22978:
Code clone detectors can flag copied code, but they rarely say why. Teeradaj Racharak and 3 co-authors use a large language model to explain detector calls after the fact. Older explainers need access inside the model or cost too much compute. Their method leans on the in-context learning skill of ChatGPT-4. The target detector is GraphCodeBERT.

The language model gave correct explanations in up to ninety-eight percent of cases. Raters judged most explanations good as well. Sample code lines from the model helped in some cases.
