Naruya Kondo, Yuto Asano, and Yoichi Ochiai present a system that turns a smartphone scan of a person into an animatable 3D avatar in about five minutes, in this 2025 conference paper. The avatars use Gaussian splatting, a rendering method that builds scenes from millions of soft colored blobs, which looks realistic but is hard to animate. Earlier approaches needed camera arrays, long processing, or powerful graphics cards.

Their method binds each splat to a skinned mesh, a conventional animated body model, and moves the splats in parallel as the mesh moves, preserving the splatted look while gaining real-time motion. Scanning and preprocessing happen on the phone itself, and avatar generation takes only about thirty seconds. Because the system is built on WebXR, the avatars run across web, mobile, and virtual or augmented reality applications, suiting social media and metaverse uses.
arxiv-2510-14078:
Randall Clark and co-authors show that a minimal machine-learning model can tell which confinement state a fusion plasma is in, using only one diagnostic, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Future fusion power plants must distinguish the low-confinement L-mode from the high-confinement H-mode for safe, efficient operation, yet they will carry far fewer instruments than today's machines.

Their framework uses electron cyclotron emission signals, which report electron temperature profiles without fragile in-vessel probes. Features are extracted with radial basis functions, localized building blocks, and a gradient boosting classifier, an ensemble of decision trees, makes the call. Test accuracy averaged about ninety-six percent correct predictions. Robustness checks and a feature study confirmed the approach is reliable rather than lucky. The authors argue state-of-the-art classification is attainable from a restricted diagnostic set, pointing toward minimalist, resilient systems for fusion power plants.
arxiv-2510-14178:
Nivedita Mahesh and co-authors study how deployment imperfections would affect a radio telescope on the far side of the Moon, in this 2025 arXiv paper. FARSIDE would spread 128 pairs of orthogonal antennas over a twelve-kilometer spiral to observe ultra-long radio wavelengths from the Moon's radio-quiet, ionosphere-free far side, a window on the early universe and exoplanets.

Because tele-operated rovers would deploy the antennas, the two elements of each pair might not sit together, creating phase offsets between polarization channels. Modeling the dipole beams with and without such offsets, the authors find the offsets leak signal into the Stokes U and V polarization channels. Using a custom simulation pipeline and a standard sky model, they produce simulated visibilities and images for both layouts. These quantify the damage to polarization response and imaging performance. They inform how precisely the rovers must place each antenna pair.
arxiv-2510-14278:
Md Mahadi Hasan Nahid and Davood Rafiei present PRISM, an agentic retrieval system for multi-hop question answering, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Such questions can only be answered by chaining several pieces of evidence together. Retrieval for such questions is delicate: missing one link breaks the chain, while piling in documents adds noise that misleads the answering model.

PRISM splits retrieval among three specialized agents working in a loop. A Question Analyzer breaks the complex query into sub-questions. A Selector identifies the most relevant context for each sub-question, optimizing precision. An Adder then hunts for evidence the Selector missed, optimizing recall, and the two iterate until the evidence set is compact yet comprehensive. On four challenging benchmarks, including HotpotQA and MuSiQue, PRISM consistently outperformed strong baselines, and downstream models using its evidence surpassed even full-context answer accuracy while reading far less irrelevant material.
arxiv-2510-14378:
Ruifeng Yuan and Lei Wu optimize the shape of manifolds that distribute rarefied gas, the gas of vacuum systems where molecules rarely collide, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Flow optimization is studied for continuum flows, but vacuum technology, from semiconductor fabrication to space simulation, needs rules for the regime governed by the Boltzmann equation.

Using an adjoint topology optimization method on a two-dimensional manifold with an inlet and outlets, aiming to maximize mass flow while keeping outflows uniform, they uncover two phenomena. A wetted-area minimum in the slip flow regime, analogous to the Knudsen minimum, arising from competition between bend losses and surface friction modified by velocity slip at walls. Second, an inlet-outlet reciprocity in the free molecular regime, where the design becomes indifferent to which side is the inlet and to the pressure ratio. They draw lessons about channel curvature, compressibility, and the uniformity constraint.
arxiv-2510-14478:
Gaofeng Fan and co-authors compute from first principles how a charmed meson decays semileptonically into a phi meson, a lepton, and a neutrino, using lattice quantum chromodynamics, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Such decays test lepton universality, the principle that electrons and muons behave identically apart from mass, and they help pin down quark-mixing parameters.

The calculation uses seven universes with different lattice spacings and pion masses, generated with two-plus-one flavors of quarks, enabling extrapolation to spacetime and to the pion mass. The form factor ratios improve precision by up to an order of magnitude over lattice studies. The team reports branching fractions for the electron and muon versions of the decay and their ratio, which lands below one, providing support for future experimental tests of universality. They also extract the quark-mixing element connecting charm and strange quarks from the rates.
arxiv-2510-14578:
Monsel and co-authors study, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a nanoscale refrigerator that behaves a little like a demon. The device is a triple quantum dot system, a tiny electronic structure, that pulls heat from a cold contact. It can cool without drawing energy on average from its power source. That source is nonthermal, meaning its energy is not spread as heat normally spreads, and it only needs to fluctuate.

Using full counting statistics and random trajectory methods, the team measured how steady the cooling power is. They compared two working regimes with strong output. One exploits information about the system, and the other exploits the resource's nonthermal character. The two differ sharply in precision. In the nonthermal regime, fluctuations in cooling power were about ten times smaller than the input fluctuations. Cross-correlations between the heat currents and the information flow backed up this reading of the two mechanisms.
arxiv-2510-14678:
Boroun, Ha, Kotikov, and Lipatov compute, in a 2025 arXiv paper, how gluons are distributed inside a proton when they carry only a tiny fraction of its momentum. This low-x regime matters for collider physics, and the distributions are usually found by heavy numerical work. The authors want formulas that are simple enough to read insight from directly.

They use the Laplace transform technique, a mathematical tool that turns convolution equations into algebra. Including leading and next-to-leading contributions, they derive compact analytical expressions for the gluon density. The formulas cover both the ordinary integrated density and the version that also tracks transverse momentum. Their results agree closely with those from other analytical and numerical approaches. The authors stress the main advantage: the expressions stay simple while capturing the essential features of far more complex calculations, in the limit where the momentum fraction tends to zero.
arxiv-2510-14878:
Karkada, Turnbull, Liu, and Simon show, in a 2025 arXiv paper, that a model's learning curve can be predicted from raw statistics of its training data. Kernel regression is usually understood through the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of its kernel on the data distribution, which are hard to compute for real images. The authors need only two measurements: the data's covariance matrix, and how the target function decomposes into polynomials.

Their key idea approximates the kernel's eigenfunctions as Hermite polynomials of the data, an ansatz they prove correct for Gaussian data. Image datasets, from handwritten digits to ImageNet, turn out to be Gaussian enough for the approximation to predict test error versus sample size in practice. The framework extends beyond kernels: neural networks in the feature-learning regime learn the same polynomial components, in the predicted order. The authors call it a proof of concept for end-to-end learning theory.
arxiv-2510-14978:
Kumari and co-authors train, in a 2025 arXiv paper, an image editing model without any paired edit examples. Editors that follow instructions like 'make the sky stormy' normally learn from datasets of input-target pairs, which barely occur naturally. Synthetic pairs are the usual workaround, but they can bake the teacher model's artifacts into the student.

The new paradigm optimizes a few-step diffusion model directly. During training the model is unrolled, generating an edit, and a vision-language model grades it: did the edit follow the instruction, and did it leave everything untouched? Those judgments become gradients for end-to-end training. A distribution matching loss keeps the outputs on the manifold of images that pre-trained models know. With no paired data, the method performed on par with editing diffusion models trained on pairs, across benchmarks. An extensive ablation study backs up which pieces matter.
arxiv-2510-15078:
Yang and a team revisit, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a decades-old mystery in the high-temperature superconductor. In YBCO, swapping yttrium for praseodymium destroys superconductivity, even though it carries the same charge and a small magnetic moment, and no other rare-earth element does this. The two standing theories blame hybridization with praseodymium's f electrons, or new states those electrons create.

Using angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, backed by density functional calculations, the team watched the electronic structure change as praseodymium content rose. They found no signature of f-electron hybridization and no new states, contradicting both models. Instead, strong electron doping appeared on the antibonding Fermi surface. The copper-oxygen bilayers decoupled, and hopping along the chains strengthened, pointing to indirect electron-release paths beyond ionization of the f shell. The authors propose the material as a platform for correlation physics in coupled one- and two-dimensional systems.
arxiv-2510-15378:
Zhentao He and Chao Ji study solutions of the nonlinear Dirac equation on graphs, in this 2025 arXiv paper. A metric graph is a network of edges with lengths, and the Dirac equation, borrowed from relativistic quantum theory, governs wave-like states living on it. The nonlinearity here acts only on a compact core of the graph, while the graph itself stretches out without bound.

The solutions are normalized, meaning their total mass is fixed at one, and the frequency appears as an unknown to be solved for alongside the state. The paper investigates the nonrelativistic limit, the regime where the speed of light is treated as huge and the Dirac equation should shade into a simpler Schrödinger-type picture. He and Ji state that, to their knowledge, this is the first study of that limit for normalized solutions on metric graphs.
arxiv-2510-15678:
Strongly correlated electrons defeat ordinary quantum chemistry methods, which matters for designing new molecules. Arpan Choudhury and three colleagues propose a quantum computing scheme for this problem in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their approach splits a molecule into fragments, entangles each fragment, then consolidates the pieces. A hardware-efficient circuit prepares entangled states within each fragment, following its actual structure. A unitary coupled cluster step then adds dynamic correlation between the fragments.

Numerical tests on strongly correlated systems show the scheme is accurate and robust. It stays flexible, since the fragment treatment can be customized per problem. The authors aim it at multireference chemistry on near-term quantum hardware.
arxiv-2510-16078:
Abdelilah Ganmati, Karim Afdel, and Lahcen Koutti fit face verification onto a smart card with very short templates. Match-on-card designs keep the biometric check inside the card. That placement protects privacy. Card hardware and standards tightly limit message size and timing, though. Their design makes compact binary templates off the card with a PCA-ITQ method. It compares them on the card by constant-time Hamming distance.

Commands follow the stated ISO and IEC card standards. Payloads have fixed length, and replies carry a decision only, so no score leaks off the card. Tests use a CelebA working set with dozens of identities and hundreds of images. Thresholds come from error curves, and full enrol-then-verify runs are replayed at those points. Even at the slowest contact rate, checks finish in tens of milliseconds. The longer code lowers the equal error rate.
arxiv-2510-16178:
Juliana Silva Canella and Norai Romeu Rocco work in pure group theory, the study of symmetry through algebra. Their target is the non-abelian tensor square of a group, a larger group built from pairs of elements. That square encodes how the group fails to be commutative, meaning its order of steps matters. They focus on finite metacyclic groups, a well-charted family built from two cyclic parts.

The authors find a full presentation for these groups when one key size is odd. A presentation is a compact set of rules that defines the tensor square. They reach it through a helper group built from the square and the group's own product with itself. From that presentation they read off three linked objects: the tensor square itself, the exterior square, and the Schur multiplier. Such presentations let algebraists compute with these groups instead of just knowing they exist.
arxiv-2510-16678:
Feyza Duman Keles and four co-authors settle an open coin problem in a 2025 paper. Picture biased coins, each with a known chance of landing heads. Flip them in some order until both heads and tails appear. The Unanimous Vote problem asks which order needs fewest flips on average.

An earlier method only promised answers within a fixed factor of best. Whether the problem was truly hard stayed unknown. The team now gives an exact method with modest running time. Simple swap arguments show the best order sits near a greedy order. They also compare fixed orders with plans that adapt mid-way. The gap between those two styles is now pinned down exactly.
arxiv-2510-16978:
Rikhil Tanugula, Dheeraj Chintapalli, and Sunkalp Chandra present a biology-inspired decision system in a 2025 paper. Their system, Lark, pairs language models with an evolving agent group. Real decisions must balance several stakeholders with competing goals. They must also avoid wordy, costly outputs.

Lark improves candidate plans through four borrowed biological tricks. Plasticity makes small adjustments to promising candidates. Duplication copies winners, then maturation specializes the copies. Stakeholder votes combine through influence-weighted ranked-choice scoring. A token penalty rewards brief answers throughout. Over thirty test rounds against fourteen systems, Lark finished near the top. It placed in the top three in most rounds. Removing any one mechanism hurt its scores measurably.
arxiv-2510-17378:
Neural networks can treat two very different inputs as the same, and Wei Xu with three co-authors probes that habit inside graph neural networks. These networks learn from data arranged as nodes and links, such as molecules or social graphs. The team builds model metamers, new graphs tuned so the network inner activity matches a reference graph even though the graphs look quite unlike each other.

Xu and his co-authors measure how large the space of such lookalike graphs is, and they find extreme levels of sameness across several classic designs. Changes to the network shape or training ease the problem only in part, falling well short of human like behaviour. The gap itself becomes a useful benchmark for judging future models.
arxiv-2510-17778:
Frédéric Déglise surveys motivic homotopy theory, a field that imports topology into algebraic geometry. The field began with work by Morel and Voevodsky. It studies algebraic varieties, meaning shapes defined by polynomial equations, with topological tools. Déglise focuses on computing the theory's homotopy sheaves, both stable and unstable.

He then describes applications by Isaksen, Wang, and Xu to stable stems. Stable stems are stable homotopy groups, a central list of numbers in topology. Those authors used a motivic version of the Adams spectral sequence. Their work also opened a path toward synthetic homotopy theory. The notes began as a Bourbaki talk, now written out.
arxiv-2510-18278:
Karelia Salinas, with Victor Barella and four co-authors, introduces ORDENA in a 2025 paper on data visualization. The data type is origin-destination flows, meaning records of movement from starting places to ending places. With massive flow data, grouping and filtering can hide the very patterns analysts seek.

ORDENA plots each flow as one point on a simple scatter plot. Origins run along one axis and destinations along the other, so the layout itself reveals spatial patterns. Extra explanation tools link each flow pattern back to its underlying attributes. Case studies built with domain experts, plus reviews by outside experts, gave strongly positive feedback.
arxiv-2510-18578:
M. Muñoz-Echeverría and thirty-three co-authors present a method for measuring the pressure profile shared by galaxy clusters, the largest structures held together by gravity. Hot gas inside a cluster pushes outward, and theory says its pressure pattern should follow one universal shape once each cluster is scaled by its mass and distance. Finding that shape requires knowing each cluster's mass, which creates a circular problem.

Their method fits the universal profile and the individual masses together for the first time, keeping track of how errors in one affect the other. Tests show the joint fit returns masses as accurate as, and more precise than, the input estimates, avoiding biases that separate fits create. The team applied the method to about twenty-five clusters observed by an X-ray heritage project, spanning a wide range of masses and redshifts.
arxiv-2510-18878:
Brij Bidhin Desai, Yukta Arvind Rajapur, Aswathi Mundayatt, and Jaya Sreevalsan-Nair present a software tool that lets users build and visualize air pollution forecasts for cities. Urban pollution threatens health and planning, yet tools that both predict pollutant levels and show their patterns over space and time in an interactive way have been missing. CityAQVis fills that gap as a machine learning sandbox.

The tool fuses satellite observations, weather data, population density, elevation, and nighttime lights to estimate ground-level pollutant concentrations. Through a graphical interface, users can train and compare predictive models and view side-by-side maps of how pollution distributes under two different urban scenarios. Pilot case studies predicting nitrogen dioxide in metropolitan regions show the tool adapts to other pollutants as well. The authors aim it at situational awareness and evidence-based air quality decisions.
arxiv-2510-18978:
Tomer Shaked and three co-authors propose a fast way to tune programmable wireless channels, such as those shaped by reconfigurable intelligent surfaces. Older methods need a simple channel model that can be tuned quickly when users move, but real channels are often too complex for such models.

Their method joins artificial intelligence with annealed Langevin dynamics, a sampling process that settles toward good settings, and skips explicit channel modeling altogether. Framed through a maximum estimate, the deep unfolded algorithm learns to search settings rapidly, which suits channels known only through simulators or direct measurements.
arxiv-2510-19178:
Runzhe Wu and nine co-authors show that gradient imbalance distorts reinforcement learning post-training when several tasks train a language model together. Mixing task datasets and optimizing them jointly assumes each task pushes the model with similar force, but the authors find some tasks produce far larger gradients than others.

Updates then lean toward the loud tasks, even though those tasks do not learn faster; some large-gradient tasks gain as little as, or less than, quiet ones. That mismatch means joint training can waste effort and starve tasks that need it. The finding pushes trainers to balance gradients deliberately rather than trust the mix.
arxiv-2510-19378:
Riccardo Messina and Philippe Ben-Abdallah build a theory of heat transfer by radiation. It covers many-body systems whose optical properties change over time. Heat exchange is usually treated at steady equilibrium. Time modulation breaks that picture. It adds memory effects and unsteady correlations.

Their formulas give heat currents for modulated systems. A Landauer-style picture covers pairwise exchange. It counts all frequency-changing channels. Near resonance, modulation boosts random heat motion across sidebands. The effect works like a tuned amplifier. It allows active control of heat flow by frequency, at the nanoscale.
arxiv-2510-19478:
Julia Wąsala and five co-authors show how missing pixels in satellite images can bias methane plume detection and test ways to remove that bias. Clouds and sensor gaps leave pixels missing in a systematic way. A model can lazily learn that images with low coverage tend to carry certain labels, then under-detect plumes exactly where coverage is poor.

Several imputation approaches are evaluated for breaking the link between coverage and label. A weighted resampling scheme during training also enforces balance across coverage levels. Fairer detection matters because methane monitoring guides real emission cuts, and biased maps would misdirect that effort.
arxiv-2510-20078:
Rina Friedberg and six co-authors tackle treatment effect learning when online experiments assign treatments in sequence over repeated sessions. An action taken in one session can carry over into later sessions, so outcomes measured afterward reflect a buildup of effects. Standard identification and inference methods can then be badly misspecified.

The team proposes T-Learners layered into the G-Formula, drawing on causal machine learning and work on identification in sequential settings. In a simple simulation, their approach prevents the steady loss of accuracy that carry-over effects otherwise cause. The result underlines why estimation tools need to match the sequential systems that are common in technology experiments.
arxiv-2510-20178:
Yun Wang and six co-authors introduce PPMStereo, a method for estimating depth from stereo video that stays consistent over time. Flickering depth breaks immersion in uses like augmented reality, yet modeling long-term consistency cheaply is hard. Earlier methods either model time only weakly for modest gains or pay a large cost for long-range temporal links.

Their pick-and-play memory picks the most relevant past frames and then weights them adaptively for aggregation, keeping the memory buffer compact and informative. The two-stage design mirrors a simple human decision pattern the authors cite. Extensive experiments show leading results in both accuracy and temporal consistency for dynamic stereo matching, with clear gains over a strong recent baseline.
arxiv-2510-20278:
Guangyu Dai, Siliang Tang, and Yueting Zhuang build a small helper model to work with a large pre-trained model. Such pairs aim to cut cost and lift skill on niche tasks. But the small model can drag scores down, add loss of past skill, and boost fake facts. Their helper, called KCM, is built on KAN nets, a type that swaps the usual perceptron blocks for spline-based units.

KAN nets are clear to view and grasp, and they lose past skill less fast. The pair is tested on text tasks, image tasks, and mixed tasks. Calls to the large model drop by a lot, while scores stay near the large model alone. Loss of past skill drops by a clear margin as well.
arxiv-2510-20778:
Padmavathi Venkatraman leads a team of fifteen co-authors plus a large science collaboration in testing lens modeling for the coming LSST survey of lensed active galaxies. Bent light from massive galaxies can time cosmic expansion, but only if the lens mass is modeled with great care.

The team built a mock set of thirteen hundred lensed systems and simulated five years of survey images for each one. A neural method then infers the key lens settings, the ring radius and the density slope, straight from the images. Both settings come back with low bias and solid precision per lens. Removing lens light first helps only when the data match the training range, a practical warning for the real survey pipeline.
arxiv-2510-20978:
Ayoub El Hanchi leads two co-authors on a shape based analysis of main component analysis, asking exactly which property of the data distribution sets its excess risk. PCA is a basic size count reduction tool, yet sharp distributional accounts of its error have been incomplete.

A central limit theorem for the estimated main subspace error is established, along with the long run distribution of excess risk under reconstruction loss. A finite sample upper bound recovers the long run picture for large samples. The key engine is a self concordance property of a Rayleigh quotient function on the Grassmannian, linking optimization geometry to statistical precision.
arxiv-2510-21178:
Flora C. Shi, with Martin J. Wainwright and Stephen Bates, studies hypothesis testing when people in a population differ and hold private information. A single test used for everyone performs worse than a test that could somehow see each person's hidden type, so uniform testing wastes accuracy.

The authors design menus of contracts that pair a test suited to each type with a payment rule, so people reveal their type by their own choice. They fully describe which menus match the ideal performance for any mixed population, and show that revealing information can cost almost nothing compared with one standard test. Numerical examples display better trade-offs between the two kinds of statistical error.
arxiv-2510-21378:
Biao Dong and Bin Cao design power control for a system that mixes sensing with edge AI on the same wireless link. Several devices first send probing signals to sense a target, then beam locally extracted features to an access point, which merges them over the air for a shared decision.

To guide the design, they define two stand-ins for quality: one that keeps the merged features as clean as possible. One that keeps different classes as separable as possible for the final decision. For both goals they derive best power settings in closed form, covering links that share time slots and links that share frequency bands. The formulas show threshold-style and splitting-style structures, and experiments confirm the theory.
arxiv-2510-21678:
Nabamita Banerjee and three co-authors add fermions to a flexible boundary regime for gravity in three-dimensional anti-de Sitter space. Boundary conditions decide which symmetries survive at infinity, and the Kac-Moody choice trades the usual Virasoro symmetry for a current algebra; giving that choice a supersymmetric upgrade is the paper's business.

For the smallest supergravity, with one supersymmetry on each side, two extensions exist. The first mirrors the bosonic story: a large gauge transformation, realized by a super-Miura map between fields and chemical potentials, links the new conditions to standard super-Virasoro ones. The second is wilder, tightly constraining the fermionic chemical potentials while enriching the boundary structure, with a geometric reading as folds in a droplet of free fermions. Quantizing it yields only bosonic soft excitations in the spectrum.
arxiv-2510-21778:
Abdelilah Ganmati, working with Karim Afdel and Lahcen Koutti, measures how much compact binary face templates change as a person ages. Faces are first turned into number patterns by a modern neural network, then compressed into short codes of sixty-four or one hundred twenty-eight bits. The change is counted directly in bits per decade.

Using hundreds of identities from the AgeDB collection, each with photos at three or more ages, the team finds a small but steady drift over time. Shorter codes drift less, so they stay more stable at a fixed matching threshold. The results matter for smart-card systems, and the authors suggest fixes such as renewing enrollment and protecting the least stable bit positions.
arxiv-2510-21978:
Hoang Phan leads a nine-author team on a side effect of teaching language models to reason harder. Training with rewards for checkable answers has become the standard recipe for sharpening math and multimodal skill. The team shows the same training quietly erodes basic abilities the model started with, such as faithful perception.

Standard guards, like penalties for straying from the original model, are computed on the training task itself. They cannot promise that broader knowledge survives, and mixing in replay data from other domains raises the question of how much weight each goal deserves. Their answer, RECAP, replays past material while dynamically reweighting objectives to protect general knowledge. The work frames reasoning gains and general competence as a balance to manage, not a free lunch.
arxiv-2510-22478:
Chenjian Wang studies pinned patterns in sets that fill a positive share of space in higher dimensions. A pinned pattern fixes one point of a shape inside the set and asks which scaled copies also fit. Wang shows a split outcome: for any fixed pattern with at least three points, some dense set can avoid all large copies pinned at its own points.

Yet a positive result also holds for every such dense set. Some pattern must occur, for each starting point, at a rich set of scales whose share stays above a fixed positive level. That level depends only on the pattern size, the dimension, and the density of the set.
arxiv-2510-22678:
Dimitri Dine and Jack J Garzella wrote a 2025 paper in algebra. They study quotient fields of perfectoid Tate algebras. Those fields come from a branch of geometry where distance works in a new way. The algebras allow roots of variables to be taken again and again, with no end.

The pair describe each quotient field with fields from Berkovich geometry. Each quotient is a semi-immediate extension of one such field. That fact pins down its value group and its residue field. A new kind of valuation drives the proof. It is called topologically simple. In one case, at least one radius in the setup must be irrational. That means it is not a ratio of whole numbers.
arxiv-2510-22778:
Many data objects are spectra, not plain number lists. Spectra are sets of eigenvalues. Swagatam Das, writing alone in 2025, builds diffusion models for such data. Eigenvalues repel each other as they move. Treating them as free coordinates gives the wrong limit.

Free probability gives the right forward process. Yet fixed strength free diffusion has one flaw. Its only balance point is the semicircle law. Das lets volatility depend on state. Then any nice compact target law can be the balance point. He gives a closed form drift for the flow. Extra conditions yield reverse dynamics and a trainable score.
arxiv-2510-22878:
Models trained on patient records may look real yet lack clinical sense. Nicholas I-Hsien Kuo, Blanca Gallego, and Louisa Jorm test that risk in 2025. They train generative models on structured medical trajectories. Sampling in those records is irregular. Visits occur at uneven times.

Two models were trained, an LSTM and a reduced Transformer. LSTM is a recurrent sequence model. Random visit gaps were added in training. Test sequences stayed complete. Generated trajectories matched feature distributions well. Yet cross feature structure was not preserved. That means local realism without clinical coherence. The authors urge domain specific evaluation before deployment.
arxiv-2510-23178:
Sumit Goel, Yiqing Yan, and Jeffrey Zeidel study how interim feedback changes bidding in a dynamic contest. Two players bid over two stages in an all-pay auction for a common-value prize, and the organizer chooses what each learns between stages. Theory characterizes outcomes as cheapest signal equilibria.

In those equilibria one player bids zero first while the other bids the cheapest amount matching some signal, and both earn zero expected payoff. Total bids sum to the prize value. The authors then run an experiment with four feedback policies, from full to cutoff rules, to see how real bidders compare with theory.
arxiv-2510-23278:
Veska Tsenkova, Peter Stanchev, Daniel Petrov, and Deyan Lazarov present hYOLO, a hierarchical extension of the YOLOv8 detector for image classification. Flat classifiers name a single object and ignore the natural hierarchy among categories. Real objects sit in families, and knowing those relations improves context and controls how bad a mistake is.

Their end-to-end model detects and classifies with hierarchical context built in. A near miss within the right family is scored more kindly than a wild error. Such graded accuracy matters in medical and industrial imaging, where some confusions cost far more than others.
arxiv-2510-23378:
Yu Yao and six co-authors investigate resonances in the Sigma baryon system with spin-parity one half minus, using the chiral quark model. They examine the system from both three-quark and five-quark perspectives. A precise few-body method, the Gaussian Expansion Method, builds the orbital wave functions of the multiquark states.

To reduce dependence on model parameters, they fit two parameter sets and check stability. Results stay stable across both sets. In the three-quark calculations, two states are obtained. The study helps clarify which observed Sigma resonances are ordinary baryons and which may be exotic five-quark states.
arxiv-2510-23778:
Halyna Hodovanets and eleven co-authors map the magnetic behavior of CeAuBi2, a strongly correlated antiferromagnet missing about eighteen percent of its gold atoms. The material orders below about thirteen degrees above absolute zero. Using magnetization, resistivity, heat capacity, and X-ray and neutron diffraction on single crystals, the team charts how applied fields reshape that order.

The crystals show strong directional preference, with an easy axis along the c direction. Along it, a spin-flop transition appears near seventy-five kilo-oersted, marked in all three bulk probes. The temperature-field phase diagram shows the transition tying into the suppression of order, which changes from second-order to first-order and splits into three transitions below one degree. An Ising model with weak frozen disorder explains the smeared look of these transitions. The authors conclude the gold vacancies alone are enough to soften the metamagnetic critical behavior.
arxiv-2510-24078:
William Yang and four co-authors propose a better way to make fake training images for fine grained image sorting. Tasks like telling bird species apart need many labeled images, and text to image models can help fill the gap. Tuning those models on a few real images can improve quality but also cause copying and reduce variety.

Their method, BOB, first pulls out traits that are not tied to the class, such as background and pose. It then trains with those traits stated clearly and averages them out when making new images. Broad tests show cleaner, more varied data and better sorting results, with less copying of the small real set.
arxiv-2510-24378:
Yann Kerverdo and four co-authors built StrokeSeg, a light tool that puts stroke lesion mapping into day to day hospital use. Top tools like nnU-Net map brain lesions very well. But they are heavy, come as one large block, and are hard to set up in a clinic. StrokeSeg splits the work into three parts. Prep, inference, and clean up are kept apart, so each part can be swapped or fixed on its own.

Prep uses the Anima toolbox and gives files in a standard form. Inference runs on ONNX Runtime with half precision numbers, which cuts the model size by about half. The tool has both a screen based form and a text command form. It ships as Python scripts or as a stand alone Windows program. Tests on hospital data show it is ready to deploy.
arxiv-2510-24678:
Jef Laga, the sole author, takes up a question left open by Poonen and Stoll on shapes called abelian varieties. A map from such a shape to its dual, called a polarization, may have no neat line set over the base field to stand for it. The question asks if a twist of the shape could hold such a set instead.

Laga gives a test for when such a twist and set exist, based just on the kernel of the map. With that test, the answer is yes when the degree is odd or small and even. But for each size from seven up, some case gives a no.
arxiv-2510-25078:
Jihye Hwang leads a team with twenty nine co-authors who map magnet fields in a huge star birth zone known as G35. Polar dust glow from the ALMA array gives the field's lay and strength. The zone is a long thread with six bright cores laid on its long line.

Field strength in the zone spans a wide range, with most parts too weak to hold back fall in by mass, while cores can be past that line. A speed grade runs on the thread's long line, in step with the field's lay at small scales. At large scales, the field lines sit cross wise to the thread. That flip marks where mass drag bends the field.
arxiv-2510-25378:
Junichiro Niimi studies hallucinated citations from language models. His 2025 paper concerns bibliographic recommendation for research papers. Models sometimes invent papers that do not exist. That problem harms trust in model assistance. He asks why some references come out correctly. Memory versus generation may explain the difference.

Highly cited papers appear more often in training data. Citation count can proxy that repeated exposure. Niimi used GPT-4.1 for his tests here. It generated one hundred bibliographic records for checking. Records covered twenty computer science domains in total. Hallucination rates varied across research domains strongly. Citation count correlated strongly with factual quality. Beyond roughly one thousand citations, records became memorized. That suggests a threshold between generalization and memorization.
arxiv-2510-25478:
Shiwei Zhu led four co-authors on magnetic bimerons. Moritz A Goerzen, Changsheng Song, and Stefan Heinze helped. Dongzhe Li closes the five-author team. Their 2025 physics paper calculates lifetimes of higher-order bimerons. They resemble skyrmions. Most studies focused on low topological charge solitons.

Ring-like high-charge bimerons are fundamentally more stable, they find. Their system is a van der Waals interface material. Lifetimes of high-charge bimerons can exceed low-charge ones hugely. The excess reaches three orders of magnitude in calculations. That trend holds even extrapolated to room temperature. Entropy dominates lifetimes rather than energy barriers there. High-charge skyrmions behave oppositely near room temperature. Their lifetimes fall as charge grows in magnitude. Distinct magnetic texture symmetries explain the difference.
arxiv-2510-25578:
Mrinal Kanti Bose and Abhay Kumar Singh construct linear codes with few weights. Their 2025 mathematics paper derives weight distributions completely. Linear codes with few weights have many applications. Secret sharing and authentication codes use them. Association schemes and strongly regular graphs also apply. They construct two distinct classes of p-ary codes.

Specific defining sets select the code constructions. Weight distributions are determined through Weil sum calculations. Detailed calculations on those sums give each distribution. Constructed codes have only few nonzero weights. Two, four, six, eight, and nine weights occur. Different cases produce different weight counts there. An infinite family of two-weight codes is obtained. Those codes are optimal regarding the Griesmer bound. Some newly constructed codes are minimal under conditions. Minimal codes have special support properties in coding theory. Their constructions expand available few-weight code families. Applications in cryptography and combinatorics may use them.
arxiv-2510-26278:
Kim Yong Tan, Yueming Lyu, Ivor Tsang, and Yew-Soon Ong present a method to make diffusion models generate samples that satisfy several goals at once. Diffusion models learn complex data patterns and are now used for high dimensional black box tuning, where the goal can only be evaluated, not worked out by calculus. Prior methods bolt an external optimizer, such as an evolution style loop, onto the model and treat generation as a black box refiner.

Their Inference time Multi target Generation algorithm instead works inside the generation process. Weighted re picking during diffusion, guided by expected combined goal values, steers samples toward a desired multi target Boltzmann pattern, a probability law that favors high goal values. They also derive a log chance score reading of that target pattern.
arxiv-2510-26678:
Friederike Ihssen, Renzo Kapust, and Jan M Pawlowski build a generative sampler for lattice field theories. Monte Carlo sampling is the workhorse for such theories, but generative models often fail outside their training domain. Their design learns the flow layer by layer, with each layer optimised on its own.

Ihssen and her two co-authors use physics-informed renormalisation group flows, which give the step between layers as a simple first-order differential equation for a kernel. Since those equations are known analytically, the kernels can be refined step by step rather than learned blind. That structure is meant to tackle out-of-domain trouble head-on. Simulations in scalar field theories show the architecture works in practice, and the authors see room for further optimisation.
arxiv-2510-26878:
Mikael Chala, Andrii Dashko, and Guilherme Guedes track how couplings run in a high-temperature effective theory. The three-dimensional effective theory describes the thermally driven electroweak phase transition of the Higgs field. How its parameters evolve with scale, their running, shapes predictions for that transition.

Chala and his two co-authors compute the two-loop running of the theory's couplings for two cases. One has a barrier present at tree level. The other has one generated radiatively by physics beyond the Standard Model. They include the leading nonrenormalizable terms. By comparing the new contributions to the beta functions with the simpler renormalizable case, they show the impact on the scalar potential that encodes the vacuum structure. The work sets up tests of these effects on phase transition dynamics in lattice simulations.
arxiv-2510-26978:
Anam Fatima, Yi Yu, Janak Kapuriya, Julien Lalanne, and Jainendra Shukla build a system that writes live comments for streaming video. On platforms like Twitch, fast chat keeps viewers engaged, but writing fitting comments on the fly is hard. Video streams carry much extra content, and older methods often ignore which frames matter most for the current chat.

Their model, SFAT, weights frames by how well they match the ongoing talk, using a vision-language tool to link images and words. A decoder then blends chat and video cues to write each comment. The team also built a large English dataset from Twitch covering eleven categories, with hundreds of hours and millions of comments, and show their model beats prior methods.
arxiv-2510-27278:
Alberto Enciso and Marc Nualart describe how stably stratified shear flows damp disturbances without viscosity. The Boussinesq equations govern buoyancy-driven flows where density varies with height, and the setting is a periodic channel with monotone shear. Using the limiting absorption principle, the pair obtain precise descriptions of inviscid damping for both velocity and density perturbations.

Decay rates depend on the local Richardson number, a ratio of stratification strength to shear, and split into four regimes: non-stratified, weak, mild, and strong. Thresholds in that number mark qualitative changes in the Green function structure. The estimates then yield quantitative sub-linear growth bounds for vorticity and density gradient. As a byproduct, the linearized operator spectrum proves purely continuous under mild hypotheses on the equilibrium profile.
arxiv-2510-27478:
Chatum Sankalpa, Ghulam Mohy-ud-din, and two other co-authors help home energy pools bid in power markets, in a 2025 paper. Aggregators bundle rooftop solar panels and home batteries from many houses into one market player. Sun and demand are unsure, so bids can misfire. Their arena is the Australian National Electricity Market, which also pays for regulation services that steady the grid.

They compare three two-stage planning methods under uncertainty: risk-neutral, robust, and chance-constrained. Each plans day-ahead bids, then adjusts as facts arrive, using the battery's flexibility. Battery charge dynamics and its charge-or-discharge rule are modeled in full. Scenario methods and affine recourse policies, simple linear adjustment rules, keep the math solvable. Across varied cases, the methods cut risk and lifted profit while keeping the plans feasible.
arxiv-2511-00378:
Yongyang Cai reviews how integrated assessment models handle uncertainty. These models link climate science, economics, and policy to test how human activity and the climate system affect each other, and officials rely on them when weighing climate strategies. Both halves of the system, the physical climate and social behavior, carry deep uncertainties that can swing the advice a model gives.

The review sorts the kinds of uncertainty these models face and surveys the modeling approaches used to manage them. It highlights recent methodological advances, including newer computational methods, and traces what they imply for policy. For model builders and policy readers alike, the overview maps where confidence is earned and where caution is due.
arxiv-2511-00478:
Robert Anderson, Haosui Duanmu, M Ali Khan, and Metin Uyanik prove that competitive markets with harmful byproducts can still reach equilibrium. Their setting is a measure-theoretic general equilibrium model, the benchmark formal picture of perfect competition, enriched with production, bads such as emissions that harm agents, and wide-ranging externalities. A famous counterexample by Hara had shown equilibrium can fail once bads enter, leaving a foundational gap.

When bads and externalities are modeled in an economically natural way, the authors show, equilibrium exists after all. Their result is the first existence theorem with bads for this class of models. The proof leans on nonstandard analysis, which supplies a systematic bridge from finite economies to infinite ones, a technique with reach beyond this problem.
arxiv-2511-00578:
Krishna Tewary, Sanjoy Biswas, and Shivam Verma explore a portal extension of the standard model built around a heavy vector-like lepton, and ask what a future multi-TeV muon collider would see. The hunting ground is associated production: a Higgs boson created together with a vector boson, either the familiar Z or a dark photon, the messenger of a hidden sector.

Producing a Higgs with a Z stays close to the standard prediction across wide parameter ranges. Producing one with a dark photon can surge instead, because the heavy lepton's interaction does not decouple. The dark channel can dwarf the Z channel by up to a hundredfold within safe theory limits. A detailed analysis of the bottom-quark plus missing-energy signature sets exclusion reach for the dark photon's mass and coupling, tied also to dark matter and muon measurements.
arxiv-2511-00878:
Ahmed Magbool, Vaibhav Kumar, Marco Di Renzo, and Mark Flanagan propose a stacked flexible intelligent metasurface for future wireless networks. A metasurface is a sheet of tiny elements that can shape radio waves. Stacking several sheets lets the system process signals in the wave domain itself.

Their new element is flexibility: each layer can be physically morphed, bent into a better shape for the channel at hand. They build transmit, receive, and channel models, then pose the task of maximizing the total data rate under power, morphing distance, and element response limits. An alternating optimization method based on gradient projection solves it, and simulations show clear gains over the rigid stacked version.
arxiv-2511-01078:
Qinwei Huang and colleagues add predictive side tasks to multi agent reinforcement learning, where several agents must cooperate while seeing only part of the world. Most systems train policies from reward alone, even though observations, messages, and other agents' behavior carry useful signal.

Their framework, BEPAL, trains each agent's policy alongside a belief model that predicts hidden state information, such as other agents' rewards or directions of motion. Training is centralized while execution stays decentralized. The extra prediction work enriches the agents' internal representations and steadies learning. On a predator prey task and on Google Research Football, BEPAL improved performance metrics by about sixteen percent on average and converged more stably than baselines.
arxiv-2511-01178:
Ming Tang and colleagues release BzScope, a Python package that computes absolute cross sections for neutron phonon scattering in crystal powders. Such calculations predict how neutrons bounce off the vibrations of a crystal lattice, and older histogramming methods struggle to reproduce sharp features and to converge over large ranges of momentum and energy.

BzScope uses an adapted integral method for one and two phonon scattering in ideal powders, staying numerically robust out to very large momentum transfer. Higher order scattering is handled through an established thermal neutron package, NCrystal, with a plugin for Monte Carlo codes. Benchmarks against nickel, lithium hydride, and beryllium readings confirm it works, and it improves accuracy for low symmetry materials by avoiding an isotropic shortcut.
arxiv-2511-01278:
Takashi Tsuboi studies bounded domains: the shapes of compact, connected three dimensional solids in ordinary Euclidean space whose boundary is one smooth connected surface. Because every such surface bounds a unique solid, the objects match compact connected surfaces, and the question is how to recognize their shapes.

Tsuboi projects the solid onto lines and studies the Reeb graphs of those height functions, summaries that track how the level sets connect and split, for both the solid and its boundary. He introduces weighted and indexed versions of those graphs. When the weights stay below a stated threshold, the solid can be deformed by isotopy into an embedded handlebody. The work is driven by a visibility question: can the solid be reshaped so every boundary point sees infinity along some ray?
arxiv-2511-01778:
Richard Evans, Max Felland, Susanna Evans, and Lindsey Sloan test a shortcut in medical statistics: letting chatbots draft the prior distributions that Bayesian analysis needs. Priors are usually elicited from busy specialists, a slow and unreliable process. Here the test case is survival in glioblastoma, an aggressive brain cancer, comparing two therapies through their hazard ratio.

Three chatbots each proposed two alternative priors for a standard Bayesian survival model fitted to real data. A radiation oncologist evaluated the proposals, and the priors were then used in a sensitivity analysis to check how much the conclusions moved. For this analysis, the AI-generated priors looked sensible and held up as a preferred alternative to expert elicitation, suggesting generative AI can safely speed up a tedious step of trial analysis.
arxiv-2511-02078:
Jessica Alessandrì and Laura Paladino work on a local-global question for elliptic curves: if a point can be divided by a prime power everywhere locally, can it be divided globally? For division by a prime itself the answer is known to be yes, but for higher powers counterexamples exist. Whether the Hasse principle holds depends on the curve, the number field, and the Galois group of the field obtained by adding the relevant torsion points.

The cases of the first two powers were settled earlier. For higher powers, the authors give conditions on the generators of that Galois group that guarantee the principle holds. They prove the conditions are necessary by building counterexamples when the conditions fail, extending a known result for the second power.
arxiv-2511-02178:
Matthew Graham and nineteen co-authors report the most powerful flare ever seen from a feeding supermassive black hole. Active galactic nuclei flicker as gas spirals into them, but this source, an AGN with the catalogue name J224554.84+374326.5, brightened by more than a factor of forty in 2018 and has been fading slowly ever since. Its total ultraviolet and optical output so far equals converting roughly a whole solar mass directly into light.

The flare outshines the previous record holder thirty times over, and very few events in the universe can release that much electromagnetic energy. The authors weigh candidate causes: a massive star torn apart by tides, gravitational lensing of a smaller flare or supernova, or an enormous supernova inside the accretion disk. They favour the tidal disruption of a star heavier than thirty suns, orbiting in the same direction the disk rotates.
arxiv-2511-02378:
Riccardo Bovo, Daniele Giunchi, Pasquale Cascarano, Eric Gonzalez, and Mar Gonzalez-Franco revive a classic idea from early human-computer interaction for modern mixed reality headsets. Richard Bolt's Put-That-There let users move things by saying so while pointing. This system pairs that concept with a large language model and a semantically segmented three-dimensional model of the room. It also uses live application metadata, and the user's speech, pointing, and head gaze.

The model turns those cues into structured window-placement commands for a panoramic workspace. Users can give explicit instructions naming an app and a surface, use deictic speech with a gesture. Or they can state a goal and let the system infer which applications are relevant and how to lay them out. One request can move several windows at once, and the relationships between tools feed the layout decisions, removing manual window juggling in immersive environments.
arxiv-2511-03478:
Jeongah Lee and Ali Sarvghad test whether breaking floor plans into vector parts helps large multimodal models read them. Such models still stumble on spatial reasoning even as their general vision improves. Floor plans make a stern test, mixing geometry, layout links, and room meaning in one drawing.

Seventy-five plans were shown to three leading models as plain images, as vector code, or as both together. Pairing vector structure with the raster image lifted comprehension scores over either input alone. Reliable plan reading could power tools that describe buildings aloud for blind and low-vision users. The study suggests structure, not just pixels, is what models lack for spatial tasks.
arxiv-2511-03578:
Mainak Singha presents a neural equation solver that cannot break the physical laws it models. Standard neural solvers often invent mass, drift shocks wrongly, or violate entropy rules while fitting data well. Constraint-Projected Learning forces every training update back onto the set of physically allowed states.

The allowed set joins conservation, shock balance, entropy, and positivity demands, and the projection step still allows gradient training at small extra cost. Extra damping calms tiny oscillations, while a staged rollout teaches long-horizon steadiness. Tests target flows where law-breaking is easiest to spot. Solvers that respect hard laws by construction could be trusted in engineering settings where a pretty but impossible answer is dangerous.
arxiv-2511-03978:
Ramsey L Karim is the lead author among eighteen authors characterising the Eagle Nebula region M16 with SOFIA FEEDBACK observations of the ionized carbon line and molecular data. Massive stars in the NGC 6611 cluster power the region and have blown at least two cavities into the parent molecular cloud.

Spectra resolve an expanding photodissociation shell toward the small N19 bubble and traces of a thin, fragmented shell toward M16. Data span cold molecular gas, warm photoionized gas, and million-degree plasma. Winds carved a cavity about twenty parsecs in radius. More than ninety percent of the mechanical wind energy escaped through breaches in the shell, limiting how strongly feedback couples to the cloud.
arxiv-2511-04078:
Zehui Feng is the lead author among seven authors on Bratrix, a framework that aligns brain signals with vision through language. Reading visual meaning from EEG, MEG, or fMRI is hard because subjects vary and visual features tangle, and aligning neural activity straight to image embeddings misses hidden semantic layers.

Bratrix splits stimuli into layered visual and language parts, then projects visual and brain representations into a shared space set by language. An uncertainty module weights alignment to handle noisy neural signals, like human perceptual trust. Two-stage training, single-mode pretraining then multimodal fine-tuning, improves precision in its tests on vision-brain alignment.
arxiv-2511-04278:
Yu Ling, Florent Pawula, Ramzy Daou, Benoit Fauque, and Kamran Behnia report careful cold transport measurements on ruthenium dioxide, a metallic oxide drawing intense recent interest. Electric resistivity follows a quadratic temperature law below about twenty kelvin, a Fermi liquid mark missed in earlier transport studies of this compound.

The quadratic prefactor matches Kadowaki-Woods scaling given the electronic specific heat, and it barely varies across four samples whose residual resistivity spans eightfold. Heat flow, split into electronic and phononic parts by field, obeys the Wiedemann-Franz law at zero temperature. A threefold mismatch between thermal and electric quadratic prefactors remains, framing ruthenium dioxide as a weakly correlated Fermi liquid.
arxiv-2511-04578:
Tiphaine Kouadou leads fourteen authors presenting wideband homodyne detectors for squeezed light. Homodyne detection reads the phase of light and characterizes continuous-variable quantum states. It works at room temperature, a practical plus for quantum information systems.

Standard detectors, though, often fail at high pulse rates due to electronic limits. The new detectors run at near-infrared and telecom wavelengths, optimized for rates up to one hundred fifty megahertz. They resolve the pulse-by-pulse structure of squeezed states at telecom wavelengths. Fast, steady detection like this is a building block for high-speed quantum communication and computing.
arxiv-2511-04678:
Yihong Sun and three colleagues define a new tracking task: following objects through transformations. Real objects get cut, melted, hatched, and reshaped, and trackers usually lose them. Appearance can change so much that the target seems to vanish.

Their Track Any State task asks systems to keep tracking while naming each state change. A new benchmark, VOST-TAS, supports the task with labeled examples. Their zero-shot system, TubeletGraph, recovers objects that other methods overlook after a change. It also maps how object states evolve over time, a step toward video tools that understand processes, not just positions.
arxiv-2511-05078:
Manan Sharma and co-authors tackle claim normalization for social media posts in many languages, as part of the CheckThat! work. The task turns noisy posts into clear claims that a checker can verify, here across 20 languages.

Their method breaks each post down with who, what, where, when, why, and how questions, which aids transfer across languages though training used English only. They fine-tuned a Qwen model with added ranked examples at run time. Scores were strongest for English and fell for some other languages, which shows the gap that cross-language work still faces.
arxiv-2511-05178:
Martin Siron and co-authors present LeMat-Bulk, a merged data set that joins three big quantum chemistry stores for materials. Fast growth in such stores aids machine-led discovery, but overlap and clashing formats make joint use hard.

LeMat-Bulk spans more than five million materials computed with one main method, plus the largest sets for two other methods. The team set one standard form and coined a hashing trick, the Bonding Algorithm Weisfeiller-Lehman, to spot copies. Tests of that hash check how well it keeps true matches while it drops exact repeats.
arxiv-2511-05278:
Hendrik Schrautzer and co-authors compute how long skyrmions and antiskyrmions live when higher-order exchange is taken into account. Skyrmions are small magnetic swirls eyed for spin devices, and their lifetime sets whether a device can hold data.

Their atom model at metal interfaces keeps all fourth-order exchange terms. With harmonic transition-state theory, they weigh both energy and entropy parts of the decay. The four-spin term raises the barrier a lot, so lifetimes grow by a large margin. The result says terms often dropped from models can decide if a skyrmion lasts.
arxiv-2511-05678:
Slobodan Simić studies the Livšic equation for a special kind of chaotic flow called an Anosov flow. Such flows stretch and squeeze space in a structured way on a closed manifold. The question is when the equation, which involves the flow's generator acting on differential forms, has a solution, and whether that solution is unique.

For flows meeting an asymmetry condition, Simić proves a unique continuous solution exists in middle degrees. Intuitively, the condition says volumes shrink fast backward in time along certain directions. He then applies the result to volume-preserving flows. There, exact forms lie in the closure of the generator's image exactly when certain bundles fit together uniquely, which forces the flow into a known form.
arxiv-2511-06478:
Murat Uzundag and colleagues observe the only known pulsating DAQ white dwarf, a merged star with a carbon and hydrogen atmosphere. Its odd composition and motion point to an origin in a white dwarf merger. Time-series photometry from three large telescopes tracked how its brightness pulses change over time.

Ten recurring pulsation peaks appeared across observing runs, with frequencies matching non-radial gravity-mode oscillations. New evolutionary models built for this rare class give a mass slightly above the Sun's and a cooling age near one point seven billion years for a carbon-oxygen core. Full asteroseismology must wait for more consistent models, and the authors call for multi-site campaigns to sharpen the signal.
arxiv-2511-06778:
Ruiheng Liu and five co-authors address a security risk in systems that let people query databases in plain language. Large language models power these interfaces, but they can leak confidential database contents or be tricked by crafted questions into giving data away. Current rule-based guards miss subtle inference attacks and block too many honest queries.

Their system, SafeNLIDB, trains models on automatically generated examples that mix hidden security reasoning with query writing, so no hand-labeled preference data is needed. New training steps, including a reasoning warm-up and alternating preference optimization, steady the learning process. In tests the system beat larger models and ideal-setting baselines on security while keeping query accuracy high.
arxiv-2511-07478:
Ruide Fu advances the local Langlands program for tori, the simplest group case of a deep number theory correspondence. For a torus, the parameter stack has a Picard structure, meaning its symmetries organize like an abelian group stack. Fu computes that structure explicitly.

The Picard dual is determined, and the Fourier-Mukai transform then yields an integral categorical form of the correspondence. A geometric version follows, whose categorical trace recovers the first result. The work settles a conjecture raised by Zhu. Though specialized, the torus case tests categorical Langlands ideas in a setting where every step can be checked completely.
arxiv-2511-07578:
Avishai Dekel, Dhruba Dutta Chowdhury, and Sharon Lapiner explain the Little Red Dots, compact red systems Webb found in the early universe. These galaxies look small yet host black holes that seem too heavy. The authors trace them to an earlier phase of feedback-free starbursts in thousands of star clusters.

After the bursts, wet compaction squeezes the galaxy while clusters sink inward. Two-body segregation and friction against the disk drag stars and black holes to the center, where clusters merge into a dense core. Young rotating clusters also seed black holes quickly. The chain turns ordinary cluster formation into the odd red dots observed.
arxiv-2511-07878:
Shihao Li, Jiachen Li, and Jiamin Xu ask what makes a practice trajectory valuable, and find the answer depends on the algorithm watching it. Using Shapley-style valuation inside an uncertain linear control problem, trajectories with strong excitation look worse under plain REINFORCE training, a negative correlation near zero point four in magnitude.

A variance mechanism explains the flip. Strong excitation lowers gradient variance, but near saddle points higher variance helps escape, raising a trajectory worth. Stabilizers such as whitening or Fisher preconditioning kill that channel and the correlation turns positive. Data valuation for control must therefore name its algorithm, not pretend worth is universal.
arxiv-2511-08278:
Chen Zhao, Haobo Jia, and Zhuqing Jia characterize the fundamental limits of robust dynamic coded distributed storage when some servers have restricted space. Coded storage spreads data so reads and updates survive server dropouts, at some communication cost. Here a subset of servers can hold only a small fraction of the message, tightening the design space beyond earlier partially constrained results.

New converse arguments and new coding designs meet, completely pinning down the minimum number of available servers needed for a feasible update. Minimum communication costs for reading and updating follow across dropout scenarios. The work extends prior converse and achievability results into a full characterization of this storage regime.
arxiv-2511-08478:
Diego Rogel Rodriguez and co-authors characterize a two dimensional mixture of active and passive Brownian particles, mapping its phases and long time motion. State diagrams at several passive concentrations show how the two species influence each other. Passive particles tend to hinder phase separation, while active particles force crystal like ordering onto the passive colloids around them, a one way imprint of activity onto quiet matter.

Long time diffusion coefficients reveal active particles inducing activity and super diffusive behavior in the passive ones. At the density where motility induced phase separation begins, active diffusivity shows an inflection point and passive diffusivity peaks. Displacement distributions confirm the change comes from altered active particle dynamics at that threshold.
arxiv-2511-08578:
Katherine Freese and six co-authors propose a route to the first supermassive black holes that starts with dark stars, early stars powered by dark matter rather than fusion. As such a star keeps pulling in matter, they show, it can grow from about ten thousand to about ten million times the mass of the Sun.

At that size a relativistic instability makes the star collapse directly into a black hole. Because dark stars skip the normal nuclear burning that ends ordinary stellar lives, they survive long enough to reach that size. The authors find the outcome barely depends on starting mass, birth time, or feeding rate. These black holes could then seed the billion-solar-mass giants already seen in the early universe.
arxiv-2511-08678:
Heather Samonski, Samir Salim, and John Salzer hunt for Green Peas, compact galaxies blazing with extreme emission lines, without waiting for spectra. Known Peas turned up mostly by luck in spectroscopic surveys, so a large hidden population may be missed, and finding it would sharpen comparisons with young galaxies in the early universe.

The hard part is contamination: stars and quasars share the Peas' colors. Their solution matches spectral energy distributions using survey photometry from confirmed stars, quasars, and galaxies, reaching eighty-five percent effectiveness with about ten percent contamination. The method yields catalogs with more than eight thousand new candidates nearby, ten times what spectra alone would give. Some are bright, many promise enormous line strengths, and a new extended class may be merging systems.
arxiv-2511-08878:
Andrea Cavallo and three co-authors design an untrained deep network that reads the covariance structure of data the way wavelets read a signal. Covariance methods are everywhere in unsupervised learning, yet the classic tool, principal component analysis, misses low-variance directions and wobbles when samples are few and eigenvalues sit close together.

Covariance Scattering Transforms apply filters tuned to specific bands of the covariance spectrum, layer by layer, with nonlinearities in between, building hierarchical representations without any training. A pruning step keeps memory and compute in check. The authors prove the finite-sample error is less sensitive to close eigenvalues than PCA's, and tests on cortical thickness data from four neurodegenerative disease cohorts bear that out. Age predictions match or beat heavier learned models, especially when data is scarce.
arxiv-2511-09078:
K. Hagino reviews how heavy-ion collisions reveal the shapes of atomic nuclei, treating the reactions themselves as a probe. Nuclei are rarely perfect spheres, and their deformations steer what happens when two of them meet at energies near the Coulomb barrier.

The single-channel story starts with the optical potential model, including microscopic modeling of its imaginary part and a visualization of quantum interference in elastic scattering. Multi-channel problems follow, where fusion reactions near the barrier prove exquisitely sensitive to the colliding nuclei's shapes, making fusion a powerful shape measurement. Hagino closes by pointing out deep similarities between these low-energy reactions and relativistic heavy-ion collisions in how shape dynamics plays out. The review emphasizes viewpoint: one physics, read through the geometry of the participants.
arxiv-2511-09278:
Jian-Min Wang and nine co-authors propose an origin for JWST's mysterious 'little red dots'. They suggest these early-universe objects are embryos of active galactic nuclei. These compact red objects look like a chimera of galaxy and active nucleus, and their nature is debated. The model places a modest central black hole inside each one.

In their picture, many stellar-mass black holes sit embedded in the central accretion disk, outweighing the central hole itself. Accretion onto those small holes powers the optical light, while the disk and nuclear starbursts supply the ultraviolet. Radiation pressure drives clumpy outflows that explain the observed Balmer absorption features. The structure forms, they argue, from collapsing primordial clouds.
arxiv-2511-09578:
Hadi Keramati, Morteza Sadeghi, and Rajeev K. Jaiman generate heat sink designs with a diffusion model steered by physics surrogates. Cooling electronics means minimizing pressure drop while keeping surface temperatures under a limit, a classic design trade-off. Their shapes are described by boundary representations of multiple fins, with training data from a multi-tier pipeline.

Two residual networks predict pressure drop and surface temperature for any proposed design. During generation, gradients from those surrogates push the diffusion process toward designs meeting both goals. The resulting samples reach pressure drops up to ten percent below what classic black-box optimization achieved, the authors report. Once trained, the generator answers new temperature constraints cheaply, without retraining or fresh topology work.
arxiv-2511-09678:
Cameron Crabb and six co-authors track how a cobalt-nickel superalloy's protective oxide skin rebuilds itself over a thousand hours in hot air. Such alloys serve in extreme engines, and long-term survival depends on the oxide scale's evolution. Samples were oxidized at eight hundred degrees Celsius for twenty, one hundred, and one thousand hours.

Mass gain, interferometry, electron microscopy, atom probe tomography, and diffraction together chart the transformation. Early nickel oxide and spinel layers, initially porous, gradually give way to a compact dual scale of chromia and alumina. Oxidation kinetics shift from near-linear to parabolic once that continuous scale forms, signaling diffusion-controlled growth. The dense, adherent scale is what protects the alloy long term, they conclude.
arxiv-2511-09778:
Sally Dawson, Arnab Roy, and German Valencia explore how the High-Luminosity LHC could reveal new invisible particles through Higgs boson decays. In their scenario the Higgs splits into a visible part and an invisible part, a semi-visible decay whose motion patterns carry information about the hidden particles. The setup could expose scalar and fermion particles with masses below about fifty GeV.

The analysis works inside a dark effective theory with a symmetry that keeps the new particles odd and ordinary ones even. Using both simple cuts and a boosted decision tree, the authors gauge the collider's reach and compare it with limits from the invisible Z width and from unitarity arguments. They also outline motion-based strategies to tell different interaction structures apart.
arxiv-2511-10678:
Tamas Almos Vami describes the Light Dark Matter eXperiment, a proposed fixed-target experiment at SLAC. It is designed to find dark matter far lighter than collider searches can reach. The Large Hadron Collider covers masses from about 1 to 10,000 GeV, but thermal dark matter models strongly motivate the largely unexplored range below 1 GeV.

LDMX would fire 8 GeV electrons from the LCLS-II beamline at a target and look for missing momentum and missing energy, the signature of dark matter particles carrying energy away unseen. Vami details the detector design and the analysis strategy, including calorimeter vetoes against ordinary processes. He also covers machine learning tools such as boosted decision trees and graph neural networks for separating signal from background.
arxiv-2511-11078:
Youssef Haouchat, Sepand Kashani, and their colleagues present SplineSplat, a method for computing scan views of a 3D volume built from smooth spline bumps. Medical and scientific tomography rebuilds a volume from many flat views, so fast and exact view math matters. Blocky voxel grids are the usual base, but they can blur fine detail.

Their ray-tracing method computes line sums through the spline volume for any scanner layout. A small neural network speeds up the share that each bump adds along a ray. In tests where data were ample for an exact rebuild, their method gave higher quality than voxel-based routes, which favors splines as a volume base.
arxiv-2511-11478:
Nhat Chung, Taisei Hanyu, and their colleagues introduce LIBERO-Mem, a task suite that stress-tests robot manipulation when the right move depends on object history, not just the current view. Robots in sequenced tasks meet visually similar objects, and key cues hide in what was touched, moved, or changed earlier. Policies without persistent object memory repeat finished steps or skip needed ones in such non-Markovian settings.

The suite mixes short- and long-horizon object tracking with timed subgoals that demand reasoning past the current frame. Their Embodied-SlotSSM framework answers with slot-based vision-language-action control: it keeps stable slot identities for objects over space and time, built for temporal scalability where token counts otherwise explode.
arxiv-2511-11678:
Yuze Liu and seven co-authors propose Co-PLMs, a framework for training large language models in the cloud together with small language models on edge devices. Cloud servers alone struggle with heavy real-time workloads and privacy limits, so pairing them with on-device models is attractive, if the two can actually learn together.

Different small models have different architectures, which blocks ordinary joint training. Distilled proxy models act as bridges, letting knowledge move between unlike models in a structure-agnostic mutual learning process. The consortium idea targets better inference for intelligent applications without shipping private user data to distant servers for every request.
arxiv-2511-11778:
Byoungjun Park and three co-authors present CATCHFed, a semi-supervised federated learning method for the common case where ordinary clients hold no labels at all and only the server owns a labeled set. Performance of earlier methods collapses as labeled data shrinks, exactly when unlabeled client data should help most.

Client-aware adaptive thresholds adjust for class difficulty, hybrid thresholds improve pseudo-label quality, and even unlabeled examples without pseudo-labels contribute through consistency regularization. Extensive tests across datasets and setups show stronger results than prior approaches. Hospitals, banks, and phone fleets all share this label-scarce shape, so robust methods widen where federated learning can honestly be used.
arxiv-2511-11878:
Fernanda Bufon Färber and five co-authors release MedPT, a large medical question answering dataset built from real patient-doctor interactions in Brazilian Portuguese. Language models for health care are trained mostly on high-resource languages, and translation misses local clinical and cultural detail, including endemic diseases.

The corpus holds three hundred eighty-four thousand ninety-five authentic question-answer pairs covering more than three thousand two hundred conditions. A multi-stage curation protocol filtered noise and enriched thousands of ambiguous questions with context. As the first resource of its scale for Brazilian Portuguese medicine, MedPT lets researchers train and test health assistants that speak the language patients actually use.
arxiv-2511-12278:
Mingqi Wu, Qiang Sun and Yi Yang introduce PCA-plus-plus, a method for finding a shared signal hidden in high-dimensional data with strong structured background noise. Classic principal component analysis can fail when that background dominates. Contrastive learning offers a clue: paired observations share the same signal but differ in background.

A baseline that aligns pairs only works when background variation is mild.
