Across three decoder-only multilingual language models, translation function vectors from a single English-to-X direction transfer to other target languages, consistently improving the rank of correct translation tokens across multiple unseen languages.
arxiv-2604-19778: Nyalang and Debbarma present KokborokMT, a neural translation system for Kokborok, a Tibeto-Burman language spoken mainly in Tripura, India by about 1.5 million people. Despite its status as an official Tripura language, Kokborok has stayed severely under-resourced, with earlier systems trained on small Bible-derived corpora scoring below 7 on the BLEU scale. The team fine-tunes the NLLB-200-distilled-600M model on a multi-source parallel corpus of 36,052 sentence pairs, mixing professionally translated, Bible-domain, and synthetic back-translated material.
arxiv-2604-19878: Traficante and eleven colleagues studied how gas clumps split into star-forming cores in 30Dor-10, a busy star-forming zone in the Large Magellanic Cloud. Their views resolve scales near 2000 astronomical units, fine enough to weigh single cores. The core mass pattern matches the classic Salpeter slope also seen in star masses. This is the first such test beyond our galaxy, and it points to later evolution, not the first split, as the source of star-mass differences.
arxiv-2604-20578: Bal shows that edge flip splits the Hashimoto map on edges into even and odd parts, giving a 2 by 2 block form. A Schur step factors the Ihara determinant into a line-graph factor times a second factor from those sectors. Although the mixed block depends on edge direction, its gauge-invariant shadows form a matrix package. Bal shows uneven non-isomorphic graphs that are adjacency-cospectral and line-graph-cospectral yet split by the correction sector. Further cases show mixed shadows splitting graphs even when the Ihara polynomial does not.
arxiv-2604-20678: Yokoyama and five colleagues study alignment fading in mixed-length rod suspensions after flow stops. The team sheared cellulose nanocrystal suspensions and tracked birefringence fading after flow stopped. Average alignment fading time falls with rising pre-shear rate. Grouped by Péclet number, data agree with theory over a shear-rate range. That trend arises because the rods shaping alignment most shift from longer to shorter rods as pre-shear rate rises. In mixed-length systems, fading time is set by flow conditions and spread, not by material alone.
arxiv-2604-20878: Zhou and Zhang introduce AITP, a multimodal large language model for assigning blame in traffic accidents. AITP sharpens reasoning with a Multimodal Chain-of-Thought method and adds legal knowledge via Retrieval-Augmented Generation. They also present DecaTARA, a ten-task benchmark that joins ten related traffic accident reasoning tasks with 67,941 annotated videos and 195,821 question-answer pairs. Tests show AITP leads the field across blame calls, crash detection, and crash understanding.
arxiv-2604-21678: Osinski and Wilson study fragments of class-sized logic, where statements may range over proper classes rather than only sets. In unrestricted class logics, key model-theoretic properties fail. The authors ban certain mixes of infinitary quantifiers and boolean connectives, and show the restricted setting behaves far better. Its compactness and Löwenheim-Skolem properties characterise large cardinals, including Weak Vopěnka's Principle, Ord is Woodin, and Shelah cardinals.
arxiv-2604-21778: Ovsiannikov and three colleagues present a fast, memory-efficient numerical method for the time-dependent unitary Tavis-Cummings model, where a multilevel spin system interacts with a cavity mode beyond the rotating-wave approximation. A change of basis by pure re-indexing brings the model into tri-diagonal form. Truncating the cavity Fock basis then makes cost linear in total system size, in both time and memory. The method suits any closed quantum system whose Hamiltonian terms can be made tri-diagonal.
arxiv-2604-21878: Barbini, Sorrentino, and Gatica-Perez propose Gradual Voluntary Participation, a framework for AI governance in journalism. Participatory design assumes users can shape tech, but AI systems resist influence through opaque data, fixed designs, and hidden goals. Talking to 10 journalists reveals a gap: trust in AI depends on feeling able to act within routines. The framework treats gradual and voluntary steps as design dimensions. It maps people involved by depth and scope in a two-way matrix. It addresses burdens, caps on who can take part, and show-only consultations.
arxiv-2604-22278: Batra, Joaquim, Prajapati and Srivastava build a particle-physics framework to explain the ATOMKI anomaly, odd features in certain nuclear transitions. Those features hint at a new boson near 17 MeV. Their chiral, flavour-specific U(1)X extension of the Standard Model makes its Z-prime boson play that role. A two-Higgs-doublet setup generates the needed axial-vector couplings while cancelling anomalies and generating fermion masses. For beryllium-8 and helium-4 signals, the viable space also survives atomic parity, beam dump, meson decay and neutrino scattering tests.
arxiv-2604-22478: In dense scattering settings, Devanand and Mankar's line-of-sight delay-Doppler estimator beats traditional single-carrier Zadoff-Chu sequences at both delay and Doppler estimation. The tests span a wide range of fading and signal-to-noise values. The win rests on two time-frequency pilot sequences inspired by Zadoff-Chu, chosen for good autocorrelation. A twisted convolution step then reads delay-Doppler straight from the received signal, so no extra transformation to the delay-Doppler domain is needed.
arxiv-2604-22578: Dioguardi Burgio and two colleagues study action representability for 2-nilpotent groups. Derived actions are described through central automorphisms of an object, and which maps into that group define an action. The category is not action representable, and weak representation hinges on amalgamation. Weak representability is proved via a strong amalgam of suitable abelian subgroups of that group. An explicit weak representing object is maps from the abelianization to the center. The category is also not locally algebraically cartesian closed.
arxiv-2604-22678: Chen and three colleagues propose BERAG and BEFT, Bayesian ensemble retrieval-augmented generation and fine-tuning, for knowledge-based visual question answering. The usual retrieval-augmented generation joins documents into one context, hiding each document's role, hurting attribution, causing the lost-in-the-middle effect where key long-context facts are missed. Joining texts scales poorly, with square-law cost growth, worst for visual data. Capping context length can still curb performance by keeping models from using deeper retrieval recall. In BERAG, language models use single retrieved documents.
arxiv-2604-23178: Soumik compares nine debiasing strategies across five judge models, three benchmarks, and four bias types. His headline result: a mid-tier model with apt debiasing beats frontier judges for far less, with Gemini 2.5 Flash plus Combined Budget reaching 71.0 percent agreement. Style bias dominates, favoring markdown over plain prose far above position bias, while verbosity bias splits by model: some favor long answers, Claude favors concise ones, GPT-4o stays neutral. Debiasing lifts several models past strict significance testing, and he releases the framework, a 375-pair dataset, and cached results.
arxiv-2604-23278: Wilson and six colleagues propose active inference as a way to phenotype agency in AI systems, beyond autonomy and goal focus. Their notion needs intentionality from beliefs and desires, rationality fitting a world model, and explainability traceable to states. They cast this as a partly observable Markov decision process under variational inference. In a T-maze test, empowerment, the channel capacity linking actions to likely outcomes, separates agency phenotypes: zero, intermediate, and high. They conclude governance must shift from outside constraints to inside tuning of prior preferences as agents forage.
arxiv-2604-23478: Bellibatlu, Raff, and Zhang ask whether judge models stay consistent when a request is reworded. Their JudgeSense benchmark spans four tasks and twenty-five judges, scoring each judge against its own agreement with itself on identical wording so that sampling noise is not blamed on phrasing. Rewording lowers agreement on every task, the ordinal task proves least stable, and larger models within a family are no steadier.
arxiv-2604-23878: Bering presents ZenBrain, a seven-layer neuroscience architecture for AI agents that unifies fifteen mechanisms under MemoryCoordinator. No system integrates more than two. Fourteen of fifteen ablations look costless under load. But raising decay over 60 days makes nine of fifteen critical, five moving from zero below minus 89 percent. The mechanisms form a cooperative survival network, so mild-load ablation underrates contributions. On LongMemEval-500, ZenBrain wins nine answer comparisons against Letta, Mem0, and A-Mem. It reaches about 91 percent of an oracle's accuracy at one-hundredth the token cost.
arxiv-2604-23978: Xu, Yang, Kirkorian, and Mutlu build a social robot that joins families at home to support school-related talk and activities. Shaped through interviews and joint design work with parents and children, the robot spent a week living with ten families. Parents steered its use in different ways, families wove it into daily routines, and the study surfaces both its promise and its privacy and practical limits for family-school partnership tools.
arxiv-2604-24078: Sussek and Heindorf explain predictions of temporal graph neural networks with Shapley values. One explainer scores single temporal events with KernelSHAP, while a second splits those event scores into feature-level Owen values, exposing layered links between events and their features. Both beat leading explainers on several metrics and datasets. The feature explainer also caught a faulty timestamp extraction in a common TGAT implementation, helping explain drops on very sparse cases.
arxiv-2604-24178: Xu and four colleagues propose Meta-Aligner, a bi-level method that tunes preferences and policy together for multi-objective language model alignment. Fixed weights waste useful trade-off data in training responses that miss the target. A weight network generates adaptive weights from prompts and learns them as parameters, while the policy learns responses under those preferences with rejection sampling. Tests on several multi-objective benchmarks show better results and steadier training than static-weight methods.
arxiv-2604-24378: Reji and four colleagues present pyTANSPEC and HxRGproc for TANSPEC data. TANSPEC, on the 3.6-meter Devasthal telescope, covers visible to near-infrared wavelengths. The pipeline handled only cross-dispersed spectra for two slits. The upgrade reduces spectra from all slits in low-resolution and cross-dispersed modes and adds wavelength and flux calibration. HxRGproc cleans slope images, correcting non-linearity and removing pink noise and cosmic rays. It now works for the H2RG detector on the TANSPEC server, so users receive pre-cleaned data.
arxiv-2604-24478: Tadjuidje, Guo, and Cheng present PersonaFlow, a tool making editable personas from repository artifacts, shown next to issue reports. In a study with 13 open-source developers, most said their understanding shifted. Over half changed responses by adding kind language, shaping explanations, or raising urgency scores. Two pathways emerged: some felt for personas as people, while others used them for triaging. Both led to more user-centered behavior. The authors offer design lessons for persona tools where speed-driven workflows obscure human elements.
arxiv-2604-24578: Chareton and four colleagues lay foundations for checking hybrid quantum programs, which mix classical and quantum control, measurement and data. Quantum programs are hard to test by running them, so proof tools matter. They introduce Hybrid Path-Sums, a symbolic way to hold sets of hybrid quantum-classical states, plus rules for simplifying those states. A core assertion language states program equivalence, state properties, and claims about program odds. It aims to let users state what a program should do and check it without running it.
arxiv-2604-24678: Chand, Nguyen, Kuntz and Pretschner report an industrial case study at BMW on using language models for enterprise domain-specific languages. They adapt code models to generate and modify multi-file DSL artifacts from a single natural-language instruction, encoding folder hierarchies as path-preserving JSON. They test two instruction-tuned code models under baseline prompting, one-shot learning and parameter-efficient fine-tuning. Fine-tuning gives the largest gains, with high exact-match accuracy and strong edit similarity.
arxiv-2604-24978: Choubey and seven colleagues propose a scalable Enterprise Deep Research system for decision-ready reports. Enterprise deep research often fails through uneven coverage, context overload and early stopping. Their system splits requests into coverage goals via outlines with reflection. It localizes context with dependency-guided runs and open information sharing. It sets evidence-based finish rules, so agents keep gathering data until sufficiency rules are met. On an internal sales task and the public DeepResearch Bench test, it beats competitive baselines overall.
arxiv-2604-25478: Khusainov and four colleagues present a shared test frame for neutral-atom code tools. Neutral-atom qubits promise quantum machines, and toolchains matter for moving qubits and side-by-side gates. Test scores hinge on uneven tuning, move models, and fidelity sources, since tools are judged under mismatched rules. Their frame brings RSQASM, a record of mapped, routed, and timed circuits, with side-by-side gates and shuttling. Adapter scripts turn tool outputs into RSQASM. For HybridMapper, DasAtom, and Enola, claimed gaps shrink or vanish once uneven rules are gone.
arxiv-2604-25578: Jiang and seven colleagues build Marco-MoE, a fully open multilingual model family. It spends far less compute by waking only about five percent of its weights for each word. That sparse design, built by reusing dense models, lets training run over five trillion tokens while still beating similar sized rivals on English and multilingual tests. The result is a top performance per compute ratio, and tuned instruct versions push past rivals that wake far more weights.
arxiv-2604-25678: The CMS Collaboration measures eight angular coefficients in Drell-Yan production of muon pairs from proton-proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider. The analysis uses data at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, with a total luminosity of 140 inverse femtobarns. Values are found across eight transverse-momentum ranges and two rapidity ranges, for muon pairs with mass between 81 and 101 GeV. Comparison with next-to-next-to-leading-order quantum chromodynamics predictions clarifies parton dynamics and Z boson production.
arxiv-2604-25778: Ebrahim and Joy ask whether code evaluation metrics, built to assess generated code, can also detect source code plagiarism. They compare five metrics, including CodeBLEU, CrystalBLEU, RUBY, and CodeBERTScore, against dedicated tools JPlag and Dolos, on two labeled datasets across six modification levels. Without preprocessing, Dolos leads overall, while CrystalBLEU, CodeBLEU, and RUBY beat JPlag. After clean-up, CrystalBLEU surpasses Dolos overall. Performance is strongest at the simplest level and drops from level four onward, though CrystalBLEU stays competitive at level six.
arxiv-2604-25978: Maguire and Dasmahapatra show that popular link prediction models can pick up a trivial heuristic that depends on mini-batches. Batch-normalization layers enable it. For a fixed graph, link scores might match node scores when graph traits are shared. That guess fails in general: the trick solves edge sorting from batch stats. Fixing for it lifts fit with node-class traits. The net, it suggests, learns a better graph picture than raw scores imply. Standard link training may thus inflate how general learned pictures are.
arxiv-2604-26178: Seo studied sample covariance matrices, grids that sum up how traits vary together, in cases where the number of traits grows far faster than the number of samples. In a spiked model, a few directions carry extra spread, and he worked out first-order limits for where the eigenvalues sit and how the eigenvectors point once the matrix is scaled. The work extends prior results on such high-dimension covariance problems.
arxiv-2604-26578: Beg, O'Donoghue, and Monahan built a pipeline that turns imperative programs and their notes into typed, attributed graphs. Reusing verification artifacts means spotting structural and semantic likeness across programs and specs. The pipeline joins syntax-tree parsing with meaning vectors from models like SentenceTransformer and CodeBERT. Tests across C/ACSL, Java/JML, and Dafny showed steady graphs across languages and note styles, grounding future matching for verification reuse.
arxiv-2604-26678: Bagon, Kichler, and Sheinin recover scene sound from the surface vibrations of solid objects with poor or highly resonant responses. Optical vibration sensing turns everyday objects into visual microphones, but prior methods favored speakers, guitar bodies, or thin membranes that vibrate readily. The team captures vibrations at multiple surface points with speckle-based vibrometry imaging, then builds a physics-guided model linking scene sound to multi-point, multi-axis vibrations through the object's modes. Reversing the resonant transfer function and fusing signals recovers the original sound, beating single-point methods.
arxiv-2604-26778: Zhao and Xiong propose a fast input spread design for ranging OFDM systems joining sensing and links under frequency-varying fading. Input spread, or signal design, balances link rate against sensing quality in such systems. Under the rate-loss framework, the best plan under real sensing limits treats signal peak shape as a stock, shared across subcarriers as needed.
arxiv-2604-26978: Tsang proves a positive energy theorem for asymptotically flat initial data, using curvature ideas and the Jang equation. He then proves a measured shielding theorem about the causal nature of the energy-momentum vector for hyperbolic manifolds. From this he proves the positive mass theorem for complete hyperbolic manifolds obeying the dominant energy rule. As a result, these extend to manifolds with locally hyperbolic ends under an assumed symmetry.
arxiv-2604-27178: Moummad and seven colleagues use knowledge distillation to make plant monitoring cheap enough for phones and edge devices. Large vision transformers and multimodal models spot plant species and disease well, but they cost too much to run where resources are thin. Distillation moves the skill of a large pretrained model into a smaller, faster model. Their broad study tests this transfer for species and disease recognition on two challenging benchmarks.
arxiv-2604-27478: Krishnan and five colleagues propose a scalable, layered software network framework for mega-constellations of thousands of low Earth orbit satellites. Their design uses graph neural networks to map orbit layout, and Koopman theory to make nonlinear dynamics linear. A Graph Koopman Autoencoder forecasts space-time moves within a per-shell linear subspace. A controller then combines shell forecasts for control. On Starlink tests, it lifts space compression by at least 42.8 percent and time forecasts by about 11 percent over baselines, while using a smaller footprint.
arxiv-2604-27678: Liu and four colleagues study proton, kaon, and lambda production in gold-gold collisions at 3 GeV with an extended transport model. For central collisions, they examine proton spectra and mean momenta by rapidity. For mid-central collisions, they examine directed and elliptic flows for protons and kaons. A momentum-dependent nuclear field fits STAR data fairly, while a momentum-independent nuclear field describes results only partly, showing momentum dependence matters for nuclear matter traits.
arxiv-2604-27878: Zerhoudi builds SimEval-IR, a free toolkit and test set for judging user simulators in search. Simulators serve two ends that tests often blur: acting like real users, and ranking systems in a sound order. The toolkit gives one session form, three runnable tests, and base scores across four data sets in two tongues and four simulator kinds. Its result flips the usual test: click-depth distance, at 0.43, and Fréchet distance over session vectors track ranking soundness far better than the popular human-likeness check, which barely predicts it.
arxiv-2604-27978: Bulíček, Los and Woźnicki build a model for heat-carrying viscoelastic fluids that stays true to thermodynamics. These fluids mix elastic and viscous conduct, and the model covers heat flow plus temperature-linked laws. They prove a global weak solution exists in three dimensions. It needs no smallness, regularity or shape limits on start data apart from basic energy and entropy caps, and no fake stress diffusion. The proof joins energy and entropy balances with compactness tools to handle velocity, temperature and elastic stress together.
arxiv-2605-00378:
William Q. Erickson studies random permutations through the lens of the Robinson-Schensted correspondence, a classic algorithm that assigns each permutation a shape, a partition drawn as a diagram. The shape famously encodes the lengths of the longest increasing and decreasing subsequences, global facts about the permutation. Erickson asks the opposite, local question: fix the shape, and ask how likely position i is to receive value j.

Using the theory of tableaux, the fillings of these diagrams, he derives explicit formulas for those probabilities for hook shapes, two-row shapes, and rectangles. Plotted as matrices, the probabilities form intricate diffraction-like patterns, which he depicts and analyzes. As a surprise application, for hook and two-row shapes the expected share of fixed points tends, as the shape grows, to a classic Wallis integral value. The paper links a global combinatorial machine to fine local statistics.
arxiv-2605-00478:
Masahiro Kaminaga studies the Anderson model, the standard model of a particle moving through a disordered medium, on a Bethe lattice, an infinite tree-like graph. In the strong-disorder regime he examines the root-averaged density of states, an averaged spectral measure at the tree's root. The single-site randomness has bounded range and a smooth density near the energies of interest.

Combining a random-walk expansion with complex analysis of the single-site transforms, Kaminaga proves the scaled resolvent extends holomorphically near the target interval once disorder is large enough. The density of states there is then real analytic, with a finite strong-disorder expansion. Its leading term is the local density of the single-site distribution. All odd corrections vanish, and the rest are finite sums over short closed walks; for the uniform distribution he computes the first nonzero correction explicitly.
arxiv-2605-00578:
Luru Jing and 3 co-authors train cancer-slide models across hospitals without moving patient data. Whole slide images are huge scans of tissue. Hospitals differ in both their model designs and their feature extractors, which breaks methods that assume all sites run the same network. Their system, FedHD, avoids exchanging model settings at all.

Each site distills its knowledge into fake feature summaries, aligned to the real data through local Gaussian-mixture modeling. Every real slide gets its own fake counterpart, keeping the full range of cases instead of squeezing it away. A staged plan folds in other sites' fake features once local gains level off, and an added module rebuilds readable patch images from the fake features so users can inspect them. On three public cancer datasets, FedHD beat leading shared-training and distillation baselines while staying design-agnostic and privacy-preserving.
arxiv-2605-00778:
Jacques Raynal, Pierre Slangen, Elsa Raynal, and Jacques Margerit study gait in a single patient with Parkinson's disease whose bite height was changed as a test constraint. Repeated walking measures were taken under six occlusal probes, meaning six bite settings. The team looked at the case at three levels, from a simple combined score to a map of fifty-five body measures.

The ranking of two close settings changed with how the score was built, and the map showed broad overlap with no separate clusters for each setting. The authors conclude that neither view can uniquely identify a distinct system state. They treat bite height as a constraint, not a proven cause, and stress the findings are exploratory.
arxiv-2605-00978:
Gene C. K. Leung and fourteen co-authors report variability in a quasar seen just 850 million years after the Big Bang, a first for such early cosmic time. In the nearby universe, quasar brightness changes help probe accretion onto supermassive black holes and measure their masses, but detecting variability so early is hard. Infrared changes across five filters trace the accretion disk, while X-ray changes probe the corona.

The variable spectrum shows the disk has a geometrically thin, optically thick structure, even while the quasar accretes at a high rate in an extreme environment. The result shows accretion physics can be characterized through variability in the early universe. Future surveys should find large samples for population studies of early black hole growth.
arxiv-2605-01378:
Muhammad Muneeb and David B Ascher built a tool that gathers genes linked to a trait or disease from many databases in one run. Finding such genes is a common first step in risk scores and drug target work, but the proof sits scattered across sources with unlike formats.

Given a trait term, PhenotypeToGeneDownloaderR pulls gene lists, puts them in a shared form, merges them, and checks each symbol against the NCBI human gene reference. Across 13 traits and 13 sources it drew well over 100,000 raw hits. It kept most symbols after checks. It also recovered nearly all genes in a gold standard set built from three trusted sources. Overlap between sources was low, which shows why pooling helps. The free tool gives later analysis a clean, repeatable starting list.
arxiv-2605-02278:
Fengming Zhang and colleagues present HELIX, a model for filling missing values in time series that gives each feature a lasting identity. Attention methods can use links across features, but they rediscover those links at every layer, with no stable anchor for what each feature means. HELIX assigns a learnable embedding to each feature that persists through the network.

Unlike graph methods, HELIX needs no predefined topology and does not assume uniform spatial links. It learns arbitrary feature dependencies from temporal co-variation, handling data that mix spatial sites with semantic variables. With hybrid temporal-feature attention, it beat sixteen baselines across five public data sets and twenty-one settings. Analysis shows its learned identities align with meaningful feature structure.
arxiv-2605-02378:
Haoyu Wang and colleagues improve multimodal in-context learning, where a vision-language model adapts from a few shown examples. Their analysis finds an inductive gap: models often give correct answers from flawed reasoning and struggle to extract consistent rules across demonstrations. Two visual obstacles widen the gap, a flood of redundant visual tokens that obscure text cues, and attention skewed toward the first image.

Their framework recasts the task as an inductive-deductive process. A similarity-based module compresses visual tokens by filtering redundant patches. A dynamic mechanism rebalances attention across all images more evenly. A chain-of-thought scheme then guides the model to state a rule from the examples before applying it by deduction to the new case.
arxiv-2605-02478:
Feiyi Liu and five co-authors model a failure mode in silicon carbide power switches used in high-voltage systems. A single energetic event can push such a switch into burnout, and near the border between recovery and runaway the outcome is not sharp. Chance variation can tip a device that should recover into failure instead.

The team builds a reduced model that couples heat and charge feedback with random terms, plus a boundary that marks failure. Fluctuations widen the sharp threshold into a band of chance, and rare excursions explain failures below the nominal limit. Timing distributions separate fast, feedback-driven runaway from slow, chance-driven failure. A phase diagram sorts the regimes, giving designers a statistical view of a limit once treated as fixed.
arxiv-2605-02678:
Nicola Apollonio proves a sharp either-or result for graphs whose vertices are colored at random. A graph's degree pattern can be summed up by a normalized quantity built from its degree sequence. When vertices take several colors, with each color keeping a fair share, the question is whether the pieces cut out by the colors match their expected sizes.

Only two regimes occur. If the normalized degree quantity shrinks toward zero, the color-class subgraphs concentrate near their means. If it stays sizable, concentration hinges on color balance: a lasting imbalance keeps the count of same-color edges away from its mean with positive chance, while a fading imbalance restores concentration. The same split holds for a broad class of randomly colored random graphs.
arxiv-2605-02978:
José Luis Delgado presents a framework for measuring whether web connections are ready for post-quantum security. Moving TLS, the protocol that secures web traffic, to quantum-safe methods needs careful evidence. That evidence must separate what a session negotiated from what an endpoint can do. It must also cover what certificates show, and why some records are missing.

The framework splits evidence into four surfaces. One is passive session records. One is active probing. One is certificate chains, and one is registry knowledge. Those map onto planes for session behavior, key setup, endpoint skill, identity checks, lifecycle, and policy. A test artifact enforces schemas on all records and keeps registries versioned. Dozens of controlled scenarios test the design, across protocol versions and key modes.
arxiv-2605-03078:
Christine P. Lee, Min Kyung Lee, and Bilge Mutlu interviewed sixteen workers in health care, finance, and management about AI that does more than assist. As systems gain agency, they can decide, assign work, and shape how staff talk to each other.

Workers described three roles: assistant that supports choices, arbiter that makes key calls staff must explain, and manager that directs work. Needs for explanation, control, and accountability shifted with each role. The authors name an authority-accountability gap, where staff carry blame for outcomes they no longer control, and draw design lessons from it.
arxiv-2605-03278:
Sahil Shikalgar and Md. Noor-E-Alam fix a flaw in doubly robust estimates of treatment effects. The flaw arises when proxy variables are endogenous. Doubly robust methods assume no hidden confounding. Yet proxies like refill rates can track the error term, through hidden behavior or noisy measurement.

Their estimator models that joint pattern with Gaussian copulas. It does so in both the treatment and outcome models. No instruments are needed, and the doubly robust property is kept. Simulations recovered unbiased effects where naive estimates were badly biased. On national survey data, a seeming blood pressure rise from counseling vanished after the fix.
arxiv-2605-03378:
Shihao Weng, Yang Feng, Jinrui Zhang, Xiaofei Xie, Jiongchi Yu, and Jia Liu defend language model agents against prompt injections that hide inside the very evidence an agent must use. Such context-aware attacks differ from generic payloads, and most benchmarks and defenses miss them because their tasks do not depend on runtime context.

Their AgentLure benchmark spans four domains and many attack vectors. Their ARGUS defense audits causal provenance: each proposed action needs a complete benign evidence chain before release. On the benchmark, attack success fell from near three in ten to under four in a hundred, with clean utility largely kept.
arxiv-2605-03978:
Areeda Ayoub, Alfonso Castillo-Gonzalez, and Eric R. Bittner show that steady-state entanglement in open quantum systems is controlled by the phase reference of a phase-sensitive reservoir. Using a covariance-matrix approach for Gaussian-preserving evolution, they show that purely local, phase-sensitive loss can create entanglement. It does so when combined with coherent coupling between modes. That coupling turns local squeezing into nonlocal correlations.

The steady state has a finite entangled region. A best squeezing strength maximizes the size of the entanglement, and how well it survives heat. Coherent coupling does not help in a simple way. It regulates the conversion of squeezing into correlations. Phase-locked rotating-frame and laboratory-frame versions of the reservoir yield clearly distinct steady states. The upshot is a controlled route to steady-state entanglement in continuous-variable systems, through such reservoirs.
arxiv-2605-04178:
Aaron Jarmusch and Sunita Chandrasekaran build analytical performance models for modern graphics processors, aiming to close the gap between theoretical peak performance and what real kernels achieve. Rapidly evolving GPU architectures add complex memory hierarchies, matrix units, and varied precision formats, which naive roofline models handle badly. Their models are grounded in systematic microbenchmark characterization of two flagship architectures.

For NVIDIA's Blackwell B200, the model captures its tensor memory, asynchronous bulk copy engine, and fifth-generation tensor cores; for AMD's CDNA3 MI300A, it captures the Infinity Cache hierarchy, register constraints, and occupancy. Validation errors were near one percent or below on dozens of kernels, while naive roofline baselines erred by over ninety-five percent. Porting the models to Hopper and CDNA2 hardware needed parameter updates but no major restructuring.
arxiv-2605-04278:
Achuth Chandrasekhar and three co-authors present a system that mines materials science papers to build structured databases automatically. Most experimental detail in the literature sits buried in text, tables, and figures, so building databases by hand is slow and hard to scale.

Their multi-agent system takes article files, converts them to readable text and figures in parallel, and assigns sub-agents to extract records paper by paper. Another agent then merges those records into one table. The design aims for production-scale extraction that a single pass or fixed rules would struggle to match.
arxiv-2605-04478:
Yida Gu and nineteen co-authors present a diagnostic system for the slow or hanging communication faults that plague large-scale model training. As clusters grow, the libraries that coordinate thousands of processors hit faults from tangled hardware, software, and environmental causes, and manual diagnosis can take days.

Their system pairs a lightweight rank-level probe with an automated analyser. The probe traces communication traffic across layers in real time. The analyser detects anomalies and locates the faulty processor rank. Deployed for a year on a four thousand processor cluster, it covered nearly all known slow or hang cases. It pinpointed affected ranks within minutes, with high precision.
arxiv-2605-04678:
Yihan Lin and six co-authors systematically compare ways of supervising vision-language-action models, the systems that connect seeing and language to robot control, using latent actions as an intermediate representation. Latent actions promise consistent training across very different data sets, but supervision strategies have been fragmented and never compared head to head.

Under one unified baseline, they test four integration strategies split between image-based latent actions, which regularise the trajectory, and action-based ones, which unify the target space. Image-based supervision helped long-horizon reasoning and scene generalisation, while action-based supervision excelled at complex motor coordination. Directly supervising the model with discrete latent action tokens worked best overall.
arxiv-2605-04778:
Aziz Takhirov and Driss Yakoubi develop a step-by-step method for solving the steady incompressible Navier-Stokes equations. Those equations govern viscous fluid flow at rest in time. Their scheme adapts a viscosity splitting, originally built for unsteady flows, to the steady problem.

At each step, the method solves one elliptic equation for velocity. It also solves one system for pressure. That system's matrix is symmetric and positive definite. It stays the same across all steps, which makes repeated solves cheap. The scheme can also be read as an algebraic splitting. The authors prove boundedness and fast convergence of the steps. Tests show the method's efficiency.
arxiv-2605-04978:
Harry Desmond introduces Exhaustive Symbolic Integration, a method that lists every symbolic function up to a set complexity and tests which ones have closed-form antiderivatives in the same family. That census defines an integrability fraction for each chosen set of building blocks, such as rational functions, powers, exponentials, logarithms, and trigonometric functions.

Desmond finds the fraction falls at high complexity and depends dramatically on the building blocks, with adding the logarithm roughly tripling it. Used as an integrator, the method solved three integrals that resisted six major computer algebra systems and often returned the simplest answer. Enumeration, he argues, can systematically find integrable forms others miss.
arxiv-2605-05278:
Mohammad Reza Deylam Salehi and Ali Khalesi analyse expert routing in mixture-of-experts models through an information-theoretic lens, treating the gate that picks experts as a noisy communication channel. The gate controls computation, communication, and accuracy at once, so the information it carries about the input matters. Finite expert banks make those information quantities measurable rather than purely theoretical.

Using pretrained convolutional experts on a digit task, the authors estimate how much the chosen model reveals about the data with a closed-form estimator. Sweeping a data-dependence parameter, their estimate tracks the generalisation gap closely. They also trace an accuracy-versus-rate curve over the expert bank, offering a practical analysis tool for resource-aware expert systems.
arxiv-2605-05478:
Learning a new task goes faster when an agent can borrow skills from old ones. Mahyar Alinejad, Yue Wang, Amrit Singh Bedi, and George Atia present LANTERN, a transfer framework for reinforcement learning with a symbolic side. Earlier methods needed hand-written task machines, one source task, and fixed rules for mixing knowledge.

LANTERN generates task automata from plain-language descriptions using a language model. It blends several source policies by semantic similarity, and it gates teaching by error and uncertainty signals. Across resource, navigation, and control tasks, sample efficiency rose forty to sixty percent over baselines, and poorly matched sources did little harm.
arxiv-2605-05878:
Moving value across a tangle of blockchains and markets creates risks no single chain explains. Basel Magableh argues the main risk is composite: part route, part sentiment, part liquidity, part the policy a system commits to. He proposes a risk intelligence design of five working engines.

A prediction engine forecasts prices, liquidity, swings, and route health. A verification subnet on Bittensor scores those predictions with money at stake. Sentiment fusion reads text, on-chain flows, and grey sources as one. An agentic engine acts under written, role-bound limits, and a scenario engine turns forecasts into pre-set action programs.
arxiv-2605-06078:
Zixuan Wang and nine co-authors train language agents for long tasks by marking milestones along the way. An agent may need dozens of steps, and plain reinforcement learning blames early good moves for late failures. Scarce successful runs also waste most of the learning signal, the authors find.

Their framework, BEACON, splits each trajectory at milestone boundaries that reflect the task's structure. Reward shaping inside each segment credits partial progress, and advantages are estimated at two scales so distant failures cannot corrupt local judgments. On three agent benchmarks BEACON beat the compared reinforcement learning methods. On long ALFWorld tasks it reached a 92.9 percent success rate, nearly double the 53.5 percent of a leading baseline, and used training samples far more effectively.
arxiv-2605-06178:
Yiming Huang and three co-authors make analog quantum simulators programmable with a hybrid control design. Analog machines evolve continuously under interactions fixed by their hardware, which restricts the Hamiltonians they can realize. That fixed structure limits what many body dynamics researchers can emulate on a given device, however good the hardware is.

Universal Analog Quantum Simulation uses optimized continuous time control fields to engineer target dynamics directly on the native evolution. No decomposition into discrete gate sequences is needed, so the analog character of the device is preserved. Numerical studies on superconducting circuits and Rydberg atom arrays show the method copying non trivial many body dynamics. Those dynamics lie beyond what the bare hardware interactions could express, turning a fixed device into a programmable simulator.
arxiv-2605-06278:
Fabian Akkerman and three co-authors shrink ensemble models by mixing pruning with fresh compression. Ensembles predict very well by pooling many weak learners, but their size blocks deployment, interpretation, and tasks like robustness verification. Pruning discards redundant learners, while compression builds new ones from scratch, and past work kept the two camps separate, the authors note.

Their framework, PACE, first generates new learners with a theoretically grounded procedure that boosts the ensemble's diversity. When no more relevant learners can be found, it prunes the enriched ensemble down. Both phases allow fine control over faithfulness to the original ensemble's behavior. Tests show the method beating prior pruning and compression methods. It also offers clear guarantees on that faithfulness, which black box shrinking methods lack.
arxiv-2605-06378:
Yuanqiu Huang and Licheng Zhang count cliques in highly connected 1-planar graphs and prove sharp bounds. A 1-planar graph can be drawn with at most one crossing per edge, and earlier work fixed the maximum clique counts for such graphs in general. Those extremal examples, though, have low connectivity, leaving the high connectivity end open, which is where this paper works, on graphs that stay connected after removing any six vertices.

Every such graph on n vertices has at most a linear number of edges, triangles, and four vertex cliques, with explicit constants for each bound. Summed together, the total number of cliques stays below a linear cap as well. All of the bounds are sharp for infinitely many sizes. The results complete the clique picture at the opposite end of connectivity from the known examples.
arxiv-2605-06778:
Sean K. Terry and fifteen co-authors present a Hubble Space Telescope imaging survey of just over one square degree toward the Milky Way's galactic bulge. The field overlaps the upcoming Roman telescope's bulge time-domain survey. Imaging it first at Hubble resolution will sharpen Roman's characterization of exoplanet systems and leave a rich legacy archive for the whole community.

Coordinated imaging with both of Hubble's wide-field cameras in two filters ran mostly in Cycle 32, with the remainder in Cycle 33. As the first paper in a series, it lays out the program and observing strategy and shows early results. The dataset will serve studies of stellar populations, dynamics, extinction, and clusters near the galactic center.
arxiv-2605-06878:
Sonu Kumar, Mukul Lokhande, Santosh Kumar Vishvakarma, and Adam Teman present CARMEN, a hardware inference engine that uses CORDIC arithmetic to run neural networks efficiently. CORDIC computes multiply-accumulate operations through shifts and additions, and its iteration depth directly sets accuracy. That lets their engine switch between approximate and precise modes at runtime with no hardware change, supporting both eight- and sixteen-bit precision.

A chip implementation in twenty-eight nanometer technology cuts computation cycles by up to a third and power by about a fifth per stage. A large configuration reaches strong compute density and energy efficiency, and a field-programmable board prototype runs real-time object detection at well under half a watt.
arxiv-2605-07078:
Zekun Wang and three co-authors test whether diffusion models can discover their own concepts at generation time. Making new combinations from familiar parts usually assumes the needed concepts are already supplied. Their method instead works from a single unusual query and the model's own learned scores.

Gradient steps recover local modes in the model's density, which are turned into clean prototypes and selected greedily. The combined teacher model can be sampled directly or used to train a small adapter. On held-out combination tests built from two image datasets, both routes beat query-only and nearest-class baselines, suggesting reusable concepts hide in the model's score patterns.
arxiv-2605-07178:
Kai Zheng and five co-authors extract text descriptions for satellite change detection from the labels already in the data. Change detection supports city monitoring and disaster assessment, but image-only models confuse real changes with look-alike variation. Added text helps, yet existing descriptions are coarse or machine-made and noisy.

Their S2M framework transcribes each labeled change region into structured facts: where it happened, what changed, how, and how many objects were involved. Training aligns images with those precise descriptions at no extra labeling cost. On a new Gaza Strip dataset built for the work, the method beat even systems that use large language models.
arxiv-2605-07578:
Aleksas Mazeliauskas reviews the first light-ion collision program at the Large Hadron Collider, which ran in July 2025. The runs collided protons with oxygen, and oxygen and neon nuclei with each other. Such mid-size systems sit between tiny proton-proton collisions and huge heavy-ion ones, making them a test bed for how collective behavior in hot quantum chromodynamics turns on.

Early results, he reports, give strong evidence that a quark-gluon plasma forms even in these small systems. The review lays out why physicists wanted light-ion runs in the first place, then walks through the initial measurements. It ties the findings to perturbative calculations, hot matter theory, and low-energy nuclear structure, showing where the three fields meet.
arxiv-2605-07978:
Qiwei Wang and three co-authors locate ground photos in three dimensions using satellite and drone imagery together. Classical cross-view localization finds only a position and a heading for a ground image on a satellite tile, because overhead views carry no cues for roll, pitch, or altitude. Those missing angles matter on slopes, ramps, and tilted mounts.

Their insight is to add one drone image as an intermediate viewpoint. It reveals the structure invisible from directly above and needs only to overlap the ground camera's view, with no known relative pose. The Cross3R model takes any combination of the three views and returns a joint point cloud, full six-degree poses for every camera, and on-tile positions. A new tri-view dataset of two hundred seventy-eight thousand images across eighty-five scenes supports training and testing.
arxiv-2605-08478:
Yihe Dong and Boris Shigida ask how to spend a fixed inference budget on competitive programming: think longer in one agent, or sample many independent attempts? They evaluate two hundred sixteen Codeforces problems from divisions one through three, varying both money cost and number of model calls.

Repeated independent sampling won on both trade-offs, across models and difficulty levels, and the gap survived prompt caching inside agent frameworks, which points to weaker per-call value from agentic reasoning. For self-contained algorithmic tasks, breadth beat depth. The authors add a budget analysis proving that a cost-optimal solver minimizes log failure likelihood per dollar.
arxiv-2605-08678:
Bohan Lyu and many coauthors introduce MLS-Bench, a test of whether AI agents can invent better machine learning methods, not merely apply known ones. Each of its one hundred forty tasks across twelve domains asks an agent to improve one targeted part of a learning system, then prove the gain holds across settings and scales. A shared community platform keeps results comparable over time.

Current agents fall well short of reliably beating human designed methods, and routine tuning proves far easier than true invention. Extra search, computing, or context alone does not close the gap, because planning and validating claims need scientific insight. AI research gains a benchmark aimed squarely at discovery itself.
arxiv-2605-08778:
Zhida He and ten coauthors improve credit assignment in multi turn jailbreak research, where harmful intent is spread across seemingly mild conversation turns. Training methods that score only the final outcome reward every turn equally, overpaying filler turns in successes and underpaying useful steps in failures. Their TRACE framework scores turns individually: masking tests measure each turn's contribution in successful attacks, while failed attempts draw penalties tied to harmfulness and relevance.

The same credit signal then serves defense training as well. Across open and closed target models, attack success rises by about a quarter over the strongest reinforcement baseline, and reuse for defense improves the safety and utility balance. Dialogue safety research gains finer supervision.
arxiv-2605-08878:
Yu Chen, Yuanhao Liu, and Qi Cao explain structurally why aligned language models can still be jailbroken. Looking at harmful inputs under smooth perturbation, they identify refusal escape directions: small shifts that move the model from refusing to answering while its grasp of the harmful meaning stays intact. A jailbreak, in this view, is a behavior transition along such a direction, not just a clever discrete prompt.

They prove these directions decompose exactly into contributions from parts of the model's operator structure, with normalization, residual wiring, and output stages analytically constrained. Removing the directions forces shared attention and feedforward modules to kill those contributions while preserving benign skill, creating a conditional safety versus utility trade off.
arxiv-2605-08978:
Xingyuan Hua, Sheng Yue, and Ju Ren teach language model agents to explore only when exploration is worth it. Agents that gather feedback before acting usually explore in a fixed, undifferentiated way, wasting effort when the task is already clear and under exploring when uncertainty runs high. Their exploration aware policy optimization scores exploratory actions by their estimated power to improve later decisions, using a variational inference based reward.

A grouping mechanism separates exploratory moves from task completing moves during training, so each is optimized on its own terms. Across demanding text based and graphical interface agent benchmarks, performance improves consistently. Agent training gains a sense of timing: investigate while confused, execute the moment the picture clears.
arxiv-2605-09078:
Charalambia Varnava and three co-authors report new telescope observations of one of the most luminous quasars known, a galaxy core buried in dust when the universe was young. The James Webb Space Telescope's mid-infrared instrument measured its light in detail, and the team fit models to the full spread of that light.

Their fits say the active black hole supplies most of the galaxy's output, with a mass billions of times the Sun's and stars forming at a furious rate. They also find clear signs of hot dust near the poles of the black hole's dust ring. The authors urge that this polar dust be included when other distant hidden quasars are modeled, since leaving it out skews the results.
arxiv-2605-09178:
Agustín Garrone studies contact Lie algebras, algebraic structures that mix symmetry operations with a contact form from geometry. His 2026 paper focuses on those that are unimodular, a volume-like condition, and asks how a special vector field called the Reeb vector acts inside them. The proof he gives is deliberately basic, avoiding heavy machinery where possible.

Garrone shows that this action must fade under repetition, except for two named algebras, which he identifies in standard notation. He then defines a wider class that includes the K-contact case and shows the same two algebras are its only centerless unimodular members. The result gives a fresh proof of a known fact about Sasakian algebras. Work in dimension five and links to Frobenius algebras and the contact Lefschetz condition round out the study.
arxiv-2605-09578:
Demchenko and fifteen colleagues ask why nitrogen doping fails to make hole current flow in beta gallium oxide, a wide band gap crystal. N has long been seen as a possible dopant, yet it never yields p type response. Using heat dependent N K edge X ray uptake on N implanted samples, the team probes the tiny scale setup of implanted N.

Spectra show a strong peak typical of molecular nitrogen, growing stronger upon heating. Theory work and scattering models show N atoms tend to form N N bonded pairs, above all in defect rich zones made by implants. That N thus forms pairs rather than lone dopants in lattice sites, solving the long standing doping failure and showing pairing as a missed uptake path.
arxiv-2605-09878:
Maity and Hamazaki bring thermodynamics together with magic, the quantum resource that separates classically simulable circuits from fully quantum ones. They define Clifford ergotropy, the most energy extractable when only Clifford operations, a restricted gate set, are allowed. Ergotropy itself is the maximum work drawn from a state by unitary evolution, and passive states are those that yield none.

The paper gives universal upper bounds on Clifford ergotropy that fall as magic rises, measured by a filtered stabilizer entropy. One- and two-qubit examples show the bounds at work, with the two-qubit case showing a sharp change in the control landscape. Even for many-body systems, where exact optimisation is hard, the analysis yields a form of the second law under Clifford operations for typical states.
arxiv-2605-10378:
Manuel Haußmann, Ramon Winterhalder, and Maria Ubiali offer a structured guide to doubt in machine learning for physics. Sound doubt estimates are vital where findings rest on validated chance statements, yet the field lacks a unified statistical view. Their 2026 overview introduces a unified taxonomy of doubt and clarifies predictive versus inference doubt across frequentist and Bayesian frameworks.

The authors discuss sound validation tools, including coverage, calibration, bias tests, and proper scoring rules, shown with simple regression and sorting examples. Coverage asks whether claimed intervals contain truth at the stated rate, while calibration checks whether stated confidences match observed rates. Readers get both a map of doubt types and practical tests for judging whether machine-learning doubt estimates in physics can be trusted.
arxiv-2605-10678:
Paul Fischill, Andreas Adelmann, and Sriramkrishnan Muralikrishnan present the first nonuniform fast Fourier transform that runs on mixed supercomputers. The nonuniform FFT serves spectral methods on uneven samples, with uses in medical imaging, molecular dynamics, and kinetic plasma runs. Old codes run only in shared memory, capping problem size at one node. Their Kokkos-based code runs the same on NVIDIA and AMD graphics processors, with spreading and interpolation kernels tuned for varied needs and machines.

Spreading kernels match or beat cuFINUFFT's single-GPU throughput at real particle densities, while adding AMD support. Strong-scaling tests on Alps, JUWELS Booster, and LUMI reach 1024 GPUs, where the spread-out FFT takes most of runtime. Applied to Particle-in-Fourier runs of Landau damping with up to a trillion Fourier modes and 8.6 billion particles, the method reaches detail levels once out of reach for spectral particle methods.
arxiv-2605-10778:
Timo Fritsch, Marvin Künnemann, Mirza Redzic, and Julian Stieß ask when sparse inputs make hard search problems easier, starting with independent sets in hypergraphs. Sparsity counts the hyperedges against the nodes, and Turán's theorem already settles very sparse cases, leaving a wide middle ground unexplored.

Above that threshold the team gives a fast algorithm whose running time is essentially optimal under standard clique hypotheses, with finer detail keyed to hyperedge sizes. They extend the study to sparse Boolean constraint problems, classifying where sparsity helps and where it does not. Algorithm designers get a near-complete map of sparsity's power for fixed-size solution search.
arxiv-2605-10878:
Tiberiu Musat answers a basic deep-learning puzzle: why does weight decay, the routine penalty on large weights, actually work? In fixed-precision networks, he proves the smallest weight norm of a looped network that outputs a given binary string equals that string's Kolmogorov complexity, up to a logarithmic factor.

Weight decay therefore imposes a prior close to Solomonoff's universal prior, the optimal prior over computable functions. The result holds for any norm, since every norm collapses to the nonzero parameter count in fixed precision, and both bounds are tight. Infinite precision breaks the story, since networks could then encode non-computable functions. Theorists get a crisp explanation for the field's most universal regularizer.
arxiv-2605-10978:
Hyunjin Seo and eighteen colleagues present a benchmark for vibe protein design. In that emerging practice, one model generates new sequences, engineers existing proteins, and reasons about protein traits through open-ended natural language. Protein design seeks amino-acid sequences that fold into stable, functional shapes.

Existing benchmarks cover only slices of the job or force objectives into rigid schemas. Their language-interfaced benchmark runs three stages mirroring a real design workflow: recognition, engineering, and generation, each grounded in expert-curated cases. Model builders get an integrated test of generalist protein-design competence under flexible, user-like intents.
arxiv-2605-11078:
Angelo Esposito, Kin Chung Fong, and Lam Hui propose an ultra-broadband axion dark-matter experiment spanning over fifteen orders of magnitude in axion mass. Axions, hypothetical pseudoscalar particles from extensions of the Standard Model, could solve the strong-CP problem and supply dark matter, but searches usually cover narrow mass bands.

Their strategy exploits observables controlled by the axion field squared, operating a DC SQUID at its flux sweet spot where voltage depends quadratically on magnetic flux, with lock-in modulation dodging low-frequency noise. Projected sensitivity beats current bounds by orders of magnitude and barely depends on axion mass. Systematic backgrounds and a nulling technique to tame them are discussed, plus adaptations for axion-fermion coupling and dark photons. Dark-matter hunters get a sweeping, practical search design.
arxiv-2605-11378: Zhou and seventeen colleagues ask whether frontier coding assistants can reliably automate agent evaluation. Judging multi-step tool use and reasoning is costly and expert work. Simply prompting them fails. Without evaluation expertise they succeed on only thirty percent of executions. They also produce bloated evaluations with over twelve metrics per agent. Their EvalAgent encodes evaluation skills into a trace-based pipeline, lifting first-run success from 17 point 5 to 65 percent. The point is that coding skill alone does not make a good judge of agent work.
arxiv-2605-11478: Namyoon Lee and Yongjune Kim introduce FibQuant, a universal fixed-rate vector quantizer for random-access key-value cache compression. Serving long contexts strains memory traffic. Rotation-based scalar codecs store a norm, rotate and quantize coordinate by coordinate, but discard the geometry created by normalization. After a Haar rotation, a block of coordinates forms a spherical-Beta source, not a product source. FibQuant keeps the same normalize-rotate-store interface with a shared radial-angular codebook, beating its scalar specialization at matched rate.
arxiv-2605-11878: Edgar Knobloch and Arik Yochelis describe relaxation oscillations near SNIPER bifurcations. There, a pair of fixed points wipes out to create a large, slow cyclic orbit. In wide media, they show, that orbit can suffer a long-wave instability, yielding rhythms patterned across space that persist on both sides of the split. The forms differ by system. One system shows a chimera state inside a theta-reaction-diffusion model. Another shows chaotic spiking inside an activator-inhibitor-substrate model.
arxiv-2605-11978: Xiaoyuan Li and seven colleagues predict a base language model's post-training promise before post-training begins. Standard benchmarks such as MMLU poorly reflect how models adapt in open-ended tasks, leading to wasteful model choice. Their RuDE system sidesteps the output gap through response sorting, building matched paired contrasts via fine-grained rubric breaks under a 4C scheme. Tests showed over 90 percent match with post-training scores, and RL checks showed it spots high-potential smaller models.
arxiv-2605-12178: Jishnu Sethumadhavan Nair and 16 colleagues ask whether business agents still need learned world models when rules can be read at run time. Business logic differs per tenant, shifts over time, and breaks models trained on past transitions when deployments change. The authors propose discovery agents that read the system's settings to recover transition rules, rather than trusting only stored models. They also build CascadeBench, a test of enterprise cascade prediction. Stored models do well in-distribution but fade under shift, while discovery agents stay robust by grounding predictions locally.
arxiv-2605-12278: Fumanal-Idocin, Fernandez-Peralta and Andreu-Perez study feature selection that buys measurements one at a time for each case, under a budget. Because the number of possible buying paths explodes, they propose Hyper-DFS, a hypernetwork that creates classifier settings on demand for each chosen feature set. A Set Transformer smooths the conditioning space, so similar tasks sit close together. The method ranks first or second across tabular and image tests and generalises to unseen feature sets.
arxiv-2605-12378: Micun and Berkholz extend a family of proof systems that write each proof line as a compact diagram for a Boolean function. Earlier systems used ordered binary decision diagrams, studied since 2004. The authors switch to sentential decision diagrams and deterministic structured DNNF circuits, which can be even more compact. Both new variants give strictly smaller refutations of unsatisfiable formulas than the older diagrams. They also map how the systems' power shifts with the derivation rules allowed.
arxiv-2605-12578: Artemasov and five colleagues estimate terahertz channels for ultra-massive MIMO in 6G, where huge antenna apertures stretch the Rayleigh distance. Users then span both near-field and far-field regions at once, and exact spatial precoding needs channel estimates that hybrid beamforming, with few digital chains, makes hard to obtain. Their block recurrent transformer, equipped with state memory, trains once and then applies iteratively for hybrid-field estimation. One trained block thus serves across the hybrid regime, rather than needing separate near- and far-field models.
arxiv-2605-12678: Corley and eight colleagues audit 152 papers on geospatial foundation models and find the field cannot yet rank its own models. Published work gives reviewers too little to judge which model fits a given task. Evaluations, protocols, released weights and pretraining controls are rarely standardised. Their audit finds 46 disagreements of at least ten points under the same model, benchmark and protocol. Ninety-four of 126 papers with usable pretraining data adopt a configuration no other paper uses. Thirty-nine percent release no model weights at all, a gap community standards can solve.
arxiv-2605-12778: Fan, Henderson and Ho improve motion in-betweening, the task of filling motion between sparse keyframes. Recent methods lose keyframe detail and break motion smoothness. Their pipeline maps implicit neural representations to sparse spatial and time cues in a latent diffusion model. From few, ambiguous keyframes, it samples representation parameters and rebuilds plausible smooth motion. Tests show better quality with few keyframes, keeping accuracy while varying the in-between motion.
arxiv-2605-12978: Zhang and six co-authors find that consolidated memories written by language models turn faulty with continuous updating, even when built from useful experience. Memory quality first rises, then falls below the no-memory baseline; GPT-5.4 fails 54% of previously solved ARC-AGI problems after consolidating from ground-truth solutions. Keeping raw episodes intact stays competitive, so the authors urge treating raw episodes as first-class evidence and gating consolidation explicitly.
arxiv-2605-13178: Lee and Choi introduce LiteLVLM, a text-guided token pruning method for pixel grounding in vision-language models. Visual tokens dominate inputs, yet pruning methods struggle with grounding, where token importance hinges on input text. Analysing CLIP, they find referent-region tokens often show low similarity to their textual representation. LiteLVLM reverses CLIP's similarity ranking, keeping tokens over referent regions while recovering context tokens for clear separation. It beats rivals by over 5% across budgets, keeping 90% of performance with a 22% speedup and 2.3 times less memory, without training.
arxiv-2605-13378: Marco Pasquale and Stefano Markidis test whether forward-mode automatic differentiation can replace finite differences inside Jacobian-free Newton-Krylov solvers. These solvers tackle stiff nonlinear equations without forming the full Jacobian matrix. Finite differences, however, make their linearisation fragile in limited precision. Holding every other solver choice fixed, the authors find automatic differentiation speeds computation by two to three orders of magnitude on processors and graphics cards alike. It also lifts the share of runs that finish from forty-two percent to at least ninety-five percent.
arxiv-2605-13878: Zhuge, Jiang, Xu and Chen build a data-driven method that recovers the governing equations of systems whose rules change over time. The approach picks an optimal set of basis functions, so it needs only simple prior assumptions. Tests on synthetic cases, including coupled Kuramoto oscillators, succeed, and the method also predicts cases such as drone navigation, chick-heart aggregates and a marine fish community.
arxiv-2605-13978: Ji and Wang construct model wavefunctions and exact parent Hamiltonians for the full Zk Read-Rezayi series of fractional quantum Hall states on a lattice. Most model wavefunctions so far live in the continuum, but theirs follow a generalized clustering rule realized on the lattice and encoded in Macdonald polynomials. That structure makes the states exact ground states, at zero energy, of local density interactions. Their gap in the particle entanglement spectrum is infinitely large.
arxiv-2605-14078: Foucoin and London survey the math traits of natural polynomials for Schwarzschild and Kerr black holes. Quasi-normal modes matter for gravitational-wave theory, signal models and data analysis, yet their math traits still pose open questions. Old theory offers a frame for studying mode orthogonality and whether modes span the space. The authors' natural polynomials, pinned by quasi-normal mode boundary rules, exactly tridiagonalize Teukolsky's radial equation. It covers three-term recurrences, ladder operators and governing equations.
arxiv-2605-14578: Wettenstein, Nadel and Boker unify several explainability tools for decision tree ensembles in one algorithm, Woodelf++. Partial dependence plots show how one feature shifts average predictions, joint plots cover feature pairs, and interaction values cover every subset. Built on Woodelf's SHAP machinery with metrics over pseudo-Boolean functions, the method is claimed to run up to six times faster than rivals on large data and far faster than scikit-learn.
arxiv-2605-14778: Baldare, Savin and Schrohe derive a Fredholm criterion for G-pseudodifferential operators, where a compact Lie group G acts smoothly on a closed manifold. Using a general Simonenko principle, the criterion covers operators over Sobolev spaces of sections of vector bundles for the manifold. When the group is finite, a further characterisation follows in terms of invertibility of suitable symbols.
arxiv-2605-14878: Singh and team study decision fusion for robust wearable affect detection. Body signals promise public health and stress-aware help, but deployments face shifting dynamics, artefacts, and missing sensors. Fixed-basis spectral features can oversmooth short-lived patterns. The authors combine Fourier-Bessel Series Expansion with EWT spectral segmentation for mode-wise transient descriptors. Signals are weighted by predictive uncertainty and reliability. On WESAD, aggregation beats or matches feature-level aggregation about eighty-four percent of the time.
arxiv-2605-15378: Sydney Montiel, Alexsandra Guadarrama, and Fabio Andrijauskas describe using the Open Science Data Federation for Big Bear Solar Observatory data distribution. The federation extends StashCache into a global network with 20 origins and 30 caches plus new access methods and monitoring. Bringing observatory data into the federation gave standard, reliable worldwide access through local caches. A pipeline built on it can apply image processing to every observatory image from anywhere on the planet. It shows the federation's value for data-intensive solar science.
arxiv-2605-15578: Shun Maeta and Miho Shito study lambda-biharmonic Riemannian submersions, a wider class than biharmonic maps. They prove no-go results for maps from spaces of constant sectional curvature. A critical value, twice the dimension-minus-one times that bend, calls the shots. With nonnegative bend, or negative bend and a different lambda, every such map must be harmonic. At the critical value with negative bend, they build examples.
arxiv-2605-15778: Robert Ghrist models liability clearing with sheaves on directed hypergraphs. A decorated debt network gives a debt sheaf. Its hyperedges split payment flows from receipt flows. Clearing setups are exactly its global sections, the equalizer of the identity and a clearing map built from payout plus intake. The build works across coefficient types, and a Clearing Invariance Theorem compares clearing tasks across payment-data types. Existence, uniqueness and iteration follow from lattice, continuity, acyclicity or contraction rules. The Eisenberg-Noe model is a special case.
arxiv-2605-15978: Anita Srbinovska and three colleagues turn police report narratives into evidence-linked facts with symbolic methods, so incident details buried in free text can be reviewed without manual reading. Their pipeline strips personal identifiers, parses sentences, maps predicates onto an ontology, and builds time-marked graphs. Tested on 450 property crime reports, it mapped most events through a PropBank-VerbNet-WordNet path, with full human agreement on incident starts, stolen items, and time cues.
arxiv-2605-16078: Wade and Teferra test how well neural-network stand-ins capture the full spread of solutions for stochastic heat conduction. Most studies check mean fields and miss the tails of the distribution. Comparing a feed-forward network with a Deep Operator Network, they find worst-case errors an order of magnitude above mean errors. The gap comes from extrapolating past training bounds, and a feed-forward network trained with a weak-form residual loss handled such extremes best.
arxiv-2605-16178: Lopez-Gomez, Brenner, and Schneider show that an agentic AI workflow can speed up seasonal streamflow forecasting for California's Sierra Nevada. Winter snowpack predicts spring and summer runoff, but shifting climate erodes forecasts trained on past data. Their agent finds data sets, pulls in prior knowledge, and tries model designs, while a code-mutation system refines each design by Monte Carlo tree search. Three XGBoost quantile models then forecast monthly natural flow at one- to six-month leads across 23 watersheds, beating the state's Bulletin 120 forecasts for early-season runoff.
arxiv-2605-16278: Gaube and others advance a hands-on guide for good human watch of AI systems in high-risk choice-making. Watch designs lack shared meanings, clear roles, and open rollout steps, leaving scholars unsure how to design, build, and test them. Drawing on CS, human-CS contact, psychology, philosophy, and law, the guide offers a working meaning, design, and steps for watch. It adds a template for writing watch designs, applied across diverse domains, plus a roundup of open research gaps.
arxiv-2605-16378: Sana and six others model iterative masked-token redraws in masked language models as Glauber dynamics chains. Masked models define local conditional distributions but usually lack one shared joint pattern, raising the question of what global outcome looped redraws induce. A rectangle test proves that model conditionals are intrinsically incompatible, a pattern found across modern models. Under bounded cross-token influence, high-temperature contraction gives O(n log n) mixing time, while a uniform local margin rule yields metastability with slow escape from semantic basins at low temperatures.
arxiv-2605-16678: Yang, Afxenti and Safari improve satellite quantum key distribution under atmospheric turbulence, which distorts the received beam while background noise stays roughly uniform. Their method uses single-photon detector arrays and activates only elements likely to register qubits, rejecting excess noise as the channel shifts. Monte Carlo simulations with diffraction, turbulence, background, and dark noise show lower quantum bit error rates and higher secret key rates than conventional schemes. Gains depend on turbulence conditions.
arxiv-2605-17178: Xu maps how light axions made in the hot early phase after inflation add to dark radiation, using a shift-symmetric effective field theory. One kinetic function drives both direct decay of the inflaton and inflaton annihilation. The two routes scale in opposite ways as the heat of that phase rises. Turning now-cast and next-wave dark-radiation limits into bounds on the theory's coefficients yields a two-dimensional map. That map can bound the heat of the early phase from both sides.
arxiv-2605-17278: Ma and colleagues build A2RBench, an automatic pipeline for generating abstract-reasoning benchmarks that can be checked formally. Language models draft tasks and expand them from validated rules, while cycle-consistency checks, running an operation forward and back, guarantee a unique answer and block hallucinations. Tests find top models far behind humans and weak on three-dimensional tasks, though richer inputs can paradoxically ease reasoning.
arxiv-2605-17378: Evgenii Vinogradov introduces UPSim, an open-source simulator for air-to-ground signal propagation in the FR3 band for drone networks. Instead of launching rays per ground point, it derives visibility regions from 3D building geometry by fast shadow projection. It then adds line-of-sight-dependent path loss and fading calibrated on over 136 million ray-tracing channels. Validation beats the 3GPP baseline sharply, cutting aggregate distance from about a third to about four hundredths.
arxiv-2605-17878: Ji Qi, Xiaojun Zhang, Honngwei Yu, and Zhihai Wang study bound states in the continuum in a two-giant-atom waveguide. Giant atoms couple to a waveguide at points, beyond the dipole approximation, enabling interference bound states for quantum tasks. They focus on coupling between two giant atoms, its phase, which prior work left unclear. They show the coupling phase controls the number of bound states and their profiles for photons and atoms. Bound states then drive dynamics, making phase engineering a tool for tailoring quantum-state evolution in interfaces.
arxiv-2605-17978: Shangzhan Li and ten colleagues propose AutoVecCoder, teaching language models to write vectorized code. Single Instruction, Multiple Data vectorization is central to high-performance computing, but compiler auto-vectorization often falls short due to static analysis. Language models also struggle with explicit vector code, given scarce corpora and strict hardware constraints. AutoVecCoder joins VecPrompt, a data synthesis line for knowledge, with VecRL, a reinforcement learning framework aligned with execution efficiency. Its 8B model leads on SSE and AVX subsets of SimdBench and sometimes beats standard -O3 optimizations.
arxiv-2605-18078: Yevhen Shcherbinin and three colleagues study where multi-agent policy-gradient methods land, using basin-entry chance for a payoff-dominance target set. For finite-unroll Meta-MAPG, the update splits into plain policy gradient plus own- and peer-learning corrections, with controlled sample noise and bias. The peer-learning correction drives selection: under local alignment, entry into the target stable-Nash set's certified region rises over plain policy gradient. Since steady correction can shift zero-update points, annealing it after entry restores plain dynamics and local stable-Nash convergence.
arxiv-2605-18178: Anas Skalli's 2026 essay weighs the thin line optical neural networks must cross to reach broad practical use. Such networks promise unmatched efficiency, bandwidth, and latency, gains that matter more as demand for neural hardware surges. Yet their value for general acceleration or niche tasks still needs proof under realistic application conditions. The essay reviews recent insights and sets out the key research priorities that would close the gap.
arxiv-2605-18278: Olena Karpel's 2026 paper studies when two generalized Bratteli diagrams count as the same, and what survives such sameness. The main result shows every such diagram matches an irreducible one. Karpel then defines completely irreducible diagrams as those matching only irreducible diagrams.
