Even through the noise, the book shows Paracelsian pharmacy at work, weighing poison against cure in grains.
books-and-characters-french-english-pg12:
Lytton Strachey gathered Books and Characters, French and English, from essays first printed in leading reviews, and London saw the book in May 1922. Strachey dedicates the volume to John Maynard Keynes. The hosted text is the Project Gutenberg release of that same first edition.

Fifteen pieces move between French and English letters. Racine, Madame du Deffand, and Henri Beyle stand on the French side. Browne, Shakespeare in his last period, Blake, and the lives of the poets stand on the English. Voltaire fills the middle with four studies and a dialogue in his own hand. Strachey writes with calm malice and perfect balance. Readers meet the essay style that made his name between the wars, at full strength.
bracton-de-legibus-twiss-vol1-1878:
Travers Twiss edited Bracton's De legibus et consuetudinibus Angliae for the Rolls Series, and the first volume appeared in 1878. Henry de Bracton, a thirteenth-century judge, wrote the treatise as a full account of English law. It is the first great book of the common law, and Twiss gave it a scholarly text with the Latin and English side by side.

Volume 1 lays out the treatise's opening: the kinds of law, the courts, and the first principles of property and persons. Bracton insists that the king himself stands under God and the law, a line quoted for centuries afterward. The treatise draws on real cases from the plea rolls, not just theory. Twiss's edition made the foundation book of English law usable by modern scholars.
bunyan-pilgrims-progress-1678:
John Bunyan was an English tinker and preacher who spent years in jail for preaching without a license. He wrote The Pilgrim's Progress during his imprisonment, and it was published in 1678. The story is told as a dream the narrator has while traveling.

A man named Christian flees the City of Destruction, carrying a heavy burden on his back. On the road to the Celestial City he meets helpers and dangers, from the Slough of Despond to Vanity Fair. Each place stands for a stage of the Christian life. Few books in English have been read by so many people, for so long.
burckhardt-renaissance-middlemore-1878:
Jacob Burckhardt's The Civilization of the Renaissance in Italy appears in S. G. C. Middlemore's translation of 1878. Burckhardt, a Swiss historian, in effect invented the Renaissance as a concept. He portrays Italy from 1300 to 1500 as the birthplace of the modern individual. The state as a work of art opens his account.

Later parts treat discovery of the world and of man, society, festivals, and morals. Burckhardt writes cultural history, not a chain of battles and kings. His method founded a whole field of study. Scholars have revised his picture for a century without displacing it. The book remains cultural history's founding masterpiece in elegant English dress.
carver-travels-interior-north-america-17:
Jonathan Carver roams the far north west in Travels Through the Interior Parts of North America, his book of 1778. Carver was a chief of troops who trekked past the great lakes to the far streams in 1766 and past. He maps lands, meets tribes, and tells of their rites, trade, and tales in brisk, clear prose for the crowd at home.

Midst his notes stands an early writ word on the great thunder bird of the tribes. The book was a huge hit in its day. It shaped how the West saw those lands. Its zest still shows.
champlain-voyages-slafter-vol-1-1878:
Samuel de Champlain founded Quebec and spent his life mapping and settling New France. His Voyages, first issued from 1613 onward, tell that work in his own words. Volume one here follows the Prince Society translation of 1878 to 1882, with Charles P Otis translating and Edmund F Slafter editing.

Champlain writes as explorer, sailor, and governor at once: coasts sounded, rivers traced, alliances made with native nations. His account is the primary record of early Canada and the Great Lakes country. No later history of French Canada can start anywhere else. The first volume opens the fullest English edition of the founder's own story, plain and exact.
champlain-voyages-slafter-vol-2-1878:
Volume two of the Prince Society Champlain continues the Voyages of Samuel de Champlain, the founder of New France. The translation of 1878 to 1882, by Charles P Otis under Edmund F Slafter's editorship, spans Champlain's works of 1613 to 1632. Volume two stands at the middle of the three-volume English set.

Champlain's narrative mixes sea craft, diplomacy, and the hard logistics of planting a colony in a cold land. He records his dealings with the native nations of Canada and the Great Lakes in detail. His maps and reports guided French policy for a generation. This volume keeps the primary record of early Canada moving, in the founder's own measured voice.
champlain-voyages-slafter-vol-3-1878:
The Prince Society translation of Champlain's Voyages closes with volume three. Samuel de Champlain's works run from 1613 to 1632. Charles P Otis Englished them, and Edmund F Slafter edited the set between 1878 and 1882. Together they tell the founding of New France from the founder's own desk, in three volumes.

Champlain governed Quebec through hunger, war, and fragile peace with native nations and English rivals. His last writings show a colony still small but rooted, and a founder still planning its growth. The Voyages remain the primary record of early Canada and the Great Lakes. Volume three completes the standard English set, ending where Champlain's own work ends.
chantry-house-pg7378:
Charlotte M. Yonge's Chantry House is a novel of childhood, schoolroom days and a country house, opening with a nursery memory. The narrator remembers his mother reading to him as he lay in his crib, and the chapters that follow trace his growth.

Contents include schoolroom days, Win and Slow, a helping hand, the valley of humiliation, the inheritance, the old house, rats, and a tuneful choir. Later chapters bring Mrs. Sophia's feud, a scrape, the mullion chamber, rational theories, cat language, and the siege of Hillside. Yonge writes with the moral warmth of The Heir of Redclyffe, and readers of Victorian family fiction will find Chantry House engaging.
cia-0000009778:
Laos is the setting for a March 1973 sighting of two American prisoners of war. The heading gives no province, which makes this one of the file's less placed reports. It arrived weeks after the Paris accords and the start of prisoner homecoming.

Unplaced sightings were the hardest to use, yet they were never thrown away. A detail inside the report might later match a camp or a route. Laotian cases stayed open longer than Vietnamese ones as a rule. This file keeps a thin report alive for that later matching, part of Laos's long unfinished accounting.
cia-0000009878:
American prisoners were reportedly detained by the Viet Cong in Tay Ninh province, an August 1966 report states. Tay Ninh, northwest of Saigon near the Cambodian border, held the Viet Cong's southern headquarters region. Prisoners taken near Saigon often vanished into that border system.

Reported detention is weaker than a sighting, and the heading keeps the hedge. Even so, Tay Ninh claims matched the known geography of southern captivity. Officials filed them for comparison with border camp reports. This early southern file shows the prison map forming in 1966, hedges and all, around the capital's own province.
cia-0000010478:
Iran's position in the East-West conflict is set out in a March 1951 CIA paper. Iran bordered the Soviet Union along a long northern frontier and held vast oil fields in the south. That geography made the country a prize neither bloc could ignore.

The paper weighs the shah's government, the nationalist movement, and Soviet pressure as parts of one problem. Weeks later, oil nationalization would seize the world's headlines. Analysts writing in March already framed Iran as a front line. This file preserves that framing at the Cold War's Persian front, before the crisis broke open.
cia-0000012278:
Vladimir I. Toumanoff sat for a debriefing in September 1960, and the CIA record of it survives with its subject partly blanked. Toumanoff was a Russian-born American who had crossed paths with figures in the Penkovsky affair. Debriefers asked him about a matter the released file will not name, blacked out in the title itself.

The record preserves the questions asked and the answers a witness gave while events were fresh. Such accounts formed the human foundation under the case's grander papers. For readers, it shows how the biggest spy case of the era was built partly from small testimonies like this one.
cia-0000012378:
Penkovskiy Case: the whole operation gets its plain title in a CIA overview from June 1963. By then the story had run its arc, from the colonel's first approach to his arrest and trial in Moscow. An overview written that summer could survey the case whole, as its handlers first understood it complete, with the ending known and the costs counted.

Such surveys became the service's own account of its greatest success and sharpest loss. They fixed the narrative officers would teach from for years. For readers, this is the closest thing to a definitive telling by the men who ran him.
cia-0000014778: Communists at a Rockefeller Colloquium are named in a CIA file dated July 3, 1953. The file calls Bernal and Wooster Communist sympathizers at the meeting. Scholars and scientists at such gatherings drew files when their politics seemed left. The record shows how deep the watch reached into lecture halls and labs.
cia-0000015378: A reported sighting of unconventional aircraft fills a CIA file dated September 3, 1955. Reported is the careful word; no one swore to the craft. The fall of 1955 brought a fresh crop of such claims. This file holds one of them, worded with the era's full and careful caution. The September sighting report is held in the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000015478: Sightings from January 19 to May 15, 1954, are gathered in a CIA record of unidentified flying objects. The title's own span is used here, since an older summary gave a shorter one. Four months of reports in one bundle let readers judge pace and pattern. Spring brought a fresh crop of claims, and the agency counted them like the seasons before.
cia-0000016878: How well Vietnamese communist forces could keep fighting in South Vietnam is weighed in a CIA paper dated in 1967. Such papers measured troops, supply, losses, and will to fight. In 1967 the war was growing, and sound judgment of enemy strength carried grave weight. The clipped title marks the paper as an original study, a core task of the agency's analysts.
cia-0000042878:
El Salvador: Update on the Jesuit Killings, number 6, is a CIA record dated April 4, 1990. By the sixth update, the case was months old and still open. The series had become the case's public diary in brief form.

Inside, the latest position of the investigation is recorded. Spring updates dealt with courts, custody, and slow legal motion. The file shows the case settling into its long middle passage. Headlines had faded by the spring, yet the numbered briefs kept coming on schedule. Their steady rhythm is itself evidence of how long justice took in this case.
cia-0000044478:
R. Zamora was interviewed on the killing of the Jesuit priests, in a CIA record dated January 4, 1990. The file is a second interview record under nearly the same title. Zamora spoke for the political opposition in El Salvador.

Inside, his account of the case is given again, weeks into the new year. Repetition let the opposition keep its charge before the public. Each interview sharpened the case against the army's account. The file shows that pressure being maintained on purpose, so the murders could not sink from view while the courts moved at their own slow pace.
cia-0000045978: Diplomats commented on a photograph said to show living American servicemen still held after the Vietnam War. A CIA item dated June 6, 1991, kept their reactions. A claim of living prisoners was the most charged kind in the missing-men dispute. The comments show officials abroad weighing the picture's power against the thin proof behind it.
cia-0000049078: El Salvador's chief of staff gave his views on criticism of the military high command in a CIA item from 1984. The criticism, much of it from Washington, blamed the command for abuses it refused to punish. His answer, preserved here, shows the brass defending its honor while the war's record grew darker.
cia-0000049178: The Joint General Staff headquarters in El Salvador evaluated public comments by a former colonel in a CIA item from 1990. A retired officer speaking out could wound the institution more than any enemy broadcast. The evaluation shows the brass grading one of their own, in the war's last, touchy phase.
cia-0000049278: A House intelligence staffer named Giza sent a follow-up request in 1985 about the Honduran death squad investigation, and a CIA item preserves it. Follow-ups were oversight's teeth: the second letter, asking why the first went unanswered. The item shows a staffer keeping a hard case alive across the years.
cia-0000049378: Guerrillas planning assassinations in El Salvador is the warning carried by declassified CIA document 0000049378, dated November 4, 1988. The item is marked for the Truth Commission and centers on a reported guerrilla plan. It survives as a brief dated notice, its title stating the alleged plot plainly for anyone tracing the agency's late-war Salvadoran reporting.
cia-0000075278: Pro-Cominform Communist Party protest of the Rosenberg sentences is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000075278, dated October 1, 1952. The heading names the protesting party line and the sentences being protested. Readers find a short declassified item from the early Cold War, preserved as a record of organized protest rather than a report on the case itself.
cia-0000096478: Decision of Balram Singh Rai to lead an alternative East Indian party is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000096478, dated July 4, 1964. The heading names Rai and the party move he chose. Readers find a short declassified political item from British Guiana, centered on one leader's decision as recorded in the agency's files.
cia-0000119578:
An April 1966 special report in the CIA's Current Intelligence Weekly takes up the problems of the Czechoslovak Communist Party. The title trails off mid-phrase in the file, but the subject is clear enough: the party that ran Czechoslovakia was in trouble. The report appeared two years before the Prague Spring.

The party's problems, as the agency framed them, grew out of reform pressure inside a system built on tight control. Analysts were watching for cracks in the Soviet bloc, and Czechoslovakia was showing them early. The report matters because it shows the strain was visible long before the famous reform movement of 1968 made headlines around the world.
cia-0000126878: Dated around August 1968, this CIA document studies the short-run economic effects of the Soviet occupation of Czechoslovakia, the heading breaking off. The first bills for the invasion came due within weeks for both sides. The paper measures that early damage as reported. Occupation bills arrived fast in fuel, transport, and broken supply lines, and a short-run study gave officials figures while the political argument over the invasion still raged.
cia-0000126978: A June 1975 CIA National Intelligence Bulletin covers Angola. The bulletin was the agency's daily product for top officials, and this issue took up a colony five months from independence. Rival armies were already racing for the capital, Luanda, as the issue went out. Daily bulletins reached the president's table, so an Angola issue in June placed the colony's race for power before the highest readers in the government that day.
cia-0000132178: Situation report 494, from January 1991, covers political developments including Soviets evacuating, the heading breaking off. Soviet advisers had served in Iraq for years, and their leaving marked Moscow's distance from Saddam. The report tracks that withdrawal. Evacuation items marked a quiet ending: the Soviet military presence built over decades in Iraq was leaving by air while the superpowers still spoke daily.
cia-0000132278: Spanish legislators reaffirming support is the headline of Situation Report 587 in the CIA's Iraq-Kuwait series. The report is dated January 3, 1991. The cause named in the headline is cut short in the record title. The missing words most likely named the United Nations or the United States. Either way, the report notes a public vote of confidence from Spain's parliament in the coalition line during the Gulf crisis.
cia-0000132578: Castro planning a return to the United Nations General Assembly fills item 11 of the CIA's Latin America series. The item is dated September 4, 1960. His 1960 visit to New York had already been a worldwide spectacle of speeches and theater. A return trip promised more of the same stagecraft. The short item tracks the early plans for that appearance.
cia-0000132678: Two items share a CIA paper dated March 2, 1961. The first reports Poland keeping up its long-term credits to Cuba. The second is item 6 of the Latin America series, cut short in the headline. Bloc credits were keeping the Cuban economy afloat through that winter. The short paper covers both halves as they were filed together that day.
cia-0000132778: Washington filed a third paper on Cuba and the Caribbean on August 4, 1960, and this briefing is that entry. Three same-day regional papers show a government watching closely, with Cuba at the center of its concerns. The declassified text survives through the CIA Reading Room mirror at the Internet Archive, cataloged as document 0000132778.
cia-0000135678: Dated 2 November 1960, this Spanish text is one of several 2506 Brigade documents bearing that same date in the declassified release. The brigade was a CIA-trained force of Cuban exiles preparing to land in Cuba. The catalog gives this item no distinguishing subject. Read together, the same-day papers suggest a busy administrative period in the camps; read alone, this one is a dated Spanish record of the brigade, preserved through the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000135978: One declassified cable from the CIA files, dated 1 February 1954, covers the trading of a burnt plane, raised as a possibility in a cable from the Lincoln station. Lincoln was where PBSUCCESS staff worked the Guatemala operation day to day, under code names, in 1953 and 1954. Nothing in the heading promises drama, yet the sheet adds one more firm date and subject to the coup record.
cia-0000136278: A cable of 1 May 1954 survives in the declassified CIA files, dealing with Instruction 15 for broadcast, the high-water mark of the numbered script series. In these files Lincoln names the field station of PBSUCCESS, the covert CIA plan to topple President Arbenz of Guatemala. What survives is the working paper itself, plain proof of how the mission was run from day to day.
cia-0000138978: Russian troop disposition is the subject of this 1946 report. The sample kept here is mostly markings. Distribution stamps limit it to American and British officials. Report numbers and dates fill the rest. The troop data itself does not appear in readable form. No honest summary of unit locations can be given. The entry's value is as an artifact. It shows early Cold War order-of-battle reporting. Its substance stays locked in the original file.
cia-03179878:
Nuclear anxiety opens the Current Intelligence Bulletin dated 15 April 1955. Ambassador Lodge warns that world concern over radiation has grown sharply in recent weeks. Bandung will almost certainly discuss it, he predicts. The peaceful-uses conference and disarmament meetings may all turn into arguments over H-bomb tests. India's moratorium proposal will resurface through Menon.

The Soviet Northern Fleet's submarine force is apparently being strengthened, masked by an auxiliary's voyage. It doubled in 1954 to forty-seven boats, at least twenty of them new long-range types. Japan will submit a Bandung peace proposal based on the UN Charter. Bao Dai directs Diem not to head the Bandung delegation. The Pathet Lao apparently resumes negotiations with the royal government, while Vientiane protests Geneva violations to the control commission. A late item ties one leader's future to Soviet-American relations.
cia-06485478:
Dispatch from Paris, partly sanitized with names redacted, reports reaction in France to the assassination of Dr. Martin Luther King. Its subject line, from a redacted source, calls the impact dramatic and profoundly disturbing. A memorial service for Dr. King in Paris is given a prominent place in the reporting.

Attachments carry much of the substance. One is the printed program of that memorial service, listing prayers, messages from the French churches, scripture lessons, and an anthem by the choir. Another is a 24 April clipping from Le Monde. It reports a press conference announcing a 29 April meeting at the Mutualite in support of Black Power, to be addressed by Jean-Paul Sartre. The dispatch notes confusion over whether Sartre had in fact agreed to speak at that meeting.
cia-06569678:
Biographic profile of Slobodan Milosevic lists him as President of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia since 1997, with a phonetic spelling of his name. The profile states he faced wide popular opposition after more than two months of NATO airstrikes had wrecked Serbia's economy. He is said to have misjudged both the chance and the scale of those attacks.

The profile states there was no sign Milosevic saw his hold on power as slipping. He was counting on divided rivals and his grip on the security forces, it says. Though his formal powers as FRY president were small, he is described as the real decision maker through the party apparatus and a wide patronage system. A personal section reports his father's and mother's suicides, his 1964 law degree in Belgrade, and posts at Technogas and the Bank of Belgrade.
cia-06712178:
Game play aid titled Cartel and Hunter Team sets out turn rules for both sides of a training game. The cartel side acts around a figure named Chapo, with cards for defenses and needs. The hunter side builds intelligence capability, plans collection, and then plans enforcement with police and marina actions.

The cartel turn allows three actions in total, with at most two Chapo defense actions. Moves include placing or moving a defense card, moving Chapo, and placing a needs disc at Chapo's location. Hunters add white pawns to a pool and place them on Nexus, Support, or Lead cards. Face-down cards are flipped, some freely and some on a die roll of 4 to 6. Enforcement pawns can reveal cards or take out a target and its linked cards, under the rules printed.
cia-06795978:
European Review, number EUR ER 86-013, is dated 6 June 1986 and marked Secret. Its briefs list opens with West Germany and the USSR under the heading New Strains After Chernobyl. Other briefs cover Finland's government challenged on nuclear policy, major military maneuvers in Ireland, unpaid workers in Portugal, and a CEMA executive committee meeting.

The Chernobyl brief reports Bonn dissatisfied with Moscow's handling of the accident. A high-ranking West German official told the American ambassador that Bonn was serious about claims for compensation. It would consult other European governments and might even go to the International Court of Justice, he added. Chancellor Kohl restated the claim in a Munich speech and drew a harsh rejoinder from Pravda. Articles in the issue cover Yugoslavia's military party congress, Bulgaria after its party congress, and Turkey's MEKO frigate program.
confessions-of-a-young-man-pg12278:
Confessions of a Young Man, by George Moore, appears here in the dress of its new edition, with a preface addressed to the book itself. Dear little book, Moore writes: belated offspring, out of print for twenty years, seen only in French all that time. It comes back to him like an old love, at once a surprise and a recollection, and he praises its prattle against his will.

A French dedication mourns a dead friend, embalmed in memory like a king in his pyramid. The preface also recalls the master at Médan, who summoned Moore to talk about the Confessions and reproved him at length, sorrowfully, among stained glass and morbid antiquities. It is the law of nature, the master said, for children to devour their parents. Paris scenes fill the confessions themselves.
davila-civil-wars-of-france-1678:
Enrico Caterino Davila, an Italian soldier who served at the side of Henri IV, wrote his Historia delle guerre civili di Francia in 1630. The English translation by Charles Cotterell and William Aylesbury, first made in 1647, appears here in the 1678 printing. Davila had seen the French wars of religion as a young man in the king's service.

His history covers the long struggle between crown, Catholics, and Huguenots that tore France apart. He writes as both witness and analyst, weighing causes with a soldier's knowledge of camps and courts. The book became the classic near-contemporary history of those wars. Its balance and detail kept it in readers' hands for two centuries.
doe-osti-3367768-final-report-for-doe-sc:
Michigan State University final report for DOE partnership grant DE-SC0022078, by John Verboncoeur, studies plasmas in gaps from below a micrometer to hundreds of micrometers across. In such gaps, electron emission from the cathode stops being a correction and becomes the physics. Breakdown shifts from thermionic emission to field emission, then to space-charge-limited flow. Those transitions were not well mapped when the project began.

Particle-in-cell, fluid, and hybrid models with emission physics built in carried the investigation, including how engineered surface shapes steer the discharge. One scaling law held until the scaling parameter passed 64, failing as argon excimer density climbed. Microplasma devices, from displays to medical tools, depend on exactly this regime; the report gives designers modeled transition boundaries instead of rules of thumb.
doe-osti-3626688-final-technical-report-:
Irena Knezevic's final report for award DE-SC0023178 covers work at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. The award ran from August 1, 2022 to December 31, 2025. Its title names the Wigner equation with electromagnetic fields, used to track electron transport in quantum materials. Thin materials such as graphene behave very unlike bulk solids when biased or lit, so new theory was needed.

The team built math and computer tools that couple electrons, driving fields, and quasiparticles such as plasmons and excitons. Three lines of work run through the report. One covers nonlinear optical traits of two-dimensional materials, where graphene sheets patterned with holes can launch plasmon waves. A second covers terahertz behaviour in the same class of materials. A third builds fresh methods for light and matter interplay. Studies of molybdenum disulfide weighed how phonons, charged impurities, and the surface below the film shape conductivity.
ebers-egypt-descriptive-vol-1-1878:
Georg Ebers showed Egypt to the crowd in Vol. 1 of Egypt: Descriptive, Historical, and Picturesque, out in English in 1878. Ebers was both a sage of Egypt and a famed tale smith. Clara Bell turned his German text to English. Great draws fill the tome: the Nile, Cairo, the heaps, and the shrines in rich, warm views.

Text and draw blend to teach as they charm. Crowds in its age learned their Egypt from these pages first. The pair of tomes was the most loved drawn guide of its time. This tome starts the tour.
ebers-egypt-descriptive-vol-2-1878:
Georg Ebers takes the tour up the Nile in Vol. 2 of Egypt: Descriptive, Historical, and Picturesque, out in English in 1878. The first tome gave the north and the great heaps. Here the trek runs south: Luxor, Karnak, the tombs of kings, and isles in the stream, all in the rich draws that made the set a craze in its age.

Ebers knew the land as a sage and loved it as a tale smith. Clara Bell's English prose keeps that warmth. The tome ends the most loved drawn guide of its time. Its charm still works.
europmc-pmc10242978:
Wang and colleagues test whether ferroptosis inducers can strengthen copper-driven cell death in liver cancer, in a 2023 study. Cuproptosis and ferroptosis are two newly defined forms of cell death, one driven by copper and one by iron. How the two pathways interact was unclear when the team began.

They treated liver cancer cells with copper-carrying drugs plus ferroptosis inducers. The combination killed more cancer cells than either approach alone in their tests. The study suggests that pairing metal-based death pathways could yield a stronger treatment for a stubborn cancer.
europmc-pmc10247378:
Martínez-Jiménez and colleagues compare the whole genomes of primary and metastatic solid tumors across many cancer types, in a 2023 study. Cancer that has spread, called metastatic cancer, is what usually kills patients. Yet most genome studies sample early tumors before spread, so the changes that come with spread were poorly mapped.

The team compared thousands of tumor genomes from both stages. They describe which changes appear early and which arise or grow during spread and treatment. The map helps explain how cancers advance and where new treatments might intervene.
europmc-pmc10281978:
Yan and colleagues report that the level of a cystine transporter called SLC7A11 decides how cancer cells answer oxidative stress, in a 2023 study. The transporter shields cancer cells from stress and is found at high levels in many tumors. The team expected more of it to always mean more protection, and found something stranger.

Moderate excess of the transporter helped cancer cells, as expected. Very high levels instead made cells fragile under stress in their tests. The surprise finding reshapes how researchers think about targeting this common cancer shield.
europmc-pmc10772178:
Zhang and co-authors reviewed ischemia-reperfusion injury in 2024, the harm that strikes when blood flow returns. A cut in flow starves tissue; its return can then deepen the damage. The Wnt signal path, a web that steers cell fate, threads through that harm. It cross-talks with many other paths in the web.

One branch of Wnt aids organ recovery, Zhang reports. The other branches make the injury worse. The paths jointly steer cell death, swelling, vessel growth, and scarring. Brain harm and a leaky brain barrier form part of the map too. The review sorts care ideas by which branch they move. Proof spans animal work, care standards, and patient trials.
europmc-pmc1088278:
Nielsen and co-authors scanned human and chimp genes for signs of rapid, favoured change in this 2005 study. Humans and chimps split about five million years ago and differ sharply in body and mind. Their DNA, though, differs only a little. The team compared 13,731 genes between the two species to find ones shaped by positive selection, where helpful changes spread fast.

Genes for smell, taste, and immune defence often carried the signal, they found. So did genes that suppress tumours, control cell death, and aid sperm making, which surprised the team. Brain genes showed little sign of such selection, while testis genes showed a lot. Genes on the X chromosome also stood out. The authors offer gene variant data for the top 50 genes as a resource.
europmc-pmc11219878:
Zhu, Chen, Masson, and Li review the signals that turn stem cells into bone-forming cells in this 2024 paper. Osteoblasts are the cells that build bone. They arise when mesenchymal stem cells, a flexible adult stem cell type, commit to the bone lineage. That commitment is governed by signal pathways and by gene-switch proteins.

Ten pathways are detailed, among them Wnt, BMP, TGF-beta, Hedgehog, and Notch. Key gene switches include Runx2, Osterix, ATF4, and SATB2. Hormones add a further layer of control over the process. Epigenetic factors, which tune gene use without altering DNA, also play critical roles. The review synthesises the latest work on each layer. The authors aim to clarify how commitment, differentiation, bone formation, and upkeep are regulated as one system.
europmc-pmc11542778:
Cross, Choma, and Onofrey examine bias in medical AI and its clinical consequences in this 2024 paper. Biases arise and compound throughout the AI lifecycle, from data collection to publication. In tools that guide clinical decisions, biased output can mean substandard care. It can also perpetuate and worsen longstanding healthcare disparities.

The authors walk through bias at each stage: data and labels, model building, testing, rollout, and publication. Small sample sizes for certain patient groups yield weak performance and clinically empty predictions for them. Missing data bias behaviour too, including diagnosis codes missing non-randomly and social determinants of health that are rarely captured. Labels annotated by experts may carry their hidden biases. The paper maps each trap so developers can design against it.
europmc-pmc1318478:
Bordone and co-authors linked an aging gene to insulin release in mice in 2006. Sirt1 is the mammal version of a known aging pathway gene. Pancreatic beta cells store and release insulin. The team tested whether Sirt1 controls that release.

Sirt1 boosted insulin secretion by repressing a gene called UCP2. It binds the UCP2 promoter directly to quiet it. Cutting Sirt1 raised UCP2 and blunted insulin output. Cells then failed to raise energy currency after glucose. Removing UCP2 restored secretion despite low Sirt1. Food deprivation also raised UCP2 in mouse pancreas.
europmc-pmc1331978:
Maksakova and co-authors reviewed retroviral elements and mouse mutations in 2006. The lab mouse is a core model for human biology. Its mutation pattern differs sharply from the human one. Transposable element insertions cause about 0.1 percent of new human mutations.

In mice the figure runs one hundred times higher. Active endogenous retroviruses drive that ongoing activity. Insertions alter gene expression and create varied mutations. The review covers how these elements interact with host cells. Maksakova argues the mouse genome is still losing its arms race against invaders. It appeared in PLoS Genetics in 2006. Mice and men share most genes, but not these rates of change.
europmc-pmc2062478:
Begun and a large team sequenced whole genomes of the fruit fly Drosophila simulans in 2007. They used shotgun sequencing of several inbred lines. Comparing variation within the species with differences from two close relatives shows how natural selection shapes genomes. The relatives were Drosophila melanogaster and Drosophila yakuba. Their goal was a population-level view of polymorphism and divergence.

They found large, previously unknown swings in variation and divergence along chromosome arms. The X chromosome carried less variation and diverged faster than other chromosomes. The team listed functional genome elements shaped by adaptive evolution. They also mapped base composition patterns in coding and non-coding DNA. The data set offers a rich resource for studying adaptation and functional variation in this species.
europmc-pmc2098778:
Cho reviewed cancer-linked microRNAs, called oncomiRs, in 2007. MicroRNAs are tiny RNA molecules, about 22 units long, that regulate genes after they are copied. Some drive cancer growth, while others suppress it. The review covers their discovery, how they act on target messages, and their use in diagnosis and prognosis across human cancers.

Several examples show the range of effects. MiR-15 and miR-16 trigger cell death by targeting the survival gene Bcl2. The miR-17-92 cluster promotes tumour formation through the gene E2F1. MiR-34a suppresses nerve tumour growth by lowering E2F3 protein. Chromosome swaps in tumours can free the growth gene HMGA2 from let-7 control. Profiling oncomiR patterns in cancers has also produced diagnostic and prognostic signatures, patterns that help classify disease and predict outcome.
europmc-pmc2124878:
Thomas Wood Hastings and Walter L. Niles of Cornell's clinical pathology department cultured sputum from common non-tuberculous chest infections in 1911. Their focus is lobar and broncho-pneumonia. Using Kitasato's careful method for handling sputum, they found pure infections rarer than assumed.

Only thirty-eight per cent of infections below the voice box proved pure. Lobar pneumonia could yield sputum with no pneumococci at all, and organisms other than the pneumococcus can undoubtedly cause it. The germs behind respiratory inflammation also shift markedly from year to year. Micrococcus catarrhalis, usually dismissed as a harmless second arrival, can take on disease-causing power, and probably does so often. Their mid-paper tables sort the streptococci into fine types by length and blood action. Readers get a corrective census of chest germs, warning against blaming one usual suspect for every pneumonia.
europmc-pmc2125178:
James W. Jobling and William Petersen of Columbia proposed a mechanism for anaphylatoxin in 1914, the fifteenth of their ferment studies. Their starting fact is that serum's protective fatty substances, the unsaturated lipoids that act as antitrypsin, can be soaked out of serum. Kaolin, starch, agar, and bacteria all absorb them from guinea pig, rabbit, and horse serum.

On their theory, an anaphylatoxin is simply a serum partly stripped this way. Diphtheria toxin and cobra venom fit the scheme, both draining antitrypsin, perhaps through a liking for lipoids. The soaking follows strict quantity rules: adsorbent in very large or very small amounts works least well. Bacteria pretreated with serum or oils lose the soaking power, and serum-treated bacteria grow tougher against trypsin. Readers get allergic poison reimagined as a missing shield.
europmc-pmc2125278:
Henry Field Smyth reported in 1915 on what happens when bacteria meet living animal tissue in culture, across more than eleven hundred cultures made in 1913 and 1914. The work looks both ways: how germs grow in tissue's company, and what the tissue's plasma might contribute to antibody making.

Diphtheria bacilli gave the prettiest result. In light or moderate plantings their colonies clustered around the individual tissue fragments and nowhere else: never in clear plasma away from tissue, never in tissue-free controls. In box cultures each fragment sat like a planet with satellite colonies. Germs sown from strong bouillon grew more freely, and comparative work with other cell types and media was planned. Readers get tissue culture turned into a meeting ground where each side's needs show.
europmc-pmc2125378:
C. H. Lenhart fed tadpoles dried thyroid gland in 1915, varying both the amount and the iodine richness of the gland, and watched development obey the dose. Differentiation comes early in proportion to quantity fed or to the iodine percentage. The gland's iodine, not iodine in other forms, carries the effect: plain iodine does nothing.

Overshoot destroys the benefit. At the largest doses and richest glands, metabolism races until the animals waste rapidly and die before they can change much. In the strongest dishes every tadpole was dead within eleven to nineteen days. Cold chills the effect, probably by lowering metabolism; cracker crumbs blunt it by feeding the animal something besides its own tissues. Differentiation peaks, one dish showed within four days, in step with iodine strength. Readers get metamorphosis as a dial, with overdose marked in deaths.
europmc-pmc2125478:
Andreas Tanberg mapped the thyroid-parathyroid relationship in 1916 through feeding and removal experiments, largely in cats. A heavy meat diet swells the thyroid; no definite swelling of the parathyroids under the same diet could be established. The parathyroid's permission, though, proves necessary for the thyroid's response.

Where parathyroid insufficiency exists, even silently, meat feeding no longer swells the thyroid. Where meat has already swollen it, removing enough parathyroid tissue makes the swelling disappear and the gland resume its ordinary look. After parathyroid removal no thyroid swelling occurs, and in chronic tetany the thyroid seems rather to shrink despite meat. Removing the thyroid entirely leaves the parathyroids structurally unchanged for years; leftover thyroid scraps, though, can swell into compact tissue that mimics parathyroid. The glands, Tanberg concludes, are independent organs, but not indifferent neighbors. Readers get a two-gland system with the dependency arrows drawn.
europmc-pmc2130978:
Philip D. McMaster and Robert Elman proved directly that bile pigments are absorbed from the intestine and return to the liver. Their paper is the third in a urobilin series, in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1925. Earlier work from the laboratory had offered indirect evidence for such a circulation of pigment; this paper feeds the pigments themselves.

Pure bilirubin fed by mouth to dogs, like whole bile, greatly increased the bilirubin in the liver's bile. Pure bilirubin placed straight into the duodenum of tubed dogs did the same. Control feedings of bile salts raised the bile quantity but changed the pigment output not at all, which separates flow from pigment. Dogs whose bile was diverted away from the gut made pigment-free bile; fed pure urobilin, they promptly showed urobilin in their bile. The gut-to-liver return of bile pigment, long inferred, stands demonstrated.
europmc-pmc2131078:
S. Burt Wolbach and Percy R. Howe mapped what the body does when fat-soluble vitamin A is taken away, in white rats and with an eye to man. Their paper appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1925. The changes concern the epithelial tissues, the linings and coverings of the body.

Across the respiratory tract, the alimentary tract, the eyes and their glands, and the urinary and genital passages, the normal lining is replaced by stratified, keratinizing epithelium, a skin-like sheet. The replacement grows from focal proliferation of cells of the original epithelium, not by conversion of existing cells. Young rats respond more promptly than adults. Growth activity of the epithelium is not diminished but greatly augmented, and in a few animals the new growth hinted at neoplastic behavior. A missing food factor, the plates argue, can rewrite the architecture of whole organ systems.
europmc-pmc2131278:
Theobald Smith and John Nelson wrote part two of their studies on a paratyphoid infection in guinea pigs, published in 1927. A breeding stock had passed from an epidemic phase into a quiet endemic phase. They asked what kept the germ alive in the stock, and whether the germ itself had grown weaker or stronger over time.

Tests showed no clear rise or fall in the germ's virulence. The organism persisted within the breeding stock, and the sows seemed the chief source, passing it to their young. Carriage in the dung was fairly brief and often went with the germ lodged in the spleen. The authors suggest the shift came from the weeding out of animals with low natural resistance, plus a slow adjustment of the germ to its host population.
europmc-pmc2140578:
William Cole, at Lake Forest College, tested the tropism theory on the horseshoe crab Limulus in a 1923 paper. Animals with one side's eyes removed or covered walk in circles, circus movements. Cole used young Limulus, twenty to sixty millimeters across, and measured their turning under set light strengths.

In the laboratory the animals are positively phototropic, circling toward the normal side when the middle and opposite side eyes are out. Fright, hunger, contact response, and light-driven motion can modify or erase the phototropism. Turning per centimeter rose directly with light intensity, while circle size shrank, and speed rose as well. The tropism theory, Cole holds, explains the reactions satisfactorily.
europmc-pmc2206478:
Bozza and colleagues profiled blood cytokines in severe sepsis patients in 2007, hunting for markers of severity. Sepsis is a whole-body response to infection that can fail organs and kill. Doctors lack accurate, quick biomarkers to group patients by risk. The team studied 60 patients in four tertiary hospitals. A multiplex assay measured 17 cytokines, immune signalling proteins, in each blood sample at once.

Nine cytokines, including IL-6, IL-8 and IL-10, ran significantly higher in septic shock than in severe sepsis without shock. IL-8 and MCP-1 tracked organ failure scores best on day one. IL-6, IL-8 and G-CSF levels in the first 24 hours predicted whether organ failure would worsen by day three. Several cytokines predicted early death well. In adjusted analysis, only MCP-1 independently predicted prognosis.
europmc-pmc2435278:
Xi, Ramirez, and Dimopoulos studied how the dengue mosquito fights the virus it carries in 2008. Aedes aegypti spreads dengue fever to humans, yet the mosquito itself resists the virus with its innate immune system. Working from the newly read mosquito genome, the team combined gene activity scans with gene-silencing tests.

One defence pathway, the Toll pathway, stood out as a real controller of dengue infection. Several Toll-linked genes changed activity after infection, and silencing pathway parts altered how well the virus did. The mosquito's natural gut microbes also mattered. They appeared to keep the Toll pathway lightly primed, so infected mosquitoes with normal microbes resisted better. The authors said this is the first full account of this mosquito's anti-dengue defence, distinct from the fruit fly systems studied before.
europmc-pmc2553778:
Redmond, Crane, and Menz established reference values in 2008 for the Foot Posture Index, a clinical score of how a standing foot is shaped. Clinicians use the index to classify foot type, but no normal ranges existed to judge a score against. The authors pooled raw data from nine research groups, totalling 1,648 observations, and derived norms from the healthy subset.

A slightly pronated foot, rolling gently inward, proved to be the normal resting posture, with an average score of plus 4. Scores followed a U-shape with age: children and older adults scored higher than mid-life adults. Sex made no difference, and body mass index showed no link to the score. Patients with high-arched feet from nerve or unknown causes scored clearly apart from the norms.
europmc-pmc2564978:
Ji and colleagues tested in 2008 whether restoring a small RNA called miR-34 could tame stomach cancer cells that had lost p53, a master tumour suppressor. MiR-34 normally works downstream of p53, and it targets genes that help cancer stem cells renew themselves and survive. The team put miR-34 back into Kato III gastric cancer cells, which carry mutant p53, and measured the effects.

Restoration lowered the target proteins Bcl-2, Notch, and HMGA2. Cells grew more slowly, stalled in the G1 resting phase, and showed more activation of caspase-3, an executioner of cell suicide. They also became more sensitive to chemotherapy when their Bcl-2 level was high. Most strikingly, treated cells largely lost the ability to form tumorspheres, the floating balls that signal stem-like self-renewal.
europmc-pmc2629778:
Corander, Marttinen, Sirén, and Tang introduced enhanced statistical tools in 2008 for their BAPS software, which infers the genetic structure of populations. Bayesian methods in BAPS sort individuals into genetic clusters, but rising data volumes and more complex questions were outgrowing the existing models. The new version adds an array of modelling options.

Users can now fit mixture models with a chosen number of clusters. They can also estimate interbreeding, called admixture, under a model that respects genetic linkage. Linkage is the tendency of nearby variants to travel together. The software can flag alleles in an individual that come from a different ancestry than the surrounding genome. It also lets researchers compare pre-specified hypotheses about population structure directly using Bayes' theorem. Computations can now be spread across several computers through a script interface.
europmc-pmc2644678:
Eden and colleagues presented in 2009 a free web tool, called GOrilla, that helps biologists make sense of long ranked lists of genes. Modern experiments often rank thousands of genes, for example by how much their activity changed. The Gene Ontology is a standard set of labels for gene jobs, and the question is which jobs cluster near the top of a list.

Older tools forced users to split their list into a chosen set and a background set first. GOrilla skips that step and scans the whole ranking directly. Its math gives an exact measure of how unlikely each cluster is by chance, without slow trial runs. Results come back as a tree diagram that shows how the winning labels relate to each other. A full scan of thousands of genes takes only seconds.
europmc-pmc2654478:
Vlachos and fellow specialists issued shared guidance in 2008 on Diamond Blackfan anaemia, a rare inherited failure to make red blood cells. The Participants of Sixth Annual Daniella Maria Arturi International Consensus Conference met to settle how the disease should be found and treated. It strikes about seven babies per million, usually in the first year of life.

The disease stems from early red cell makers that die too readily, and it often comes with birth defects and a raised cancer risk. The group reviewed the three main treatments: steroid drugs, regular blood transfusions, and stem cell transplants. They set out who should get which option, and how care should be planned over a lifetime. Because the disease is rare, much advice rests on expert judgment rather than trials, which the authors state plainly.
europmc-pmc2695778:
Lindgren and colleagues, with the Giant Consortium and partner groups, merged 16 genome studies in 2009 to find genes controlling where the body stores fat. Belly fat matters more for diabetes and heart disease than total weight, yet its genetics lagged behind. The combined scan covered 38,580 adults measured for waist size and waist-to-hip ratio.

Twenty-six candidate variants went forward for checking in up to 70,689 more people. Three regions confirmed. Two, near genes called TFAP2B and MSRA, moved waist size, apparently through overall fatness. The third, near LYPLAL1, shifted waist-to-hip ratio in women only, a pure fat-distribution effect. The split is the point: some genes make people fatter, while others decide where the fat goes, and the second kind can harm even at the same total weight.
europmc-pmc2714578:
Wassmer and co-authors mapped in 2009 how the retromer complex, a protein coat that sorts cargo inside cells, links sorting to transport. Retromer pulls chosen cargo from early endosomes, small sorting sacs, back to the trans-Golgi network, a shipping hub. Mammals were known to use several sorting nexins, proteins that bend membranes, but how they paired up stayed unclear.

They found four mammalian retromers, each with a distinct mix of sorting nexins one, two, five, and six. Two nexins bind the dynactin activator of dynein, a motor that hauls cargo along cell tracks, which sets the layout of the network. Another nexin binds a tether at the Golgi hub, which completes the route.
europmc-pmc2736378:
Welch and co-authors tested in 2009 which design choices control how much protein a synthetic gene makes in E. coli bacteria. Synthetic genes are now a standard route to make therapeutic and research proteins, but redesign rules rested on little direct evidence. They synthesized two sets of forty genes for two valuable proteins, varying only in synonymous codons, alternate spellings for the same building block.

Protein output ranged from undetectable to thirty percent of all cell protein, driven strongly by codons for a subset of amino acids. Favorable codons were those read by transfer RNAs that stay most charged during amino acid starvation, not the codons commonest in highly expressed native genes. New genes designed by their model performed as predicted.
europmc-pmc2745878:
Terwilliger described in 2003 an automated method for building protein models. It builds the main chain into an X-ray electron-density map. It works by template matching and iterative fragment extension. Model building is the first reading of the map in terms of atom positions, and at low resolution errors are hard for later refinement to fix. Manual building can take a day or far longer when maps are unclear.

The method finds likely helices, strands, and other fragments by matching templates against the map, then extends fragments step by step to trace the chain. It builds on earlier tracing and fragment-fitting methods but automates the search decisions. Faster automated building speeds the whole structure determination process, especially for difficult, low-resolution cases.
europmc-pmc2760878:
Wu and Eisen presented AMPHORA in 2008, an automated pipeline for phylogenomic inference that builds organism trees from many protein markers at once. Microbial classification long rested on a single ribosomal RNA gene, the gold standard, yet single genes can misplace distant organisms due to composition bias. Whole genomes now supply every protein gene, but cloning and aligning many markers by hand was slow.

AMPHORA automates marker choice, alignment, and tree building for large data sets, using protein sequences that are less prone to nucleotide bias. It lets researchers corroborate ribosomal trees with genome-wide evidence at scale. The pipeline aims to make robust, multi-gene phylogeny a routine step in microbial systematics and ecology rather than a bespoke effort.
europmc-pmc2816178:
Thornton and Woods reviewed primary microcephaly in 2009, an inherited condition where the brain grows far too small before birth while its structure stays normal. Studying it offers a clean window on how the fetal brain builds its outer layer, the cerebral cortex, which is unusually large in humans.

Eight gene locations and five genes had been pinned to the condition when the review was written. Surprisingly, every known protein from those genes spends part of the cell cycle at the centrosome, a hub that organizes cell division. One gene, ASPM, accounts for about half of all cases. The authors argue the centrosome acts as a meeting point where many control pathways for early brain growth converge.
europmc-pmc2848978:
Hackl, Grillari, and a large team hunted in 2010 for microRNAs, tiny gene regulators, that change consistently as human cells age. Single studies had tied scattered microRNAs to aging, but no shared signature had emerged. The team profiled seven aging models: four cell types aged in dishes, plus foreskin, stem cells, and immune cells taken from young and old donors.

Four microRNAs fell across nearly every model. MiR-17 dropped in all seven, and three close relatives dropped in most. As they fell, some of their target genes rose, notably p21, a brake on cell division long tied to cell aging. The authors propose the four as shared markers of human cellular aging.
europmc-pmc2868878:
Slater, Spanlang, Sanchez-Vives, and Blanke showed in 2010 that a person can feel a virtual body as their own without any matching touch. Earlier illusions, like the rubber hand trick, needed touch seen and felt at the same moment. Here men put on immersive virtual reality and saw a life-sized female body from its own viewpoint, standing where their body should be.

That first-person view alone created a strong sense of owning the virtual body, reported on questionnaires. When the virtual body was threatened, the men's heart rates slowed in the classic fear response, as if their own body were at risk. The result shows vision from inside a body can outweigh touch cues, and it gives science a tool for probing how the brain builds the sense of self.
europmc-pmc2873978:
Patel, Bhattacharya, and Butte ran in 2010 a scan of the environment for type 2 diabetes modeled on genome-wide scans. Instead of testing genes one study at a time, they tested two hundred sixty-six measured exposures, from nutrients to pollutants, against diabetes in national survey cohorts. Diabetes status came from fasting blood sugar, and models adjusted for age, sex, weight, ethnicity, and income level.

Two signals survived strict checks and repeated in separate cohorts. A breakdown product of the banned pesticide heptachlor raised the odds of diabetes notably per step up in exposure. A form of vitamin E called gamma-tocopherol also tracked higher odds, a surprise for a nutrient often seen as protective. The pilot proved the scan approach can flag overlooked environmental suspects.
europmc-pmc2936378:
Van Herck and co-authors systematically reviewed pay-for-performance schemes in health care in a 2010 article, gathering studies published over roughly two decades. Such schemes pay doctors or hospitals extra for meeting quality targets and vary widely in design.

More than a hundred evaluation studies offered a large but cautious body of evidence, strongest for clinical quality and fairness of care. Far less was known about teamwork, patient focus, or value for money. Results hinged on how schemes were built and on local context. The review maps which design choices seem to help or hinder.
europmc-pmc2944278:
Agusti and the ECLIPSE investigators described the wide variety of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in a 2010 cohort study. The lung condition mixes airway damage with problems elsewhere in the body, and patients differ greatly.

Over two thousand stable patients were compared with smokers whose lungs tested normal and with people who never smoked. Patients carried more other illnesses than controls at every severity stage. Standard airflow grades matched poorly with breathlessness, exercise ability, flare-ups, and general health, and values spread widely within each grade. Even severe airflow blockage sometimes came with few symptoms, underlining the condition's patchwork nature.
europmc-pmc3014878:
Szarka and colleagues ran a 2010 study of immune signal molecules in blood. They compared healthy pregnancies with preeclampsia. That dangerous complication of pregnancy is marked by body-wide inflammation. Single markers had given a patchy picture.

Sixty patients, sixty healthy pregnant women, and about sixty non-pregnant controls were compared using a multiplex array plus targeted tests. Normal pregnancy already shifted the circulating mix, and preeclampsia shifted it further in characteristic directions. The team related the patterns to clinical features and to markers of vessel activation, oxidative stress, and debris from the placenta.
europmc-pmc3044678:
Wang and coauthors tested in 2011 whether the switch from juvenile to adult growth in trees uses the same small RNA controls known from small annual plants. In annuals, one tiny RNA is high in seedlings and falls as the plant matures, while a second rises. The team tracked both RNAs in several woody species with clear young and adult forms, including eucalyptus, acacia, ivy, and oak.

The same opposing pattern appeared in the trees. Forcing a poplar hybrid to keep making the juvenile RNA held back its target genes and the adult RNA, and the trees stayed juvenile far longer than normal. The result shows the phase change clock is shared across plant lineages that split long ago. Breeders and foresters who need to speed or delay maturity can use that shared switch as a handle.
europmc-pmc3252278:
Hisato Kobayashi and colleagues produced single-letter-resolution maps of DNA methylation in mouse eggs and sperm, in this 2012 paper in PLoS Genetics. Methylation patterns are rewritten in the germline and carry imprinting, the parent-of-origin marks that control some genes. Using whole-genome bisulfite sequencing alongside RNA sequencing, the team compared the two gametes directly.

The maps turned out strikingly different. In eggs, methylation tracked with gene activity, concentrating in the bodies of active genes. In sperm, methylation covered nearly everything except CpG-rich islands, and promoter methylation ran opposite to expression. The comparison found over sixteen hundred regions methylated differently between egg and sperm, beyond the known imprinting control regions, and about half resisted the wiping that follows fertilization. Most egg-specific marks needed the protein Dnmt3L, splitting egg methylation into two functional types.
europmc-pmc3306778:
Kool led an international team that pooled data on a childhood brain tumor called medulloblastoma, reporting in 2012. It is the most common malignant brain tumor of childhood, yet studies disagreed on how many distinct kinds exist. Gene based work suggested the tumor is really several diseases wearing one name, so the team merged results from seven studies covering hundreds of tumors.

The combined data support exactly four core subgroups, labeled WNT, SHH, Group 3, and Group 4. Each group differs sharply in gene activity, DNA changes, patient age and sex patterns, and survival chances. A second large group of tumors, sorted with a simpler tissue test, gave nearly the same picture. The authors say future trials should treat and study each subgroup on its own terms.
europmc-pmc3320478:
Hayes led a companion review on how West Nile virus spreads and circulates, published in 2005. Since its 1999 arrival in New York, the virus had caused more than sixteen thousand reported cases in the United States. Birds carry the virus in their blood, and Culex mosquitoes pick it up and pass it to people, horses, and other animals.

The review explains what drives the intensity of spread in a place, from mosquito numbers and feeding habits to local weather and human behavior. Reported infection rates in hard hit neighborhoods were surprisingly low, meaning whole populations remain vulnerable in later seasons. Rarer routes, including blood transfusion, organ transplants, and infection before birth, are also covered. The authors gather the first five years of Western Hemisphere experience into one account of the virus's ecology.
europmc-pmc3346778:
Braun and colleagues tested how steady urine markers of two common chemical exposures are across pregnancy, in a 2012 study. Phthalates, used in plastics and personal care products, and bisphenol A, used in can linings and plastics, may affect mother and child health. Most studies measure them once, in a single urine sample, which is only fair if levels hold steady over time.

The team collected over a thousand samples from one hundred thirty seven women, before and during pregnancy. Average levels looked similar in both periods, but steadiness varied sharply by chemical. Two phthalate markers were moderately stable, so one sample sorted women's exposure reasonably well. Bisphenol A and several other markers swung widely, meaning one sample can badly misclassify exposure. The authors advise repeat sampling for the jumpier chemicals in pregnancy research.
europmc-pmc3366978:
Linden and colleagues piloted a therapy in which people with depression learn to regulate their own emotion circuits using real-time brain scanning. Many patients respond incompletely to drugs or talking therapy, so the team tested whether neurofeedback from functional MRI could add a self-directed route to improvement.

Eight patients completed four neurofeedback sessions, learning to boost activity in areas involved in positive emotion, including the ventrolateral prefrontal cortex and insula, while viewing their own brain signals. Their scores on a standard depression rating scale improved significantly. A comparison group using the same mental strategies without feedback did not improve. The authors call for blinded randomised trials to rule out placebo effects.
europmc-pmc3373078:
Chadha and colleagues reported in 2006 that Nipah virus had caused a 2001 outbreak of brain fever in Siliguri, India. The virus had never been detected in India before. Patients in four hospitals, their family contacts, and medical staff fell ill with fever and confusion during January and February of that year.

Tests at the time found no culprit, and Japanese encephalitis was first blamed. Years later, stored samples were checked because the Siliguri cases resembled Nipah outbreaks in nearby Bangladesh. The re-analysis linked the outbreak to Nipah, a bat-borne virus that killed a large share of its victims elsewhere. The finding extended the virus's known map into India.
europmc-pmc3482178:
Keshari and co-authors studied how inflammatory signals push white blood cells to cast out DNA traps, in a 2012 PLoS ONE paper. The traps, webs of DNA and germ-killing proteins, catch microbes but can also harm tissue. The team worked with patients who had a whole-body inflammatory state, a dangerous condition that can follow injury or infection even without germs.

Blood from those patients carried more trap material, and their isolated cells made extra traps and reactive chemicals. Plasma from patients made healthy cells do the same. Three inflammatory signals drove the effect, and blocking them cut trap release. Keshari's group shows these signals act through two enzymes in the cells. The chain helps explain tissue damage in severe inflammation.
europmc-pmc3523078:
Changing daily habits can dissolve metabolic syndrome, and Kazue Yamaoka and Toshiro Tango measure how well in 2012. Their meta-analysis gathers randomized trials from 1966 to 2011 with at least six months of follow-up, comparing lifestyle programs against usual education or no treatment.

The share of patients whose metabolic syndrome resolves runs about twice as high in lifestyle groups as in controls. Five of the six syndrome components improve significantly: blood sugar, waist size, triglycerides, and both blood pressures. HDL cholesterol is the exception. Programs aim at weight loss through diet and activity. The pooled evidence, checked by sensitivity analyses, supports structured lifestyle change as treatment, not just advice.
europmc-pmc3605278:
Clémentine Schilte and colleagues followed chikungunya patients for three years in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2013. The mosquito-borne virus struck the island of La Réunion in 2006 with fever and joint pain, and doctors there enrolled 180 patients during the acute illness. Chikungunya was known to linger, but the long joint story needed a prospective record. Patients returned for checks at four, six, fourteen, and thirty-six months.

Across the three years, sixty percent suffered joint pain at some point, mostly in waves of relapse and relief. The typical pattern hit many joints, usually on both sides of the body, with swelling, deep tiredness, and low mood riding along; most called it highly disabling. Being over thirty-five, or still aching at four months, predicted the long course. Blood tests showed none of the markers of autoimmune joint disease, setting this pain apart from rheumatoid arthritis.
europmc-pmc3608878:
Jianguo Xia and colleagues wrote a tutorial on biomarker hunting in metabolomics for the journal Metabolomics in 2013. Metabolomics, the census of small molecules in a sample, is often aimed at finding markers that flag disease early, predict its course, or sort patients by risk. Papers in the field, the authors complain, report their candidate markers loosely. Few give sensitivity or specificity, and fewer still show the standard accuracy plot, the ROC curve, with its uncertainty range. Almost none publish the model behind the curve.

Part one teaches ROC craft from the ground up: building the curve, reading the area beneath it whole or in the clinically relevant part, and attaching confidence intervals. Part two moves to the multi-marker models metabolomics needs, comparing statistical and machine-learning recipes and their traps. The goal is a shared reporting language so markers can survive the trip from discovery papers to clinic use.
europmc-pmc3647278:
Skin disease and heart danger move together in a 2013 meta-analysis by Armstrong, Harskamp and Armstrong in the Journal of the American Heart Association. Psoriasis is a long-term swelling skin condition, and past studies hinted it raised the odds of heart attack and stroke. The team searched three large data banks for studies in English from 1980 to early 2012 and pooled what they found.

Nine studies covered 201,239 people with mild psoriasis and 17,415 with severe psoriasis. Mild disease still tied to higher risk of heart attack and stroke once other factors were counted. Severe disease tied to higher risk of heart death as well, with the heart attack risk up by about seven-tenths. The authors put the yearly toll at about 11,500 extra major heart events and call for fuller counts of other risk factors in future work.
europmc-pmc3651278:
How active older adults really are is less clear than health drives assume, Sun, Norman and While find in a 2013 systematic review in BMC Public Health. Activity guards against disease, keeps older people self-reliant and lifts life quality. The team searched for studies since 2000 that gave activity levels for adults aged 60 and over who live at home, plus the share who met set activity goals.

Fifty-three papers made the cut. The share meeting the goals ran from 2.4 percent to 83.0 percent across studies, a spread too wide to settle the question. Goal wording and ways of counting activity shifted from study to study, which bent the results. Older age bands moved less than younger ones, and women moved less than men, above all in free time. The authors call for random samples and one shared, sound way to count.
europmc-pmc3653278:
Joined-up care needs a map, and Valentijn, Schepman, Opheij and Bruijnzeels draw one in a 2013 article in the International Journal of Integrated Care. First-contact care, they argue, is the natural hub for joining services. Yet loose wording around joined-up care had blocked clear study of it. Their method mixed data bank searches, hand searches and talks with field workers.

The map weds the jobs of first-contact care to the layers of joined-up care. Care centred on the person and care aimed at whole populations act as guiding rules. Joining works at three levels: the clinic, the professions and offices, and the whole system. Shared tools and shared values keep the levels tied. The map is a first step toward a shared grasp of the layers.
europmc-pmc3656778:
A national weight program for veterans landed unevenly, and Damschroder and Lowery ask why in a 2013 Implementation Science study. The program, called MOVE! in the text, was rolled out to veterans' medical centres across the United States, where weight problems run high. The pair used a theory framework of 31 factors, called CFIR in the text, to sort facts from five centres picked for wide spread in success and place.

Talks with 24 staff and leaders fed the check. Ten factors split high- and low-success centres sharply. Six of the ten sat inside the centres: staff networks, felt need for change, program rank, goal feedback, learning climate and leader backing. Their step-by-step method may help other teams judge why sound programs stall or fly.
europmc-pmc3665478:
A web server judges whether a single protein change is likely to harm, Capriotti, Calabrese, Fariselli, Martelli, Altman and Casadio present in a 2013 BMC Genomics article. Their method, SNPs&GO, reads a protein's sequence, its shape when known, and its job labels from a job bank. It was built to flag single amino acid swaps that tie to human disease. The server version runs two updated engines, one sequence-based and one shape-based.

On a balanced test set of over 38,000 swaps, the sequence engine scored 81 percent accuracy. On the near 6,600 swaps with known shapes, the shape engine scored 84 percent. On a fresh blind set, the two scored 79 and 83 percent. The server is free online and folds sequence, shape, family history and job facts into one call. For labs drowning in variant lists, it offers a first sort.
europmc-pmc3687078:
Mellins and Malee review what is known about the mental health of children and teenagers who have lived with HIV since birth. Treatment has turned perinatal HIV into a chronic condition. Questions about behaviour, mood, learning, and psychiatric illness have moved to the front.

Rates of psychiatric problems run above those in the general population. Yet HIV itself may not be the whole cause. Young people exposed to the virus but not infected show similar difficulties in some studies. Family stability, illness burden, and poverty all shape outcomes. The reviewers call for proven mental health interventions, tested properly and delivered where most affected youth live, in lower-income countries.
europmc-pmc3695978:
Moles and colleagues charted the bacteria in the first stool of premature babies and followed how the gut community changed over the first weeks of life. They sampled meconium and later feces from fourteen preterm infants in hospital. They combined culture methods with DNA-based profiling.

Meconium carried its own distinct community, dominated by Staphylococcus and other Firmicutes, rather than being sterile. Later samples shifted toward Proteobacteria, with Enterococcus and gut bacteria such as Escherichia and Klebsiella becoming common by the third week. One genus, Serratia, tracked with greater immaturity and with hospital factors such as antibiotic treatment and breathing support. The authors argue that colonization starts from a specific early community, not a blank slate.
europmc-pmc3722478:
Przemyslaw Kardas, Pawel Lewek, and Michal Matyjaszczyk published a review of systematic reviews in Frontiers in Pharmacology in 2013 on why patients do or do not take their medicines as prescribed. They searched six databases for reviews from 2000 to 2009 that named factors behind non-adherence to medicines for home use.

They kept 51 reviews covering 19 disease areas, and pulled out 771 separate factor items. Most items concerned day-to-day taking of medicine; only 47 concerned sticking with it over time. Clear factors fell into groups tied to money and social position, the care team and system, the illness, the treatment, and the patient. Because definitions and measures varied so much, the authors say no single patient's adherence is easy to predict.
europmc-pmc3765378:
Sophie Billingham, Amy Whitehead, and Steven Julious published an audit in BMC Medical Research Methodology in 2013 on sample sizes in British pilot and feasibility trials. Such early trials test whether a bigger trial can work, yet little guidance exists on how many participants they need. The team mined a national research network database.

From 513 studies screened, 79 trials qualified. Half were labeled pilot trials, about a third feasibility, and some both. Most had two arms. Pilot trials planned a median of about 30 participants per arm, against about 36 for feasibility trials. Publicly funded pilot trials ran larger than industry ones. None of the summaries justified the chosen size. The authors say every study needs a size justification, though early trials may not need a formal calculation.
europmc-pmc3772378:
Sefaattin Tongay and a large group of co-authors reported a physics study in Scientific Reports in 2013 on light emission from two-dimensional semiconductors. Single-layer materials such as molybdenum disulfide can emit light, and defects in the crystal can trap charge carriers and the energy packets called excitons. The team created missing-anion defects in controlled amounts with alpha-particle exposure or heating.

A new emission peak appeared below the main band, and overall light emission grew stronger as defects were added. Oddly, both effects vanished in a vacuum, which points to a role for molecules from the air sitting at the defect sites. The authors draw a sharp lesson: brightness at room temperature cannot be trusted as a sign of crystal quality in these materials. They also propose defect engineering as a way to tune optical properties.
europmc-pmc3846878:
Min Zhao, Qingguo Wang, Quan Wang, Peilin Jia, and Zhongming Zhao review software for copy number changes in BMC Bioinformatics in 2013. Such changes leave a genome with too many or too few copies of a large stretch. Next generation sequencing now lets labs spot them from raw read data.

Older chip methods set the prior standard but read at coarse scale. A wave of new tools has grown up around sequence data, for both whole genomes and just the coding parts. The review sorts the tools by how they work and weighs strong and weak points of each. It closes with advice on where tool building should go next, so detection grows sharper and more even across the genome.
europmc-pmc3883678:
Ovarian cancer sphere cells are the focus of a PLoS One study, dated 2014 in the record, by Jianqun Liao and co-authors. Some ovarian cancer cells grow as floating spheres and act like stem cells. Such cells are blamed for spread and drug resistance, the main reasons this cancer kills.

Sphere cells from cancer lines and patient fluid proved potent. A few thousand seeded full tumors in mice, while far more ordinary cancer cells could not. The sphere cells bore stem cell marks, renewed themselves, and shrugged off low oxygen through their metabolism. They also grew, moved, and invaded more fiercely, and resisted chemotherapy. The work ties the stem-like state to a hardy fuel style, and names that link as a drug target.
europmc-pmc3900378:
Jean Daunizeau, Vincent Adam, and Lionel Rigoux present a modeling toolbox in PLoS Computational Biology, with the record dated 2014. Brain and behavior models have grown rich and nonlinear, with unknown settings that must be fit to data. Without a formal stats frame, such model studies are hard to repeat or refute.

Their toolbox, VBA, gives one probabilistic answer to three shared jobs. It can simulate data from a model, fit settings and pick between rival models, and tune study design to sharpen the next test. The tools are built to be generic, fast, and robust across model types. The authors aim at a quantitative science of mind and brain where models earn their keep against data, patient by patient where illness varies widely.
europmc-pmc3906378:
Jeff Alstott, Ed Bullmore, and Dietmar Plenz present a Python package in PLoS One, with the record dated 2014. Power law patterns, where big events stay common far into the tail, show up across nature and society. Fitting them well takes care, and sound methods were hard for non-experts to use.

Their package, powerlaw, wraps the best fitting methods in simple commands. It handles basic fits and model checks and offers a wide set of options for varied needs. The code is public and built for extension. Heavy tails can break standard statistics, since even the average may not settle, so careless fits mislead. The tool aims to put sound practice within reach of any researcher with data in hand.
europmc-pmc3935878:
Daniel L. Rabosky introduces a method for finding shifts in the pace of evolution on family trees, in PLoS ONE in 2014. Biologists want to know where speciation sped up or slowed down, whether from a key new trait, a change over time, or crowding as species pile up. Existing tools forced researchers to guess where the shifts were before testing them.

Rabosky's approach lets the data decide.
