A statistical sampler moves between models with different numbers of diversification regimes placed anywhere on the tree, mixing steady, time-varying, and diversity-dependent processes. Tests on simulated trees showed it could recover complex mixtures, and it matched or beat a leading older method. As a real example, he applies it to the radiation of modern whales, tracing how their speciation and extinction unfolded.
europmc-pmc4021678:
Piotr Wojdasiewicz, Łukasz A. Poniatowski, and Dariusz Szukiewicz review the push and pull of signal proteins in osteoarthritis, in Mediators of Inflammation in 2014. Osteoarthritis is the most common long-term joint disease. It harms all joint tissues, and inflammation runs through it from an early stage, at varied strength.

Joint breakdown is not a one-way slide. Wear-down processes run beside repair processes at all times. A network of signal proteins called cytokines steers both sides. One group fans inflammation, with named members that drive cartilage loss. A rival group calms it and backs repair. The review maps these signals, the cells that send and receive them, and the inner pathways they trigger. How the balance shifts as the disease builds is still under study. Knowing the network in detail may point to new drugs that tip the balance toward repair.
europmc-pmc4053778:
Petra Leidinger and colleagues build a blood test signature for Alzheimer's disease from twelve small RNAs, in Genome Biology in 2013. Alzheimer's is the commonest dementia, yet early, gentle diagnosis still lacks a reliable marker. Small RNAs in blood shift with disease and can be measured without touching the brain.

Sequencing blood from patients and healthy controls found well over a hundred small RNAs at changed levels. The team picked twelve and rechecked them in a larger set of two hundred samples. That set added look-alike brain diseases and a mild impairment stage. The dozen separated Alzheimer's from healthy controls with accuracy above ninety percent. Telling it apart from other brain diseases was harder but still workable. The targets of the twelve point to nerve development and wiring. The authors propose blood small RNAs as a practical route toward earlier, kinder diagnosis.
europmc-pmc4056078:
Donat R. Spahn, Rolf Rossaint, and a multidisciplinary task force update the European guideline for managing bleeding after major trauma, in Critical Care in 2013. Uncontrolled bleeding remains a leading cause of preventable death in the injured. The task force has issued guidance since the middle of the previous decade; this is its second update.

Recommendations were rebuilt from a fresh literature review and graded by evidence strength. New ground includes when to use blood-pressure-raising and heart-supporting drugs, and how to handle the growing share of patients who arrive on blood thinners or anti-clotting tablets. Clot prevention after injury gets fuller treatment. The largest addition is organisational: every hospital should run a written, evidence-based protocol for the bleeding trauma patient and stick to it. Older advice was rechecked against newer studies and shifts in available products.
europmc-pmc4102778:
James A. McCubrey and a large team reviewed GSK-3, an enzyme first studied for its role in sugar storage, as a possible cancer drug target. Their review appeared in Oncotarget in 2014. The enzyme touches many cell processes, and faulty activity is linked to diseases from bipolar disorder and Alzheimer's to diabetes and cancer.

In cancer its role is double-edged. In some tumours, shutting GSK-3 down helps growth, making it act like a tumour suppressor. In others it steadies a growth-driving complex around beta-catenin, acting like an oncogene. Many blocking drugs exist, but this ambiguity makes their use controversial. The review weighs the enzyme's varied roles in solid tumours and its newer link to cancer stem cells.
europmc-pmc4185378:
Hideyuki Yaginuma, Hiromi Imamura, and six co-authors built a sensor to measure energy levels inside single bacteria in Scientific Reports in 2014. ATP is the fuel that powers most cell reactions, yet no method could give an exact ATP level for one living cell. Group averages hid how much cells differ from each other.

Their sensor, named QUEEN, joins a glowing protein to a bacterial ATP-binding protein, so brightness tracks ATP directly. Readings from QUEEN matched the standard firefly luciferase test on whole cultures, and the sensor barely reacted to changes in growth rate. Aiming it at single Escherichia coli cells from one culture, the team found ATP levels varied widely from cell to cell, even though the cells were genetically identical.
europmc-pmc4193278:
Anastasia N. Vlasova, Linda J. Saif, and six co-authors sequenced pig diarrhea virus strains in Emerging Infectious Diseases in 2014. Porcine epidemic diarrhea virus, a coronavirus, reached North America in 2013 after decades in Europe and Asia. It kills suckling piglets at high rates and costs pork producers heavily.

The team compared 74 strains collected in North America from May 2013 to February 2014. The viruses were not one uniform invader: sequences varied, and the highly virulent strains carried distinct molecular marks alongside milder variants. Tracing those marks helps show where the strains came from and how they were changing as they spread. The picture warns that the virus evolves fast in new herds, so control plans must track its forms, not just its presence.
europmc-pmc4201578:
Sophie S. Abby, Eduardo P. C. Rocha, and four co-authors built a genome mining program called MacSyFinder in PLoS ONE in 2014. Many cell machines, from secretion systems to CRISPR defences, are built from sets of parts that sit together in the genome. Finding such systems in new genomes by hand is slow.

MacSyFinder lets researchers write a model of a system's parts and layout, then scans genomes or raw metagenome data for matches. It finds parts by protein similarity, then checks whether the hits obey the model's rules on content and spacing. A companion viewer, MacSyView, draws the results in context. As a test, the team built models for CRISPR-Cas defence systems and sorted them accurately with public protein profiles. The program is free and open source.
europmc-pmc4237778:
Michael Inouye, Kathryn E. Holt, and six co-authors built a rapid bacteria typing program in Genome Medicine in 2014. Hospital and public health labs need to type germs fast: which strain is it, and does it carry resistance or virulence genes? Whole genome sequencing holds all those answers, but extracting them from raw reads usually means slow assembly first.

Their program, SRST2, reads the raw output directly and reports the genes found and the exact allele of each, skipping assembly. In tests it beat assembly-based methods on both gene detection and allele calls. A public health laboratory validated it in routine use, and the team showed it tracking germs inside a hospital. With resistance rising, they offer it as a surveillance tool any sequencing lab can run.
europmc-pmc4277278:
Binod Neupane and five co-authors compare free software packages that run network meta-analysis in R. Their review appeared in PLoS ONE in 2014. Network meta-analysis lets researchers compare many treatments at once by combining direct trial results with indirect links through shared comparison drugs.

Three packages are walked through in detail: gemtc, pcnetmeta, and netmeta. The authors test what each can do, how each handles data and models, and how much coding effort each demands. The side by side account helps clinical researchers pick the tool that fits their question instead of learning each package from scratch.
europmc-pmc4293378:
Fatemeh Seyednasrollah, Asta Laiho, and Laura L Elo compared eight software packages that find genes switched up or down between sample groups in RNA sequencing data. Their comparison appeared in Briefings in Bioinformatics in 2015. RNA-seq had become the standard way to read gene activity, yet no agreement existed on which analysis pipeline a typical lab should trust.

The team ran each package on the same tasks and weighed accuracy, consistency, and ease of use from the view of a basic user. Packages differed in how they handled small sample counts and noisy genes, and no single tool won on every count. The paper closes with practical guidelines for picking a pipeline that stays robust in real research settings.
europmc-pmc4315878:
Theodoros Grigoratos and Giorgio Martini review the dust thrown off by vehicle brakes, an overlooked slice of city air pollution. Their review appeared in Environmental Science and Pollution Research in 2015. As exhaust controls tightened, non-exhaust traffic particles from brakes, tires, clutches, and road wear grew in relative share, together matching exhaust as a source.

Brake wear alone can supply over half of non-exhaust traffic particles in dense city driving, where braking is constant, and a fifth of all traffic particles. On freeways the share drops. The review gathers emission rates, particle sizes, and metal content, and weighs how brake materials and driving patterns change the yield. It makes the case for standards in an area regulation had ignored.
europmc-pmc4382178:
Andrés Cózar and co-authors measured floating plastic across the Mediterranean Sea, in PLoS ONE in 2015. The five great ocean gyres are known plastic traps, but whether this enclosed sea is another was open. Ships sampled surface water throughout the basin, counting and sizing plastic pieces. The sea borders dense coasts and heavy shipping, and its water exits mainly through a deep layer, which could hold floating debris in.

Plastic appeared at every site sampled, at an average density of one item per four square meters, matching the gyre traps. Pieces were mostly millimeter-sized fragments, yet large objects were more common than in ocean gyres, reflecting nearby pollution sources. Total floating plastic was estimated between 1,000 and 3,000 tons. Given the sea's rich life and busy coasts, the authors expect harm to marine and human life to be frequent.
europmc-pmc4383978:
Noe Fernandez-Pozo and co-authors described the Sol Genomics Network in Nucleic Acids Research in 2015. The network serves the nightshade family, Solanaceae, which includes tomato, potato, pepper, eggplant, and tobacco. It stores whole genomes for a growing list of family members, plus gene loci and trait data that researchers can upload and edit through friendly web pages. Analysis tools include sequence search, genome browsers, expression and map viewers, and a system for trait-mapping studies.

A newer tool designs gene-silencing constructs, which let researchers switch off one gene to see its role. With genomic and trait data piling up, the network is now building web-based breeding tools, so growers can use marker data in crossing decisions. Its code and database design are also being adapted for other plant groups, spreading the model beyond one family.
europmc-pmc4406678:
Steve Horvath and co-authors tested whether Down syndrome truly speeds biological aging, in Aging Cell in 2015. People with Down syndrome, caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21, face many age-linked conditions early, from immune decline to Alzheimer's disease. That pattern suggested their tissues are biologically older, but molecular proof was sparse. The team applied the epigenetic clock, a marker that reads age from chemical marks on DNA, to blood and brain tissue.

Trisomy 21 raised the clock's age estimate significantly, by 6.6 years on average across the tissues tested. The effect held in both blood and brain, two very different tissues. A molecular measure thus backs the clinical impression of accelerated aging. The clock also gives researchers a yardstick for testing whether future treatments slow that acceleration.
europmc-pmc4479078:
Angela Acheampong and Jean-Louis Vincent studied fluid balance in sepsis patients in Critical Care in 2015. Giving intravenous fluid is a cornerstone of sepsis care, yet patients who end up with more fluid in than out tend to fare worse. Whether a positive balance itself predicts death, or merely marks sicker patients, matters for how hard doctors should push fluids.

The team tracked intake and output daily for a week in consecutive adults treated for sepsis in their intensive care unit. Patients who died had taken in more fluid and carried a daily positive balance more than twice that of survivors, whose output volumes were similar. The longer a positive balance persisted, the higher the mortality, and the link held after adjusting for other risk factors in a time-dependent model. The authors urge attention to cumulative balance, not just early resuscitation.
europmc-pmc4518278:
Cheng Bi and five co-authors found a way to grow better crystals for solar cells, reported in Nature Communications in 2015. Their material is organolead trihalide perovskite, a cheap crystal that turns light into power. Thin films of it usually form small grains, and each grain edge is a spot where charge is lost, capping how well the cell works.

Growing the film on slick, non-wetting layers spaced the starting seeds farther apart and let grain edges move freely. The crystals grew tall and wide, with aspect ratios from 2.3 to 7.9, and charge losses fell to single-crystal levels. Solar cells built this way reached a steady 18.3% efficiency under standard sunlight, using low-temperature processing. The trick is simple enough to carry to other light devices.
europmc-pmc4522678:
Troy D. Hubbard leads an eight-author team showing how a human sensor protein learned to read gut microbes, in Scientific Reports in 2015. The aryl hydrocarbon receptor, or AHR, is a protein that switches genes on when certain molecules bind it. In the gut it helps keep peace between the body and its microbes, but which natural molecule flips it there was unclear.

Combining binding tests, gene measures, and computer models of the sensor's pocket, the team fingered indole. Gut microbes make indole from tryptophan, a food building block. Human AHR responds to indole strongly and seems to bind two indole molecules at once, unlike its classic triggers. The finding frames human AHR as a dedicated indole reader, a channel for microbe-to-host signaling.
europmc-pmc4525178:
Jordan A. Ramilowski leads an eleven-author team drafting the wiring diagram of human cell talk, in Nature Communications in 2015. Cells coordinate through ligands, messenger molecules one cell releases, and receptors, the locks they fit on another cell's surface. A full map of such pairs across cell types had been missing.

Drawing on gene data from 144 primary human cell types, the team charted which cells send and which receive each signal. Most cells express tens to hundreds of ligands and receptors, weaving a dense network. About two-thirds of pairs may also act on the same cell that sent them. Surface and secreted proteins proved the most cell-specific, and receptors mostly evolved before their ligands. An online tool lets others query the map.
europmc-pmc4525378:
Neelja Singhal, Manish Kumar, Pawan K. Kanaujia, and Jugsharan S. Virdi review a fast way to name microbes in Frontiers in Microbiology in 2015. The trusted standard reads marker genes, which is slow and costly. The newer method, MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry, weighs a microbe's protein pattern and matches the fingerprint against a library.

The method works on whole cells or extracts and is rapid, sensitive, and cheap in labor and supplies. Labs already use it to identify species, type strains, trace outbreaks, and spot germs in water, food, blood, and urine, plus drug resistance. Its limit is plain: a new isolate can be named only if its reference fingerprint sits in the database. The review maps where the tool stands.
europmc-pmc4531078:
Yi Zhu leads a twelve-author team hunting drugs that kill aged cells, in Aging Cell in 2015. Senescent cells are worn-out cells that stop dividing but refuse to die, and they pile up with age. Mice live healthier when such cells are removed by a built-in suicide gene; a pill that did the same could ease many age-linked diseases.

Reading gene activity in senescent cells, the team found survival networks turned up high, matching the cells' known death resistance. Silencing key nodes of that network killed senescent cells while sparing dividing and resting ones. Two existing drugs hit the same nodes: dasatinib cleared senescent fat-cell precursors, quercetin worked better on vessel and marrow cells, and together they cut the senescent load in old mice.
europmc-pmc4579478:
Tracy D. Ainsworth leads a twelve-author team finding the core microbes every coral carries, in The ISME Journal in 2015. Corals are simple animals hosting some of the richest microbial communities known. Within that crowd, telling true symbionts from hangers-on had been impossible, yet it decides what bacteria actually do for the coral.

Sampling corals separated by thousands of kilometers of ocean, the team found seven bacterial types universal to the core microbiome. Distinct micro-habitats inside the coral held distinct communities. The two most abundant core types sat precisely with the coral's tenant algae and the host cells housing them. The authors argue these bacterial partnerships help the famous coral-algae symbiosis thrive across varied seas.
europmc-pmc4632578:
Masaki Miya and colleagues brought out a 2015 study presenting universal DNA primers for identifying fish from water samples. Fish shed DNA into their surroundings, and reading it can survey species without catching them. Their primers target a short, variable stretch of a mitochondrial gene. The design drew on whole mitochondrial genomes from 880 species. The work appeared in Royal Society Open Science.

Tested in four aquarium tanks holding 180 known species, the method detected 168 of them. Reef water samples near the aquarium added more, bringing the total to 232 species from 70 families. The approach proved cheaper, faster, and more sensitive than traditional surveys, and it works from sharks and rays to reef fish. Conservation teams gain a non-invasive census tool.
europmc-pmc4635978:
Morten T. Venø, together with colleagues, released a 2015 study charting circular RNA production during pig brain development. Circular RNAs had been found in many tissues, but never tracked across brain growth in a large animal. The team profiled five brain tissues at up to six fetal time points. The work appeared in Genome Biology.

Thousands of circular RNAs followed intricate patterns across place and time. Expression peaked in the cortex at day sixty of pregnancy, with 4,634 distinct circles from 2,195 genes. Some genes produced many circle variants, each shifting differently over development. Long flanking introns and repeated elements nearby seemed to favour circle formation. A new staining method showed circles moving within cells as development proceeds, hinting at active roles.
europmc-pmc4673178:
David M. Goldenberg and colleagues' 2015 study centres on sacituzumab govitecan, an antibody-drug conjugate aimed at Trop-2, a surface protein abundant on many solid cancers. The drug links a Trop-2 antibody to SN-38, a moderately toxic chemotherapy agent, at an unusually high loading. The work appeared in Oncotarget.

The conjugate delivered up to 136 times more SN-38 to human tumours grown in mice than irinotecan, the standard prodrug of SN-38. It releases its payload gradually and in its most active form, which may explain milder severe diarrhoea than irinotecan causes. Early patient results showed promise across several metastatic cancers, including triple-negative breast and lung cancers. The authors present the design as a new template for conjugates carrying mid-strength drugs.
europmc-pmc4702778:
Christopher Southan, Joanna L. Sharman, Helen E. Benson, and nine colleagues plus the NC-IUPHAR group updated the Guide to PHARMACOLOGY in Nucleic Acids Research in 2016. The guide records expert-checked links between drugs and the proteins they act on in the human body. Expert subcommittees work with in-house curators to pull measured binding values from journal papers. This update spans seven database releases since the 2014 report.

The resource now covers about thirteen hundred protein targets and six thousand ligands, from small molecules to peptides and medical antibodies. Measured strength values anchor each claimed interaction. Together the links sketch a data-backed druggable genome of about seven percent of human proteins. New website features and download options widened access. The guide also feeds a printed compendium issued every two years. For drug hunters, it offers curated facts instead of scattered claims.
europmc-pmc4765878:
Artem Tarasov and four co-authors introduce a speed tool for genome data files in Bioinformatics in 2015. Sequencing labs store aligned reads in SAM, BAM, and CRAM files, and the standard tool for handling them leans on a single processor core. As data sets swell, that step slows whole pipelines, including hospital screening where hours can matter.

Their tool, Sambamba, spreads the work across many cores at once. In their test it converted a large compressed file far faster than the standard tool. Beyond speed, it adds deep coverage checks and strong filters for pulling out just the reads a study needs. The software is free and open source. The authors report that sequencing centers were already picking it up for daily work.
europmc-pmc4783878:
Xing Du leads nine authors in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences in 2016. Their review covers how proteins grip small molecules. That grip is called protein-ligand binding. It underlies nearly every job in the cell. It also underlies nearly every drug's action. Reading it well is basic for biology and for drug design.

The review starts with the physics of the grip. It covers speeds, heat, and the forces that pull partners together. It then walks through three classic pictures. One is a rigid lock and key. One is a glove that molds on contact. One is a partner that picks a ready shape from a shifting crowd. A final section weighs lab and computer methods for measuring grip strength. It gives the strengths and limits of each.
europmc-pmc4834578:
Cintia S. de Paiva leads a wide author team in Scientific Reports in 2016 on gut microbes in Sjögren syndrome, an autoimmune disease that dries the eyes and mouth. Gut imbalance has been tied to immune misbehavior elsewhere, so the team profiled microbes from patients' eyes, tongues, and stool, and recreated the imbalance in a mouse dry-eye model.

Patients' stool carried more of several possibly harmful genera and fewer of the usual helpful residents. The lower the gut diversity, the worse the eye and body disease scores ran. In mice, antibiotics plus drying stress produced a worse dry eye than either alone, with a matching gut shift and fewer mucus-making cells. The findings tie the syndrome to a gut pattern and suggest the gut helps set its severity.
europmc-pmc4841778:
Hanjie Zhao and seventeen co-authors reported in 2016 that exosomes from tumor-support cells rewire how cancer cells burn fuel. Exosomes are tiny sacs that cells shed. Those from cancer-associated fibroblasts, the support cells in many solid tumors, were taken up by cancer cells and changed their energy machinery in deep ways.

The sacs slowed the cells' oxygen-based energy path and pushed them toward sugar breakdown and a second route that uses glutamine. Labeled-atom tests showed the sacs also hand over ready-made building blocks, such as amino acids, fats, and cycle intermediates, which starved cancer cells use at once. The work recasts tumor support cells as direct food suppliers, not just signal senders.
europmc-pmc4873978:
Hiroaki Semba and co-authors reported in Nature Communications in 2016 that a low-oxygen switch drives the fuel use macrophages need to move. Macrophages crawl toward inflamed tissue as oxygen thins along the way. A factor called HIF-1 alpha turns on a gene, PDK1, that diverts sugar away from full burning. The team found this switch also fires in mild low oxygen, where normal burning still works.

A sugar-burning enzyme, PKM2, gathered in the cell's crawling feelers and powered local energy supply. Blocking the axis stalled macrophage movement. Migration thus runs on fast sugar burning at the cell edge, not just on the cell's main engines. The route may matter for wound repair and tumor spread.
europmc-pmc4878278:
Alistair E. W. Johnson and co-authors released MIMIC-III in Scientific Data in 2016, a free critical care database. It holds de-identified records for patients in intensive care at one large hospital: vital signs, drugs, lab results, staff notes, fluid balance, procedure and diagnosis codes, imaging reports, stay length, and survival.

Open access lets academics, companies, and students all work the same rich data. Uses span outcome research, care quality checks, and course projects. Single-center data carry limits, which the release notes plainly. A shared, free dataset raises the floor for critical care research, since small teams can test ideas once locked inside hospital walls.
europmc-pmc4985278:
Bambang Parmanto, Allen Nelson Lewis, Kristin M. Graham, and Marnie H. Bertolet build a new survey for rating telehealth visits. Their paper appeared in the International Journal of Telerehabilitation in 2016. Older surveys assumed telehealth meant clinic video systems. Care has since moved to home computers and common software. A scale built for that world was missing, so the team built one and tested how well it holds up.

The survey scores both the screen tools patients and clinicians face and the quality of the remote visit itself. Checks showed the tool is sound and works across many uses. The authors argue ease of use is not a small point: a system patients cannot run delivers no care at all. They offer the survey for judging new telehealth programs and for weighing one platform against another.
europmc-pmc5055678:
Chandan Pal, Johan Bengtsson-Palme, Erik Kristiansson, and D. G. Joakim Larsson map antibiotic resistance genes across life and landscapes in Microbiome in 2016. Resistance genes only threaten health when they reach pathogens, so knowing where mobile resistance genes abound matters. The team analyzed 864 deeply sequenced metagenomes from humans, animals, and outside environments, reading resistance genes, mobile elements, and the bacterial mix.

Human and animal communities were narrow in species, with few biocide and metal resistance genes, but relatively rich in antibiotic resistance genes. Outside environments were the reverse: species diversity with many metal and biocide resistance genes and mobile elements, but few known antibiotic resistance genes in water, sediment, and soil. Wastewater matched the human gut, and the richest hotspots were sites polluted by antibiotic factories and a set of city air samples. The authors urge tighter control of factory waste and more watch on air as a route.
europmc-pmc5116078:
Jianping Ji and a large team of co-authors grew a new two-dimensional material, reporting in Nature Communications in 2016. Antimonene, a sheet of antimony atoms one or a few layers thick, was predicted to be stable and useful, unlike black phosphorus sheets that decay in air. Making good crystals had proved hard.

The team grew few-layer antimonene crystals as neat polygons on several surfaces, including bendable ones, by a gentle deposition method. Tests showed the predicted buckled structure. After 30 days in air the sheets stayed intact, and simulations backed antimonene's resistance to oxygen at room temperature. The sheets also conduct electricity well and let visible light through, which points to use in clear conductive coatings for screens and other devices.
europmc-pmc521178:
Bino John, Anton J. Enright, Alexei Aravin, Thomas Tuschl, Chris Sander, and Debora S. Marks predicted human targets of microRNAs in PLoS Biology in 2004. MicroRNAs are tiny RNA molecules that bind matching sites on messenger RNAs and either cut the message or block its use, but the targets of most mammalian microRNAs were unknown.

Their method searched the tail regions of human gene transcripts for sites matching all 218 known mammalian microRNAs, demanding strong matching rules and conservation across species. It found about 2,000 human genes with sites conserved in mammals and about 250 also conserved in fish. Predicted targets clustered among transcription factors, the microRNA machinery itself, and protein breakdown systems, hinting at feedback loops. Their estimate suggests microRNA genes, about one percent of human genes, may tune output for a tenth or more of all human genes.
europmc-pmc526178:
Alekos Athanasiadis, Alexander Rich, and Stefan Maas mapped A-to-I RNA editing across the human transcriptome in PLoS Biology in 2004. Editing swaps one letter of an RNA message after copying from DNA, which can change the protein built from it. Few edited human genes were known, though far more were suspected. The team hunted in Alu elements, repeats that litter human genes.

Facing Alu pairs inside one RNA can fold into the shape the editing enzymes attack. Tests confirmed editing in 43 genes, and a scan of over 100,000 messages found 1,445 edited at more than 14,500 sites. Editing levels tracked the pairs' spacing and match and varied by tissue, highest in brain, windpipe, and thymus. Such edits can even create or erase splice signals.
europmc-pmc5305778:
James W. Dawson gave an opening address to the Edinburgh Women's Medical Society in October 1920, printed in the Edinburgh Medical Journal in 1924. He spoke as a fellow worker, not a master, to women starting in medicine. His theme was the balance of work and rest in a doctor's life, framed as a modern form of the old Religio Medici.

Dawson argued that no one can live by work alone. Play and amusement are basic needs of human nature, not soft extras. Outdoor pastimes that give sound exercise can steady the temper and refresh the mind. Leisure, used well, makes a person a fitter tool for the work that must be done. The address mixes counsel on study, duty, and joy drawn from a long working life.
europmc-pmc5348978:
Zhangyuan Yin, Clarence Pascual, and Daniel J. Klionsky reviewed self-eating in cells in Microbial Cell in 2016. In autophagy, a cell wraps worn parts and spare material in a sac and breaks them down for reuse. The process is old in evolution and runs in all complex life. A set of named Atg proteins builds the sac in set steps.

Once seen as a mere stress reply, the process now reads as a core housekeeper. It holds cell balance, guides growth and development, and backs immune defense. When it slips out of tune, disease can follow in many organs. The review sums up the machine parts, the switches and signals that tune them, and the roles of self-eating in health and illness. Its plain scheme of the steps gives new readers a firm entry point.
europmc-pmc5389178:
Thomas M. Stubbs and his co-authors, with the BI Ageing Clock Team, build an age clock for mice in a 2017 Genome Biology paper. In humans, chemical marks at set DNA sites can predict age with fair accuracy. The team asked whether mice share such a clock. They mapped these marks across many mouse tissues and ages at single-letter detail.

Many sites shifted with age in the same way across tissues. A model built on a few hundred sites guessed a mouse's age to within a few weeks. The clock also picked up real effects: removing the ovaries sped it up in females, and diet fat content shifted it too. The authors offer the clock as a tool to test what speeds or slows aging.
europmc-pmc5422478:
Fröhlich and Wahl review what thyroid antibodies do inside and outside the thyroid gland. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. Autoimmune thyroid disease is among the most common autoimmune disorders. Its hallmark antibodies target three structures. They are thyroid peroxidase, thyroglobulin, and the TSH receptor. The antibodies also appear in people with no clear thyroid fault. That spread raises questions about wider effects.

Receptor antibodies drive Graves' disease and its eye problems. The review traces causes and mechanisms of the thyroid diseases first. It then weighs claimed links beyond the gland. Breast cancer gets close attention. Some data hint the antibodies may help tumors start. Other data link them to better outcomes once cancer exists. The authors stress weak spots in the proof. Test methods vary, and hormone shifts can confound results. Prospective studies are still missing.
europmc-pmc544578:
Hoet and co-authors review what was known, and not known, about nanoparticle risks to health. Their review appeared in the Journal of Nanobiotechnology. Manmade nanoparticles already fill car tires and plastics. Tiny glowing quantum dots mark cells in labs. Investment in nanoscience was surging worldwide. New consumer goods were sure to follow. Talk of possible harm had barely begun. Hard data were thin on both sides.

The review gathers the early evidence on hazard. Particles can enter through the lungs, gut, or skin. From the lungs they may cross swiftly into the blood. They can then reach vital organs. Carbon black particles disturb cell signaling in tests. Carbon nanotubes wrap with DNA, raising concern. The authors trace likely paths inside the body. They weigh drug delivery and toxicology studies for clues. Their verdict is caution, not alarm. The field needed far more testing.
europmc-pmc5487478:
Donat and co-authors present a review in Frontiers in Aging Neuroscience on microglia after traumatic brain injury. Microglia are the brain's resident immune cells. They switch on fast when the brain is hurt. Early activation may help restore balance in the tissue. If it stays on for years, it can deepen the damage.

The review tracks microglial shape and behavior over time after injury. Animal work and human imaging both feature. Scans show activation far from the injury site itself. The old split into good and bad states looks too simple, they argue. New therapies aim to nudge microglia toward repair.
europmc-pmc5491678:
Camara and co-authors present a review in Frontiers in Physiology on VDAC1, a channel protein in mitochondria. VDAC1 sits in the outer membrane and gates all traffic in and out. Metabolites, nucleotides, and ions pass through it. It also binds proteins that control cell death. Its failure is tied to heart, brain, and cancer diseases.

The review explains how the channel opens, closes, and is tuned by other proteins. Partners such as hexokinase and Bcl-2 family members shape its role in survival. Disease sections cover cardiac injury and Alzheimer's disease, among others. The authors weigh VDAC1 as a drug target. Selective control could protect cells in many tissues.
europmc-pmc5492678:
Snoek and co-authors report a genetics study in BMC Genomics on hidden gene variation in C. elegans. Cryptic genetic variation stays silent under normal conditions. Stress can unlock it and reveal new traits. The team asks which gene regulators drive that unlocking. They used a bred worm population and a brief heat shock.

Gene activity was measured in control, heat stress, and recovery states. Heat changed the activity of 3,305 genes, they report. Nearby gene regulators behaved alike across all states. Distant regulators, called trans-eQTL, were far more state-specific. About 67 percent of them appeared in only one state. Heat stress produced the most unique ones.
europmc-pmc5500878:
Biancur and co-authors report a cancer metabolism study in Nature Communications. Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma is hard to treat and often deadly. These tumors lean heavily on glutamine, an amino acid, for growth. Blocking an early glutamine enzyme, GLS, looked like a sound drug plan. The team tested a potent GLS blocker called CB-839.

The drug slowed pancreatic cancer cells strongly at first, they report. The cells then adapted and kept growing, in dishes and in mice. Protein and metabolite profiling revealed the backup routes they used. Pairing the blocker with drugs against those routes worked better. The authors argue that such rational pairs may help patients.
europmc-pmc5508778:
Ghurye and co-authors present a software study in BMC Genomics on genome assembly. Long-read machines now produce far longer DNA pieces than older tools. Even so, the pieces rarely span a whole chromosome. Joining them into chromosome-scale scaffolds needs long-range clues. Hi-C data, which maps DNA contacts inside the nucleus, supply such clues.

The team built an algorithm named SALSA for this task. It uses contact patterns to order and orient the pieces. Tests ran on human and goat assemblies. SALSA produced more accurate scaffolds than LACHESIS, the leading rival, they report. The method is built to scale to large genomes.
europmc-pmc5518378:
Beatson presents a clinical paper in the Transactions of the Medico-Chirurgical Society of Edinburgh. It addresses breast cancer cases too advanced for surgery. At the time, such patients had no curative options at all. Beatson, surgeon to the Glasgow Cancer Hospital, proposed a new line of attack. His approach rejected the view of cancer as a local parasite.

Three cases illustrate the method in detail. The core step was removal of the ovaries, sometimes with thyroid extract added. Beatson reasoned that ovarian influence could drive the tumor's growth. Cutting that influence off, he argued, might shrink inoperable disease. The paper became a founding document of hormone therapy for cancer.
europmc-pmc5542178:
Gong and co-authors present a research article in Oncotarget. Their subject is how stem cells help new blood vessels grow. Mesenchymal stem cells release tiny packets called exosomes. The team tests whether those packets carry helpful signals to vessel-lining cells.

Experiments used human vein cells in dishes and gel plugs placed in mice. Exosomes from the stem cells raised tube-like growth in the vein cells. They also drew vessel cells into the plugs and raised blood flow there. Tracking showed the packets entered the cells fast. They carried microRNAs that favor vessel growth, such as miR-30b. Blocking or changing those signals altered the effect. Readers see a clear route for stem cell help without the cells themselves.
europmc-pmc5549378:
Aisen and co-authors present a review article on Alzheimer's disease. They argue the disease is best seen as a continuum. Brain changes begin many years before symptoms appear. The range runs from no symptoms at all to severe impairment.

Defining the disease by symptoms alone is too narrow, they say. Biomarkers can show disease well before memory fails. The authors trace the continuum through biology, biomarkers, and clinical signs. That view matters for trials of drugs that aim to slow the disease. It also shapes early diagnosis and care. Readers get a clear case for treating Alzheimer's as one long process, not set stages.
europmc-pmc5554778:
Mohammed and co-authors present a research article in Cell Reports. They used single-cell RNA sequencing on mouse embryos. The stages run from day 3.5 to day 6.5 of development. That window covers implantation and the start of gastrulation, when body layers first form.

The team charts how gene activity shifts as the epiblast grows and splits into new cell fates. They track the X chromosome switching back on, then off again. Gene noise ran high in cells not yet committed to a fate. By contrast, primitive streak cells at day 6.5 acted in close sync. Readers get a detailed map of the choices that launch the body plan.
europmc-pmc5567978:
Katzman and co-authors review adult ADHD and its frequent partner disorders in BMC Psychiatry. About 2.5 percent of adults have ADHD. As many as 80 percent also have another psychiatric condition. Mood, anxiety, substance use, and personality disorders are the most common partners.

Shared family links and brain traits tie these conditions together. Overlapping symptoms make diagnosis hard. The authors favor a dimensional approach, judging traits by degree, not just by label. Validated scales and sharp clinical questions can flag missed cases. Guidelines say to treat the most impairing condition first. Early care may change the course of later illness. Readers get a practical guide for a complex clinic problem.
europmc-pmc5574878:
Nguyen, Green, and Mecsas review how neutrophils make a killing burst of reactive oxygen. Neutrophils are front-line immune cells. An enzyme complex called NADPH oxidase lets them flood germ traps with these harsh molecules. Too little output means repeat infections. Too much harms tissue.

Cell surface receptors prime or trigger the burst. Signals then build and switch on the oxidase complex. The reactive oxygen can wake up stored proteases and help cast neutrophil traps. It also crosses into bacteria and damages their DNA, proteins, and membranes. Bacteria fight back with repair systems and secreted blockers. The review weighs both sides of that arms race. Readers get a deep guide to a core immune weapon.
europmc-pmc5660078:
Akaike and co-authors report a biochemistry study in Nature Communications. It identifies how cells make cysteine hydropersulfide, or CysSSH. This sulfur compound occurs widely in living things. Its production route and roles were unclear. The team shows that cysteinyl-tRNA synthetases drive its synthesis. These enzymes normally help build proteins from cysteine. Tests spanned bacteria, human cells, and mice.

Deleting the mitochondrial form of the enzyme cut CysSSH output. That result marks these enzymes as the main persulfide synthases in vivo. They also add sulfur chains to proteins during translation. Their work links to mitochondrial growth and energy output. The authors suggest relevance for redox signaling and stress diseases.
europmc-pmc5729478:
Staudacher and Brown ask how antibody drug conjugates kill nearby cancer cells. Such drugs pair a tumor seeking antibody with a strong cell killing payload. A linker joins the two parts and controls drug release. Released drug can drift into nearby cells, a process called bystander killing.

The review checks whether the conjugate must first be taken inside a target cell. Older views held that entry, linker cutting, and release inside were all required. Newer work shows some linker and drug pairs can be cut outside the cell instead. The authors use two approved drugs to show both paths at work.
europmc-pmc5759778:
Reynolds and co-authors review chronic disease care programs in primary and community care. Long term conditions need steady, well run management in these settings. The team searched work from 2006 to 2014, updating a 2006 review. They kept 165 articles covering 157 studies.

Programs were sorted by the Chronic Care Model and its parts. Support for self management was the most common element. It most often improved patient level outcomes, above all in diabetes and hypertension. Delivery design helped both staff and patients, but for fewer conditions. Decision support mainly changed staff behavior, such as medication use.
europmc-pmc5777078:
Ferron and co-authors study how coronaviruses correct errors in their RNA. These viruses copy large RNA genomes with a sloppy main enzyme. A second enzyme, nsp14, cuts out wrong building blocks and also caps the RNA. The team solved the structure of nsp14 and tested its work.

They show that nsp14 can excise ribavirin, a drug slipped into the genome. That removal explains why the drug fails against these viruses. The structure looks unlike other cap enzymes, a sign of a swapped past. This proofreading gear let coronavirus genomes grow large, but it also shields them from some drugs.
europmc-pmc5777978:
Wang, Mathieu, and Brezski review ways to engineer the Fc tail of IgG antibodies. Antibodies bind targets with one end and recruit immune action with the other. Most approved antibody drugs use the IgG1 subclass, which engages many immune parts. Small tail changes can tune that recruitment up or down.

The review sorts engineering efforts by their aim, from stronger killing to better safety. It explains how each change alters contact with immune components. Examples from clinical studies show the ideas at work in patients. The goal is antibody drugs that beat the natural isotype on both effect and safety.
europmc-pmc5808178:
Savio and co-authors review the P2X7 receptor in inflammatory disease. Stressed or dying cells spill ATP, the cell's fuel. Outside cells, ATP acts as a danger alarm. The P2X7 receptor hears that alarm and fires up immunity.

Once active, the receptor helps release IL-1beta and other attack signals. It can also open a pore that kills the cell. In infections and cancer its role flips with context. In brain diseases it seems to drive harm. The review weighs blockers as possible drugs. Readers get both faces of a receptor the authors call angel or demon.
europmc-pmc5850278:
Waterhouse and co-authors unveil BUSCO version 3, a yardstick for genome completeness. Their paper appeared in Molecular Biology and Evolution. BUSCO hunts for genes every species in a lineage should carry. Missing or broken copies expose gaps in a genome assembly.

The rewrite makes the code faster and easier to extend. Forty lineage data sets now span vertebrates to plants and protists. Example studies stretch the tool past simple quality checks. It trains gene predictors on trustworthy reference genes. It picks sound species for comparisons and markers for family trees. Metagenome surveys borrow the same yardstick.
europmc-pmc5854578:
Senapati and co-authors review drug delivery vehicles for cancer treatment. Their article appeared in Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy. Standard chemotherapy has clear flaws, the authors note. Drugs spread through the whole body and harm healthy tissue. High doses are often needed, and resistance can develop. Carriers aim to bring drugs to tumour sites and spare other tissue.

The review covers carriers made from polymers, lipids, and other materials. It explains how their structure shapes how well drugs work. Tiny carriers can pool in tumours and enter cells more readily. The authors also weigh safety issues such as poor breakdown in the body. Readers get a broad survey of carrier types and their performance.
europmc-pmc5870778:
Brown and co-authors present FQC Dashboard, a tool for sequencing quality control. Their article appeared in Bioinformatics. FASTQ files hold raw sequence reads plus quality scores. The FastQC program sums up quality for single files. FQC runs that check, parses the results, and gathers them. Findings appear in a web dashboard that users can explore.

Runs are grouped in dropdown menus for easy browsing. Plain configuration files control the pages and tabs. Extra data in CSV form can extend the display. The tool is written in Python and JavaScript. It is free under an MIT license, with code online. Sequencing staff can spot failing runs more quickly.
europmc-pmc5905078:
Edington wrote a note on the skull of Dr. Pritchard, the Glasgow poisoner. The note appeared in the Glasgow Medical Journal in 1912. Pritchard was convicted of poisoning his wife and her mother. He was hanged in 1865 before a huge crowd. It was Glasgow's last public execution. A cast of his head was taken before burial.

Demolition of the old court buildings led to exhumation in 1910. Bodies buried in the prison courtyard were uncovered then. Edington reports the state of the remains found. Pritchard's boots and coat fragments were still recognisable. The note links a famous trial to physical remains. It is part medical record, part local history.
europmc-pmc5928078:
Xu and co-authors make nitrogen-rich carbon nanofibers for potassium-ion batteries. Their article appeared in Nature Communications. Potassium is plentiful, unlike lithium used in most batteries. Slow potassium uptake has limited electrode choices, though. Their soft carbon anode is packed with nitrogen. It aims for fast charging and long life.

The anode stored charge well even at very high rates, they report. It still worked after 4,000 cycles at a strong rate. Storage happened mostly at the surface, tests showed. A full cell with a Prussian blue cathode also performed well. Low cost and lasting materials add appeal. The work may guide searches for better potassium storage.
europmc-pmc5946678:
Egerton and co-authors review the gut microbiota of marine fish. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Microbiology. Work on fish gut microbes is dwarfed by work on humans. Yet the field has grown with the aquaculture industry. Recent focus falls on shaping gut microbes through diet. The aim is to meet farming needs while keeping fish healthy. Wild fish baseline data are still scarce.

The review covers factors that shape the marine fish gut community. Fish live amid dense microbial life in the oceans. Their gut microbes aid nutrition, metabolism, and immune defence. The authors flag gaps in knowledge about specific microbes' roles. Fish diversity makes single baselines hard to set.
europmc-pmc5952578:
Rana and Musto review the role of inflammation in the development of epilepsy. Their review appeared in the Journal of Neuroinflammation. Epilepsy often follows earlier injury to the nervous system. Poor control of inflammation in injured tissue may be a key step. How that imbalance drives epilepsy is still unclear. The authors trace inflammatory pathways that may link the two.

They review inflammatory molecules in brain and body-wide disorders. Rheumatoid arthritis, Crohn's disease, and type 1 diabetes are covered. Such molecules could feed the process that ends in seizures. Blood-brain barrier breakdown also features in the picture. The authors argue this knowledge could yield risk markers. It may also point to new preventive treatments.
europmc-pmc5969978:
Lamont exhibits a specimen of cystic pneumatosis of the bowel and reviews the rare condition. He spoke at a Glasgow medical society meeting in January 1929. The paper appeared in the Glasgow Medical Journal. The condition puts gas-filled cysts in the bowel wall. Recorded cases are very few, he notes. About ten were published in Britain and America over two centuries. Continental literature held some eighty more.

An Amsterdam catalogue from 1737 gives an early reference. Gas cysts also appear often in swine intestines, Lamont adds. John Hunter linked them to air escaping through diseased vessels. Lamont describes his specimen's morbid anatomy in detail.
europmc-pmc5984078:
Kelly and a huge team of co-authors map white matter differences in schizophrenia across thousands of brains. Their study appeared in Molecular Psychiatry. Single studies had given scattered pictures of these differences. The ENIGMA working group coordinated 29 international studies. Data covered 2,359 healthy controls and 1,963 patients. Diffusion imaging was processed the same way at every site.

Fractional anisotropy was lower in patients across most regions, they report. Twenty of 25 regions showed significant reductions. The whole white matter skeleton peaked at an effect size of 0.42. The anterior corona radiata and corpus callosum stood out. No effects of onset age or drug dose appeared.
europmc-pmc5997778:
Allen and co-authors make the case that mitochondrial dysfunction is a key player in depression. Their paper appeared in Frontiers in Neuroscience. Depression was long tied to monoamine changes and neuron growth. New data point to wider losses of cell plasticity. Mitochondria power the cell and steer brain function. They also drive oxidative stress and apoptosis. Faults in their energy work may precede depressive symptoms.

Drug data on mitochondria point both ways, the authors note. Some antidepressants help them, others worsen their state. The link still deserves deeper study, they argue. Mitochondria could be targets for new antidepressant drugs. Specific faults might serve as personal treatment markers.
europmc-pmc6007078:
Street and co-authors introduce Slingshot, a method for inferring cell lineages and pseudotime from single-cell data. Their paper appeared in BMC Genomics. Single-cell sequencing reveals mixed cell communities in detail. Stem cells can be charted as they mature into types. Tracing several branching paths at once stays hard. Slingshot was built for exactly that problem. It combines stable techniques suited to noisy data.

On published data sets it found one to three true trajectories, they report. Simulations showed more accurate pseudotimes than rival methods. The tool stays flexible across varied data shapes. Accurate lineage maps expose how gene activity changes over time.
europmc-pmc6020378:
Chuai and co-authors present DeepCRISPR, a design platform for gene editing. Their article appeared in Genome Biology. CRISPR uses a guide RNA to direct cutting. A good guide hits its target strongly. It should also avoid cutting at wrong sites.

DeepCRISPR predicts both effects in one framework. It uses deep learning trained on guide data. The system also finds sequence traits that shape success. Epigenetic features, tied to how DNA is packaged, matter too. The authors report it beat existing design tools. Automated feature finding removes much manual guesswork. Readers get a guide to choosing safer, stronger guides. The platform is free online for research use.
europmc-pmc6033178:
Griffiths and co-authors review missed nursing care and staffing levels. Their systematic review appeared in the Journal of Advanced Nursing. Missed care means needed care is delayed or omitted. It has been proposed as a direct staffing signal. Death rates alone give a blurrier picture.

The team searched major databases for quantitative studies. Eighteen studies reported missed care from nurse surveys. In most, three quarters or more reported omitting care. Fourteen studies tied low staffing to more missed care. Adding support workers showed little clear benefit. The authors call missed care a promising quality indicator. They note that reported omissions may not equal real failures. Readers get a careful summary for policy and practice.
europmc-pmc6054678:
Zarrinpar and co-authors study what wiping out gut microbes does to metabolism. Their research article appeared in Nature Communications. Antibiotics are often used to deplete microbes in mice. Such mice help test the microbiome's role in disease. Their own metabolic shifts were not well mapped.

Depleted mice had lower baseline blood sugar. They also handled glucose loads better than normal mice. Insulin sensitivity improved without any change in fatness. Gut levels of short-chain fatty acids fell sharply. Bile acid pools shifted in gut and body. Colon cells changed their fuel use in response. They burned glucose instead of fatty acids. Gut hormone signaling also changed with depletion. Readers get a baseline map for interpreting such experiments.
europmc-pmc6064978:
Prins and Kingdom argue for formal model comparison in psychophysics. Their article appeared in Frontiers in Psychology. Researchers there often estimate thresholds condition by condition. They then eyeball whether the pattern fits a claim. Formal hypothesis tests stay rare in the field.

The authors blame training gaps and missing software. They present Palamedes, a Matlab toolbox built for this task. Its model-comparison approach targets exact research hypotheses. Users gain freedom in how tests are framed. The article explains the method in plain, non-technical terms. Readers get tools for sharper inference from perception data.
europmc-pmc6156078:
Donovan and co-authors present a research article in eLife on how thalidomide breaks down a key development protein. Thalidomide once caused severe birth defects when used for morning sickness. Yet thalidomide and related drugs are now a mainstay of cancer care. How they work at the molecular level was unclear.

The team shows these drugs trigger destruction of several zinc finger transcription factors. One is SALL4, a protein that guides early development. People born with faulty SALL4 show defects much like thalidomide's, including the Duane Radial Ray syndrome pattern. The finding explains the drug's birth defects. It also clarifies how the drugs attack cancer cells.
europmc-pmc6192678:
Thompson and co-authors present a meta-analysis in Nature, with the Earth Microbiome Project Consortium, cataloguing Earth's microbe diversity. How much microbes matter is now clear, yet the basic shape of their world stayed dim. Studies used mismatched methods, so their results could not be compared.

Hundreds of researchers gathered samples under shared project rules and shared ways of reading them. New methods track exact DNA sequences across studies in place of rough groupings. That lets microbe communities be compared across places and scales. The catalogue shows patterns in microbe life across the planet. The authors note gaps in the map, both in place and in soil and water traits. Their frame can grow to fill those gaps in time.
europmc-pmc6248078:
Schoemaker and co-authors pooled data on body weight and breast cancer risk before menopause. Their pooled analysis appeared in JAMA Oncology. The data cover more than 758,000 women who had not yet reached menopause. Weight was tracked through body mass index at several ages. Earlier single studies were too small to test age bands and tumour types well.

The team found that higher body mass index went with lower breast cancer risk. The link was strongest for weight at ages eighteen to twenty-four. It held across the full weight range. Hormone sensitive tumours showed the clearest pattern. The authors note that fat after menopause raises risk instead. The contrast by life stage is a key puzzle for prevention research. Their result does not mean weight gain is safe overall.
europmc-pmc6255378:
Mirjalili and co-authors review the active compounds of the herb ashwagandha. Their review appeared in Molecules. The plant, Withania somnifera, has served Ayurvedic medicine for over 3,000 years. Its key compounds are called withanolides. They are steroid like molecules built on a shared ring frame. Modern labs have tested the extracts for many effects.

Two compounds draw special focus in the review. Withaferin A slowed tumours and blocked new blood vessel growth in tests. Withanolide A showed effects of interest for Alzheimer's disease. The authors lay out the structures of the wider compound family. They also weigh its broader medical actions. A final part covers growing the compounds with biotechnology. Plant cell methods may supply them without harvesting wild plants.
europmc-pmc6268778:
Rivas and co-authors tested the handed forms of pinene, a scent compound from pine oils. Their study appeared in Molecules. Pinene comes in two shapes, alpha and beta. Each shape also has a left and right handed form. The team tested all forms against bacteria and fungi. Only the positive handed forms killed microbes.

Strength was measured as the lowest dose that stopped or killed each germ. The positive forms killed Candida yeast within an hour. They killed resistant Staphylococcus aureus within six hours. Paired with a standard antibiotic, they boosted action against that resistant strain. They also blocked biofilm growth by Candida at low doses. Harm to mouse immune cells was checked as well. Handedness, the study shows, can decide whether a natural compound works at all.
europmc-pmc6269478:
Jain and co-authors built a fast method to compare whole genomes and test species borders. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. The method is called FastANI. It estimates average nucleotide identity, a shared measure of genome likeness. Older tools were too slow for today's genome flood. FastANI skips direct alignment and uses near matching instead. It runs up to a thousand times faster.

The team compared about ninety thousand microbe genomes against each other. That meant roughly eight billion pairs. Nearly all pairs fell into two clear bands. Genomes of one species matched above ninety-five percent. Genomes of distinct species fell below eighty-three percent. The gap held even when common species were removed. Clear borders, not a smooth blend, seem to rule microbe diversity. Fast tools make such global checks possible at all.
europmc-pmc6325578:
Cai and co-authors review metal-organic frameworks that release drugs on cue. Their review appeared in Advanced Science. These materials, called MOFs, form spongy crystal lattices. Their pores can be tuned in size. Their surfaces are easy to change as well. Such traits suit them to carrying medicine.

Smart delivery systems respond to signals in the body. Others respond to triggers applied from outside. The review sorts MOF systems by their trigger. Acid level, magnets, ions, and heat are covered. Light, moisture, pressure, and chemical state appear too. Some systems answer several triggers at once. Most work so far targets anticancer drugs. The authors close with design problems still to solve. They point to what safer, smarter carriers will need.
europmc-pmc6417278:
Woodward and co-authors present a new implementation framework in Implementation Science. Health equity and implementation science have long run as separate fields. Their Health Equity Implementation Framework joins the two.

The framework maps factors at patient, provider, and system levels that block fair care. The team applied it to hepatitis C treatment among Black veterans. That case showed where the rollout fell short for those patients. The authors argue the framework can guide fair rollout of any new treatment. It turns equity from an afterthought into a design step.
europmc-pmc6425178:
Su and co-authors review how whole-genome sequencing can predict whether a bacterium will resist antibiotics, without waiting for culture-based tests. Labs have long grown bacteria and exposed them to drugs to learn what works. Reading the genome instead promises faster answers plus rich data for tracking outbreaks.

Recent studies show sequence data can forecast resistance for many known drug-and-bug combinations, sometimes from samples sequenced directly. Gaps remain where the genetic basis of resistance is poorly mapped, so the authors expect sequencing and classic testing to support each other. Clinicians reading this gain a grounded view of where genome-based testing already helps and where caution is still required.
europmc-pmc6452778:
Mulani and co-authors review other ways to fight the ESKAPE pathogens, six hospital germs known for shrugging off many drugs. The six are Enterococcus faecium, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Enterobacter species. Strains that build enzymes able to break even last-line drugs have left doctors short of options that work.

The options surveyed include drug pairings and boosters, phages, germ-killing peptides, tiny particles, and light-based therapy. Each is weighed for how it works and its promise in living animals. Trial status and limits count too, such as harm from peptides and the cost of making them. Pairing two or more ways earns special stress, since each can cover the other's weak spots and stretch the working life of drugs already on the shelf.
europmc-pmc6535078:
Yousufuddin and Young review how aging drives ischemic stroke, writing in the journal Aging. Stroke risk doubles every ten years after age 55, and three quarters of strokes strike people aged 65 or more. Of 795,000 strokes a year in the United States, 87% are ischemic, caused by blocked blood flow to the brain.

Aging also stiffens and narrows the brain's vessels and weakens their self-control of flow. Silent damage is common: hidden infarcts, white matter disease and tiny bleeds that raise later stroke risk. Risk factors such as high blood pressure, diabetes and atrial fibrillation cluster in older adults, and most older stroke patients carry several chronic conditions. Trial proof for prevention drugs in the oldest patients stays thin, leaving hard choices for doctors.
europmc-pmc6598278:
Lin and co-authors report a research article in the Journal of Neuroinflammation. They study people with Parkinson's disease in Taiwan. The work links gut bacteria with immune signals in the blood. Earlier work hinted that gut changes may feed brain inflammation. This group tests that idea in an Asian patient group, where past data are thin.

The team sequenced stool samples from 80 patients and 77 matched controls. They also measured nine plasma cytokines with a multiplex assay. Patients' gut communities held more Verrucomicrobia, Lactobacillus, and Bacteroides. Prevotella was more common in controls. Bacteroides levels tracked motor score severity. Two cytokines, TNFα and IFNγ, ran higher in patients. A second cohort of 120 patients and 120 controls confirmed those raised levels.
europmc-pmc6650278:
Lloyd-Price and co-authors present a multi-omics portrait of the gut ecosystem in inflammatory bowel disease. Their study appears in Nature. Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis affect millions worldwide. The work sits inside the Integrative Human Microbiome Project. Researchers followed 132 subjects for a full year each. Sampling reached 24 time points per person. In total they gathered 2,965 stool, biopsy, and blood specimens.

During disease activity, gut communities shifted in a set pattern. Facultative anaerobes rose at the expense of obligate ones. Microbial transcription and metabolite pools were disrupted. Bile acids and short-chain fatty acids changed in step. Periods of activity also showed greater temporal variability. All data feed the public IBDMDB resource.
europmc-pmc6656778:
Porcu and co-authors present TWMR, a method linking gene expression to complex traits causally. Their paper appears in Nature Communications. Genome-wide studies find thousands of trait variants. Most sit outside genes and lack clear meaning. Many overlap expression QTLs that tune gene activity. TWMR applies Mendelian randomization across the transcriptome. It uses many variants as instruments at once. It also models many expression traits together. That design handles pleiotropy better than rivals.

Applied to 43 human phenotypes, the method found 3,913 associations. The authors call these putatively causal gene-trait links. Over a third had no strong GWAS signal nearby. Most were missed for power reasons, checks suggested. One link tied BSCL2 to educational attainment.
europmc-pmc6798078:
Zhao and Cao review engineered T cell therapy for cancer in the clinic. T cells are central to cell-based immunity in the body. Two strategies reprogram them: CAR T cells, given a synthetic receptor, and TCR T cells, given a new natural-style receptor. Both have produced encouraging results in trials against malignant tumors. Solid tumors remain harder, shielded by dense matrix and suppressive cells.

The article surveys worldwide clinical uses of both therapies in patients. Design details matter for success: adding helper domains such as ICOS and 4-1BB improved cell persistence and anticancer effect in one design. Surface levels of the receptor also shaped how well cells worked. The authors predict engineered T cells will become safe, well-tolerated, and effective standard treatments.
europmc-pmc6876278:
Dimitrov and co-authors present an updated naming system for Newcastle disease virus, in Infection, Genetics and Evolution. The virus, also called avian paramyxovirus 1, infects birds worldwide and can devastate poultry. Several rival schemes for sorting its strains grew up over the years. They rested on different methods and vague cutoffs, so studies clashed and comparisons broke down.

A 2012 scheme by Diel and co-workers introduced objective criteria, but uptake was partial and the virus kept evolving. This update revises the classification and nomenclature together, applying the criteria across the full set of known genotypes. Eight virus sequences still fit no genotype. The authors aim for one shared language for surveillance and research.
europmc-pmc6884778:
Ma and co-authors report a study in the Journal for ImmunoTherapy of Cancer on worn-out T cells in liver cancer. Inside tumours, killer CD8 T cells often slide into an exhausted state and stop fighting. The marker PD1 rises as they tire. How the depth of that exhaustion relates to a patient's outlook in hepatocellular carcinoma was not mapped.

The team profiled cells from fresh tumours of 56 patients, plus archived samples from cohorts of 358 and 254 patients. Cells with the very highest PD1 levels carried the fullest exhaustion signature. Patients whose tumours held many such cells did worse. Broader CD8 presence alone, by contrast, tracked with longer survival.
europmc-pmc6964678:
Koundouros and Poulogiannis review how cancer cells rewire their fat metabolism. Their review appeared in the British Journal of Cancer. Cancer cells reshape their chemistry to keep energy and building blocks flowing for growth. Fatty acids matter beyond membranes: they carry signals and serve as fuel.

The authors organise the field into four areas. First, how cells balance making fatty acids against importing them. Second, how cancer-driving pathways, such as PI3K-AKT-mTOR, seize control of fat handling, and how tumour variety complicates that picture. Third, how fatty acids help cancers progress and spread by reshaping their surroundings. Fourth, strategies and pitfalls in drugging fat metabolism. Untangling the interplay between cancer signals and fat chemistry, they argue, should expose new weak points.
europmc-pmc6995578:
Abu Samaan and co-authors review paclitaxel, a flagship chemotherapy drug, in breast cancer care. Their review appeared in Biomolecules. Paclitaxel is among the most widely used anticancer drugs and a first-line choice for breast cancer. It kills cells through several routes that end in programmed death.

Resistance is the central problem. Tumour cells dodge the drug using pump proteins, small regulatory RNAs, and gene mutations. Side effects, including nerve damage and allergic reactions tied to its solvent, add to the burden. A newer albumin-bound form raises efficiency and lowers some risks. Nanoparticle versions aim the drug at tumours for steadier effect. The authors summarise lab and clinical evidence, and judge where this drug's future in breast cancer lies.
europmc-pmc7014278:
Wang and co-authors review chitosan derivatives in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Chitosan comes from chitin, a natural material found widely in shells and fungi. It is safe and breaks down in the body. One flaw limits its use in medicine, though: it barely dissolves in water.

The review covers four ways to change chitosan chemically. They are acylation, carboxylation, alkylation, and quaternization. Each change aims to raise solubility, add pH sensitivity, or improve targeting. The authors then survey medical uses of the changed forms. They include antibacterial materials, slow-release systems, and carriers that deliver drugs or vaccines to chosen sites. The review maps a fast-growing route toward new drug products.
europmc-pmc7033178:
Patel and co-authors report a nanoparticle study in Nature Communications. Lipid nanoparticles carry mRNA into cells, but most particles get trapped in endosomes. Only a small share of the cargo escapes. The team tested whether natural variants of cholesterol could improve that escape.

They built particles with plant sterols that have a C-24 alkyl tail. These particles took a polyhedral shape instead of a round one. Cells took them up more and kept them longer, the authors report. Tracking of single particles showed faster movement inside cells. Gene transfer improved as well. The tail length, ring flexibility, and a hydroxyl group all mattered. The work links particle surface makeup to delivery success.
europmc-pmc7044178:
Manisalidis and co-authors review the environmental and health impacts of air pollution in Frontiers in Public Health. Air pollution drives climate change and also damages bodies directly, raising illness and death rates. The review names the main culprits. Particulate matter slips deep into the lungs by inhalation. Ground-level ozone harms the breathing and circulatory systems, while nitrogen oxides, sulfur dioxide, and organic compounds add their own injury.

Carbon monoxide can poison outright at high levels, and heavy metals such as lead cause poisoning or slow intoxication once absorbed. The diseases that follow include chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, asthma, bronchiolitis, lung cancer, cardiovascular events, and disorders of the nervous system and skin. Effects vary with the pollutant, its source and dose, and with place and season. The authors frame clean air as a basic condition for a healthy population.
europmc-pmc7075278:
Xia and co-authors probe how the new coronavirus fuses with cells in Cellular and Molecular Immunology. The virus, 2019-nCoV, had caused more than 17,388 confirmed cases and 361 deaths as of 3 February 2020. Like SARS-CoV, it uses the human ACE2 receptor and belongs to lineage B betacoronaviruses. Entry depends on the spike protein's S2 subunit, where two regions, HR1 and HR2, zip together into a six-helix bundle that pulls virus and cell membranes together.

The authors had previously built fusion inhibitors against SARS and MERS by targeting that machinery. Sequence comparison located the corresponding domains in the new virus, though its HR1 core carries notable mutations compared with older SARS-like viruses. They designed peptide inhibitors based on the HR1 and HR2 regions to jam the bundle's formation. The letter maps a concrete drug target and a tested design strategy, transferred from two earlier coronavirus emergencies to the third.
europmc-pmc7076378:
Wadhwa and co-authors review the delivery of mRNA vaccines in the journal Pharmaceutics. Messenger RNA has become a hot therapeutic format, aimed at infectious disease vaccines, cancer immunotherapy, protein replacement, and genetic disease. Three obstacles block the road: the molecule is very large, it is intrinsically unstable and easily chewed up by enzymes, and it provokes the immune system.

Chemical tweaks solve part of the problem, but getting the molecule inside cells remains the major hurdle. A working drug needs delivery technology that keeps mRNA stable under body conditions until it arrives. The review concentrates on non-viral delivery systems, including lipids, polymers, and nanoparticles, and weighs their strengths for vaccines. It then reports the clinical status of mRNA vaccine candidates and closes with perspectives on the future. Written before any mRNA vaccine reached market, it maps the delivery science such products would stand on.
europmc-pmc7230578:
Helmy and co-authors offer a comprehensive review of the COVID-19 pandemic, from the virus's family tree to control measures. Their article appeared in the Journal of Clinical Medicine. The outbreak began with unexplained pneumonia in Wuhan in December 2019. It was tied to a seafood wholesale market there. The cause proved to be a new coronavirus, SARS-CoV-2.

Genetic analysis shows the virus is 96.3 percent similar to a bat coronavirus. Spread between people was confirmed, even from carriers without symptoms. By the time of writing, at least 200 countries had cases. The review organizes what was known about genetics, spread, diagnosis, and treatment. It also covers prevention and control at population level. Readers get one wide briefing on a fast-moving emergency.
europmc-pmc7250878:
Littlejohns and co-authors describe the UK Biobank imaging project in Nature Communications. UK Biobank first recruited half a million adults aged 40 to 69. Starting in 2014, it invited 100,000 of them back for detailed body and brain scans. The goal was to build the world's largest study of its kind.

The scans include brain, heart and belly MRI. They also include bone density scans and neck artery ultrasound. The team explains how scans are collected, checked, stored and shared. By early 2020, more than 45,000 people had been scanned. The authors also plan repeat scans for at least 10,000 people. Readers learn how this linked scan, health and gene data can support research on many diseases.
europmc-pmc7253578:
Muhammad and co-authors review bacterial biofilms and ways to control or promote them. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Microbiology. A biofilm is a community of bacteria stuck to a surface. The cells hold together in a self-made matrix of sugars, proteins and DNA. Such films cause trouble in hospitals, food plants and water systems.

Formation runs through five stages, from loose attachment to mature growth and dispersal. The authors list methods that block attachment or disrupt cell signals called quorum sensing. Other methods attack the matrix itself. Biofilms can also help clean waste water, protect plants and slow corrosion. Those uses get equal space, with ideas for growing helpful films on purpose.
europmc-pmc7310678:
Grant and co-authors pool 148 studies from 9 countries to find how common each COVID-19 symptom really is. Their systematic review and meta-analysis appeared in PLoS ONE. The analysis covers 24,410 adults with laboratory-confirmed infection, in literature searched on April 5, 2020. Clear symptom rates were needed to write sensible quarantine and testing rules.

Fever was the most prevalent symptom at 78%, followed by cough at 57% and fatigue at 31%. Among hospitalized patients, 19% needed non-invasive ventilation and 17% needed intensive care. Rates varied considerably between studies, a warning against single-source figures. The pooled estimates give policy makers a firmer base for deciding which symptoms should trigger testing or isolation.
europmc-pmc7360778:
Brumpton and co-authors show how family structure can bias gene-based causal studies, in Nature Communications. Mendelian randomization uses inherited variants as natural experiments to test whether a trait causes a disease. Studies of unrelated people, though, can be skewed by population mixing, mate choice, and parents shaping children's environments.

Using siblings removes much of that bias, since brothers and sisters share family background. The team tested the idea in simulations and in 61,008 siblings from Norwegian and UK studies, plus 222,368 siblings from 23andMe. Known effects, such as lower body mass cutting diabetes risk, held up. Claims that height or body mass raise education largely faded within families. Family data, they argue, should check such findings.
europmc-pmc7366678:
Strunz and co-authors trace how injured lungs rebuild their air sacs, in Nature Communications. They sequenced single cells over time in a mouse lung injury model and resolved 28 cell types. Lineage tracing then showed where each repairing cell came from.

Airway and alveolar stem cells converge on one transitional state, marked by the protein Krt8, before becoming the flat cells that line air sacs. These in-between cells look squamous, show stress and aging signals, and appear in several injury models. In human lung fibrosis they fail to move on and persist, forming their own signaling network with support cells and macrophages. Stalled repair, the authors propose, is part of what makes fibrosis permanent.
europmc-pmc7398478:
Weersma and co-authors review the two-way traffic between common drugs and gut microbes in Gut. The gut microbiome mediates how a person meets their environment, and drugs are part of that meeting.
