The review stresses non-antibiotic drugs, whose microbial effects are less obvious than antibiotics'.

Drugs reshape the gut community, and the community reshapes drugs in return. Microbes chemically transform drug structures, changing how much is available, how active it is, and how toxic. Microbes also sway responses to cancer immunotherapy indirectly. Common medicines such as stomach acid blockers leave clear fingerprints on the microbiome. Understanding this traffic, the authors argue, could let doctors tune the microbiome to make treatments work better.
europmc-pmc7432778:
Furue reviews how skin barrier proteins are controlled in atopic dermatitis. The disease is an itchy eczema with a weak skin barrier. Three proteins, filaggrin, loricrin, and involucrin, help keep that barrier strong.

Signals IL-4 and IL-13 switch these proteins down through STAT6 and STAT3. IL-22 and IL-17A likely add to the block. In contrast, ligands that activate the AHR receptor switch the proteins up. Coal tar, glyteer, and tapinarof act this way and also switch on the protective factor NRF2. Since the harmful signals cause oxidative stress, these dual activators work well in treatment. The review links each signal to clear steps in disease and care.
europmc-pmc7478978:
Yang and co-authors show that gut microbe products drive IL-22 output and guard gut immunity. IL-22, made by innate lymphoid cells and CD4+ T cells, is vital for intestinal defense. The microbes' role in its control was unclear.

Short-chain fatty acids from gut microbes raised IL-22 output in both cell types. They acted through the receptor GPR41 and by blocking histone deacetylase. The acids lifted two factors, AhR and HIF1-alpha, that switch on the IL-22 gene. Feeding the acids to animals protected intestines from inflammation. Human CD4+ T cells responded the same way. The findings tie diet-shaped microbes to a core gut defense. They also name paths that food or drugs might tune to calm bowel disease.
europmc-pmc7484178:
Maynard and co-authors use single-cell RNA sequencing to track how lung cancer changes under targeted therapy. Lung cancer is the top cause of cancer death. Its variety helps it adapt and dodge treatment.

The team profiled 49 biopsies from 30 patients with metastatic disease, taken before and during therapy. Over 20,000 single-cell profiles covered cancer and surrounding cells. Surviving cancer cells in residual disease took a primitive, alveolar-like state. Cells at progress switched on kynurenine, plasminogen, and gap-junction pathways. Active T cells marked residual disease, while suppressive states marked progress. Traits from the cell data predicted outcomes in other patient groups. The study shows therapy reshaping a whole tumor ecosystem.
europmc-pmc7566278:
Wu and co-authors measure SARS-CoV-2 levels in wastewater and compare them with case counts. The virus is shed in stool early in illness. Many infected people show no symptoms at all.

The team built a lab protocol using qPCR on raw sewage. Sequencing checks validated the measurement approach. Viral levels implied far more infections than confirmed cases. The gap was orders of magnitude in size. Such data may change views of case fatality rates. Catchment-level estimates could guide distancing choices over time. They could also guide when to scale measures back. The work supports wastewater checks as an early warning tool for outbreaks.
europmc-pmc7766078:
Schaufeli and co-authors build and test a new scale for burnout at work. The classic burnout scale dates from an older concept of the state. The authors first interviewed 49 practitioners on how burnout looks. Four core traits emerged: exhaustion, mental distance, and impaired emotional and cognitive control.

The new Burnout Assessment Tool was tested in 1500 Flemish employees. Its core items formed one general burnout factor, as designed. Secondary items, such as low mood and bodily complaints, formed two factors, not the expected three. Scores were reliable and matched older burnout scales well. The tool also split cleanly from engagement and workaholism.
europmc-pmc7784378:
Ragonnaud and Biragyn argue that gut microbes are key controllers of healthy aging. Diet and lifestyle shape how people age. They act in part through the gut microbiome. Microbes colonize the gut after birth and settle by about age three. Their mix keeps shifting into adulthood.

A major shift in that mix is called dysbiosis. It can spark harmful local and body-wide inflammation. The authors note that dysbiosis grows more common with age. Older guts hold more pro-inflammatory microbes and fewer helpful ones. They link this shift to leaky gut and changed metabolite levels. Their view treats dysbiosis as a prime driver of age-related illness. Fixing it could help older people live longer in good health.
europmc-pmc7798278:
Sorokina and co-authors present COCONUT, an open online database of natural products. Natural products are small molecules made by living organisms. Many are active in the body, which sparks drug research. Databases for them have multiplied over the years.

No single online source had gathered all known natural products. COCONUT fills that gap. It merges records from open sources into one dataset. Both confirmed and predicted products are included. A web interface lets users browse and search the collection. Downloads are quick and free. The authors built it to ease screening and other computer-based work.
europmc-pmc7859578:
Nannoni and co-authors review stroke in people with COVID-19. The virus became a world pandemic within months. Its link to acute blood vessel disease in the brain stayed unclear. Case reports hinted at real risk. The team searched three medical databases.

The authors pooled the studies they found. They counted how often stroke struck COVID-19 patients. Risk factors for stroke in this group were sorted. Scan and clinical patterns were described as well. Outcomes after stroke were tallied. COVID-19 strokes skewed toward large vessel blockage. Patients were often younger than typical stroke cases. The synthesis gives clinicians a first firm map of the problem.
europmc-pmc7927678:
Singer and Singer present a historical essay on Girolamo Fracastoro and his theory of infection. Fracastoro was a physician of Verona who lived from 1478? to 1553. He came from a family of noted doctors and trained at Padua in the Renaissance. His idea that disease spreads by tiny seeds shaped later thought on contagion. The essay weighs his place in the science of his age.

The authors first sketch his life, character, and writings. They then trace where his infection theory came from. Its form and reach are examined in depth. The essay asks how far his claims rested on the learning of his time. It also follows the mark the theory left on later medicine. Written in the early twentieth century, the piece treats Fracastoro as a forerunner of germ theory. It remains a study in how a bold idea grows from older roots.
europmc-pmc8068178:
Medina-Leyte and co-authors review endothelial dysfunction and inflammation as drivers of coronary artery disease. The endothelium lines the arteries and guards blood flow. When it fails, atherosclerosis takes hold. That failure raises the risk of heart attacks and other events. New tools, from liquid biopsies to molecular assays, keep finding fresh markers of the damage.

The review first sets out how a healthy endothelium works. It then sorts the markers of dysfunction into old and new. Molecular and cellular markers from recent work dominate the list. Some markers may also serve as drug targets. The authors close with ways to shield or repair the lining. Drugs and lifestyle measures both feature in that survey. Prevention of coronary disease is the end goal throughout.
europmc-pmc8078878:
Menni and co-authors track vaccine side effects and later infections in users of a UK symptom app. The prospective study drew on the COVID Symptom Study community. Between December 8, 2020 and March 10, 2021, 627,383 people reported a vaccination. Their reports covered 655,590 doses of the Pfizer-BioNTech and Oxford-AstraZeneca vaccines. Users logged local and body-wide effects within 8 days.

Systemic side effects followed 13.5% of first Pfizer doses and 33.7% of first AstraZeneca doses in the reports. A sore arm was far more common than either. People who had already caught the virus reported stronger effects. Infection risk fell from about 12 days after a first dose. By 21 to 44 days, risk was cut by 69% for the Pfizer vaccine and 60% for the AstraZeneca one in tested users.
europmc-pmc8233978:
Gold and co-authors probe long COVID prevalence and a possible link to Epstein-Barr virus. Some patients keep symptoms such as fatigue and brain fog for months. The team first surveyed 185 people who had COVID-19.

Long COVID symptoms appeared in 30.3% of those surveyed. Four people with no acute symptoms later developed them. The team then tested 68 patients for Epstein-Barr reactivation. Two thirds of the long COVID group showed reactivation signs. The rate was far lower in those without lasting symptoms. The authors flag a link that larger studies should test.
europmc-pmc8547878:
Yang and co-authors make the case for Oscillospira as a next-generation probiotic candidate. This gut genus shows up often in sequencing data but has never been grown pure in culture. It lives widely in animal and human intestines. Its levels track with leanness, obesity, and health.

Links also reach gallstones and chronic constipation. Sequencing and metabolic data suggest it makes short-chain fatty acids such as butyrate. Those products matter for gut health. Gains in obesity-linked metabolic disease look hopeful in early work. The review gathers that case in one place. Food, health care, and drug uses may follow if culture hurdles fall.
europmc-pmc8695578:
Vos and co-authors report a trial of immune therapy given before surgery for head and neck cancer. Patients got two doses of nivolumab, some with one dose of ipilimumab, in the weeks before their operation. The trial held 32 patients with advanced local disease. Surgery timing and tumor response were the main measures.

No surgery was delayed in the first phase. Major tumor response, near total loss of live tumor cells, came in 35 percent of the combo group. The single-drug group reached 17 percent. Serious immune side effects hit about a third of patients in each group. No patient with a major response saw the cancer return in follow-up.
europmc-pmc8748878:
de Hond and co-authors map guidance for artificial intelligence prediction models in health care. Such models promise much, but complex data-driven tools need quality checks before daily use. The team ran a scoping review across major databases and asked AI experts for input. They sorted guidance into six phases of model work.

From 2,683 unique hits, 72 guidance documents were kept. Strong guidance covered data preparation, model building, and validation. Later phases drew far less attention. Software building, impact checks, and rollout in clinics were thin spots. The review names these gaps for engineers, data scientists, and clinicians who build or judge such models.
europmc-pmc8812578:
Fang and co-authors review a fix for a known flaw in drug delivery. Coating tiny drug carriers with polyethylene glycol, or PEG, keeps them in the blood longer. Yet the coating also blocks cells from taking the drug in. It also hinders escape once inside the cell. The authors call this tension the PEG dilemma. Their focus is PEG layers that can be cut loose at the target.

The review sorts cleavable PEG designs by what triggers the cut. Some bonds break inside the cell. Others respond to conditions around a tumor. The authors weigh each design against older, fixed coatings. They argue that smart shedding keeps the gains of PEG while restoring drug action. That balance, they suggest, could aid future cancer treatment.
europmc-pmc8899578:
Zhang and co-authors review platinum drugs in cancer therapy and the push to improve them. Cisplatin, carboplatin, and oxaliplatin are clinic mainstays. They kill cancer cells by damaging DNA. Their flaws are serious, though. They lack selectivity and strain the whole body. Tumors also learn to resist them. The review tracks how chemists answer those flaws. Nanotechnology offers many of the new designs.

The authors trace the first-line drugs' development first. Cisplatin's mechanism gets a detailed account. Sections then cover modified platinum compounds. Platinum nanoclusters earn special focus. These tiny clusters act through fresh mechanisms. They promise better tumor targeting. Early clinical signs encourage the authors. Challenges for nanodrugs are stated plainly. The review gives a full arc from accidental discovery to engineered particles.
europmc-pmc8901678:
Chen and co-authors review the many faces of ferroptosis in liver disease. Ferroptosis is iron-driven cell death marked by fat oxidation in membranes. The liver handles both iron and nutrients, so it sits exposed. Liver disease now causes about two million deaths a year worldwide. Ferroptosis shows up across its forms. Injury, fatty liver, scarring, and cancer all involve it. The direction of harm, though, flips by disease.

In injury and fibrosis, liver cells die too easily by ferroptosis. In liver cancer, tumor cells resist it or learn resistance. The authors explain liver iron handling first. They then set out how ferroptosis is regulated. Disease sections follow one by one. Open questions are listed frankly. Biomarkers for the process are still missing. The authors weigh drugs that block or trigger ferroptosis. Timing and cell targeting are the crux.
europmc-pmc9013078:
Rong and co-authors review new treatments for glioblastoma, the most common and deadly primary brain tumor in adults. Standard care still leaves patients with very poor survival, so fresh strategies are urgent. Better genetic and immune profiling of tumors now feeds a wave of trials. The authors cover immune checkpoint blockade, CAR T cell therapy, oncolytic viruses, and vaccines.

They also review ways to cross the blood-brain barrier, including focused ultrasound for targeted delivery. Combination treatments aim to raise response rates while limiting side effects. The authors close by weighing the hurdles that still block lasting benefit for most patients.
europmc-pmc9032478:
Hersh and co-authors review how nanoparticles may carry drugs across the blood-brain barrier to treat brain tumors. The barrier blocks most drugs, and survival for malignant brain tumors stays poor. Particles small enough to slip through can also target tumor cells. The review explains routes across the barrier, including passage between cells and transport through them.

It surveys particle types, from polymer carriers and liposomes to metals and nanogels. Particles can also carry imaging probes that outline tumors and track treatment. The authors close with the limits that still keep these tools from routine care.
europmc-pmc9205778:
Qi and co-authors report interim results of a phase 1 trial of Claudin18.2-specific CAR T cells in digestive cancers. CAR T therapy works well in blood cancers but poorly in solid tumors. Claudin18.2 is common in gastric and other digestive cancers, which makes it a target. The trial treated patients whose cancers had already had other therapy.

In all, 37 patients got one of three cell doses. All had grade 3 or higher blood toxicity, and most had mild cytokine release syndrome. No severe syndrome, nerve toxicity, or treatment deaths occurred. The overall response rate reached 48.6%, and disease control was high across the group. Response in gastric cancer was higher still. The authors call the early results promising for heavily treated patients.
europmc-pmc9654278:
Rawat and co-authors summarize the role of phosphorylated tau in Alzheimer's disease and other tauopathies. Alzheimer's is the lead cause of dementia in older people. Its marks are amyloid beta deposits and tau tangles in the brain. Tau normally steadies the microtubule rails inside nerve cells.

In disease, tau takes on too many phosphate groups. The loaded protein stops doing its rail work well. Synapses falter and neurons waste away in the process. The review covers tau structure and its normal duties. Protein changes after birth and gene faults get sections. Tau spread through the brain is traced in detail. The tauopathy family spans Pick's disease and frontotemporal dementia. Progressive supranuclear palsy and Huntington's disease also join. Links with amyloid, synapses, and mitochondria are weighed. Drug work aimed at the loaded protein closes the survey.
europmc-pmc9718678:
Hendra and co-authors present m6Anet, a method that finds m6A marks from direct RNA sequencing reads. The m6A mark adds a layer of control to RNA messages. Nanopore reads carry the mark in their raw current signal. Training data, though, labels whole sites and not single molecules.

That gap is where most learning tools stumble at the start. m6Anet uses a multiple instance learning frame to bridge it. The frame learns from site labels while scoring single reads. Tests showed it beat rival computing methods on the task. Its calls matched wet lab method accuracy in the checks. It also worked on new cell lines and species with no retraining. Read level scores gave a sense of mark rates per site. One run can thus both find and size marks genome wide.
europmc-pmc9753778:
Siebner and co-authors write a consensus paper on what transcranial magnetic stimulation actually stimulates in the brain. The method is the standard way to switch brain areas on without surgery. A pulse through the skull sets up a shifting electric field. That field can fire nerve cells in the cortex below.

The group stresses that the response is more tangled than often assumed. The field hits hardest near the tops of surface folds. Axons of both excitatory and quieting cells likely fire. Whether a fiber fires depends on its shape and angle. The cell's own state at that moment matters too. Models point to axon tips at fold crowns as prime targets. Firing then spreads along links to near and far regions. Ear and skin nerves also get co-fired by each pulse. The authors urge care in reading what TMS effects mean.
frus-1861-d178:
A letter of 3 September 1861 went from William H. Seward to Carl Schurz in Madrid. The letter is document 178 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

September orders to Spain dealt with the watch on ports and trade. Cuba's harbors lay close to the blockade's edge. Seward's letter kept Schurz alert to any Spanish step that might let Southern ships find shelter or supplies. Cuba's governor took orders from Madrid, which made Schurz's post a guard on the island too. A guard on the island, kept by letter, cost the Union no ships at all.
frus-1861-d278:
News and judgment from Mr. Angel reached Seward's desk in a letter dated 10 June 1861. It was printed as Document 278 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. It was written in the opening months of the Civil War, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1861-d78:
Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 9 September 1861. The dispatch is document 78 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Two Adams letters in three days mark a full week at the London post. Notes, calls, and press talk filled the envoy's days. The second letter shows how fast fresh points could pile up, each one needing a clear report home. Fast work in September kept the small points from growing into open quarrels. Small points, met fast, stayed small; that was the whole art of the autumn.
frus-1862-d178:
On 30 October 1862 Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward from London, in a report printed as Document 178 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It is one of two Adams letters under that date.

The end of October found the French plan for a joint truce proposal nearly ready, while Britain hung back. Adams's reports from these days are prized because he heard British doubts at close range. This letter forms part of the closing record of October, the month when European action on the war came closest and then began to recede. Earl Russell, the British foreign secretary, was the minister Adams dealt with most in London.
frus-1862-d278:
Dated 12 May 1862, Document 278 is a dispatch from Secretary of State William H. Seward to William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris. It is printed in the France section of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

By mid-May, France was digesting its check at Puebla and reinforcing its army in Mexico. Washington saw a chance: a France busy in Mexico might think twice about the Confederacy. Seward's letters of this period, this one among them, probed that opening while keeping formal ties smooth with the French government. Southern agents were active in Paris too, seeking loans, ships, and friends at court.
frus-1862-d378: A translated paper dated 19 September 1862 stands as Document 378 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Filed in the French section between letters of Viscount Treilhard and Secretary Seward. The heading marks it only as a translation, with no author or reader named. So the entry rests on its date, its form, and its place in that file.
frus-1862-d478:
On 11 August 1862 James E. Harvey reported from Lisbon to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is Document 478 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the President's annual message.

Harvey wrote in the weeks when the Confederate cruiser Alabama had just slipped to sea and begun her raids. Portuguese waters, including the Azores, were among the places such ships might use. A report from Lisbon in that month spoke directly to the Union's effort against the raiders. The Union hoped to hem them in by law. It could not reach them by force. Harvey's letters give the State Department's side of that effort, from one of the ports where it was actually decided.
frus-1862-d578:
On 23 July 1862 James Watson Webb reported from Rio de Janeiro to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is Document 578 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed for Congress.

Webb's July reports came as the war at sea was spreading south in prospect. Confederate cruisers were fitting out to raid American commerce. Their hunting ground would be the ocean routes. Brazil's many ports could shelter such ships or shut them out, depending on the rules Rio enforced. A minister's report on Brazilian intentions was therefore practical intelligence, not ceremony. The letter belongs to the maritime side of the volume, where the Union fought to turn neutral law into a wall around its merchant fleet.
frus-1862-d678:
Anson Burlingame wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 24 July 1862. The dispatch comes from Burlingame's post as American minister to China. It is document 678 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, in the heart of the summer mail.

Summer letters from China brought word on trade and on the Qing court's long fight with the Taiping revolt. Burlingame's reports also served Americans who lived and traded in the treaty ports, whose safety rested on his work. This dispatch is one of the last in his 1862 run, and it shows an envoy settled into the rhythm of a hard, distant post.
frus-1862-d78:
In a letter dated 9 June 1862, William H. Seward gave Charles Francis Adams his latest word from Washington. It was printed as Document 78 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. The date falls in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1863p1-d178:
A dispatch dated 1 May 1863 carried news from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. It is document 178 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

The CSS Alabama, built in a British yard, had escaped to sea in 1862 and was burning Union merchant ships. London's handling of such ships hung over every report Adams sent home. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d278: Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, sent this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 3 September 1863. It is document 278 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, part of the London correspondence on Britain and the Civil War. Letters on this route carried Adams's reading of British policy while Washington worked to keep Britain from backing the Confederacy.
frus-1863p1-d378:
Writing in Washington on 30 January 1863, Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, addressed Secretary of State William H. Seward on British business. The paper is document 378 in the 1863 volume. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Taken as a run, these notes chart Britain slowly accepting that the Union would not collapse. That judgment, formed in Washington, helped keep Britain out of the war. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d478:
One entry in the 1863 papers is a 25 April 1863 letter from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it.

The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. A reader gets the feel of diplomacy done by hand: formal greetings, careful wording, and hard points pressed without open threats. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d578:
Secretary William H. Seward addressed a formal note to Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington on 25 June 1863. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863. The letter is one piece of the steady stream of notes that passed between the two governments in the early summer of 1863.

A reader gets the feel of diplomacy done by hand: formal greetings, careful wording, and hard points pressed without open threats. For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d678:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams, his minister in London, on 30 November 1863. The letter appears as document 678 in Foreign Relations of the United States for 1863. Adams was the main American voice in Britain through the whole Civil War.

The Union's great fear was that Britain might back the South or treat it as a full nation. Seward's London mail worked against that risk day after day. This dispatch is one small part of that steady push. Read with its neighbors, it helps show how talks stayed open and calm even while a hard war went on at home.
frus-1863p1-d78:
Charles Francis Adams wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 13 February 1863. Three Adams letters in the volume bear the date. Adams was the American minister in London, and this letter is document 78 in part one of the 1863 volume.

A three-letter day at the legation meant a full plate: talks, papers, and people to report on. Adams kept each sheet to its own head, a habit that makes his file easy to read still. This one opens the set of 13 February. In a volume built from such days, it is one more proof of the post's pace at the heart of the war.
frus-1878:
The 1878 papers open with Hayes counting blessings and one disaster. Yellow fever has swept the lower Mississippi that summer. He reports about twenty thousand deaths from the pestilence. The correspondence then spreads across the usual map. Mexico takes the longest country run. Britain, France, Germany, and Italy follow. Greece earns an unusually full section.

Japan's file catches a nation displaying itself. It prints the closing of a national industrial exhibition. The emperor graces the ceremony in person. Ten years since the restoration, his minister says, industry must grow. China, Haiti, and Peru fill their standard places. Turkey and Egypt close the list. The volume mixes epidemic grief with steady routine. Its Japan pages show modernization as spectacle.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d178: American delegation minutes of the final meeting of the Moscow Conference, held on October 30, 1943, form Document 178 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The final session sealed three weeks of talks and set the texts the ministers signed that day. Minutes of a closing meeting carry the formal end of a story the letters in this volume tell in pieces. The volume prints them in the Moscow section.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d278:
A long Cairo meeting of 26 November 1943 left no official record, and an editorial note in the volume covers it instead. The Log dates the start at half past four, but other accounts suggest it ran at least two hours, with Churchill and the Chiangs at Roosevelt's villa for much of the afternoon.

Elliott Roosevelt describes a final political conference in the garden, with Harriman, Eden, and Cadogan present, framing the words of the Cairo communiqué. For security, that statement was held back until after Tehran, and until Stalin approved its text. Stilwell's account adds that Chiang agreed to Burma points he had rejected the day before. The note closes with a long list of other Roosevelt-Chiang topics, from a billion-dollar loan to the Chengtu airfield costs.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d378:
Charles Bohlen's minutes record a private talk between President Roosevelt and Marshal Stalin at Tehran on 1 December 1943, at twenty past three. Roosevelt had asked Stalin to come to him to speak briefly and frankly, and the subject was American domestic politics.

Roosevelt explains that an election falls in 1944, that he may have to run again if the war continues. Six or seven million Americans of Polish descent must not be lost as voters. Personally he favors moving Poland's eastern border west and her western border to the Oder, but he cannot join any decision at Tehran or speak publicly now. On the Baltic states, he jokes he will not go to war when Soviet armies reoccupy them, but asks for some public expression of the people's will in time. Stalin answers that chances for that will come under the Soviet constitution, with no international control.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d478:
A further memorandum by the United States Chiefs of Staff bears the date December 4, 1943, the first day of the Second Cairo Conference. The American chiefs were pressing to convert the broad Tehran understandings into fixed plans. The State Department included the paper in its Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

Written positions mattered at Cairo because the two allies still differed over the balance between the cross-Channel attack and operations in the Mediterranean. The American chiefs stated their case in papers like this before arguing it in session. For readers, the memorandum is evidence from inside that argument, showing how the United States framed its demands at the summit's military level.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d78: Roosevelt wrote to Chiang Kai-shek on October 30, 1943, his second letter to China's leader in four days. It is Document 78 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The Cairo meeting, where Chiang would sit with Roosevelt and Churchill, was now set for late November, and the letters of these weeks arranged it. The record gives the date and the names. The text in the Foreign Relations series holds the details.
frus-1944-quebec-d178:
What passed between Roosevelt and Churchill at lunch on September 13, 1944, is known only at second hand. The editors draw on a memorandum by Harry White, the Treasury official, recording what Roosevelt told Morgenthau later that day. Churchill had been very glum during the conversation, according to this account.

Roosevelt said he had asked Churchill how he would like to have the steel business of Europe for twenty or thirty years. Churchill, he reported, seemed much excited over the possibility. The note also records a suggestion made at one of the day's meetings: that Fiorello La Guardia go to Italy as the president's representative and attend meetings of the Allied Control Commission.
frus-1944-quebec-d278: A one-sentence British memorandum, C.C.S. 682 of September 15, 1944, asks the American chiefs to take note of a single fact: Operation Highball would be available in the Eastern Theatre at the end of November 1944. The Combined Chiefs noted the paper at their 175th meeting the same day. No details of the operation are given in the memorandum itself.
frus-1944-quebec-d78: The editorial note listed as Document 78 was drafted by State Department historians. It sits inside the Quebec 1944 volume of conference papers. Editorial notes explain what the documents leave unsaid. They give background and point readers to related records in the series. Behind the note stands the September 1944 Quebec meeting. Roosevelt hosted Churchill there as Allied armies entered Germany. The note guides readers through the preparations for that summit.
frus-1945-50-intel-d178:
The meeting named in the title took place on 26 November 1946, and these minutes are its formal record. In the printed Foreign Relations series it is document 178, in the volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The first peace-time setup paired the National Intelligence Authority at the top with the Central Intelligence Group below it.

The record runs item by item, the way the meeting itself ran, with each topic closed by the group's choice on it. Read with the papers before and after it, the record shows a policy taking shape one meeting at a time. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d278:
On 24 May 1948, Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter sent a memorandum to the National Security Council. Readers meet it as document 278 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The CIA had its law and its first chiefs; what it still lacked was a settled sense of its own limits.

The form is plain on purpose: a named sender, a named reader, and a short statement of the matter at hand. A reader can watch the system think on paper: a fact here, a doubt there, a choice asked for at the end. Pages like this one are the bricks of the story: plain, dated, and load-bearing.
frus-1945-50-intel-d378:
A memorandum from the Under Secretary of State (Webb) reached the Executive Secretary of the National Security Council (Souers) on 4 April 1949. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 378 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. With the Dulles Report now public inside the government, agencies were sorting out what to change and what to defend.

The memo form let a staff officer speak straight to a chief: here is the point, here are the facts, here is what is asked. Kept in sequence, such memos form the true diary of the office that sent them. Pages like this one are the bricks of the story: plain, dated, and load-bearing.
frus-1945-50-intel-d78:
McCormack wrote to William Benton, assistant secretary for public and cultural relations, on 23 October 1945. Both men ran newish empires inside the State Department, Benton's being information and culture. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Where intelligence ends and public information begins was a live border question in 1945, since wartime agencies had mixed spying, analysis, and propaganda. McCormack writing to Benton shows the two office heads sorting that border between them. Readers get a look at a forgotten seam of the postwar build. The men who told America's story abroad had to share a department with the men who read the world's secrets. Neither side could swallow the other.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d178:
A way out of the Yugoslav deadlock appeared on 27 January 1945. Acting Secretary Grew's top secret report to the Secretary of State, traveling with the President's party, carries the news in excerpt. It is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

Subasic has accepted King Peter's latest proposal. The exile government will resign and be formed again at once under Subasic, on a wider basis. The new government will then put the Tito–Subasic agreement into force, taking account of the King's two objections. If the counter-proposal fails, the King will agree to the regency clause instead. Tito has consented to Subasic's coming to Belgrade to carry the agreement out, the appointment of a regency among the steps. Subasic plans to leave on 29 January.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d278:
Prisoners of war head the matters Winant put to Stettinius on 28 January 1945. His letter from London, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, was written on the eve of the conference. The Russians, he explains, feel deeply about this problem, and the letter shows why.

Hundreds of thousands of Soviet people, brutally treated by the Germans, are being freed in growing numbers by the allied armies. Moscow is pressing London and Washington, through the military missions, for two-way agreements. Each government would treat the other's freed nationals by the standard it applies to its own soldiers. Civilians count the same as soldiers in the Russian view. Winant adds a confession of difficulty. The European Advisory Commission never got to grips with the question. Its special subcommittee never met, for want of instructions to him.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d378: Get this referred to the foreign ministers before there is trouble. That is the whole of Harry Hopkins's advice to the President in this note of February 7, 1945, passed during the fourth plenary meeting. The slip is one sentence long, signed with Hopkins's first name. Its link to that session rests on internal evidence and on a later account the editors cite. Small as it is, the note shows the adviser steering a heated debate toward the ministers' table, where bargains could be drafted in cooler language.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d478:
What Polish democrats wanted is summed up in this cable from Grew of February 6, 1945. The summary covers a memorandum by former Premier Mikolajczyk. The Polish people at home, it said, desired to regulate Polish-Soviet relations. They feared Poland would be forced into communism. Their hopes of independence rested on Britain and the United States.

The memorandum urged a guarantee by all three great powers. Frontier changes should embrace all frontiers at once. The eastern frontier should be settled by compromise, not unilateral dictation, and should favor Poland more than the Curzon Line did. Restitution should include Danzig and East Prussia. Grew's summary reached Yalta as the leaders drew the map the memorandum dreaded.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d78:
Two open items had to be settled before a United Nations conference could even be called. Acting Secretary Stettinius told the President so on 15 November 1944, in a memorandum printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. The items were Security Council voting and invitations with initial membership.

Stettinius then lists the ways to reach agreement. The most promising, he writes, is a meeting of the three heads of government. Failing that, the three foreign ministers might meet, preferably in London. A third option sends the Under Secretary to London. The paper is a direct step toward the Big Three meeting that became Yalta.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d178:
General Eisenhower suggested putting the Danube question on the summit agenda in a message dated July 3, 1945. Only a paraphrased extract is printed, as document 178 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The full text appears in the second volume, as an enclosure to another document.

The surviving lines discuss an international problem: the internationalization of the Danube river. They say its urgency would suggest adding it to the agenda of the coming Big Three conference, if that action is thought proper. Control of the Danube, Europe's great east-west waterway, was contested ground. The Soviet Union dominated its lower course, while the Western powers wanted the river opened to free navigation. Even this fragment shows a field commander feeding a policy question up to the summit.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d278:
A briefing paper described the pending Austrian occupation zones in a paper dated June 23, 1945. The paper is document 278 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It covers the agreements the European Advisory Commission was finishing in London for Austria's zones of occupation and control machinery.

The zones are largely settled. Salzburg and Upper Austria south of the Danube go to the United States. Burgenland and Lower Austria go to the Soviets. Styria and Carinthia go to the British. The Tirol and Vorarlberg go to the French. The one main obstacle is the zoning of Vienna itself. After a recent reconnaissance mission, most differences look solvable except the airfields. Washington, London, and Paris each press for a field of their own near the capital. Moscow has so far offered only one field for all three. Talks to settle the point were under way.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d378:
Notes on reparation, drafted at Babelsberg on July 14, 1945, try to fix the scope of the term before any division among claimants. Agreement, the paper argues, should first be sought on how reparation relates to other forms of compensation by Germany. Only then should the allies argue over shares.

War booty, it says, should be defined narrowly, ideally as only the equipment and supplies of the German armed forces. The net value of labor services by Germans outside Germany should be credited to the reparations account. Restitution should count both property Germany destroyed and property it carried off. The paper was used the next day with the British.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d478:
Allied Force Headquarters is defended in Kirk's top secret cable from Caserta of July 7, 1945. His mission had made clear, he writes, how essential it held the retention of allied troops in Europe, and American troops in particular, to the preservation of order. He need not stress its concurrence in the supreme commander's views along those lines.

So long as an allied military commitment lasts in the area, Kirk argues, the headquarters should preserve an allied character. It should be reduced in size and moved to Trieste, the vital strategic point in southeastern Europe. He also proposes abolishing the political adviser's office, its useful work passing to a liaison officer attached to the Rome embassy.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d578:
Moscow ambassador Averell Harriman reported again to the President and Secretary of State on July 13, 1945. His top secret wire is document 578 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It details the last, best offer China's T. V. Soong put to Stalin and Molotov.

Soong proposed joint railways with an equal board and a Chinese chairman. The Chinese Eastern line would have a Russian manager, the South Manchurian line a Chinese one. Dairen would stay a free port under Chinese rule, with docks leased to the Soviets for trade. Port Arthur would be a naval base under Soviet control for joint use. Stalin called the plan unsatisfactory and gave nothing back. Soong left for Chungking to consult Chiang, hoping Truman might win a compromise at Potsdam.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d678:
An extract from James Dunn's Potsdam memo of July 14, 1945, covers Tangier. It is document 678 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers, drawn from his talk with Sir Alexander Cadogan. Dunn reported the item to Secretary Byrnes among many agenda points.

Cadogan reported that the Paris talks on Tangier had been suspended. His government had not yet answered the Russian request to join them. It felt it could not refuse, since the United States had already joined the talks. Dunn replied that he saw no basis for keeping Russia out. Cadogan then suggested a wider table if Russia came in. All the interested powers should be invited, the Belgians, Dutch, and Swedes among them. The Spaniards, he added, presumably would not be.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d78:
Ambassador Harriman appealed to Soviet official Andrei Vyshinsky in a letter dated June 19, 1945. The letter is document 78 in the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Eisenhower needed his advance party in Berlin the next day. They had to prepare housing, food, and communications for the American delegation. But the Soviet General Staff wanted to wait for Zhukov's return on June 28.

Harriman sets out the request in detail: General Parks, 50 officers, 175 enlisted men, and 50 trucks. He also asks free use of the Dessau-Berlin highway and the Halle-Berlin air route. A little over two weeks after June 28, he argues, would not leave enough time to get ready. He asks for approval that night so the movement can start in the morning.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1078:
Ambassador Alexander Kirk sent this extract of a telegram from Caserta on July 24, 1945. It reports a sharp exchange in Belgrade between the British ambassador and Marshal Tito. The ambassador had been ordered to protest Yugoslav radio and press propaganda, and fiery statements by Yugoslav leaders, on the Greek frontier and Venezia Giulia questions.

Tito answered that his own speeches only keep his people informed. Yugoslav propaganda on Greece, he said, replies to Greek attacks, and British newspapers share blame for the Venezia Giulia row. He rejected the argument, but agreed to seek direct talks with Athens to settle difficulties. The ambassador doubted the Yugoslav press would change its line.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1178:
In a less common direction, the Acting Secretary of State wrote to the Secretary of State himself on 31 July 1945. Joseph Grew ran the department from Washington while Secretary Byrnes was at Potsdam. His message reported home-front business up to his chief at the talks.

The flow of cables usually ran from the summit to the capital. This one runs the other way: the home office briefing the team abroad. It shows the department's two halves keeping each other posted in the last days. A reader gets the whole circuit in one note, Washington speaking and Potsdam listening.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1278:
President Truman wrote to Generalissimo Stalin on 21 July 1945. Leader-to-leader notes were the summit's most direct channel. This one went from the American president to the Soviet chief in the middle of the talks' first week.

Such a message carried the sender's personal weight. It could soften a session, press a claim, or test the other man's mood between meetings. This note belongs to the pair of Truman-Stalin exchanges in the volume. Read with Stalin's reply of the following week, it shows the top of the alliance at work in its own words.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1378:
Charles Yost, executive secretary of the conference's central secretariat, wrote a memorandum on 9 August 1945, a week after Potsdam ended. The secretariat kept the summit's records, lists, and drafts in order. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Papers written after a conference closes often explain how its texts were made and filed. Yost's post at the secretariat put him at the center of that housekeeping. His memorandum helps readers trust the record itself, since it comes from the man charged with keeping it. It is a fitting late entry in the volume: the staff view of how a great meeting was wound up and its papers put away.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-78:
A dozen shipping topics fill the subject list of another unrecorded Potsdam conversation. Its editorial note is the seventy-eighth unnumbered item following document 710 in volume two. Troop shipping for the Pacific war dominates the list.

British vessels in the Pacific for Operation Coronet head the list. The United States agreed not to request conversion of eighteen British cargo vessels to troopships. That concession was tied to the allocation of the liner Milwaukee to the United States. Whether the Milwaukee would be converted in America or Britain, and crewed by which nation, was also debated. Britain's inability to supply France with coal that winter comes up, with U.S. shipping and coal support in view. Italian charter payments, Italian membership in the Maritime Authority, and the disposition of captured German vessels close a very full agenda.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d778:
A second Kirk report from Rome bears the date July 20, 1945, as document 778. Two dispatches in one day mark a full in-tray at the embassy. The ambassador in Italy kept Washington current as Potsdam began. This report joined the second Potsdam volume beside the first.

Paired same-day reports let readers split a post's business by theme. One may carry politics, the other a pressing case. Kirk's pair shows an embassy working several lines at once. The documents together give Rome's week a fuller shape. They show how much of diplomacy is simply keeping many threads from tangling.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d878:
Written for Assistant Secretary of State William Clayton on July 23, 1945, this working paper lays out advice on German economic matters at Potsdam. Its author is not named. The paper assumes the three powers will accept the supply policy set out in a memorandum on Poland's western boundary.

The advice would wind up the Reparations Commission and hand reparations to the zone commanders. Only broad deals struck in the Control Council would bind them. It also urges deleting Principle 18 and rewriting a clause on foreign credits to Germany. Two small edits would add currency, banking, and customs to the list of shared policy fields.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d978:
William Clayton cabled the Secretary of State from London on August 14, 1945, about captured German gold. At Potsdam, the Soviets gave up any claim to gold taken by Allied troops in Germany. Clayton stresses the reach of those words. Allied includes Soviet forces, and Germany includes the Soviet zone.

No big power, he adds, gave up its voice in deciding the gold's fate. Clayton backs the Gold Pot theory, pooling the gold for shared settlement. He advises handling its disposal with the general restitution problem, first through Pauley and the Reparations Commission. Failing agreement there, Generals Eisenhower and Clay would act in the Control Council.
frus-1969-76v10-d278: An editorial note in Volume X of the 1969-1976 series records the final U.S. evacuation of Saigon in April 1975. Ambassador Martin left by helicopter at 2058Z on April 29. The last Marine guards left the embassy grounds at 2346Z. In Operation Frequent Wind, U.S. forces lifted out 7,806 U.S. citizens and foreign nationals. Operation Eagle Pull had earlier removed 276 people from Phnom Penh. The note adds that 131,399 Cambodian and Vietnamese refugees entered the U.S. system between March and June 1975.
gao-gaoreports-b-297078:
Lifecare Management Partners protested an Army award for medical coding work in GAO decision B-297078, dated November 21, 2005. The winner was Wright Solutions. The site was Walter Reed Army Medical Center in Washington. The work was certified coding of medical records. The firm hit a late start date and tech marks. Part of its case was late.

GAO denied the case in part and cut part as late. A shift in start date came from award delays. One delay came from the firm's own agency-level protest. That shift was fair. Marks were sound and fit the tests. One claim came more than 10 days after the firm knew of the loss at agency level.
gao-gaoreports-b-297378:
Meggitt Safety Systems protested a sole-source Army award in GAO decision B-297378, dated January 12, 2006. The holder was Kidde Dual Spectrum. The goods were auto fire control systems. They would go in Marine light armored vehicles. War use in Iraq had shown a need for more armor and fire control. The firm said it could meet the need.

GAO denied the protest. The agency did check the firm's skill with care. It found the firm could not meet the time need. That find was sound. Urgent need can back a sole deal when a rival cannot meet the clock. A full check of the rival must come first, and it did here.
gao-gaoreports-b-298478:
Eagle Home Medical Corporation protested the rejection of its proposal by the Department of Veterans Affairs. The buy covered home oxygen services and supplies. The work served a VA medical center in Columbia, South Carolina. The set-aside was for HUBZone small firms. GAO ruled in B-298478 on October 13, 2006.

VA rejected the offer as priced too high. The price stood 39 percent above the government estimate. That estimate rested in large part on a recent deal with the prior contractor. GAO found the comparison fair and the call sound. A price that far above a sound estimate can be turned down. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299978:
AlliedBarton Security Services protested a second Federal Emergency Management Agency guard order in Louisiana. This order went to Knight Protective Services for sites near Baton Rouge. The Stafford Act again set the eligibility test. GAO ruled in the B-299978 series on October 9, 2007.

The agency found the firm was not a Louisiana-based firm. GAO found that call fair on the record. The firm also attacked the winner's eligibility call. It lacked standing to raise that point. Even a win on it would not put the firm next in line. A third vendor stood ahead of it. Both lines of attack thus failed. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-278:
Defense Microelectronics, GAO-05-278 of March 11, 2005, maps the labs where Pentagon cash backs chip work at the edge. War gear leans on fast-shifting chip tech. Trade chips fit most needs, but some war needs are the Pentagon's alone. Its edge in the field rests on work no shop will fund for it.

Congress asked for a full list. GAO names each Pentagon and federally funded site that makes or tests chip designs with defense cash. It tells what each site does. It then shows how the Pentagon steers its chip spend across them, so the bets back each other up in place of clash.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-378:
National Park Service, GAO-05-378 of April 15, 2005, makes a full roll of the park land held in the capital. The District of Columbia draws an estimated 20 million guests a year to its shrines and green space. Crowds grow at home too. Park chiefs must weigh play fields, calm green, and shrine care on the same tight land. No full roll of that land stood in one place.

GAO lists each park plot in the District. It lists the play and sport grounds on them, and their shape. It tells what new play uses the grand plans float. It weighs how care of a plot could pass to the city.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-478:
Keeping voter registration lists accurate is the topic of GAO-05-478, a report GAO issued on June 10, 2005. Reports of ineligible people signing up to vote had raised concern about state checks. The Help America Vote Act of 2002 set a deadline for statewide lists and checks on them. GAO studied seven states to see how they verify who may vote and what problems they face.

Methods differed greatly by state. Some states relied on the word of the person signing up. Others used return mail or checked lists of felons and the dead. Arizona met the January 1, 2004, deadline for a statewide list. The other six states took a waiver to January 1, 2006. GAO found that federal data could help states spot felons and non-citizens on their lists. The numbers involved may be small, GAO noted, but a few votes can decide an election.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-878:
The hidden costs of the tax system are summed up in GAO-05-878, released August 26, 2005. Americans will pay about $2.1 trillion in federal taxes in 2005. That is about 16.8 percent of gross domestic product. But taxes paid are not the whole cost. Time and money spent complying add more. So does economic loss when tax rules warp choices. Congress asked GAO to size those extra costs.

GAO made no estimates of its own. It gathered studies by others and showed why the math is hard. No one keeps steady accounts of compliance time or cost. Even the lowest study figures add up: about $107 billion a year for personal and business income tax compliance. Efficiency costs have no full estimate at all. Two big studies put them at 2 to 5 percent of product each year, as of the mid-1990s.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-378:
Congress gets floods of agency data, yet not always in a useful form. GAO's March 8, 2006 report, GAO-06-378, uses the Federal Aviation Administration as a case study. Agencies produce much performance, budget, and financial information under law. Agencies often grasp poorly what Congress needs. Members and staff may miss data that could aid oversight.

GAO names FAA information that could sharpen congressional review. It points to other technology and information tools as well. It also asks how committee access could be faster and more useful. The case study shows how existing records can support oversight. Readers get a model that reaches beyond one agency.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-678:
Trends in corrected company financial statements are updated in GAO-06-678, a GAO report dated July 24, 2006. A restatement is a public fix to past financial reports, caused by fraud or accounting error. In 2002, GAO found that restatements had grown sharply from 1997 to mid-2002. Those fixes wiped billions of dollars from the market value of the firms involved. Congress asked GAO to update that work.

GAO found that the share of companies announcing restatements rose from 3.7 percent to 6.8 percent between 2002 and September 2005. The count of announcements grew by about 67 percent. Cost or expense errors were the main reason for the fixes. Most restatements were prompted by insiders, such as managers or internal auditors, and GAO also tracked enforcement actions.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-978:
Trade in conflict diamonds, and U.S. steps to curb it, are reviewed in GAO report GAO-06-978, dated September 27, 2006. Rough diamonds had fueled grave wars in Africa. In 2003 the United States and other nations began a joint scheme to certify clean stones. A U.S. law, the Clean Diamond Trade Act, set the home frame for that scheme.

The law told GAO to report on U.S. work. GAO mapped the offices and rules set up to run the act. It checked how home rules work, and the snags they face. It weighed U.S. aid to the world scheme, and its weak points. More agency action is needed, GAO found.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1078:
Flood insurance payments to private firms need closer watch, GAO finds in report GAO-07-1078, dated September 5, 2007. The National Flood Insurance Program is run by the Federal Emergency Management Agency. Private insurers sell and service most policies, and settle claims, under a program called Write Your Own.

Recent floods raised doubts on the flood fund's health. GAO asked how much the agency paid those firms in recent years, and how it set the sums. It tested if the sums match firms' true costs fairly. It checked the money and management controls in place. The report, made on the Comptroller General's authority, urges better care of those payments.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-278:
Congress will not fund the border visitor program without a spending plan it can trust. GAO reviewed the latest plan in GAO-07-278, a report dated February 14, 2007. The program logs foreign visitors with fingerprint checks. Law requires a plan that meets set conditions. GAO judged the fiscal year 2006 plan against those terms. It also followed up on past advice.

Several weak spots stood out in the plan, GAO found. Exit pilot projects lacked clear definitions and cost support. The plan did not place the program among sister border efforts. Program management costs had risen sharply. Development costs had fallen over the same span. The plan explained neither shift. GAO urged the department to define exit work before funding it. It also pressed for a clearer map of how border programs fit together.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-478:
Permit reviews paid for by the applicants raise fairness doubts, and GAO-07-478, a GAO report issued May 16, 2007, checks the practice. Cities and counties that build near waters and wetlands need permits from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers. Section 214 of a 2000 water law lets the Corps take funds from such bodies to speed the reviews. The Corps must still follow its normal steps plus extra safeguards.

Only four districts had in fact taken and used such funds when GAO looked. They had received more than $2 million in all. Practice varied widely among them. Some staff did not know which rules or records applied. GAO found the risk plain: paid speed can look like bought favor. It urged tighter oversight so each choice stays open and even-handed as use of the authority grows.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-578:
Spy planes and drones multiply under separate services, and GAO-07-578, a GAO report of May 17, 2007, hunts for overlap. Demand for intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) keeps climbing in wartime. Over the next 7 years, the Defense Department plans to spend over $28 billion on airborne ISR systems, old and new. That marks a sharp rise over past spending.

GAO lined the platforms up side by side. It compared their missions, sensors, and ways of working for shared ground. It also checked each program's cost and schedule health. The familiar pattern showed: weak business cases and thin testing push costs up. Delays then force old aircraft to fly years past their planned end, at extra cost. Studies inside the department aim at joint planning, GAO notes, but choices still get made service by service. The report urges an enterprise view before the next $28 billion is split.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-678:
Pay for performance at bank regulators is graded in GAO-07-678, a GAO report dated June 18, 2007. Congress let financial regulators set their own pay systems. It told them to keep pay and benefits broadly in line with each other, so they do not poach staff. GAO reviewed 10 such agencies. It matched their systems against six key practices for sound performance management.

Most regulators use many of the practices, GAO found. The weak spots recur: staff doubt the fairness of ratings, and top and middle scores blur together. The study also tracks how each agency works to keep its package comparable. Personnel files show how staff moved among agencies or left, across fiscal years 1990 through 2006. The report treats the systems as works in progress. Its advice aims at trust: publish the overall rating and raise results, so staff can see how work links to pay.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-78:
Drug control in Afghanistan is assessed in GAO-07-78, a report dated November 15, 2006. Opium poppy farming and trafficking threaten the Afghan government's stability. The U.S. plan rests on five pillars. They span farm alternatives, crop eradication, interdiction, justice work, and public information. A 2005 funding law told GAO to track fiscal year 2005 funds. The U.S. Agency for International Development and the State Department ran the programs. GAO made no recommendations in this report.

Both agencies started projects under each pillar. USAID spent $180 million on farm alternatives such as seed, credit, and cash-for-work. State spent $258 million backing crop eradication by Afghan forces. Delays from poor security and weak roads limited gains. Many projects were too new to judge. Results varied by region and by safety risks. GAO warned that worsening security threatens the whole effort. Drug money could again shelter traffickers and terrorists.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-1078:
The next air traffic system and its slow build-out are assessed in GAO report GAO-08-1078 (September 11, 2008). A joint office inside the Federal Aviation Administration plans the shift to the new system, called NextGen. The change spans many agencies and private partners. GAO has classed air traffic system buying as high-risk since 1995.

This report reviews the agency's work to buy new control systems on time and on budget. It also weighs planning and transition issues for NextGen as a whole. Key hurdles include aligning many partners and new technology. GAO drew on cost and schedule data and talks with 24 aviation stakeholders, among others.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-678:
Leaving teen care for adult life is hard for young people with serious mental illness. GAO-08-678, dated June 23, 2008, counts those young adults, lists the blocks they face, and shows how some states and federal agencies help. The study covers ages 18 through 26.

At least 2.4 million young adults, 6.5 percent of that age group, had a serious mental illness in 2006. Nearly 90 percent had more than one disorder, and school completion lagged peers. Services built for teens or for older adults often fit them poorly. About 186,000 drew disability benefits for mental illness in 2006. The report maps the gap and early fixes.
geber-works-russell-1678:
Richard Russell gave The Works of Geber English dress in 1678. Geber was the Latin name for tracts tied to Jabir ibn Hayyan. The core work is the Summa Perfectionis, the Sum of Perfection. It is a root text of the alchemy of the West.

Clear rules tell how to test, purge, and join the base stuffs of the art. Geber gives the first clear tale of strong acids and their use. He sorts metals by their make and tells how each may be raised. The book set the lab craft of alchemy on a firm base.
hardy-return-native-1878:
Thomas Hardy published The Return of the Native in 1878, setting it on the wild Egdon Heath in his fictional Wessex. Hardy knew this Dorset landscape from childhood. The heath itself broods over the story almost like a character.

Clym Yeobright, the native, returns from Paris hoping to teach the local people. He marries the restless Eustacia Vye, who dreams only of escaping the heath for a glamorous life. Their mismatch pulls in a former lover, a reddleman, and Clym's stern mother. Misread letters and chance meetings steer everyone toward tragedy. The novel is one of Hardy's most admired studies of longing and fate.
haug-essays-sacred-language-parsis-1878:
Martin Haug's Essays on the Sacred Language, Writings, and Religion of the Parsis appeared at London in 1878. The second edition was edited and enlarged by E. W. West. Haug, a German scholar who worked in India, founded the Western study of the Avesta, the Zoroastrian scriptures. His essays sort the Gathas, the oldest hymns ascribed to Zoroaster himself, from later layers of the texts.

An outline of a Pahlavi-Pazand glossary closes the volume, a tool for students of Middle Persian. Haug's work established Pahlavi studies and put Parsi religion on a scholarly footing in Europe. The book became the most cited nineteenth-century work on its subject. West's enlargement kept it current after Haug's early death. It still introduces the field's history.
history-of-the-united-netherlands-from-t:
John Lothrop Motley's chapters forty-five and forty-six move his History of the United Netherlands toward peace. Preparations for the campaign of 1606 open the portion, with Maurice's authority diminished by years of stalemate. A general desire for peace spreads across Europe. Three kings — of England, France, and Spain — bend their designs on the provinces.

Henry IV secretly wishes to annex the Netherlands to France, and Barneveld parries him with artifice. Spain's matrimonial schemes and secret missions reach the Hague. An eight months' armistice is arranged as the chapters close. Motley writes diplomacy now instead of sieges, and the change of key is the story. The republic that begged for protectors in 1584 is courted by all of them in 1606. Exhaustion, not conversion, makes the peacemakers.
james-daisy-miller-1878:
Henry James published Daisy Miller in 1878, first in an English magazine after American editors balked. James was then an expatriate writer shuttling between America and Europe. The novella made his name on both sides of the Atlantic and defined his great theme: the American abroad.

Daisy Miller, a pretty, free-spirited girl from Schenectady, tours Switzerland and Rome with no sense of European rules. The young American Winterbourne watches her, torn between attraction and the colony's snobbish verdict. Her friendship with an Italian escort ruins her name, and a Roman fever ends the story. James never quite says whether Daisy was innocent or foolish. Readers have argued it for a century.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aaron-ben-moses:
Aaron ben Moses Teomim was a rabbinical scholar born about 1630, probably in Prague. His family, the Teomim-Fränkel family, had settled there from Vienna. After preaching in Prague, he was called as rabbi to Worms in 1670.

During a grave illness on Passover evening, 1675, Aaron vowed to write a commentary on the Haggadah if he recovered. The result, "Maṭṭeh Aharon," appeared in 1678 and was reprinted three times. In 1690 he accepted a call to Cracow. Three months later he was arrested at Chmelnik and died of fright and ill treatment on the way to prison.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abbasi-abbas-mo: Moses Abbasi was a disciple of Rabbi Ḥasdai ben Solomon, of Valencia and Tudela. That is the first of the few facts the entry gives for him. He wrote letters to Isaac ben Sheshet, a leading rabbi of the age. He also wrote to the poet Solomon da Piera. No book, post, birth year, or death year of his is named. His place in the record rests on his teacher and on the two men he corresponded with, as the short entry presents them.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abiezer-judah-b: Judah ben Isaac Abiezer, of Tiktin, was a Jewish author of the nineteenth century who lived in Jerusalem. He wrote "Mishmeret ha-Berit," a defense of Judaism against the godless, printed at Jerusalem in 1846. His "Sha'are Ẓedeḳ," of 1848, treats the rights of the Holy Land. It also holds rich detail on the woes of Jerusalem and of Safed in his own century. A third work, on the treatise Berakot, came out at Lemberg in 1851. Rabbis count him a great authority.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-ben-jos:
Karaite author Abraham ben Josiah of Jerusalem flourished in the first half of the eighteenth century. He traveled from Palestine to the Crimea. There, in 1712, he finished Emunah Omen, a work on Karaite theology printed at Eupatoria in 1846.

Its themes are God's nature, the unchanging Law, and the chief points between Karaite and Rabbinite teaching. It also weighs how science relates to religion. The entry finds no new thought in it, but praises his wide grasp of rabbinic writing. He honored Maimonides and Ibn Ezra highly. In 1715 he wrote on slaughter rules under another name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adda-b-ahabah-a:
Adda b. Ahabah was a Babylonian amora of the second line. He is quoted in both Talmuds. Lore says he was born the day Judah I. died. He learned under Abba Arika, called Rab. At Rab's funeral he rent his clothes twice in grief. At Pumbedita he drew a crowd of pupils. He taught at times in the open streets. He lived to a great age.

Asked what earned him that long life, he gave a plain rule of days. He was first to the synagogue and last to leave it. He kept his mind on the Law as he walked. He bore no grudge to sleep and kept a calm house. Once he rebuked a woman in the street for bold dress. She proved to be a Samaritan, and he paid a fine of 400 zuz. Tales of his prayer in drought close the account.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-agriculture-143:
Agriculture was the base of Israel's life as a nation. State and Temple alike stood on it. At the start the Hebrews show as a herding tribe. The fathers kept sheep and stock on common land. Yet Isaac sowed in Gerar and reaped a hundredfold. Jacob's sons went down to Egypt as herdsmen. Some clans kept to herding long after the rest took to the plow.

The whole law of Moses fits a people set to hold Canaan. The three feasts of the year turn on the farm year. Poor laws claim the gleanings of field, vine, and olive grove for the poor and the stranger. The Sabbatical year and the Jubilee rest on farm life too. So does the view of God as the giver of rain and crop. Blessing and curse are told in terms of the soil's yield.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ahiasaf-978:
Ahiasaf was a Hebrew annual published in Warsaw by the Ahiasaf Publication Society. It was founded in 1893 and met with quick success, both literary and financial. Though an almanac in form, its real strength lay in its literary pages, which formed the bulk of each volume.

The annual served the revival of the Hebrew tongue in Russia. It also helped build a modern Hebrew literature. Many of the best Hebrew writers of the day wrote for it as regular contributors. The entry names Ahad-ha-'Am, that is A. Ginzberg, along with Lillienblum and Brainin, among others.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-albelda-formerl:
Albelda, once spelled Albeilda, is a town of Old Castile, near Logrono. Jews lived there as early as the eleventh century. The congregation answered to the bishop of Calahorra. By order of Alfonso X., its taxes went to the bishop or to the chapter. In the thirteenth century the flock counted thirty-five families.

Its dues were paid partly in kind. Three days before each Ash Wednesday, the Jews owed the chapter thirteen hens. When the bishop visited, they owed him linen for himself and his suite. The chapter also kept all fines laid on the Jews, and it jailed them at times. With the flock of Alfacel, Albelda owed a yearly tax of 11,648 silver maravedis.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alexis-mikhailo:
Alexis Mikhailovich was the second czar of the Romanof dynasty. He was born at Moscow on March 29, 1629. He died on February 9, 1676. He succeeded his father on July 26, 1645. In his reign many Jews lived in Moscow and inner Russia. Their numbers grew under Stephan von Gaden, the czar's Jewish physician. Samuel Collins, another court physician, reports the same.

Alexis often gave Jews red-seal passports, needed by any foreigner entering the interior. They traveled to Moscow freely, dealing in cloth and jewels. The court even sent Jewish merchants abroad on errands. In 1672 Samuel Jakovlev was charged to buy Hungarian wine. Yet Alexis also drove the Jews from Mohilev in 1654, Wilna in 1658, and Kiev in 1660. By the treaty of 1667, Jews in the new Russian towns could stay under his rule. The entry judges him kindly disposed for his age.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-almanzi-joseph-:
Joseph Almanzi was a book lover and poet of Padua. He was born on March 25, 1801. He died at Triest on March 7, 1860. His father was a rich merchant. Home tutors gave him a strong schooling. By age twenty he was deep in Jewish letters. He also gathered Hebrew books with great zeal.

His library grew into one of the best in private hands. He bought the famed library of Azulai and added to it. Scholars like Luzzatto and Zunz used its riches. Books he could not buy, he copied by hand. After his death Luzzatto printed his letters and poems. A list of his library came out as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ambrosius-moses: Moses Ambrosius was one of the first Jews in New York. The city was then called New Amsterdam. He came with a party of twenty-three Jews. They reached the New Netherlands in Sept. 1654. They had left Bahia in Brazil after its fall. Each man had pledged his own credit for all. The party could not pay the fare in full. Ambrosius was one of two men held by the town. He was freed in a short time and did well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-anathoth-1478: Anathoth was a town in the territory of Benjamin in Palestine. The entry counts it among the first Levitical cities, citing Joshua and First Chronicles. Robinson identified it with the modern village of 'Anata, about two and one-half miles northeast of Jerusalem. It was home to Abiathar and to the prophet Jeremiah. Returning exiles likely settled there too. The entry adds that its high site gave it a strong position.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-antigonus-anton:
Antigonus, also called Antoninus in some sources, was a Palestinian scholar of the last tannaitic generation, in the second and third centuries. Very little of his teaching survives. The entry counts just two Haggadot and one Halakah in his name.

One saying retells a verse from Exodus, where God leads Israel by a pillar of cloud. Antigonus pictures a king who, after holding court till dark, lights the way for his sons himself. When courtiers offer to carry the torch, the king refuses. He wants to show his love openly, so the world will honor his sons. The entry notes source mix-ups that tangled his name with an emperor's and with Rabbi's.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aquinas-thomas-:
Thomas Aquinas was the most eminent Christian theological philosopher of the Middle Ages, born in 1227 at Aquino, in the kingdom of Naples, and dead in 1274. Like his teacher Albertus Magnus, he made philosophy his chief study and sought to harmonize it with religion.

The entry states his rule that all knowledge of principles in us comes from God, so nothing true can contradict divine wisdom. Though a Dominican with no kindly feelings toward Jews, he drew deeply on Jewish philosophy, the entry argues. His Summa shows a profound knowledge of Ibn Gabirol and of all Jewish philosophical works then known. Of his five proofs of God's existence, three, the entry says, come directly from Jewish thinkers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ark-of-the-law-:
Synagogue worship centers on the Ark of the Law, the chest that holds the Torah scrolls. It stands in or against the wall that faces Jerusalem, raised a few feet above the floor and reached by steps. A lamp hangs before it, and a rich curtain, the paroket, often screens it. When the Ark is opened, the entry says, the congregation rises out of respect for the Torah inside.

Its name, Aron ha-Kodesh, the Holy Ark, links it to the Ark of the Covenant in the Tabernacle and Temple. The synagogue itself was viewed as a sanctuary next to the Temple, and its Ark matched the Holy of Holies.
