Clinicians advising patients with early memory problems can use the ranking to suggest exercise types with the best support.
plos-pone-0358578: Liang and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on HIV testing among men who have sex with men in Southern China. They examined how often these men test and how testing links to sexual behavior. They also looked at use of preventive medication against HIV. Regular testing and prevention work best together, so knowing how they pair up helps clinics design outreach.
plos-pone-0358778:
Retna Sheeja Pushpa Raj and Prakash Babu Kodali measure what caesarean births cost mothers in Tamil Nadu, India, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Just over half of the four hundred seventy-five recently delivered mothers they surveyed, in mid 2023, had given birth by caesarean, a strikingly high share. The study linked how a woman delivered to her out of pocket spending and her physical and mental quality of life in the weeks after birth.

High risk pregnancies and private facilities were the strongest predictors of a caesarean. Mothers who delivered surgically faced roughly double the odds of heavy out of pocket costs, and markedly worse physical quality of life scores, while the mental side differed less. The authors say the pattern, surgical birth concentrated in private care and paid for by families, deserves policy attention in a state where one in two births now arrives by operation.
plos-pone-0359278: Kinsman and two co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on psychiatric prescribing in Botswana. At the country's only referral institute for mental illness, they counted how many adult patients receive many psychiatric drugs at once, a practice called polypharmacy. The snapshot design covered patients at one point in time. Many drugs at once can help, yet raise risks, so a clear count guides safer care.
plos-pone-0359778:
Yi-Chao Zhou, Yi-Chang Chou, Yin-Ling Hung, and Yen-Jung Chang wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on ageing in Taiwan. It is a longitudinal cohort study running from 2005 to 2016. The authors link marital status to incident screen-positive cognitive impairment, new cases flagged by screening tests for thinking decline.

The title itself warns that the links vary with the cognitive screening instrument chosen, meaning the answer depends on which test defines impairment. That caution matters for every study that sorts people by a single screen. Researchers of marriage, widowhood, and dementia risk are the readers, and they gain a lesson in measurement as well as a result.
plos-pone-0359878:
Jingmei Liang, Yuyun Hu, and Bing Liao traced in 2026 a chain of signals that injures kidney filter cells in acute kidney injury. The cells are podocytes, which wrap the kidney's tiny blood vessels and keep protein out of the urine. The authors show that signaling between cells through a pair of proteins, GAS6 and its receptor AXL, can trigger a form of cell death called cuproptosis in these podocytes.

Above that pair sits a regulator named CEBPD, which the team places upstream of the signal. Acute kidney injury strikes suddenly, often during severe illness, and has few targeted treatments. Mapping a death pathway step by step gives drug researchers named points where the chain might be cut.
plos-pone-0360478:
Wen Li and colleagues piloted in 2026 a blend of music therapy and artificial intelligence for university students. Their exploratory randomized study added verbal suggestions, generated by a large language model and adapted to the students' culture, into music therapy sessions. The spoken guidance was designed to deepen the therapy's calming and focusing effects.

As a pilot, the study's job is to test whether the approach is workable and promising enough to justify a larger trial, rather than to settle its value. Culturally adapted wording matters because therapeutic language lands differently across backgrounds. The work sits at a new crossing point, where universities search for scalable mental health support and AI tools are eager to supply it, with evidence still catching up.
pmc-10652478:
Born hand differences that shorten fingers have many surgical answers, and a research team led by Bartsch reviewed them all for results, in work from twenty twenty-three. Twenty-four studies held more than five hundred patients and over a thousand fixed digits. Study quality ran low to middling throughout.

Finger movement, the main reported outcome, improved modestly under every technique. Looks were reported rarely, and read as pleasing where they were. Only one study pitted two methods head to head. The field, the authors imply, needs shared outcome sets before any winner can be named.
pmc-10654378:
Zahra Abbasi Ranjbar and co-authors present a 2023 study on whether a simple blood measure can help spot ectopic pregnancy early. In this dangerous condition, a pregnancy grows outside the womb, usually in a tube. A screening of chemical signals had pointed to lactic acid as a possible marker.

The case-control study enrolled ninety-five women in early pregnancy: fifty with confirmed tubal ectopic pregnancies and forty-five with normal pregnancies of the same age. Blood samples were tested for plasma lactate. The ectopic group skewed older with higher parity and body weight, though not significantly. Lactate ran slightly higher in the ectopic group. The authors weigh whether such a cheap test could join early diagnosis, ahead of rupture.
pmc-10656378:
Haoyu Ma and co-authors build a feather-light foam that swallows microwaves and hides heat in a 2023 paper. The material is a nano-aerogel laced with carbon nanotubes, made by polymer chemistry, gel setting, and special drying. Its pores measure only tens of nanometers, and air fills over ninety percent of its volume.

The tiny pores block heat flow, the mixed interfaces reflect infrared and soak up microwave energy, and the airy build matches signals into the material instead of bouncing them off. The foam covered a full radar band in absorption tests and masked a heat gap of over sixty degrees. Paired with a graphene film, it became a thin shield that absorbs far more than it reflects, suiting stealth and electronics protection.
pmc-10656478:
Woo-Hyeon Son and co-authors test, in a 2023 trial, whether plain walking can cut body fat and vessel inflammation in older women. After menopause, hormone shifts favor fat gain and steady inflammation, which raise heart disease risk. Walking is cheap, easy, and needs no gear. The team signed up twenty-six postmenopausal women with obesity and split them by chance into a walking group and a control group.

The walking group trained at a moderate pace for twelve weeks. Body measures and blood tests were taken before and after. Weight, body mass index, and body fat share all fell in the walkers. So did several blood markers tied to vessel inflammation. One growth factor linked to vessel health trended upward. The authors say a simple walking habit may help guard these women's hearts.
pmc-10656878:
When a heart stops outside a hospital, a phone guide can talk a bystander through chest pushes that keep blood moving. Rebecca Hvidt Tuffley and co-authors asked in 2023 if a caller's stress changes how that help plays out. They reviewed more than six hundred real calls from the Danish capital region.

Chest pushes began at much the same rate for stressed and calm callers, and the wait before they began was much the same too. Guides were more apt to cheer stressed callers on and to coach the speed and depth of pushes. Blocks to care, such as fear or a locked door, came up more often on stressed calls. Stress, the team finds, shapes the call more than the outcome.
pmc-10671078:
Jessica A Clark and co-authors published a study in 2023 on two inherited dog eye diseases and how breeding choices moved their gene frequencies worldwide. One disease slowly blinds by killing the retina's light sensors; the other deforms the eye from birth in collies and relatives. Commercial DNA tests for both have existed for years.

The team analyzed test results for over eighty-six thousand dogs for the blinding disease and nearly thirty-four thousand for the eye anomaly, spanning fifteen years, eighty-two countries, and sixty-seven breeds. Frequencies differed sharply by breed and shifted over time, mostly downward as breeders used the tests. Yet dogs carrying two copies of the blinding variant still appeared fourteen years after testing began. Testing works, the authors conclude, but only where breeders keep using it.
pmc-10673478:
Yang Liu and co-authors work out the mechanical, electronic, and optical traits of a set of caesium lead halide materials. Their 2023 study uses first-principles density functional theory. It runs across four types, split by which halogen they hold.

All four materials showed good stability in the sums, and good elastic modulus, hardness, and wear resistance. Each acted as a semiconductor with a direct band gap. The gap shrank as the halogen atom grew in size. The sums for light found peaks in the dielectric values at low energy. They found the most strong absorption in ultraviolet light. Absorption moved toward the red end of the scale, and grew in strength, across the set. The team puts the results forth as a guide, based on theory, for devices in microelectronics and in optoelectronics.
pmc-10688678:
Drew Duckett, Kailee Calder, Jack Sullivan, David Tank, and Bryan Carstens test if reduced data approaches match whole genome sequencing for common place based heredity studies, using the North American water vole. Study design forces a choice among many marker types. The study came out in twenty twenty three.

The team gathered five data kinds, from single genes up to low depth whole genomes, for the same voles. Genetic gaps, population structure, and past population swings were each estimated per data kind and compared. Results differed by marker, above all in fine detail. A cost check found genotype by sequencing markers the most cost effective route.
pmc-10689478:
A color change test that needs no DNA extraction can spot mpox and its relatives, report Zhiru Li and co-authors in a 2023 study. Their method uses loop mediated amplification, a technique that copies DNA at one steady temperature, paired with a probe that tells mpox apart from other Old World poxviruses.

Swab fluid goes straight into the test, which skips the lab step that low resource settings struggle with. The team also mapped 200 poxvirus genomes to place the assay on firm ground. They offer the test as a fast, scalable tool for diagnosis and outbreak watching where it is needed most.
pmc-10691378:
Abdullah Al Zubaer, Michael Granitzer, and Jelena Mitrovic test large language models on legal argument mining in a 2023 study. Argument mining pulls premises and conclusions out of text, and legal writing is a hard test case. The team probed GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 by prompting alone, varying wording and the examples shown, picked by semantic search.

The corpus came from European Court of Human Rights cases, and runs were repeated for sound statistics. Surprisingly, smaller models trained for the domain beat both big models on premise and conclusion scores, by 1.9 and 12 percent. Prompt wording still shifted results a lot. The authors trace the gap to the dense structure of the legal data.
pmc-10692078:
Ahmed Abdel Gawad and four co-authors measured natural radioactivity in Nubian sandstone from Egypt, in a study from twenty twenty-three. Builders use this stone widely, so its safety matters. The team checked levels of uranium, thorium, and potassium isotopes in samples of the rock.

All three came in below world average limits for building materials. The dose people would absorb from the stone, and the added lifetime cancer risk, also sat below world means. Statistical tools showed the three elements drive what little risk exists. The authors conclude the sandstone is safe to use. Its radioactivity is too low to pose a health risk under normal use.
pmc-10692178:
Takashi Nishida and co-authors compare, in a 2023 study, a new two-eyed visual field tester against the standard machine used to track glaucoma. The Humphrey analyzer tests one eye at a time and anchors clinic practice. The TEMPO device tests both eyes together with a quicker estimation routine. Seven hundred forty eyes, spanning healthy, suspect, and glaucomatous, took both tests on the same day in random order.

Headline scores agreed closely between the machines. The new tester's readings tied slightly more strongly to nerve fiber layer thickness measured by tomography, a sign of validity. It also finished much faster, taking a bit over four minutes against more than seven. The authors say the binocular approach merits study for long-term monitoring, where visit burden shapes whether patients keep coming.
pmc-10692878:
Sonia Ponzo and co-authors review in 2023 the apps that claim to spot signs of autism from phone data. Diagnosis can lag three years behind first symptoms, which harms children and families. Apps could speed the process by feeding clinicians timely readings, if they prove accurate.

The scoping review found just four studies covering four products, one sold commercially and three built for research. Accuracy ranged widely, from twenty-eight to about eighty-one percent, and the balance of hits and misses varied just as much. The thin evidence base, the authors conclude, is not yet enough to guide adoption in clinics or research.
pmc-10693078:
Soha Mohammadi and co-authors describe a surgical workaround for the riskiest plumbing in free-flap reconstruction. Rebuilding a lip after cancer surgery with tissue moved from the forearm depends on stitching tiny veins together; a size mismatch or a doubtful join can starve the flap. Their patient, a 77-year-old man, had a lower lip tumour removed with a safety margin, neck glands cleared, and the lip rebuilt with a forearm flap.

Faced with a venous join they did not fully trust, the surgeons did not redo it. Instead they added a second vein connection in a Y configuration, so the flap's outflow had two supports. The authors argue the Y anastomosis eases the operation and cuts the complications that size mismatches cause. A literature review accompanies the case, which they offer as an option when a single venous join looks doubtful.
pmc-10693578:
Fathizadeh studies how heat vibrations help push a pure spin current along DNA. The 2023 paper works in molecular spintronics, where spin, not charge, carries the signal. A voltage gate across the chain sets the current going.

Analysis of the state's fractal pattern shows the spin current stays nearly pure. Warmer conditions strengthened it rather than wrecking it. Vibrations of the chain hand their twist to the electron spin, spreading the spin state wider. Longer chains held spin better than short ones, with higher selectivity. The author suggests devices could be tuned by managing heat and vibration. The study joins sound, heat, and spin in one model of spin flow in a biological chain.
pmc-10693878:
Samrachana Adhikari and co-authors describe a new research cohort in a 2023 paper. The cohort was built to study whether heart failure patients take their medicines as directed. Missed chances to help are common because doctors cannot easily spot who is at risk of skipping doses.

The team linked electronic health records with pharmacy refill data and neighborhood social data. Patients came from a large New York City health system and had heart failure or weak heart pumping. All had active prescriptions for at least one of the four main drug types. The linked data aim to improve models that flag patients likely to miss doses.
pmc-10694578:
Erin Jay Feliciano and a large team of co-authors call for action on cancer disparities in Southeast Asia in a two thousand twenty-three commentary. The region holds over six hundred eighty million people, and cancer incidence and mortality are projected to climb.

The authors argue disparities run deeper than country-level statistics. Within each nation, minoritized groups face unequal risk, screening, treatment access, and survivorship along lines of ethnicity, gender, wealth, religion, and geography. Their lens is intersectionality: overlapping identities compound disadvantage in ways single categories miss. Pandemic-driven poverty has widened the gaps. The piece urges researchers and policymakers to study and serve these overlooked populations directly.
pmc-10694878:
Five researchers led by Koichiro Hirayama asked how arm skill scores relate to real arm use in people soon after a stroke. They studied two hundred three patients with a first stroke. One test scores how well the weak arm moves, and the other logs how much the patient uses it in daily life.

A split-point method found the link changed at a score near forty-five. Below that point, more skill did not mean much more use. Above it, use rose more steeply. The authors say rehab plans should push arm use with longer practice once patients pass that score. The finding helps match training to each stage of recovery.
pmc-10694978:
Giving the right amount of fluid during big abdominal surgery can speed recovery. Yanxia Sun and co-authors ran a randomized trial of goal-directed fluid therapy in one hundred patients having major cancer surgery on the abdomen. One group got fluids guided by two heart measures, with set targets. The other got standard care based on blood pressure and vein pressure. Neither patients nor assessors knew the groups.

The guided group left hospital in about nine days, against twelve for standard care. Gut problems after surgery struck two guided patients but sixteen in the other group. The guided group also passed gas sooner and ate sooner. The trial supports measure-guided fluids for major abdominal operations.
pmc-10695378:
Jin-Sung Yuk and Ji Young Park linked menopause hormone therapy to gallstones in a 2023 Korean cohort study. Hormone care eases menopause symptoms, but its effect on the gallbladder was worth a hard look at national scale. The team also asked whether it shifts gallbladder cancer risk.

They drew on national health insurance records from 2002 to 2019. Women on hormone care were set against those never on it, and the care group was split by drug form, from combined pills to skin-applied estrogen. Gallstone rates ran higher in the care group. Such data help women and doctors weigh symptom relief against gall risk.
pmc-10696078:
Ju-Ryoung Kim and co-authors ask in a 2023 study whether weak muscles near a joint help drive osteoarthritis. The disease is often seen as wear in the smooth tissue that caps the joint. Yet muscles around the joint change too as the disease grows. The team used mice whose knee joints were made unstable by surgery, a standard way to trigger the disease.

Muscles near the joint shrank, grew scar-like tissue, and lost cells that help repair them. When the team weakened those muscles further with a toxin, joint harm and pain got worse. Mice bred to lack myostatin, a protein that holds muscle growth back, had stronger muscles. Those mice showed less joint harm and no pain response after the same surgery.
pmc-10696678:
Shahjada Selim and co-authors check cholesterol control in Bangladeshi diabetes care in a 2023 study. Lipid targets matter because heart disease is the big killer in type 2 diabetes. National data on who actually hits those targets were scarce.

Clinics at several tertiary hospitals enrolled 3,060 adults who had diabetes for at least a year and lipid drugs for at least three months. Interviews and fasting blood tests fed the audit. Targets were set for total cholesterol, triglycerides, and the harmful and protective fractions. The average patient was about forty-five, and women were the majority. The paper charts how far real control lags the guideline numbers.
pmc-10698478:
Hansraj Gautam and Vidya study conflict among female Asian elephants in a 2023 paper. A long-standing model links animal conflict to how food is spread out and how many rivals live nearby. Clumped, rich food should spark fights between groups, while scattered food should not.

The pair watched elephant clans in the Kabini grassland of southern India. Fights between clans were stronger there than in nearby forests, and females fought outsiders more than clan mates. The grassland is a rich food patch, which fits the model's forecast. Fights within clans were also common, though they did not track the expected factors as neatly. The study refines how food maps onto social tension in a species that splits and rejoins often.
pmc-10699878:
Davalos-Dehullu, Mank and their co-authors present a chromosome-level genome for the blacktail brush lizard in 2023. The lizard lives only on the Baja California Peninsula in Mexico, and its genome can reveal how sex chromosomes work in reptiles.

Long-read sequencing and scaffolding produced an assembly held mostly in a small set of large pieces, with many protein-coding genes predicted. Repeat content was high and old, and chromosome layout proved well conserved across reptiles. One small chromosome was identified as the X, with perfect dosage compensation between males and females. Past population size appeared extremely low.
pmc-10700278:
Louise Baucher and co-authors describe severe infections in patients taking ibrutinib for blood cancers. The drug is now standard care for several lymphoid diseases, and it calms the immune system in broad ways beyond its main target. That breadth can open the door to harsh and unusual infections.

Their 2023 study gathers cases from ten French intensive care units over six years. Patients had been on the drug for months before illness struck. Fungal infections made up a large share of the severe cases, led by invasive aspergillosis, with pneumocystis pneumonia next. The multicenter cohort sets out the features and outcomes of these crises, data meant to sharpen watchfulness in clinics that use the drug.
pmc-10702278:
Mykaihla Sternick, James Gates, Allen Champion, and Andrew Yampolsky present in 2023 a new way to treat a stubborn wound inside the mouth. Vacuum-assisted wound therapy lowers air pressure over a wound, drains fluid, and helps tissue heal without surgery. It is used often in the head and neck, but reports on using it through the mouth are scarce.

Their patient had a wound joining the mouth to the skin that had resisted many prior operations, including tissue flap repairs. The team built a mouth-fitted vacuum device and managed to keep a watertight seal in place. The patient stayed with the treatment, and the wound was managed with success. The authors urge doctors to consider the approach for similar hard-to-treat oral wounds. The case adds a worked example to a thin record.
pmc-10704678:
Hyung Jun Park, Joon Hyeok Boo, Dong Hun Suh, and Jae Gyoon Kim study why two leg alignment X-rays disagree after knee bone surgery, in a study from 2023. Good alignment after the wedge surgery drives good results. One view ends at the ankle bone, and a longer view ends at the heel, which may better reflect the true load line.

They compared both views in fifty-one patients and split them by how far the load line measures differed. The heel view read higher in the mismatch group. Ankle tilt before and after surgery and a shin angle before surgery set the groups apart, which helps surgeons judge which view to trust.
pmc-10704778:
Gianni Rossi and colleagues check rural parent habits on early allergen feeding in Australia, in work from 2023. Guidance since the prior decade urges early allergen food in the first year to cut allergy risk. Australia has high food allergy rates, and rural parent practice was poorly known before this survey.

More than three hundred women in two rural districts who were pregnant or new mothers replied. Most children met all four feeding rules checked in the survey. Rules covered allergen timing, solid food timing, and milk feeding during first solids. School level, past allergy, and pregnancy care type showed no clear link with rule following. Parents called the guidance realistic and trusted, though child pace shaped choices.
pmc-10705778:
Zhaoxin Jing and co-authors study how chronic heat stress damages the kidneys of Siberian sturgeon, in a 2023 paper. Warming waters threaten farmed and wild fish alike. The kidney controls water and salts in the fish body. How heat injures that organ was little known.

Tanks were warmed step by step from mild to high heat stress. Fish were then held at those temperatures for twelve days. Tissue slices, cell tests, and gene measures tracked the damage. Cell death, inflammation, and heat shock proteins all shifted with temperature. Higher heat brought heavier kidney injury. Fish farmers gain warning signs for heat waves. The work also informs breeding and cooling strategies for sturgeon aquaculture.
pmc-10706478:
Xiaofeng Lu and nine co-authors seek a way to make oolong tea that keeps its healthy catechins high while still tasting good. Catechins give tea much of its flavor and health value, but high levels and good taste are hard to get at once. The study came out in twenty twenty-three.

The team varied one step at a time through the full tea making run, then used chem-ical sorting methods to weigh the results. Their best route uses red light wilting, leaf turning with long rests, drum roasting, cold rolling, and microwave drying, each for set times. This route kept far more catechins and gave a smooth, brisk taste, the authors report.
pmc-10707278:
Anna Kitaeva and co-authors trace which plant calls drive the age die-off at the tip of pea root knots in heat. Heat caps pulse crops, and the knot tip, where gas fix crafts run, dies first in warm runs. Their 2023 study warms nod pea lines and reads three call kinds in the fix zone: a stress call, a ripe call's seed part, and a growth call. Dye marks place each call in the cells by day.

Both the stress call and the ripe seed rise in one day of heat. The growth call falls in the same span. Fed growth call holds the fix zone whole for more days. Senescence, heat, and guard script lines dim in the fed knots too. Plant calls thus run the heat death of the knot tip as a team.
pmc-10707778:
Marta Redondo and co-authors coat tiny particles with a germ killer in a 2023 study of water disinfection. The killer, a quaternary ammonium compound, usually leaches into water as it works. Their plan was to lock it onto particles so it kills on contact and stays put.

Layers were built up on three core types: a bone-like mineral, chalk, and glass beads. Tests against a common water bacterium showed full kill in four hours at a mid dose for the mineral-core particles. Checks over two weeks found no killer leaking into the water. That supports contact killing, a cleaner route for stored or treated water.
pmc-10708378:
Huang, Wang, and Tang catalog the ZF-HD gene family in moso bamboo. These zinc finger proteins guide plant growth, development, and stress responses. Knowledge of their history in bamboo was limited before this work. The team found 24 family genes spread unevenly on 12 chromosomes. Two subfamilies emerged from the family tree: ZHD and MIF types. ZHD genes split further into seven groups by kinship with rice and Arabidopsis.

Whole-genome and segmental duplications grew the family over time. Ratio tests showed purifying selection on all duplicate pairs. Promoter scans found stress and hormone response elements in most genes. Many genes switched on under abiotic stress in expression tests. The authors map structure, motifs, and control elements per gene.
pmc-10708578:
Miguel Gutiérrez Gaitán and co-authors analyze coding schemes that protect vehicle to vehicle radio links from fading, in work published in 2023. Signals between moving cars bounce off the ground and scatter, which creates deep dropouts. Fast motion also shifts frequencies and breaks code alignment.

Simulations with a multi ray ground model showed the codes cancel many self interference fades across car distances and speed related shifts. In deep fades they beat receiver only diversity, despite the loss of perfect alignment in changing channels. Higher order codes with lower rates still gained when paired with multi antenna receivers. The authors offer the results as guidance for transmit diversity in car networks.
pmc-10708678:
Felici-Castell and five colleagues build a low cost air pollution sensor network in twenty twenty-three. Cheap sensors can densify air quality monitoring in cities, where breathing problems are rising. Their raw data are error prone and need correction and processing. The team pairs such sensors with 5G links and neural networks.

The goal is to forecast pollutant readings twenty-four hours ahead for early warnings. Four network designs were trained and compared on a large prepared data set. A long short term memory design performed best overall. Average estimation error was about seven percent across pollutants. Carbon dioxide forecasts were especially accurate, and fine particles also scored well. The authors target support for citizens with respiratory problems.
pmc-10708878:
Peijie Xu and co-authors build a head worn aid for blind walkers in a 2023 paper. People with low or no sight face real danger from obstacles, above all when alone. Their device spots blocks ahead in real time and warns the wearer, while staying small and fast enough for head gear.

The team tried more than thirty model variants with distinct tuning and weighed their scores side by side. The pick had to balance sharp reads with real time speed on a tiny kit. Natural head turns, which can skew sensor reads, were part of the design brief. Tests showed the aid can flag obstacles with high accuracy.
pmc-10709078:
Swati Dhasmana and co-authors make the computational case for a cell-division protein as a pancreatic cancer target, in a 2023 study. Pancreatic cancer is among the deadliest malignancies and is usually caught late. The protein TRIP13 helps manage chromosome handling during cell division. Mining large molecular data sets, the team tracked its levels across disease stages.

TRIP13 ran high in tumors, and its partner genes clustered in pathways central to cancer growth. Lab checks on tissue and cells backed the data analysis. Enrichment results tied the protein's network to key physiological processes gone wrong. The authors propose TRIP13 as both a diagnostic marker and a drug target. Early detection tools for this cancer are so scarce that any solid lead matters.
pmc-10709578:
Anna Akanteva, David Dick, Shirin Amiraslani, and Jane Heffernan built a data set in 2023 that tracks Covid-19 rules across Canada. Each province and territory set its own public health steps during the pandemic. The team recorded those steps in a shared format so they could be compared over time and place.

Measures are scored on a four-point scale, from none to strong, in three areas: schools, work, and other settings. The result is a near real-time record in a form that is easy to use. It lets researchers study how rules affected spread and lets modelers test ideas on real policy data rather than rough guesses.
pmc-10709878:
Kang Huang and nine co-authors test whether small gene variants in a fat-processing gene shift heart disease risk in Han Chinese. Their case-control study was published in twenty twenty-three.

The study matched four hundred and eighty-seven heart patients with the same number of healthy people. Five variants in the gene CYP4V2 were typed. One variant's T form raised risk by about a third overall. The link was sharper in people over sixty, men, smokers, and drinkers. A second variant raised risk in drinkers, while a third lowered risk when diabetes joined the picture. The gene handles fatty acids, which fits a heart role. The findings add population-specific markers to heart risk research.
pmc-10710178:
Qiping Liu and four co-authors test contrast enhanced ultrasound for judging kidney masses found on routine scans. The method injects a contrast agent and watches blood flow through the mass in real time. Flow patterns can hint at whether a growth is cancer or benign.

Sixty-seven patients with kidney masses had the contrast scan, and results were checked against surgery findings. The group held fifty-five cancers and twelve benign growths. The scan sorted cases with high sensitivity and an overall accuracy of about ninety-one percent. Specificity was lower, at about two thirds. The authors conclude the method has high value for telling benign from malignant kidney lesions.
pmc-10710578:
Toshihide Tanaka and co-authors report a trial of drug treatment given before surgery for a harsh brain tumor, in a paper from 2023. The tumor type is malignant glioma, most often glioblastoma. One drug, bevacizumab, is standard before surgery in bowel cancer but not in brain tumors. The multi-center trial tested safety first, then looked for signs of gain.

Fifteen patients got the drug plus a chemo pill before their operations. Surgery followed about three weeks later. Two patients had severe side effects tied to the drugs, such as wound infection and low blood counts. Tumors shrank in nearly all cases, and patient function scores improved before surgery. Average time before the disease grew again was about nine and a half months. The authors call the plan safe and worth study for some patients.
pmc-10711178:
Sanjal Desai and co-authors measured how long patients live after Hodgkin lymphoma returns following a stem cell transplant, in a 2023 study. In the past, such patients lived a median of two to three years after relapse. Since then, two drug types, checkpoint inhibitors and a targeted antibody drug, have deepened and lengthened responses. The team gathered records from fifteen centers to update the outlook in this new era.

Of nearly twelve hundred transplant patients, three hundred sixty-seven saw their cancer progress. Their median survival after relapse reached about nine and a half years, far beyond the old figure. Older age, fast relapse, and a hot scan before transplant marked worse odds. Patients whose first salvage used a checkpoint inhibitor lived longer than those who got neither new drug. A second, donor transplant did not add survival in this group.
pmc-10714478:
Reda and seven co-authors sequenced malaria parasites across Ethiopia in this study from twenty twenty-three. Parasite genetics can reveal how intensely malaria spreads and whether control works. The team collected dried blood spots from trial patients at three endemic sites. Five highly variable gene markers were read deeply in one hundred eighty-one infections.

Diversity ran high across all markers. About seventeen percent of infections carried multiple parasite strains. Two sites' parasite populations looked nearly identical in twenty fifteen, while others stood apart. The pattern suggests frequent parasite flow between sites with moderate local structure. The authors offer the data as a baseline for tracking future control efforts.
pmc-10714678:
Jorian Prudhomme, Jérôme Depaquit, Johanna Fite, Elsa Quillery, Emilie Bouhsira, and Emmanuel Liénard published a 2023 systematic review of blood feeding arthropods found on cattle in France. Ticks, flies, midges, and their kin carry pathogens that can hit farms hard. Yet records of which species occur where were scattered and rough.

The team gathered more than nine thousand documents, read about a thousand closely, and analyzed 290 in depth. They covered ten groups, from biting flies and mosquitoes to lice and ticks. From the data they built maps of distribution and abundance for species of medical and veterinary interest. Farm level detail was often missing, though, and many groups lack counts over time. The review sets a baseline for surveillance.
pmc-10716178:
Ritsch and Armanios put forth a way in twenty twenty-three to use built works as a social sense tool to spot groups at risk in a crisis. Past work reads bias in built works after the fact, as a kind of post-mortem. Their way reads gaps live to guide aid to the right spots fast.

They test if county web reach rates can guess job loss rates in the Covid wave in the United States. A two-by-two map shows where the sense is sharp or blunt and where it errs each way. Adding bridge, build, and library web facts makes an array that reads more sharp. The plan aims at fast, fit aid.
pmc-10716378:
Daniele Antermite and co-authors found a late-stage way to build drug-like chimera molecules in a 2023 chemistry paper. PROTACs are two-headed molecules that drag a target protein to the cell's trash system. Making them is slow, since each head and the link must be built and joined with care.

Their method uses a ruthenium catalyst to add the second head at a late step, by direct work on a carbon-hydrogen bond. It starts from parts that are easy to buy or make. A modular route like this lets chemists spin out many variants fast. That speed helps map which shapes degrade targets best.
pmc-10716978:
Heart rate variability, the small timing changes between heartbeats, reflects how well the body's automatic systems are working. Donghoon Kim and co-authors studied 417 older Korean patients at a veterans' hospital in 2023, split between those with cognitive impairment and those with normal cognition. They asked whether quality of life tracked with heart rate variability in each group, using standard measures of both.

A link appeared only in the group with cognitive impairment: higher quality of life went with higher variability on several measures. No such link showed in the normal cognition group. Because the study took one snapshot in time, the authors cannot say which factor drives the other, and they call for follow-up work.
pmc-10717178:
Gianluca Scalia and co-authors report a very rare brain tumor case from 2023. A 55-year-old man had a tumor in the brain that had been partly removed and treated with radiation. The tumor type tends to strike young children and can return, but spread outside the nervous system is exceedingly rare.

Four years later the man grew a large mass under the scalp on the left side of his head. Surgeons from two teams removed the mass with a rim of healthy skin, opened the skull where bone had thinned, and rebuilt the area with his own skin grafts. Lab tests showed the scalp growth was the same tumor. Drug treatment later kept the disease stable.
pmc-10718278:
Audrey Huang and co-authors report, in a 2023 case study, a rare join of two arm nerves found in an 8-year-old boy in surgery. The boy had weak elbow bend after a spinal cord injury that ate the nerve coat. Surgeons planned to move a spare strand from one nerve to the biceps branch, to bring back elbow bend. On the table, the biceps branch was found mid upper arm as planned. A shock test on the nerve trunk past it, though, moved the hand and lit up the median nerve's muscles on the trace.

Cut work then showed the two nerves, median and musculocutaneous, fused as one thick trunk. The team used median strands as the donor in the biceps' place. The case is the first found live in surgery and proved by shock tests, the team says. Surgeons should know this variant can occur.
pmc-10719078:
Yu and co-authors train machine learning to predict delirium after child surgery. Emergence delirium is a distressed wake-up state in children. Records came from one large children's hospital, 2015 to 2019. The data held 54,776 visits across 43,830 patients. Four common learning models were built and compared. The set held a shrinkage model, a ridge model, a random forest, and a boosted tree model.

All four models scored near 0.74 to 0.75 on curve tests. Adenoid and tonsil surgery raised predicted risk. Younger age raised risk as well. Midazolam before surgery and ondansetron added risk too. IV induction and ketorolac linked to lower risk in the data.
pmc-10719278:
Bereneice Sephton and colleagues demonstrate a way to send rich information with quantum light, in a 2023 study. Quantum networks aim to share information between distant parties without moving the particles that carry it. Packing more dimensions into each particle raises capacity and resists noise, but doing so has been hard.

The team's method uses a nonlinear crystal process, boosted by a strong laser field, to read the shape of a single photon's light pattern. One photon of an entangled pair was converted to a new color, which carried its spatial pattern across. The channel handled fifteen distinct states. They faithfully sent patterns shaped as twists, grids, and blended forms, without knowing in advance what was sent. The work joins two young fields: shaping light and quantum processing.
pmc-10719378:
Jeppesen and André combine two tools to predict the shapes of large, symmetric protein assemblies. AlphaFold predicts protein shapes well, but it has limits on chain and residue counts. Symmetric docking can place copies of a known subunit into ordered shells. The team joined the two: AlphaFold first folds the single unit, then docking builds the full shell. The method targets assemblies with cubic symmetry types.

On 27 test systems, the built assemblies matched the true shapes closely. The median match score was 0.99, and most models rated acceptable to high quality. The finished models are energy-tuned for study of contacts between subunits. The work extends accurate shape prediction to very large protein shells.
pmc-10719578:
JongCheol Pyo and co-authors review a deep learning method used to forecast water quality in lakes and rivers, in a paper from 2023. The method, called long short-term memory, reads sequences and holds onto long past patterns. Water quality shifts with weather, land use, and seasons, so long memory helps. The network is the most used of its kind for this task.

The review first weighs the plain network against physics-based models and other learning tools. It then covers add-ons that clean the data before training. Later sections pair the network with image-style layers, attention steps, and transfer from other sites. Those pairings beat the plain form in most tests. The authors also flag the role of fixed traits like land shape. They close with open problems for the field.
pmc-10720078:
Measuring the pulmonary artery on scans usually means widths or areas, but a full 3D volume might say more about pulmonary hypertension. The six authors studied 59 patients who had both right heart catheterization and CT pulmonary angiography. They split patients into 18 without and 41 with pulmonary hypertension, measured artery diameters by hand, and used 3D software to get cross-sectional areas and volumes of the central pulmonary arteries.

Every scan measure ran higher in the hypertension group and tracked the catheter pressures. For the main and right pulmonary arteries, 3D measures correlated more strongly than widths or areas. The right artery volume beat its width and area clearly in curve analysis, and decision curve analysis favored the 3D measures. The team also built simple equations that estimate catheter pressures from the main artery volume and width.
pmc-10720278:
Epoxy resins that come ready-mixed in one part are easier to use than two-part mixes, but they need a curing agent that sleeps until heated. Taha Behroozi Kohlan and co-authors built such agents in 2023 by pairing a common curing chemical with water-and-oil-loving polymers. Mixing the pair by a simple solvent method lets them tune the agent's behavior.

They varied the polymer's side chains, its mix ratio, and its dose in a standard epoxy, then watched curing with heat scans. Some blends stayed stable at room conditions yet cured fast when heated, the profile factories want. The authors say the flexible recipe can be adjusted for different resins and processes, widening the reach of one-part epoxies.
pmc-10721378:
Hazal Saltık and co-authors survey older women about osteoporosis, in a study published in 2023. The disease thins bones and raises fracture risk, and women after menopause face the highest risk. Good habits can delay it, but only if women know and act on the facts. The team measured knowledge, attitudes, and daily behavior in this group.

They surveyed 225 women at a large hospital's family medicine and bone density clinics in 2018 and 2019. The average age was about fifty-eight, and the median knowledge score was only seven of nineteen points. About half scored low. Even among high scorers, many smoked, skipped sun, ate too little calcium, or exercised too little. University graduates and those taught by health staff knew more. The authors call for direct teaching by clinicians.
pmc-10722978:
Dandan Tian and co-authors present a 2023 study of banana resistance to Fusarium wilt. The fungus behind it, race 4 of Fusarium oxysporum, is the most lethal banana disease in Asia. Roots of a resistant variety and a susceptible one are compared after infection. Gene activity and metabolite profiles are both measured. The susceptible variety changes only 172 genes, while the resistant one changes 1,856. Between the two varieties, 800 genes differ directly.

Those genes cluster in oxidation control, cell wall building, and protective chemistry paths. Plant breeders get named candidate genes for resistance work. The contrast is the lesson: resistance looks like a broad, fast mobilization, not a single gene. Banana farming feeds millions and the crop is genetically narrow, so wilt resistance is a food security topic. Dual profiling ties gene switches to the chemicals that actually fight the fungus.
pmc-10723178:
Jia Li and co-authors link a blood inflammation score to nerve damage in people with type 2 diabetes, in a 2023 study. The nerve damage, a common complication, causes numbness and pain in the feet and hands.

The score combines platelet and white cell counts into one index of body-wide inflammation. Among 1,460 hospitalized patients, higher scores went with worse vibration sense and more nerve damage. The top quarter of scores carried clearly higher risk than the bottom quarter, even after adjusting for other factors. Links held in men, younger patients, and those with longer disease. The authors propose the cheap score as an early warning marker.
pmc-10725178:
Ricardo Martín-Moya and co-authors compare movement quality and fitness in male and female semi-professional soccer players in this 2023 study. Twenty-eight players, evenly split by sex, took a seven-part movement screen plus sprint, agility, and endurance tests. The goal was to see whether screen scores predict field performance.

Men changed direction faster, but movement screen totals did not differ between the sexes. Screen-related factors predicted a fair share of endurance and sprint variation in combined models, though relationships varied by person. The authors conclude that no single test tells the story: coaches should combine several field tests and weigh training history and individual traits when reading results.
pmc-10725278:
Mary Moran and three co-authors test if patient-filled health forms can be gathered in one region in a 2023 study. Mind health shapes how trauma patients fare, near and far, yet forms that track it over time are rarely filled. A top trauma plan urges such forms, mind data in the set.

The team ran hour-long group talks with a mixed care team to vet a draft form plan. A set guide drew out what would help or block the work. Their themes show the plan's fit for the region. Form drives gain ground truth before launch this way.
pmc-10725978:
Lei Cai, Chenmin Yang, and their co-authors report the first case series linking a gene called PPP2R1A to a rare womb cancer type. Their 2023 paper covers mesonephric like adenocarcinoma of the endometrium, in two women aged 57 and 77. Both cases were caught at an early stage.

Care, tissue study, stain tests, and gene tests were all recorded. One tumor had shallow spread into the womb wall and carried a KRAS gene change. The other grew deeper, had entered small vessels, and carried three gene changes, including the PPP2R1A one. Both tumors shared a stain pattern across many markers. The authors say the PPP2R1A change has not been reported for this cancer type in English before.
pmc-10728678:
Keyhole surgery has clear advantages over open surgery, less pain and faster recovery, and guidelines already urge it for emergency appendix and gallbladder operations. Min Hyeong Jo and Heung-Kwon Oh comment on the first nationwide Korean study of laparoscopic emergency surgery, which compared it with the open approach across many hospitals. Most appendix and gallbladder removals, about 94 and 88 percent, were already done by keyhole in Korea.

For the small bowel, stomach, and large bowel, open surgery still dominated, reflecting harder cases and sicker patients. Korea's rates differed from foreign reports in both directions, and the commentators note the study's retrospective design lets surgeon preference skew the results. They call the work a necessary baseline and ask for follow-up research explaining why Korea's pattern diverges.
pmc-10729078:
James McGowan and co-authors (2023) asked what makes quality improvement collaboratives work, using the Michigan programme as the case. Such teams, where hospitals join to raise care quality, show mixed results elsewhere. The Michigan programme has lifted care across many fields for years. The team spoke with 38 clinicians, managers, and programme staff from ten sites. They watched meetings and read programme papers.

Five traits marked the programme's success. It learns from positive deviants, the sites that quietly excel. Coordination is strong, checks are strict, and sites share honest score feedback. These levers are used with care, not to punish. Senior professionals are drawn in as leaders, building community. Winning buy-in, duties, and sparing sites needless forms all helped. The authors offer the findings as a design guide for leaders building such teams. Michigan's lesson, in short, is that structure and culture must be built as one.
pmc-10734478:
Yiping Zou, Michael Glenn Mason, and Jose Ramon Botella build a cheap, portable reader for DNA-based tests, in this 2023 paper. Tests that copy DNA to detect disease are prized for their accuracy and speed. The weak link is reading the result where the patient is: village clinics and farms lack lab gear, and staff have little training. A reader that works at the point of need could close that gap.

Their device is small, low-cost, and simple enough for users with minimal training. It handles the readout step for amplification tests, turning the copied DNA signal into a clear result. The same box serves two readout functions, which cuts the kit a field worker must carry. Faster, surer answers at the site mean treatment or crop action can start the same day.
pmc-10735378:
Jane Lowers and co-authors interview adults who live alone with early dementia in a paper from two thousand twenty-three. About one in three people with dementia lives solo, though care needs grow over time. The team asked what helps and what hinders these adults as they plan ahead.

Fifteen solo adults named their assets: speaking up for themselves, friend networks, money, and care institutions. A self-reliant streak, fear of being a burden, and worry about being exploited held them back from asking for help. Asking felt easier when help seemed rewarding for the giver, when favors could be returned, or when framed as self-advocacy. The authors stress the strengths these adults bring.
pmc-10735578:
Jessica Blaxton and Cindy Bergeman study how stress and depression move together within a person across the years, in a 2023 conference abstract. Older adults often handle emotions and resist stress well. Yet when stress does get to them, they may recover more slowly. The team asked whether age changes the within-person links among felt stress, stress reactivity, and depression.

They used data from 572 adults in a long-running Notre Dame health study, each measured over two to four yearly waves. Only midlife adults showed a sharper effect: in years when their stress reactivity ran high, felt stress hit depression harder. Reactivity in one year also carried the effect of stress from the year before into depression the year after. Older adults looked protected at this yearly scale. The authors suggest midlife adults with reactive years would gain most from stress management and depression monitoring.
pmc-10735878:
Haiyu Jin asks in 2023 whether feeling healthy can blunt the care costs that come with frailty in China. Frailty's root biology is unclear, so care tends to target function and symptoms. Self-rated health, a one-line self-score, may mark which frail people are in fact more resilient.

Data came from a large China aging survey, with people classed as not frail, pre-frail, or frail, and self-scores split into poor and good. Frailty and poor self-scores often went together, Jin notes, yet over a third of frail people rated their health good. Models split costs into clinic, hospital, and self-care lines. If a good self-score truly cuts frail people's costs, a cheap survey line could help target scarce elder care funds.
pmc-10735978:
Feeling cut off from others may age the body in ways that show up years later as a dementia warning sign. Xiang Qi and co-authors tracked over three thousand older Americans from 2012 to 2020 in a 2023 study. They measured isolation and loneliness first, then chemical aging marks on DNA in 2016, and new cases of a syndrome pairing memory complaints with slow walking.

Isolation, more than loneliness, predicted the syndrome: isolated participants faced about a third higher risk. Isolation also matched older DNA-based age and a faster pace of aging, and those aging marks carried a small but real share of the isolation effect, up to about a sixth. The authors suggest fighting isolation may slow one road toward dementia.
pmc-10736178:
Jenny van der Steen and Ida Korfage report a study, published in two thousand twenty-three, that asked experts in thirty-three countries how to plan care ahead with people who have dementia. The work came from the European Association for Palliative Care.

Over four rounds, a panel of one hundred seven experts agreed on a shared framework for advance care planning in dementia. It rests on three themes: a person's capacity, the role of family, and steady contact and talk. The authors also share advice given directly by people living with dementia, which the panel found eye-opening. The framework treats planning as an ongoing talk, not a one-time form, and adjusts as capacity changes.
pmc-10736478:
Michael Vale wrote this research paper, published in 2023, on loneliness among sexual minority adults and how it ties to minority stress, the strain of living with stigma. The study spans ages eighteen to ninety.

Vale first examined baseline data from 333 people, weighing seven kinds of minority stress against loneliness. Older participants reported less loneliness and less stress than younger ones. But age changed how some stressors bit: hidden shame, expected rejection, and family stigma tracked loneliness more strongly at some ages than others. A second part followed 112 people over twenty-one days. On days when people hid their identity or felt more inner shame, loneliness rose. On days they disclosed it, loneliness fell. The paper shows loneliness in this group shifts with both age and daily experience.
pmc-10736578:
Katherine Wang and co-authors compare how income and schooling gaps link to daily function among older Americans of four racial and ethnic groups. Their 2023 study draws on a national health survey from 2011 to 2018. It covers White, Black, Hispanic, and Asian adults aged sixty and over, and tests memory, word fluency, and basic self-care tasks.

Asian elders with a high school education or less showed the highest rate of memory trouble of any group. Black and Hispanic elders had higher odds of disability and thinking problems than White elders. Asian elders matched White elders on self-care but did worse on word fluency. The gaps tied to schooling were widest among Asian elders, for both self-care and memory.
pmc-10736778:
Yuri Jang and co-authors adapt a caregiver course for Korean American families who tend kin with dementia. Such carers in small ethnic groups miss out on proved courses when tongue and culture bar the door. Their 2023 pilot reshapes the Savvy Caregiver course and runs it for six weeks with two Korean-speaking, course-trained leads. Thirteen carers take part.

None drop out, and near all class meets are kept. Low mood scores fall for each carer by course end, a big drop by test marks. Six months on, the gain holds, with no clear slip. Paths of change vary by carer, the team notes. The pilot backs tongue-fit, culture-fit courses as a fair path to proved help.
pmc-10736878:
Jessica Maras and Kate Leger track in 2023 how daily discrimination and daily stress response move together within a person. More than thirteen hundred adults report across three survey waves over twenty years. Eight-day diaries at each wave log daily stress reactions.

On days and waves when a person faces more unfair treatment than usual, stress reactions also run hotter. Past work saw this link only between people, not within them. The swing holds across the full twenty-year span of reports. Daily fairness climate thus tracks daily stress load in one life.
pmc-10736978:
Darina Petrovsky and Anne Mitchell introduce a symposium in two thousand twenty-three on age-friendly care built around the 4Ms framework. The framework names four evidence-based elements of good care for older adults: What Matters, Medication, Mentation, and Mobility. Following it makes high-quality, needs-based care more likely.

The session gathers four nurse scientists, one for each element cutting across the others. Talks include disparities in advance care planning across social groups, drawn from a national retirement study. Another reports a pilot trial of primary palliative care for nursing home residents with serious illness, testing whether the approach is workable and welcome.
pmc-10737078:
Donnette Narine and Takashi Yamashita studied breast cancer screening in an often-overlooked group in a 2023 paper. Black women die of breast cancer at far higher rates than white women, yet research often treats them as one block. Caribbean Black women differ in background and culture, with many immigrants among them.

Using seven years of a national health survey, the authors analyzed 552 non-Hispanic Caribbean Black women aged 40 to 75 in the United States. The longer a woman had lived in the country, the more likely she had been screened in the past year. Age itself showed no link. The authors urge prevention work aimed at this subgroup, above all at newcomers.
pmc-10737178:
Sin, Cheng, Roseman, Zamrini, and Ahmed study tiny strokes found in the brain after death and their link to dementia, in this 2023 paper. These microinfarcts are common in older adults and may quietly erode thinking. Whether the link differs between women and men was the open question.

The team used autopsy data from 727 community-dwelling older adults, about half of whom had dementia. Microinfarcts appeared in roughly half the brains. Having two or more was more common among those with dementia. Deep-brain microinfarcts carried a significant link to dementia, while surface ones did not. The pattern looked similar in women and men. The authors see location as the telling detail.
pmc-10737278:
Evan Plys and Melissa Gerald share field lessons on enrolling hard to reach groups in a 2023 symposium paper. Some communities are shut out of research by place, poverty, or past neglect, yet their voices are key to fair health gains. Four talks give worked cases.

One covers poor short stay nursing home residents and their care partners, with tips on budgets and community boards. A second follows Hispanic families caring for elders with dementia, through translation and culture fit work. A third enters prisons and addiction clinics. Recruitment and protocol bends fill the set.
pmc-10737378:
Guo Yu, Zhenmei Zhang, and Quanbao Jiang study how caring for a spouse relates to memory and thinking in later life in China. Their 2023 paper uses four rounds of a large health survey from 2011 to 2018. The sample covers 3,137 couples aged 45 and older, and thinking skills were scored with a short test.

Couples tended to change together over the eight years, the authors find. Men started with higher scores but lost ground faster than women. Giving care was linked to slower loss for men, but not for women. Getting care was linked to faster loss for both, so help should reach both partners.
pmc-10737478:
Gemmae Fix, Janet Clark, and Allen Gifford wrote a 2023 study on bringing a whole-health care model into HIV clinics. The US Department of Veterans Affairs is rolling out Whole Health, a patient-centered approach that aligns care with what matters most to each patient. Rollout centers on primary care, but HIV clinics have long provided both HIV and primary care.

People with HIV are aging into complex health and life situations that fit the Whole Health approach well. The team interviewed 11 physicians, psychologists, nurses, and leaders at three clinics, using story vignettes to spark discussion. Findings were mapped onto an implementation framework. Most staff knew of Whole Health and wanted it, yet no clinic offered its services and few had training. The study lists what clinics need to adopt the model.
pmc-10737578:
Niranjani Nagarajan and Joshua Ehrlich report new vision measures and impairment rates from a national study of older adults. Published in 2023, the work uses the National Health and Aging Trends Study in the United States. In 2021 that study added tablet based tests of distance acuity, near acuity, and contrast sensitivity. The tests can run in people's homes.

The home tests agreed well with clinical standards. About 28 percent of adults over seventy had at least one kind of impairment, with near vision loss the most common. Rates ran higher among the oldest and the less schooled. Lower income groups, and Hispanic and non-White adults, also showed higher rates. Each impairment type went with a higher adjusted rate of dementia.
pmc-10737778:
Huei-wern Shen and Yi Wang untangle how volunteering and everyday discrimination each relate to life satisfaction after age 50. Discrimination is known to drag satisfaction down at many ages. Volunteering tends to lift it, at least in older adults. Whether volunteering softens the discrimination effect, and whether that differs by age, was unknown.

Their 2023 study uses 5,791 respondents from a 2016 national retirement survey. About 3,191 were 65 or older; 2,600 were 51 to 64. Across the whole group, discrimination tracked with lower satisfaction and volunteering with higher. In the younger group, volunteering did not carry, or mediate, the link between discrimination and satisfaction. The analysis adjusted for health, income, and social traits.
pmc-10737878:
Björn Slaug and seven co-authors catalogued life changes around retirement age in Sweden and Germany, in a study from twenty twenty-three. Lives alternate between stable spans and events that force adjustment. How changes cluster, and in what order they arrive, may matter as much as each change alone.

Interviews with fifty people covered about ten years around retirement. Each person faced close to four changes on average, and a quarter faced more than five. Retirement and moving home often came together. Illness often followed a chain of earlier events, while a new partner often started one. Gaps between events varied widely. The study maps how change piles up in this stage of life.
pmc-10737978:
Vera Gorbunova wrote this conference paper, published in 2023, introducing a session on what gene activity patterns can reveal about aging and long life. The session compared these patterns across species with very different lifespans.

Gene activity in cells shifts fast and in steady ways when the body faces stress or change, so it offers a close-up view of aging. The talks covered shared gene patterns tied to long life across species. They also covered ways to merge gene data with protein data. Other speakers presented clocks that estimate biological age from gene activity. Still others covered single-cell studies of immune aging in humans. One talk dealt with how joining the blood flow of young and old animals can renew old tissue.
pmc-10738078:
David Russell, Christina Miyawaki, and Erin Bouldin interview dementia caregivers in rural Appalachia about services they cannot get, in a 2023 study. Dementia risk runs higher in rural areas while help runs thinner. The team wanted the local picture in western North Carolina.

They spoke with twenty-two caregivers and people with dementia between 2021 and 2022, recruited through local agencies. Families described fragile support networks, confusion about what services exist, and feeling behind in planning for the future. Whether they used a service turned on the illness's stage and family context as much as on supply. The study gives rural planners ground-level detail: names of the gaps, in the words of the people who live with them.
pmc-10738178:
Kexin Yu and colleagues described in 2023 how an online dementia research registry kept its Asian American volunteers engaged. Recruiting minority older adults is one of the hardest problems in Alzheimer's research, and weak recruitment slows treatment development. The registry, based in Oregon and Washington, lets adults enroll themselves online for future studies. By early 2023 it held just under five hundred participants.

The paper reports response and retention patterns and the adaptations the team made to recruit Asian Americans. Registry members averaged about sixty-four years old, and twenty research projects had already drawn participants from it. Most studies that tried the registry used it again. The lessons are practical: which outreach adjustments moved enrollment, and how an online-first design can still build trust with communities that research has historically underserved.
pmc-10738278:
Juyoung Park and co-authors present a 2023 study on the combined mental health risk of elder mistreatment and social isolation. Each risk alone is known to harm the mental health of older adults. Their joint effect, though, has drawn little study, and the concern is sharp among older Asian immigrants.

The sample held over two thousand older Korean Americans, with an average age in the early seventies. About a third reported one kind of mistreatment in the past year, and a quarter were socially isolated. Both risks raised mental distress on their own. Facing several kinds of mistreatment while isolated added a further, clear risk.
pmc-10738378:
Patrik Marier and Loïc Trabut compare how France and Quebec used market tools to deliver home care, in a 2023 paper. Quebec runs a managed market: regional health bodies buy services from community groups and firms to cut long-term care costs. France chose a consumer-driven route, giving older adults a cash benefit to pick their own provider.

The authors track both systems across rural, urban, and declining industrial areas. Despite the contrast, both hit the same wall: rural areas lack enough providers for any real choice, so officials must step in and build market-like conditions by hand. Market tools, they argue, were designed with cities in mind and drift toward austerity elsewhere.
pmc-10738478:
Alisha Thompson, Scott Wilks, and Rhonda Bardales tested in 2023 how social life links to quality of life in older adults living at home. Longer lives have not been matched by equal effort to raise later-life quality. Rich ties are thought to help body, mind, and thinking health.

Data came from a national survey of 746 adults aged sixty-five and older. Measures covered how much people engage with others and how good those ties feel. Quality of life rose with engagement and with each health measure. Being unmarried, being male, and certain ethnic backgrounds also shaped scores. The authors discuss what the pattern means for services that support older adults.
pmc-10738578:
Ray Merrill and Ian Gibbons track in 2023 how prostate cancer survival gaps between White and Black men in the United States have changed. Survival depends on tumor stage, age, and marital status at diagnosis. Using national cancer registry data for cases from 2000 to 2015, with follow up through 2020, they estimate five year relative survival.

Over that time, survival fell for White men and rose for Black men, so by 2015 the rates were about the same. Stage by stage, the racial gap was not significant once other factors were counted. Marital status and very young or very old age mattered for some stages. Race did not change those other links.
pmc-10738878:
Kylie Schiloski and Margie Lachman asked whether believing in control protects the aging mind in two thousand twenty-three. People who feel in charge of their thinking often perform better. Whether that belief slows decline was unclear. A national midlife study supplied two waves a decade apart. About two thousand five hundred adults took part. Memory and executive function were tested at both waves.

Baseline beliefs were set against later change. Starting skill, schooling, and health were held constant. Age was tested as a possible modifier. Belief in control tracked with better maintenance for some. The pattern hints mindset shapes cognitive aging. Interventions might train control beliefs deliberately. Long horizons make the finding valuable.
pmc-10740178:
YangHao Fu, TianDuo Wang, and John Ronald built a blood test that reports what immune cells are doing inside a tumor, in a study from twenty twenty-three. Cell therapies work well against blood cancers, but doctors lack cheap ways to watch the cells at work inside solid tumors. Blood signals rarely mirror tumor activity.

Their trick uses a synthetic receptor that switches on a custom gene when the immune cell touches its target. Engineered T cells carrying the receptor released a marker enzyme only when they met target-positive cancer cells. In mice, blood levels of the marker rose for target-positive tumors and stayed flat otherwise. The authors say the system could help explain why responses differ across patients.
pmc-10740578:
Liquan Cai and co-authors study, in twenty twenty-three, a cell pump and its control of heart cell power plants. The pump, Na/K-ATPase, moves sodium and potassium across the cell wall. It also talks to a kinase called Src, a switch protein. That talk has emerged as a way to tune mitochondria, the cell's power plants. The team used gene editing in human stem cells to make a pump variant that cannot signal through Src. Total pump activity stayed the same, but Src and related signals fell sharply.

Both normal and mutant stem cells grew into heart muscle cells, with markers and beating to prove it. Yet the mutant heart cells breathed much less at rest and at max. The axis thus shapes heart energy use.
pmc-10741078:
A team of researchers links common pain relievers to gut inflammation through mitochondrial stress in a paper from 2023. Crohn's disease mixes genetic risk with environmental triggers. Certain gene variants weaken a recycling process in gut cells, and pain drugs called NSAIDs are known triggers. The team showed these drugs stress mitochondria, the cell's energy units, in intestinal cells. In tissue models from Crohn's patients, the drugs switched on a mitochondrial stress response.

Stressed cells released mitochondrial parts that act as danger signals. Gut biopsies from patients in remission or with mild disease showed the same stress pathway active. Severe cases did not. The authors argue mitochondrial stress helps explain flare-ups after NSAID use.
pmc-10741178:
Menconi and co-authors sweep worm risks from fresh fish in Italy and kin lands. Fish fare has surged in Europe as a health food of late. Fresh fish holds weight for lake folk and guests who seek old dishes. That surge lit risks from worms borne in fish to men. Such worms now rank as world food germs in the text. Clans span round worms, fluke worms, and tape worms in the set.

Past 50 worm kinds can strike men from raw fish fare. Half-cooked fare with live worms drives those strikes in hosts. Yet such worms get less note than peer food germs in print. Slow ill pace and dim finds drive that gap in care. The sweep homes on six fresh-fish worms in the zone. Their rates in fish and hosts form the core facts.
pmc-10741778:
Paul Holvoet presents a 2023 review on why stem cells from fat tissue disappoint in heart disease trials. In animal studies these cells shielded arteries and hearts from stress and inflammation. In patients, the same cells have shown little benefit, and the author searched the literature for the reason.

Aging and metabolic change are the likely culprits. Older stem cells divide less, tire faster, and lose mitochondrial power. They also stir more inflammation and lay down more fat, weakening their ability to grow blood vessels and save heart muscle. The review names small regulatory RNAs whose rise or fall tracks these failures. Fixing that RNA pattern might restore the cells' healing power.
pmc-10741878:
Ji-In Woo and co-authors isolated hormone-making bacteria from coastal soil in 2023 and tested whether they help seeds sprout under salty conditions. Salt harms plant growth and threatens farm yields. Certain root-zone bacteria can soften that harm, and some make gibberellin, a plant hormone that drives germination.

Seven isolates were screened for growth-promoting traits and for tolerance of two salt levels. Two isolates stood out for making the hormone and related helpful compounds. Seeds of mallow and broccoli were then tested under salt stress with the bacteria. The study aims to show which isolates best support sprouting when salt would otherwise stall it. Readers get a candidate bio-treatment for saline soils, built from bacteria that already live where salt is normal.
pmc-10742678:
Domenik Popp and co-authors ask whether the COVID-19 pandemic changed the fate of hip fracture patients in Austria. Lockdowns and strained hospitals raised fears that delayed surgery would cost lives. Their 2023 study compares patients treated for fractures near the top of the thigh bone across three spans: before, during, and after the emergency years.

The team enrolled 246 patients from the 2020 and 2021 emergency period at a large trauma center. They compared them with 494 patients from the same months in 2017 to 2019 and with 313 patients from 2022 and 2023. Admissions fell by about a fifth during the pandemic, and the mix of sex and accident place shifted. Death rates within thirty days, though, sat close across the spans, around fifteen percent. The study tests whether care truly returned to normal or settled into a new pattern.
pmc-10742778:
Alejandro Nunez-Trull and colleagues asked in 2023 whether the structure of lower-limb tendons shapes how people walk. Walking relies on rocker motions of the foot and on tendons that stretch and recoil. The team measured the patellar tendon, Achilles tendon, and plantar fascia in thirty-nine healthy men with ultrasound, then timed their gait phases on a pressure platform.

Men with thicker patellar tendons spent longer in the first rocker phase of each step. A like trend appeared for thicker Achilles tendons, though it was weaker. Plantar fascia form showed no clear tie to rocker timing. The authors read tendon thickness as one factor that stretches the early stance phase of walking.
pmc-10742878:
Fairuz Bestari and co-authors pool studies on ultra-processed food and chronic disease in a 2023 analysis. Such foods, classed by the NOVA system, are engineered for taste and shelf life. They tend to pack energy, salt, sugar, and fat, while shorting fiber. The team gathered eighteen studies to measure dose-response links with major diseases.

Eating more of these foods raised intakes of sugar, salt, saturated fat, and energy by wide margins. Fiber intake fell far below the advised level. Each ten percent rise in their share of the diet tracked with higher hazard for diabetes most strongly. Heart disease, obesity, and cancer followed with smaller but clear links. The authors say capping daily intake of ultra-processed foods could help prevent obesity and its companion diseases. They frame dose, not mere presence, as the measure that matters.
pmc-10742978:
A research team published a research paper in 2023 on how well teeth can reveal a young person's age, tested in a large multiethnic sample. Age checks matter when migrants arrive without documents, and courts need to know if someone is a minor. The team compared three dental methods on jaw X-rays from 324 patients aged four to twenty.

All three methods overestimated age on average. After age eighteen, accuracy within one year fell below half for every method. Two methods missed by roughly 1.2 to 1.3 years on average, while the third missed by about two years. The authors conclude dental estimates alone cannot reliably decide minority.
pmc-10743178:
Mónica Guerra and co-authors build magnetic nanofibers carrying an enzyme in a 2023 materials study. Nanofibers offer huge surface area for their weight, which suits drug delivery and targeted treatment. The team loaded lysozyme, a bacteria-fighting enzyme, into fibers of two plastics, one blended with chitosan.

Fibers were spun electrically, crosslinked with boron-based compounds, and dotted with magnetic iron beads. Microscopy checked their form. Tests measured how much enzyme stuck, how active it stayed, and how it leaked out in fluids that mimic body and cancer settings. Cancer cell survival after contact with the fibers was also checked. The system aims at guided delivery in future care.
pmc-10743878:
Wenya Zhai and co-authors test what a signaling protein does in fish liver during bacterial infection, in a 2023 study. The protein, called IL-6, rises with infection stress and is tied to harmful oxygen byproducts. Its role in fish liver was unclear. The team bred zebrafish with the gene knocked out and infected them with a common fish germ.

Knockout fish showed milder liver damage than normal fish. Gene scans found thousands of genes shifted, many tied to oxygen handling. Knockout livers held less of a harm marker and more of a guard enzyme after infection. The results suggest that losing IL-6 eases oxidative stress in the liver during such infections.
pmc-10744078:
Muftah Mahmud, Swati Vasireddy, Krisstina Gowin, and Akshay Amaraneni review a family of blood diseases in which the marrow makes too many blood cells, in a 2023 paper. These diseases, and the overlap forms that share traits with a second group, can look very unlike from patient to patient. That range makes them hard to name and sort.

The review covers gene faults, chemical marks on genes, and chromosome changes, plus how they interact with immune cells. It then walks through signs, sorting rules, and treatments. New gene reading tools have widened what doctors know, the authors note. For advanced disease, a stem cell transplant remains the main path, even as drug care improves.
pmc-10744178:
Margo Hammond and co-authors published this transplant study in 2023. It asks whether traits of a heart donor predict whether the person who receives the heart later dies of heart-related causes.
