The authors reasoned that some causes of donor death stir the immune system strongly, and that this early immune activity could harm the recipient over time. They linked records for local adult donors to the outcomes of their recipients.

Donor age was known for 706 donors and donor sex for 730. Three donor traits went with more heart-related deaths among recipients: donor age over 40, female donor sex, and donor death from bleeding inside the skull. The authors suggest that watching for and calming donor immune activation might protect recipients. They note the study covers a single center, so wider checks are needed.
pmc-10744878:
A 32-year-old woman with an underactive thyroid from Hashimoto's disease arrived at hospital with worsening muscle pain, weakness, and frequent falls. Ergeta Ktona, Blerta Budani, Ioannis Kostas-Agnantis, and Alma Idrizi report her case because the trigger turned out to be unusual. Two weeks earlier she had been treated for what looked like ordinary flu.

Blood tests showed normal thyroid function but high levels of muscle damage markers. Antibody and DNA tests pointed to a heavy cytomegalovirus infection. Scans showed fierce inflammation across the muscles of her pelvis, thighs, and calves. A muscle biopsy on day seven confirmed polymyositis, an autoimmune attack on muscle. With medicine and physical therapy she improved markedly within two weeks. The authors discuss how virus and autoimmunity may intertwine.
pmc-10746078:
Children with inflammatory bowel disease face risks to growth and bone health. Their skeletons are still developing, which raises the stakes. Moon Bae Ahn and In Hyuk Yoo studied 51 Korean children and adolescents with newly diagnosed disease. The patients were aged 10 to 18. All had Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis. The team measured bone mineral density in the spine and thigh bone at diagnosis. They compared the scores with body measurements and blood markers.

More than half the children had scores in the low-normal range. About one in five had thigh bone scores below minus 2. The authors report how common low density is at diagnosis. They also name the risk factors clinicians should watch.
pmc-10746478:
Siyang Cao and co-authors map the world literature where ferroptosis, an iron-driven form of cell death, meets bone and joint disease. Links to osteoporosis and osteoarthritis have piled up for a decade. Their 2023 bibliometric study pulls every paper and review on the pair from the Web of Science, spanning 2012 to mid-2023.

Software built for science mapping charts who publishes, where, and with whom. China, the United States, and Italy together produced over four fifths of the shelf. Three Chinese universities led the institution table. The maps also trace hot topics and the teams shaping them. Newcomers to the field get a chart of its centers and currents instead of a cold start.
pmc-10746978:
Claudio Cubillos and co-authors review, in 2023, digital tests that measure thinking skills in older adults. Spotting decline early matters, and software could make testing cheaper and wider. The team searched three databases and, after screening, kept twenty studies of apps and platforms for this purpose.

Most tools were computerized versions of paper tests, or test batteries run on computers, tablets, or the web. A few used simulators, virtual settings, or games built around daily tasks. The review maps which thinking skills were tested and how the tools were validated, and it flags gaps, such as thin evidence on some accuracy measures, for future developers.
pmc-10747078:
Muhammad Zahaib Ilyas and co-authors map the genetics of drought-linked traits in maize. Their 2023 study profiles 41 inbred lines with 200 DNA markers. Maize feeds much of the world yet suffers badly under dry conditions.

Over a thousand marker variants were found, and the lines split into two main groups plus a mixed set. Two statistical models tied markers to seven chemical and leaf traits, from phenolic acids to moisture content. Eighty-five links passed the bar in the simpler model and 31 in the stricter one. Some markers tracked several traits at once. The authors offer the list to breeders for marker-guided selection.
pmc-10747478:
Anton Poroykov and four colleagues published a 2023 paper on measuring error in close-range photogrammetry. This method builds 3D shapes from flat photos, giving touch-free measures of a surface. It is used in fields from engineering to medicine.

Because the method chains many steps, its true error is hard to pin down. Math estimates and computer models miss real-world factors like lighting and lens flaws. The team built a system that gauges error from real test setups instead. A known test object lets them compare measured shape with truth. Direct checks give users a firmer sense of how much to trust each measure.
pmc-10747678:
A team of surgeons studies CT scans to plan nose-based pituitary surgery in a paper from 2023. The operation reaches the pituitary gland through the nose and a thin wall called the septum. Cutting away less septum is gentler, but the surgeon still needs room to work. The team simulated tool insertion on scans from twenty patients and compared the results with cadaver dissections.

The average predicted cut was about thirteen millimeters. In cadavers, a one-centimeter cut let a straight tool reach the key artery edge. A two-centimeter cut gave wider reach and a better view. Nasal width measures did not predict the needed cut. The authors say one centimeter suffices for standard tumors.
pmc-10747778:
Beltran Martinez and co-authors tested whether breaks or stretching during a shift reduce muscle fatigue in material handling work. Fatigue is a main driver of work-related muscle and joint disorders. Volunteers repeated a handling task under three schedules: no breaks, small breaks, and breaks with a stretching routine. Muscle activity sensors and a wearable-based movement score tracked fatigue objectively.

Both rest schedules cut fatigue significantly compared with working straight through, and stretching added no clear extra benefit over breaks alone in the reported results. Output did not drop under any schedule. The authors conclude that small breaks during a shift can meaningfully lower fatigue, and with it the likely risk of workplace disorders, at no cost to productivity. The text byline names fewer authors than the catalog record, so team framing is used.
pmc-10747878:
Jiahong Yang and five co-authors build a machine learning system to detect autism spectrum disorder from brain scans and personal data, in a two thousand twenty-three neuroimaging paper. Autism's causes remain elusive, but its fingerprints appear in functional brain activity.

Their framework first prunes the imaging features with recursive feature elimination, then feeds survivors into a graph neural network over brain connectivity. A separate extractor handles phenotypic information such as age and test scores, and the two streams are fused. On the ABIDE benchmark the combined system reached about seventy-nine to eighty-one percent accuracy, competitive with leading methods. The authors present it as a step toward objective diagnostic support.
pmc-10747978:
Jiajun Ran and co-authors build a reliable gene-transfer system for watercress. Their 2023 paper improves how the salad plant takes up new genes. Watercress germplasm holds promise, but gene studies lacked a working pipeline. A strong regeneration method in their lab gave them the base.

Pretreatment, co-culture, and differentiation steps were each tuned. A marker gene for the hormone auxin was inserted as proof. Glow checks and DNA tests confirmed the transformed plants. The inserted reporter maps where auxin gathers during growth. The system now supports gene function studies in this crop. Breeders gain a tool for a small but valued plant.
pmc-10748078:
Olivia Leslie, David Córdova Bulens, and Stephen Redmond build a fingertip sensor that feels in six axes in this 2023 paper. Dexterous robots need touch that reports force and slip across the whole contact patch, not just at one point. Without it, grips stay clumsy.

Their optical sensor, shaped like a human thumb tip, estimates force and displacement at ten spots on its surface. It also sums the total force and torque. Light inside the fingertip carries the signals, keeping the device thin. It mounts onto existing robot fingers without rebuilding the gripper. The team details the build and bench tests of the design.
pmc-10748378:
Kang He and co-authors test whether charcoal in the soil helps peanuts ride out a sudden drought, in a 2023 study. Short, sharp droughts are growing more common, and biochar is known to soften water stress, but its effects run through soil life as much as through the plant.

The team grew peanuts under an extreme short drought with biochar mixed in at three rates. The amendment raised soil nitrites and available phosphorus and reshaped the bacterial community more strongly than the fungal one. Soil chemistry shifted alongside the microbes. Plants in biochar soil resisted the drought better. The work ties a simple soil additive to a whole underground support system for crops under stress.
pmc-10751078:
Akshay Athavale and Bridin Murnion review a drug family used for seizures and nerve pain. The drugs are gabapentinoids, sold for a short list of cleared uses. In Australia they are cleared for stubborn focal epilepsy and nerve pain. Use for vague back or leg pain is common, yet proof for it is thin.

The drugs can cause a mild high, sleepiness, and loose control, which invites misuse. Harm from misuse, both by chance and on purpose, has climbed. Long use can breed dependence, and a sudden stop can bring withdrawal. If the reason for use is murky, the authors urge a slow taper off. Kidney trouble raises the risk of harm. Each new script, they say, needs a clear weighing of help against harm.
pmc-10751778:
Tiantao Liu and co-authors add reaction type clues to AI tools that plan how to build new compounds. Their 2023 paper works with template-free models, which learn to plan builds straight from data. Such models can miss the chemical logic a skilled chemist would use. The new framework, named SynCluster, groups reactions by type with no labels, then feeds those groups into the base models as extra cues.

On the task of working back from a target compound, the cues lifted top scores by clear margins. Gains held when the framework was paired with a second known model. Forward build and reagent choice tasks also scored high, which the authors take as a sign of broad use.
pmc-10753878:
Some tumors wall themselves off with stiff scar tissue that immune cells cannot cross, so checkpoint drugs fail at the gate. Fotios Mpekris and thirteen co-authors soften the wall with nano-sized drug bubbles in this 2023 study. The bubbles carry pirfenidone, a drug that loosens the tumor's mechanics, packaged so a hundredth of the usual dose does the work.

In mice with breast tumors and a fibrous skin cancer, the bubbles restored the tumor interior much as the free drug does. Adding a checkpoint drug then slowed growth, extended survival, and in one breast model cured the animals outright. Tumor tissue showed more helper and killer T cells after the pairing. The authors call the approach mechanotherapy: fix the physics first, then let immunity in.
pmc-10754578:
Mamdouh Ali Kotb and co-authors measure neck nerve roots with ultrasound in people with type 2 diabetes in this 2023 paper. Diabetes can damage nerves, including those of the neck and shoulder bundle. The study used people with no nerve symptoms, to catch early changes.

They scanned twenty-five patients with diabetes and eighteen people without it. Both sides of the neck were imaged at three nerve root levels. Two of the three roots were clearly thinner in the diabetes group. Worse blood sugar scores and longer time with diabetes went with thinner roots. The authors suggest ultrasound can reveal early nerve change before symptoms start. That could help doctors watch nerve health in diabetes care.
pmc-10756078:
People who live in care homes often have frailty and several long-term illnesses, so their medical care is complex. Lauren McCarthy and co-authors set out in 2023 to define what doctors working in care homes should be able to do. They first searched the research and grey literature, gathering 124 candidate skills across 21 areas, and mapped them to the national framework for doctors.

A panel of 23 experts then voted over three rounds, keeping items with at least 80 percent agreement. The final list holds 109 skills across 19 areas. Agreement came easiest for general skills around frailty and less easily for specialist topics and leadership duties. The authors offer the list as the base for training doctors in care home medicine.
pmc-10758678:
Sumit Acharya, Suraj Lama, and Durga Anil Kanigicherla published a review in twenty twenty-three on anti-thymocyte globulin, a frontline rescue drug when a transplanted kidney faces T-cell attack. The antibody preparation, made in rabbits or horses, depletes the T cells driving rejection, including cases that resist steroids. It is powerful but not benign.

The review walks through how the drug works beyond simple cell depletion and compares the commercial products. Trials disagree on the best dose and course length, leaving no firm standard. Early side effects like fever and rash contrast with long-term infection and cancer risks from deep immune suppression. The authors synthesize the efficacy evidence for reversing rejection episodes.
pmc-10772578:
Savary and a large team of co-authors grow mini-tumors in the lab to test drug pairs against a childhood muscle cancer. Rhabdomyosarcoma cure rates after relapse have stalled for two decades, partly for lack of good lab models. Their organoids come from relapsed tumors of the fusion-negative type.

The mini-tumors kept the molecular marks of the original cancers and grew for months. That stability suits them to drug screening with long follow-up. As a proof of concept, the team retested drugs that trigger cell death, guided by gene activity data. The authors present the model as a sharper way to pick drug combinations worth trying in patients.
pmc-10773678:
Martin Dufwenberg and four co-authors propose flushing the fluid that bathes the brain and cord with clean fluid as a way to guard nerves after harm. Brain and cord ills are hard to treat since the system is sealed by bone and a tight barrier. The article came out in twenty twenty-three.

That seal traps swelling agents, germs, and toxic waste near a wound, which can feed a harmful loop. Neck level access points can reach the fluid, though back taps are the norm. With tiny tubes and fluid filters now at hand, the authors ask if two tubes, one in and one out, could wash the fluid and break the loop. They lay out the case for trials of this flush idea.
pmc-10774478:
Hoang Kieu Chi Ngo, Hoang Le, and Young-Joon Surh wrote a perspective article in 2023 on a protein that controls how cells handle chemical stress. In healthy cells, turning the protein on helps block the start of cancer. In cells that are already cancerous, the same protein can help tumors grow, spread, and resist chemotherapy and radiation. Changes in its gene can lock it in an active state, and patients with that pattern tend to fare worse.

The authors review what is known about those gene changes and what they mean for judging a patient's outlook. They also weigh treatment ideas aimed at the protein, including small drug molecules, gene-silencing tools, and gene editing. For readers, the piece frames why a single target can be both protective and dangerous, and why treatment may need to match each tumor's exact state.
pmc-10776078:
Ting Ma, Caihong Zhang, and Jia Huang sequence the first complete mitochondrial genome of a blow fly species, in a 2023 paper. The genus Isomyia has had frequent taxonomic revisions, and its place in the family tree was unsettled. A full genome can help place it.

The genome is 16,438 bases long and holds the standard set of protein-coding genes, transfer RNAs, and ribosomal RNAs, plus a rich non-coding region. Family trees built by two methods from twenty-three genomes support the unity of the family and several subfamilies. The species branched early in its group. The data add a reference for fly evolution studies.
pmc-10792178:
Amirhossein Mirzaei and co-authors offer a 2023 systematic review of two citrus flavonoids, hesperidin and hesperetin, against diabetes and its complications. Plant compounds with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory actions are much studied as add-on therapies. Proof from cells and molecules needed to sit in one place.

Three databases were searched through mid 2023. Hesperetin calmed inflammatory signalling through a major immune pathway. Hesperidin kept nerves safe in diabetes by switching on an antioxidant defence switch. Effects ran from cell level to whole-body metabolism across the studies covered. The pair emerge as credible options for human testing under tight control.
pmc-10797378:
Heart surgeons can repair a mitral valve through small cuts, by hand-held camera or by robot, often while freezing stray heart rhythms back to normal. Magdalena Rufa and co-authors compared the two approaches in 2023 at one center, matching patients closely on twenty-two traits before surgery. Each group held fifty-two patients, followed for a median of two years.

Outcomes were strikingly alike. No patient died in hospital or within thirty days, survival matched between groups, and about seventy-six percent kept a normal rhythm at follow-up. Most had the rhythm procedure on the left side of the heart, and many also had a second valve fixed. The authors conclude both routes are safe and effective in matched hands.
pmc-10800478:
Miwako Nishio and co-authors read antibody patterns in a rare, fatal disease where the Epstein-Barr virus infects the body's own killer cells. Their study appeared in 2023, though the catalog lists 2024. Using a Japanese nationwide survey, they analyzed 84 patients across childhood to old age. Antibodies against the virus's hidden nuclear protein appeared in most patients, but at lower levels than in healthy people. Antibodies against the virus's outer shell ran higher.

Patients with strong shell and early-protein antibody levels survived better at three years than those with weak ones. The authors read the pattern as a dulled immune aim at infected cells, partly compensated by anti-particle responses. They suggest antibody profiles could help predict the disease's course.
pmc-10806278:
Eduardo López-Caneda, Séverine Lannoy, Salvatore Campanella, and Carina Carbia introduce the second volume of a research collection on binge drinking and the young brain. Alcohol is the world's most used psychoactive substance, tied to about three million deaths a year. It accounts for nearly three in ten deaths among people aged fifteen to twenty-nine in Europe and the Americas. Binge drinking means downing five or more drinks, four for women, within about two hours.

The editors stress why the pattern worries researchers: adolescence and young adulthood are windows when the brain is still maturing, up to about age twenty-four, and when many mental disorders first appear. Heavy episodic drinking in this window is linked to structural and functional harm in still-developing regions such as the prefrontal cortex, plus deficits in executive skills like impulse control. The volume gathers studies probing these effects.
pmc-10808478:
Fangxiang Mu and co-authors survey what women with repeated pregnancy loss know and do about their condition in a 2023 study from Lanzhou, China. Self-management matters greatly in this condition, so 497 patients answered a questionnaire on knowledge, attitude, and daily practice.

Knowledge scored poor at about 58 percent of the maximum, attitudes were middling, and practice was surprisingly proactive at about 81 percent. Education and income fed knowledge, which in turn shaped attitudes and habits. Age mattered in a curved way, helping only under thirty-two. The authors pinpoint weak knowledge items for targeted teaching and groups needing extra support, so self-care guidance can close the knowing-doing gap they documented.
pmc-10824978:
Emma Curran and eight co-authors review in 2024 how biological threat agents can harm the eyes. Governments group mass-casualty hazards under a framework covering chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear, and explosive events, from attacks and bioterrorism to fires and spills of dangerous material.

The review walks through the eye effects of the biological agents in that framework: how they injure the eye, how those injuries show up, and what they mean for care. Eye doctors are often first to see certain signs of exposure. The authors give clinicians a reference for spotting and handling these rare but serious cases.
pmc-10826878:
Andreea Manole and a large team show how a rare gene fault clogs human neurons with protein clumps. Faults in the gene for the enzyme NGLY1 cause a disease with slow development, nerve harm, and seizures. Their 2023 study turns patient stem cells into working cortex neurons in the lab. Gene, protein, and function checks then map what goes wrong inside.

The sick neurons cleared protein clumps poorly. Their energy hubs and their synaptic links also faltered. Adding back a healthy copy of the gene fixed the faults. Mature neurons showed the harm while star-shaped support cells did not. A laser capture step let the team list the clumps' contents in fine detail. That list may guide future drug hunts.
pmc-10834778:
Letian Lv and co-authors build a nanoplatform to strengthen photodynamic therapy against cancer, in this 2024 Europe PMC paper. Photodynamic therapy kills tumor cells with light-activated reactive oxygen, but many tumors resist the cell death it triggers. Mitochondria, the cell's energy hubs, are a promising lever for breaking that resistance.

Their system, PyroFPSH, is a metal-organic framework decorated with nanozymes that mimic two enzymes. It drains the tumor's glutathione defenses and keeps generating reactive oxygen species. It also carries sulfasalazine, a drug that depolarizes mitochondria and cuts tumor energy supply. Lab results show the combined actions raise therapy effectiveness, expanding what enzyme-mimicking nanocarriers can do in cancer treatment.
pmc-10862378:
Madison Edwards and co-authors coax the fats in a drop of biofluid to an interface where they can be read and reacted in place. Their 2023 paper serves disease diagnostics, where lipids flag progression and treatment response, yet their look-alike isomers defeat standard mass spectrometry. Tiny samples make the handling worse.

Their method electromigrates a thin film of sample to the air-liquid surface at the tip of a theta-shaped capillary. Extraction and a fast chemical tagging happen right there, separating isomers that would otherwise blur together. The integration of steps, from drop to answer, is the advance, aimed at small-volume samples like a newborn's heel-prick blood.
pmc-10863778:
When brain arteries narrow, doctors need to know how badly blood flow reserve has failed in each brain territory. Martina Sebök and co-authors tested whether an MRI-based measure can stage that failure as well as the standard PET method. Patients with one-sided narrowing had both scans. Experts staged each territory by eye on the PET images. The MRI measure, based on blood oxygen changes with carbon dioxide, was then matched against those stages.

The team derived cutoff values that split territories into failure stages. Training and test splits checked that the cutoffs held up. A working MRI cutoff would spare patients a scarce, costly PET scan. The study moves the MRI method toward routine stroke-risk care.
pmc-10867578:
Haavard Koppang, Søren Wenstøp, and Jaime Pineda ask how charming deceit bends moral judgment, in a 2023 paper. Deception strains stock takes on moral acts, so the authors frame beguiling mechanisms: deceptiveness with a seductive charm that diverts. Such tricks work in the gray zones of moral dilemmas, where the right call is unclear. The effect cuts two ways, which the authors stress.

Morals, in their frame, grow from basic innate leanings that stack into mindsets and then acts, steered by feeling and social reading more than cold reason. Brain wiring for morals mixes levels, shifts with context, and bears marks of early social life. The beguiling case shows the blend at work.
pmc-10871078:
Ana Rumora and co-authors report in 2023 on a hunt for bacteria in soil that can make electric current. The team sampled seven soils in and near Bergen Community College in New Jersey. Such germs matter because they power soil fuel cells, small devices that turn the work of microbes into power.

Five of the seven soils made current in the test cells, with an average output of 155 microwatts. The best cell gave 143 microwatts and held billions of the current-making bacteria after fifteen days. Gene tests on that cell found that half its anode community belonged to one large group of bacteria, with other known groups and many unknown ones making up the rest. The authors note that such devices could one day aid power supply, waste treatment, and sensing.
pmc-10875678:
Le Li and a large team scale up production of a human growth factor used in wound healing research and care, in work published in 2023. The protein, basic fibroblast growth factor, drives many cell processes and is in high demand. The team builds a 500 liter fermentation and purification process in a common bacterial host.

Growth conditions were tuned with a statistical design method and then validated at full scale. A three step column purification yields the mature protein, whose identity was confirmed by several analytic methods. Activity tests in cells and in a diabetic wound model in animals check healing effect. The process aims to supply research and clinical needs at larger volume with consistent quality.
pmc-10883078:
Mehmet Efe Biresselioglu and co-authors surveyed experts in eleven Lighthouse Cities about cutting greenhouse gases, in a study published in 2023. These cities, from Baku to Cape Town, joined a shared project to shift daily habits toward lower emissions. The team asked eighty-nine experts how their cities work on climate at the local level.

Experts named raising awareness and sharing information as a core part of city plans. For habit change, they put saving energy and green travel first. The side-by-side read shows what leading cities lean on and where their powers stop. The authors argue city halls hold real, if bounded, leverage over how residents live.
pmc-10907978:
Yi Jiang and co-authors uncover a self-reinforcing loop that keeps a liver cancer signal switched on. The signal, a transcription factor called STAT3, drives many cancers when stuck active. A fat tag attached by the enzyme DHHC7 holds it on; patient data link high DHHC7 to poor outcomes. In liver cancer cells the loop closes through a low-oxygen factor.

Tagged STAT3 raises that factor, HIF1α, and a kinase steadies it; HIF1α then switches on the gene for DHHC7, making more of the tagging enzyme. Breaking the loop at any point slowed tumor growth in mice. All three players crowd human tumor tissue too. The authors nominate the loop as a drug target worth attacking.
pmc-10909078:
Aoi Kataoka and four co-authors review in 2023 studies that link cancer registries with stored tissue data to study colorectal cancer. Such linkage joins outcomes and lifestyle facts with gene-level material. It can power studies of incidence and prognosis that neither source allows alone.

Searches across two databases to late 2021 gather 2793 papers, of which 81 qualify. Site-specific registries and cohort designs dominate the set. Registries mostly serve to pick patients or cases, while tissue data mostly supply prognosis factors. Consent handling and sample sizes are charted by design. The authors weigh how wider linkage could enrich future work, with care for privacy and data quality.
pmc-10962678:
Halil Koyu, Serdar Demir, and Mehmet Haznedaroglu study microwave extraction of red cabbage. Their study from twenty twenty-three seeks brain active compounds in the plant. Good extraction should cut solvent, time, and energy use.

Red cabbage is a mass grown food plant with health promise. Microwave settings were tuned for two enzyme block targets. Phenol, flavone, and pigment content were measured in extracts. Best settings split by which target was in focus. Microwave extracts beat standard solvent extracts on both counts. A key pigment fraction was isolated for more checks.
pmc-11018978:
Silage, the fermented feed that carries livestock through winter, depends on the microbes that arrive on the plants themselves. Xiaolong Tang and co-authors asked how much the source of those microbes matters. They took the natural microbe communities from alfalfa, from corn, and from the two mixed, and seeded each into alfalfa and corn mixed silage. The alfalfa born community performed best: it kept ammonia and acidity low while building more lactic acid, the preservative that good silage needs.

Silage seeded with the alfalfa community also kept more sugar and protein and less tough fiber than the other batches. Its bacterial community stayed richer and more diverse late into storage. The authors conclude that where the starter microbes come from shapes the whole fermentation, through competition during airless storage. The paper, published in 2023, suggests farmers could improve feed quality by managing the microbes riding on their forage.
pmc-11182278:
Tais Estrela and Linda Dagi review optic nerve damage in children born with fused skull seams in a paper published in 2023. The catalog lists 2024, but the journal record in the text gives 2023. Fused seams can raise pressure inside the skull. That pressure swells and then wastes the optic nerve. Sleep apnea, odd vein growth, and a brain malformation can add to the harm.

The review walks through causes, checks, and care for the nerve damage. Eye doctors also manage crossed eyes, uneven focus, and exposure damage in these children. Their reports help decide when skull surgery must be done or redone. Early spotting of nerve swelling is the main defense against permanent sight loss.
pmc-11225478:
Tumwine wrote an editorial in twenty twenty-three welcoming readers to a December issue of African Health Sciences. He surveys the papers chosen for that issue. The issue appeared while the COP28 climate talks met in the Middle East amid major conflict.

The papers cover infections such as tuberculosis and COVID-19, plus other bacterial, fungal, and viral illness. Others deal with breast cancer, high blood pressure, and diabetes, along with goiter, kidney disease, and trauma. Further sets cover sexual and reproductive health, nutrition, and mental health. Tumwine closes by hoping the goodwill at the climate talks spreads, and he wishes readers a peaceful festive season.
pmc-11273078:
Zeynie Chekol Degu and Flimon Hadaro Hando track in 2024 how women have fared in Ethiopia's top leadership posts since 1991. Fair seats at the decision table matter for good rule, peace, and shared growth, they note. Their study covers the three federal arms: those who make, enforce, and judge the laws.

Records from government offices fed a mixed study, read by content review and plain counts. Seats for women have grown notably in recent years, they report, yet across thirty years women stayed under-represented at the top. Some posts, the prime minister's among them, have never been held by a woman and seem barred in practice. Growth at the edges has not yet cracked the summit.
pmc-11446378:
Ziman Chen and co-authors published a report in 2023 on China's first national student competition for carbon dioxide capture, conversion, and use. The contest, called the Bloomag Cup, was launched by professors at Beijing University of Chemical Technology and held in Beijing in July 2023. Universities will take turns hosting it each year.

Students and researchers from across the country presented ideas for trapping carbon and turning it into useful products. Organizers say the point is to surface breakthroughs early, train new talent, and push the young field forward. The hope is that the yearly contest keeps seeding technology that helps curb climate change while supporting greener growth.
pmc-11532478:
Shuhui Hou, Hui Xu, Shating Lei, and Dong Zhao studied an enzyme that runs high in tissue from women with endometriosis, in a paper from twenty twenty-four. In this condition, tissue like the womb lining grows where it should not, causing pain. The enzyme helps control cell chemistry, and its role in the disease was unclear.

The enzyme was higher in patient tissue and in lab-grown cells from patients. Blocking it slowed cell growth, movement, and spread, and shrank lesions in mice. The hormone estrogen and signals from immune cells both raised the enzyme. Cutting it lowered activity in a growth pathway inside the cells. The authors name this pathway as a possible drug target.
pmc-11533278:
Siyu Miao and co-authors predict nasal tumor regrowth with machine learning in a 2024 study. Sinonasal inverted papilloma is benign yet returns after surgery in a fifth of cases. The team followed two hundred ten operated patients over more than a decade and trained six survival learning models to flag who relapses.

One fifth of patients recurred, at a median of about thirty five months. Abnormal cell change in the tumor was an independent risk factor. An extra survival trees model predicted best, with strong accuracy in training and solid accuracy in testing. Explanation scores spotlighted bone defects, eye socket involvement, smoking, untreated attachment sites, and drinking as the top warning features for follow up planning.
pmc-11536478:
David Dillon and a large team lay out a care bundle to stop rearrest after a heart restarts in a 2024 paper. When a heart restarts outside a hospital, it can stop again before the patient reaches the emergency room. That second stop is a major barrier to survival, and guidance for crews in that window is thin.

The bundle sets clear targets for blood pressure, airway, oxygen, and breathing in the first minutes after restart. It was built from the best available evidence by a California outcomes group. The paper explains the logic and how the bundle was formed. Crews get a shared checklist for a chaotic moment.
pmc-11536678:
Kei Mukawa, Yutaka Iba, and Nobuyoshi Kawaharada report a rare late surgical problem in a 2024 case paper. A fifty-five-year-old man had a heart banding operation as a baby, then corrective surgery as a toddler. Ten years of worsening breathlessness led to checks that found severe narrowing above his pulmonary valve, a late scar of the old band.

A patch alone could not fix the ring-shaped narrowing. The surgeons rebuilt the pulmonary root with a remodeling technique borrowed from aortic repair. The pressure gradient fell from sixty to eleven, and recovery was smooth. Readers get a repair option for this rare adult case.
pmc-11539678:
Rui Li and eleven co-authors published this study in 2024. It compares the milk-producing cells of two sheep breeds at the gene level. East Friesian sheep are champion milkers; Sewa sheep, a hardy breed of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, give far less milk, and the difference's genetic roots are sought here.

The team grew mammary cell lines from both breeds and confirmed their identity with marker stains. Sequencing the cells' active genes found 1,813 differences, over eleven hundred turned up in Sewa cells and the rest turned down. The differing genes clustered in signaling, metabolism, and cell-process categories, with signal transduction the largest single group. Two genes, ATF3 and MPP7, emerged as candidate regulators of lactation. The authors offer the comparison as a starting map for breeding and gene studies aimed at milk yield. They note the work is in cultured cells, so whole-animal confirmation must follow.
pmc-11542478:
Yu-Lin Zhong and five co-authors scan the brains of patients with diabetic eye disease for changes in the white matter, in a 2024 study. Diabetic retinopathy damages the retina, but its fingerprints may reach the brain's wiring too.

Forty-six patients and 43 matched controls underwent functional scans. Several wiring hubs showed stronger activity or connectivity in patients, including bridges between the hemispheres. One visual pathway region showed weaker local coordination. Machine learning separated patients from controls with up to 89 percent accuracy using these measures. Alterations clustered in the corpus callosum and radiating fibers. The authors suggest the eye disease rides with a broader network disturbance, worth tracking alongside vision.
pmc-11549878:
Zehua Yang and co-authors screened lung disease risk models with machine learning in two thousand twenty-four. COPD grows from genes and environment together. Which gene variants best predict it was the question. Patients and healthy controls gave DNA samples. A genotyping platform measured their variant profiles. Several algorithms competed to build the sharpest model.

Regression first thinned the variant list. Shrinkage and forest methods refined it further. Accuracy curves ranked the candidate models. The winning model then flagged candidate risk variants. Such panels could target screening to high-risk smokers. Early detection is COPD care's biggest lever. The pipeline suits other gene-environment diseases too.
pmc-11552578:
Anette Viftrup and co-authors measure the harm patients report when their planned surgery is cancelled in a 2024 study. Cancellations close to the date are common at busy hospitals, but their human cost is rarely quantified. At a Danish university hospital, seven hundred eighty-five patients whose operations were cancelled for hospital reasons were surveyed; over half replied.

Forty-two percent reported physical worsening and forty-eight percent emotional strain. A third could no longer manage daily activities, and over a quarter needed stronger painkillers. Disappointment and loneliness were common, and nine percent feared dying. Women reported emotional strain more than men, and waits over thirty days nearly doubled the risk of physical decline. The authors argue cancellation is a clinical event, not an administrative one.
pmc-11561678:
Kurt and seven co-authors map how symptoms of three mental disorders connect in refugees and asylum seekers in Turkey. Their study is from two thousand twenty-four. Displaced people face high rates of trauma stress, depression, and anxiety. The cultural mix of these groups makes the links between symptoms hard to guess from other populations.

Large online surveys reached seven hundred eighty-five Afghan and seven hundred ninety-eight Syrian participants. Network analysis found the symptoms that hold the whole web together. For Afghan participants, feeling blue, restlessness, and panic spells were most central. For Syrian participants, worry, feeling blue, and tension led instead. The two webs had the same overall strength but differed in shape. Such maps can point care toward the symptoms that unlock others.
pmc-11569378:
Jinxing Wei and four co-authors review how small RNAs steer cell self-eating and drug proof in cancer. Their review appeared in twenty twenty-four. Small RNAs tune gene use post-birth and can switch self-eat paths on or off. Self-eat keeps cells in line but can help tumors live and shrug off chemo.

Some small RNAs act as tumor drivers and some as brakes, by which self-eat path they hit. That split makes the RNA and self-eat pair a rich cure field. The review maps the links by gene and path in each cancer kind. It then weighs cures that tune the pair and calls for deep work on the webs.
pmc-11571878:
Liqin Lu and co-authors present a 2024 journal article building a questionnaire on what university students know, feel, and do about novel psychoactive substances. These lab-made drugs spread fast on campuses, and educators need a sound measuring tool. The team drafted items from the literature and expert advice, then tested the survey on 587 students in Fujian.

Weak items were cut through statistical screens, and factor analysis settled on five subdimensions. The final model fit well, with reliability scores above 0.9 overall. One weakness remained in separating the dimensions cleanly. The authors offer the tool for gauging drug education needs and effects.
pmc-11574078:
So Min Ahn and co-authors compare two devices for measuring eye length in a 2024 study. Eye length guides cataract surgery choices, and two optical methods compete: one built on tomography scans, one on interferometry. Whether they agree in diseased eyes was the question.

Records covered 123 eyes from 73 patients with various retina and choroid diseases. Readings from the two devices correlated strongly, and repeat readings were steady for each. Still, the scan-based device read about a tenth of a millimeter shorter on average, a real if small gap. A membrane on the retina widened the gap further. The authors warn the two methods are not interchangeable when planning surgery.
pmc-11574278:
Ali Mert Sendil and co-authors tested a structured exercise program for preschool children in a 2024 paper. The program trained motor skills such as side stepping, galloping, jumping, and running, in half hour sessions twice a week for eight weeks. It aimed to lift physical fitness, motor competence, and the mental skill of stopping a wrong response. Children in the other group followed the normal kindergarten program.

Forty one children aged five to six took part, split between exercise and control groups. Balance, agility, and jumping tests measured fitness, and a standard battery measured motor skills, including eye and hand coordination. A go and no go task measured stopping control. The exercise group gained more than controls on static balance and on two motor battery parts, with clear group by time effects. The abstract reports those gains in detail for the motor and balance measures.
pmc-11574478:
Yu-Wei Lin and co-authors pool trials to find the best dose of a drug for bipolar depression in a 2024 review. Five trials with over two thousand patients fed a dose response model. Outcomes covered mood, worry, function, dropout, and body chemistry shifts. Six week courses formed the typical test window.

Forty to sixty milligrams daily gave the best balance in the model. Mood gains peaked near fifty milligrams across several scales. Side effects rose with dose, while dropout and mood switch risks stayed flat. Weight crept up at low doses and blood sugar at high ones. A hormone marker rose in both sexes with dose. The authors name the mid range as the reasonable choice.
pmc-11575178:
Lingying Liu and co-authors test stem cell doses for deep burns in pigs in a 2024 study. Deep partial burns harm body and mind and heal slowly. The team used miniature pigs, whose skin suits preclinical trials. Five dose levels of cord stem cells were injected into round burn wounds.

All doses sped healing and cut healing time, with gains rising by dose. Treated wounds grew new surface skin faster and showed less swelling and redness. New tiny blood vessels grew in greater numbers. Collagen layout also improved toward normal skin patterns. The highest dose worked best of all groups. Dose choice will matter if the therapy moves toward clinic use.
pmc-11575778:
Islam and co-authors warn that landfill leachate quietly harms soils in the temperate Himalayas. Landfills are the cheapest, most common waste option in much of the world. In developing nations such as India, poorly managed dumps let hazardous liquid seep into the ground around them.

That liquid, called leachate, is a strong point source of pollution for soil, water, and other media. The study examines how it lowers soil quality near Himalayan dump sites. Mountain soils recover slowly, so damage can last for decades. The authors press for better dump control in fragile highland regions.
pmc-11578878:
Zhisong He and a large team of co-authors present a 2024 paper building a cell atlas of human neural organoids, the lab-grown mini-brains made from stem cells. Labs use dozens of recipes to grow them, but nobody knew how completely the recipes cover the real brain or how faithful each is. The team merged thirty-six single-cell datasets from twenty-six protocols, totaling over 1.7 million cells.

By mapping organoid cells onto developing human brain references, the atlas shows which cell types each protocol produces and how closely they match their natural counterparts. A public interface lets researchers annotate new data against the atlas. The team also used it as a healthy control set to spot what goes wrong in organoid models of brain disease.
pmc-11579678:
Brönneke, Herr, Reif, and Stern wrote a 2023 paper on health technology assessment for digital health tools. Their case is Germany, where a 2019 law created a payment path for prescribable health apps. Doctors can prescribe these apps, and public insurance pays for them.

The authors argue that standard assessment methods fit these apps poorly. Apps change often, and full trial evidence may come after listing. They make the case for a dynamic form of assessment that uses real-world data over time. Such ongoing checks, they say, can improve the quality of apps on the market.
pmc-11584978:
Vicente Esparza-Villalpando and co-authors weighed the safety of oral ketorolac in a 2024 review. Ketorolac is a strong pain drug taken by mouth, and doctors need a clear picture of its harms before choosing it over other options.

The team pooled 50 clinical trials and compared side effects across placebo and rival drugs. A single dose brought more adverse events than placebo, while repeated doses over one to ten days looked safer than active rivals. Doses of 5, 10, or 20 milligrams in multi-day courses did not raise risk in the pooled data. The review gives prescribers a trial-based map of when this painkiller's risks stay modest.
pmc-11585978:
Yongping Cao, Mengyun Zhou, and Tianhong Xu report a 2024 study on whether three joint diseases cause a scaly skin disease. The three diseases attack joints in adults and in children, and the skin disease often shows up near their diagnosis. Shared genes may drive both, which a gene-based method can test without a trial.

The team drew gene data from a large open bank for all four diseases. Single-disease checks found causal links from each of the three joint diseases to the skin disease. Checks for bias and noise backed those finds. A joint check that weighed all three at once kept two as risk factors, while the adult joint disease lost its effect. The work adds to grasp of how the skin disease starts.
pmc-11586978:
Som Singh and colleagues wrote an opinion article in 2024 arguing that medicine's favorite yardstick for patient handouts measures less than its users think. Pamphlets and digital handouts increasingly carry the work of explaining care, and readability formulas grade how hard their text is to comprehend. Study after study finds medical materials missing the recommended sixth to eighth grade reading level, and the field has responded by demanding simpler text.

Reviewing the literature across pediatrics, internal medicine, prevention, and surgery, the authors caution that readability is not health literacy, and neither is the same as a patient actually understanding and acting. A formula counting syllables cannot see layout, prior knowledge, fear, or trust. Their nominated frontier is generative artificial intelligence, which might rewrite and personalize materials on demand, though they note few current tools match that promise, so the innovation gap remains open.
pmc-11587678:
Immune cells can be rebuilt by design to do jobs they never evolved for, and Naoki Hosen, a solo author, introduces a series of reviews on these designer immune cells. The model case is CAR T-cell therapy, where a patient's T cells are fitted with a synthetic receptor that hunts cancer. Versions aimed at blood cancers have shown striking power in the clinic.

Other cell types are joining in, including natural killer cells, macrophages, and cells grown from stem cells, armed with a growing range of synthetic receptors. The reviews he gathers cover stem-cell-grown killer T cells, fresh cancer targets, T-cell wear-out and how to beat it, and gene editing tools. Hosen frames the field as a new kind of medicine built from living cells.
pmc-11588578:
Lucie Riglet and Isabelle Fobis-Loisy give a fast imaging method for plant mating cells in a 2024 protocol paper. A flower's stigma is where pollen first lands and is accepted or refused. Watching that first contact in fine detail used to need slow confocal microscopy and specially bred glowing marker plants. Their method swaps that for a benchtop electron microscope.

Fresh samples go in without fixation or marker lines. Images catch pollen as it drinks water minutes after landing, and later as its tube grows through the stigma. The path of the tube is easy to follow. Work shown uses a small model plant, but the method suits other species and pollen from varied genetic backgrounds. It should speed up studies of plant fertility.
pmc-11588678:
Niels Brevé and co-authors published this habitat study in 2024 on the European sturgeon, a critically endangered fish. Bringing it back to the Rhine needs proof the river still offers spawning and nursery ground. The team reviewed the fish's needs, then modeled depth and flow over more than 350 kilometers of the delta and lower Rhine, in two lands.

Prime spawning ground came to just 0.75 square kilometers, enough for about 2,500 females. That is ample, since at most 750 adults of the fish are thought to live. Most spawning ground sits in Germany's North Rhine-Westphalia, and most nursery ground in the Netherlands. Dams and shipping lanes cut the true supply. The authors say the map can guide where to guard or restore habitat, and the method can travel to other rivers.
pmc-11588778:
Paul Lehrer and co-authors review how stress care affects the body of people under money stress in a 2024 paper. Money trouble is known to raise mental stress, and stress in turn changes body measures tied to disease. The team searched for trials that tested whether talk and stress based care changed those body measures.

Of more than 5,000 papers screened, 16 fit, and 11 had control groups. Taken together, care gave a small to moderate benefit. Gains were largest for heart rate variation and for swelling markers, and smallest for cortisol. All studies were in people with long term poverty, and none tested financial planning as part of care.
pmc-11590278:
Qiaoqiao Zhang and colleagues report a rare success against a brain lymphoma tied to HIV, in this report from twenty twenty-four. The cancer, a diffuse large B-cell lymphoma growing in the brain, is one of the most common tumors in people with AIDS. Its outlook is usually grim. Whether surgery helps was long debated.

Their patient was a man of thirty with AIDS. He arrived with dizziness and headache, after a first hospital read his scans as a different tumor. New scans and tissue tests showed the lymphoma in the left cerebellar hemisphere. Surgeons removed it. He then had two weeks of radiotherapy and seven rounds of a drug mix, DA-EPOCH. His symptoms eased, the cancer vanished on follow-up, and four years on it had not returned. The authors argue that surgery fits lone, reachable tumors, best when paired with radiation and drugs.
pmc-11590478:
Yuki Suzuki and colleagues tested a local antibiotic method in 2024 for infected knee replacements. Infections around artificial knees are among the hardest problems in bone care. The method washes the joint nonstop with strong antibiotic fluid. The team reviewed fourteen patients with such infections. Acute cases got cleaning surgery plus the wash, keeping the implant. Chronic cases got a two-stage implant swap with the wash. Gentamicin flowed into the joint daily for two weeks. Vein antibiotics ran alongside in all cases.

All acute patients kept their implants after one-stage care. Most chronic patients cleared infection with the two-stage plan. Two chronic patients failed the first attempt at keeping implants. A later two-stage redo succeeded for both. No side effects from the local drug were reported. Follow-up ran well over a year on average. The authors judge the wash safe and likely helpful.
pmc-11591478:
Antonio Carlos Mota Porto and co-authors described a gene-edited eucalyptus tree that tolerates glyphosate weed killer in 2024. Eucalyptus is among the most productive trees for large farms in Brazil. Weeds must be controlled, yet the trees are harmed by the main herbicide, so spraying needs care and often wastes chemical.

The team checked body traits and long-term field growth of the edited trees. Seedlings in a greenhouse and young trees in the field were sprayed directly. In all trials, sprayed edited trees grew as well as unsprayed normal trees and kept like body measures. Brazil has approved the trees for farm use, and the authors present them as a step forward for weed control.
pmc-11591578:
Yu and co-authors test whether chatbots can diagnose a mouth disease from photos in this 2024 study. Oral lichen planus is a chronic inflammatory condition that is hard to spot early. Diagnosis usually rests on a clinician's experience and judgment.

The team gathered lesion images from 128 confirmed patients. Three AI platforms judged the images, first cold and then after feature training. Training lifted recognition sharply: one model rose from 59 to 77 percent, another from 68 to 80, and a third from 15 to 50. Cheek lesions were easiest, reaching the mid-90s for two models. Gum lesions stayed hard, near 60 percent at best. The authors see promise with clear site limits.
pmc-11592978:
Murad Alrashdi and co-authors ask whether cleaning out a baby tooth's pulp before capping it changes how long the cap lasts, in a 2024 study. Ready-made zirconia crowns are favored for young children's teeth for looks and grip, but their stiff fit can expose the pulp during shaping. The pulp step, a pulpotomy, is sometimes done first.

Charts covered 81 upper front baby teeth in children aged two to five, checked every six months for two years. Teeth with and without the pulp step fared the same: success rates and survival curves showed no real gap. The authors conclude the pulpotomy step did not move crown success within two years, which may spare some children an extra procedure.
pmc-11593278:
Man Jia and co-authors trace a signal loop that helps kidney cancer grow, centered on a protein called FGF7. Their 2024 study looks at clear cell renal cell carcinoma and the support cells around the tumor. Those support cells, known as cancer-associated fibroblasts, are the main stromal cells in this cancer's surroundings.

The support cells release FGF7, which switches on a growth path inside tumor cells and helps them spread. Tumor cells answer by raising FGF7 output in the support cells even further. Tumors rich in these cells and FGF7 also held more M2 macrophages, a cell type that aids tumors. In mice, removing FGF7 slowed the cancer, marking it as a drug target.
pmc-11593578:
Xiulin Nong and six co-authors measured how crowding during transport stresses young yellowfin seabream, in this 2024 study. Fish fry are shipped live in bags, and cramming in too many saves money but fouls the water and can kill the cargo. The right density is a balance every hatchery must strike.

The team simulated a twelve-hour journey at six densities, small fry in the hundreds per pouch and larger fry in the low hundreds. Afterward they counted survivors and read two health dials. One dial was the activity of antioxidant enzymes in liver and gut, the body's defense against chemical stress. The other was the switching of two genes tied to stress and cell death. Density and recovery time both shaped the readings. The results give fish farmers a firmer basis for choosing packing densities that keep fry alive and vigorous on arrival.
pmc-11595178:
Gabriela Fonseca-Camarillo and colleagues measure guidance proteins in inflamed bowel tissue. Their study from twenty twenty-four covers semaphorins and their plexin receptors. These proteins steer cells and regulate immune activity. Their pattern in inflammatory bowel disease was unknown before.

Fifty-four patients and twenty controls supplied intestinal tissue. Gene and protein levels were measured for the family. One guidance gene fell in ulcerative colitis tissue. Its receptor fell too, while another receptor rose. Stains located the proteins near immune cell types. Expression levels tracked clinical disease features in patients. Immune steering molecules may shape bowel inflammation course.
pmc-11595578:
Scherer and five co-authors mine a German trauma registry for how often badly injured patients lose a limb. Their data covered 32,572 severely injured patients with limb fractures treated between 2009 and 2019. Car crashes caused most injuries, and over half the patients also had severe chest trauma.

Amputation stayed rare: 242 upper-limb and 422 lower-limb cases. The share rose steeply when overall injury severity passed the highest band. Patients with severe chest injuries were amputated more often in both limb groups. The authors offer the numbers as a planning base for trauma centers. They note the salvage-versus-amputation call still hinges on the limb's state and the patient's stability.
pmc-11597078:
Four researchers review dual targeting cancer drugs built on a short protein tag in a 2024 paper. The tag, known by its three letter code RGD, homes to integrins, grip proteins that help tumors grow, spread, and sprout blood vessels. Drugs built on the tag can scan or treat tumors.

Past agents hit limits: target levels vary, and the body clears the drugs too fast. The review covers fresh designs that aim at two targets at once to sharpen the hit. New agents pair the tag with a second homing part or a stronger payload. The authors argue the dual route can lift both diagnosis and therapy.
pmc-11597378:
Yushuo Wu and co-authors test a fungicide, thifluzamide, against a rot that attacks stored Huangguan pears. The fungus Rhizoctonia solani breaks into fruit by releasing enzymes that chew through cell walls. The team measured how the treatment changed those enzymes in lab culture, and how it changed the pear's own defense chemistry.

After three days, the treatment clearly slowed all six wall-breaking enzymes the fungus makes. In the fruit, it raised the work of three defense-linked enzymes and lifted levels of flavonoids and total phenols, compounds that help plants resist attack. Gene activity in the same defense pathway rose as well. The authors conclude the fungicide fights the rot two ways at once: it weakens the fungus's tools and primes the fruit to defend itself.
pmc-11598678:
Zhikang Yang and eight co-authors built a near-infrared vein imaging system for robot blood draws in a 2024 paper. A robot's success starts with seeing the vein clearly. The team tuned imaging settings by simulation, then trained a segmentation network that grafts residual blocks into a U-shaped design.

Self-taught pretraining let the network learn from few labeled images. Against the plain U-shaped net, the hybrid cut loss and boundary error while raising overlap scores by wide margins. A smarter stereo matching method, with weights that vary by region, cut its average error by about a quarter. The authors plan to wire the system into a full robotic blood collection rig for live puncture guidance.
pmc-11599278:
Yan-li Zhang, Chao Ran, and Wei Li present a 2024 study of scan traits in lung infection by a fungus called cryptococcus. Patients answer care at unlike speeds, and scans may show who will lag. The team compared records and images from 70 patients: 37 full responders and 33 partial ones. They hunted scan and clinical traits that split the groups and weighed each trait's call power.

Partial responders more often had weak immunity, mid-course spread, and disease on both sides. Fluid near the lung and swollen chest nodes also clustered in that group. Three traits stood as lone risk marks: weak immunity, mid progress, and two-sided spread. Joined, the three called the outcome well. Scan reads could warn teams early about slow cases.
pmc-11599578:
Cecilia Liberati and co-authors report a two step program to tame antibiotic use in a children's blood and cancer unit in Padua, in a 2024 paper. The patients are fragile, and excess antibiotics breed resistant germs. The study ran from 2019 to 2022 as a before and after check.

Step one spread clear pathways for fever care in children with low white cell counts, and use shifted between drug classes at once. Step two put the pathways in an app and added twice weekly audits with feedback. Total use fell again, with clear drops in three heavy drug classes. The authors credit teamwork and trust, not rules alone.
pmc-11600878:
Collin Sakal, Wenxing Zhao, Wenxin Xu, and Xinyue Li present a 2024 study of caffeine, sleep, and activity in older adults living their normal lives. Good sleep and daily movement both support a long life after sixty-five. Caffeine might lift activity, but it could also cost sleep, and that trade off was untested in daily life.

The team used data from a national health survey of adults aged sixty-five and older, from 2011 to 2014. Wrist sensors gave sleep and activity measures, worked out with a learning method. Caffeine intake was sorted by dose, both by body weight and by total amount. The study then looked for links across the dose groups.
pmc-11600978:
Duan and co-authors test if depression raises the risk of acid reflux disease, using genetics as a tool. Reports link depression with gastroesophageal reflux, but cause and effect were unclear. Mendelian randomization uses gene variants tied to depression to probe that direction of influence.

The method is less prone to the lifestyle mix-ups that cloud watch-based studies. The team also asked which risk factors carry part of any effect, acting as middle steps. Traits like body weight or smoking may sit on the path. Results help explain how mood and reflux connect and where prevention may work.
pmc-11601978:
Fayez Alrohaimi and co-authors cut a spare cheek-gland growth out through the mouth, sans a face cut. Such growths are rare and hard: face cuts risk scars and the face nerve. Their 2024 case is a man in his late thirties with the mild kind of gland growth in the spare gland. The mouth path takes the whole growth out clean.

No scar and no nerve harm ride the heal. Full pre-cut checks are stressed as the base of the win. Mouth paths can serve more spare-gland cases, the team holds, with more reads owed. Looks and use both gain when the cut hides.
pmc-11602778:
Sana Barakat, Mohamed Abdel-Fadeel, Ola Sharaki, Mohamed El Shafei, Basant Elbanna, and Aml Mahfouz wrote a 2024 paper on a stomach bacterium and fatty liver in children. The bacterium, Helicobacter pylori, lives in many stomachs and can cause ulcers. Fatty liver not caused by alcohol is also rising in children. The team asked whether the infection raises the odds of the liver disease.

They compared one hundred children with fatty liver, found by ultrasound, with one hundred without it. Stool tests found the bacterium in sixty-four percent of the liver group and twenty-five percent of the others. Blood tests then checked which strains the infected children carried. A link this strong in children argues for more study of whether treating the infection helps the liver.
pmc-11602878:
Fatemeh Estaji and co-authors present a 2024 review of Epstein-Barr virus in stomach cancer. Stomach cancer stays a top cause of cancer death worldwide. Its causes join lifestyle, family history, gene faults, and infections. Epstein-Barr virus infects over ninety-five percent of people, usually silently for life. It was the first virus found in a human tumor. Its role in stomach cancer is now a settled research topic, though key mechanisms stay disputed.

The review centers on epigenetic mechanisms: chemical marks that switch genes without changing DNA. Immune shifts and gene mutations get coverage as well. Contradictions on whether the virus worsens outlook are weighed openly. Oncologists get a map of how a near-universal virus can drive one cancer in a small minority. That minority question is the puzzle: the marks the virus leaves may explain why only some carriers develop tumors.
pmc-11603178:
Li and seven colleagues publish the full gene map of the Suminoe oyster from south China in twenty twenty-four. The oyster is a key species for both sea ecology and fishery trade around the world. Their map spans the full set of ten chromosomes, built from three kinds of gene reading tools. It is sharper and more complete than past maps of the species.

The map holds close to thirty thousand protein coding genes, most with known roles. More than half of the genome is made of repeated stretches. The team also logged over a thousand non coding RNA genes. The map can guide breeding, stock care, and study of oyster diversity and evolution.
pmc-11604678:
Yuki Hamano and co-authors map brain hubs for two-hand sequence learning in a 2024 study. Thirty-five healthy right-handed volunteers practice a cued two-hand reaction task in a scanner. The task splits hand chord forming from sequence learning, with mirror and harder parallel modes. Reaction times fall in both random and fixed sequence runs, showing learning.

Harder random practice cuts task activity most in the left primary motor cortex and the cerebellar vermis, they find. Those spots also link more strongly with other areas during learning and show sequence specific gains. The authors call the left motor cortex and vermis critical hubs for this skill.
pmc-11604778:
Vaibhav Verma and Geeti Sharma review a fast growing cancer drug class in a 2024 paper. The drugs, called bispecific antibodies, grab two targets at once and can pull immune T cells onto cancer cells. They have shown gains in blood cancers that came back after care.

The review walks through each approved use, how well the drugs work, and their side effects. Early signs suggest they match a rival cell therapy in effect while being gentler to take. They can also be given off the shelf to any patient, unlike cell therapy made per person. No head to head trial has yet set the best order of the two.
pmc-11604978:
Llaó-Cid, Peguera, and co-authors wrote a 2024 study identifying a vein protein that guides blood vessel growth and barrier formation in the brain. Veins turn out to seed all other vessel cell types during new growth. The protein FLRT2, found on vessel walls, had no known role in that process.

Deleting FLRT2 in young mice damaged retinal veins specifically. Endothelial cells multiplied and sprouted less, and fewer tip cells led the growing front. The protein partners with VE-cadherin, the glue of vessel junctions, and with an endocytic adaptor to shape those junctions. Expansion microscopy showed the glue's distribution shift in mutant tissue. In cortical vessels, FLRT2 also coordinated tight junctions, which build the blood-brain barrier. The work names FLRT2 a vein-specific regulator of brain vasculature.
pmc-11605578:
Yuki Koyahara and ten co-authors report two cases in this 2024 conference paper on hunting for the source of cancer that has spread to the brain. When a brain tumor turns out to be spread from elsewhere, doctors must find the first tumor to plan care. The team used a whole-body MRI method called DWIBS, which builds one wide image from many body slices.

In the first case, scans and surgery pointed to spread from cancer of the food pipe. In the second, early searches found no source, but the whole-body MRI lit up at the spot where lung cancer later appeared. The authors note the method runs on standard MRI machines, which are common in Japan. They suggest it as an option where PET scans are hard to get, while calling for more cases to be gathered.
pmc-11606078:
Junping Li and co-authors present a software toolkit for reading complex genome rearrangements from contact maps, in a 2024 paper. Such rearrangements reshape how DNA folds, and they show up as odd blocks in maps made by a capture method that logs which DNA parts touch. Those blocks reveal where fragments sit and which way they face. No hands-on graphics tool existed for turning blocks into full rearrangement calls.

Their Python toolkit runs in four parts. One filters out simple rearrangements and logs break points. A second assembles the complex ones and draws the process as it goes. A third checks each call by faking a map from it and comparing that map with the real one. A fourth rebuilds the map so users can see the fold change directly. The authors aim the tool at biologists who work from contact maps daily.
pmc-11606178:
Caitlin Caspi and eight co-authors ask how low-wage parents fared with COVID-19 relief aid. Aid ranged from cash payments and food support to a larger child tax credit and a pause on evictions. The team held long interviews in 2022 with forty parents in two United States cities. Parents named red tape, office errors, and poor information as blocks, even when they clearly qualified.

Aid that arrived on its own, with no forms to file, reached families best. Most parents spoke well of the help once it came. The paper draws lessons for how relief can reach working families with less strain.
pmc-11606978:
Layered oxides called Ruddlesden-Popper phases can be tuned for fuel cells and catalysts by swapping their metals, but the recipe interacts with how the metal atoms arrange themselves. Dina Fazlizhanova and Sergey Levchenko compute the behavior of one such family in 2024, built from lanthanum, strontium, cobalt, and iron. Their quantum calculations cover three blends, from no strontium to full replacement. They also average over many atomic arrangements, since real crystals mix them.

Handy shortcut numbers for rating these oxides, covering defect formation and oxygen movement, swing widely with the arrangement. Yet their averages still march in a clean line as strontium rises. One further wrinkle: the correction term for electron behavior differs between sites in the same crystal.
pmc-11607278:
Fei Teng and co-authors published this study in 2024. It hunts for shared roots between preeclampsia, a dangerous pregnancy condition, and endometrial cancer of the womb lining. Both involve immune imbalance, vessel trouble, and new blood vessel growth. The team mined gene and immune data for overlaps. From that search they built a five-gene risk model for the cancer.

The model split patients into high- and low-risk groups with clearly different survival. Low-risk patients lived longer and showed richer immune activity in their tumors. The five genes also play roles in preeclampsia, backing the shared-roots idea. The authors suggest the genes could serve as outlook markers for the cancer. They also see a path toward treatment plans tuned to each patient's risk profile.
pmc-11607378:
Niizato, Sakamoto, Mototake, Murakami, and Tomaru apply a theory of integrated information to a school of ayu fish. The theory was built to gauge consciousness, but it can also describe other systems poised at a critical state. Their 2024 study watches how group unity rises and falls as the school moves.

Group unity peaked when the school sat at its critical state, a balance point between order and disorder. Several levels of criticality appeared at once, in subgroups inside the whole school. High criticality subgroups were scattered unevenly in time and space. Core fish in those subgroups were less swayed by inside and outside cues. The authors say the pattern fits older views of critical systems.
pmc-11607878:
Kiyoshi Shikino and co-authors tested, in a 2024 study, a video-based exam that probes whether young Japanese doctors can diagnose, not just recall. Written in-training tests measure knowledge well but say little about bedside reasoning. Their add-on shows a simulated emergency room case and asks for the diagnosis.

A total of 4,677 residents took both the standard test and the video exam in early 2023. Only one in ten landed the video case's diagnosis. Yet the video scores separated strong from weak performers sharply across every domain, from basic knowledge to physical exam skill. Hospital and doctor traits tied to success were also mapped. The authors argue a short simulation video adds a competence signal that paper tests miss, cheaply and at national scale.
pmc-11607978:
Ching-Hua Yeh and co-authors study a gene that is switched off in liver cancer and helps tumors spread, in this 2024 paper. The gene, PAX6, guides early body development and is often silenced by chemical tags in cancer. Its role in liver cancer was unclear.

The team confirmed that heavy tagging silences the gene in tumor cells. Restoring it slowed cell growth and invasion in dishes and shrank tumors in mice. Blocking it had the opposite effect, speeding growth. Gene-reading work then traced which target genes carry out its protective effect. The findings name a possible new lever against liver cancer spread.
pmc-11608478:
Haoru Li and co-authors track tiny blood vessel loss in severely nearsighted eyes in a 2024 study. Some such eyes grow a bulge at the back, posterior staphyloma, which can worsen over time. The team used a vessel imaging scan to compare flow loss rates in eyes with and without the bulge, following over one hundred patients for at least a year.

Bulge eyes showed faster growth in prescription, eye length, and back wall height, plus faster loss of small vessel coverage in two choroid measures. Starting prescription, wall thickness, bulge height, and yearly change in one vessel index predicted which eyes progressed. The results support vessel checks as an early warning tool.
pmc-11608878:
Luana Maroja and co-authors re-examined a famous hybrid zone where two field cricket species meet and interbreed. Earlier genome scans found patches of strong difference between Gryllus firmus and Gryllus pennsylvanicus, mostly on the X chromosome. Those patches were read as islands where genes cannot cross between species, set in a sea of free exchange. The team sequenced a reference genome and sampled eight populations far from the hybrid zone to test that reading.

Away from the zone, the high-difference patches did not show the high absolute divergence the islands model predicts. Nuclear DNA also put the species split near eight hundred thousand years ago, four times older than mitochondrial estimates. The authors argue the island story needs rethinking, and that some patches may reflect other forces.
pmc-11609178:
Mario Cioce and co-authors review how cancer cells rewire their use of fats to survive treatment, in this 2024 paper. Drug resistance is the main reason cancer therapy fails. Fat handling turns out to be one of the tools tumors use to push through hard times and keep growing.

The changes range from altered fat pathways inside tumor cells to exchanges with nearby tissue in the tumor's setting. Some cell groups lead this rewiring and drag the whole tumor along. The review maps these routes and argues that blocking them could make standard drugs work again for patients whose cancers no longer respond.
pmc-11609278:
K Deepthi, Aditya Shastry, and E Naresh present a deep learning method to sharpen satellite images in 2024. The images record many bands of light but are often low in detail. That limits their use for analysis. Their method works without labeled training pairs. It cleans the image in stages before the main model runs.

Steps remove noise, fix tone, and boost edges. Patches of the image are then grouped and fed to a network that builds a sharper image. A special tuning method guides the training. Tests gave high scores for accuracy and image quality. Times for grouping and training were lower than in rival methods. The team reports the method beat known state of the art tools.
pmc-11609778:
Mark Forsberg and Marina Konopleva review therapy for acute myeloid leukemia in older and unfit adults in a 2024 paper. Strong classic chemo can cure some patients, but a month in hospital and real death risk rule it out for many older adults.

The past few years brought nine new targeted drugs and many new regimens for this blood cancer. Most early gains sat in relapse care or strong regimens for fit patients. A landmark trial then paired venetoclax with azacitidine for new patients who could not take strong chemo. That pair raised response and survival over the older standard. The review maps choices for a group once left with few options.
pmc-11609878:
Stine Gerhardt and co-authors use Danish national registers in 2024 to study aggressive care at the end of life for people with gastrointestinal cancers. Knowing what drives such care helps plan better palliative support. Their group covers everyone in Denmark who died from these cancers over a decade long span covered by the registers.

Many patients were in hospital in their last month, and a large share died in hospital, while smaller shares had surgery, scans, or anti cancer treatment near the end. Pancreatic cancer was linked to most forms of aggressive care. People in specialized palliative care had lower odds of aggressive care and of dying in hospital. Other illness burden and being divorced also raised the odds of hospital care at the end of life.
pmc-11610178:
Julia Chan and three co-authors compare how cancer survivors with poor sleep experience it at different distress levels, in a qualitative study from 2024. Distress and broken sleep often travel together after cancer, but the links between them are murky. Lived experience can reveal what numbers miss.

Thirty-three Cantonese-speaking survivors in a community program, all poor sleepers, were interviewed and split by distress score. Shared triggers included lingering treatment effects, intrusive cancer thoughts, and poor sleep routines. Highly distressed survivors added thought suppression, worry about worrying, and thin social support. Low-distress survivors coped better through reprioritizing health and positive reappraisal.
pmc-11611378:
Christine Li, Michael Guo, Ahmer Karimuddin and many co-authors present abstracts from the 2024 Canadian Surgery Forum, a conference collection published in 2024. The collection gathers short reports across surgical practice in Canada. One featured study weighs the cost of sterile water used in endoscopy. Its authors note that tap water use in scope work is supported by evidence.

In that study, one unit switched most procedures to tap water for a month. Sterile water use fell sharply, and cost per procedure dropped by over half. Waste fell by a meaningful amount each month, and the carbon cost of bottle production was counted too. Advanced procedures kept sterile water in both periods. The authors call tap water protocols a simple step toward greener endoscopy. The wider collection continues with further surgical studies.
pmc-11612178:
Giulio Rosati and co-authors print microneedles entirely with an inkjet printer for living-tissue sensing, in a 2024 paper.
