Microneedles serve pain-free drug delivery and wearable sensing, and farmers could use them to probe plants. Making them usually takes costly tools and cleanroom steps, which blocks mass production.

The team's method prints conductive microneedles from silver nanoparticle ink, and the recipe extends to other metal inks. No cleanroom is required, so the needles can be made cheaply and at scale. As a first demonstration, the printed needles monitored the electrochemical state of plants from inside the tissue. The authors present the approach as a route to disposable sensors for medicine and precision farming alike.
pmc-11612278:
Badhon Khan and seven co-authors hunt drug-proof germs in hospital air in Dhaka in a 2024 study. Germs that shrug off drugs are a world health threat, and wards are hot spots where they breed and spread. Air dust in wards can carry live germs, yet that route had been little probed in Bangladesh.

The team took air and dust samples in four hospitals and two outdoor spots in greater Dhaka. Fine dust levels were logged in real time while filters caught the germ load. Caught germs were grown and faced with drug disks. The study maps a hidden spread path in wards.
pmc-11612378:
Bive Bive Zono and a team including Marie-Pierre Hayette screen people with advanced HIV in Kinshasa for a hidden fungal infection. Their study was published in twenty twenty-four. The fungus, Cryptococcus neoformans, can invade the brain and kill, yet it can sit silent in the blood first.

The team tested two hundred and sixty-two outpatients whose immune counts were very low. Forty-seven, about eighteen in each hundred, tested positive for the fungal marker in blood. Half of those who agreed to a spinal tap turned out to have the fungus in their spinal fluid, though they had no symptoms. The team typed the fungi and compared them with strains from sick patients in the same clinics. The results back routine screening so treatment can start before the brain is hit.
pmc-11612478:
Yanxia Zhu and five co-authors published in 2024 the full genome of a Chinese medicinal herb whose dried roots are used as a drug. The plant has a large genome, so the team joined two modern methods: long, exact DNA reads and a mapping step that shows how pieces sit on each chromosome. The result covers nearly the whole genome across thirty-five chromosomes.

Most chromosomes were built end to end, and the team found over thirty-two thousand protein-coding genes, nearly all with a known role. Repeat DNA makes up most of the genome, a fact the build now makes plain. Breeders can use the map to raise plants with more of the active compounds that give the roots their value.
pmc-11612578:
Huitong Ding, Katherine Gifford, Ludy Shih, and a large team ask older adults what they think of brain health technology in this two thousand twenty-four cohort study. Digital platforms promise earlier Alzheimer's risk prediction and monitoring, but older users' perspectives had not been studied. Twenty-eight participants from a Boston University Alzheimer's research center used a digital brain health platform. The initial assessment period lasted fourteen days. Semistructured interviews about their experiences were transcribed and analyzed with natural language processing.

Word counts leaned positive: like, well, and good were the most frequent positive terms. Words like problem and hard flagged real friction points in using the platform. Sentiment analysis showed a slightly positive overall emotional tone toward the tool. The authors present the study as early evidence on acceptability. A monitoring platform only works if intended users actually engage with it; this study probes that human side.
pmc-11613378:
Xiao Zheng and Jinjuan Xu test a liver-protecting drug during tuberculosis treatment in a study from two thousand twenty-four. TB drugs strain the liver, and a licorice-derived compound may shield it. Records of one hundred thirteen patients at one hospital were reviewed.

Fifty-eight patients got the compound alongside standard TB therapy; fifty-five got therapy alone. The protected group fared better overall and suffered less liver injury. Liver blood markers rose in both groups during treatment, but stayed lower with the compound. Side effect rates did not differ between groups. The authors conclude the add-on improves the treatment's overall effect while easing liver harm. They frame it as a practical companion to standard regimens.
pmc-11614578:
Eight authors, led by Hongli Liu, survey in 2024 the health related life quality of family caregivers of people with dementia in southwest China. Caring for a parent or spouse with dementia wears down body and mind, yet hard local data were scarce. The team compared three groups: dementia carers, other carers, and people with no care load.

Over six hundred valid surveys came back from three provinces. Dementia carers scored lowest on both body and mind health scales. Other carers sat in the middle, and the care free group scored highest. A joint model hunted for traits that drag scores down. The results feed plans to support carers.
pmc-11614878:
Finding the slip face a slope will fail on is a search with many false floors. Wei Qin and Jiancheng Zhao breed computer guesses at the face in 2024 with a tuned gene-style search. Their cross-breeding step mixes two codings at once, a tweak they first set right on six toy puzzles with known bests. The slope's safety score comes from a classic slice method.

On five slopes from past studies, the search found the true worst face and its score, matching the known answers. Knob tests showed the count of face-shaping points is the make-or-break set. Head to head, the search beat two rival hunters on the same slopes. The team pitch it for dam and road cuts where a missed face costs lives.
pmc-11615078:
Yaqi Guo and co-authors read the gut microbes of arthritis patients for two overlooked kinds of genes: those that resist antibiotics and those that help germs cause harm. Earlier work mapped which microbes live in the guts of people with osteoarthritis or rheumatoid arthritis, but not what those genes do. Drawing on gene catalogs from stool samples, the team compared patients with healthy controls.

Both patient groups carried a richer variety of resistance genes than controls, while virulence genes were clearly richer only in the rheumatoid group. The overall gene profiles separated the three groups cleanly, and a few genes stood out as enriched in one disease or the other. A random forest model using these gene patterns told patients from controls with accuracy between about 75 and 84 percent. The authors propose resistance and virulence genes as candidate markers that could one day support diagnosis of both arthritis types.
pmc-11615178:
Haiqian Zhu and co-authors mapped, in a 2024 study, how genes tied to a new cell death mode shape head and neck cancer. The death mode, disulfidptosis, strikes cells under disulfide stress. Almost nothing was known about its genes in this cancer.

Sorting atlas tumors by those genes split patients into two clusters. One cluster fared worse, with more stromal cells and fewer killer T cells nearby. A fresh risk model built from the genes predicted outcomes and held up in the team's own patient group. Single-cell and spatial data then traced where the genes act, spotlighting fibroblasts that support the tumor. The work ties a fresh death pathway to prognosis and to the tumor's neighborhood, suggesting new angles for therapy.
pmc-11615278:
Eric Cortada and co-authors compare how hearts in fish and mice react to injury, cell by cell. Their twenty twenty-four paper uses single-cell RNA reads after heart damage. Adult zebrafish regrow heart tissue, while adult mice and humans mostly scar.

Fish hearts were frozen to injure them, and mouse hearts were tied off at an artery. The team also tracked reactions in tissues far from the heart. Heart macrophages stood out as key players in the heal-or-scar choice. Some cell groups and gene programs matched across species, while others split apart. The map may show what to copy from fish for human repair.
pmc-11615378:
Yang Chen and co-authors reviewed chromatin accessibility in a 2024 paper. A cell's DNA is packed into chromatin, and only the open stretches can be read, copied, or repaired. Closed zones sit in dense heterochromatin, while open ones hold fewer packing spools and far more control switches.

The review maps what open chromatin does, how the cell tunes it, and how genes, marks, and surroundings all play in. It then turns to therapy: drugs that pry chromatin open or seal it shut. Reading the open map has become a standard lens on disease, from cancer to rare syndromes.
pmc-11616378:
Bo Xiong, Yuxiao Chen, and Ning Chen ask, in twenty twenty-four, whether living longer means living healthier, across two hundred four countries from nineteen ninety to twenty nineteen. Life expectancy and healthy life expectancy both rose globally, but at different rates. The gap between them is years lived in poor health. Using Global Burden of Disease data, the team tracked both measures at birth and at age sixty-five. Countries were sorted into three types: optimization, low deterioration, and high deterioration, by how the gap moved.

Statistical models then weighed which risks drive each type: environmental, behavioral, and metabolic. For men at birth, drug use mattered most in optimization countries. Low physical activity led in low deterioration ones. Childhood abuse and bullying led in high deterioration ones.
pmc-11618378:
Stephanie Vermeulen and co-authors evaluate, in a 2024 study, a new drug candidate that steadies the cell's internal scaffolding to fight cancer. Drugs of the taxane family do the same job and are front line treatments for many cancers. Their grip on the scaffold disrupts cell division, and the cell dies. But taxanes bring heavy side effects, and cancers often learn to resist them.

The candidate, Pelophen B, is a synthetic cousin of a natural marine product. It steadies the same scaffolding, but grips it at a different site from the taxanes. That different grip may dodge some resistance routes. The team tested its anticancer effect across many tumor types. They used established cell lines, fresh early cultures, and tumor derived cultures that keep the tumor's three dimensional structure. The authors present the results as promising preclinical grounds for further work.
pmc-11618478:
Cai Chen and co-authors map street greenery with explainable machine learning in a 2024 study. The green view index scores how much plant life fills a pedestrian's view. Older methods struggle with the bent, uneven links between surroundings and that score. The team joined street view photos, satellite images, and other data in one frame that also respects place to place variation.

A geographically weighted forest model learns each area's own pattern. A second tool then explains which factors drive the score in each place, and how their push bends at high or low values. City planners gain more than a map: they learn where a new row of trees would move the needle most.
pmc-11618578:
Milan Rusko and co-authors describe a new Slovak speech database built to help detect brain diseases early from the voice, in a 2024 paper. The database holds recordings from 1,649 speakers doing tasks such as holding a vowel, rapid syllable repeats, naming, and describing a picture. Speakers include people with Alzheimer's disease, mild cognitive impairment, and Parkinson's disease, plus healthy controls.

The paper walks through how the database was built: choosing tasks, recruiting patients and controls, and running the recording sessions. It details the file structure and formats so other teams can use the data. The authors expect the collection to support systems that predict these diagnoses from speech and language features, a promising route to cheap early screening.
pmc-11618678:
Tatsuki Kimura and co-authors tell of a stroke that returned within a week because a clot hid the true culprit. A forty-seven-year-old woman arrived with speech loss and right-side weakness that had already eased. Scans first blamed a narrowed neck artery with a web-like shelf, a carotid web, partly masked by thrombus sitting on it. She was treated for a transient attack from artery-to-artery embolism.

Six days later the same symptoms struck, now with a blocked brain artery and a fresh infarct. Removing the clot by catheter revealed the web's shelf clearly for the first time. A stent followed, and she left hospital with only mild tingling in her right fingers. The authors warn that thrombus can camouflage a web on first imaging.
pmc-11619178:
Andrea Mudd and co-authors present a 2024 analysis of how health research uses a complex systems lens. The lens treats health inequality as the product of many linked parts, with feedback loops and delays. It has grown popular in studies of income gaps in health and behavior, but its use may lag behind its fame.

Building on a prior scoping review, the authors graded studies with a traffic-light tool. They checked how fully eight key ideas, such as feedback loops, were applied and reported. Studies that used more of the ideas also reported the direction of links more often. The deepest level of the paradigm was rarely reached. The authors call for reporting guidelines so future work states its methods plainly.
pmc-11619778:
Sebastian Steiner and co-authors explored superacid chemistry in two thousand twenty-four. Superacids can force a proton onto reluctant molecules. Oxalyl chloride had never been protonated before this work. The team reacted it in two superacid mixtures. One form gained a single proton on oxygen. That salt was isolated as the first of its kind.

A doubly protonated form survived only in solution. Related reactions yielded salts of a small carbon cation. Crystals grew from a fluorinated solvent at low temperature. Spectra and X-ray structures confirmed the products. Colorless salts were handled under strict cold conditions. The work extends the map of stable exotic cations. It also shows superacids can tame acyl chlorides.
pmc-11620478:
Xie and a large team of co-authors test whether farm pesticide use shows up in the dust of farmers' homes. Earlier work found higher pesticide levels in such homes, but rarely compared the dust against careful records of how much pesticide each person actually used.

The team measured thirty-two pesticides in 295 dust samples from 213 participants and matched them with records of recent and lifetime use. More days of use meant higher dust levels for chemicals such as malathion, metolachlor, and atrazine. Home and garden use also raised some levels. The results confirm that farm work follows people indoors, which matters for protecting children and other household members.
pmc-11620678:
Xinmei Li and co-authors compare two ways to track where a drug spreads in the body, in a study from 2024. The drug is mefuparib, a cancer drug, tagged so its spread can be measured. The team worked with two common types of lab rat and asked if the method or the rat type changed the results.

One method takes images of thin slices of the whole body, and the other burns tissue samples and counts the tag. Both methods found the drug in the same set of tissues, and most results matched well. Blood and brain results were alike in both rat types. Liver and kidney levels, though, were much higher in one rat type. The work helps labs choose methods and animals for such tests.
pmc-11620878:
Jerry Nboyine and co-authors field-test a pest-proof cowpea in a 2024 study from West Africa. The cowpea weevil can wipe out a whole stored harvest within six months. A modified cowpea line, event CSI-32, makes a bean protein in its seeds that stalls weevil growth, and regulators needed proof it farms like the original.

Trials in Ghana and Nigeria during 2023 set the new line against its parent and three released varieties. Growth, pest damage, and yield in the field came out much the same as the parent line. Harvested grain then faced lab-reared weevils in storage jars. Egg laying, adult emergence, and grain damage were logged, with development timing and a susceptibility index computed per line. The storage arm tests whether the built-in shield holds after harvest.
pmc-11620978:
Mariachiara Ippolito and co-authors reported a rare case in 2024 of fat from a broken bone reaching a young man's brain. The man, aged 26, came to hospital after a motorcycle crash with a car, with fractures of the shin and thigh bones and a dislocated shoulder.

After surgery to fix the bones, he had a seizure, fell into a coma, and his breathing failed. Scans ruled out bleeding and stroke, then showed the pattern of fat embolism in the brain. A heart test suggested a small hole between the heart's upper chambers, a likely route for the fat. Early diagnosis guided care, including an early airway procedure. He survived and regained many abilities in rehab.
pmc-11622478:
Jinghui Chi, Shuping Li, and eight co-authors studied loneliness in people with schizophrenia in China, in work from twenty twenty-four. Loneliness is the felt sense of being cut off; social isolation is the plain fact of few ties. Both run high in this group. The team asked if the two differ by sex, and how each ties to symptoms and thinking skills.

They assessed three hundred twenty-three long-term patients, more women than men. Set scales scored mood symptoms, brain skills, loneliness, and isolation side by side. The team then weighed the pull of each factor, alone and paired, for men and women apart. The aim is care that fits the distinct needs each sex shows.
pmc-11622678:
Jerome Tan and co-authors used a magnetic scan trick in 2024 to judge the quality of lab-grown spinal cord starter cells. Such cells, made from reprogrammed body cells, could one day replace tissue lost to cord injury. Batches vary, though, and standard checks are slow, costly, and destroy the sample.

Their method reads how fast a magnetic signal fades, which tracks iron inside the cells. Starter cells and their parent cells gave clearly different readings. The scan could count leftover parent cells in a batch and even forecast, from day one readings, how well cells would mature weeks later. Poor batches stood out early. The authors offer the scan as a fast, gentle quality gate for cell factories.
pmc-11623478:
Jinhuan Tang and co-authors present a study from two thousand twenty-four on rivalry between car makers under a green policy. China's dual credit policy pushes makers of new energy vehicles and gasoline vehicles to balance output and emissions. The authors model the two sides as a long-term game played with production delays.

Using complex system theory, they track stable zones, sudden splits in behavior, and chaos in the joint decisions. Fast adjustment by either side can tip the system into disorder. In stable zones, gasoline makers' emission changes did not move output for either side. Delayed production choices, they find, can help steady the market.
pmc-11623978:
Six clinicians report a rare immune side effect of a cancer drug in a case report from 2024. The drug, durvalumab, boosts the immune system against tumors but can turn it against healthy tissue. A seventy-two-year-old man treated for lung cancer developed muscle weakness and skin hardening. He was admitted with breathing failure from weak muscles and raised lung pressure. Tests pointed to scleroderma triggered by the drug, alongside muscle inflammation.

Nerve damage and a specific antibody were also found. Such combined cases are rare in the literature. As these drugs spread, the authors warn, similar events may grow more common. They urge early recognition and prompt treatment to limit harm.
pmc-11624478: Mehdi Heidarizadeh and Maryam Mohebiniya report a chance find in a 2024 case note. A patient set for nose surgery had scans taken for planning. Those scans showed an osteoma, a benign bone growth, in the frontal sinus. Such growths are the most common tumor of their tissue type. The growth had nothing to do with the planned surgery. The authors stress that knowing the scan look of these growths aids early care and follow-up.
pmc-11624778:
Brooke Nichols and co-authors tot up ten years of gains from South Africa's gene-based testing program for HIV, tuberculosis, and COVID-19. Their 2024 study counts the tests actually run and the healthy years of life they saved. Such counting, the authors say, helps governments see what lab testing is truly worth.

Since the program began, its tests averted about 4.3 million years of healthy life lost. Those gains carry an estimated worth of over twenty-eight billion dollars. Each dollar spent returned about fourteen dollars of value on average. Early testing of infants for HIV paid back most of all. The authors rank the program beside childhood vaccination as a top-value health buy.
pmc-11625078:
Jeongwon Jeon and seven colleagues published a 2024 study of blood vessel aging and the small RNA molecules that may signal it. Vascular aging means arteries gradually lose elasticity, stiffen, and collect fatty deposits, raising the risk of stroke and hypertension in older people.

The researchers measured the reactive hyperemia index, a test of how well blood vessel linings respond, in Korean subjects. They then compared microRNAs carried in extracellular vesicles, tiny parcels shed by cells into the blood, between subjects with better and worse vessel function. Several microRNAs differed in abundance. The pathways they point to involve endocrine hormone regulation. Such circulating signals could become blood tests for vascular age.
pmc-11625278:
Yimamu and co-authors cooked in 2024 nanoparticles of cadmium zirconium sulphide by a sol-gel route and asked how baking temperature changes them. The particles matter for sensors and solar cells. Samples were annealed at rising temperatures and probed for structure, shape, composition, and light behavior.

The crystals kept a mix of hexagonal and cubic forms at every setting, while their grains shrank as the heat rose. At the top temperature the particles clumped heavily. Element checks confirmed all three ingredients throughout. The energy gap narrowed steeply with heat, sliding from about 2.6 to 1.6 electron volts. Glow spectra showed two peaks, one from the crystal itself and one from sulfur gaps. The authors say heat is a tuning knob for the material's optics.
pmc-11625578:
Xincong Chen, Jiayu Wang, Wenwen Liu, and Yihui Zhang studied flexibility in an invasive salt marsh plant in a 2024 paper. A plant's ability to change traits with conditions helps invaders settle in new ranges. Both outside climate and internal links among traits may limit that flexibility.

Seeds came from seven groups across the plant's range in China and grew in two shared gardens at the range edges. Flexibility differed by trait and was highest for a trait tied to fitness. Temperature at the home site was the main outside driver of trait variation. The work helps explain how invaders respond and persist under climate change.
pmc-11625678:
Jocelyn Moyes and eleven co-authors pilot in 2024 home-based flu testing in South Africa as a way to gauge how well flu vaccines work. Standard surveillance leans on clinic visits, which many sick people skip. A self-referral system in three provinces mailed swab kits to adults with fresh respiratory symptoms.

Of 1,456 samples returned, 5 percent held flu, 3 percent RSV, and 27 percent the COVID virus. Flu strains split across the two A subtypes and B/Victoria. Comparing vaccinated and unvaccinated positives gave a workable vaccine estimate. Home testing reached people outside clinics and still produced usable data, a model that could widen surveillance where clinic networks are thin.
pmc-11626178:
Sebastian Susperreguy and co-authors use gene-edited mice to clear a suspect family of calcium channels in a 2024 study. When cell calcium stores empty, entry channels open, and the TRPC family long stood accused of forming them. Mice and cells with all seven TRPC genes knocked out gave a clean test.

Store-driven calcium entry ran normally without any TRPC protein, carried instead by Orai channels, with Orai1 in the lead. Receptor-driven entry also stood, again leaning on Orai1. The signature currents were untouched too. The verdict reshapes a decades-old debate about how cells refill their calcium.
pmc-11626978:
Vasily Lukyanov and co-authors weighed costs in 2024 for heart checks after a stroke whose cause is not clear. Finding a hidden irregular beat early can let doctors start blood-thinning drugs sooner. The study compared a wearable patch worn for a stretch of time with a small device placed under the skin.

A cost model was adapted for the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, and Sweden, for one thousand patients over one year. The patch path saved money in all three lands. Savings came from lower device costs and fewer repeat strokes after earlier treatment. Per patient with a found irregular beat, the saving was several times the patch cost. The three health systems gave the test scope beyond one country.
pmc-11627078:
Alexandro Barbosa and co-authors feed a tropical pasture grass with the help of microbes in 2024. Acid soils starve the grass of phosphorus and nitrogen. Phosphate rock holds phosphorus but releases it too slowly, so the team paired it with a fungus that dissolves rock and a bacterium that fixes nitrogen from air.

Lab and greenhouse tests picked the best bacterium for the pairing. In the field, pastures getting the microbes grew more herbage and took up more nitrogen and phosphorus across five harvests. Adding phosphate rock alone made no clear difference. The authors recommend the microbial mix as a biofertilizer for established pastures on poor acid soils.
pmc-11627378:
Suxu Lin and three colleagues test whether households that adopt digital tools also use energy more wisely, in a 2024 study. Home consumption drives a large share of emissions, so household change matters for green goals.

Data from a 2019 national finance survey of Chinese households grounded the analysis. Digital transformation at home linked to clearly higher energy efficiency at every level of use. Gains were largest for food, housing, and miscellaneous spending, and stronger in homes with elderly members. Income carried part of the effect, while education changed its strength. The authors say the micro-level evidence, rare in a field of national studies, can guide policies that push digital adoption for savings.
pmc-11628578:
Shengyuan Fu and co-authors review lab models for a rare childhood blood cancer. Their review from 2024 deals with juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia, which strikes infants and young children. The disease shrugs off standard chemo drugs, and the only cure path, stem cell transplant, still carries a high relapse risk.

New care ideas are badly needed, but the rarity of the disease makes patient material hard to gather. Labs have built a range of stand in systems: models grown from patient cells, plain cell models, and animal models. The review sets out how each type is made and judged, and what each can show about the disease inner workings. It aims to serve as a working reference for the field.
pmc-11628678:
Seven authors led by Chunyun Li pin a gene switch, YAP1, as a must-have for sperm stem cell fate and male fertility. These stem cells must both renew and ripen into sperm across a man life. Lab tests in dish and mouse showed YAP1 sits in the core of human stem cells of this kind. Mute the gene and the cells slow, copy less DNA, and die more.

A gene mate, NEDD4, fell as the switch target in the read chain. A third part, RAD21, teams with the switch to drive that target. Men with no-sperm states held low switch marks and gene typos in a near eight hundred man scan. Mice bred to lack the switch in germ cells stalled sperm make.
pmc-11628978:
Kent and a large team ask in twenty twenty-four whether survival results from the United States can stand in for the United Kingdom in judging lung cancer drugs. The cancer type is advanced lung cancer of the most common form, treated first with chemo, immune, or targeted drugs. Health bodies often face thin local data when they weigh new treatments.

The team compared about one thousand UK patients with several thousand US patients from health records. After adjusting the US group to match the UK group, survival was much alike for each drug class. Curves for immune and targeted drugs nearly overlapped. The authors say US data could fill gaps in UK reviews where local data are sparse.
pmc-11629278:
Kaixuan Ma and co-authors describe tiny gel spheres designed to help repair damaged bone. Bone defects often have uneven shapes, so a repair material must fit the gap and still support new growth. The team made the spheres from methacrylated silk fibroin through microfluidic electrospray. Each sphere holds magnesium ascorbyl phosphate, which leaves slowly over time. That slow release helps new blood vessels form and helps cells develop into bone cells.

The spheres carry a polydopamine coating, part of the mussel-inspired design. That sticky layer lets them join together in place and match the shape of the defect. The same layer can turn light into mild heat, which adds further support for bone growth. In tests in living animals, the joined spheres helped defects heal well. The authors present the design as a flexible approach for bone repair.
pmc-11629878:
Nayla Léveillé and co-authors unravel a tuberculosis scare that turned out to be a lab mix-up in two thousand twenty-four. Five patients at separate Montreal sites tested culture-positive for the TB germ after their samples passed one central lab. One was an organ donor with slim odds of true TB, which raised doubts.

Charts, risk factors, and each sample's path through the lab were retraced. Classic strain typing and full genome reads on a portable sequencer compared the germs. Two patients had real exposure and symptoms to match. The rest traced to cross-contamination inside the lab, where one true sample can seed false positives for others, a known flaw in up to two percent of cultures. Genome data backed the verdict.
pmc-11631078:
Allison Gatz and co-authors hunt social drivers of dangerous blood acidity in this 2024 study. Severe acidosis can kill, and its burden may fall unevenly across society. The All of Us program offers health records, social surveys, and genetic data in one cohort.

The team matched about thirteen thousand participants, one case to four controls. They modeled acidosis risk against social factors like insurance, adjusting for health and demographics. Employer-provided insurance stood out in the early results. Separating social from medical causes points policy at fixable gaps. The study shows big diverse cohorts can expose disparities that smaller ones miss.
pmc-11632478:
Gupta and Rawat report a rare case of metallosis after hip replacement surgery. Metallosis means metal debris gathers in tissue near a joint. It is most often linked to metal-on-metal bearings, yet this case followed a metal-on-polyethylene total hip replacement, a pairing where the problem is very rare.

A 70-year-old man came in with unusual hip pain after trauma to the replaced joint. Finding the cause proved hard, since his bearing type made metallosis an unlikely suspect. The report walks through the diagnosis and care steps, and warns surgeons to keep this cause in mind.
pmc-11634178:
Bowen Chang, Jay Park, and Vivek Buch review the use of normative atlases in deep brain stimulation in this 2024 paper. The treatment sends electric pulses into precise brain spots to ease disorders of the brain and mind, so hitting the right target matters. Normative atlases are standard reference maps of the brain built from many scans.

The review explains how these atlases guide surgeons to the target, help tailor electrode placement to each patient, and support predictions of how stimulation will turn out. It also weighs the problems: atlases differ from each other, and using them well is technically demanding. Looking ahead, the authors point to better imaging and to machine learning tools that could sharpen the maps. Their bottom line is that shared reference atlases make the therapy more exact and more personal.
pmc-11634578:
Jette Bloemberg, Zola Fung-A-Jou, Paul Breedveld, and Aimée Sakes published a study in 2024 on a surgical needle modeled on a parasitic wasp's egg-laying tube. Medical needles pushed through tissue tend to buckle, which limits how deep and how straight they can go. The wasp's tool avoids this by sliding its parts back and forth so the whole never bears a hard push.

Their needle joins six thin steel wires driven by a hand unit built around a low-friction ball spline. One wire advances while the rest retreat, so grip and cutting forces mostly cancel. In gel blocks standing in for tissue, the needle advanced with modest slip at several drive speeds. Softer gels let it travel more truly. The manual unit brings the design closer to the clinic.
pmc-11634778:
Yanli Xu and co-authors trace how one gene switch drives early heart growth in work from 2024. The switch, called HAND2, helps build the heart and other organs. How it turns on its target genes was still partly unclear.

Working in zebrafish and mouse stem cells, the team made gene edits that broke parts of the switch. Edits that stopped the switch from pairing blocked heart growth fully. A gene called pdgfra stood out among targets and could rescue heart cell movement when restored. The team also found the DNA spot where the switch binds near that gene. The link held in both fish and mouse cells, hinting at a shared early step.
pmc-11634878:
Lei Jiang and a team of co-authors compared two exercise plans for heart patients who had a stent procedure, in a 2024 study. Sixty patients with coronary heart disease joined rehab training for three months. One group did steady moderate exercise, while the other did short bursts of hard effort.

Both groups improved, but the hard-burst group gained more in a six-minute walk test and in peak oxygen use. Patients who had suffered a heart attack gained the most from the harder plan. Blood and stool tests showed shifts in gut microbes and body chemicals tied to walking gains. The authors say hard interval training may aid recovery through the gut as well.
pmc-11635178:
Cutting out liver spread of stomach cancer doubled median survival in registry data, and Wuhui Sun and Xiawei Li weigh that claim with care, in work from twenty twenty-four. Near three thousand seven hundred patients from a United States registry were split by whether cancer-led surgery was done. Weighting tricks balanced the groups against cherry-picking.

Median survival ran twelve months with surgery against six without. The death hazard fell by near half in the cut group, even among patients with grim traits. Only about one in ten patients had surgery. The authors call for trials to name who truly gains.
pmc-11635378:
Microplastics, shards and fibers under five millimeters, now drift through water, food, and air, and the gut is where many land. Sudipta Bora and co-authors review in 2024 how these particles disturb the gut microbiome, the inner ecosystem whose balance guards digestion and immunity. The particles also ferry hitchhiking pollutants and heavy metals into the body.

Imbalance in the microbiome ties to gut disorders, body-wide inflammation, and chronic disease, and the gut-brain axis may carry the harm to the mind. The authors call the threat quiet but pervasive and press for studies that pin down how exposure becomes illness.
pmc-11635478:
Simou Sun and co-authors present in 2024 a direct imaging method that can sort and describe single tiny particles released by cells. Such particles may serve as disease markers or drug carriers, but they vary a lot even within one cell type. The team labels particles on several dimensions with a new membrane probe, then views single particles fixed on a soft surface with a sensitive microscope.

A stronger algorithm checks how labels overlap on each particle. Particles from one cell type split into seven groups, some true vesicles and others not. Four cell types gave clearly different group mixes. Within each group, the method counts marker proteins, sizes particles, and links cargo patterns.
pmc-11635678:
Yanfang Guan and twelve co-authors present a 2024 paper on soft robots made from a conductive jelly-like material that moves under electromagnetic drive. The elastomer mixes gelatin and glycerol as its base, threaded with carbon nanotubes and silver nanowires to carry current. Tuning the recipe gave a soft, easily molded material with strong conductivity and resistance to twisting fatigue. Two bio-inspired robots were built from it.

An inchworm-style robot crawled at about three millimeters per second, and still moved while carrying grains or a capsule. A spider-style robot carried up to twenty-two grams. The authors report the material keeps its performance over repeated use. They pitch such quiet, low-energy soft robots for goods transport, safety monitoring, and disaster relief work. The study is a materials demonstration with working prototypes.
pmc-11635878:
Kasie Gebeyehu Tiruneh and co-authors tracked dangerous blood sugar emergencies in Ethiopian diabetes patients in a 2024 study. These emergencies are among the deadliest acute complications of diabetes and are rising worldwide. The team followed more than five hundred adults under care at public hospitals in two southern regions across four years. Records were pulled with a standard checklist and analyzed with survival methods.

The analysis estimated how often emergencies struck and which traits predicted them. Survival curves compared groups, and a regression model singled out predictor variables. The authors note that despite the burden these crises place on patients, hospitals, and families, local evidence on who is at risk has stayed thin. Their study aims to guide prevention where the events are common.
pmc-11635978:
Yutao Li and co-authors refine force field values for metal nodes in porous frames in a 2024 paper. The frames, metal-organic frameworks, can trap carbon dioxide. Sim runs guess trap skill, but stock force fields err. They give each element one set of values, while frames hold rich local chem states. For frames with hard metals the stock set reads gas uptake high. The team built a cheap work flow to fit fresh values.

Live uptake curves serve as the input truth. A math trick ties the loss score to the force values, so fits run fast. The work spans two metal groups and a range of link arms. The new values aim at true uptake reads for carbon work. The authors pitch the flow as a low-cost path to sound sims for gas trap design.
pmc-11636178:
Youssef, Nabil, Atiya, and El-Mahy compare two wrist surgery options for active patients with a worn wrist joint. The joint damage follows an old break of the scaphoid bone that never healed. Their trial, reported in 2024, followed patients for about two years.

Thirty four patients got one of two fusion operations between 2019 and 2021. One joins four wrist bones, and the other joins three while keeping a small bone the older plan removes. Both groups gained about the same motion, grip strength, and pain relief. The three bone operation took much less time in surgery. Scores used a standard wrist scale, and pain was rated on a simple line scale.
pmc-11636578:
Quang Dinh Le, Nhan Quang Le, and Duc Trong Quach published this 2024 analysis of two ways to snare flat colorectal growths during colonoscopy. Laterally spreading tumors of ten to thirty millimeters can be lifted and cut conventionally, or resected underwater, where buoyancy floats the lesion into the snare. This post hoc look re-cut the data of a randomized trial, 88 patients with one tumor each.

Clean-margin resection rates tied between the methods. The underwater route, though, removed tumors in one piece far more often, especially the big ones from twenty to thirty millimeters: 100 percent against 42.9. It was also much faster, a median of 85 seconds against 207. Bleeding and clip counts matched. The authors read the water as the better tool for larger flat lesions.
pmc-11637378:
Scott Wegner, Hahn Kim, and José Avalos go fishing in the pharmacy shelf for drugs that block lactate transport in cancer cells. Tumors shuttle lactate through gate proteins MCT1 and MCT4, and blocking both is attractive but years from the clinic. Using yeast fitted with a light-based sensor, the team screened a library of approved drugs for anything that slowed MCT1.

About one percent of the library hit, including a cluster of common pain and inflammation drugs, the NSAIDs. Seven approved drugs in that cluster blocked MCT1 at doses humans already tolerate, and their shapes resemble known blockers of the sister gate. The authors propose these familiar drugs as fast candidates for trials.
pmc-11637478:
How common is psoriatic arthritis, the joint disease that follows some psoriasis cases? Lembke, Macfarlane, and Jones gather thirty studies from around the world and pool them with care. They keep population surveys separate from health record studies, since the two designs can skew results in different ways. Their combined estimate puts the rate at about 112 cases per 100,000 adults.

Europe showed the highest rates in both designs, near or above 175 per 100,000, while Asia and South America ran far lower. The authors note wide gaps between regions and thin data in many places. They offer the figures as the best current map for planning care.
pmc-11638078:
Qingxin Yang and co-authors build plant spore microrobots to deliver a cancer drug inside the bladder in a 2024 study. Bladder cancer returns often after standard care. The robots use spores of a traditional Chinese medicine plant loaded with the drug doxorubicin and magnetic iron oxide particles.

A rotating magnetic field steers the robots, which moved well and held course in body like fluids. In mice with bladder tumors, guided robots stayed in the bladder longer and clung to its wall. Tumor growth fell more in the guided group than in control groups, and tissue checks confirmed strong shrinkage. The design needs no fuel, running on the outside field alone.
pmc-11638478:
Mengze Li, Qiannan Jia, Tifei Yuan, and five colleagues map, published in 2024, how emotion habits and mental health linked up in students during the COVID-19 emergency. Eleven hundred university students filled surveys on depression, anxiety, body symptoms, and nine habits for handling feelings. Instead of simple scores, the team drew networks: symptoms as nodes, links as ties between them. In the anxiety web, runaway worry anchored the pattern.

Across all three webs, two habits kept bridging the feeling side and the symptom side: self-blame and catastrophizing. Rumination joined them in the body-symptom web. Bridge nodes matter because change there can spread through the whole web. The authors suggest therapy aimed squarely at self-blame and worst-case thinking. Such focus, they argue, buys the widest relief when a crisis strains a whole campus at once.
pmc-11639778:
Veysel Yusuf Cambay and co-authors present a 2024 method to spot fibromyalgia from heart signals. The disease causes wide pain and is hard to confirm with a single test. Heart tracings may carry a faint print of it. The team built a simple tool that reads the highs and lows of the signal in short blocks.

Their tool, MinMaxPat, splits the tracing into blocks of 16 points. It logs where the peak and trough fall in each block, then builds a feature map from those spots. A histogram of the map becomes the input for sorting. A selection step trims weak features, and a neighbor-based sorter makes the call. On a public data set, the model topped 80 percent accuracy. Simple signal tools could aid clinics that lack costly tests.
pmc-11639878:
Healthcare workers face a burnout crisis that feeds on itself: exhausted staff leave, morale drops, and those who remain burn out faster. Cheryl Connors, Matt Norvell, and Albert Wu describe RISE, a peer support program at Johns Hopkins that sends trained peers to staff after stressful events, day or night. The focus here is the role leaders play in making such a program work.

RISE began in 2011 and has since spread to more than 140 healthcare organizations. Leaders share the burden of emotional support, gain skills for their own work, and model openness by joining program design and use. The authors argue this creates a virtuous cycle: supported leaders support staff, and staff resilience strengthens the whole organization.
pmc-11639978:
Wesley, Escalona, Kannourakis, and Ahmed study plakin proteins in ovarian cancer in twenty twenty-four. Epithelial ovarian cancer is aggressive and causes many deaths in women. Plakins are proteins that hold the cell skeleton together and support key cell processes. The team asked how plakin levels change as tumors progress.

They stained tissue from forty-eight patients for plakins and for markers of a change called EMT. That change helps cancer cells spread. Two plakins, periplakin and plectin, were lower in high grade than in low grade tumors. High levels of them tracked with an epithelial, less mobile cell state. Public data sets and cell lines supported the tissue findings. The authors suggest partial loss of plakins may free signaling that starts EMT.
pmc-11640178:
Louise Doculara and co-authors test, in a 2024 study, whether DNA shed by leukemia cells into the blood can track treatment response in infant leukemia. Babies with a rearranged gene form of the disease face early relapse. Response is now checked by repeated bone marrow biopsies, which are invasive and hard to repeat often in infants.

Tumor DNA in blood offers a gentler route, if its levels mirror the disease well. The team used mice grafted with leukemia from three infant patients. They tracked tumor DNA before and after a menin blocking drug. Before treatment, DNA levels matched the leukemia load closely as the grafts grew. After the drug, the picture grew more complex. The study weighs when blood DNA can stand in for marrow checks, and when it may mislead, a key step before clinic use.
pmc-11640378:
Carvalho and co-authors review how sunlight-driven damage in skin interacts with p53, a protein that normally guards cells against cancer. When ultraviolet light hits skin, a working p53 helps damaged cells repair or die. A mutated form loses that guard role and can aid tumor growth. The review explains this response and then turns to a treatment idea: drugs that reactivate mutant p53 so it behaves like the healthy form again.

A second thread links p53 with the vitamin D receptor, one of its target genes, in holding back skin tumors. That link suggests pairing p53 reactivators with vitamin D in prevention strategies. The authors present this as a research direction with real promise, not a proven therapy. The review ties damage response, a famous tumor suppressor, and a hormone pathway into one map of where prevention drugs might act.
pmc-11640478:
George Ayoub proposes that autism risk is set in early windows when the developing brain needs folate and calm immune conditions. His paper was published in twenty twenty-four. Autism affects over two in a hundred eight-year-olds worldwide.

One window hinges on folate, a vitamin that donates the chemical tags regulating DNA; shortage is tied to autism risk. Another involves oxidative stress and inflammation in the fetal brain, possibly from immature immune cells there. Ayoub suggests early supplementation with reduced folate and the amino acid taurine, before and after birth, might soften symptom severity by steering development toward typical paths. The piece is a hypothesis, offered for testing.
pmc-11640578:
Matilda Cloves and Troy Margrie build a microscope that watches two brain layers at once in a 2024 paper. Brain cortex works through patterns that span all its layers. Three photon imaging can reach the full depth of mouse cortex with single cell clarity. Until now, no setup caught two layers at the same moment.

Remote focusing plus adaptive optics split the view into two planes. The planes can sit up to six hundred micrometers apart. Activity from marked cell types in any layer pair can be recorded together. That opens direct tests of how layers talk during thought and action. The method extends deep imaging from still depth to live cross layer timing.
pmc-11640678:
Cindy Nabuurs and an international team of colleagues asked whether radiation after surgery helps early cancer of the ear canal. Squamous cell carcinoma of the external auditory canal is rare, and opinion is split on adding radiotherapy for stage pT1 and pT2 tumors removed with clean margins. The twenty twenty-four study gathered records from fourteen hospitals worldwide. It included 112 early-stage cases, forty-eight of which received postoperative radiotherapy.

Five-year disease-free survival did not differ significantly between the radiated and non-radiated groups. For T1 tumors the figures were 92.9 percent with radiation and one hundred percent without. Patients given radiation more often had aggressive growth features, which likely influenced their doctors' choices. The results suggest routine radiation may add little for these early, cleanly removed cancers.
pmc-11640978:
Sheila Cano-Carrillo and co-authors study two long non-coding RNAs in the heart in a 2024 paper. Early in growth, the heart gains an outer skin whose cells dive in and seed new heart cell kinds. Two gene switches steer that skin, and each pairs with a long RNA that does not build protein.

One RNA sits by the switch in chicks, the other by its kin switch in mice. The team shows the two switches drive the two RNAs in split ways. Those drives shape how skin cells move into the heart wall. The work adds a layer to heart growth rules.
pmc-11641078:
Tyreasa Washington and co-authors frame how kin caregiving may raise Alzheimer's risk for African Americans, in this 2024 paper. About three and a half million relatives, grandparents above all, raise kin children in the United States, and Black families take this role most often. The work brings money strain, open-ended duty, and chronic stress, itself a driver of Alzheimer's and heart disease.

Structural racism adds its own stress load on top. The authors map the chain from caregiving stress through heart risk to brain disease, and they call for research on the changeable links where support could cut the risk.
pmc-11641278:
Tadeusz Paszko and co-authors (2024) explain how weed killers stick to the organic matter in soil. The herbicides are the phenoxyalkanoic family, six of which are used in the European Union. The soil partners are humic and fulvic acids, the complex leftovers of decayed life. The group's work showed these acids do most of the binding. In acid soil the herbicides bind in their neutral form. In less acid soil their charged forms attach through bridges built by aluminum ions held in the acids.

Now the team combines infrared spectroscopy, heat measurements of the binding, and molecular modeling to say why. They report the enthalpy of the binding and trace which sites on each acid do the work. The aluminum-based sites in fulvic acid change with acidity, while those in humic acid do not. The mechanisms matter for predicting how long herbicides linger and where they travel.
pmc-11641378:
Diego Rojas and co-authors test whether a lipid drug can undo alcohol's damage to rat lungs, in a 2024 study. Heavy drinking stirs body-wide inflammation, and lungs pay with swelling, mucus flood, and scar tissue that breeds infection. Fenofibrate, a fat-drug that fires a cell switch called PPAR alpha, is known to cool inflammation elsewhere. Rats drank alcohol, with or without the drug to follow.

Alcohol alone thickened the lungs with immune cells and raised flame signals inside them. It also pushed up a mucus protein and laid collagen collars around the airways. Fenofibrate after alcohol pulled each mark back down, the collagen near to the level of sober controls. The authors read alcohol as a clear lung toxin in this model. They glimpse a second career for the old drug, as a lung anti-inflammatory worth testing in drink-linked lung disease.
pmc-11641578:
Adriana Franca and co-authors review coffee silverskin in two thousand twenty-four and test it in chocolate cake. Silverskin is the thin layer shed during coffee roasting, rich in fiber and antioxidants. Turning this by-product into a food ingredient could add value to waste.

The team baked cakes with three levels of silverskin and measured fiber, antioxidant power, and phenolic content, all of which rose with the addition. Tasters scored color, smell, taste, texture, and overall liking on a nine-point scale. Cakes with the two lower levels pleased tasters about equally, while the highest level was liked least. Even the lowest level passed the bar for an antioxidant fiber source. Taste and overall impression drove acceptance most.
pmc-11641678:
Marina Barreda Gutierrez and co-authors study the digital divide among older Europeans in a 2024 paper. Young people grew up with phones and computers, while many older adults met them late in life, with less skill and less access. The team asks whether that gap in tech use tracks with worse mental health, and whether the harm has grown over time.

They draw on a large survey of health, aging, and retirement across Europe. Their checks show that the age-driven tech gap does link to poorer mental health in older adults. The authors urge that closing the gap be treated as a public health task. Bringing older people into digital life, they argue, could lift mood and well-being for many.
pmc-11641978:
Belmont-Sánchez and co-authors compare two copper based crystal compounds that share the same three copper core. One compound was known, and the team made a second one where simple charged ions act as spacers. Their 2024 study looks at structure, heat stability, light based tests, and magnetic behavior for both.

The core holds three copper centers in a line, bound by a shared helper molecule. The two compounds differ in how that helper's free arm reaches the central copper, which stretches the copper to copper gap. In the new compound, paired spacer ions stack in neat opposing rows. Computer based checks support the claim that the spacers keep the cores magnetically apart.
pmc-11642078:
Ruth Rodrigues, Edson de Almeida, Fabio Kruger, Edson Silva-Filho, and Edvani Muniz make water-holding gels to help cure cement in two thousand twenty-four. The gels blend a synthetic polymer with pectin, a plant gum, and ash from rice husks. Such gels soak up water and release it slowly, which can feed the hardening of cement from inside.

Three gel doses were mixed into mortar and checked at one week and at four weeks. The mid dose did best, beating plain mortar on strength at both checks. Lab tests with light, X-rays, and imaging described the gel's makeup and form. The work shows waste ash can play a useful role in building materials.
pmc-11642278:
Jules Tianyu Zhang-Yin and co-authors report a case in two thousand twenty-four about a scan result that looked like cancer spread but was not. The scan is a PET/CT method widely used for neuroendocrine tumors. It lights up tissue that carries a certain receptor, and it has largely replaced an older, blurrier scan.

In this patient, a bright spot near the base of the neck first read as a likely metastasis in the neck. The spot in fact sat in a nerve cluster called the stellate ganglion, which can take up the tracer in a harmless way. A follow-up scan showed no neck spread. The case warns readers about this rare trap.
pmc-11642378:
Sperm production depends on a nursery: stem cells in the testis that must balance making more of themselves against maturing into sperm. Ali Sadek, Yulia Khramtsova, and Boris Yushkov review an underappreciated resident of that nursery — mast cells, the immune cells best known for allergy. They carry a cargo of active substances that can steer the tissues around them.

The review gathers evidence on how testicular mast cells influence the stem cells, support or disturb sperm formation in health and disease, and interact with the other cells of the niche. Because the niche is defined by function rather than anatomy, every signalling neighbour matters. The authors argue that mast cells may hold a critical, overlooked influence on male fertility, and they map the interactions future experiments should test.
pmc-11642478:
Ronald Blab and co-authors test road bitumen mixed with crumb rubber from old tires in a study from 2024. Waste tires pile up worldwide and pollute land and water. Melting their rubber into road tar could cut waste and improve roads at once.

The team first set design temperatures for Malaysian regions using the SUPERPAVE system. Hourly air data and a pavement heat model gave the ranges. Standard bitumen and rubber-mixed bitumen were then tested at many temperatures and aging stages. Shear, viscosity, and bending tests measured stiffness and cracking risk. The goal is a mix tuned to Malaysia's hot climate. Recycled rubber roads could serve the tropics well.
pmc-11642678:
The authors present a case they call the first of its kind: a womb twisted a full three turns that quietly severed the cervix. The patient was a woman who was not pregnant and felt no symptoms. Uterine torsion is rare and hard to spot, since pain is often its only sign. Most cases surface only during surgery.

Inside, surgeons found the uterus rotated 1080 degrees, a fibroid larger than fifteen centimeters, and a large ovarian tumor. The cervix was missing from its place and turned up fully detached from the uterine body. The team completed the operation, and the woman went home on day eight. Two months later she had no complications. The authors urge fast imaging and action whenever this twist is suspected, especially after menopause.
pmc-11642978:
Fuel cells that run on polymer electrolyte membranes work well but lean on costly platinum catalysts. The authors of a 2024 study answer with a one-step recipe that starts from crystal-structure prediction. Guided by theory, they made a low-platinum alloy called CaPt2 by arc melting in a single step, with no hazardous waste. The product matched the predicted structure. Adding calcium enriched electrons on the platinum surface. It also changed how oxygen intermediates bind and move during the oxygen reduction reaction.

The alloy carries a third less platinum by mole fraction, which lowers feedstock cost on top of the cheaper making process. The team presents the route as a model for designing other working catalysts at lower cost.
pmc-11643278:
Eike Bauer and co-authors review ten years of work in 2024 on an iron-based compound used to speed chemical reactions. The compound and its charged form are cheap, stable, and easy to change, which makes them handy tools for making new compounds. The review covers their growing use as catalysts, the helpers that speed reactions without being used up.

Key ground includes reactions that add oxygen, join carbon parts, build long chains, and switch on or off with electric charge. The charged form also works as an acid-type catalyst in its own right. The authors sort the main advances so chemists can see where these iron tools fit best.
pmc-11643378:
Suchocki tested a plant-based alcohol called hexanol as a partial fuel for a small jet turbine. Interest in green flight fuels is rising, and hexanol can be made from biomass. Trials ran on a JETPOL turbine at speeds from forty thousand to one hundred ten thousand turns per minute. The fuel blends mixed one quarter and one half hexanol into standard jet fuel.

At high speeds, both blends matched the plain fuel in heat efficiency, though they burned more fuel because hexanol carries less energy. Carbon monoxide output fell sharply at higher speeds, showing cleaner burning. The study weighs thrust, fuel use, and gas output side by side. It offers early evidence that such blends could work in small turbines.
pmc-11643578:
Zimo Wang and co-authors report new ring-shaped compounds from a fungus in a 2024 paper. The fungus lives inside plants and makes cyclic depsipeptides, small rings mixing amino and hydroxy acids, a family known for killing cells and germs.

Guided by activity tests, the team pulled seven such rings from the fungus, two of them new to science. Spectroscopic tools and chemical tricks pinned down each ring's full three-dimensional build. Four of the rings slowed two human lung cancer cell lines at modest doses. Two also hit a staph germ and a yeast hard at low levels. The results add fresh candidates to the search for cell-killing and germ-killing leads.
pmc-11643678:
Daniel Martínez-Cisterna and co-authors review silver nanoparticles as a spray against farm pests. Their 2024 review gathers work on how the tiny silver grains are made and what they do to insects. Bugs from four orders are covered, among them flies, beetles, and moths.

Trials report stunted growth, weight loss, and higher death rates in treated pests. The grains can pass cell walls, break up DNA copying, and stir up harmful oxygen forms inside the bug. Making the grains from plants or microbes is one of the routes the review compares. The authors sum up the proof and the open questions for farm use, and note the need for care with dose and spread.
pmc-11643878:
Xiaoyu Wu and co-authors build a battery anode from vanadium nitride dots fixed on carbon fibers, in a study published in two thousand twenty-four. Sodium-ion batteries are cheaper than lithium ones, and vanadium compounds can hold much charge, but they swell and break down as sodium moves in and out. Carbon fibers stay stable and give the dots a firm frame with wide surface area.

The woven fiber mat lets sodium ions move fast and keeps charge transfer easy. As an anode, the material held a steady charge level after five hundred cycles at a mid rate. It still held most of that after a thousand cycles at a fast rate. The authors present the design as a strong pick for sodium storage.
pmc-11644078:
Roman Puzanskiy and a large team follow a famous plant cell culture from first division to death, reading its chemistry at each stage, in a 2024 study. Tobacco BY-2 cells are a standard model in plant biology because they grow in step and stretch in a polar way. In a closed batch, they pass through lag, growth, elongation, and rest phases while the medium itself changes sharply.

Sugar vanished fast, simpler sugars rose then fell, and acidity dipped then climbed. Against that moving backdrop, the team profiled the cells’ metabolites across the whole life arc. The map shows how inner programs and outer conditions trade signals to produce each phase. Anyone using BY-2 as a model gains a timetable of what the cells are doing chemically, hour by hour.
pmc-11644178:
Qun Hu and co-authors study how the timing of a mid season nitrogen top up affects carbon and nitrogen use in high yield rice, in a paper from 2024. Rice needs nitrogen through its growth, and giving some of it mid season is a common tactic. When exactly to give it, though, can shift how the plant stores and moves sugars and nitrogen.

Two top japonica types were grown under five nitrogen plans, with top ups at three growth stages, none, or no nitrogen at all. The middle timing gave the highest plant nitrogen uptake at heading, at maturity, and during grain filling, plus the best nitrogen use efficiency. Later top ups lowered sugar and starch stores in plant tissues. The winning plan also built the largest store of sugars that later moved into the grain.
pmc-11644278:
Ruxue Pan and seven colleagues exposed rice to silver nanoparticles at two life stages and found the plant's vulnerability changes with age. Silver nanoparticles are widely used and can reach farmland. Seeds were exposed during germination, or seedlings after sprouting, at matched concentrations. Growth, photosynthesis, nutrient content, and antioxidant defenses were measured. Particles accumulated more in seedlings, and roots always held more than shoots.

Exposure during germination, even at the highest dose, barely affected the young plants. Seedlings hit with the same doses grew less, photosynthesized worse, and lost nutrients significantly. Timing, not just dose, decides nanoparticle risk. The twenty twenty-four study warns that safety tests run only on germinating seeds will understate the hazard to established crops, and regulators should test the sensitive stage.
pmc-11644378:
Xuanan Lu and co-authors blend two plastics and a ceramic dust into a safer electrolyte for lithium batteries. Liquid electrolytes carry fire and leak risks, so solid polymer films are prized, but single polymers rarely meet every demand at once. Their film mixes polyacrylonitrile with polyurethane, adds a lithium-conducting ceramic, and takes a lithium salt, all cast from solution.

The best mix carried ions well at room temperature and stayed stable across a wide voltage range. More than a third of the current was borne by lithium ions themselves. A test cell with an iron phosphate cathode cycled steadily and kept its pace under faster drains. It delivered a solid capacity at a one-hour rate. The authors pitch the film for room-temperature solid batteries.
pmc-11644478:
Putthiwat Thongwong and co-authors test a snack-like film meant to protect the brain after stroke, in a 2024 study. The melt-in-mouth film carries silkworm pupae extract plus holy basil and ginger, a blend called JP1 with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory leanings. Rats stressed for two weeks, then given a blocked brain artery, received the film before and after the stroke.

Memory for places and objects improved under treatment. Brains showed less oxidative stress, inflammation, and cell death, better chemical signaling, and gut floras richer in friendly bacteria, while the stress hormone fell. The blend is a candidate worth carrying toward human trials for post-stroke thinking problems.
pmc-11644678:
Taegyun Kim, Seung Min Kang, Kanghyun Kim, and Geon Hwee Kim make oil-soaking sponges from recycled foam plastic in 2024. A 3D electrospinning step with a dash of phosphoric acid builds the porous sponge in one pass. The sponge shuns water and loves oil, a pair of traits that suit spill cleanup.

Sponges from recycled stock matched those from fresh stock in soak tests. Acid dose was tuned for top uptake in the trials. The work shows waste foam can turn into a high-value tool for oil and water splits, the authors report.
pmc-11644778:
Omari Chaligava and co-authors track air pollution across Georgia using moss as a living sensor, in a 2024 study. Mosses soak up airborne metals and particles, so their tissue records local air quality. The team gathered close to one hundred moss samples nationwide over five years. Lab analysis measured fifteen major and trace elements in each sample.

Statistical sorting split the elements into three source families: natural ground dust, human activity, and local oddities. Maps built from the data show pollution load across the country. Results were compared with the country's first moss survey from the prior decade, exposing trends. An ecological risk assessment rounds out the picture for policy makers.
pmc-11644878:
Wu, Guo, Peng, Su, Ahamod, and Han classify damaged three dimensional point clouds in twenty twenty-four. Point clouds from scanners guide self driving and face recognition systems. Real data often suffer occlusion, rotation, and noise. Tuning network structure alone did not fix the accuracy drop.

Their approach extracts local feature descriptors before classification. A new network design is built around those descriptors. Training data were augmented for ten chosen object categories. Tests covered occlusion and coordinate changes against leading models. Their model kept higher accuracy under heavy corruption. Depth camera trials on real objects confirmed the gains. The authors say feature preprocessing is the key to robustness.
pmc-11644978:
Wang and co-authors build a neural net to sharpen long-wave infrared spectral images. Such imaging aids gas checks, mineral hunts, and fire spotting. A snapshot device now captures these images in real time. Its output has low spectral detail and heavy noise. Training data for this band are also scarce.

Their Hierarchical Spectral Transformer learns from single-pixel spectral records. Pixel-level learning sidesteps the lack of full image sets. The design aims to catch both local and global spectral links. Past nets based on convolution or attention missed one of those scales. The authors claim finer spectral rebuilds for noisy long-wave input.
pmc-11645078:
Kamil Bancik and nine co-authors published an energy harvesting study in twenty twenty-four on powering farm sensors from the temperature gap between air and soil. Fields need more monitoring, but batteries are awkward in remote plots. A thermoelectric generator turns even a small heat difference into electricity, day and night.

The team reviewed existing devices, built an improved one around a Peltier cell, and measured it outdoors for twelve months. It harvested about seventy-eight hundred joules over the year while logging the temperatures across the generator. The yield is modest but continuous and maintenance-free. The authors judge the approach viable for off-grid agricultural sensing where battery swaps are impractical.
pmc-11646378:
Francesco Coppolino and co-authors published this 2024 case series on easing pain after lung surgery. Removing a lung lobe by keyhole surgery still leaves many patients with severe, lasting chest pain. A nerve block beside the spine helps, but its numbing fades fast and the drug can spread unevenly.

Six patients received the block with a standard numbing drug plus dexmedetomidine, a sedative that stretches the effect of the block, and methylene blue dye to show the spread on camera. Pain scores stayed below four on a ten-point scale at every check over two days, and opioid use fell. No patient had a slow heart rate or vomiting, the team report. The small series suggests the mix is worth a fuller trial.
pmc-11647178:
The EFSA Panel on Additives and Products or Substances used in Animal Feed issued a 2024 opinion on Bafasal, a feed additive made of four bacteriophages. Bacteriophages are viruses that infect bacteria, not animals. These four target a Salmonella strain, and the product is meant for all poultry, given in drinking water or liquid feed.

Europe's food safety body had judged the product before and found it safe for birds, consumers, and the environment. It is not a skin or eye irritant, though it should be treated as a possible trigger for breathing allergies. The new opinion weighs fresh evidence on how well it works. Earlier work showed it could lower counts of two Salmonella types. The panel's task was to say whether the claimed gains in carcass cleanliness and bird performance hold up.
pmc-11647278:
Yuanying and co-authors track mid life hospital stays in south Anhui, China, in a 2024 paper. Mid life patients, aged forty five to fifty nine, form a key work force group. Their disease mix and early death risks shape family and state costs.

Over one hundred fifty thousand stays from a decade of records were sorted. The mid life share of stays shot up over the decade in alarm. Cancer led the disease list, then injury and gut disease. Age fifty was a peak year for entry in the data. Risk traits for early death were drawn from the same set.
pmc-11647378:
Auden Steane and co-authors set out, in a 2024 protocol, a plan to gather what is known about the hard parts of going home after bowel surgery. Care during the hospital-to-home move has improved, yet no one has mapped which teaching and support steps help these patients most. The review will cover countries with public health systems.

The team will search four major databases for studies since 2012. At least two reviewers will screen and extract data on their own, then merge their work. Patient challenges will be sorted with a standard coding frame tied to known quality aims. The map should show where support is thin and where new programs could help most.
pmc-11647478:
Valeria Hasenmajer and co-authors study how a long-term excess of cortisol disrupts daily immune rhythms, published in 2024. Cortisol-like hormones are strong setters of the body clock. Their effect under chronic human exposure, though, had not been studied in depth before this trial.

Cushing's syndrome, a rare condition where a tumor drives excess hormone, offers a chance to see those effects in people. In a year-long multicentre trial, patients and matched controls gave blood samples at five points in a day. Several immune cell groups showed changed levels, swing size, and rhythm during active disease. Those changes were only partly restored after remission. Clock genes in the same cells also showed a flattened daily swing.
pmc-11647878:
Soares, Freitas, Queirós, Purwidyantri, Alpuim, and Nieder watch single DNA molecules pair up in real time. Their sensor is a sheet of graphene carrying fluorophore-labeled DNA hairpins. Graphene quenches the labels in a distance-dependent way, so hybridization changes the light signal as hairpins move. A wide-field fluorescence microscope with a sensitive camera captured signals from single hairpins at low target concentration.

The team used the signals for super-resolution localization of each hairpin and measured how fast single hairpins unfold, at about 7 seconds. Some molecules paused in partly hybridized states, which more than doubled the unfolding time. A semiempirical model helped explain the observed kinetics.
pmc-11648078:
Christos Gatsios, Maximilian Dreher, and co-authors scan two twin build films to see how pack ways bend their charge traits, in a 2024 study. Twin builds share the same parts in unlike links, a clean test of form. Film charge flow had to be read from flat to thick coats on one base.

Both twins lie near flat at thin coats on the base in scope views. Top fill state marks let shake costs fall out for each twin. One twin reads as the better charge flow pick by those costs. Its thick coat top state splits wide, traced to field pull not wave mix. Pack ways thus rule film traits as much as build.
pmc-11648678:
Ekemiri and colleagues surveyed in 2024 computer vision syndrome among bankers in Trinidad and Tobago, whose jobs mean long hours at screens. About three quarters of those enrolled reported the syndrome. Working in a rural branch more than doubled the odds. Wearing prescription glasses was linked to lower odds. The authors call the condition common yet easily preventable.

They recommend workplace changes, including anti-glare screens and glasses for staff with heavy screen time. The study adds Caribbean data to a problem usually studied elsewhere. Bank managers, they argue, should treat eye strain as an occupational health issue.
pmc-11648878:
Jiuyang Xu and five co-authors report a case where an inflamed-vessel disease caused both a brain blockage and a brain bleed, in a 2024 report with a literature review. The disease attacks small vessels across the body and is tied to a blood antibody marker. Brain involvement is uncommon, and having both stroke types in one patient had not been reported.

Their patient was a 67-year-old man, previously healthy, with fever, fatigue, coughing of blood, skin lesions, and hearing loss. Chest scans showed nodules that grew and merged, and antibody tests were strongly positive. Steroid treatment helped only partly. New dizziness and clumsiness then marked the brain events. The case warns doctors to watch the brain even as other organs improve.
pmc-11649078:
Chunxue Han, Ruichao Li, and Haigang Li show that when rain falls matters as much as how much, for a dry Inner Mongolian steppe, in a 2024 study. Sixty years of records from the growing season sorted into four rain patterns: bunched in July, bunched in August, split early and late, or spread thin and even. The team replayed all four on field plots through one season.

Plant kinds, variety, and counts barely moved between patterns, save one evenness score after July. Total plant growth, though, leapt under the July bunch: over half again as much as any other pattern. One annual forb did most of the extra growing. July rain near two fifths of the year's average, with base needs met in other months, hit the steppe's sweet spot. The authors suggest timed watering could lift forage where rain timing drifts.
pmc-11649378:
Glick and co-authors compared gene architecture across 590 species, in a study published in 2024. Most genes in complex organisms are split: coding stretches are broken by non-coding introns. Introns bring benefits, yet why they persist and how they evolve is only partly clear. The team gathered whole-genome data across the main branches of eukaryotes, the group holding animals, plants, and fungi. They measured intron length, intron counts, and the balance between introns and coding parts.

The analysis wraps those measures in a family-tree framework, so shared ancestry does not fake a pattern. Basic gene structure proved to differ sharply between the major lineages. Some groups favor many short introns; others carry few, long ones. The patterns suggest each lineage tuned its gene layout under its own pressures. The study gives gene evolution a broad, tree-aware baseline.
pmc-11649578:
Hujie Wang and three co-authors surveyed hospital teams in rural China in two thousand twenty-four on how leader ties shape team results. More than a thousand staff from three hundred teams in four hospitals took part. National reform puts teamwork in rural hospitals high on the agenda, so the link matters for policy.

Staff who felt similar to their leader, or who accepted a power gap, both spoke up more and stayed silent more, a mixed pattern. Speaking up linked to better rated care and higher job satisfaction. Silence cut the other way. The study shows leaders shape team voice, which in turn shapes how care feels for staff and patients.
pmc-11650078:
Lingzi Luo and co-authors survey, in a 2024 study, whether Shanghai residents planned to seek mental health help during the strict COVID lockdown of 2022. The lockdown ran for over two months and covered twenty-five million people. Most mental health care moved online during that time, yet public intent to use it was little known.

An online survey reached more than three thousand adults across all districts of the city. About thirty percent screened positive for depression or anxiety signs. Fewer than one in four said they planned to use mobile mental health services. The study links intent to health status, lockdown stress, and past experience, giving planners a view of unmet need in a crisis.
pmc-11650778:
Jing Yu and co-authors assemble a toolkit for watching sulfur batteries at work in a 2024 review. Sulfur cathodes promise cheap, strong, and greener storage than today's cells. Yet migrating sulfur chains, swelling, and slow chemistry block the road to market.

Live monitoring methods, used in place or during operation, can catch those failures as they form. The review covers tools that track structure, shape, chemistry, stress, and ion flow inside a running cell. Each failure mode needs its own window into the battery.
