A shared toolbox lets labs compare methods and pick the right probe. Better watching is a shortcut to better sulfur cell design.
pmc-11651278:
Yanping Zong and co-authors present a 2024 map of world research on flu and two key T cell types that fight it. They mined a major database for work from the mid-1980s to 2023. Their tools chart who writes what, where, and on which themes, across more than a thousand papers.

Output rose year by year, led by teams in the United States, Australia, and China. One Melbourne institute topped the list, and one scholar there was the most prolific author. Team links were sparse and mostly stayed within one country. Hot themes point to cell based flu vaccines as a major next step. The study helps new researchers see the shape of the field.
pmc-11651478:
Xiaoxiao Zhao and colleagues report a two thousand twenty-four diagnostic study of a rapid RNA test for tuberculosis that standard smears miss. Smear-negative lung tuberculosis is hard to confirm quickly. A test that amplifies the germ's RNA live could help.

Patients with suspected smear-negative disease gave sputum or lung wash samples. Both the RNA test and a leading cartridge test were run on each. The RNA test caught about half of true cases while never flagging healthy samples. Agreement between the two tests was substantial. The authors weigh where the faster, cheaper RNA method fits in practice.
pmc-11652078:
Xiaobing Wang and four co-authors describe a combined procedure for a blocked portal vein in a man with advanced liver disease. Their 2024 case report concerns a 69-year-old man who arrived with black stools and vomited blood after four days of bleeding. Scans showed the portal vein blocked and rerouted, with cirrhosis, a swollen spleen, and fluid in the belly.

A team review ruled out standard endoscopic, surgical, and tumor treatments. Care centered on two goals: reopening the vein and sampling the blockage to check for cancer. The doctors paired a shunt placed through the jugular vein with ultrasound-guided endoscopy for the recanalization and biopsy. Combining the two routes let them treat and diagnose in one plan. The report offers the pairing as an option when a malignant blockage leaves few choices.
pmc-11652478:
Wanno Wallole, Abraham Alano, and Misganu Endriyas study a women's network in southern Ethiopia and what helps or hurts its work, in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. The network was set up in two thousand ten to support growth and health in rural areas. The team used group talks and key interviews to learn how the network now runs.

Women said the network helped them pay for food, clothes, health care, and schooling. It also raised use of mother and child health care and cleaner home habits. But unpaid work strained members, and support from health staff and from men was uneven. Some trained women also kept their distance. Readers learn why such groups fade without steady backing.
pmc-11652878:
Abdelrahman AlAshqar and co-authors report a rare womb tumor case in a 2024 paper. Such tumors, called teratomas, hold tissue from all germ layers, but they are far less common in the womb than in the ovary. Scans rarely settle the diagnosis, so it is usually made after surgery, and where the tumor starts has been debated.

A woman aged forty four had four weeks of bleeding from a womb mass, and tests gave no clear answer. She chose full womb removal, and the tumor proved to be a mature cystic teratoma. Gene repeat tests on tumor and tube tissue showed near match with the host, which rules out an unfertilized egg or leftover fetal tissue as the source.
pmc-11653578:
Francesco Grippo and co-authors build an algorithm that reads all the causes on a death certificate, not just the headline one, in a 2024 paper. Long-lived populations often die with several diseases at once. Official statistics usually crown a single underlying cause. That habit hides the true weight of multimorbidity. Death certificates list more causes than the headline.

Their method uses the relationships among listed causes to assign each a role. Some started the fatal chain, and others hastened it. The World Health Organization's rules guide the logic. Countries can then track dying with multiple diseases more honestly. Health planners gain better maps of end-of-life burden. The algorithm works on data that registries already hold.
pmc-11653678:
Turki Aljuhani and seven colleagues survey what blocks clear talk between rehab therapists and their patients in Saudi Arabia. The study gathered survey answers from 228 patients and 46 physical and occupational therapists in one rehab department. Most patients reported high satisfaction, yet barriers stood out on both sides.

Patients cited short visit time most often. Therapists pointed to poor patient history-taking, cramped physical setups, and time pressure. Therapists who spoke only Arabic struggled more to follow the language used. Younger therapists found juggling many problems harder. The authors recommend targeted training, better clinic structures, and better electronic records to raise satisfaction and outcomes.
pmc-11653778:
Karly Cini and a large team tie long-ill risk marks to mind health in Indonesian teens. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. Such risks start in youth but are framed as grown folk fears. Near one thousand three hundred school teens aged sixteen to eighteen in Jakarta and South Sulawesi were taped or told on five risk fields, from fat to food. Jakarta teens gave blood reads too.

Risk packs were the rule: most teens bore risks in three or more fields. Any risk tied to more mind strain, most for long screen sits. More risks meant worse mind scores and life grades all round. Blood marks tied too.
pmc-11653978:
Manoj Kumar and three co-authors compare two ways of giving a calming drug to children in this twenty twenty-four trial. Children often swallow coins, magnets, or button cells, which must be pulled out with a scope. The team tested a drug that calms and eases pain, given as an aid to the main sleep drug.

Children were assigned at random to get the drug through the nose or through a vein. Staff who judged the results did not know which route each child got. The study weighs how well each route worked for pulling objects stuck at the top of the food pipe. Findings can help doctors pick the kinder route for small children.
pmc-11654078:
Binyun Pan and co-authors chart the genes and small molecules that remodel the pig ovary from birth to pregnancy, in a 2024 paper. The ovary makes eggs and hormones, and its orderly cycling drives fertility. Which genes and metabolites run its development and sustain gestation was only partly known.

The team sequenced RNA and profiled metabolites in Chenghua pig ovaries at four stages: newborn, puberty, one year, and late pregnancy. Thousands of genes changed across development, hundreds across pregnancy. Cholesterol-building genes steered early growth, while one enzyme, boosted in lab cells, raised estrogen-making genes and cell growth. The atlas names concrete levers for breeding and fertility research in pigs, with echoes for human ovarian biology.
pmc-11654178:
Duo Chen and co-authors map the genes that build triterpenoids in Cyclocarya paliurus, a valuable Chinese tree used in health teas. These compounds drive much of the tea's reputed benefit. Their 2024 study pairs chemistry with gene activity data: a metabolite census of the leaves set against which genes switch on alongside each compound.

Sixty-nine terpenoids turned up, with triterpenoids making up over four fifths. Five abundant ones, including corosolic and ursolic acids, were tracked closely. Certain P450 genes rose and fell with the enzymes that shape the two main triterpenoid families, marking them as likely builders. Gene families such as MYB and WRKY look like regulators. Plant biochemists get a short list of genes to test.
pmc-11654278:
Yohei Fujiishi, Wakako Ohyama, and Emiko Okada study a safety test problem in a 2024 paper. To check whether probiotic candidates damage genes, labs grow the bacteria with human cells in a standard test. The catch: the bacteria sour the medium, and sour conditions alone can fake a positive result.

The team mapped how low the acidity must fall before the test cell line shows false damage, using three food acids the bacteria make. They then found the strongest doses of three antibiotics that stop the bacteria without skewing the test. A run with live lactic bacteria confirmed the antibiotics keep the test honest. The work gives labs a cleaner way to screen probiotic strains.
pmc-11654378:
Guann-Ming Chang and co-authors examine whether steady, well-linked care cuts wasteful medical services, in this 2024 nationwide study from Taiwan. Seeing the same doctor over time is called continuity, while how closely a patient's doctors share work is called coordination. Past work linked each one to less overuse on its own. The team compared their relative weight using insurance data.

They studied about 1.46 million people sampled from Taiwan's national insurance rolls in 2015. Overuse was counted across eighteen services classed as low value. People with high continuity had notably lower odds of overuse than the middle group. High coordination also linked to lower overuse, by a smaller margin. The authors say helping patients keep steady, connected care may trim low-value services.
pmc-11654778:
Ziwei Zhu wrote a 2024 paper comparing two sedatives for painless stomach and bowel scope exams in older patients. Such exams need a drug that works fast, wears off fast, and keeps blood pressure and breathing steady. The two drugs tested were remimazolam besylate and ciprofol.

Thirty-one patients got each drug. The remimazolam group fell asleep faster, woke faster, and left the recovery room sooner. Their pain relief rated higher, and their blood pressure, heart rate, and oxygen held steadier during the exam. Memory test scores after the exam were also higher. Side effects were about the same in both groups. The results favor remimazolam for older patients, though the study was small and at one site.
pmc-11655178:
Matthew Trone, Joshua Stover, Alejandro Almarza, and Robert Bowles argue that acidity is an overlooked driver of back pain from worn spinal disks, in a 2024 review. Known pain suspects include matrix breakdown, changed mechanics, and inflammation, yet treatments aimed there help little.

The review gathers what is known about low pH inside damaged disks. Acidity speeds the breakdown of disk cells and their matrix. It also invites nerve growth into the disk, alters how cells sense mechanical load, and raises inflammatory signals and pain-related ion channels. Big gaps remain in linking acidity to the sensation of pain itself. The authors map those gaps and propose studies to fill them. Better grasp of acid-driven pain, they say, is a route to better drugs.
pmc-11655478:
Vinicius Hernandes and co-authors present autoMEA, a software tool described in 2024 for reading multi-electrode array data. Such arrays record the firing of neuron networks in real time, but the datasets are large and complex. Older analysis tools depend on fixed settings chosen by hand, which takes time and invites bias.

AutoMEA uses machine learning to detect bursts of activity automatically. The team demonstrates it on primary hippocampal neurons from wild-type mice grown on multi-well array plates. They also test it on two other neuronal network models to benchmark its performance. The tool aims to make network activity analysis faster and more consistent across labs.
pmc-11655578:
Felicitas Zöllner and seven co-authors check how well fissure sealants protect children's molars. Their 2024 study examines eight- to ten-year-olds across a population sample. Some children have molar-incisor hypomineralization, a flaw that weakens enamel. Whether sealants still help those teeth was an open question.

Over five thousand four hundred children were examined with standard dental tools. About fifty-nine percent had at least one sealant. Sealant quality ranged from fully intact to nearly lost. Caries levels stayed low overall, near zero point two on the index. Children with sealants showed lower decay scores, with or without the enamel flaw. Mixed models confirmed a real protective effect. Sealing pays off even on weakened teeth.
pmc-11655778:

Raw trimmed scans erred badly, by about minus twenty-two percent on the lung shunt share and plus thirty-four on lung dose. Stretching the partial data evenly did little better. A fitted model that predicts the missing counts cut errors to about eleven percent. Using only the left lung made all methods agree closely. The corrections also held together on 31 real partial scans. The authors say planning can proceed safely even when the lungs are incompletely imaged.
pmc-11655878:
Ji Hye Shin and eleven co-authors show that a protein called USP21 protects a growth receptor and helps colorectal cancer spread, in a 2024 study. Cancer cells with the gene knocked out grew, migrated, and formed colonies and spheres far more slowly, and tumors in mice shrank markedly. A drug that blocks USP21 also curbed sphere formation. The authors propose the USP21-EGFR axis as a treatment target.
pmc-11655978:
Velmarini Vasquez and colleagues trace Parkinson's cell harm to loss of a mitochondrial gate protein, in work from 2024. Clumped alpha synuclein is a hallmark protein in Parkinson's disease brain tissue. Mitochondria fail in that disease, yet the chain from clumps to failure stayed partly hidden.

Mutant synuclein placed at mitochondria drove gate loss in cultured nerve cells. Stress factors that clump synuclein made the loss worse in patient cells. Restoring the gate or cutting clumps eased cell energy faults.
pmc-11656078:
Eddy Roccati and co-authors test free university study as a shield for the aging brain in a 2024 paper. The ISLAND Campus scheme in Tasmania offered fee free study to adults in mid and later life, in person or online. The aim was to cut dementia risk factors that can still be changed and to lift thinking skills.

Campus learners were matched with non learners of like age and sex from the same large study. Close to a thousand people in all took surveys on health and risk, gave blood for gene and protein tests, and did memory tasks online. The design lets the team weigh whether late study truly moves risk and cognition.
pmc-11656378:
Haotian Jiang and co-authors test a self leveling slurry made from industrial byproducts in a 2024 study. The mix joins slag, steel slag, and a sulfur removal residue in a geopolymer base meant to flow flat and harden strong. Turning waste powders into building material cuts both landfill load and cement use.

Two mix ratios were compared, and three activator chemicals were ranked by the strength they unlocked. A lime based activator worked best, ahead of a silicate and a caustic soda option. Microscope views showed needle crystals and gels forming as the mix set, signs of the binding reaction. Surface blooming after water curing left pores inside, a flaw the authors flag for follow up work.
pmc-11656678:
Bor-Uei Shyr and co-authors ask in a 2024 study whether obesity worsens outcomes for robot-assisted pancreas surgery. The operation, a pancreaticoduodenectomy, is among the most demanding in general surgery. How body weight affects results with the robot route had rarely been documented.

The study covered eight hundred eighty-six patients who had either robot-assisted or open surgery. Groups were formed for obese robot cases, non-obese robot cases, and obese open cases, then matched by propensity scores. Operations took longer for obese robot patients, yet blood loss was lower in both robot groups than in open surgery. Death and complication rates stayed much the same across all three groups. Delayed stomach emptying was also less common with the robot. The authors conclude the robot route is safe for obese patients.
pmc-11656778:
Samuel Steiner and Craig Roy develop CRISPR-Cas9 tools for genetic analysis of Coxiella burnetii, in work from 2024. The bacterium grows inside host cells and uses a secretion system to send over 100 effector proteins into the cell. Directed mutation has been hard, which has blocked systematic study of those effectors and their interactions.

One method, CRISPRi, silences genes and matched known mutant effects. A second method uses cytosine base editing to create stop codons and loss-of-function mutants, even double mutants in one step. A double mutant lacking cig57 and cig2 showed a strong added growth defect. The tools widen what genetic studies of this pathogen can test.
pmc-11656878:
Hamid Reza Heidarzadeh and co-authors link eye blood flow to artery stiffness in healthy adults, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. About three hundred adults from an Iranian cohort had eye scans and artery checks. The eye scans measured tiny vessels near the center of sight, plus the clear zone at its core.

Age went with lower vessel counts in both shallow and deep eye layers. Women had higher deep-layer counts and a larger clear zone. A stiffer artery signal went with lower deep vessel counts near the center. The authors suggest eye scans may flag early artery disease.
pmc-11656978:
Shaimaa Amin and co-authors measure stress and unmet needs among caregivers of children with cancer. Their 2024 study surveys 258 caregivers at an Egyptian oncology center outpatient clinic. Two validated scales score stress and resource needs.

Average stress lands in the moderate-to-high band. Age, schooling, marital status, and income each predict stress strongly. Lower income and higher schooling both push stress up. The number of children, the child age, and time since diagnosis matter as well. Correlations between stress and needs round out the picture. The authors argue support systems must be built on what caregivers actually lack, since their strain spills into the care children receive. Their factor map tells clinics where help lands hardest.
pmc-11657178:
Shi-Yu Gao and co-authors weigh one-shot ray care in surgery next to whole-breast ray care for early breast cancer. The study appeared in 2024. The one-shot form is a handy pick for fit cases. A 2023 guide sorts cases as fit, half-fit, or unfit for part-breast rays.

Over seven hundred cases from five years of care fed the read, with near five years of checks. In the fit group, flare-back rates sat near two in a hundred for both forms. In the half-fit and unfit groups, one-shot rates ran clear high, near eleven and fourteen in a hundred. The guide's sort held up in the split.
pmc-11657278:
Sornpaisarn and a large team of co-authors wrote this paper in twenty twenty-four on teamwork against long-term diseases in Thailand. Such diseases are a top health threat, and beating them needs action beyond the health sector. Thailand had a ten-year joint plan led by the prime minister, yet not one meeting was held in that time. The authors set out to build a fresh approach that might work better.

Their plan rests on three ideas. It seeks commitment from middle managers rather than top leaders. It produces research aimed at specific, reachable policies. It uses knowledge brokers to keep ministries in real contact. Officials from the farm, finance, and education ministries agreed to join and picked target policies. The paper also lays out the study that will test the approach.
pmc-11657378:
Older adults with cancer often carry other health problems that shape which treatments they can handle. Sharon He, Heather Shepherd, Meera Agar, and Joanne Shaw gathered the review evidence in 2024 on whether full geriatric assessments improve outcomes for these patients.

The umbrella review covered 26 systematic reviews across six databases. Weaknesses found by assessment predicted most outcomes studied, though the exact domains that mattered varied from review to review. Patients whose care included an assessment plus follow-up management had lower treatment toxicity than those on standard care. pmc-11657578:

The team asked how place, social traits, and milk habits shape knowledge, attitudes, and views of that risk. Such traits vary a lot between lands and groups. The aim is a clear map of where buyers are well informed and where gaps leave them exposed, to guide public health work in each setting.
pmc-11657678:
The authors build a drug-loaded gel meant to fight myeloma where it hides: inside damaged bone. Multiple myeloma fills bone marrow with malignant plasma cells and eats holes in bone in eighty percent of patients. Cells that survive treatment shelter in those lesions and block healing. A local material could brace the bone and bathe the hiding cells in drug doses the whole body could never tolerate.

Their xerogels blend silica and collagen into a dry implant. One version slowly releases bortezomib, a standard myeloma drug. Lab tests tracked the release with precision instruments and checked effects on bone-building and bone-eating cells. Animal work followed, in rats and in a myeloma mouse model, with imaging and tissue checks. The authors present the gels as a candidate platform for treating bone lesions and leftover disease in one move.
pmc-11657778:
Ilyes Benhalima and co-authors report, in a 2024 case study, a meningitis case whose culprit hid from every standard test. A seventy-three-year-old man with past throat and food-pipe cancers arrived with sudden fever and confusion. Early cultures and scans found nothing, and first antibiotics failed to help.

Fluid from a spinal tap teemed with white cells, and a stain hinted at a common meningitis germ, but panel tests stayed negative. Only gene sequencing of the fluid named the true cause: Gemella, a mouth bacterium that rarely invades the brain. With continued targeted antibiotics the patient improved. The authors review past Gemella cases and urge sequencing when routine tests stall.
pmc-11657978:
Yucao Sun and colleagues combine sound-based therapy with copper-driven cell death against liver cancer. Their study from twenty twenty-four builds drug-loaded nanobubbles. Sonodynamic therapy uses sound to activate a drug inside tumours. Tumour antioxidants blunt that attack by soaking up reactive molecules.

Copper ions consume those antioxidants and stress the tumour. Extra copper also triggers a distinct death route called cuproptosis. The bubbles carry a sound activator and a tumour-seeking peptide. Gene profiling traced how the combined therapy rewires tumours. Immune checkpoint treatment worked better after this reprogramming. Two death routes attacking together may beat resistant liver tumours.
pmc-11659278:
Shitou Xia, Fernando, and Junxing Lu introduce a research topic on soilborne fungal diseases in a 2024 editorial. Fungi living in soil cause wilting, stunting, and death across many crops, and they persist without a host, which makes them hard to beat. Understanding their survival and spread is the first step to control.

The editors summarize the topic's four research articles and three reviews. Two studies on the Ganoderma genus open the collection, with further work on systematics, pathogenesis, and greener control methods. Molecular and genomic tools thread through the issue. The editorial frames a field moving from chemical dependence toward biological control of stubborn soil diseases.
pmc-11659678:
Cornelius and co-authors test in 2024 whether captive finches respond to short food shortages differently by season, and whether watching others helps. Winter threatens songbirds with cold and scarce food. They compared red crossbills and pine siskins under timed feeding limits in summer and late winter, tracking body mass change as the main response measure.

Both species lost less mass during late winter restrictions than in summer. Social information did not vary by season: crossbills benefited from observing food-restricted flockmates in both periods. The results suggest seasonal tuning of the stress response to food shortage. Behavior and body state together maintain balance.
pmc-11661678:
Hila Ariela Dafny and six co-authors interview the teachers who supervise nursing students on clinical placement about violence from patients and others. Eleven clinical facilitators in South Australia spoke in hour-long interviews during late 2022. Violence against students came in verbal and physical forms. Facilitators did not always learn that an incident had happened, and their power to repair the harm varied.

Most saw themselves as disempowered visitors in the facilities, unable to give students the backing they needed. Views also differed on what counts as violence and what is acceptable. The authors say any fix must reckon with the facilitator's weak formal authority.
pmc-11662678:
Yuhao Mao and co-authors study sawtooth waves in dream sleep among sleep apnea patients in a 2024 paper. Sawtooth waves are a hallmark brain pattern of rapid eye movement sleep, the stage when breathing pauses often hit hardest.

Sleep lab records came from twenty patients with moderate to severe apnea and sixteen healthy controls. Waves tied to breathing pauses were weaker than lone waves. With airway pressure treatment, wave share and strength rose to healthy levels. Wave rate did not change much. Links with deep sleep length were also checked. The work shows treatment restores a key dream sleep brain pattern in apnea.
pmc-11663378:
Dongru Du, Jianjun Luo, Weiling Cai, and six colleagues ask, published in 2024, whether sleep apnea signs track with kidney stones in American survey data. The national survey covered nearly ten thousand adults from 2015 to 2020. About one in nine reported having had a kidney stone. Three apnea signs were self-reported: snoring, snorting or stopped breathing, and daytime sleepiness. After adjusting for other risk factors, plain snoring showed no link to stones. The other two signs did.

People who often snorted or stopped breathing in sleep had about two-thirds higher odds of stones. So did people who often felt sleepy by day. Marriage and smoking status changed the strength of the breathing link. The authors stress the design: one slice in time cannot prove apnea causes stones. Still, the two stronger signs may flag patients worth screening. They call for follow-up studies that watch people over time.
pmc-11663578:
Elizabeth Robbins and Steven Kelly traced photosynthesis evolution across flowering plants in 2024. Photosynthesis powers nearly all life here. Photosystems start the light conversion process. Their parts are encoded in plastid DNA. Hundreds of species were compared residue by residue.

More than seven hundred species were included. Adaptive changes clustered in key spots. Some changes affected cofactor binding directly. Others reshaped contacts between protein parts. One repair protein kept changing repeatedly. Changes may ease its replacement cycle. Damaged photosystems would repair faster then. Plant adaptation paths are now clearer. Repair speed may shape plant success.
pmc-11663878:
Hollis and van Gent open a study set in twenty twenty-four on rare types of ovarian cancer. Ovarian cancer is not one disease but many, and they differ in origin, gene traits, and response to drugs. The most common type draws most research and has gained new targeted drugs in recent years.

The rarer types, by contrast, stay poorly studied and short on options, the editors argue. The set they introduce includes work on a rare and fast-growing type that mixes two cell forms. Cases, gene studies, and treatment reports in the set aim to build basic knowledge. That groundwork is needed before better targeted care can follow.
pmc-11663978:
Wiwik Dahan and co-authors present data on pulling rare earth elements from tin mine waste on Bangka Island, Indonesia, in a 2024 data paper. Rare earths feed many modern products, from batteries to phone screens. The team used froth flotation, a foam separation method, on finely ground tailings. A fatty soap like chemical collected the target minerals while another chemical held back the rest, across a range of acidity levels.

The paper reports measured shares of cerium, neodymium, and thorium in both the collected foam and the leftover tailings. It also tracks how changing the dose of the holding chemical shifted recovery. The richest cerium and neodymium catches came at one low dose, while thorium peaked with none of that chemical at all. The authors offer the data set as a new route to rare earth recovery from tin waste.
pmc-11664278:
Ziping Ai and co-authors published a research paper in 2024 comparing four ways to dry gardenia fruit, a plant used as food and herbal medicine for pain, pressure, and inflammation. Drying shapes both shelf quality and active ingredient content. The team tested hot air, infrared, pulsed vacuum, and radio-frequency-assisted hot air.

The vacuum and radio methods opened tiny channels inside the fruit that let moisture escape, cutting drying time by roughly a third to two fifths. They also kept more of the key compound geniposide and preserved color better. Radio-frequency hot air gave the strongest antioxidant activity and the richest active ingredients overall. The authors recommend it for industrial gardenia processing.
pmc-11664478:
Rhubarb root has been used in Chinese medicine against tumors for thousands of years, and its anthraquinone compounds are the suspected active part. Linyuan Yu and four co-authors review what is known about these compounds against liver cancer. They search three major databases for work on effects, signaling pathways, toxicity, and how the body handles the compounds.

Five anthraquinones, including emodin and rhein, show anti-liver-cancer activity, marking them as possible drug leads. The catch is toxicity: the same compounds can harm the body, which has slowed deeper study. The authors call for work that finds the balance point between benefit and harm, and for stronger experiments overall. The review appears in 2024.
pmc-11664578:
Hannah Buttner and co-authors show in 2024 how a helpful soil fungus kills predatory worms that attack crops. The fungus is already used as a biocontrol agent, but how it fought worms was a riddle. The team found it makes soapy peptide compounds, malpinins, in large amounts. Tests with natural and lab-made versions showed one unusual building block is key to the killing power.

Glow-tagged versions let them watch the compounds travel into the worm's gut and gather there. The work solves the riddle and explains the fungus's protective value in soil. It may guide greener crop protection that borrows the fungus's own chemistry.
pmc-11665178:
Surgeons in Iran tracked how many knee patients got back to their old activity level after ligament repair. The ligament at stake, the ACL, tears often in sport and can lead to early joint wear if care is poor. The study used the patient own hamstring tendon as the graft, a common choice. Staff then polled activity and fear of movement over 18 months of follow-up.

The group held 76 patients with a mean age near 26 years, about two in five of them female. Fear of movement split the results sharply. Of patients with such fear, just one in eight got back to full activity. Of those with no fear, near all did. Activity scores dipped at six months, then rose by the last check. The team urges fear screening as part of rehab.
pmc-11665478:
Ürün and co-authors ask whether body weight at diagnosis predicts survival in advanced lung cancer, in a 2024 single-center study. They reviewed 289 patients with metastatic non-small cell lung cancer treated from 2010 to 2017. Patients were split at a body mass index of 25. Survival models weighed weight alongside diagnosis type and response to first treatment.

Patients with the higher index lived longer, with predicted survival of 13.0 months against 9.3 months for the leaner group. Weight, tumor type, and full response to first-line therapy each predicted survival on their own. The pattern fits the obesity paradox reported in other cancers. The authors treat body mass as a useful prognostic sign and call for larger prospective studies.
pmc-11666378:
Alex Chauca-Cerrutti and four co-authors optimize a green method for extracting oil from lucuma seeds. Their study is from two thousand twenty-four. Lucuma is a fruit whose seeds are usually thrown away, yet their oil holds antioxidants prized for health. The method uses carbon dioxide squeezed to a fluid-like state, which leaves no solvent residue.

They varied heat, pressure, and gas flow in a planned set of runs. Two modeling styles were compared: a classic response surface and a neural network tuned by a genetic search. Both fit the data well, and the network fit slightly better. The best settings recovered about ninety-seven percent of the seed's oil. That oil beat solvent-extracted oil on several quality measures and held more healthy fats.
pmc-11666478:
Schütz and co-authors report strong survival in men whose prostate cancer had spread to only a few sites at diagnosis. Care for spread disease usually leans on hormone therapy, newer hormone drugs, and chemotherapy, while surgery's role stays debated. Their 2024 review covers 43 men at one center who all had the prostate removed as part of a tailored multi-pronged plan.

Thirteen men who combined surgery, hormone therapy, radiation, and targeted treatment of spread sites saw no cancer deaths over up to ten years. Ten men who needed chemotherapy fared far worse on both progression and survival. A middle group getting fewer combined treatments landed in between, without clear statistical separation. The authors call for markers that sort patients by risk.
pmc-11667178:
Martin Hallbeck and co-authors find Parkinson's-linked protein damage in the liver of a mouse model of the disease, in a study from 2024. The protein alpha-synuclein clumps in the brain in Parkinson's, but clumps also turn up in a few organs outside it. The liver's part in handling that burden was unclear.

Livers from mice carrying a human disease mutation carried the same chemical edits on the protein that mark it in patients. Human liver cells in dishes added those edits when fed protein fibers, and slowly broke the fibers down. A stickier form, small clumps, resisted breakdown unless cell recycling was boosted. The authors suggest the liver helps detoxify this protein, a possible support route in the disease.
pmc-11667778:
Eight reviewers in China examine the sugar code on the surface of cancer stem cells, in a review published in 2024. Cells coat their proteins with sugar chains whose patterns carry information, much like a code. Proteins that read the code steer cell talk, immune response, and disease course. Cancer stem cells, the stubborn seeds of tumors, show altered sugar patterns as their metabolism shifts.

The review explains the main ways sugars attach to proteins and the letters of the sugar alphabet. It then traces how changed coatings help tumors grow, dodge immune attack, and spread. Enzymes that build or trim the sugars rise and fall in cancer, driving those changes. The authors argue that cracking the sugar code could expose weak points in cancer stem cells. That knowledge may guide drugs aimed at the cells that regrow tumors after treatment.
pmc-11668278:
Giada Vanacore, Jens Bager Christensen, and Sumru Bayin wrote this 2024 review on why young brains heal better than old ones. A baby mammal's brain can replace lost cells with ease. Adult brains, by contrast, often lose tissue for good after injury. Stem cells in the brain change with age, and the tissue around them grows hostile, with swelling and scarring.

The review walks through how the young brain mounts repair after injury or cell loss. It then lists the age-linked changes that blunt each step. Gene marks lock stem cells down, while the aged setting blocks fresh growth. The authors close with treatment ideas that might lift those brakes. The piece maps a path toward helping adult brains rebuild.
pmc-11668778:
Hong and ten co-authors isolate a predatory bacterium from fish pond water, in work from twenty twenty-four. Fish farms lose stock heavily to bacterial disease. Sustainable, non antibiotic disease control is a pressing need for aquaculture.

Bdellovibrio bacteriovorus is a bacterium that hunts and kills other bacteria. A strain, designated FWA, was isolated from pond water and characterized in the laboratory. A living predator that targets pathogens could protect farmed fish without drug residues. Characterization covers its prey range and growth traits, the first facts needed before any pond trial can be designed.
pmc-11668978:
Jacques-Henri Veyron and co-authors test an alert system meant to keep very old people out of hospital. Their 2024 trial ran in seven assisted living homes in France. Care staff filled in a phone questionnaire on each resident, and a learning system scored the risk of a near-term crisis.

Of 194 eligible residents, 118 joined and had at least one check. The system raised 92 alerts for 47 people. Half the alerts led to care steps, and those cases ended in few hospital stays. The other half, with no steps taken, led to many more stays. The authors read this as early proof the alerts can guide timely care for frail residents in such homes.
pmc-11669878:
A large research team built EyeGPT, a language model tuned for eye care, in this 2024 study. General chat models often lack deep knowledge of a narrow field like ophthalmology, the study of the eye. EyeGPT starts from a general model called Llama2. The team reshaped it to answer patient questions and support medical teaching.

Three moves did the reshaping: role-play prompts, fine-tuning on about eighty-four thousand eye-related samples, and lookup in a medical database plus fourteen eye textbooks. Four eye doctors graded answers to one hundred twenty questions, simple and complex. They scored accuracy, clarity, trust, and empathy, and counted made-up answers. The best version beat the base model and is compared with doctors alone and doctors aided by the model.
pmc-11669978:
Thirugnanasambandan Sunder, writing solo in 2024, reflects on recent articles about restarting the heart. His letter ranges over two papers on cardiac arrest. One covers machines that pump the chest automatically in hostile settings like moving vehicles or disaster zones. The other presents a model that predicts outcomes after arrests outside hospital.

He traces how resuscitation evolved over centuries into modern practice, and notes how slowly the medical community sometimes adopts techniques that clearly work. In-hospital and out-of-hospital arrests get separate attention, along with current guidelines and strategies that raise survival. He closes by pointing at open questions for future research. Letters like this are how a field talks to itself: a veteran reader connecting new papers to old lessons and naming what to study next.
pmc-11670078:
Lea Youssef Baby and four co-workers review two ways to probe the body with small electric currents. One way builds pictures of tissue. The next probes how muscle acts. Both send a tiny current in and note how tissue reacts at distinct pitch bands. The 2024 review maps the past, the present, and the likely path ahead for both ways.

Silver chloride pads are the most used type. Staff most often send current in, since that route copes with worn pads best. New kits have moved to digital capture with sources that work at more than one pitch. The review sets side by side the math used to build pictures and the kits on sale. The picture method helps find growths and watch lung health. The muscle method serves to find and track nerve and muscle disease. The part played by machine learning grows in both fields.
pmc-11670978:
Xuanyin Cui and co-authors test worm-derived antigens against ulcerative colitis in mice in a 2024 study. Ulcerative colitis is a chronic bowel inflammation with unknown cause and hard treatment. Some worms and their products are known to calm inflammatory diseases, a paradox that researchers are learning to use.

The effect ran through a signaling path that promotes intestinal stem cell growth. The findings support parasite-inspired therapies for bowel disease.
pmc-11671478:
Shiqi Chen and nine co-authors build machine learning models to predict stroke after heart bypass surgery. Bypass grafting treats blocked heart arteries, but a stroke afterward can harm long-term recovery. Their 2024 study hunts for warning signs present before and after the operation.

Records came from 1,200 patients treated at Wuhan Union Hospital between 2016 and 2022. The team gathered 33 pre-surgery traits and four post-surgery complications for each patient. A selection method narrowed the list, and six learning models were trained and compared. A tool called SHAP explained which traits drove each prediction. The group also released a free online calculator so clinicians can estimate a patient's risk quickly.
pmc-11671878:
British military casualties in Afghanistan often developed pressure sores at the back of the head while lying on the standard service stretcher. Pain is not injury, but it offers a first guide where no guideline existed. Twenty-six healthy service members lay motionless until pain or discomfort stopped the test.

Twenty of them first felt pressure pain at the back of the head, after about thirty-one minutes on average. The rest stopped for aches from the awkward position itself. Women were more sensitive to pain, but the time until head pain was similar for both sexes. The authors suggest repositioning patients who cannot move themselves well before the half hour mark.
pmc-11672478:
Aminu Yusuf and Sedat Ballikaya studied a small power system for remote sensors in two thousand twenty-four. Sensors at sea or in the wild need durable power with little upkeep. Their system combines a thermoelectric generator, which makes electricity from heat gaps, with a phase change material that stores heat.

They added a heat sink coated to radiate heat to the sky, which cools one side of the generator. The combined design gave a ten-fold gain over radiative cooling alone. The melting point of the phase change material proved key for night operation, since it must release stored energy then. On a summer day the system reached its best power density in Istanbul among three cities tested.
pmc-11672578:
Taichi Aono and co-authors mine the skin of a Japanese island frog for defensive peptides, and turn one assay toward detecting bacterial toxins. Frog skin is a rich source of host defense peptides, small proteins that kill microbes. Their 2024 paper clones the genes for nine such peptides from Tago's brown frog of Yakushima, spanning known families plus one new peptide they name yakushimin.

Lab-made versions of the peptides were tested against bacteria, fungi signals, and cell harm. One brevinin peptide killed Staphylococcus aureus, and two peptides visibly warped the cells of common bacteria. Several also attacked rice and plant pathogens in dose-dependent fashion. The team further built a detection system for bacterial endotoxin in serum based on peptide binding. The work joins natural-product discovery with a practical diagnostic, both drawn from one small frog's skin chemistry.
pmc-11672978:
Jillian Stafford and four co-authors asked if a leader tail kills the punch of a natural peptide. Their study, from twenty twenty-four, deals with microviridins, a clan of made then trimmed peptides. Such goods draw eyes for library screens of new drug leads. Screens run best if the leader tail can stay on. The team made lead forms with the tail kept in a lab bacterium.

They then read if the forms still block elastase, a cut enzyme, by a glow test. Decay was tracked by fine liquid reads. Readers who hunt peptide drugs learn if this clan can be screened tail on, which saves a trim step per test.
pmc-11673078:
Raina, Samuel, and Fuchs test a plant soap as a switch for a guard gene in cells in this twenty twenty-four study. Swell storms drive long ills when the body can't curb its rage scents. One gene switch can curb those scents by cross-talk with a core swell path.

Dock sims show the soap could grip the switch much like a known drug does. A dye race test found no grip, so the true bind spot stays to be firm. The team casts the soap's calm as a fresh route in print.
pmc-11673378:
Pedro Gil-LaOrden and co-authors test the place of guilt in burnout in a 2024 study. Burnout grows from long work stress and can bring body complaints with no clear cause. In the other, complaints come first and guilt last. The first model fit the data well and the rival fit poorly. The authors urge care teams to weigh guilt when they assess burnout.
pmc-11673478:
Yu-Ling Wu and twelve co-authors published a neuroprotection study in twenty twenty-four on a mushroom extract against spinocerebellar ataxia type 3. The inherited disease comes from a stretched repeat in the ataxin-3 protein, which clumps in neurons and weakens antioxidant defenses. The extract, from lion's mane mycelium, is rich in a compound called erinacine A.

In cell models it boosted antioxidant power and cellular cleanup, lowering the mutant protein and its aggregates. The mechanism ran through Nrf2, the master switch for detoxification genes. The authors propose the extract as a candidate therapy worth clinical exploration.
pmc-11673578:
Josef Boronski, Agamemnon Crumpton, and Simon Aldridge report a new nickel compound in a 2024 chemistry paper. Nickel in high valence states is thought to appear briefly in industrial reactions and in enzyme cycles. A few four-valent forms had been captured in crystals, but nothing higher had been identified.

The team made a stable crystal by inserting zero-valent nickel into three beryllium bonds. The product is a sixteen-electron compound with an inverted ligand field and a defined threefold shape. Capturing such a species in solid form lets chemists test ideas about how high-valent nickel behaves in real reactions.
pmc-11673778:
Li Zeng, Xiaojun Zhou, Yuge Lei, and Jiayan Chen study depression in drug users. Their work from twenty twenty-four deals with illicit drug use in Hubei, China. Depression is a common ill among such users.

A random sample of users filled four scored forms. Forms covered addiction memory, family life, mood, and self esteem. Model tests asked if self esteem sits between the other traits. Strong addiction memory went with more depression in the group. Good family life went with less depression instead. Self esteem carried part of both of those links.
pmc-11673878:
Jeffrey Wang and co-authors check if blood fats and swelling move together in schizophrenia, in a 2024 paper. High triglycerides and body wide swelling are common in this group and raise heart risk. In the general public those fats link to swelling, but whether they link in schizophrenia was unclear.

The team tested fasting fats, cholesterol forms, and many swelling markers in 147 patients on long term antipsychotic drugs and 56 matched healthy peers. Patients had higher fats and clear signs of swelling. Yet the fats did not track the swelling markers in patients as they do in other groups. That discord hints that heart risk in schizophrenia may run on apart paths.
pmc-11673978:
Hao Chen and a large team of co-authors test in 2024 whether late-life alcohol exposure worsens memory decline in mice. Alcohol is thought to affect Alzheimer's risk, possibly through a cell cleanup pathway. That pathway is controlled by a factor that boosts waste disposal genes in the brain.

Young and aged mice were fed alcohol in two patterns, then checked with lab and behavior tests. Aged mice had lower activity of the factor and worse maze memory. Alcohol did not worsen the age-related drop in the factor. It slightly impaired memory in young mice only, the authors report.
pmc-11674278:
Jose Roberto Alegretti and co-authors grow mouse, cow, and human embryos in gently flowing microfluidic chips and find they develop better than in still drops, in work from twenty twenty-four. Wombs and fallopian tubes are moving fluids, while lab culture sits static. Whether flow helps across species was untested.

A randomized trial cultured hundreds of fertilized eggs per species both ways. Flowing culture improved development in mouse and cow embryos. In human sibling eggs, it raised cell counts at the cleavage stage, cut cell fragmentation and death, and lifted blastocyst formation and quality. A placental gene marker also shifted. Media, temperature, and gas were held equal, so flow itself gets the credit.
pmc-11674378:
Luis Larrea Murillo, Conor Sugden, Bela Ozsvari, and four colleagues characterize an odd hybrid state in breast cancer stem cells in this two thousand twenty-four paper. Cancer stem cells are rare but drive progression, spread, and treatment resistance, and high aldehyde dehydrogenase activity marks them. The team isolated human breast cancer cells with high versus low enzyme levels and compared their traits in depth.

In metabolism they were revved up, with more mitochondrial DNA and mass and higher mitochondrial and glycolytic activity. pmc-11674578:
Erika Novoa-Bolivar and a large team test whether cell counts in lung wash fluid can forecast the course of interstitial lung disease. Their twenty twenty-four article uses bronchoalveolar lavage, which samples the deep lung. Flow cytometry gives fast, exact counts of lymphocytes and neutrophils in that fluid.

Over a thousand real-life patients were studied, with their scans, pathology, lung function, and outcomes. Two cut-offs split patients into three risk groups. The favorable group, with more lymphocytes and fewer neutrophils, lived far longer than the unfavorable group. pmc-11674678:
Ran Pu and nine co-authors study color-linked chemistry in an orchid used in medicine, in a paper from 2024. The plant comes in a green form and a purple-red form, and both are rich in plant compounds tied to health effects. The team asks why color and chemistry differ by form and stem age.

They paired chemical profiling with gene activity maps for half-year and full-year stems. They found hundreds of color compounds, with two pigment groups dominant in the red form. High activity in pigment-making genes explained the color shift. They name key genes and control switches that likely steer the pathway.
pmc-11674878:
Marta Sannino and co-authors explore whether creative thinking in children tracks with greener behavior, in a 2024 study. The environmental crisis will shape the lives of today's children. Values and beliefs behind green action are well studied. The role of thinking style is less settled. Divergent thinking means generating many varied ideas.

The team measured divergent thinking and pro-environmental behaviors in children. They also tested whether the link differs for boys and girls. Gender turned out to moderate the association. The study adds a cognitive angle to a field led by attitudes. Child psychologists gain a fresh hypothesis to test.
pmc-11675178:
Cracking eggs to measure them wastes the product, and a research team showed that scan images plus deep learning can take the measures whole, in work from twenty twenty-four. Height, width, shell depth, and volume came out of the cut images. Scores reached near full agreement with hand measures. The method suits farms and labs that grade eggs at scale: no breakage, fast runs, and repeatable numbers. The team frames scan-plus-learning as a stand-in for the calipers and the cracked shell.
pmc-11675278:
Andre Bovell and co-authors price the care of cervical cancer in Antigua and Barbuda in a 2024 study. The disease ranks among the top five cancers for women in the twin-island state, yet its costs had never been counted.

Patient records from four sites covering 2017 to 2021 fed a prevalence-based cost study. Total direct medical costs came to about 240,000 US dollars a year. Treatment was the biggest driver, followed by care for side effects after treatment, then diagnosis. The head byline lists five names while the catalog lists six, so the count is left open here. The authors offer the figures to guide prevention spending and cost control.
pmc-11675578:
Aleksandr Kashurin and co-authors build self-set gels from two plant-and-flesh based chains and test mix grades. The study appeared in 2024. Green aims push care work to raw stuff from life. Gels from the pair had shown weak hold in past forms.

Mix grades were set by the share of charged groups on each chain. Past a set grade, gel firm strength rose four-fold next to a plain flesh-chain gel. Near that grade, gels drank more water and drank it fast. They also stood up to salt baths with a rot aid far past weak forms. Salt baths and gut-like baths held their swell down.
pmc-11675878:

Band patterns then show each strain's toxin profile. The authors also report how often each toxin gene appeared. Hospital labs gain a low-cost tool for surveillance. Infection control teams can act sooner on risky strains.
pmc-11675978:
Wenna Yao and co-authors compared gut microbes and chemistry in two sheep breeds in 2024 to ask why one resists disease better. Hu sheep are hardy, while East Friesian sheep give much milk but fall ill more easily.

The gut flora and chemistry differed between the breeds at this age, when diarrhea risk is highest. Such differences may help explain the hardiness gap, and could point to microbes that support disease resistance in farm animals.
pmc-11676078:
Liu and co-authors build glowing terbium compounds with a twist in a 2024 study. The goal is bright green light that spins in a set direction, a trait valued for displays and sensors. Their design pairs three light-harvesting arms with a handed helper molecule around one terbium center. Two mirror forms of the compound were made and checked.

The arms drank in light strongly and fed it to the metal with high yield. The glow came out pure green, and its spin bias was clear and steady. Combined brightness scores topped six hundred units, a strong mark for this class. The authors offer the pairing trick as a route to better handed light sources.
pmc-11676478:
Ulrike Steiner and Erich-Christian Oerke used microscopes to re-examine how the apple scab fungus feeds, in a 2024 study. The fungus was classed as a half-and-half feeder, living off live cells first and dead cells later. Their close views of infected apple leaves told a different story: the fungus stays a live-cell feeder throughout.

They saw knob-like pads pressed to leaf cells within a day of entry, and thin fan cells spreading through the cell's hollow. The fungus slips enzymes through the leaf skin and reshapes host cells into transfer cells that stream food toward it. The pair model this as a blend of live feeding and scavenging, with no killing stage at all.
pmc-11676678:
Bibi Aliya Seelarbokus and four co-authors measured addictive-like eating in patients recovering from a first minor or moderate stroke at a French hospital. Diet is a known stroke risk factor, but disordered eating itself is rarely studied in this group. The team screened 101 patients over four months with the Yale Food Addiction Scale, then tested links with obesity, high blood pressure, cholesterol problems, and diabetes.

Five percent of patients met the full diagnosis of food addiction. Far more, 38.6 percent, showed at least one symptom, most often feeling unable to cut down. Cholesterol problems were the only risk factor tied to the diagnosis itself. A more severe addictive profile was also tied to cholesterol problems and to diabetes. The authors present the study as an early look at a neglected corner of stroke care.
pmc-11676778:
Immacolata Rulli and co-authors review steroid use in child septic shock in a 2024 paper. Septic shock in kids can shrug off fluids and heart drugs. Guides then leave steroid picks to the doctor's call. The team swept ten years of work, 63 papers from 399 finds. Death and grade marks face off across the set. One big review backs a death cut; next reads show flat or worse marks.

Ward stay may shrink with one steroid form. Harm marks run mild: weak limbs, high salt, high sugar. Gland tests fail to call who gains. A side group with weak glands may gain most, the team say. Firm rules wait on that call.
pmc-11676878:
Sahsikala Thangasparan and four co-authors review how oxidized low-density lipoprotein drives cardiovascular disease, in a two thousand twenty-four evidence review. Atherosclerosis, the plaque disease behind most heart deaths, begins with harm to vessel linings and inflammation.

Oxidized LDL stirs both innate and adaptive immunity and sustains the inflammatory signaling, with molecules such as interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor alpha, that grows plaques. The review gathers cell culture and animal evidence pathway by pathway, noting where the map of workings still has gaps. Because oxidized LDL sits at the center of triggering and maintaining vessel-lining injury, the authors present it as a hopeful target for more precise anti-atherosclerosis treatments.
pmc-11676978:
Huiguang Li and co-authors weigh three near-twin heat guard genes in a wild shrub. The study appeared in 2024. The genes came from past copy events but now read quite apart in code. All three sit in the cell core of the plant.

Plants of a lab species with extra copies of two of the genes beat wild plants in heat. The third gene's boost did near nothing for heat strength. In shrub sprouts, all three raised the call of six heat genes, but to distinct degrees. One gene was the top driver on most counts. Swap tests in yeast cells bore out the split in strength.
pmc-11677178:
Arzu Şahin Mantı and co-authors test how rinse fluids used in root canal care affect a repair material's grip in a 2024 study. The repair paste, called MTA, must bond well to the filling placed over it. Five rinse options were compared, some based on chitosan, a natural polymer.

Sixty paste samples were split into six groups, one for each rinse plus plain water. After a five-minute soak, each sample got a filling and its bond strength was measured. One common rinse, EDTA, gave the weakest bond and ate into the surface. Chitosan mixed with a germ-killing rinse gave the strongest bond and left the surface intact. Most breaks happened inside the paste itself, not at the joint.
pmc-11677378:
Mengjun Xiao, Tao Wang, Chuyu Tang, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2024. It tracks how the fats inside Cordyceps sinensis, a prized medicinal fungus, change under four ways of handling: fresh, freeze-dried, oven-dried, and air-dried.

Drying decides how well the fungus keeps its useful compounds, yet its fat profile had barely been studied. Using a sensitive mass-based method, the team cataloged 765 distinct fat species. One broad class, the membrane fats, was most abundant, followed by storage fats and signaling fats. Nearly nine in ten of the cataloged fats shifted in amount between treatments, with storage fats most concentrated. The authors say the map helps producers pick drying methods that protect quality, for uses in food and medicine.
pmc-11677578:
Nan Li and co-authors trace how a pest weevil's immune system answers attack by a fungal parasite in this 2024 study. The weevil damages alfalfa crops, and the fungus Beauveria bassiana is used as a living pest control. Knowing how the insect fights back could sharpen that control.

The team infected weevils and sampled gene activity and small molecules at three times after infection. Gene data showed a broad immune boost touching energy use, detox pathways, cell cleanup, and programmed cell death. Chemical data found whole families of fats and acids rising in response. Matching the two datasets linked key genes to key chemicals, and network analysis named hub genes for each stage, including sensors that spot invaders and enzymes that clear poisons. Two processes, self-eating of cell parts and a fatty acid pathway, stood out as central to the defense.
pmc-11677978:
Miguel Rincón-Cervera and co-authors wrote a 2024 paper on turning an invasive seaweed into a farm resource. The brown alga has spread across the western Mediterranean and harms local ecosystems. Yet it holds useful compounds: alginate for gels, mannitol, and a family of plant-boosting tannins.

The team collected the alga on the Spanish coast and tested extraction recipes, varying time, heat, and mix ratios in a planned design. The best yields reached about twenty-nine grams of alginate and twelve grams of mannitol per hundred grams of alga. Turning a pest into feedstock for biofertilizers and soil cleanup could pay for its removal. The study pins down the conditions that get the most from each batch.
pmc-11678178:
Lisa Borgatti and co-authors give in 2024 a math method to gauge how thick a landslide is from height data shot from space. True depth is a core need for hazard calls and safety work. Mass balance turns the depth task into a reverse math task with many fits.

Their fix picks smooth fits and tunes the trade off with a balance rule. Fake data sets with known depth test the method at split noise loads. It held up well as noise rose. On a real slide in Alaska, the depth map matched past geology reads, which backs its field worth.
pmc-11678478:
Ao Gu and co-authors study how chronic oxidative stress builds stress granules in ALS neurons carrying a UBQLN2 mutation, published in 2024. The gene helps cells clear damaged proteins and guards against oxidative stress. In motor neurons grown from patient stem cells, the disease picture included misplaced TDP-43 protein, more cell death, and weaker survival.

A chemical stressor triggered the formation of stress granules, droplet-like assemblies tied to stalled protein production. Faulty recycling of cell waste made the degeneration worse. Two treatments, one that halts protein production and a cancer drug, cut the buildup of tagged waste proteins and eased the damage. The authors read the findings as a map of how stress and granule biology drive this form of ALS, with drug targets along the way.
pmc-11678778:
Berenika Szczęśniak-Sięga and six co-authors published a 2024 chemistry study on a new family of anti inflammatory compounds and how they meet cell membranes. The molecules belong to the 1,2-benzothiazine family, chemical cousins of some established pain drugs. Any drug candidate must cross lipid membranes, calm inflammation, and avoid excess harm.

The team tested how the compounds interact with model phospholipid membranes, a stand in for cell walls. Enzyme assays and computer docking measured their blocking of the two cyclooxygenase enzymes and their selectivity between them. Cell tests tracked inflammatory signal genes, and standard assays measured antioxidant power against free radicals. Quantum calculations rounded out the profile. The combined data rank the family members as starting points for safer anti inflammatory drugs.
pmc-11678878:
Yash Brahmbhatt leads a team on severe gum disease and cognitive decline. Their study from twenty twenty-four uses US survey data. Gum disease is a progressive swelling ill of the mouth.

It disturbs mouth germs and spills swelling signals to the body. Data came from adults aged sixty-five and older in the survey. Severe gum disease was set by a standard case definition. Models tested links between gum disease and mind scores. An enzyme tied to swelling was checked as a modifier. Each mind score point cut gum disease odds slightly.
pmc-11679078:
Mingkun Feng and co-authors present a 2024 journal article on rebuilding images from compressed measurements. Deep unfolding networks turn an iterative solver into a trainable network, keeping the steps readable, but many grow heavy and leak features between stages. The team's design adds a content-aware adaptive move inside the descent step, so each stage grabs the features it actually needs.

A second version borrows the brain's memory trick, carrying deep information across stages instead of letting it fade. On standard test sets the base model beat rival methods while training more cheaply. The authors pitch the design as accuracy without the usual parameter bloat.
pmc-11679478:
Elena Ivanova and co-authors measure mercury in the fur of bats living in a quiet stretch of Russian middle taiga. Mercury ranks among the most dangerous elements for wildlife and climbs from water into land food webs. Many bats hunt over water and eat insects that began life in it, which makes them sensitive recorders of contamination. Their 2024 study samples five insect-eating species in summer habitats with little human pressure.

Mercury levels rose in a steady order across species, from about 3.3 micrograms per gram in Daubenton's bat to about 8.4 in the noctule. How each species hunts explained the ranking better than anything else: what a bat eats, and where, sets its dose. Adults carried more mercury than youngsters in the same species. The authors offer fur readings as a gentle, non-lethal way to track pollution in remote forests.
pmc-11679678:
Hilda Dinah Kyomuhimbo, Usisipho Feleni, Nils Hendrik Haneklaus, and Hendrik Gideon Brink built an enzyme-tipped sensor to detect a common disinfectant chemical in water, in this 2024 study. The chemical, CTAB, is a cationic surfactant found in many products, and its runoff can harm microbes, plants, and people. Fast field tests for it are scarce.

The team coated a carbon electrode with a zinc oxide and polyaniline mix, then anchored laccase enzymes under a thin polymer film. Light and microscopy checks confirmed each layer formed as planned. The sensor read the chemical across three wide ranges with high sensitivity and a very low detection limit. In tap water and wastewater trials, it recovered most of the known amount, showing promise for routine checks.
pmc-11679878:
Saleh Alsunaydi, Abdulaziz Alharbi, Abdulrahman Al-Soqeer, and Mohamed Motawei study how nitrogen fertilization and water deficit affect Mombasa grass, a forage cultivar. Their 2024 paper aims to improve forage production in harsh environments.

Four irrigation levels and three nitrogen doses were tested in combination. Higher irrigation gave greater fresh and dry weights across cuts, compared with deficit conditions. Under moderate stress, though, one late harvest matched the well-watered plots in dry weight. Water deficit cut the protein content of the grass significantly. The results help growers balance yield and feed quality where water is scarce.
pmc-11679978:
Anil Fastenau and co-authors argue for a stronger role for local people in the fight against leprosy. Their 2024 piece draws on case studies from Brazil, India, and Nigeria. Leprosy control is held back by stigma and by poor access to care in many places. Local action can raise awareness and help find cases early.

The authors show how community-led work cut stigma and helped people stick with treatment. They stress health teaching that fits local culture and includes all groups. Such steps can strengthen national programs and support the World Health Organization Zero Leprosy plan. Even in places with few resources, they argue, this path can bring lasting gains.
pmc-11680078:
Pietro Bellini and co-authors review whether radioactive iodine helps when thyroid cancer grows inside an ovarian tumor, in a 2024 paper. Struma ovarii is an ovarian growth made largely of thyroid tissue. Rarely, that tissue turns cancerous. Treatment then borrows from thyroid cancer care, but the rules are murky. Surgery alone may or may not suffice.

The team searched major databases for treated cases. Eleven studies met their quality checks. All were retrospective, reflecting how rare the condition is. Radioiodine's role was weighed against recurrence and survival patterns. The synthesis helps tumor boards advise patients with few precedents. It also shows where a registry could settle open questions. Rare cancer care advances through exactly such pooling.
pmc-11680178:
Nneka Vivian Iduu and co-authors published this 2024 study on a Salmonella strain that lost some of its punch. This Salmonella type spreads through poultry and sickens people worldwide. A rough-surfaced variant found on a US farm seemed weaker than its smooth kin. The team compared the two forms gene by gene to find out why.

Whole genome reads showed the pair were near twins. One change stood out: a frameshift error in a gene that helps build the germ's outer coat sugars. The error cuts the gene's protein short. In chicken embryo tests, the smooth strain killed far more embryos than the rough one. The authors link the coat defect to the drop in virulence, a clue for tracking risky strains.
pmc-11680278:
The authors study why some people fail to build protection after a hepatitis B vaccine, focusing on slow drift in gene-control marks. Their 2024 study looks at rare methylation changes in B cells, the immune cells that make antibodies. Up to ten percent of vaccinated people stay unprotected.

Samples came from forty-one responders and thirty non-responders, aged twenty-two to sixty-two. Non-responders carried more of the rare marks, mostly of the added-methyl kind. Certain chromosomes and immune-linked genes held clusters of them. Mark load also tracked with aging clocks and with a disorder score in men. The authors read failed response as partly an aging drift in gene control. They note the drift links may not drive the weak immunity itself.
pmc-11680378:
Levente Zsichla and co-authors compare four free software pipelines that stitch full virus genomes from sequencing reads, in a 2024 study. Labs lean on such tools for diagnosis and outbreak tracking, yet picking one without a head-to-head test is guesswork.

The team ran all four on fake and real HIV data sets with factory settings. All built accurate genomes when the guide sequence closely matched the sample. Two tools, shiver and SmaltAlign, stayed sturdy even when the sample's strain diverged from the guide. Run times split the field too: two finished about ten times faster than the others. The authors lay out the trade-offs in features, ease of use, and computing cost.
pmc-11681278:
Denise Reis Costa and five co-authors published this study in 2024. It describes how immune checkpoint drugs were used for skin melanoma across Norway after the drugs entered care between 2014 and 2017. Norway has some of the highest melanoma rates in the world, so the stakes are high.

Using national registries, the team tracked 2,083 adults who got these drugs through 2021. Nearly half started on one drug, nivolumab, for disease that had spread. Real-world patients were older than trial patients and more often had cancer in the brain. About one in five would have been barred from the trials because of other immune diseases. The authors note that this gap raises fair questions about how well trial results carry over to everyday patients.
pmc-11681378:
Carina Zhang-Petersen and co-authors trace US breast cancer patterns after a 2009 screening guideline change, in a 2024 study. The task force shift cooled mammography use, and critics feared later-stage finds and heavier surgery. The team mined a national cancer registry from 2004 to 2019.

The cohort held just over two million women aged forty and up. In situ cancer rates, the earliest form, fell after the change in the tracked data. Stage-by-stage rates and the mix of surgeries, partial removal, full removal, and full removal with rebuilding, were charted by age band. The study gives the screening debate a long, population-wide ledger instead of clinic anecdotes.
pmc-11682778:
Mostafa El-Sayed El-Sheikh and co-authors survey, in a 2024 study, a contagious cattle disease in Egypt's Gharbia governorate. Infectious bovine rhinotracheitis, caused by a herpes virus, costs dairy farms worldwide through illness, lost calves, and breeding trouble. The team compared smallholder farms with commercial ones, none of which vaccinated against the virus.

Blood from four hundred animals, mostly cattle with some buffalo, was tested for antibodies. About twenty-two percent carried them, with rates a bit higher on traditional farms than commercial ones. Winter carried far higher odds than autumn. Young stock showed more exposure than adults, and animals in open free-stall housing or with recent breathing trouble were hit more. The authors urge a proper vaccination program to shield the dairy trade.
pmc-11683578:
Kamau and MacNaughton read Kenya's model health coverage program through a human rights lens. Makueni County's scheme, MakueniCare, is widely praised as a working path to universal coverage, the United Nations goal for 2030. Their 2024 study draws on international, national, and county law plus thirty interviews with officials and civil society leaders.

Key principles come from a global covenant on social rights and Kenya's 2010 constitution, above all the right to health. The analysis traces how those principles shaped both the program's adoption and its daily running. The authors close with ways the scheme could hew closer to its rights roots. They present the county as a lesson in rights-driven health policy.
pmc-11684878:
Fraser Barbour, John Hayes, and Ahmad Khalifa report an unusual urology case in 2024: an elderly man inserted a pencil into his urethra, where it became lodged. Foreign body insertion is uncommon in urology practice. It can cause bleeding, infection, blocked urine flow, and tearing that later scars into a narrowing of the passage.

Under regional anesthesia, the team removed the pencil with forceps. Camera checks showed a false passage torn in the urethra wall. A catheter was placed over a guidewire and left for six weeks to let the tissue heal. The patient later developed a urinary infection needing extended intravenous antibiotics. The title admits there was no single right way.
pmc-11685278:
Jin-Hong Yoo introduces the contents of a journal issue dated 30 December 2024 in this editorial summary. The issue holds one review and four original research articles. Rather than a study of its own, the piece walks through each article in turn, giving the main question, the data, and the headline result. It serves as a guided table of contents for readers of the journal.

The first summary covers a study of a tumour protein in 229 surgically removed small intestine cancers, where high levels meant better survival. The second looks at genetic testing in 1,554 Korean patients with suspected heart muscle disease, which found disease-causing variants in over forty percent. Later summaries take up caesarean delivery on request and other topics. The piece lets busy clinicians scan the issue's worth in a few minutes.
pmc-11688078:
Li Yang and co-authors published a study in 2024 on a mucus gene and coal workers' lung scarring disease. The team compared healthy men, dust-exposed workers, and patients at two disease stages, over five hundred Han Chinese men in all. Three variants in the MUC5B gene were typed, and the gene's activity in blood cells was measured.

Two variants showed no link to disease. The third variant's forms appeared more often in patients, and those same forms came with lower gene activity. Patients' gene activity ran well below that of exposed and healthy men. A cutoff test flagged the measure as a sensitive early marker. The authors suggest screening dust workers by this gene.
pmc-11688178:
Nizar Mourad and Pierre Gianello review, in a 2024 paper, a new line of pigs bred so their insulin-making cells release far more insulin. Pig islet transplants could treat diabetes, but pig cells respond weakly to sugar, so huge cell numbers are now needed. Most gene edits in donor pigs aim to calm the immune attack on the graft.

Recent work found signal pathways that amplify insulin release in pig cells, as they do in mice and humans. Pigs were bred with those pathways switched on only in insulin cells. Their islets released more insulin in the body, in the dish, and after transplant into diabetic mice. Stronger cells could cut the dose each patient needs.
pmc-11688378:
Abainash Tekola and co-authors measure disordered eating among school teens in Harar, Ethiopia, in work from 2024. Harmful eating patterns stunt teen growth and shadow adult health. Data from Ethiopia, and from this town in particular, were nearly absent.

Over 1,100 secondary students answered questionnaires in mid-2022. A standard twenty-six-item test flagged risky eating attitudes at a set score. About twenty-eight percent of students screened positive by that rule. Regression analysis sorted which background factors tracked the risk. The study gives local schools and clinics a first baseline. Screening and support planning can build on the measured rate.
pmc-11688578:
Maria Incoronata Corbo and co-authors survey hand hygiene knowledge among staff at a large Italian university hospital, in a 2024 study. Clean hands are a front-line defense against hospital infections, so gaps in knowledge matter. A 17-item questionnaire, modeled on a World Health Organization tool, drew 542 replies from about 6,749 staff, with nurses and doctors answering most.

Average knowledge landed near 74 percent, which the authors call moderate. Weak spots included correct use of hand rub and cleaning after patient contact. Longer service and certain qualifications predicted stronger knowledge. The authors link knowledge to compliance and call for steady training with feedback, tuned to the weak points the survey exposed.
pmc-11688778:
Korijna Valenti and Sara Bybee present a set of studies on the health care needs of older adults who are gay, trans, or in kin groups summed up as LGBTQIA+. The set is from two thousand twenty-four.

The studies look at bias, being made welcome, and clear talk in care. One drew on twenty trained doctors who treat the very ill, and asked how they speak with such patients and their chosen care partners. One asked care home heads in a midwest state how they find and treat such residents, and what blocks full welcome. The set argues that these older adults have needs of their own, in voice, in policy, and in daily support.
pmc-11688878:
Marjolein Broese Van Groenou and Norah Keating introduce a symposium on how older Dutch adults' social worlds and care networks shape their well-being, in this 2024 paper. Long-term care reform across western countries has shifted weight onto families, raising a practical question: can relatives organize broad care networks, and does breadth protect the person receiving care?

Three studies, all from the thirty-year Longitudinal Aging Study Amsterdam, attack the question in sequence. One asks which social network traits predict a care network rich in informal helpers. A second tests how care network types relate to psychological well-being, and whether loneliness, control, and feeling adequately cared for carry the effect. A third joins the models and asks how societal context changes the links. The editors frame the session around lessons for supporting both care recipients and their informal caregivers.
pmc-11688978:
Ryan McGrath, Kelly Parker, and Jeremy Hamm test whether finer grip measures detect cognitive impairment in older adults better than raw strength, in work published in 2024. An electronic grip device can record more than peak force. It can also capture how steadily a person holds a set force and how fast force rises.

The study covered 125 adults aged 65 and over. Thinking status was graded with a standard mental status exam. People with impairment held a grip at a quarter of their peak far less steadily than intact peers. Men with impairment also raised force more slowly.
