Peak strength itself did not differ between groups. The authors suggest the finer measures, which respond to behaviour change, may flag early decline that strength misses.
pmc-11689078:
Hae-Ra Han and co-authors measure in 2024 how much hearing loss affects older Korean immigrants in the United States, screening them through ethnic churches. Hearing loss is common with age, yet data on minority groups with limited English are thin. National samples mostly cover English speakers, and screening rarely reaches these communities.

Older Korean Americans are one of the fastest growing aging groups in the country, and many speak little English. The team worked with faith organizations in the Baltimore and Washington area. They screened community dwelling adults aged 60 and over where they already gather. Church based screening shows a way to reach elders whom clinics miss. The counts can guide hearing services in their own language.
pmc-11689178:
Jeremy Holloway tests a program that pairs trained college students with lonely older adults in the northern Midwest. His 2024 study deals with Tellegacy, a project built to cut isolation and lift wellness. Students trained in goal setting, calm focus, and listening met eleven older adults each week, in person and by phone. Life story talks formed the core of the meets, and each elder got a book of their own stories at the end.

Scores for loneliness fell, while life satisfaction and mood scores rose. Students also told of gains of their own from the meets. Holloway reads the pilot as proof the model can work and calls for larger studies of its health effects.
pmc-11689378:
Alexander Garbin presents a 2024 conference presentation summary on screening older veterans' fall risk through video visits. Primary care often lacks time for full fall assessments. The study used the veterans' health system's video platform to measure risk remotely in patients already flagged as high risk. Tests adapted for the home included a sit-to-stand measure, fear-of-falling and home-hazard surveys, and a medication review tool.

Interviews with veterans and their primary care providers explored how fall risk is currently handled and how telehealth fits. The presentation reports the prevalence of falls and risk factors found, plus the perceived barriers and facilitators of virtual assessment. Garbin argues virtual platforms can carry much of this work outside crowded clinics. The piece aims to reassure clinicians worried about safety and measurement quality at a distance.
pmc-11689478:
Niloufar Hadidi and co-authors ran this 2024 feasibility study on training community members to teach stroke prevention. African Americans face about fifty percent higher stroke risk than White Americans. Higher rates of blood pressure, diabetes, and obesity drive much of that gap. The team tested a train-the-trainer plan built around local Stroke Champions in the Minneapolis-Saint Paul area.

Twelve champions were recruited to teach warning signs, risk factors, and ways to cut risk. The team built a stroke education website for their use. Champions found the site helpful, easy, and valuable. They also said they needed more backup from the research team to deliver sessions well. The one-arm study shows the approach can run and where it needs shoring up.
pmc-11689578:
Emma Nichols and five co-authors ask, in twenty twenty-four, if the time taken on brain tests adds useful facts in surveys. Fast tests have long hinted that speed holds a signal. Surveys often record time per item but rarely use it. The team used a large India aging study with more than four thousand people. It held thirty-five test items, from simple facts to hard recall tasks.

Taking longer than the middle group linked to worse brain scores on many items. Answering fast linked to better scores on simple items. But fast answers linked to worse scores on hard items. The authors say time is worth using, but its meaning flips by task type.
pmc-11689678:
Kimberly Kennedy and six co-authors share recruitment lessons from a large aging study at two United States sites, in a 2024 paper. The study probes how muscle biology drives mobility loss after seventy. It enrolled eight hundred seventy-nine older adults. Volunteers had to walk at set speeds and tolerate biopsies and scans. Recruitment ran from twenty eighteen to twenty twenty-one, spanning the pandemic.

Phone screening reached over four thousand people. About a third passed to the next stage. Direct mail postcards proved the best and cheapest draw. Three quarters of screened people came from mailings. Information sessions converted most attendees into enrollees. Session talks covered the multi-day exam and consent in detail. Costs per enrollee stayed near one hundred dollars. The authors show exam-heavy studies can fill even in hard times.
pmc-11689778:
Amy Kelley presented this session description in 2024. It introduces the National Institute on Aging, part of the United States National Institutes of Health. The session was aimed at researchers who are early in their careers and want to know what the institute funds.

The institute supports research on aging across the lifespan, from basic biology to the care of older adults. It gives special weight to Alzheimer's disease and related dementias. The session outlines the kinds of grants on offer and gives advice on applying, with tips for students, junior faculty, and new scholars. It ends with small group talks led by institute staff, where attendees could ask about paths that fit their own stage.
pmc-11689878:
Ashley Fromenthal and Rebecca Allen studied loneliness in older adults in two thousand twenty-four. Later life brings money strain, weaker health, and shrinking social ties. Housing trouble or a forced move can deepen the strain. The authors asked what helps older people stay resilient. They focused on taking part in community and social life.

The study used survey data from several thousand older Americans. It tested how felt health links to loneliness. It also tested whether life threats carry that link. Social and community activity were checked as buffers. The work rests on a classic stress and coping model. Findings can guide programs that keep older adults connected. Strong ties may blunt the harm of hard life changes.
pmc-11689978:
Older patients often stay in bed during hospital stays, and family caregivers at the bedside can sway whether they get moving. Shulyaev and co-authors compare how caregivers from different cultural groups in Israel view in-hospital mobility for their older relatives.

The study covered 156 patient-caregiver pairs: Israeli Arabs, immigrants from the former USSR, and veteran Israeli Jews. Caregivers in all groups leaned positive toward mobility, but scores differed. Arab caregivers scored lowest, at 3.48 on a five-point scale, against 3.69 and 3.82 for the other groups, and the gap held after adjusting for patient health and function. The authors urge care teams to address cultural views that may keep older patients in bed.
pmc-11690178:
Rodriguez-Manas and co-authors report two studies of a tech platform for frailty care in a 2024 paper. Frail older adults need close watch at home, and proof that gadgets help has been thin. The platform grades health, tracks function, and sends tailored steps back: exercise plans, food advice, and drug reviews. One study was a six-month trial across three European lands; the other ran in normal clinic care in Madrid.

Both studies saw frailty scores ease and walking skill improve after six months. Users rated the platform near the top for ease of use. Enjoyment scores also rose over the project. The authors say the results back tech-guided frailty care at home.
pmc-11690278:
Wenjin Wang and co-authors merge in a 2024 review the walking-interview studies of how people with dementia live in their neighborhoods. Most such people still live at home and spend much time nearby. Seventeen studies, with one hundred eighty-six people in all, let them speak while walking their own streets.

Three themes arose. Streets, signs, and transport shape whether they can get about and feel at ease. Care and social ties guard their health and sense of self. Phones and other tech can bridge gaps in daily contact. The review centers the voices of people with dementia themselves.
pmc-11690378:
Kristen Beavers and five co-authors report a trial on weight loss and bone health in older adults. Their twenty twenty-four paper covers the INVEST trial. Weight loss can thin bone and raise fracture risk. The trial asked if wearing a weighted vest, to replace lost weight, could guard bone. A third group did strength training instead of vest use.

One hundred fifty adults joined, and most finished the year-long trial. All groups lost about nine to eleven percent of body weight. Vest users wore the vest about seven hours a day. They replaced most lost weight in the vest. Strength group members came to most of their sessions.
pmc-11690778:
DeGroot develops in 2024 a digital palliative care tool that includes the patient's social convoy, the partners, family, and friends who give care. Digital health often leaves that circle out. The Convoy-Pal program was built with user centered design input from clinicians, older adults with serious illness, and their convoys, 81 people in all.

The twelve week program gives a tablet, a smartwatch, and phone access options, shared between patient and convoy. It tracks symptoms and offers care resources based on answers. Early users rated its information highly. A small waitlist trial with 46 people then tested feasibility, with retention at 67.4 percent and caregiver recruitment the main strain.
pmc-11690878:
Megumi Inoue and four co-authors tested a group video game program for people living with early or moderate dementia in a 2024 study. The program ran for twenty weeks at an adult day health center and used a system called Obie. Players move, think, and socialize as they play, for example by swatting at bright balloons that float across a board or floor.

The study followed twenty-four people with tests before and during the program. Scores on a standard thinking test barely moved between the start and the midpoint, and mood and behavior scores also held steady. Staff watching the sessions saw early-stage players join in with more energy and clear enjoyment than those at the moderate stage.
pmc-11691178:
Two researchers studied how trust in science and science literacy shape climate views among older adults worldwide, in a paper published in 2024. Older people both sway climate policy and suffer its effects keenly, yet their views are little studied. The team drew on a 2020 global survey of over thirty-three thousand adults aged fifty to ninety-nine in 113 countries. They tested whether literacy and trust predict understanding of climate change, seeing it as a major threat, or denying it.

Both literacy and trust predicted greater understanding and stronger threat views, but neither predicted denial. Trust also carried part of the link from literacy to climate views, acting as a bridge. The authors suggest that building both knowledge and confidence in science can help aging populations prepare for a warming world.
pmc-11691278:
Alex Laffer and co-authors published this 2024 quality improvement report on training nurse practitioners for hospice and palliative care inside the Veterans Administration. Palliative services are scarce because the workforce is thin, and clinicians who grow interested mid-career face steep routes back to school. The project builds the training into the job instead.

The twelve-month program asks at least 500 clinical hours from nurse practitioners working in a VA Community Living Center. Its curriculum is mostly practical: interprofessional teamwork, hard conversations, and medical, psychosocial, cultural, spiritual, and ethical content woven longitudinally. Two protected hours a day pair hospice experiences with team learning, while participants keep their regular duties. The authors offer the model as a workforce lever other centers can copy.
pmc-11691578:
Xiaochuan Wang and Eman Zaman review dental care inside long-term care homes in this 2024 paper. Fewer than one in five residents gets proper oral care, by recent estimates. The reviewers searched the literature from 2013 to 2023 and kept sixteen studies. Residents suffer when mouth care ranks low among many competing needs.

The papers point to the same fixes. Care should be integrated into daily nursing, insurance access widened, and staff trained to value oral hygiene. Poor mouth care drags on mental, physical, and social health in this frail group. The authors call for education programs that lift oral health from afterthought to routine.
pmc-11691678:
Hui-Ching Weng and three co-authors published a study in 2024 comparing preferences and attitudes toward advance directives in Taiwan and Thailand. An advance directive is a written document that states what medical treatment a person wants if they later become unable to speak for themselves.

The researchers matched 259 pairs of people from the two countries by sex, age, education, and background in medical work. Both groups felt much the same about the need for advance directives at their current stage of life, and both supported family decision-making during hospitalization. Differences appeared in how comfortable people felt discussing death and end-of-life care, with comfort higher in Taiwan. People in Taiwan also had more confidence that peers their own age would consider advance directives. All eight qualities sought in a health care proxy were rated higher in Taiwan.
pmc-11691778:
Erik Knight and co-authors published a 2024 study on a mundane question with real consequences: does eating before a blood draw change hormone readings in older adults? Biomarker studies usually demand fasting samples, yet the same volunteers often do thinking tests fed. If a meal shifts hormone levels, mixing the two states corrupts the science.

Thirty older adults, averaging sixty-seven years, attended two morning lab sessions after fasting overnight. Blood was drawn hourly, four times per session. A meal arrived after the second draw in one session and after the fourth in the other, so each person served as their own control. Eight hormones were measured with precise chemistry. The team modeled the meal's effect with Bayesian methods. The study is the kind of methodological housekeeping that quietly decides whether flashier findings can be trusted. Aging research leans on these markers; knowing their meal sensitivity protects every study downstream.
pmc-11691878:
Emma Quach, Lauren Moo, Emily Franzosa, Pengsheng Ni, Shibei Zhao, and Christine Hartmann wrote a 2024 paper on home services for veterans with dementia in the United States. Home care and adult day programs help such veterans stay in the community. The team asked which veterans use them, and whether the kind of care team they belong to matters.

They used 2019 records for more than one hundred forty-three thousand veterans with dementia. Patients were grouped by their other illnesses and by team type, such as home-based primary care or a dementia clinic. Use of both services together was linked with every team type at every illness level. The results show care teams act as gateways to support at home.
pmc-11692078:
Victoria Cirone and six co-authors published a pilot study in 2024 on high-intensity interval training for women in perimenopause, the transition period before menopause. Hormonal changes during this stage can harm memory and brain health. Interval training alternates short bursts of intense exercise with periods of active recovery, and it may help while fitting into busy lives.

Six women took part over twelve weeks, recruited across seventeen months. Most adhered to the program, with a high attendance rate. One woman withdrew, slightly above the team's target rate. Cardiovascular fitness barely changed. Delayed recall of word lists, however, improved by a large and statistically clear margin. Brain scans also tracked the volume of a key memory region and the state of myelin, the insulation around nerve fibers. The team describes the program as feasible and worth testing in a larger trial.
pmc-11692278:
Yeonjung Lee and co-authors ask whether a risk gene changes which pastimes protect the aging mind. Work, volunteering, and leisure have all been tied to sharper cognition late in life. The APOE ε4 variant pulls the other way, raising Alzheimer's risk. Using national survey data on over seven thousand five hundred older Americans across two waves, the team split the analysis by carrier status.

In the whole group, employment, volunteering at any intensity, and both thinking and social leisure all came with better later cognition, while carrying ε4 predicted worse. Among non-carriers, jobs and rich leisure helped broadly. Among carriers, only gentle volunteering and mental or physical leisure kept their link. The gene, the authors conclude, narrows the menu of protective habits rather than erasing it.
pmc-11692378:
Bettina Beech and co-authors study in 2024 how loneliness and social engagement relate to thinking skills in older Black and White adults in the United States. Social connection shapes health, and its absence raises the risk of cognitive impairment. Few studies have asked how those links differ by race and sex.

The team drew on a national retirement study, using its 2016 core survey and its leave behind questionnaire. They compared loneliness, engagement, and cognitive status across the four race and sex groups. The design can show whether the same loneliness weighs more on one group than another. Such gaps would argue for support programs shaped by community, not one size for all elders.
pmc-11692478:
Where an older person lives may shape how long they live, beyond money and health alone. Seoyeon Ahn, Sojung Park, Eunsun Kwon, and BoRin Kim followed over six thousand Americans aged seventy and up across twelve survey waves to 2022. They sorted them into five housing types, from subsidized senior buildings to ordinary homes, split by income and housing cost strain.

Low income or heavy housing costs raised death risk in every setting, and chronic illness plus deep isolation did the same. One result cut the other way: isolated elders died less often in senior housing than in traditional homes. The authors read congregate housing as a shelter for the socially exposed.
pmc-11692578:
Yeonsu Song and seven co-authors look, in 2024 work, at poor sleep among people who care for kin with dementia. Such carers face a higher risk of dementia themselves, and poor sleep is common in the group. The team asked whether poor sleep tracks with blood marks of nerve decay.

The data came from a sleep training trial, with just eighteen carers at the start and fewer later. More time awake at night went with higher levels of two such marks. Worse sleep depth also tracked with higher marks, and fewer good nights tracked with a worse ratio of two marks. Training did not shift the marks in this small set. The team calls for larger work to test if better sleep cuts the risk.
pmc-11692678:
Family caregivers of people with dementia walk very different paths depending on culture and income. Jung-Ah Lee and co-authors compare twenty-three caregivers in California: White, Latino, Korean, and Vietnamese. During the pandemic, nursing students supported them with weekly calls, and the team analyzed the caregiving experience thematically.

Eighty-one percent of minority care recipients relied on Medicaid; none of the White recipients were low-income. White caregivers showed more active problem-solving and wider social circles. Minority caregivers with limited English more often endured problems quietly, kept tight social boundaries, and engaged their relatives less in shared activities. The 2024 study presses for support shaped to each community's reality.
pmc-11692778:
Jennifer Albrecht, a solo author, reports early findings on thinking decline in older adults after traumatic brain injury. Brain injury is a known risk factor for dementia, but recovery paths in older people are less clear. The 2024 report comes from an ongoing cohort study of adults aged sixty-five and up treated at a major trauma center.

Forty-two people with at least two thinking tests were tracked over six months. About a third showed decline. That group more often had a history of depression and lived alone. Their losses centered on visual-spatial skills and immediate memory. Albrecht cautions that the study is preliminary and still enrolling, but says the pattern marks who may need closer follow-up after injury.
pmc-11692878:
Jessica Bibbo and five co-authors evaluate an online training that teaches prison staff about dementia. Their study came out in 2024. People aging in prison develop dementia at higher rates than the general population, and the share of older inmates is rising fast, yet staff training is rare.

The course, built with Ohio's corrections department, was offered to all staff; several hundred took optional surveys around it. Knowledge improved on a key item about environment and dementia. Attitudes improved on five measures, including confidence in interacting with people who have dementia. About nine in ten respondents called the material useful and said they would recommend it to co-workers. The authors see e-learning as a scalable way to fill a neglected training gap.
pmc-11692978:
Duy Nguyen and three co-authors ask, in a 2024 study, whether early childhood experiences shape cognitive function in late life. They study older adults in China, a group often overlooked in past work on childhood adversity. Their data come from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study, a national survey that tracks health and life history, with waves from 2011 to 2020.

The sample held 9,941 people aged 50 and over at the start, all free of cognitive impairment then and still living at the last wave. Weak neighborhood quality and social cohesion in childhood, poor social relationships, and poor childhood health all tracked with worse cognitive scores in late life. Self-rated memory told the same story. The authors argue that steps to improve child health and social bonds could protect minds decades later, in China and beyond its borders.
pmc-11693078:
Young Min Jee and co-authors test, in a 2024 study, a suction dressing for older patients after surgery to rebuild pressure sores. Sores on the tailbone area are hard to heal, sitting near a source of contamination. After surgeons cover the wound with a flap of nearby tissue, care focuses on keeping the join clean and dry. Their method seals the closed wound under gentle negative pressure.

Fifty-two patients were split between the suction dressing and a standard one. Every flap survived in both groups. The suction group had fewer flap complications and drained far less fluid by the seventh day. The standard group saw one infection and three wounds that split open. The suction group saw none of either. The authors judge the sealed method the stronger choice for these fragile recoveries.
pmc-11693178:
Esther Shin, BoRin Kim, and Sojung Park sort the long care paths of older adults who live at home and tie them to well being, in a 2024 journal article. Care can come from kin for free or from paid hands, and the mix shifts with health, wealth, and place. Past work often read one source alone.

Using a national aging study from 2011 to 2022, the team kept 1,200 adults over seventy who had care all through. A joint path model found four patterns: thin care all along, one kin carer for most, many kin carers, and a dual mix of kin and paid help. Most sat in the one kin group. The thin care group was more often unwed, schooled, and living alone with movement ills. The authors map who lands where.
pmc-11693378:
Lucas Hamilton and Brea Perry study how the social worlds of older adults with and without dementia overlap with those of their close ties, in a 2024 conference abstract. Dementia strains family systems and weakens key social bonds. Isolation is linked with worse outcomes for patients and with raised dementia risk in caregivers. The team ask which ties are shared between an older adult and a close informant.

Data come from 124 pairs, where the informant is typically a spouse or a child. Seventy-three focal adults were cognitively normal, and fifty-one had dementia-related impairment. Each person named, in a separate interview, the people they talk with about important or health matters. Family members and people who give emotional support were more likely to be shared ties.
pmc-11695478:
Won-Young Lee reflects on twelve years as editor-in-chief of a medical journal in this 2024 editorial. He took over Endocrinology and Metabolism in 2013, asked by the incoming society president, after earlier work turning another journal into an English language, PubMed indexed title.

His charge was to do the same for this journal, and the essay looks back on that run as he hands the role to a successor. He writes against a hard year, when conflict between doctors and the government left professors carrying hospital and emergency duties while still doing research. The piece is a personal farewell and a thank-you to the colleagues who kept the journal going.
pmc-11695878:
Eman Abdellatif and Emad Hamouda test whether a simple ratio of two blood markers can forecast survival in sepsis, in this 2024 study. One hundred seventy intensive care patients in Alexandria were followed, with the ratio of C-reactive protein to procalcitonin taken on admission and again on day three. Standard severity scores were recorded beside it.

Patients who died carried a markedly lower ratio at both time points, and the ratio also ran lower in septic shock. A low ratio tracked with worse severity scores across the board. As a day-one predictor of death, the ratio scored close to the best standard score and beat either marker alone. The authors propose it as a cheap early warning.
pmc-11699078:
Mengyao Li and co-authors read spinal fluid proteins to watch a last-resort antibiotic fight a resistant brain infection. Their 2024 case study follows a sixty-nine-year-old patient whose brain ventricles were infected with a multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter strain after hospital care. Polymyxin B was given three ways at once: into the fluid spaces and by vein.

Fluid samples came before the first dose and at one day, one week, and nearly four weeks after. Within a day of dosing, the innate immune system flared: pathways for invader capture, cell eating, and neutrophil activity all rose. The blood-brain barrier showed signs of strain in the protein mix. The authors use the single case to map how host, germ, and drug interact inside the ventricle, aiming to tune dosing of a drug with few rivals left.
pmc-11699278:
Joanne Bruno and eight co-authors test early time restricted eating in adults with prediabetes in a 2024 study. The plan packs all food into the first six to eight hours of the day. It can help blood sugar even when weight holds still, but how much was unclear. Their feeding trial held weight steady on purpose to isolate the clock effect.

Ten adults were fed on an early plan and a usual plan for one week each, in swapped order. On the early plan, four fifths of food landed before two in the afternoon. Worn sugar sensors showed smaller sugar swings and less time spent above the high mark. Two swelling marks in the blood did not move. The authors pitch the plan as a weight free lever for shaky blood sugar.
pmc-11709378:
Cory Funk, Tom Paterson, Jennifer Rohrs, and Timothy Hohman published this Alzheimer's study in 2025. It explores a tipping-point idea about microglia, the brain's cleanup cells. These cells swallow debris and store its fats in droplets. The authors propose that disease accelerates when the droplets saturate and the buffering fails. They tested the idea on data from the ADNI cohort, grouping 608 people by a cognitive score and comparing blood fats with spinal fluid proteins across the groups.

One score band stood out sharply, the range where people slip from normal thinking toward mild impairment. Within it sat two groups progressing at different speeds. The faster group's proteins pointed to droplet signaling in microglia and to fat-processing changes. Certain gene variants tied to Alzheimer's risk also split between the groups. The authors say the signature might one day help predict, at diagnosis, whose disease will move fast.
pmc-11709578:
Cristian Bernabe and nine co-authors test an Alzheimer risk gene variant in mice in a 2025 paper. Genome wide studies tied the ABCA7 gene to late onset Alzheimer's disease. One variant, A1527G, was flagged as a likely risk factor. What it does in a living brain was unknown.

Gene editing inserted the variant into mouse lines already carrying other risk genes. Brains were profiled for gene activity at several ages. The variant shifted expression patterns resembling known disease changes. A second, fuller model line received the variant as well. Those mice faced behavior, imaging, fluid marker, and tissue checks up to two years old. The consortium's pipeline aims to judge whether this variant deserves drug targeting. Results build the case step by step.
pmc-11709678:
Shama Rao and co-authors test whether tiny packages released by stem cells can protect neurons from Alzheimer's-related harm in a 2025 study. Amyloid-beta, a protein that builds up in the disease, drives cell stress, inflammation, and neuron death. Neural stem cells grown from reprogrammed human cells release vesicles loaded with proteins and small RNAs.

The team collected those vesicles and added them to mature human neurons exposed to a toxic form of amyloid. Treated neurons survived better on standard viability tests. Measures of cell stress fell, and genes tied to cell death, energy production, and cleanup shifted in protective directions. Tau protein changes, another mark of the disease, were also tracked. The results support vesicles as a candidate shield for neurons.
pmc-11709878:
Julia Cho and co-authors present a 2025 study of a fast, adaptive version of a classic picture naming test used in memory clinics. The full test shows sixty drawings and takes up to half an hour. Their version picks about ten items on the fly, tuned to the patient by item response maths.

Seven patients took both a thirty item standard form and the adaptive form. The adaptive test took about a minute, against ten for the standard. Scores from the two tracked each other almost exactly. The authors say the short form could ease clinic load while keeping a trusted measure. Testing continues to firm up the result.
pmc-11709978:
Isabelle Maia and co-authors published a study in 2025 on how schooling level affects the accuracy of a questionnaire for cognitive decline. The tool, filled in by informants, covers attention, memory, language, and other domains. It had been checked against a known questionnaire, but not across education levels. The team applied both tools to informants for just under two hundred older adults in Brazil.

Adults were split into low, middle, and high schooling groups. The total score held good to excellent accuracy in all groups. The memory domain scored best in the higher schooling groups, while some domains stayed weak throughout. The authors say checks by schooling level are needed, given wide gaps in schooling quality.
pmc-11710078:
Wenjie Luo and Hao Chen share a 2025 conference abstract on a microglia adapter protein in tau disease. The protein, DAP12, passes signals for receptors such as TREM2, a known risk gene. Mice without it resist tau harm despite more tau buildup, and the team set out to learn why, using gene readouts from cortex and hippocampus.

Without DAP12, tau inclusions rose, yet inflammation and synapse loss were blocked. Microglia stayed in their calm state instead of shifting to a disease state. Tau also pushed insulation-making cells into a weak middle state, and removing DAP12 blocked that shift and raised myelination. The work maps cross-talk among three cell types.
pmc-11710278:
Mark S Overby and co-authors compared two versions of a common thinking test used in Alzheimer's trials, in a study published in 2025. The standard test, called ADAS-Cog, can miss mild memory problems because some scores bunch at the top. Their longer version adds tasks for speed, language, learning, and space skills.

The team grouped scores from healthy older adults, people with mild memory loss, and people with likely Alzheimer's into a few broad factors. For the standard test, a general factor split all three groups apart, while a hands-on skills factor did not split the mild group from controls. Both factors from the longer test split the groups well. The results suggest the added tasks make the test sharper for early stages.
pmc-11710378:
Moorthi Ponnusamy and co-authors study in 2025 how the BIN1 gene shapes tau spread in Alzheimer-like mouse brains. BIN1 is the second strongest genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer's disease. Brain BIN1 levels fall in patients, and the protein binds tau in lab tests.

Mice bred to lack BIN1 in forebrain nerve cells grow tau tangles in a set pattern. Seeded tau spreads less after the loss in key brain regions. Memory areas like the hippocampus show lighter tau load and less cell loss. The region-specific shield hints that BIN1 loss slows disease in some zones.
pmc-11710578:
Yoav Piura and co-authors describe a rare form of dementia that strikes within a single week, in a 2025 paper. Doctors know the broader class of rapidly progressive dementia, where thinking collapses within a year or two. A small share of patients fall faster still, reaching full incapacity within seven days of the first symptom. What causes that abrupt form, and how those patients look, was not known.

The team drew on 187 patients with rapidly progressive dementia enrolled at Mayo Clinic and Washington University between 2016 and 2023. Those whose collapse took a week or less were classed as abrupt onset. The authors charted their features, test results, and final causes. They also searched published reports to sharpen the list of possible causes. The work gives doctors a clearer approach for these rare, urgent cases.
pmc-11710678:
Sunghwan Ko studies how estrogen shapes the range of microglia, the immune cells that live in the brain, in the female mouse hippocampus. When the ovaries fail at menopause, the hormone falls fast, and swelling in the brain climbs with age. The hormone, acting through its alpha receptor on these cells, is thought to calm that swelling, but the routes it uses are still not known.

Ko weighs three groups of mice: normal females, females that lack that receptor, and females whose hormone was drained by a chemical that ages the ovaries. Gene reads from single cells sorted the cells of that brain region into five subtypes. The study tracks how each change shifts those subtypes and their gene programs. It tests if loss of the hormone drives the cells toward active states tied to Alzheimer's risk.
pmc-11710778:
Nattayaporn Apaijai and co-authors test a diabetes drug in rats with heart failure in a 2025 study. The drug, dapagliflozin, blocks a sugar transporter and is now standard care in heart failure. It had also helped thinking in older adults with diabetes. The team asked whether it protects the brain when heart failure follows a heart attack.

Rats with surgery-induced heart failure showed weak hearts, poor thinking, and damaged brain mitochondria, the cells' power units. Eight weeks of the drug improved heart pumping and thinking about as well as a standard heart drug, enalapril. Both drugs cut swelling and voltage loss in the power units, though not oxidative stress. The authors say the drug guards the brain through its power units.
pmc-11710878:
Callie Moran and a large team of co-authors survey disinfectant use in health sites, in a paper dated twenty twenty-four. The study asks whether use of quaternary ammonium compounds rose during the COVID-19 pandemic. These chemicals fill most sprays approved against the virus, yet animal and human studies link them to harm.

The team phoned hospitals, private offices, and dental sites in six states picked to mirror national health data. Staff answered open and closed questions on how their cleaning habits changed. The paper pairs that survey with known risks: fertility harm in animals and weaker cell energy in humans. It flags a cleaning gain that may carry quiet costs.
pmc-11712078:
Natalia Palacios and co-authors trace care paths for United States veterans with Alzheimer's disease in a 2025 records study. Veterans face distinct risks and can face hurdles in reaching new treatments through the VA health system. The team used health records from late 2015 to early 2024.

They found more than 110,000 veterans with an Alzheimer's code in their records. Over forty percent were first coded by a primary care doctor, far more than by any specialist type. Within a year, about a quarter saw a neurologist or a dementia clinic. Black veterans moved to specialist care more often than white or Hispanic veterans. The authors see room to strengthen follow-up care after a first diagnosis.
pmc-11712178:
Louisa I Thompson and co-authors report early data on digital screening for memory problems in primary care in a 2025 Rhode Island study. New Alzheimer's drugs have raised the need for fast, timely diagnosis, and digital tests could speed referrals. The team tried three routes: an online test taken at home, the same test self-run in the waiting room, and a tablet test given by the doctor.

Thirty-four older adults were screened and twenty-three joined the study. Most finished the home test by smartphone, and all who tried it completed it before their visit. Most said they preferred screening at home. The doctor-run tablet test succeeded in nine of eleven visits, with time pressure and tech faults causing misses. The waiting room option was dropped for lack of space and staff.
pmc-11712378:
Psychedelic drugs as a path to treat Alzheimer dementia are reviewed by Jitendra Kumar Sinha and co-authors in work dated 2025. Such drugs were long tied to rite and leisure use. They act on a serotonin switch and can boost brain wiring growth through two signal webs. Their role in brain-wasting disease has stayed near untouched till now.

Fresh work shows three named drugs ease signal faults tied to Alzheimer disease. Paths in view span a growth factor chain, a cell growth switch, and cell self-cleaning. Dose sets the line between help and harm. Long-term safety proof is still owed, the team stresses.
pmc-11712478:
Yejin Kang and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on signs of cell rust in people with mild memory loss tied to blood vessel damage. The work sat inside a trial that tested a supplement meant to mop up that rust. The team asked whether rust markers set these patients apart from healthy peers and hinted at who would gain from the treatment.

Patients came from a heart rehab program and were split by test scores into a mild loss group and a healthy group. One rust marker ran lower in the loss group while a second ran higher, a mixed picture. The loss group then took the supplement or a dummy pill for half a year. The study shows rust signs in vessel-based loss are not simple.
pmc-11712578:
Bery Mohammediyan and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on sleep and the pace of Alzheimer's changes in older adults who still think clearly. Poor sleep has been tied to the disease, but which comes first was murky. The team followed 220 adults from a cohort of people with a parent who had dementia.

Sleep was tracked by surveys and wrist devices, while scans measured amyloid and tau over about four years. About a hundred people had repeat scans, and thirty-two went on to mild impairment. Higher amyloid went with more broken sleep from night to night. The study helps sort out how sleep and brain changes feed each other before symptoms start.
pmc-11712678:
Most dementia cases go unnoticed for years, and the pen-and-paper screening tests are slow and can misjudge people with little schooling. Laili Soleimani and co-authors build an alternative in a 2025 study: software that reads doctors' notes for warning signs. The cohort drew on more than four thousand older patients at one New York health system, using their last five notes before a memory test.

The software pulled out hundreds of clinical features, and a forest of decision trees learned to flag risk. On held-back patients the flag caught most true cases with few false alarms, though a stricter test set scored lower. A live screening rollout at the hospital comes next.
pmc-11712778:
Aygun Badalova published a research paper in 2025 on an app that helps people with dementia relearn the names of family and friends. Forgetting the names of loved ones is a common and painful part of the illness. The app, called Gotcha!, trains one face a day with photos and gentle, error-free practice.

Before the six-week training block, patients took weekly naming tests to set a baseline. A speech checker in the app gives feedback at once when a name is spoken. Among the first twenty users, four in five named faces better during training, and eight gains passed strict checks. Group tests backed the trend. The team also asked why patients join such projects.
pmc-11712878:
Jean-Paul Soucy and co-authors present a 2025 research paper on how to group brain scan data when modeling the spread of tau in Alzheimer's disease. The team worked with data from the TRIAD cohort at McGill University. The study asks how much fine detail a model needs before its forecasts stop getting better.

Inside, the authors compare four ways of grouping the data, from one pool for the whole brain to groups split by both brain region and brain network. They used scans from 113 people who each had tau PET and MRI at least twice, a year or more apart. The work helps researchers pick a model size that stays accurate without needless cost.
pmc-11712978:
Katherine Britt and co-authors published a study in 2025 on what helps or blocks cognitive care planning in primary care. Such planning means regularly checking a patient's needs and writing down steps to meet them. It can lift health and quality of life for people with dementia, yet formal plans remain rare. The team asked providers about their own experience.

Eight primary care providers who treat older adults took part in phone interviews. Many knew general cognitive care but lacked a clear step-by-step method. Five themes emerged, covering buy-in, family presence, time and staffing, structure, and training. Providers valued a structured approach, family involvement, and support at each level from patient to organization.
pmc-11713078:
Jung-Ah Lee, Jiuchen Zhang, Amir Rahmani, and Annie Qu use smart rings to watch the sleep of people caring for relatives with dementia, in this 2025 study. Caregivers sleep badly under constant burden, and self-report surveys miss those with limited English. One hundred three caregivers in California, mostly older women from white, Hispanic, Korean, and Vietnamese backgrounds, wore the rings for three months.

Half received a culturally tailored home support program; half served as an attention control. The rings streamed sleep stages, timing, and awakenings to phones and the cloud in real time. Deep dream sleep crept up slightly in the support group while slipping in controls. Adult-child caregivers fell asleep faster after the program, landing in the healthy range, while spousal caregivers gained less. Participants liked seeing their own sleep data. The authors call the wearable approach feasible for diverse caregivers.
pmc-11713178:
Axelle Vanparys and co-authors describe a project on protein tagging in tau diseases, in a 2025 paper. These diseases involve abnormal buildup of the tau protein in brain cells, and Alzheimer disease is the most common of them. No test cleanly separates the tau diseases from each other.

Tagging proteins with ubiquitin is a normal cell process that may go wrong in these diseases. The project separates soluble and clumped brain proteins from patients with four tau diseases and from healthy subjects. Mass spectrometry then catalogs the proteins in each fraction. The aim is twofold: find tag based markers that tell the diseases apart, and learn whether tagging drives tau clumping. Such markers could sharpen diagnosis where current methods fall short.
pmc-11713278:
Soumilee Chaudhuri and a large team of co-authors present a 2025 study from a Korean brain aging cohort on how heart risk and amyloid plaques combine to affect thinking. The cohort, called KBASE, follows older adults across the Alzheimer's spectrum. The team split 526 participants into four groups by cardiovascular risk score and by whether brain amyloid was present.

Cognition differed across the groups in every domain tested, including memory, language, and executive function. Even without amyloid, cognitively normal elders with high heart risk scored notably worse on memory than their low-risk peers. Four years of follow-up tracked how the gaps evolved. The authors argue that vascular care may protect memory even before Alzheimer's pathology appears.
pmc-11713378:
John Alam and co-authors report blood test results from a drug trial in dementia with Lewy bodies, in this 2025 paper. The drug, neflamapimod, had earlier improved thinking and movement scores in a sixteen-week trial with ninety-one patients. The team now asked what the drug did to two proteins in the blood.

Stored blood samples were tested for GFAP and a second marker linked to nerve harm. Levels were checked in all patients and in those with pure Lewy body disease, without Alzheimer's changes. The title reports that the drug lowered GFAP levels in the pure group, a sign worth tracking in later trials.
pmc-11713478:
Gallen Triana-Baltzer presents a 2025 report on a blood test from Janssen that measures a tau form tied to Alzheimer's disease. Blood tests for the disease have grown from spinal fluid tests and brain scans that track plaques and tangles years before symptoms. The test here reads p217+tau, a marker that falls when a drug works.

The test began as a spinal fluid assay in 2017 and was reshaped for blood, where levels run near one percent of fluid levels. Over four years it was checked in more than ten large patient groups. It sorted people by plaque or tau status with high accuracy, and its cut-off values held from sick patients to healthy ones. More work is still needed on early use.
pmc-11713578:
Pierrick Bourgeat and co-authors clean up brain amyloid measurements with a learning method that watches change over time, in this 2025 paper. PET scans gauge amyloid with a ratio that leans on a reference brain region, and noise there corrupts the score. Their network, DeepSUVR, learns a per-scan correction by penalizing changes that make no biological sense, like amyloid shrinking over time.

Trained on thousands of repeated scans, the method tightened agreement between different tracers and steadied each person's trend across visits. Corrections run on single scans, so clinics need no history to use it.
pmc-11713678:
Apoorva Safai and co-authors link poor neighborhoods to changes in brain layout in a 2025 study. People in poor areas tend to have worse health and weaker thinking skills in old age. The team uses a new scan method that maps how alike the shapes of brain regions are. They ask whether this map can show how neighborhood strain gets into the brain.

The study covers 526 adults with no thinking problems from two Wisconsin research programs. Each person's home area got a hardship score based on income, schooling, jobs, and housing. The team compared the brain maps of people from the hardest-hit areas with those from the best-off areas. Shape patterns differed between the groups. Such maps may help explain how place shapes later memory loss.
pmc-11713778:
Lucia Crivelli and co-authors describe a lifestyle trial for dementia prevention across Latin America in a 2025 paper. The trial, called LatAm FINGERS, is the first of its kind to span the region. It covers twelve countries, from Mexico to Argentina and Uruguay. The team writes about how to recruit fairly in places that drug research often leaves out.

The trial randomly assigns older adults to a lifestyle program shaped for local food, habits, and culture. Staff used outreach methods that respect local customs and languages. The paper shares what worked and what proved hard. Broad trials like this one matter because results from one rich country may not fit the rest of the world.
pmc-11713878:
Ellen Singleton and co-authors test whether sex changes how tau buildup tracks with mental decline. Tau is a protein that piles up in Alzheimer's disease. Women seem to gather tau faster yet hold up better for a time. The team followed a large Swedish group of amyloid positive adults with tau scans and thinking tests.

In people still thinking clearly, higher starting tau tied to odd patterns by sex across many brain zones. In impaired people, tau in some zones tied to faster decline. Split by tau load, women matched men's thinking paths at low and mid loads. The study adds nuance to how sex shapes disease course.
pmc-11713978:
Illhwan Cho and co-authors build a test plate that maps where drugs grip amyloid in this 2025 paper. Amyloid-beta clumps drive Alzheimer disease, but their messy shapes hide drug binding sites. The team fixed thirty-seven short amyloid fragments, each six units long, onto a plate. Known amyloid-active compounds were then washed over it.

Each compound lit up its own set of fragments. An imaging dye gripped three spots along the chain. Curcumin blocked three regions, while a sugar alcohol hit three others. Two breaker drugs worked hardest on the tail end of the chain. The authors offer the plate as a shortcut for designing diagnostics and treatments.
pmc-11714078:
Kylie Meyer and co-authors report a 2025 study of a support program for Latino caregivers. Family members who care for a person with dementia face high care costs and lost work time. Latino caregivers in the United States bear a heavier share of that strain than most groups.

The five-week group program, CONFIDENCE, ran online through a Los Angeles community group. About half of those who signed up came to at least one session, and guests rated it highly. A small trial group showed lower money strain after the program and stronger coping scores two months later. Low attendance was the weak point. The program is now being cut to four sessions with a phone app and AI help added.
pmc-11714278:
A landmark 2020 report listed twelve changeable risk factors for dementia across the life span. Matěj Kučera tests how many of those factors truly predict dementia in the Czech Republic in a solo 2025 study.

The analysis used a European aging survey and followed more than thirty-five hundred adults aged 65 and over who began dementia-free. Of ten factors with usable data, five tied to later dementia after adjustment. Physical inactivity carried the strongest risk, ahead of low education, diabetes, and depression. Living alone also ranked among the five. Sex seemed to modify a few links, including alcohol use and living alone. Local evidence can help national prevention plans aim at the factors that matter most at home.
pmc-11714478:
Luisa Figueredo and co-authors scan a mind bridge in sleep apnea souls whose minds still test sound, in a study from 2025. Apnea chops sleep and starves the brain of air in bursts. It oft dulls recall, and may court Alzheimer disease. The fornix, a white bridge out of the recall hub, is a prime spot to look.

One hundred forty-five souls took a night sleep read, mind tests, and spread scans of two kinds. Mean age sat near sixty-five, with mind scores at the sound line. Breath-stop counts and sleep span marks were set by the bridge's build marks. The ask in full: does apnea wear the bridge ere it wears the mind? The scan pair gives two reads on that wear.
pmc-11714578:
Suzanna Joseph and co-authors, with the iMIND research group, photographed the blood vessels of the retina in people with mild cognitive impairment, in this 2025 study. The retina is part of the brain's family, and its vessels may mirror changes tied to memory decline. Earlier small studies with a narrower scanning method gave mixed signals about vessel thinning in early impairment.

The team used an ultra-widefield camera that captures far more of the retina in one shot, including its deep choroidal layer. Special software measured vessel widths, twisting, branching complexity, and density in 131 eyes of patients with mild impairment, compared with people of normal cognition. Wide views might catch vessel changes that narrow scans miss. If eye images reliably flag early brain change, they could become a cheap screening window in memory clinics.
pmc-11714678:
Kazuya Igarashi and co-authors report a 2025 study of a spinal fluid protein and its tie to brain loss in Alzheimer's disease. The protein sits at nerve junctions, so its level may mark junction harm. The team drew fluid samples from 177 people in a Japanese imaging study, across healthy, mild-loss, and dementia groups.

Levels ran higher in the mild and dementia groups than in the healthy group, and higher levels tracked lower thinking scores. People in the top bands faced a higher risk of slipping into dementia. The protein also tied to known disease markers and brain size measures.
pmc-11714778:
Yan-Jhu Su and co-authors use a national retirement study to link chronic illness with cognitive function in older United States adults, in a 2025 study. Thinking ability ties to physical health and to traits such as race and ethnicity, but few studies weigh them together. The team ask whether illness links differ by group.

Their cross-sectional sample covers 8,310 adults aged sixty-five and older who were employed in 2018. A standard phone-based test measures cognition. Models relate single illnesses and illness counts to scores, with race and ethnicity as moderators. The design shows how health and social position may jointly shape later-life thinking.
pmc-11714878:
Joseph Geraci and co-authors report a 2025 project that uses phone and wearable data to spot early loss of thinking skills. Such devices can gather health data all day without a clinic visit. The team built data sets that mix many kinds of measure for each person. They also set up ways to share the data while guarding privacy. A first study drew on sixty-four people from a Boston research center.

A new machine learning tool sorted the people with loss of skills into clear sub-groups. One small group stood out for sleep measures, such as drops in blood oxygen at night. A second group stood out for high heart rate readings. Most members of both groups did have loss of skills. The team calls the results early, but they show how daily data might sort patients in useful ways.
pmc-11714978:
Prevention clinics for Alzheimer's disease tailor diet, exercise, and other steps to each patient's risks. Kellyann Niotis and a large team of co-authors ask whether blood markers can show if that tailored care works. They describe a study enrolling adults with a family history of the disease, plus some already diagnosed. Staff collect gene type, thinking scores, and blood markers such as amyloid ratio and tau forms. Some blood tests use a finger-prick card done at home.

Repeated marker readings could track whether risk care slows disease change. The study also gathers markers tied to Lewy body disease, which shares risks with Alzheimer's disease. If blood markers prove steady, clinics could judge care plans without costly brain scans. The paper sets out the study design and its goals.
pmc-11715078:
Robyn A Honea and co-authors weighed how genes tied to cell power plants shape brain fuel use. The power plants, called mitochondria, carry their own small set of genes. Brain fuel use drops early in Alzheimer's disease, which hints that these genes may play a part. Two genes near the cell core were in the frame as well.

The team used data from a Kansas aging cohort with three groups of adults. One group had the disease, one had mild thought loss, and one had neither. All had scans that map how much sugar each brain zone burns. Carriers of a known risk gene burned less sugar in zones at the front and midline of the brain. Two other gene marks showed no such link in the healthy group. The split points to the risk gene, not the power-plant genes, as the driver here.
pmc-11715378:
Single DNA methylation sites linked to Alzheimer's disease carry weak signals each, so Lidija Milicic and co-authors borrow the genetics trick of summing many sites into a risk score. They run epigenome-wide scans in an Australian cohort of 707 people against eight traits, from disease risk to brain volumes and memory scores, then build methylation risk scores from the results.

No single site survived strict correction. Several combined scores did associate with Alzheimer's risk in the second cohort of 620 people, even after correction. The 2025 study suggests the methylation signal for Alzheimer's is real but spread thin, readable only in aggregate.
pmc-11715478:
Yi Ling Clare Low and co-authors present a 2025 study of immune cells in the blood of people with Alzheimer's disease. The team also studied people with mild memory loss and people with normal thinking. A key gap, they note, is how immune cells in the blood link to swelling and harm in the brain. Blood samples came from a large Australian health study.

Flow tests sorted B cells and T cells in samples from 142 people in the three groups. The Alzheimer's group had fewer of one type of calming T cell and more of a rare T cell type. The mild loss group stood out in another cell group. Readers see which blood cell patterns differ by stage of memory loss.
pmc-11715678:
Kseniya Nevzorova and co-authors ask how often the logopenic variant of primary progressive aphasia rests on Alzheimer's disease as its underlying pathology. The variant centers on language impairment, with word and speech faults. Spinal fluid tests can show whether the hallmark Alzheimer's proteins sit behind the signs. Their 2025 study examined 20 such patients at one clinic. Each patient had a lumbar puncture so the fluid could be analyzed.

Fluid results split the group into four established cases, eight probable cases, and eight patients with no sign of Alzheimer's. In all, three in five patients had the disease at the root. Onset ran a little younger in that group, but the gap was not significant. Test scores hinted that worse memory with less speech loss may flag the disease before laboratory work. The team urges fluid testing for all such patients, since the root guides the choice of care.
pmc-11715878:
Christian Lachner and co-authors measure dementia risk factors in a 2025 study of Latino and Black adults. These groups carry a higher dementia burden than white adults in the United States, for reasons tied to health care access rather than biology. Many risk factors, such as high blood pressure, can be treated if they are found.

The study enrolled 86 cognitively normal adults at a Florida clinic and tested them directly. Risk factors were strikingly common: high blood pressure, high cholesterol, and diabetes each affected about half or more of the group. Worse, large shares of those cases were unrecognised or poorly controlled. Depression and low vitamin B12 also appeared. The authors argue that finding and treating these factors is a concrete step toward fairer brain health.
pmc-11715978:
Gyujin Heo and five co-authors scan nearly seven thousand blood proteins to find a strong signature of Alzheimer's disease, in this 2025 study. Single blood markers exist, but each is weaker than spinal fluid tests. A wide sweep across the protein set might find a panel that closes the gap.

The sweep covered more than 3,300 people across three study groups. Two hundred fifty-seven proteins differed between patients and controls in both discovery and check samples. A machine learning model built on eighty-nine of them sorted patients well and did not fire for Parkinson's disease, which supports its specificity. The signature also flagged faster decline and marked some healthy people at very high later risk. Pathways pointed to fat transport in the blood.
pmc-11716078:
Anisa Dhana and co-authors track in 2025 whether visit-to-visit blood pressure swings link to thinking scores in older Black and White adults. Swings may harm brain vessels apart from high average pressure. The Chicago cohort gives an eighteen-year view on that question.

Near five thousand adults aged sixty five and up took part in the city health study. Pressure was read every three years by trained staff, and swings were scored from gaps between visits. Thinking was graded by four standard tests at the last visit. Models adjust for age, schooling, habits, mood, and major diseases to isolate the swing effect.
pmc-11716178:
Jordan Teague and co-authors model when tau buildup starts in each person's brain and how fast it grows, in a 2025 paper. Tau is one of the two proteins that mark Alzheimer's disease, and its timing differs from person to person. A method first built for amyloid scans estimates the age at which buildup begins. The team checked whether the same method works for tau scans across several cohorts.

The main sample held 273 people from two Wisconsin studies, with repeat tau scans over time. Their average starting age was about seventy-one. The model produced a personal estimate of tau onset age for each participant. The authors then tested how well it forecast later scans and how well past scans fit the curve. Work like this helps trials pick the right moment to treat and judge whether a drug slows the clock.
pmc-11716378:
Ismail and four colleagues review the evidence linking cigarette smoking to Alzheimer's disease, in a study published in two thousand twenty-five. They also ask what happens neurologically when smokers switch to e-cigarettes. Nicotine's effects on the brain, they note, have been studied far less than smoking's effects on heart and lungs.

The authors searched MEDLINE, PsycINFO, and the Cochrane trial register through October two thousand twenty-three. They also checked several clinical trial registries for ongoing work. The findings conflict. Some studies report nicotine improving cognition and easing deficits. Others link active smoking to higher Alzheimer's risk. The review lays out this unsettled picture and the need for clearer evidence.
pmc-11716478:
Jinghang Li and ten co-authors published a study in 2025 on a brain-age score built only from white matter in midlife women. Brain-age models guess a brain's age from scans, and a gap from real age signals poorer health. The team wanted a version focused on white matter, where vessel damage tied to Alzheimer's risk shows up.

Their deep learning model was trained on healthy adults and then tested in 239 women in a midlife brain study. They compared the white matter age gap with blood markers of amyloid, tau, and nerve damage. A focused score like this could help track vessel-related brain risk in women before symptoms start.
pmc-11716578:
Trevor Lohman and thirteen co-authors link the brain's control of body rhythms to a blood marker of Alzheimer's disease. The central autonomic network is a web of brain regions that manages heart rate, blood pressure, and similar automatic jobs. Its ties to Alzheimer's blood markers had not been explored.

The team recruited 76 independent older adults from the community for brain scans and blood draws. Resting scans measured how strongly the autonomic network's parts sync with each other. Blood tests gave the ratio of two amyloid forms, a marker that falls as Alzheimer's pathology builds. Heart and vessel risk factors were recorded through interviews. A well-known resting network served as a comparison, to check that any link is specific.
pmc-11716678:
Smriti Ghildiyal and co-authors ask whether the ApoE4 gene variant changes how blood vessel risks and brain blood flow shape thinking in older Singaporeans. Their 2025 study draws 601 adults from a community dementia cohort, split between midlife and later life. Participants carry diagnoses from subjective decline through dementia.

Each person took thinking tests, gave blood pressure and blood sugar readings, and was genotyped for the ApoE variants. Brain perfusion was measured with a spin-labeling MRI method. The design lets the team test whether carrying ApoE4 strengthens or weakens the links among vessel risk, blood flow, and test scores, within each age band. Southeast Asian data on this interplay were scarce. The study frames gene status as a lens that clinics may need when reading vascular risk.
pmc-11716778:
Michael Edler and co-authors describe in 2025 three sample banks at Indiana University that serve research on brain degeneration diseases. Ready access to good samples from many and varied donors speeds work on diseases such as Alzheimer and Parkinson disease. Housing three banks in one place lets them share methods, staff, and tools.

The banks store many sample types, from blood and spinal fluid to brain tissue and stem cells made from donor tissue. Shared standard procedures keep quality steady across studies. Together the banks hold over four million sample portions from more than 150 studies and about 142,000 people. More than 600,000 portions have gone out to over 370 research teams, feeding almost a thousand papers. Online catalogs help researchers pick samples and manage requests across all three banks.
pmc-11716878:
Pedro de Castro Lopes and co-authors check whether early memory and thinking problems already raise the risk of malnutrition in older adults, in a study from 2025. Malnutrition stalks advanced dementia, but its foothold in early impairment is less charted. The cross-sectional study enrolled 87 community-dwelling elders in Brazil.

A ten-point cognitive screen sorted participants into no impairment, mild-to-moderate impairment, and, by exclusion, severe cases, who were not enrolled. A standard nutrition questionnaire flagged risk at scores under twelve. The team then tested whether impairment status and malnutrition risk traveled together. The head text ends as the statistics are introduced, so this summary reports the design and aims rather than a verdict. The question matters because early, cheap nutrition support could blunt decline.
pmc-11716978:
Pauline Maillard and co-authors tested a brain imaging marker for small vessel disease in 2025. Free water in white matter, read from diffusion scans, tracks the vessel damage behind vascular memory loss. The marker is one of a standard kit a research consortium is validating.

Two hundred seventy-five people had baseline scans and checks, then a follow-up visit a bit over a year later. The team asked whether baseline free water forecasts change in executive function scores. Models accounted for age, sex, education, and time. Past work already showed the marker is reliable to measure and sensitive to thinking scores. This study extends the test to decline over time, toward early spotting of at-risk patients.
pmc-11721078:
Timo Risch and co-authors trace how Escherichia coli escapes a new antibiotic family in a 2024 study. Cystobactamids attack the bacterial machinery that untangles DNA, and they break through many existing resistances. Knowing how resistance to them arises guides development, so the team bred highly resistant mutants and read their genomes.

Every mutant carried a single-letter change in the control region of one gene, ygiV, which turned up production of its protein. The protein latches onto the drug tightly and keeps it from its targets, and exposure to the drug pushed production higher still. Unlike a related drug class, resistance here came from a control tweak, not gene copying. A side benefit appeared too: the mutants dialed down several virulence factors.
pmc-11724678:
Daniel Rabin, Max Spiro, Connor Rachford, Timothy Fahey, and John Farrell report a rare chain of complications from a common antibiotic in a case report from 2024. A twenty-six-year-old woman with a congenital heart condition was treated with ceftriaxone for a heart valve infection. On day twenty-one she returned with a septic, clot-infected spleen. The trigger was acute pancreatitis caused by the drug itself, only the third such case in a decade.

Stopping the antibiotic brought steady improvement and falling inflammation markers. No surgery was needed in the end. The authors credit close teamwork across specialties. The case warns that a routine drug can set off an unusual cascade.
pmc-11726878:
Zhihe Yang and co-authors wrote this 2024 review of lab models used to study biofilms, the slime bound communities microbes form on surfaces. Inside a biofilm, microbes resist drugs far better than when floating free. Sound models are needed to study their traits and defenses.

The review sorts the designs in use, from classic flow cells and plates to newer printed and chip based setups. Each design's strengths and limits are laid out in turn. The authors note where lab models drift from real life conditions. They close with ways that three dimensional printing and other new tools could close that gap.
pmc-11727178:
Teng and co-authors redesign a fat-splitting enzyme to survive the heat of food processing. The lipase from the fungus Rhizomucor miehei is a useful green catalyst, but it wilts at working temperatures. Screening computationally with two stability-predicting tools, the team nominates eight single changes and confirms three as promising building blocks.

Combining the three into one mutant raises the enzyme's best working temperature by ten degrees, to fifty-five, and stretches its half-life at fifty degrees from forty-six minutes to over seven hours. Activity on camphor tree seed oil jumps by one hundred forty percent, useful for making structured lipids. Simulations explain the gain at the molecular level. The authors offer the mutant as an industrial biocatalyst.
pmc-11727278:
Laura Acquaticci and six co-authors measure the active compounds in acorn flour extracts. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four. Acorns from an oak tree hold many plant compounds that may aid health. The team asks how the heat of extraction changes what comes out, and how strong the extracts act.

They scan extracts made at four heat levels with a fine mass tool. The mid-heat extract holds the most of two key acids and shows the strongest anti-oxidant action. It also blocks two enzymes tied to diabetes and to nerve decay. That extract stands out as a hopeful base for health, drug, and skin products.
pmc-11727778:
Ahmet Kurtoğlu and co-authors study how lifting experience reshapes the heart in a paper from 2024. Resistance training is now a daily habit for millions, amateur and pro. Knowing how years of lifting change heart shape helps trainers balance gain against strain.

Forty-five healthy adults who lifted regularly took part. Their training histories ranged from fresh to veteran. Ultrasound measured the left ventricle's squeeze and relax phases. The left atrium's mechanical work was scored as well. Patterns linked longer experience to distinct heart traits. Tailoring training loads to the heart's response may keep lifters safer. The study adds data where athlete-heart research favors endurance sports.
pmc-11727878:
Angeliki-Erato Sterpi and a large team of co-authors report, in 2024, a case of brain lesions that look like multiple sclerosis but arose after radiation treatment. Radiation can harm nerve support cells and their precursors, which may yield a pattern much like that disease on scans. The authors pair their case with a systematic search of past reports.

Their patient was a thirty-seven-year-old woman whose scan showed white matter lesions after her radiation sessions. The search found seven prior cases that met strict scan criteria, with a mean age near thirty-nine. The paper maps how these lesions present and how they differ from true disease, which helps clinicians avoid a wrong diagnosis and needless treatment.
pmc-11728078:
Restoring blood to a starved heart saves muscle yet injures it too, and several scripted forms of cell death drive that injury. Shinya Tsurusaki and Eddy Kizana review those death programs in this 2024 paper. Necrosis was once dismissed as accidental, but some of it runs on molecular rails like ordinary programmed death. Three such routes — necroptosis, ferroptosis, and pyroptosis — draw special focus.

Reperfusion floods tissue with reactive oxygen, the trigger for much of the damage. Dying heart cells then spark inflammation, scarring, and eventual heart failure. Each death route offers drug targets at its control points. Blocking the right route at the right hour could shrink heart attacks' long shadow.
pmc-11728178:
Mengjie Zhao and co-authors find a gene that links bud timing to cold hardiness in mulberry trees, in a 2024 study. Winter dormancy protects woody plants from cold. When buds wake, frost risk rises. The team scanned two hundred one natural mulberry populations. A gene called MaFAD2 showed the strongest tie to bud break timing. The gene was already known for cold resistance. Its activity peaked in dormant buds and faded as dormancy ended.

Trees from cold regions carried selected versions of the gene. Forcing the gene on in early-budding lines delayed bud break. That confirmed a causal role. The findings tie the two traits at one locus. Breeders can use bud timing as a visible proxy. Selecting later buds may buy cold tolerance. The work serves silk regions where mulberry is a crop. Climate swings make such markers more valuable.
pmc-11728278:
Park and Park sequence the full chloroplast genome of Sium serra, a plant found in Korea, China, and Japan. Some Sium species serve as herbal medicine and get confused with a look-alike plant. The species was first placed in another genus, then moved to Sium. Chinese sources still file it under the old name, so its genome had been skipped. The team took DNA from fresh leaves and read it on a high-throughput machine.

Software assembled and labeled the genome, and related species were compared. The analysis places the plant within the Sium group. The work gives a firm genetic reference for telling this herb from its look-alikes. It also adds to knowledge of diversity in the genus.
pmc-11728578:
Schuerger and co-authors gauge wet loss in mass gravel bike races in the field. Gravel race is a new bike form, with first worlds in 2022. It blends road, cross, and mount traits in long, hard runs. Stops for food and drink are rare in such race spans. Three race spans gave the facts at an April 2023 meet. In sum, 121 racers filled pre-race forms for the work.

Of those, 53 gave pre-race weight and spit salt marks. Just 38 racers came back for post-race tests in the set. Past one fifth, 22.6 percent, were wet-full pre race. Most were mild-dry at 56.6 percent in the pre counts. Post race, just 15 percent stayed wet-full in the set. Mid-dry rose to 47.5 percent and grave-dry to 17.5 percent. Weight fell and spit salt rose from pre to post reads.
pmc-11736378:
Qurrat-Ul-Ain and co-authors fed goats in 2024 with garlic and papaya leaf powders to test growth, gut health, and methane-linked germs. Forty male goats were split into five groups: plain feed, a chemical methane blocker, garlic leaf, papaya leaf, or both leaves. Weight gain, feed use, blood marks, rumen germ counts, gut wall traits, and meat quality were all read.

The mixed-leaf group gained best, with better feed use and blood protein. Papaya leaf cut the methane-maker count by about a tenth. Garlic leaf held rumen germs lowest, and all leaf groups grew taller gut wall folds. Meat quality held steady. The team sees the leaves as a green aid, with more work owed on dose and on other herd animals.
pmc-11738078:
Saif Azzam and seven co-authors shared a review in twenty twenty-four on borderline personality disorder. People with this condition have emotions that shift a lot. Their ties to others shift too, and so does their sense of self. The review looks at how it is found and how it is treated. It looks at where experts still do not agree.

The authors weigh the set and proposed criteria used to find the disorder. They note the limits of the tools in use. They note how common it is and what else often comes with it. They weigh four psychotherapies. Two of them are dialectical behavior therapy and mentalization-based treatment. They set those next to the small role of drugs. They take up misdiagnosis, the role of trauma, and stigma. They ask if recovery is possible. The aim is to ground research and day-to-day clinical choices.
pmc-11740078:
Hao Shen and Mingjun Yang test a genetic link between a lung infection and lung cancer in a 2024 paper. The infection involves cousins of the tuberculosis germ. It often appears beside lung cancer, raising cause and effect questions. Gene based instruments can probe causality without a trial's cost.

Four methods all found no causal push from infection to cancer. Checks spotted uneven data, yet removing outliers kept the null result. The reverse direction also showed no support in their analysis. The authors conclude genes give no backing to a causal claim.
pmc-11749278:
Maria Rodriguez-Camacho and co-authors study barriers that stop Roma women in Spain from reaching reproductive rights. Their 2024 paper uses talks with service providers as its source. Nine semi structured interviews were held in person from April to June 2019. Topics held skills across cultures, views on gender bias, and resources to fight it. Networks of actors were also covered.

Three focal areas emerged: stereotypes, discrimination, and cross cultural skills. In each, some provider discourse blocked access while other discourse helped. Models of the tie between professionals and Roma users project stereotypes that hinder access, the authors found. The right of Roma women to keep their culture is not secured in public policy. Nor is their right to take part in policies that affect them, despite stated aims of inclusion.
pmc-11757878:
Andrew McCrary and co-authors track how a heart rhythm fault develops in babies after surgery for a birth defect, in a study published in 2024. The defect, tetralogy of Fallot, is repaired in infancy. Surgery often leaves a blocked signal path in the right heart, which in older patients ties to weaker exercise ability.

The team scanned twenty infants soon after repair with ultrasound and heart tracings. Before surgery, all had shown even contraction and normal tracings. After surgery, strain imaging sorted each baby's right heart pattern as even, mistimed, or unclear. The setup lets the team ask whether the electrical block and the mechanical mistiming arrive together. Results follow in the full report.
pmc-11758278:
Haiqin Zhu, Qintuo Pan, Zhaoliang Zhang, and co-authors compare two operations for a torn retina in this study, published in 2024. The condition is a retinal detachment that splits the center of vision in eyes that still hold their natural lens. Surgeons can fix it from outside the eye with a buckle, or from inside by removing the gel inside the eye.
