The team reviewed 101 patients under fifty-five, with fifty-one eyes treated by buckling and fifty by the inside operation. Both methods reattached the retina in every case by the end. Clear vision at six months was reached by about six in ten buckle cases and about four in ten of the others, a gap that was not firm. Side effects differed: the inside operation brought more growth of scar-like tissue on the retina. The authors advise care in picking the method for each patient.
pmc-11769678:
Jeanine Liebold and co-authors predict transcription factors from a protein's three-dimensional shape rather than its sequence alone. The head of the text dates the work to 2024, though the catalog lists 2025. Transcription factors switch genes on and off by binding DNA. Older predictors flag any protein carrying a known binding domain, so they miss genuinely new factors with unfamiliar domains.

Their deep learning method, StrucTFactor, is the first to use 3D secondary structure for this task. Tested on about 525,000 proteins across twelve data sets, it beat current sequence-based methods with clear statistical confidence. The gain over the closest rival reached seventeen percent on a balanced accuracy measure. Structure, the authors argue, carries signal that sequence hides.
pmc-11772178:
Yajie Zhang, Cong Lu, Lili Li, and Hongyu Li study a cholesterol ratio and infertility in United States women, in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. The ratio compares non-HDL cholesterol to HDL cholesterol in the blood. Its link to infertility had not been well explored.

They used national survey data from two thousand thirteen to two thousand eighteen, covering two thousand nine hundred forty-seven women aged twenty to forty-five. About eleven percent reported infertility. Higher values of the ratio were tied to higher odds of infertility, and the top third showed the strongest link. Subgroup checks gave near-consistent results. The authors say more work is needed on the link and its causes.
pmc-11772278:
Alberto Pauletti and co-authors study brain infection and seizures in mice in a study whose head gives 2024. Infections of the brain can trigger seizures, and new neuron growth in adults might one day help repair harm. That growth centers on a zone in the dentate gyrus where stem cells divide.

Using a virus model of seizure, the team tracked stem and young cells at three points after infection. They found the pool of young cells fell fast and growth patterns changed. The result differs from drug-induced seizures, which can briefly raise growth. Knowing the true path may steer repair research in a better direction.
pmc-11782278:
Luis Felipe Oliveira Ribeiro and ten co-authors published a forestry study in twenty twenty-five on spraying eucalyptus sprouts from a remotely piloted aircraft. Drone spraying is spreading in agriculture, but its quality in forestry was poorly documented. The team also measured how much spray reaches the workers doing the job.

They flew a DJI AGRAS T40 at three swath widths and three droplet sizes, comparing it with a manual backpack sprayer. Sensor cards placed in the sprout canopy measured droplet spread at upper, middle, and lower layers. Protective clothing captured exposure on the applicators. Narrower ranges with finer droplets distributed spray best through the canopy.
pmc-11788178:
Pik Fang Kho and a large team of co-authors compared body fat and insulin response in South Asians and Europeans in a study published in 2024. South Asians tend toward insulin resistance at lower weights, for reasons not fully known. Guessing fat from height and weight may hide the true link.

Forty-six South Asian and forty-one European volunteers took gold-standard tests: a body scan for fat, a hard exercise test for fitness, and a direct insulin suppression test. Sixteen measures tracked with insulin response, most of them precise fat measures rather than rough ones. A subset also gave blood for eleven proteins tied to resistance, five of which tracked with the response. After adjustment, the precise measures carried the story. The authors say accurate fat measurement is key to understanding this group's diabetes risk.
pmc-11798978:
Guillaume Sarrabayrouse and co-authors follow a blood drug into the gut in a 2025 immunology study. Erythropoietin, best known for boosting red cells in anemia treatment, has side effects that hint at wider immune effects, and its impact on intestinal balance had never been mapped in health.

Healthy mice dosed for twenty-eight days developed a disturbed gut flora: more bacteria overall, less diversity, shifted species. Along the small intestine and colon, key immune populations thinned out, including regulatory T cells and antibody-secreting plasma cells in the ileum. A hormone given for blood, the study shows, quietly remodels the gut's immune garrison.
pmc-11801778:
Kadam and colleagues ran in 2025 a wastewater surveillance program for the coronavirus in Mumbai's slum communities, where clinical testing often misses silent cases. For eleven months they sampled open drains and treatment plants and sequenced viral material. Wastewater signals tracked reported city cases. New variants showed up in sewage about three weeks before clinical detection.

Viral loads rose in summer and monsoon months, patterns the team links to weather and droplet behavior. The authors call wastewater monitoring a cheap early warning system. For crowded, vulnerable settlements it can guide targeted responses ahead of case counts.
pmc-11802378:
Ya-Jie Zhai and six colleagues studied how body composition and resting energy use relate to thinking decline in Chinese diabetes patients, in a study published in 2024. The patients all had type 2 diabetes and were over forty-five. Central obesity and low muscle mass were the suspected risks.

The cross-sectional study enrolled 1,243 patients and tested thinking with a standard exam. Patients with impairment burned less energy at rest by every adjusted measure and carried less muscle and more waist fat. The top quarter of resting energy use came with roughly half the impairment risk of the bottom. Prediction improved when energy use and fat-free mass were combined. Mediation analysis suggested the size-adjusted energy measure carried about half the effect of waist and muscle on risk. The authors propose the measure as a screening aid for this group.
pmc-11803678:
Elizabeth Haudrich and four co-authors track stress day by day in teens at raised risk for psychosis in a 2024 study. Risk ran in the family for half the group. Phones pinged the teens through the day across a year, asking about stress, while nights logged their sleep and past trauma was scored.

The at-risk teens carried heavier trauma loads and slept less than the comparison group. Across all teens, worse trauma and a short night both foretold a tenser next day. Which group a teen was in did not change that link. The findings point to sleep as a daily lever on stress.
pmc-11807978:
Fereshteh Asgharzadeh and co-authors test a fruit extract for womb scarring in this study. The head of the text dates the work to 2024. Scar bands inside the uterus can block fertility, and gentle oral treatments are scarce.

Rats with induced uterine adhesions received the jujube extract by mouth. The team measured scar bands, womb shortening, and regrowth of the inner lining. Gland counts and lining thickness showed how well the tissue healed. Inflammation signals and antioxidant enzyme activity were tracked in the tissue. Treated animals showed far less fibrosis on staining and marker tests. Pregnancy outcomes in the model improved alongside the tissue repair.
pmc-11810978:
Two writers review whether pharmacists can act as gatekeepers against suicide in poorer countries, in a paper published in 2024. About seventy percent of self-poisoning deaths occur in low- and middle-income countries. Bans on farm poisons cut such deaths there, but drug overdoses have risen in their place. The review gathers studies from 2014 to 2024 on training community pharmacists to spot and help suicidal customers.

Only eight studies turned up, and none measured whether the training actually lowered deaths. Trained pharmacists did grow more confident, willing, and skilled at responding to suicidal intent. Nearly all of that evidence, though, comes from rich countries where pharmacists see customers often. The authors argue the approach can travel to poorer settings if it is reshaped for local conditions. They call for research that tests adapted versions where the need is greatest.
pmc-11814178:
Shifeng Du, Yashuai Yang, Hongbo Yuan, and Man Cheng build a system that spots and counts a harmful invasive weed from drone video in real time. The weed, Solanum rostratum, has spread across many countries and threatens farms and ecosystems. Their system, TrackSolanum, chains four parts: a detector that finds the plant, a tracker that follows each plant across frames, and a locator that pins its position. A counter then tallies plants as they cross a line. The study was published in 2024.

Field tests flew at two heights. At 2 meters, the system reached precision of 0.950 and recall of 0.970, with a counting error of 2.438 percent at 17 frames per second. At 3 meters it stayed close, with a 4.634 percent counting error and much faster processing. The authors offer the tool for judging infestations and guiding precise weed control.
pmc-11822478:
Sreyashi Chakraborty, Melinda Simon, and Alessandro Bellofiore argue in a 2024 review that mechanical heart valves need a fresh look at design and testing. Valves with two flaps are still a sound choice for the heart's main exit, above all for young patients and for poorer regions. They last very well, but people who get them face a raised risk of clots and strokes.

That risk forces most patients to take blood thinning drugs for life. The next wave of valves should resist clots well enough to drop that need. The authors say design work is held back by strict rules, by weak grasp of why clots form on these valves, and by poor test methods. They set out new ways to test how a design change affects both blood flow and clot risk. Better tests would speed safer designs.
pmc-11825778:
Katrine Beck and co-authors present a study published in 2024 on joy in indoor cycling. Joy may be a key reason people stay active. Indoor cycling, or spinning, can be done in a group or alone, and the group effect on joy was not clear. Twenty active adults, with a mean age of 56, did both forms in the study.

Each person rode a 44-minute group session and a solo session, both led by an instructor. Power, heart rate, and pedal rate were much the same in both. Joy scores were a bit higher for the group ride. The gap was small and of minor weight in real terms. The authors judge the group element to be of minor importance for joy.
pmc-11827678:
Dana Rocio Chavez-Yacolca and co-authors study how internet addiction feeds study delay among university students in Peru, in a paper whose journal record is dated 2024. Putting off schoolwork is common, and heavy internet use is a suspect cause. The team asked whether belief in one's own study skills sits in the middle of that link. They surveyed 334 students with three standard scales covering addiction, delay, and academic self-belief.

Stronger internet addiction came with weaker self-belief, and weaker self-belief came with more delay. Addiction also raised delay directly. Put together, self-belief carried part, but not all, of the addiction effect, which makes it a partial bridge between the two. The authors suggest universities build students' confidence in their study skills as one lever against procrastination, alongside tackling the internet habits themselves.
pmc-11831278:
Xurong Gao and co-authors hunt for brain-wave markers of methamphetamine addiction in a paper whose text is dated 2024. Scalp recordings flicker through brief stable patterns called microstates, each tied to a large brain network. Such patterns might serve as fingerprints of the disorder if read at the right rhythm band.

The team analyzed microstate behavior across frequency bands and tasks, then trained classifiers to separate patients from healthy controls. At rest, the alpha band worked best, reaching about 85 percent accuracy. One pattern class, microstate A, carried the most weight in the calls. The authors present the band-specific marker as a reliable biomarker lead.
pmc-11840278:
Minjun Zhao and co-authors compare, in a 2024 study, how DNA is packed in pig egg cells versus pig embryo cells. Packing units called nucleosomes wrap the DNA and help control which genes switch on. Egg cells at the germinal vesicle stage will later halve their DNA for fertilization, while body cells divide in the usual way. Knowing how their packing differs could aid cloning by nuclear transfer.

Eggs from large follicles showed higher nucleosome coverage near gene start sites than the embryo cells did. Gene activity data turned up dozens of genes switched on in only one cell type. In body cells, packing near a gene's start tracked its activity level. In eggs, that link broke down. The contrast shows how packing rules shift across cell types.
pmc-11854978:
Michael Haller and co-authors present the 2024 update of international guidelines on finding and staging type 1 diabetes early in young people, in a 2024 consensus document. The guidelines come from the International Society for Pediatric and Adolescent Diabetes, whose recommendations are the main global reference for diabetes care in children, teens, and young adults. This chapter updates the 2022 guidance on staging the disease before symptoms appear.

New material gives evidence-based advice on screening for risk and on monitoring young people already in early stages. The chapter reviews trials aiming to delay the move to full, insulin-dependent disease, and efforts to preserve the pancreas's own insulin-making cells after diagnosis. It also weighs the chances and difficulties raised by a recent United States approval of teplizumab, an immune therapy that slows progression. The authors frame early detection as a practical path to gentler disease.
pmc-11970178:
Ping Zou, Ke Li, Yiting Qian, Tingting Wu, and Yue Qian present a 2024 study on predicting outcomes in breast cancer from blood tests. Doctors already track several tumor markers in the blood. The team asked whether adding immune and inflammation counts sharpens the forecast of a patient's three-year course.

They followed 112 patients who had surgery for breast cancer. Patients with poor outcomes had higher levels of the three tumor markers and of several cell counts and inflammation scores. Regression analysis kept five measures as real predictors. A combined model using the three markers with two cell counts reached a strong accuracy score. Such a cheap blood panel could help flag patients who need closer follow-up.
pmc-11976078:
Bader Alzaben and seven co-authors measured a jaw hollow that can complicate implant work in the east of Saudi Arabia, in a study published in 2024. The hollow sits on the tongue side of the lower jaw, near the first molar. A drill that breaks into it can cause bleeding or numbness. Their set held 256 cone-beam scans of that spot, sorted by ridge shape: round, flat, or cut in.

The cut-in shape led, at more than half the scans. Its depth and slant ran nearly even for men and women. One height reading split by sex; the rest did not. The authors warn that most jaws in their group hold the hollow. They urge a scan check of the spot before each implant in the zone.
pmc-11983578:
Lore Remmerie and co-authors co-create a framework for young people's sexual well-being in a study dated 2024. Health research often defines well-being for youth rather than with them, and in ways that clash across cultures. Fifteen young professionals from four continents joined a three-round online Delphi process.

The group framed sexual well-being as personal and varied, with an open view of sexual activity and intimacy. They named core capabilities: informed choice, bodily autonomy, consent, exploration, self-awareness, pleasure, communication, comfort, safety, and self-esteem. Those capabilities need an enabling setting with real access to information and services, plus acceptance and freedom from coercion.
pmc-12082678:
George and co-authors present a 2024 review of breastfeeding and chest infections in Nigerian infants. Twelve studies over two decades were gathered. Babies not exclusively breastfed faced about four times the infection risk of those who were.

Breast milk carries immune factors that blunt infections like pneumonia. Yet only a quarter to two fifths of Nigerian babies get exclusive breastfeeding for six months. Beliefs, mothers' jobs, and low schooling hold rates down. The authors call for targeted public health work and policy support to lift practice, given how steeply the protection runs in the local data.
pmc-12091078:
Seyed Abdosaleh Jafari and co-authors ask whether a person can be stripped of human dignity in a 2024 philosophy paper. Schools of thought disagree on what grants dignity in the first place. The authors take free choice of good and virtue as the mark. They then ask how anyone can tell that mark is present in a real person.

The paper draws on Islamic sources, above all the Qur'an, to find signs of dignity in action. It compares how people differ in showing those signs. Hard cases that strain each school's rules are worked through one by one. The authors argue that ideas like right and good are matters of judgment, so dignity shows itself in more than one way.
pmc-12110478:
Aimable Mutayomba and Japheths Ogendi screen road crash survivors in Kigali for post-traumatic stress disorder. The condition stalks crash survivors worldwide yet draws little clinical attention in Rwanda. The pair checked patients returning for follow-up care at three public hospitals over two months in 2023.

Of 288 survivors assessed with a clinician-run scale, fifty, about seventeen percent, met the diagnosis. Risk clustered in the thirty-two to forty-five age band. No formal schooling, family conflict at home, severe injuries, and earlier traumas each raised the odds. The authors argue crash follow-up in Rwanda should build PTSD screening in as standard care, not an afterthought.
pmc-12199978:
A team of doctors report a 2024 case of a rare bacterial infection in a small child. The germ is Chryseobacterium gleum, a Gram-negative bacterium that usually strikes people with weak immune systems. It can cause infections of the belly lining, lungs, urinary tract, and brain lining, but no case in a child had been published.

The patient was a two-year-old who came to a pediatric clinic with fever that kept returning. The child also had swollen glands under the jaw and a skin rash. Blood tests showed microcytic anemia and a high level of C-reactive protein, a marker of inflammation. A chest X-ray showed mild thickening of the bronchial pattern. Blood films showed red cells of uneven size and shape. The case is presented as the first of its kind after COVID-19 in a child.
pmc-12218478:
Selma Korlat, Christina Ristl, and Jana Nikitin wrote this 2024 study on what stirs adults to care for future generations. Such care, called generativity, may fade as age shortens one's time horizon. One hundred fifteen people aged eighteen to eighty-five reported their time outlook and generative aims, then logged nature contact in daily life through a sampling study.

Time in nature lifted concern for future people and the planet in middle-aged and older adults whose horizons ran short. The young showed no such lift. The authors suggest nature contact as a lever for drawing older adults into social and green causes, with gains for their own well-being and for those who come after.
pmc-12479978:
Jieun Park and co-authors recount a tuberculosis outbreak inside a psychiatric hospital in Daegu, South Korea. Such closed wards are prime ground for spread, since patients stay long and share air. In early twenty twenty three, one infectious case was reported. A field team then traced contacts across the hospital.

The search found two more active cases and dozens of silent infections. Later checks added a few more cases, all among the first found contacts. Gene tests tied every case to one strain from a single long stay patient. The authors stress fast case finding and treatment of both active and silent infection in such high risk sites.
pmc-12480278:
Lee, Kwon, and Lee report shot rates for young youth in South Korea for the year twenty twenty-two, in a report from twenty twenty-three. Shots are the cheapest way to stop spread of many germs. The state gives shots free and aims for rates above ninety-five percent. This report checks if that aim held for each age group.

The team used records for about one point two million youth. Rates were high at age one and fell with age. By age six, the rate was below eighty-nine percent. Rates also varied by place and by shot type. The authors say more work is needed for groups that miss shots and for those who doubt or refuse them.
pmc-12625778:
Liu leads a large team mapping pig genomes to find selection marks and trait-linked loci in a 2024 paper. Pigs vary widely between Eastern and Western breeds, and the genetic basis is murky. The team built a pan-genome from many assemblies and resequenced genomes.

They catalogued millions of small variants plus large structural changes and many new genes. Domestication left marks near genes tied to fat growth and lung immune response. Muscle data across developmental stages showed how selection reshaped chemical marks on DNA. Those shifts altered timing genes differently in Eastern and Western breeds. The resource should aid breeding programs and trait biology. It spans genomes, transcripts, and methylation in one study.
pmc-12659078:
Weihao Qi and a large team present a simple method to rebuild three-dimensional animal movement paths from a single camera video, in a 2025 paper. Movement data guide ecology research, but multi-camera setups are costly and complex. Their method combines deep learning tools with a pinhole camera model.

Tests in air and on the ground showed small average position errors, and distance estimates stayed robust when the animal was partly hidden. The team extracted speed and gait measures from the rebuilt paths and applied them to a bat predation study. The system needs only one low-cost camera and no precise calibration. The authors aim at field studies of wild animals.
pmc-12660678:
Juliana Nyasordzi and co-authors grade the safety of store bought baby foods in Ghana in a 2025 paper. Pureed weaning foods can carry fungi, their toxins, and toxic metals. Babies are the least able to bear such loads.

All sampled foods held fungi, with yeasts and two mold groups most common. Toxin levels from molds sat in low ranges across brands. Trace lead, cadmium, mercury, arsenic, and copper were found as well. Daily intake math put all loads below set safe caps. Cancer risk marks also sat in the safe zone. The foods passed this round, with watch still urged on makers.
pmc-12660778:
Forghani leads a team pooling studies on blood-borne tumor DNA in an aggressive lymphoma in a 2025 review. Circulating tumor DNA offers a needle-light way to track disease burden and change. Dozens of studies linked it to survival.

High starting levels meant higher progression risk. Tumor DNA still present at the end of treatment carried the strongest warning by far. In scan-negative patients, a positive DNA result was highly specific for coming relapse. In scan-positive patients, a negative DNA result cut the relapse risk sharply. The authors say DNA readings refine what scans show. Standardizing test protocols is the main need. DNA-guided management trials come next.
pmc-12660978:
Quanming Pu and co-authors hunted the genes that turn radish leaves purple, in a 2025 study. The purple comes from anthocyanins, pigments with health appeal and defense roles in plants. Root color genetics in radish were known, but leaf color was not. The team crossed a purple-leaf line with a green-leaf line and bred several generations from them.

Leaf color proved to be set by nuclear genes, with purple partly dominant. Mixing DNA from extreme offspring of the second generation pointed to one stretch of chromosome seven. That stretch holds thirty-nine genes, and activity tests sorted them by leaf type. One gene, akin to a known color switch called MYB114, was active only in the purple line. The authors name it the likely master switch for radish leaf color.
pmc-12662978:
Hope K Fiadjoe and co-authors study an enzyme in liver cancers in a 2025 paper. The enzyme, called HAL, starts the breakdown of histidine, an amino acid, and its level can sway how cancer cells respond to some drugs. Its role in the two main primary liver cancers was unknown.

Using a large public cancer database plus lab tests on patient tissue, the team found HAL turned down sharply in these tumors. Lower levels may help tumors grow or resist treatment by letting histidine build up. The finding names a possible marker for sorting patients and a fresh angle for drug research in liver cancer.
pmc-12663478:
Pengcheng Yan and co-authors uncover a protective protein's role in viral heart inflammation in a 2025 paper. Acute viral myocarditis, often triggered by coxsackievirus B3, kills heart cells through apoptosis and can turn severe. The protein DJ-1 is known to guard cells against death, but its part in this disease was obscure.

The team found DJ-1 levels fell in infected heart cells and in mouse hearts with myocarditis. Mice lacking DJ-1 suffered worse disease and more cell death, while restoring the protein protected both cells and animals. The chain runs through a second protein, Dusp1: losing DJ-1 lowers Dusp1, which unleashes a stress pathway that drives apoptosis. The authors present DJ-1 as a promising treatment target.
pmc-12664178:
Joaquim Domingos Lequechane and seven co-authors poll, in 2025 work, what a rural Mozambique town knows and does about malaria. The fever still weighs hard there, and town views shape what cures can land. House heads were polled before and after a kill-the-germ project ran in the zone.

Heads knew the signs, the bite path, the guards, and the cures at high rates both times, near nine in ten or more. No gaps split the project and plain zones, nor the before and after reads. The team reads the flat tale plain: the town's high fever load does not spring from poor knowledge. Other bars must drive it.
pmc-12664778:
Hamza Alrabai and co-authors review a hard-to-spot cause of buttock pain in this 2025 paper. In piriformis syndrome, a deep hip muscle squeezes the sciatic nerve. The pain mimics pain from the lower spine, so the condition is often missed, even though it may cause 5 to 8 percent of low back pain cases.

Sitting or hip movement often worsens the pain. Standard scans frequently show nothing specific, which adds to the delay. A nerve-focused magnetic scan can reveal nerve swelling and improve accuracy. The authors argue that pairing a careful clinical exam with targeted imaging gives the best path to a correct diagnosis and to treatment that fits the cause.
pmc-12669978:
Mai Sri Lena and colleagues built and validated a questionnaire about how parents support young children learning English in Indonesian primary schools. Parental help shapes motivation and effort, but no trusted local tool measured the roles parents play. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team drafted items from the literature and expert feedback, then surveyed parents of fifth graders at public and private schools in Padang. Statistical factor methods were used to test whether the items grouped sensibly and measured steadily.

Five dimensions emerged: general involvement, expectations, access to resources, enrichment, and out-of-school activities. A confirmatory analysis fit the five-part model well, and reliability scores passed standard cutoffs. The authors offer the questionnaire as a diagnostic tool for schools and researchers who want to understand and strengthen home support for language learning.
pmc-12679078:
Hemorrhoids after childbirth are common and painful, and Chinese herbal care offers two topical treatments for them. Xiao-Hui Wang and co-authors compared a combined routine against a standard one in two hundred sixty-eight patients at a Hebei hospital. One group used a herbal lotion sitz bath plus an ointment. The other used a magnesium compress plus the same ointment. Each group held one hundred thirty-four patients treated between twenty twenty-three and twenty twenty-five.

Before care, the groups matched in swelling and hemorrhoid size. After care, the herbal bath group showed smaller hemorrhoids and less swelling. Pain, comfort, mood, and cooperation with care were also compared. The authors report an edge for the combined herbal routine, with few side effects.
pmc-12685978:
Alessandro Ruffolo and nine co-authors pool evidence on combined surgery for prolapse affecting several pelvic compartments at once. Two operations, one lifting the rectum and one lifting the vagina or uterus, can be done together. Past studies were mostly backward looking, leaving the joint benefit unclear.

Six studies entered the pooled analysis. After combined surgery, constipation and blocked emptying improved clearly, as did stool leakage. Reported return of prolapse stayed low, under one in ten by both patient report and exam. No serious adverse events appeared. The authors call the joint approach safe and effective for these women. They still ask for larger, longer, controlled studies.
pmc-12690778:
Xuqian Wei and co-authors describe two families with severe clotting from inherited antithrombin deficiency in this 2025 study. Antithrombin is one of the blood's main natural brakes. Lacking it is among the worst inherited clotting risks. The condition is rare and often missed by standard checks. One patient, a man of thirty-nine, had extensive leg vein clots. The other, a woman of twenty-one, had a risky lung clot.

Both had antithrombin activity near half of normal. Lab tests measured the protein directly as well. Gene faults that cut the protein short were found in the gene. Family studies like this guide screening of relatives. Early knowledge can prevent a first fatal clot. The paper is a genetic case series.
pmc-12690978:
George John and a large team at a cancer center in India report on multiple myeloma in adults aged forty or younger, in a study published in twenty twenty-five. This blood cancer mostly strikes older people, so facts about young patients are scarce.

The team looked back at new cases treated from twenty thirteen to twenty twenty-one. Of one thousand nine hundred and eighty people screened, one hundred and ten were forty or younger, with a middle age of thirty-six. Bone harm was very common, seen in more than nine in ten, while high calcium and kidney harm were less so. More than a third had the most advanced stage at diagnosis. Common drug mixes paired bortezomib with other drugs, and about a quarter got a stem cell transplant.
pmc-12692678:
Maksym Zoziuk and co-authors scan in 2025 the small regulatory RNAs called microRNAs across human cancers, hunting for stable patterns and a cross kingdom twist. These tiny RNAs tune gene activity and often go off track in cancer, but most studies chase one at a time. The team merged proven interaction data with expression data from many cancers, and used a strict cutoff to name the most strongly shifted regulators.

They found sets of microRNAs that were turned down or up again and again across cancers, with matching shifts in their target genes. A sweep of plant microRNAs from many species found some that match the turned down human ones closely in sequence. The patterns give future studies firm leads.
pmc-12694378:
Mohsen Ramadan and co-authors chart in 2025 how an out land seed beetle in Hawaii spreads to new hosts, with a dual role in the wild. The beetle, from Africa, eats the seeds of the isles' own coral tree. A kin tree from its home land now stands as a new host.

Eggs clump on both trees, more thick on the home tree. Young live as well on both, though home tree bugs grow big ger. A food bean takes eggs with low live rate; two kin beans take none. Light seed harm from one young bug lifts sprout rates on the home tree.
pmc-12694978:
Olaleke Abraham Fasasi and co-authors test low, everyday-like doses of monosodium glutamate on male rat reproduction, in this 2025 Europe PMC paper. The flavor enhancer is widespread in processed food, and its safety is debated, though most studies use unrealistically high doses. Thirty rats received one of four doses or plain water for thirty days.

Treated rats gained more weight, and their reproductive measures worsened in step with dose. At the highest dose, sperm concentration fell by well over half, normal sperm shape dropped, and defects of head, neck and tail rose. Motility fell sharply, with half the sperm non-motile at the top dose. The authors urge caution on chronic intake.
pmc-12695478:
Propylene glycol is added to feed to give fattening lambs more usable energy, but what it does to their fat tissue over time is murky. Akın Yakan and co-authors run a grid experiment in Akkaraman lambs: two doses of the additive or none, with tissue sampled after 60, 90, and 120 days. They read gene messages, proteins, and fatty acid mixes in rump fat.

Early on, the higher dose tripled one fat-handling protein while lowering a master fat switch. With longer feeding, other fat-building factors rose and the fat itself shifted toward healthier unsaturated kinds, most clearly at the lower dose. Three fatty acids made up over 70 percent of the fat throughout. The authors say dose and timing both matter for fat quality in sheep, reporting in 2025.
pmc-12695878:
Stem cells grown in the lab can form beta cells, the insulin producing cells destroyed in type 1 diabetes, yet the lab grown versions stay immature and work poorly. Anne Lietzke and co-authors compared these cells with real human islets and found weak output from their energy centers. Genes driven by a regulator called PPAR alpha, which sets up fat burning inside those centers, were largely switched off, even though the cells' mass and structure looked normal.

Treating the growing cells with a drug that activates that regulator switched the missing genes back on. The treated cells secreted insulin better and formed many more beta cells, both in dishes and after transplant. The authors argue that fixing this energy program early in growth could make lab grown replacements stronger and more useful for people with type 1 diabetes.
pmc-12699378:
Wei Cong, Jingfu Sun, Zhanyu Hao, and Maosong Gong tested a plant compound, called IDET, as a booster for a standard cancer drug in thyroid cancer. The drug, paclitaxel, often loses force as tumors resist. The team paired the two in cancer cells and in tumor-bearing mice.

Together, the pair curbed cell growth, movement, and invasion more than the drug alone, while sparing normal thyroid cells. They jammed a defense switch that tumors use to clear cell stress, so harmful oxygen byproducts piled up and drove cell death. Tumors in mice shrank more with the pair, and organs and blood stayed sound. The compound looks like a safe sensitizer.
pmc-12699978:
Ghazaleh Falahati and co-authors estimate how often menstrual problems followed COVID-19, using a method built to resist publication bias. Reports during the pandemic linked the infection to cycle changes, but studies with striking results are more likely to be published, which can warp pooled numbers. Their 2025 analysis applies a robust Bayesian model averaging method alongside classic ones to the same evidence.

The bias-adjusted estimates put missed periods at about twelve percent of survivors and bleeding between periods at seventeen. Changes in cycle regularity reached twenty-four percent, and changes in duration, volume, and pain landed between twelve and seventeen. Overall, about nine percent had some disorder. Classic methods gave clearly different pooled sizes, which is the point of the exercise. The authors urge health education and support services for affected women.
pmc-12700378:
Alexander Truchon and co-authors mapped the marks on a giant virus's DNA in two thousand twenty-five. New long-read tools can read these marks at scale. Giant viruses carry a rich kit for tagging their own DNA. This one, which infects algae, was thought to hold six tagging enzymes. Tests showed its DNA is tagged in a strict, set pattern. Nine short motifs bore the tags.

Tag levels shifted from motif to motif. The virus sits in a group of huge DNA viruses. Its enzymes echo kin across that wide group. Tags may guard its vast genome from harm. They may tune gene use mid-infection too. Such viruses steer algal blooms in the seas. Mark maps open a fresh lens on their lives.
pmc-12700878:
Giraud and co-authors characterize the SARS-CoV-2 variant BA two point eight six in the lab, testing its drug sensitivity, infectivity, and fitness. In late 2023 it co-circulated with EG five point one, raising fears of stronger immune escape. Their 2025 study uses live viruses, checks antibody and antiviral responses, and runs head to head growth contests.

BA two point eight six fully escaped one therapeutic antibody, matching a known escape mutation, while EG five point one stayed sensitive like its ancestor. Both variants stayed sensitive to antiviral drugs. In hamsters, BA two point eight six grew far less in lungs and somewhat less in upper airways than an older strain. In nasal cells it also lost the direct contest with EG five point one. The authors conclude the variant's spread potential is limited despite its escape.
pmc-12701878:
Nine authors present a study in two thousand twenty-five on treating fully blocked hip arteries through the wrist. Catheter treatment of aortoiliac disease increasingly uses the radial artery in the wrist, thanks to purpose-built tools. Whether the wrist route can handle total blockages was unclear.

One center reviewed forty-six wrist-route procedures drawn from one hundred five blockage cases treated over five years. Patients averaged about seventy-four years, with long lesions, mostly severe. Stents were placed successfully in every patient, most often bare metal ones, guided by ultrasound imaging inside the vessel.
pmc-12702278:
Haskly Mokoena and co-authors review heart risk in people living with HIV who take standard drug therapy, in a 2025 paper. Even on treatment, these patients face higher rates of heart and vessel disease. The review asks whether raised inflammation and activation of the vessel lining help explain that extra risk.

The authors searched major databases and graded the quality of the studies they found. Fifteen reports, covering more than seven thousand patients, met their rules. Both short and long treatment courses came with higher levels of several inflammation markers. Markers of vessel lining activation were also raised. The pattern supports a link between ongoing inflammation in treated HIV and later heart disease, and points to targets for prevention.
pmc-12704978:
Teja and five co-authors report a rare tumor found behind common belly pain in a young man. Their twenty twenty-five case report comes from a family medicine clinic. Abdominal pain is an everyday complaint, but this case had red flags: three months of right loin pain, ten kilograms of weight loss, and a month of cough.

Scans showed a large, mixed mass above the right kidney, with spread to nearby nodes and the chest lining. The picture fit a malignant pheochromocytoma, a rare adrenal tumor. The patient was sent to endocrinology for care. The authors stress the family doctor's role in spotting red flags early and pushing fast referral, which can change outcomes in serious disease.
pmc-12705778:
Ronja Kardinal and Dagmar Wachten review how macrophages, the immune system's scavenger cells, drive the slow inflammation of obesity, in a 2025 paper. That chronic, low-grade state, called metaflammation, links excess weight to insulin resistance and organ damage. In white fat, obesity flips macrophages from calming to inflammatory types, stiffening tissue as they go.

The review extends to brown and beige fat, where macrophages tune heat production, and to the liver, the other metabolic front line. There, liver macrophages promote the fatty liver disease of metabolism, feeding inflammation, fat buildup, and scarring. The authors map these roles to guide therapies aimed at reprogramming macrophages rather than merely suppressing them.
pmc-12705978:
In ulcerative colitis, inflammation sometimes gathers around the appendix opening even when the rest of the colon looks calm. Ting Yi and co-authors asked whether that local swelling tracks with structural changes in the appendix itself. They reviewed 169 patients with the disease, scoring inflammation near the appendix during colonoscopy and measuring the appendix on CT scans where available.

About 17 percent of patients had a narrowed or vanished appendix opening, and the odds rose with age and with stronger nearby inflammation. Among the 42 patients scanned, 69 percent had a thickened appendix body, yet none showed signs of ordinary appendicitis. Appendix width also rose with the local score. The authors suggest the inflammation grade near the appendix can serve as an indirect sign of appendix involvement in this disease.
pmc-12706078:
Hiroshi Ageta and co-authors find that common cholesterol drugs may quietly help cancer immunotherapy. Tumors shed tiny vesicles carrying PD-L1, a protein that switches off immune attack, and patients with many such vesicles answer checkpoint drugs poorly. The team shows PD-L1 gets tagged by a small modifier called UBL3, and that tag is what routes it into the vesicles.

Statins block that tagging. In patients with heavily PD-L1-positive tumors, those already taking statins had clearly fewer PD-L1 vesicles in their blood. Gene data also tied UBL3 and PD-L1 levels to lung cancer survival. The authors propose adding statins to existing combination therapies as a cheap way to cut the vesicle traffic and sharpen immunotherapy, a hypothesis ready for clinical testing.
pmc-12706978:
Anna Gal-Pottyondy and five co-authors built reference values for the physical load on young basketball players in a 2025 study. Knowing game demands helps shape training and guard against injury. The players, 224 in all, came from Hungarian national youth teams across three age groups and both sexes.

Tracking gear recorded movement and heart data across fifty-one prep matches. Tables of reference values were built for outside load, such as speed and bursts. Inside load data, from heart measures, suffered too much loss to serve as reference. Boys led on burst distance and top speed, while girls led on mean speed and heart rate zones. Age gaps also showed. The authors offer the tables for coaches planning youth work.
pmc-12707678:
Jean-Baptiste Guimbaud and three co-authors present a 2025 neural network, SEANN, built for health studies that respects what the field already knows. Classic tools for linking traits to health are rigid, while plain neural networks are flexible but data-hungry, and health data is often thin. SEANN feeds the network a form of settled knowledge: pooled effect sizes from past meta-studies.

Those pooled sizes enter the training goal itself, steering the network toward links the field already trusts. In controlled simulations, the informed network beat a plain one at forecasting new cases. Its learned links also looked more sound to an epidemiologist's eye. The authors offer the design as a way to make machine learning usable where data is scarce but past studies are rich.
pmc-12708878:
Four authors describe a 2025 device that gathers power from millimeter-wave signals to run smart city sensors with no batteries. Billions of small devices need cell changes that cost time and harm the environment. Fifth-generation networks can carry both data and usable energy at the same time.

Each unit pairs a round-polarized antenna with a rectifier and a glass lens that widens the catch angle. One unit caught up to 20 milliwatts in tests. A two-by-two array caught up to 82 milliwatts with two senders, with a peak near 105 milliwatts in theory at full network power.
pmc-12709778:
Kumlgn Tesfa, Debaka Belete, Meseret Mulu, and Aschalew Gelaw survey urinary tract infections at a large hospital in Gondar, Ethiopia. Such infections are among the most common worldwide, and local data on which drugs still work were thin. Their 2025 study enrolls 320 patients suspected of the infection over seven months in 2023, testing urine samples and quizzing patients on risk factors.

About 22 percent of the patients truly had an infection, and seventy bacterial strains were grown. Most strains were gram-negative, led by Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae. Two drugs, meropenem and nitrofurantoin, still worked well against those bacteria. Alarmingly, about 71 percent of strains resisted several drugs at once. Nearly half of the gram-negative strains made an enzyme that breaks a whole class of antibiotics. The authors call for local drug testing to guide treatment rather than habit.
pmc-12710078:
The EFSA Panel on Food Enzymes gave a safety view in 2025 on a food enzyme made by a mold strain. The enzyme cuts a plant fiber found in grains and is made by a non-tweaked strain of a known mold. It is meant for use in eleven food-making steps. In three of them the enzyme is stripped out at the end, so intake was judged for the other eight in European crowds.

Gene harm tests raised no fears. A ninety-day rat feed study set the top safe dose at the highest amount tried, which stands far above the judged intake. A scan of its build found no match to known allergens, though a small allergy risk can not be ruled out in full. The panel found no safety bar to its use as planned.
pmc-12711078:
Stachowicz and co-authors compare in 2025 the physiques of elite Polish swimmers with non training peers, split by sex and by sprint or distance training. Body measures guide weight targets and training plans, and may also mark health risk. Thirty women and thirty men at top level were measured.

Swimmers had lower body mass index and waist to hip ratios than peers in the reported groups. Body fat was lower in the female sprint group. Long distance groups were very small, with six per sex. The authors ask how far elite swimming physiques match health promoting profiles, given the low fat and lean build found.
pmc-12711378:
Andrea Cosenza and co-authors report five-year outcomes for a light-based focal therapy in men with low-risk prostate cancer treated at a specialist center. Standard cures, surgery or radiation, control the cancer well but often harm erection and bladder control. Focal therapy treats only the diseased part of the gland, guided by scans and targeted samples.

The therapy uses a drug that, once lit inside blood vessels, chokes off the tumor's supply. Men with low-risk disease are the group most likely to be overtreated by full surgery, so a gentler option matters to them. The report tracks cancer control and side effects over five years. Long follow-up from a referral center helps men weigh focal care against watching and waiting.
pmc-12711878:
Mateen Jangda and co-authors build an AI model that warns when tube-fed patients in intensive care will be underfed, in a 2025 paper. Patients on breathing machines often get too few calories, which slows recovery.

Their model, NutriSighT, reads the stream of patient data and predicts underfeeding between days three and seven of ventilation. It was trained on about 3,300 patients from an Amsterdam database and checked on about 6,500 from a United States one. Its accuracy scores, around 0.81 at home and 0.76 abroad, clearly beat a standard rival model. The model is built to show its reasoning, which matters at the bedside. Early warnings could let staff adjust feeding plans in time.
pmc-12712678:
Yasmin Begum and co-authors make gold particles with a plant extract and test them on dye and germs, in work from 2025. The particles broke down a common orange dye fast under visible light, clearing over ninety percent in ten minutes with a helper compound. They kept most of that strength after four reuse rounds. Tests also showed germ killing against two species.

Computer models probed the particles' energy gaps and stability to back the lab work. Three learning models then forecast those gaps, with one tree model landing closest to the computer values. The authors pitch the particles for cleanup work.
pmc-12712778:
Yusuke Hoshino, Sachiko Horie, Masayuki Maki, and Ikumi Dohzono report a 2025 study on how a wild plant copes with pollen from a new kin species. Pollen from the wrong species can cut seed yield, yet plants that live near kin may have grown some guard over time. Proof from species with a known contact past is rare, so the team used two sorrel kin in Japan.

One sorrel is native and the other is a new arrival, and each grows both near and far from the other. Crosses with the wrong pollen cut seed yield in the native plant, most of all in groups that live near the kin. A second test, with right pollen first and wrong pollen next, also cut seed yield. The pattern defies the plain hope that near groups guard best.
pmc-12714078:
El-Sayed, Alsenany, Asal, and Alasqah build and test a scale for AI addiction among researchers in twenty twenty-five. Heavy use of AI tools boosts output but raises fears of over reliance. No validated measure existed for addictive use in research settings. The team drafted items from literature and interviews.

Data came from seven hundred eighteen nursing researchers. The final scale has twenty-two items across five dimensions. Those dimensions cover compulsive use, over dependency, harm to function, withdrawal, and tolerance. Factor analyses confirmed the five part structure, explaining most variance. Reliability scores were excellent across several measures. The authors say the tool can flag unhealthy dependence on AI in academia.
pmc-12714278: Joanna Clarke, writing for the staff editors of PLOS Biology, reflects on the year 2025 in the life sciences in an editorial from 2025. The year brought upheaval and uncertainty for many in the research community, she notes. The piece looks back over the year and picks out research achievements that give reasons for thanks, framing resilience and resourcefulness as the year's defining traits for the field.
pmc-12714778:
Fangxing Wang, Jie Zhao, Weijie He, Huazheng He, and Qiang Wang model crooked knee parts in partial knee replacement in a 2025 study. Half knee implants spare the joint, but fixed bearing designs punish small placement errors, and their stress effects were little mapped.

A standard knee model hosts thigh parts shifted or tilted in set ways. Sideways shift raised insert stress by near nine percent at five millimeters. Tilt either way raised it more, past eleven percent. Ligament and spare cartilage stresses shifted in telling patterns too. The maps give surgeons placement targets that keep stresses low.
pmc-12715378:
Two ways of reaching the hip joint during partial hip replacement differ in cost as well as technique, and a Dutch team priced both inside a randomized trial. Esser and co-authors followed 555 hip fracture patients for six months after cemented hemiarthroplasty. Quality-adjusted life years differed by a trivial 0.02 between the posterolateral and direct lateral approaches. Costs leaned slightly higher for one approach, but the confidence ranges crossed zero from both healthcare and societal viewpoints.

The chance of either approach being cost-effective hovered near fifty-fifty at generous payment thresholds. The authors conclude the two approaches are economically interchangeable.
pmc-12715778:
Patients with chronic sinus disease often need endoscopic surgery, and many have recently had COVID-19. Ella Prebel Jackert, Oluwatobiloba Ayo-Ajibola, and Eric Wei ask in 2025 whether a recent infection makes that surgery riskier. They mine a large health database covering nearly 50,000 sinus operations from 2020 to 2024. Matching balances the groups by age, health, and background. They compare patients infected within two months of surgery, those infected earlier, and those never infected.

A recent infection raised the risk of nosebleeds and congestion after surgery by roughly a quarter. Major complications showed no increase in any group. The authors conclude the operation stays broadly safe, while timing still deserves a thought in care planning.
pmc-12716478:
Kofi Aduo-Adjei, James Akazili, Øystein Ariansen Haaland, and Lumbwe Chola measure how often blood pressure care crushes household budgets in Ghana's Greater Accra Region, in a 2025 study. Ghana's national insurance aims to keep care from pushing families into poverty, yet out-of-pocket costs stay high. The team surveyed 382 patients at two district clinics about direct and indirect costs of managing hypertension.

By the lower threshold, 65 percent of patients faced catastrophic spending; by the stricter one, 58 percent did. Most respondents were women, and nearly all were Christian. Widowhood and joblessness linked to lower odds in the team's model, while larger households raised them. The authors conclude that hypertension care still imposes a heavy financial burden despite insurance, and they call for stronger protection for these patients.
pmc-12716578:
Charlott Terschluse and ten co-authors ask if a freeze biopsy adds value in lung checks for two granuloma illnesses. Both illnesses leave lumps of immune cells in lung tissue, and standard scope tools oft miss them. They review more than three hundred patients at one center over a decade.

Single tools hit in a tight mid range, with freeze biopsy at the top of that range. Pairing needle draw with freeze biopsy lifted hits to near nine in ten cases. Freeze biopsy shone most when scans showed no lung field change. Harms ran a bit higher than forceps, but not by a firm margin.
pmc-12717178:
Yinan Xing and seven co-authors test whether metformin, a diabetes drug, can calm airway inflammation in obese mice with asthma. Obesity makes asthma worse and blunts standard treatment. The team built the model by feeding mice a high-fat diet and exposing them to egg protein, a trigger. They measured inflammation markers in blood and lung fluid and checked lung tissue under the microscope.

The obese asthmatic mice showed stronger airway inflammation than lean asthmatic mice, with more white blood cells in lung fluid. A signaling route driving inflammation was switched up, while a calming energy sensor was switched down. Metformin reversed that pattern: the energy sensor rose, the inflammation route fell, and key inflammatory chemicals dropped. The authors say the results support metformin as a candidate add-on for obesity-linked asthma, through that paired pathway. Further work is needed before any use in patients.
pmc-12718578:
Yihong Ding and co-authors study frailty and depression together as dementia risks in a 2025 analysis of three aging cohorts. The two conditions may share roots, yet most past work judged each alone.

More than two hundred twenty thousand people aged sixty and over were followed across British and American cohorts, for nearly three million person years in total. About nine thousand developed dementia. Frail participants faced about two and a half times the risk of the robust. Depression alone raised risk about one and a half times. The paper then weighs the pair together, asking whether having both is worse than the sum of its parts, and reports the interaction in full.
pmc-12720278:
A European Food Safety Authority plant health panel weighs the pest risk of sweet chestnut plants shipped from the United Kingdom, in work from twenty twenty-five. The trees move as graftwood, whips, bare root stock, and potted plants. Import rules list the commodity as high risk.

All pests tied to the commodity were screened against set criteria. Three regulated pests found in the United Kingdom counted as relevant. One unregulated fungus like organism, Phytophthora kernoviae, passed every test for deeper review. Experts judged the stated safeguards and rated pest freedom per product type. Bare root and potted plants carried the pest most often in expectation. High confidence bounds were given for clean units.
pmc-12720378:
Alexander Reznik and co-authors track the mental health of female university students in Ukraine across three years of war. The war brings fear, low mood, loneliness, and burnout to civilians. Their 2025 study surveyed more than three thousand students at three points, from the first year of the full war to late 2024. Most had stayed in place, while some had fled within or beyond the land.

Fear of war, low mood, and burnout all eased in the second year, then rose again in the third. At every point, low mood and loneliness tracked closely with fear and burnout. Step-by-step models tied burnout to fear, low mood, and loneliness together. The authors say the results can guide campus mental health services and training for staff.
pmc-12720978:
Modar Doyya and co-authors present a 2025 case report on spleen removal to treat a blood disorder in late pregnancy. A woman in Syria, aged thirty-eight and at full term, had immune thrombocytopenia, a state in which the body destroys its own platelets. Drugs given for a month had failed to lift her very low platelet count, and labor had begun.

The team gave platelet transfusions, delivered a healthy baby by cesarean birth, and removed her spleen in the same operation. They also found and removed a small extra spleen. Her platelet count rose sharply after surgery. The authors note that spleen removal is now most often done in mid-pregnancy, but this case shows it can work at full term when drugs fail.
pmc-12721078:
Motaz AlAqeel and co-authors report a rare tumor case in the forearm in 2025. A woman in her late forties noticed a slow growing, painless lump in her upper forearm. She also developed wrist drop, a sign of nerve trouble. Scans showed a smooth, mucus rich growth inside a forearm muscle that turns the hand.

Tissue tests confirmed a benign tumor type that seldom appears in the forearm. Surgery removed the growth, which was pressing on a nearby nerve. Her wrist lift then improved step by step, with no return of the tumor. The report pairs the case with a review of past cases.
pmc-12722278:
Franziska Meinert and co-authors checked the accuracy of frameless brain biopsy guided by scans, in a 2025 study. Guided biopsy is the standard way to diagnose brain lesions that cannot be removed. Frameless systems steer the needle with MRI data, but MRI can warp shapes and hurt targeting. CT gives truer geometry, so some teams fuse the two scan types for navigation. The study compared the two routes in routine care.

Ninety nine patients who had the biopsy over about two and a half years were split by navigation type. Most used MRI alone, and a smaller group used the fused scans. Miss distance at entry and at target was much the same in both groups. Lesion size, target depth, and procedure time also matched. Complication rates differed on paper but not in a statistically clear way, and the authors treat overall accuracy as comparable.
pmc-12722478:
Ivo Sedláček and co-authors describe, in a 2025 taxonomy study, two cold-tolerant bacterial species new to science, found in Magellanic penguin droppings in Argentine Patagonia. Samples gathered in 2016 and 2017 yielded two strains that early gene reads placed in the genus Erwinia, a group better known from plants.

Whole-genome comparisons showed the strains match no named species, and differ enough from each other to count as two. Form and chemistry tests backed the split. They are named Erwinia psychrophila and Erwinia magellanica, and their type strains now sit in two public collections. Since some Erwinia species blight crops, knowing the family's wild members sharpens both ecology and plant protection. Penguin colonies, it seems, host more than birds.
pmc-12722778:
Pneumonia caught outside hospitals still sends many older adults into wards each year in Korea. Kyeo Rae Ju and co-authors chart who those patients are and what infects them in a 2025 study at one large hospital.

From more than seven thousand people with pneumonia signs between 2005 and 2019, the team confirmed about four thousand cases. The average age was seventy, and two thirds were men. Chronic lung disease was the most common background condition, ahead of cancer and weakened immunity. Sputum cultures most often grew a Klebsiella species, with staph and other bacteria behind it. Regional maps of this kind help doctors choose first antibiotics before lab results return.
pmc-12722878: DeBroff reviews the history of double optic capture, a method for seating artificial lenses during cataract surgery. The lens optic is held through openings in both the front and back walls of the lens capsule. The grip keeps the lens centered and can cut later membrane growth behind it. The review traces how the method was done and how it has changed. Newer variants serve both child and adult cataract cases. DeBroff also weighs wider use in routine adult surgery to prevent haze behind the lens.
pmc-12723078:
After breast cancer treatment ends, many women live with a nagging fear that the cancer will return, and that fear can shadow daily life. Zhensheng Li and co-authors follow that fear through radiation treatment in this 2025 study from a hospital in Hebei, China. They track anxiety, depression, and quality of life in women receiving radiation after surgery.

Four hundred and eighty-six women joined the study in 2015 and 2016 and filled in standard questionnaires before and after their radiation course. Fear of return was gauged by a single worry question borrowed from a quality-of-life scale. The team modeled how strongly that fear lined up with anxiety and depression scores, taking pain and poor sleep into account as well. Their title states the headline finding: the fear contributes largely to distress and to poorer quality of life.
pmc-12723178:
Haiping Zhang and co-authors trace, in 2025, a chain of RNA signals that drives inflammation in artery disease. Immune cells called macrophages fuel the disease when fat metabolism goes wrong. A long noncoding RNA was found at high levels in such cells after exposure to oxidized cholesterol, a key trigger.

Silencing that RNA calmed the inflammatory response. It works by soaking up a small RNA, which frees a third factor that switches inflammation on. Raising the long RNA raised that factor, confirming the chain. The authors propose blocking the long RNA as a treatment strategy for atherosclerotic heart disease, to be tested beyond the dish.
pmc-12723878:
Jeehae Chung and co-authors survey nurses on digital skills, burnout, and engagement in a 2025 study. Hospital tech now demands strong digital literacy and informatics skill. Such skills may act as job resources that shield nurses from burnout. A demands-resources model frames the question.

In June 2025, 130 nurses at a Korean tertiary hospital filled the survey. Wards, intensive care, and emergency units all took part. Regression models link digital skills to burnout and engagement. Mediation tests ask if a positive work culture carries part of the effect. The study maps where training investment may pay off in nurse well-being and retention.
pmc-12724478:
Leon Gerardo Kreis and co-authors weigh the costs and gains of auto feedback after online depression screening in a 2025 study. Adults who screened positive but had no diagnosis joined a trial with three arms. One group got no feedback, one got plain feedback, and one got feedback shaped to their symptoms, wishes, and local care. All feedback shared the result and urged pro advice.

Over six months, with just over one thousand people in the study, cost and health gaps between groups were not firm in statistical terms. Yet plain feedback looked worse than both no feedback and shaped feedback on value for money. Curves and extra checks probed how sure that ranking was. Readers learn that more contact after screening is not always better value.
pmc-12727178:
Siyu Zou and co-authors review drug shots for jaw joint pain in a paper from 2025. The focus is on people whose jaw joint disorder limits how wide they can open the mouth. The team compares thirteen kinds of shots given right into the joint.

The authors searched four large databases for trials that tested these shots. They checked each trial for bias and pulled out data on mouth opening and pain. They also tracked side moves of the jaw, such as shifts to the side. By pooling the trials in one network, the review ranks the shots side by side. Clinicians can use the ranks when they pick a drug for a stiff, sore jaw.
pmc-12729078:
Semahat Incikabi and Oktay Erbay test if math fit tween math and science class plans steers kids' science marks. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Six hundred twenty fifth and sixth grade kids in eleven Turkish state schools took science tests. Each test item was classed as math-linked or math-split by its fit to the grade math plan.

Kids scored far low on split items, though talks showed they oft held the science but tripped on math forms past their class scope. The pair hold that plan gaps put kids at a loss and split their grasp. They urge plan teams, teachers, and law heads to bind the two plans tight.
pmc-12729178:
Chen and co-authors compare two stitch materials for repairing a torn Achilles tendon, the thick cord at the back of the ankle. One material dissolves over time and the other stays. Their 2025 study matches fifty patients of each kind from repairs done between 2013 and 2024, then checks healing with ultrasound and function scores at six and twelve months.

At six months the dissolving-stitch group had thinner tendons, better gliding, and higher function scores. Blood flow at the repair site ran higher in that group as well. By twelve months every gap had closed, and outcomes looked the same. Complications were few in both groups. The authors say dissolving stitches speed early healing without changing the end result.
pmc-12729278:
Ruben Nurmohamed and a large team published a 2025 study on a new attack against infections on medical implants. Germs on implants form biofilms, slimy shields where dormant bacteria hide. Inside a biofilm, standard antibiotics lose much of their power, which feeds the wider crisis of drug resistance.

The team's plan is radioimmunotherapy. Antibodies that home to one germ type are linked to radioactive atoms, actinium-225 or lutetium-177. The antibodies carry the radiation straight to the biofilm, where it can kill the sheltered bacteria. Tests in living animals give the first proof that the idea can work. Success could open a path for infections that drugs alone cannot clear.
pmc-12729678:
Manoela Neves and co-authors model how a growth on the vocal folds changes the voice in a 2025 study. Growths on the top surface can alter tissue stiffness and cause hoarseness. Past models rarely placed a lesion inside a true-to-life model of the voice box.

The team built a layered, three-dimensional model from a human scan, with a bleeding polyp as the lesion. Air flow and tissue motion were simulated together so each could move the other. That setup lets them trace how the lesion shifts airflow and fold vibration. Voice doctors and engineers may use such models to plan care.
pmc-12729978:
Flora Philine Reemtsma and co-authors present a 2025 field study on blood changes in eventing horses during cross-country rides. Amino acids in blood shift as muscles adapt to hard effort, and those shifts might forecast how well a horse performs. The team followed horses across a full season of events.

Twenty horses from nine breeds were sampled at up to seven events over twenty-three weeks. Blood was drawn before the ride, shortly after, and the next morning. A few amino acids shifted with the calendar week, and four measures linked to ride scores. Early leucine and later histidine levels stood out. Such markers could one day guide training and care.
pmc-12730178:
Aiman Abdullah Sanosi, writing alone in 2025, reports a case where a vitamin dose made long-term migraine worse. The patient was a woman whose classic migraine had been calm and well held for 20 years. She then began two months of daily, severe head pain that drugs could not ease.

The turn came after she started a high dose of biotin, a B vitamin sold for hair and nails. She took 10,000 micrograms a day. Her attacks grew daily, sent her to emergency care more than once, and cut her quality of life. When she stopped the dose, attacks fell back to rare and mild. Sanosi thinks the dose may stir cell energy paths that feed head pain. He calls for more study of the link.
pmc-12730278:
Ugo Testa and co-authors published a 2025 review on gene therapy for two inherited blood diseases. Sickle cell disease and beta-thalassemia both stem from faults in the gene for a hemoglobin part. In severe cases they demand lifelong intensive care, and the only cure, a donor stem cell transplant, is open to few patients. Gene therapy offers a way to use the patient's own cells instead.

The review draws on a systematic search of the literature. In this approach, the patient's blood stem cells are collected and fixed outside the body, then returned. One route adds or silences genes using a lentivirus shuttle. Another edits the faulty code directly, with CRISPR tools or base editing. Several products have now been tested in patients. Many achieved freedom from transfusions and lasting correction of blood measures. Some products have won approval, offering a possible cure without a donor.
pmc-12730378:
Tomasz Gebarowski and co-workers compare smell-related repair cells grown from two sources in dogs, in a 2025 paper. Olfactory ensheathing cells are studied for nerve repair. They can be taken from the olfactory bulb in the brain or from the lining of the nose, which is easier to reach.

Using matched donors and identical lab conditions, the team grew both culture types. Bulb cultures held a higher share of the target cells and grew faster. Nose cultures were more mixed and included an epithelial component. The authors say source shapes culture makeup, and nose-based methods need more refinement before functional tests of repair.
pmc-12730678:
Gregory Kelly and co-authors review new immunotherapy approaches for colorectal cancer, published in 2025. Immunotherapy uses the body's own immune system to target tumor cells more precisely than standard chemotherapy. Drugs that block immune checkpoints such as PD-1, PD-L1, or CTLA-4 have produced durable responses in some patients.

Yet most cases gain little from a single checkpoint drug. The field needs markers that pick out likely responders, plus new targets that make tumors sensitive to blockade. That search is hampered by an incomplete grasp of how these therapies reshape the immune response to cancer. The review highlights genome-wide screening, mouse models, and organoid co-culture systems as tools for finding targets for combination treatment.
pmc-12730878:
Svetlana Miroshnichenko and co-authors test a way to make hard cancer cells drug-soft again in a 2025 study. Repeat chemo can breed cells that shrug off many drugs at once. The team aimed small blockers at three tiny RNA bits that help cells resist. The blockers use a new chemical build. Their test bed was a human skin cancer cell line bred to resist two core drugs, cisplatin and doxorubicin.

Pairs of blocker and drug worked as well as the sum of parts, and at times a touch more. With blockers in play, drug doses fell five to twenty-fold while cell kill held strong. A key drug-pump mark dropped in level. Three fresh marks tied to resistance also fell. The authors see the blockers as add-ons that could stretch old drugs. Cell tests come first here, so animal and human steps still lie ahead.
pmc-12731078: Guest editors Negin Imani, Brenda Vale, and Derek Clements-Croome open a 2025 special issue on buildings that borrow ideas from living things. They argue that the outer skin of a building is moving toward change and self-control, much like the skin of a plant or animal. In their view, treating buildings as living systems, not fixed blocks, is a key path for facing climate change. The short editorial sets up the issue's theme: walls and roofs that sense, adjust, and respond to their setting.
pmc-12731378:
Mehmet Siddik Cadirci develops new goodness-of-fit tests in a statistics paper from two thousand twenty-five, written alone. Such tests check whether data match a claimed distribution. The tests rest on Tsallis entropy, a generalized measure of uncertainty, with emphasis on two flexible distribution families.

The test statistic compares a closed-form entropy under the assumed model with a neighbor-based estimate from the data. Cadirci proves the estimator settles on the true value under mild conditions. Cutoff values come from resampling methods. Wide simulations report the tests' false alarm rates, power, and running time across settings. An applied example shows how to calibrate the tests in practice.
pmc-12731578:
Filipe Stoyell-Conti and co-authors film in this 2025 study, at the gene level, how a vein remodels after surgeons join it to an artery for dialysis access. The mouse fistula model is popular, but how faithfully it mirrors human change was unproven. Gene reads, bulk and single-cell, tracked the jugular vein across the days after surgery.

Inflammation struck first, then a matrix-building wave cresting at day ten. Immune cells flooded in, some turning pro-scarring, while wall fibroblasts became the chief matrix layers by day five. Matched against human samples, the mouse replayed the core inflammation-to-fibrosis axis, backing the model for mechanism hunts. Drug tests in the model gain firmer ground.
pmc-12731678:
Feifer and six co-authors link social conditions with what palliative care visits cover for children with cancer, in work from twenty twenty-five. Pediatric palliative care improves symptom control and end of life outcomes. Access to it is unequal by social determinants of health.

Less was known about how visit content itself varies by race, income, or language. The retrospective cohort included patients up to twenty-seven years old with cancer. Domains addressed in each visit were charted against family social factors. Content gaps matter as much as access gaps: a visit that skips financial or spiritual needs serves a family less fully.
pmc-12732078:
Deniz Kamaci Sener and co-authors test whether a blood-based stress index forecasts death after back-of-brain strokes, in a 2025 paper. Vessel lining injury drives stroke damage, and the EASIX index, built from creatinine, an enzyme, and platelet counts, gauges that injury. The study covers posterior circulation strokes reopened by clot retrieval.

Fifty-eight patients treated with mechanical thrombectomy, some with clot-busting drugs too, had index values drawn from first-day labs. The index predicted ninety-day death only modestly, and the link missed statistical significance. Still, patients above the cutoff carried a several-fold higher mortality risk and tended to be older with more lipid trouble. The authors call for bigger cohorts before the cheap score guides care.
pmc-12732278:
Busra Bulbul and thirteen co-authors hunt for real world marks of survival in spread breast cancer treated with CDK4/6 blockers, a standard first line care for hormone driven cases. High estrogen receptor levels may mark who lives longer. The study came out in twenty twenty-five.

Records came from many centers for hundreds of patients treated across four years with one of two drugs of this class. Single factor checks tied longer survival to no prior hormone care, no liver spread, bone only spread, and a second hormone mark. Very high estrogen receptor levels showed a strong trend the same way. In joined models, no prior hormone care kept its link to better survival.
pmc-12732578:
Laelson Rochelle Milanês Sousa and co-authors study HIV risk behavior among men who have sex with men in Brazil, in this 2025 survey study. The group faces high HIV rates, and a daily preventive pill, known as PrEP, is one of the main tools offered. The team asked which men both skip condoms and skip that pill.

An online survey run in 2020, spread through social media and dating apps, drew one thousand three hundred fifty-seven men. About sixty-nine percent reported condomless anal sex without PrEP use in the past year. The pattern was more common among younger men, among men with a steady partner, and among those who had already had a sexually transmitted infection. The authors call for prevention work shaped to these men, with more effort to raise PrEP use and sharpen risk awareness.
pmc-12732878:
Sonja Zrilić and co-authors study a weak kind of bond that turns out strong in metal complexes holding phenanthroline, in a paper published in twenty twenty-five. The bond links a carbon-hydrogen group to oxygen. In the setting studied, the oxygen comes from water sitting just outside the metal's inner shell.

The team mined a crystal database and found thousands of these contacts in stored structures. They then computed bond strengths for the free molecule and for complexes with cobalt and palladium. Binding the molecule to a metal made the bonds much stronger. The strongest matched the bond between two water molecules. Strength tracked the electric charge felt at the hydrogen atom almost perfectly.
pmc-12732978:
Flaminia Coluzzi and co-authors review brain immune cell activity in nociplastic pain. Their twenty twenty-five paper covers a third kind of chronic pain, driven by changed pain sensing itself. No clear nerve damage or tissue trigger explains it, so diagnosis rests on ruling other causes out.

PET scans with tracers for microglia, the brain immune cells, show a strong link with this pain. Fibromyalgia, the model form of the condition, shows the clearest signal. Brain maps tie swelling to pain processing areas. The review moves from animal models to human scans, then to treatment ideas that target microglia. A biomarker from such scans could end the diagnosis-by-exclusion era.
pmc-12733078:
City design can move chronic patients, and Mercedes Gil-Lespinard and co-authors ran a practice circle to co-design fixes in Barcelona, in work from twenty twenty-five. Twenty-five people sat in: patients, clinicians, planners, and officials. Three sessions mapped what blocks walking and what helps it.

Shade, walkable routes, and green links led the wish list. Four neighborhood spots were picked for upgrades: more shade, friendlier paths, richer green space. Spaces that flex and connect beat grand single projects, the group found. The project offers the circle method to other cities with aging, ill populations.
pmc-12733178: Marie Nour Karam and co-authors review acute leukemia in teens and young adults with Down syndrome in a 2025 study. Records at one center cover 41 children and seven teens and young adults, all treated with a child style drug regimen.
