Two year event free survival sat at 28.6% for the older group against 84.9% for the children. The authors call for more research aimed at this understudied group.
pmc-12733278:
Suhaila Saad, Nurulhuda Mohd Satar, and Roza Hazli Zakaria wrote this 2025 study on what dialysis patients in Malaysia pay from their own pockets. Dialysis keeps people with failed kidneys alive, but the steady cost of treatment, supplies, and travel falls partly on patients. The team surveyed 220 patients at two public hospitals, some on center-based blood dialysis and some on home fluid dialysis.

Monthly out-of-pocket spending was far higher for the center group, with a median near 388 ringgit against about 160 for the home group. The gap held after other traits were weighed. Spending also rose with the distance from home to the center, with other illnesses, and with longer time on treatment. The authors say the choice of method shapes family budgets as much as clinic budgets, a fact that should enter treatment planning.
pmc-12733478:
Ghaith Mansour and co-authors review a decade of change in blood cancer care in a 2025 paper. Leukemias, lymphomas, myelomas, and related syndromes form the field covered. Treatment once relied on blunt chemotherapy alone for nearly every patient treated.

Molecular knowledge has redrawn treatment maps since then, disease by disease. Engineered cell therapies and bispecific antibodies lead the immune treatment wave. Targeted pills block single drivers like BTK and BCL-2 proteins inside cells. Combination strategies that pair old and new drugs are assessed in depth. Long-term outcomes and resistance problems temper the celebration throughout. Readers get a guided tour of precision medicine's biggest success field.
pmc-12733578:
A research team compared blood markers of one cell process across four joint and immune diseases in this 2025 study. The process is called NETosis, a way white blood cells release web-like strands that can fuel inflammation. The diseases studied were lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, and ankylosing spondylitis.

The team measured free DNA in blood plus two markers tied to the webs, and compared patients with healthy subjects. Free DNA was higher in all four diseases, but the two web markers stood out most in lupus, where they also linked to heart and vessel disease. A signal protein that can trigger the process was raised in all four groups. The pattern suggests the process is strongest in lupus, present in arthritis, and weaker in the other two diseases.
pmc-12733778:
Dong Gyu Kim, Kyung Ah Lee, and their co-authors report a 2025 case of rebuilding the perineum, the area between the legs, after Fournier's gangrene. That rare infection kills tissue fast in the genital and anal area, and wide removal of dead tissue leaves hard wounds to close. Their patient was a man aged 43 whose infection followed colon cancer.

After the dead tissue was cut away in stages, the team closed the wound with a flap of skin and tissue from the upper inner thigh. The flap was planned around small vessels found with a handheld sound device and turned to cover the gap. It lived in full, with no wound problems, and the man recovered good function. The case adds one more option for a hard repair.
pmc-12733878:
Hashimoto and co-authors evaluate a new bone cement mix for joint and spine repair. Standard PMMA cement is the clinical mainstay, but it is far stiffer than spongy bone, never resorbs, and can heat tissue as it sets. Those flaws can loosen implants and harm nearby bone over time.

Their composite blends cyanoacrylate glue with round, porous particles of beta-tricalcium phosphate that were sintered for strength. The phosphate ceramic can conduct new bone growth and slowly resorb. Tests weighed handling, strength, and setting traits of the mix. The aim is a cement that works more like living bone.
pmc-12733978:
Ines Abreu Marques and co-authors present a 2025 review of a less known side of Crohn's disease: perianal damage that does not form fistulas. Cracks, deep ulcers, narrowings, and skin tags near the anus affect many patients and drag down daily life. The review pulls work up to late 2025 that sets these apart from fistula cases.

Close to half of patients develop such signs during their illness. Many heal with standard Crohn's care or simple measures. Deep ulcers and narrowings warn of a rougher course. Surgery is kept for stubborn cases, since risk is high. A link to anal cancer stays unproven. The authors call for set labels, closer watch, and trials of modern drugs.
pmc-12734278:
Nuria Andrea Tort and colleagues tested in two thousand twenty-five whether hydrogen-rich water boosts standard painkillers for nerve pain in mice. Nerve pain often needs long, high-dose treatment with heavy side effects. Male mice with a tied sciatic nerve received a cannabis-like drug, a gabapentin-like drug, the water, or combinations.

Each treatment eased pain behaviors in a dose-related way, and combinations worked better than single drugs. Brain-related tissue checks showed less oxidation, inflammation, and overactive pain signaling with combined care. The results suggest an add-on that might let patients use lower drug doses, though human testing remains far away.
pmc-12734578:
Mamta Dhyani and co-authors show that a workhorse power transistor ages by rules its standard theory does not predict in a 2025 study. The devices are 1700-volt silicon carbide MOSFETs, prized in electric vehicles and grid gear. Under heat and voltage stress, their turn-on threshold drifts, a wear-out called bias temperature instability.

Textbooks model that drift with reaction-diffusion theory and a fixed power-law exponent. Switching the devices at realistic speed under combined gate and drain stress, the team found the exponent itself changes. Lifetime forecasts built on the fixed rule would then mislead. Power electronics designers need the corrected picture before these parts anchor fast chargers and drives at scale.
pmc-12734878:
Alfredo Morales-Sánchez and co-authors test how one layer's thickness changes a memory device's behavior in this 2025 study. The device stores data by switching electrical resistance in a stack of silicon and silicon oxide layers. Three stacks were built, differing only in the middle silicon layer's thickness.

After heating, the two thinner stacks broke down as silicon layers bled into each other, growing larger crystals. The thickest stack kept its layered shape. That stack switched on at a much lower voltage and held stable on-off behavior. The broken stacks behaved erratically and needed far higher voltage to form. The study ties clean layer structure to reliable switching.
pmc-12735278:
Diana Tatarciuc and her co-authors offer a 2025 narrative review on how the mouth's microbes may affect stomach health. Most attention goes to Helicobacter pylori, a stomach germ tied to gastritis. Yet the mouth hosts a vast microbial community, and its imbalance may feed stomach disease. The authors gathered studies from 2000 to 2025, favoring reviews and strong human research.

They describe three pathways linking the mouth to the stomach. Germs can travel down and settle in the stomach, swelling from gum disease can prime body-wide inflammation, and disturbed mouth chemistry can alter helpful nitrate processing. Early trials suggest treating gum disease may help clear the stomach germ and cut its return. Still, shared habits like smoking blur the picture. The authors urge dentists and stomach doctors to work together on this link.
pmc-12735478:
Mittelman and colleagues show that mice learn to release insulin at the taste of a known food in twenty twenty-five. This early insulin pulse, before food is absorbed, helps keep blood sugar steady after meals. The team tested whether mice give the pulse for two lab chows of like makeup. One chow was the mice's daily food, the other was new to them.

A few seconds of chewing the known chow was enough to trigger the pulse. The new chow triggered none until weeks of eating it had passed. Mice raised on the second chow showed the mirror pattern. Smell loss killed the learned pulse for one chow but not the other. Flavor learning drives the pulse.
pmc-12735778:
Ceylan Buse Atlas Okut and Ayşe Türkhan purified and profiled an enzyme from sickleweed, an edible and medicinal plant. The enzyme, polyphenol oxidase, drives the browning that spoils the look and value of cut fruits and vegetables. Knowing how it behaves in a given plant helps food makers control it.

Using a binding-based purification, they concentrated the enzyme about fifteen-fold. For all three test compounds, it worked best at a neutral acidity and at twenty degrees. One compound, 4-methylcatechol, bound most strongly, and the team used it to test stability against heat and acidity. Of three common anti-browning agents, ascorbic acid blocked the enzyme best, ahead of citric acid and sodium metabisulphite.
pmc-12736178:
Dorina Pjetraj and co-authors published a review in 2025 on picky eating in children. Many young children refuse foods, and parents worry whether the phase will pass or cause harm. The review asks when picky eating is a normal stage and when it signals a deeper problem.

The team searched five databases for work from 2015 to 2025 on children up to age eighteen. Picky eating shows in thirteen to fifty percent of children, peaking between ages two and six. Causes span genes, touch and taste sensitivity, temperament, and family habits at meals. The review separates the trait from two harsher feeding disorders that carry real risk. Care rests on parent teaching, calm repeated offers of new foods, and expert help when growth suffers.
pmc-12736278:
Nguyen Phuc An Khang and co-authors review ways to make gold nanoclusters glow brighter in electric light tests, in a 2025 paper. These tiny gold specks shine when a voltage drives reactions around them, a method used in sensing. Helper chemicals called co-reactants spark the glow, yet weak output and wasted energy limit the clusters.

The review sorts fixes into four families. Newer co-reactants swap in safer, body-friendly options. Accelerators cut the voltage needed and raise output. Bundling the parts into one nano-assembly shortens the energy path. Host shells can cradle the helpers and steady their radicals. Together, these designs lift brightness and stability for gold cluster light tests in labs and clinics.
pmc-12736378:
Mónica Sánchez-Ceja and co-authors pair natural agents with an antibiotic against a cow udder germ in a 2025 study. Mastitis, an udder infection, costs dairy farms worldwide. The germ at issue shrugs off the standard drug and builds slime shields called biofilms.

Two helpers were tested: nisin, a germ-made peptide, and chitosan, a shell-derived polymer. At low doses, each boosted the drug's power against two farm strains and a lab strain. The chitosan mix worked best of all. Stain and live-count tests showed the pairs also broke into pre-made biofilms and killed cells inside. The authors pitch the pairs as aids to prevent or control mastitis with less drug.
pmc-12736478:
Ahmed Elfallaki Elidrissi and co-authors study a plant as a source of a natural diuretic, in work from twenty twenty-five. The plant is Astragalus boeticus, and its extracts were checked for makeup, urine effects, and safety signs. Plant diuretics draw interest as a gentler choice than synthetic drugs.

Lab reads found fourteen phenolic compounds, led by trans-resveratrol. Computer safety checks flagged no harm to liver, genes, or nerves for that compound. In rats, both extracts raised urine output and salt loss over fifteen days. Kidney and liver blood signs stayed stable. The authors link the effect to the phenol mix and urge more work on how it acts.
pmc-12736878:
Maria Mondéjar-López and co-authors report a 2025 study on a plant-based spray meant to protect crops from fungi. Fungal disease cuts crop yields by large margins, and rules now limit some chemical sprays, so growers need safer options. The team loaded an extract of the plant Sideritis serrata into tiny particles made of chitosan, a material drawn from natural sources.

The particles were made by a gel method and tuned for size and for how much extract they carried. In lab tests, the loaded particles fought fungi far better than the free extract, with the largest gain against one Aspergillus strain. Tests on wheat seeds showed about ninety-five percent sprouting, with stronger root and shoot growth. The authors see the product as a promising green tool, with field trials still to come.
pmc-12736978:
Ivan Timofeenko and co-authors shine extra light kinds on red-leaf lettuce in a 2025 study. Two kinds of lettuce, unlike in leaf shape and red depth, grew under a mid white light. The team added blue light, a low dose of the burn ray past violet, or both, by day and by night.

They ran the burn ray for two full days at a low rate. Leaf food-making, guard marks against cell harm, and plant size were all read. Red depth in the leaf may shield or strain the plant under such light. Growers of lit greens gain dose lore for lights that can help or hurt.
pmc-12737078:
Tatiana Grodetskaya and seven co-authors compare how young oaks from different mother trees handle drought, low nitrogen, and both stresses at once. Pedunculate oak faces growing climate pressure, and family-level differences could guide planting choices. The team raised half-sibling families from five mother trees and measured water content, growth, leaf pigments, and protective enzymes under each treatment. Water stress dried the leaves of every family, but the chemical responses diverged sharply.

Some families piled up proline, a stress shield, while two families lost it. Combined stress stunted the growth of only some families, and nitrogen shortage cut chlorophyll in two. Two families, numbered 303.32 and 339.57, stood out as the most resilient across all three stresses. Others were sensitive to one stress or both. The authors offer the ranking as a basis for choosing tough oak stock for forestry and conservation.
pmc-12737178:
Bora and a team including Bhuyan review membrane filters for clearing fine particles from air in twenty twenty-five. Dirty air harms health worldwide, and membranes offer a sharp sieve. Five membrane kinds get the tour, from nanofiber mats to light active sheets. Fresh traits like germ killing, flame resistance, and reuse are weighed.

Separation paths, physical, chemical, and biological, are laid out in depth. A cost and merit face off with classic filters favors membranes on several counts. Market status and scale up hurdles are charted. Green making, smart materials, and AI aided design mark the road ahead.
pmc-12737278:
Camille Dumont and co-authors compare capsule types for dry powder inhalers, a factor that had been little studied. Five capsules were tested: two gelatin-based forms and three hypromellose-based forms. All held the same model blend of phenytoin and lactose, and spray performance was measured with a standard impactor set-up.

Hypromellose capsules gave clearly higher drug delivery than gelatin ones. The best form sent fifty-one percent of the nominal dose toward lung uptake, with strong batch-to-batch steadiness. Inner surface traits differed by polymer family, yet no neat link tied roughness or charge to performance. All capsules held up well in strength tests. Capsule choice, the authors conclude, is a key design factor.
pmc-12737478:
Jiunn Luh Tan and eleven colleagues survey raspberry viruses across the Czech Republic and report a brand-new one, in a study from twenty twenty-five. Global raspberry production has grown, yet viruses threaten it. Samples of plants and arthropods came from five regions over two years. Tests covered the certification scheme's virus list plus two more.

Raspberry bushy dwarf virus was most prevalent, infecting about half the plants. Two other viruses followed at substantial rates. Four listed viruses were not detected at all. One virus turned up in a new host plant, and a leaf blotch virus was experimentally transmitted with its mite partner. Only two of the arthropod species carrying viruses are known vectors. Sequencing showed high variability in several viruses. Continued monitoring, the authors urge, is essential.
pmc-12737678:
Qiaoyu Fang and co-authors screen approved drugs against two viral enzymes of SARS-CoV-2 in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The enzymes, Mpro and PLpro, drive virus copying and blunt host defenses. Blocking them could slow infection, and old drugs offer a fast track.

Using chip screening, enzyme tests, a fake-virus assay, and computer docking, the team found two standouts: oxytocin and risedronate sodium. Both shifted the enzymes' activity and kept the virus from copying in the tests. The authors say these drugs, and cephalosporins as a class, widen the library of candidates for coronavirus care. More study is needed before any clinical use.
pmc-12737778:
Daniele Henriques and co-authors studied liver changes after two rounds of dengue infection in marmosets in two thousand twenty-five. Dengue can injure the human liver, above all in severe cases. A second infection with a different dengue type is a known risk pattern, so a primate model helps trace what happens.

Twenty-six marmosets first received one dengue type, and half later received a second type two months on. Viral proteins appeared in liver cells and scavenger cells. Damage included cell death, inflammation, and iron deposits. Immune cell counts rose in both rounds, but the mix of signals differed, with the second round higher in several inflammatory markers. The model mirrors human severe dengue liver change.
pmc-12738078:
Daniel Álvarez, Stefano Vanni, and Sriraksha Srinivasan present a 2025 methods paper on lipid transfer proteins. These proteins ferry fatty molecules between cell membranes, and many act as bridges. Knowing where the lipid sits inside the protein is key, yet most structures lack that detail.

The authors built a simulation pipeline on free software, using coarse-grained dynamics with the Martini 3 force field. A lipid starts free in solvent and is watched as it binds the protein on its own. The method finds binding pockets reliably and even hints at entry routes, which docking tools miss. It needs no prior knowledge beyond the protein's shape. The pipeline is shared openly so other labs can repeat it.
pmc-12738278:
Decision capacity in people with mental illness in India is gauged by Rajshekhar Bipeta, Madhur Rathi, and Umashankar Molanguri in work dated 2025. Seventy-four patients took a set of scales on illness depth, choice capacity, advance wishes, and insight. Most, near nine in ten, could choose on entry, care, and treatment. Capacity tied to sex and to insight in firm ways.

Most gave advance directives for future care. Clinic care and psychiatrists led their picks, and parents led as named stand-ins. The team urges routine capacity and directive checks in care.
pmc-12738578:
Hasibul Hassain Emon and six co-authors present a 2025 study of what female university students in Bangladesh know about HPV and its vaccine. The virus is a top cause of cervical cancer, the second most common cancer in Bangladeshi women as of 2020. Vaccination prevents it, but false beliefs about safety can hold uptake down.

The team interviewed 800 students face to face with a structured questionnaire. Questions covered the virus, the cancer, and the vaccine, plus attitudes and willingness to be vaccinated. The study sorts which facts students know, which they miss, and what blocks acceptance. The results can aim campus health campaigns.
pmc-12738778:
Yuanjian Zhang and colleagues struck layered rock samples in two thousand twenty-five. Real rock masses mix hard and soft layers. A soft interlayer sits between hard sections. Its thickness may change how the mass breaks. The team used a split-bar impact device. Sandstone and granite played soft and hard roles. Computer simulation tracked cracks and damage growth.

Thicker interlayers resisted crack growth more strongly. They also absorbed more energy before failing. Stored elastic energy built up under impact. The interlayer reached its limit first and failed fast. Its failure then drove the whole mass apart. Mining and tunnel engineers gain failure insight.
pmc-12738878:
Stefano Cantella and seven co-authors make a 3D-printing filament that mixes a common plastic with collagen peptides, in a research paper from 2025. The plastic, PCL, is used in medical implants but has no biological activity of its own. Collagen peptides could add that activity for healing tissues.

The team blended the materials without toxic solvents and extruded them on a custom desktop system. Tests confirmed the plastic kept its core structure and heat traits, while the peptides added stiffness and biological benefit. The material printed into lattice scaffolds, broke down at a tunable rate, and proved friendly to cells. Both fresh and recycled plastic worked as the base.
pmc-12740878:
Alba Xifra-Porxas and co-authors ask whether a common cleanup step for brain scans removes real brain signals. Their 2025 study uses brain scans taken at rest, paired with electric brain records plus heart and breath records. The step in question removes a shared signal found across the whole brain. Critics fear it may also strip out true nerve activity.

Body rhythms such as heart rate and breathing explain a large share of the shared signal. Electric brain activity explains a smaller share. After cleanup, false links tied to body rhythms drop, while links tied to brain waves in two key bands stay in place. The results suggest the step cleans the data without erasing the nerve patterns that rest-scan studies care about most.
pmc-12741578:
Huimin Guo and co-authors use nature's randomization to test whether inflammation helps cause rare gut and pancreas tumors. Their 2025 study applies Mendelian randomization, which treats inherited genetic variants as instruments, to ninety-one inflammatory proteins and hundreds of immune cell traits. The outcomes are five subtypes of gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine neoplasms.

After correction for multiple testing, three immune signals stood out, all involving a monocyte marker tied to stomach tumors of this family. The strongest more than tripled the odds. Reverse analysis found no sign the tumors drive the inflammation instead. Because genes are fixed at conception, such results resist the reverse-causation traps of ordinary observation. The authors read the monocyte signals as clues to how these tumors arise and where immune-targeted treatment might bite. Rare cancers offer few trial patients, making genetic evidence like this disproportionately valuable.
pmc-12742078:
Benedict Leonard-Hawkhead and five co-authors mapped ways to improve sleep for people with vision loss. Their scoping review, from twenty twenty-five, searched three big databases plus extra web checks. They kept studies in English on adults with vision impairment that tested sleep help. Animal work and off topic work were cut. Two reviewers screened and pulled data on their own, with a shared tool.

The map shows which aids have been tried, where the studies cluster by land, and where gaps sit. Sleep disorders in this group need care tuned to low sight, not plain sleep advice. Readers who run eye and sleep services get a chart of what proof exists and what trials are owed next.
pmc-12742378: Rob Vernelen, Charlotte Vanhoenacker, and Filip Vanhoenacker offer a short teaching point on spotting sarcoidosis in muscle on MRI scans. Sarcoidosis can affect muscle, and its scan pattern can be confusing without the right clues. Two named signs give the key: a dark star pattern on cross-section images and a three-stripe pattern on lengthwise images. Knowing both signs helps radiologists name the condition with more confidence.
pmc-12743478:
Chen and co-authors screen over two thousand infertile men in China for missing pieces of the Y chromosome in this 2025 study. Such microdeletions remove genes needed for sperm production. The patients attended a Fujian hospital between 2022 and 2025.

Microdeletions appeared in 8.66 percent of the 2,010 men. Among the 174 carriers, the AZFc region accounted for 85.63 percent of deletions. Other regions were far rarer, and a few men lacked several regions at once. Semen volume and two hormone levels did not differ by deletion type. Sperm concentration and forward motility did differ significantly. The mapping helps doctors counsel men on fertility options by deletion pattern.
pmc-12745978: Angelina Wang, Daniel Ho, and Sanmi Koyejo argue that offline tests misjudge how language models act in real use, in a short paper from twenty twenty-five. Set bench tests grade a model in a vacuum. In the field, users shape the model to them self, and that personal touch shifts its acts deep. The team shows proof: eight hundred real users of two chat tools put bench and other questions to their own tuned chats. Field replies split from the offline scores in clear ways.
pmc-12747078:
Natalia Milczarska and co-authors report a rare case of a giant tumor growing from womb remnants in a woman born without a womb. Their case report from 2025 deals with Müllerian agenesis, a birth fault that hits about one in five thousand female births. The womb and upper birth canal fail to form when ducts do not fuse in the womb.

The patient was a woman aged forty six who had never had periods, with lasting lower belly pain and swelling. The tumor was a benign muscle growth on the remnant buds. Full removal of the tumor with both ovaries and tubes was chosen as care. The authors stress exact diagnosis and a care plan fit to the rare pairing.
pmc-12747978:
Emergency rooms are rich places to learn, but short rotations and time pressure can keep junior doctors from forming strong teaching ties with senior physicians. Satoru Yoshida and co-authors explored how those ties grow in 2025, interviewing fourteen junior residents after a two-month emergency rotation at a center in Japan. They used a framework built on shared goals, agreed strategies, and mutual trust.

Nine themes emerged. Residents stated and reshaped their goals through both formal talks and casual contact, and they forged their own styles while coping with uneven teaching habits among seniors. One-way instruction sometimes cut their autonomy. Trust grew slowly from seniors' attitudes and judgment, and it deepened engagement. The authors stress that senior engagement drives the whole process.
pmc-12748578:
Reza Ahmadvand, Sarah Safura Sharif, and Yaser Mike Banad build a neuromorphic framework that jointly estimates state and controls a dynamical system using spiking neural networks. Robots must infer their state from noisy measurements while they steer, and the two jobs feed each other. Their 2025 framework joins a spiking network, whose neurons fire in bursts, with a robust filter and a classic control law. No training is used: the network weights are set from the system's own model.

A firing rule in the network acts like predictive coding drawn from neuroscience. Tests ran on a benchmark task and on a spacecraft rendezvous path. Next to the same pairing without spikes, and to the textbook gold-standard pairing, the spiking framework held its accuracy and robustness. It also ran leaner, which suits constrained craft. The team pitches it for demanding, fast-moving systems.
pmc-12749078:
Five authors, led by Shiwei Lin, present a 2025 paper on better path planning for robots. The A* algorithm is a standard way to plan a route across a map, but it can waste time on extra nodes and search too wide an area. The team's new method builds on A* and adapts itself as it goes.

The method, called ODDEA*, changes the weight of its guide function based on how dense the obstacles are nearby. It steers the robot toward open areas and adds a local penalty near blocks. Tests used small, medium, and large grid maps, plus 50 random medium maps. Against A*, Theta*, and BA*, the new method used fewer nodes and less time. It took less than half the planning time of A* and searched about a fifth of the space.
pmc-12749678:
Mahendran and Gomathy designed a hybrid learning model for smart power grids in this 2025 paper. Smart grids record huge streams of data on how people use electricity, and grid operators need good short-term forecasts of demand to keep supply and demand in balance. Older forecasting methods struggle with the scale of this data.

The proposed model pairs a memory-based neural network, known as LSTM, with a neuro-fuzzy system that handles vague or shifting patterns. Together they learn from past use patterns and predict demand over different time spans. The authors argue that deep learning reads consumer patterns better than standard methods. They also stress that short-term load forecasts matter most for keeping the grid stable day to day.
pmc-12750578:
Voshtani and seven co-authors studied a growth factor in human muscle stem cells for this paper from twenty twenty-five. Satellite cells repair and build skeletal muscle. The factor IGF2 is known to shape muscle growth, but its exact roles in human cells were murky. The team grew primary human satellite cells under set conditions.

Adding IGF2 sped cell division and pushed cells to mature into muscle. It switched on the master genes of muscle formation through a known receptor path. Removing the cells' own IGF2 stalled both growth and maturing. The factor also boosted the cells' power plants, raising oxygen use and energy output. The authors name IGF2 a candidate target for muscle-wasting diseases.
pmc-12750678:
Ultrasound can check where a newborn's central line tip sits, Fiorentino Grasso and co-authors test in a 2025 study. Misplaced or drifting tips in these thin catheters cause grave harm in intensive care nurseries. Ten newborn units joined the prospective study across one year.

Ultrasound confirmed the tip at placement, then rechecked across the first week. The study counts how often tips wander and when, plus traits that predict drift. A bedside sound scan spares babies repeated X-rays and transport. If the checks hold up, nurseries gain a safer routine for the tiniest patients' most delicate lines.
pmc-12751678:
Handan Özçılnak Ünver and Çiğdem Yüksel validate a listening scale for nursing students in a 2025 paper. Active-empathic listening is a core skill in therapeutic communication and person-centered care. The study adapted the scale into Turkish and tested its quality.

The sample held 405 nursing students who answered an online survey. The team checked language and content validity, then ran factor analysis to confirm the scale's structure. Fit indices were strong, and the content validity score was perfect. Item links and a reliability coefficient supported the scale's consistency. The authors offer the Turkish version as a sound tool for nursing education.
pmc-12751778:
Guangyao Zhao and three co-authors study how soybean roots hunt for phosphorus in a 2025 paper. Phosphorus is a key plant nutrient that soils often lack. Roots can grow finer, leak acids, or partner with fungi to get it. The team asked how plants trade off those strategies as supply changes.

Five soybean types grew under five levels of phosphorus supply. Gene reads and chemical profiles came from their roots. At moderate shortage, fungal partnership surged and root chemistry shifted. At severe shortage, acid leakage rose many fold and roots grew longer per gram. Types with fine roots coped better when supply was worst. The results map the switch points between strategies for breeders.
pmc-12751878:
Jingjing He and co-authors set out the plan for a large nutrition biobank in China. Their 2025 protocol paper describes a long-term study of diet, genes, body traits, and early chronic disease. Chronic diseases are starting younger, and people respond to the same diet in very different ways.

The study will recruit adults in three phases, from a small pilot group to a main group drawn from cities and villages across many provinces. Staff will collect social data, health records, and weighed food records over a decade. The goal is diet advice tuned to the person, not one rule for all. The protocol paper lets other researchers see the design in full before results arrive, and it invites checks on the methods.
pmc-12751978:
Tonnies Buckman and fourteen co-authors update survival odds for colon and rectal cancer in Ghana, in a 2025 study. Cases have climbed in Ghana, yet late finds keep survival low. The team read records of 281 patients treated at a Kumasi teaching hospital from 2016 to 2022. Charts gave age, tumor site and type, stage, and fate.

Half the patients were in their mid-fifties, and over a quarter were under 45, a young skew. Tumors split near evenly between colon and rectum, and most were the common gland type. About seven in ten arrived at stage III or IV. Median survival ran about 45 months, with about four in ten alive at five years. Stage drove the odds most, the models showed. The authors press for screening that catches the disease before it spreads.
pmc-12752078:
Busra Ekinci and Murat Canpolat present a 2025 study on love, marriage views, and flexible thinking in young adults. The pair asked whether a happy love relationship shapes views on marriage in part through flexible thought. Flexible thought means the skill of shifting views and finding new ways to cope. The study site was Turkiye.

The sample held 436 young adults who had been in a love relationship. Each filled in scales on relationship joy, marriage views, and flexible thought. Content partners held better views on marriage and thought in more flexible ways. Flexible thought also linked to better marriage views on its own. It carried part of the link between joy and views. The authors offer tips for practice.
pmc-12752178:
Alex Abramovich and five co-authors reviewed what is known about homeless queer and trans youth in a 2025 paper. Such youth are far more common among homeless young people than in the wider youth pool. They are also understudied, so their needs and lives hold big gaps in the record, which this review set out to fill.

The search swept journals and grey reports alike and kept one hundred twelve sources from around the world. Most told of harm at home, from strife to rejection, and of abuse on the street. Stigma in housing programs, poor mental health, survival sex, and blocks to jobs and school all recurred. So did shut doors to community support. The authors map the gaps that study and policy must close.
pmc-12752378:
Jingjing Song, Yilan Lei, Yi Zhang, and Xintong Hu examined why evening-type students procrastinate more on schoolwork. Chronotype, a person's natural sleep-wake preference, had been linked to procrastination without a clear mechanism. The twenty twenty-five study surveyed 774 college students with questionnaires. It measured chronotype, academic procrastination, future self-continuity, and self-control. Future self-continuity is how connected someone feels to their later self.

Later chronotype scores went with more procrastination. Statistical analysis suggested two mediators carried part of that link. Feeling disconnected from one's future self weakened self-control, which then allowed more delay. The chain ran from chronotype through both mediators in sequence. The authors say the findings offer a new angle for preventing academic procrastination, for example by strengthening students' future-self connection.
pmc-12752878:
Waraporn Appamano and co-authors test a probiotic for farmed Asian seabass in a 2025 study. Fish farms are hunting non-antibiotic ways to keep stock healthy as resistance spreads and buyers watch chemical use.

The candidate bacterium was pulled from shrimp pond mud and wrapped, spores and all, in algae-derived gels. In the lab its spores formed efficiently, survived stomach-strength acid and bile, and blocked slime building by two disease bacteria, with clean safety checks. The team then fed 120 young seabass one of four diets, plain or with free or wrapped spores, and tracked growth and immunity. A hardy, well-wrapped probiotic could give fish farmers a greener line of defense.
pmc-12752978:
Liu Wei and co-authors report a 2025 study of black pigment in a Chinese chicken breed with black bones. In breeding, the depth of black tends to split apart when lines cross. The gene and chemical drivers of that pigment in early growth were not yet pinned down.

The team joined gene read data with chemical read data from the birds. Five compounds stood out as key varied chemicals, tied to paths that build the amino acids used in pigment. A set of 73 genes also shifted, among them two named candidates. The joint map aims to give breeders firm markers for selecting birds that keep the deep black trait.
pmc-12753378:
Aditya Dash and four co-authors wrote this 2025 review of why killer T cells often fail to clear cancers of covering tissues. These T cells are a strong arm of the immune system. In the best case, they learn a tumor's markers, move in, and kill the cancer cells.

The review explains the many blocks that stop that path, with a focus on lung cancer. The zone around a tumor can bar entry, dull the cells, or shut them down. Getting trained cells into tumor nests is one hard step; keeping them active is another. The authors weigh these blocks with an eye to care that could lift them.
pmc-12753578:
Salwa Al-Maraghi and co-authors asked whether blood sugar swings early in pregnancy foretell diabetes of pregnancy, in a study from twenty twenty-five. The condition is usually found near the end of the second trimester, and it was not known if sugar shifts show up sooner. The team used health records from Qatar's public system, for women tested before twenty weeks and again in the early third trimester.

A weighted average sugar measure was used to gauge early swings. Women who later developed the condition had early values that stayed in the normal range but ran higher than in women who stayed free of it. Past a set threshold, the odds of later diabetes roughly tripled. The authors say early sugar swings can flag high-risk women in time for earlier care.
pmc-12753778:
Panan Suntornsaratoon and co-authors test in a 2025 rat study whether pandan leaf extract can lower uric acid, the gout driver, and calm its side damage. Rats were made uric-acid-high with a chemical blocker. The sick rats excreted less uric acid, lost antioxidants, and showed blood sugar trouble, kidney harm, and fatty liver.

Fourteen days of the extract cut the acid-making enzyme and blood uric acid, rivaling a standard drug, by both slowing reabsorption and boosting excretion through kidney and gut. Insulin action improved, liver fat and inflammation fell. A kitchen leaf, the study hints, acts on several fronts of this metabolic tangle.
pmc-12753978:
Date palms earn over thirteen billion dollars a year in dry regions, yet pests like the red palm weevil and diseases such as Bayoud and Black Scorch cut yields hard. Checking trees by eye is slow and subjective. Abid Iqbal builds one AI framework that handles the whole diagnostic chain: naming the disease, locating it, outlining the damaged area, and grading its severity.

The pipeline mixes several recent tools. A generative model creates extra training images, CLIP sorts the disease class, and PaliGemma2 finds the spots from text prompts. A pairing of Grounding DINO with SAM 2.1 outlines them without prior examples of the exact class. A vision transformer then scores severity. Across two datasets the system reached 98 percent classification accuracy and detection between 94 and 98 percent. Iqbal presents the unified design as a scalable way to watch palm health.
pmc-12754178:
Yongcheng Chen and four co-authors study soil microbes as native desert soil becomes alfalfa farmland in Xinjiang, China, in a 2025 paper. Planting alfalfa is a known way to heal degraded soils, but how the change unfolds in a high altitude sand area was unclear. The team compared native soil, cultivated soil, and soil around alfalfa roots.

Cultivation reshaped the microbial mix, raising helpful bacteria tied to nutrient cycling and lowering some decomposers. Over time, diversity recovered and became more even across sites. Soil organic matter and acidity were the main drivers of the change. A shared core of microbes appeared in all three soils. Networks of microbe interactions were more complex in native and root soils than in cultivated soil.
pmc-12754878:
Maryam Alizadeh, Shirin Bahrami, Zeinabe Saeedi, and Loghman Khaninezhad review team learning for ethics teaching in 2025. Team-based learning has drawn interest as a way to build ethical reasoning in health students. Evidence on its results, though, was scattered across many small studies.

The review searched four databases for peer-reviewed studies from 2000 to early 2025. Fifteen studies with more than two thousand learners qualified, mostly from Asia and North America. Judged on a four-level outcome ladder, team learning scored well on learner reaction and beyond. A narrative synthesis was used, since the studies differed too much to pool.
pmc-12755078:
Guoku Hu and co-authors review tiny cell-made parcels as both villains and vehicles in brain disease, in this 2025 paper. These parcels, called extracellular vesicles, carry proteins and genetic scraps between cells. They can spread the toxic proteins behind Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and other diseases.

The same parcels cross into the brain with ease, which makes them attractive drug carriers. Their surfaces can be tuned to deliver calming or protective cargo to the right cells. The authors highlight parcels from colostrum, the first milk, as a natural and scalable source. They argue that steering these two-faced carriers could yield immune-based treatments for brain disease.
pmc-12755878:
Anastasia Unitt and co-authors forge a naming code in 2025 for a germ that spreads by sex. The germ swaps genes so freely that family trees blur, which makes its groups hard to name in a steady way. Steady names matter more as the germ learns to shrug off drugs.

Their code rests on a barcode scheme built from the germ core set of genes, more than a thousand strong. It names groups at more than one depth, from broad clan to fine branch. Past typing kits failed to hold a stable map of the germ kinds. Health teams gain names they can share across labs and years.
pmc-12756478:
Xuehai Liu and nine co-authors test an herbal decoction against bone-cell injury caused by thin air. At high altitude, low oxygen harms osteoblasts, the cells that build bone, and may feed osteoporosis. Their remedy pairs aconite with ginger, a warming-yang formula in Chinese medicine. Using bone-forming cells cultured in a 4,500-meter hypoxic chamber, the team profiled gene activity and ran a battery of cell-health assays.

Gene profiling pointed to the HIF-1 signaling pathway as the hub of the injury. Hypoxia suppressed that pathway's key members and its growth signal VEGF, while reactive oxygen and calcium flooded the cells, mitochondria faltered, division stalled, and death rose. The decoction reversed much of this: viability improved, oxygen radicals and calcium fell, mitochondrial health returned, and the HIF-1/VEGF axis recovered. The authors propose the formula protects bone cells by restoring that oxygen-sensing pathway.
pmc-12757278:
Anna Maria Pfefferkorn and twelve co-authors trace how a kidney protein calms the immune attack on transplanted kidneys in mice. The protein, lipocalin-2, is known as an early alarm marker for kidney injury, and the team's earlier work showed a lab-made form protects grafts. Here they ask how. Mice receiving kidneys from a different strain got the protein or not, and immune cells from graft, spleen, lymph nodes, and blood were profiled days after surgery.

By day seven the treated mice carried fewer killer and helper T cells of the memory kind across all sites. Their graft-invading T cells also released less of two attack molecules and shed fewer granules. Effects on the innate immune side were small and spotty. Same-strain grafts showed no change in plain injury, so the protein's gift is immune tuning, not tissue shielding.
pmc-12763978:
Health checks done for India by its own review body are summed up by Varshini Neethi Mohan and co-authors in work dated 2025. The body, HTAIn, weighs new health tools to help public funds serve more than a billion people well. The team read most of the studies the body had posted by late 2023. They charted what each study checked and if it paid off.

Most studies dealt with care for mothers and newborns, tools, or screening. All weighed cost gains, and most weighed health gains too. Scores for study quality spread wide. Fairness across groups scored worst. The team urges a clear frame for picking what to check next.
pmc-12764878:
Malak Alamri and three co-authors propose a trust aware edge computing model for connected healthcare. Sensors and wearable devices stream physiological data for monitoring and diagnosis, and edge computing cuts response time. Battery powered devices have limited resources, though, and malicious devices on the network can corrupt accuracy and reliability.

Their Edge-Cloud Trusted Intelligence model lowers computing overhead on devices. Multi level security protects privacy by adopting trusted behavior when devices communicate in a distributed setting. The design targets personalized healthcare systems that must stay responsive under diverse network conditions. Trust checks aim to keep suspicious processes from degrading medical decisions that depend on the data streams.
pmc-12764978:
Anoushka Mukharya and Srinivas Mutalik build a quality by design method to measure quercetin in silver frameworks in a 2025 paper. Quercetin is a plant compound of medical interest, held here in a silver metal organic framework. A sound liquid based test is needed to measure it accurately, in line with global guidelines.

A design of experiments plan tuned the key settings and gave strong linearity, high sensitivity, and robust results. Stress tests showed the compound held up under mild acid, light, and oxidation at room temperature, but broke down under base, strong acid, and heat. A greenness score rated the method fair, with low energy use in a short run and moderate solvent use.
pmc-12767078:
Haiyu Liu and co-authors test, in a 2025 study, whether caffeine can protect retinal pigment epithelium cells from oxidative damage. These cells guard the back of the eye and support the light-sensing layer. Oxidative damage plays a part in age-related degeneration of the retina. The team stressed a laboratory line of these cells with hydrogen peroxide, a strong oxidant, then added caffeine.

Caffeine kept more cells alive and reduced both cell death and DNA fragmentation. It shifted key proteins that control cell death in a protective direction and lowered markers of damage inside the cells. Gene expression data hinted that caffeine also affects immune defense pathways and fat handling. In mice with drug-induced retinal degeneration, long-term caffeine eased damage to the protective layer and kept the retina's structure more intact. The authors see caffeine as a protection worth more study.
pmc-12767378:
Daniel Waszczuk and co-authors review stem cell care for recovery after stroke, in work from 2025. Stroke is a top cause of death and disability worldwide, and standard care often fails to restore full function. Stem cells may help repair the brain and bring back lost skills.

The review covers three main cell types and how each may act in the body. One type calms immune response and supports new blood vessels and nerve growth. The authors weigh trial data on how well each type works. They also trace the path from lab work to patient care and the hurdles that remain.
pmc-12768678:
Jaqueline Horvath, Barbara Silva, and Maria Ferreira reviewed in 2025 how Brazil's public health system judged new obesity treatments over a decade. A national committee must weigh benefit, safety, and cost before the system adopts a technology. The team read the committee's public reports for obesity care from twenty twelve to twenty twenty-two.

Four technologies were judged: two appetite drugs, one further drug, and laparoscopic bariatric surgery. Only the surgery was adopted, in twenty seventeen. The appetite drugs were turned down for weak benefit and safety concerns. The third drug worked but was refused for its high cost and budget impact. The authors say obesity has been under-prioritized in this process.
pmc-12768778:
Calvin Young and co-authors wrote a 2025 report on the first full review of a smart software tool by Canada's Drug Agency. The tool, called RapidAI, helps doctors spot strokes in brain scans. The agency used the case to test how it should judge software tools that learn from data.

The review weighed how well the tool finds two kinds of stroke, what it costs, and what clinics need to run it. Ethics and fairness were checked throughout, with input from patients and experts. Patients stressed speed and accuracy in stroke diagnosis. The proof on health gains was rated low in certainty. An expert panel then gave advice on fit use of the tool. The report shares lessons for later reviews of such tools.
pmc-12770578:
Jiankui Bai, Qingnan Lou, Chengcheng Zhang, Junyi Guo, Guangqing Wei, Baojun Wang, and Bin Shi tune a fiber sensor shaped as a thin tube in a 2025 paper. The sensor hears sound and shakes along a fiber line, which suits wide-area watch tasks. Weak signals slip past it, though, so the team sought a build that hears more.

They varied three build traits: how stiff the tube is, how thick its wall is, and how wide it runs. A softer, thinner tube boosted the signal sharply, up to a top score in their tests. A wider tube added gain in a steady line. The rules give a clear recipe for sharper sensors for quake and ground work.
pmc-12771178:
Bill Aparicio-Huacarpuma and co-authors computed the traits of a family of atom-thin semiconductors in two thousand twenty-five. The materials pair silicon, germanium, tin, or lead with iodine in single layers. Such two-dimensional sheets could serve in solar cells and light-based electronics.

Using first-principles and semiempirical calculations, they checked stability plus electronic, mechanical, and optical properties. All four sheets were semiconductors, with band gaps in a range suited to light harvesting. Bound electron-hole pairs, called excitons, were strongly held, which shapes how the sheets absorb light. Estimated peak solar efficiency reached about sixteen percent at a standard limit. The authors see strong response to visible and ultraviolet light.
pmc-12772078:
Liang Chen, Ting Yu, and Yanqing Pan report two cases where targeted lung cancer drugs also melted away hazy lung spots. Their 2025 paper follows patients with several ground-glass opacities alongside adenocarcinoma carrying EGFR mutations. After surgery removed the main tumors, both patients took gefitinib, a drug aimed at that mutation.

In the first case, a remaining hazy spot in the left upper lobe shrank within a month and vanished by three months. The second patient's matching spot also shrank after one month on the drug. The authors suggest this drug class offers a useful option after surgery for such patients. They caution that the best timing and approach still need study in larger groups.
pmc-12772178:
Nine authors, led by Mengzhan Li, report a 2025 study of how two plant enzymes switch off a growth hormone signal. Brassinosteroids are hormones that drive plant growth and development. Their signal runs through a receptor called BRI1, whose activity is set by phosphate tags that are added and removed.

The removing side was poorly known. The team shows that two phosphatases, PP2C-D2 and PP2C-D5, erase key phosphate tags on BRI1 and so damp the signal. The pair only become active when two copies join into a dimer. Hormone action fights that joining: BRI1's own phosphorylation, and binding by a small protein called SAUR15, both break the dimers apart. The enzymes then fall back to a single, inactive form. The study reveals a full on-off loop for the hormone pathway.
pmc-12772578:
Anna Hillenmayer and co-authors teach a neural network to grade urgency in an eye emergency room in this 2025 study. Sorting who needs care first guards safety and saves resources. The team used language processing to read patients' own words.

On arrival, 1,715 patients filled a form with free text and checkboxes. Staff labeled each case urgent or not from the final diagnosis. A BERT network trained on most forms and was tested on the rest. The study checks how well the model matches expert sorting. A reliable tool could speed triage, though human judgment stays in charge of the final call.
pmc-12774878:
Francesco Troisi, Hannes Hübener, Angel Rubio, and Simone Latini propose a way to trap excitons with patterned light cavities in this 2025 paper. Excitons are bound pairs of an electron and a hole in a material. Twisted layered materials trap them in moiré patterns, but twisting is hard to control. The team instead uses optical cavities with a periodic structure. Coupling to trapped light, and even to its quantum flicker, can reshape the exciton bands.

Their theory treats strongly coupled excitons and photons beyond simple approximations. In a laser driven cavity, the light pattern mimics moiré confinement directly. In a dark cavity, quantum fluctuations alone shifted the exciton bands and changed their effective mass. The team traces both effects to long range interactions between excitons, carried by the cavity. They propose structured cavities as a tool for engineering materials with light. No twisting step is needed.
pmc-12780378:
Fei Qi and co-authors chart what makes the hardest lung segment operation slow, costly, or complicated. Basal segmentectomy works deep in the lung where vessels and airways vary wildly. The team reviewed one hundred ninety thoracoscopic cases at a Beijing hospital, splitting out the one hundred twenty that included the tricky lowest segments.

Operating time averaged a little over two hours. Regression showed approach, procedure type, and bleeding drove operating time, while procedure type drove total cost, and a poorly split lung fissure lengthened drainage. The learning curve bent at case one hundred nineteen: before it, a surgeon still learning; after it, proficiency. The authors say single-port access shortened operations, and they offer the numbers as planning references for teams adopting the operation.
pmc-12780578:
Junbei Zhu, Jianhao Huang, Qiang Wang, and Kai He built a prediction chart for survival after curative liver cancer surgery from a simple blood ratio, in a 2025 study. The ratio divides prealbumin, a nutrition-linked protein, by a platelet size spread measure. Records covered 205 patients operated on at one hospital from 2016 to 2021, split into training and validation sets.

A cutoff from the training data divided patients into risk groups, and the ratio tracked with survival in the analysis. The team folded it into a nomogram, a point-based chart, for individualized forecasts. They offer it as a cheap aid for follow-up planning.
pmc-12780678:
Mary Junak and co-authors review surgical records for rectal cancer patients, in a study published in 2025. Many such patients get a stoma, a temporary opening for waste, which is later closed. A leak where the bowel is rejoined is a feared problem after closure. The team asked whether prior chemo and radiation, given before the first surgery, raise that risk.

Using a national surgical database for cases from 2005 to 2012, they found 461 patients who had elective stoma closure. About half had received the prior treatment. Leak rates were near seven percent in both groups, and major problems, death rates, and hospital stays also matched. The authors conclude that earlier chemo and radiation did not worsen closure outcomes in this data.
pmc-12781478:
Mahmoud Badawy and co-authors describe a three-wire trick for fixing stubborn elbow fractures in children, in this 2025 study. The fracture, just above the elbow, usually yields to closed manipulation, but a stubborn minority once forced open surgery. Their method turns the fixation wires themselves into levers for correction.

Two wires are placed in the loose fragment and one above the elbow socket, all before the bone is aligned. Working the three wires corrects tilt, shift, and rotation at the break. Twenty children treated this way all achieved acceptable alignment without open surgery. Operations averaged about thirty-three minutes. Five mild pin infections cleared within a week of wire removal.
pmc-12785078:
Yifan Nie and co-authors feed pregnant ewes, in a 2025 study, a protected form of glutamine to see if it lifts lamb growth and health. Late pregnancy is a window when a mother's diet shapes her offspring's growth and later resilience.

A moderate dose improved lamb birth weight, weight at fifteen days, and daily gain. In the ewes, the supplement improved fat handling and one liver enzyme measure, and it lowered stress markers in lamb muscle. Antioxidant defenses rose in both mothers and lambs. Gut microbe mixes shifted toward helpful types, with signs of mother-to-lamb transfer. Body chemistry profiles changed in step, adding detail to the growth gains.
pmc-12785178:
Cold snaps cut cotton yields, and Ni Yang and co-authors hunted the gene switches that help one cotton line stand the cold, in work from twenty twenty-five. A tough line and a weak line were sampled before and after six hours of cold. Gene reads, chemical scans, and gene-access maps were joined in one hunt.

The tough line alone lit up fat-making paths under cold. Thousands of switch genes were found across the checks, led by four big switch families. Net tools grouped the switches into nine teams and named hub switches. Fat chemicals made up a tenth of the shifted chemicals, and most switch teams tracked them tight. Open gene zones add a map of where cold flips the switches.
pmc-12785578:
Wei-Ming Lin and colleagues published a cancer study in 2025 on liver tumors that invade the portal vein. That invasion is a severe complication with poor outlook. Some patients, though, live well past a year on combined treatment. The authors described what those longer survivors looked like on scans and records.

The study covered twenty-six such patients at one center. Most had extensive vein invasion at the start. Liver function was usually well preserved despite the spread. Scans were checked at the start and again at six months. Most patients showed a measurable tumor response to therapy. The report aims to help doctors recognize which treated patients may do better.
pmc-12785678:
Letícia de Oliveira Carneiro and six co-authors built a light-based method to grade polished white rice lots for sale, in this 2025 study. Rice quality is usually judged by eye and hand, sorting lots into commercial types. The team instead scanned grains with visible and infrared light and let machine learning read the spectra, alongside lab measures of moisture, starch, and protein.

Top learning models sorted the commercial batches with accuracy above ninety-five percent. One wavelength in the short-wave infrared carried much of the signal. High-grade lots reflected less light in the infrared bands, hinting at richer makeup. Adding chemical measures let the team suggest simpler commercial categories. The authors say the method can speed lot sorting in storage and processing plants.
pmc-12785978:
Misong Kim and three co-authors test whether spit can stand in for blood in checking rheumatoid arthritis, in a 2025 journal article. The illness is a long immune attack on the joints. Blood tests now in use work well but need a needle, which some patients dread.

The team took spit from 58 patients and fifty healthy adults and read two marks in it. One mark, calprotectin, rises with swelling. The other is an antibody long tied to the illness. Both ran far higher in patients. The first mark caught most cases, while the second rarely fired in health. A joint model with clinic facts split the groups with fine skill. The authors say a spit test could ease checks.
pmc-12786078:
Duangjai Todsaporn and eight colleagues hunt for new inhibitors of JAK2, a signaling enzyme that drives cervical cancer, starting from plant-derived sesquiterpene lactones. Computer docking screened forty derivatives. Scores for drug-likeness and toxicity cut the field to six, which the team made and tested.

Two compounds blocked JAK2 at low nanomolar levels, more strongly than the standard drug ruxolitinib, and killed cervical cancer cells while sparing others. Cell studies showed they triggered apoptosis, with a surge of reactive oxygen species. Computer models showed how they bind so tightly, through hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic contacts. The authors nominate both molecules as scaffolds for building therapy aimed at JAK2 for this cancer.
pmc-12786178:
Josée Boucher and colleagues report spine gains without new surgery after fusion hardware removal, in a case from 2025. Adult scoliosis after fusion plus hardware loss can bend the spine in two planes at once. Revision surgery is often advised, yet it holds large risks for older or frail patients.

One woman fused at age twenty-four lost her rods two years later due to infection. Over two decades her chest curve worsened and she lost much standing height. At forty-seven she chose Schroth based therapy plus part time bracing over new surgery. Over twenty-eight months her curves shrank, height rose, and lung volume grew by one third.
pmc-12786878:
Lee Kyang and co-authors test, in a 2025 study, a numbers-based way to judge blood flow in the stomach tube built during esophagus removal surgery. Leaks where the tube joins the remaining gullet are devastating, and a dye that glows under special light can reveal weak perfusion before the join is made.

Six patients had the dye test quantified as a relative perfusion ratio against the duodenum set at one hundred percent. Join sites were chosen where the ratio topped eighty percent, and values ran from eighty to one hundred. No leaks occurred. The small series supports measured dye guidance over eyeballing alone.
pmc-12787278:
Eran Leshem and co-authors study how frailty affects patients who have a heart procedure to fix atrial fibrillation, a faulty heart rhythm. The procedure burns small spots inside the heart to block stray signals. Frail patients face higher risk around such work, but past studies mixed risks together or looked far ahead.

Records for about forty-three thousand hospital stays were split by a frailty score into low, middle, and high groups. Death in hospital hit about six in a hundred in the high group, against one in a hundred in the low group. Stroke, lung failure, and blood infection were also far more common. The authors urge scoring frailty before the procedure.
pmc-12787478:
Akhileshwar Singh and co-authors catalog the terpene-making genes of lettuce and test how a plant hormone switches them on in this 2025 study. Terpenes are scent and defense compounds with wide roles in plant life. Their control in lettuce, a major salad crop, was poorly mapped.

Young seedlings exposed to methyl jasmonate released a fresh terpene blend. Untreated seedlings released none that instruments could detect. The team matched those scents to the synthase genes behind them. Gene-by-gene lab tests confirmed which enzyme makes which compound. Flavor, pest defense, and shelf life all touch terpene output. Breeders gain targets for tuning lettuce chemistry on purpose. The catalog itself is a lasting output of the work.
pmc-12787978:
Anxin Guo and co-authors build, in a 2025 paper, an unsupervised framework that helps drones make sense of their own sensor streams. Situation awareness depends on fusing GPS, motion, and radar feeds in real time. Standard deep generative models wobble badly when trained on such flight data.

Their model steadies training with weighted uncertainty and a mixture output that handles many flight styles. In tests, ordinary versions of the model often failed to converge on this data. The stabilized version extracted usable features from nonlinear time series. No labeled examples guide the learning, which suits raw flight logs. Reliable self-monitoring is a step toward drones that can judge their own state.
pmc-12788478:
Navyasri Chappa and co-authors wrote a 2025 narrative review of metal-free dental implants, with zirconia as the leading material. Many patients and dentists want implants without metal, for looks and for body compatibility. The review surveys where the field stands and which new materials are coming.

The authors discuss the biological, mechanical, and esthetic properties of zirconia implants. They also review polymer-based and ceramic options now in development. Clinical outcomes, bonding with bone, and current limits all get attention. Readers come away with a plain summary of what zirconia implants can do today and what future materials may offer for safer, better-looking tooth replacement.
pmc-12789678:
Abilasha and Karthikeyan present a joint energy-saving and attack defense method for cognitive radio sensor networks, in a paper from 2025. Such networks borrow idle spectrum, but fake primary users can trick sensors into vacating channels. Wasteful routing and unfair channel sharing also drain performance.

Their algorithm blends attack detection, a moth-flame search for fair channel assignment, and tuned cluster sizes with multi-hop relay to extend life. The channel fading model reflects real signal weakening. Simulations show higher throughput, longer network life, and less attack damage than prior methods. Fairness among secondary users is built into the assignment step.
pmc-12796378:
Jinzhong Zhang and co-authors train neural networks with a bird-inspired search in a 2025 paper. Feedforward networks pass data one way, with no loops, and fit many sorting and guessing tasks. Training them means setting link weights well, which plain methods can do poorly.

The search copies a magpie flock: scouting for food, chasing prey, and storing extra finds. Those moves balance wide search with fine local tuning. The team use it to set weights and offsets, scoring each try by error size. Tests on seventeen data sets back claims of fast settling, sharp scores, and steady runs. Fewer control knobs add to the draw.
pmc-12797778:
Xinyou Liu and seven co-authors show that a contact protein drives stomach cancer growth by rewiring fat use, in a 2025 study. The protein, called EPDR1, was high in tumor tissue and cell lines and tracked with poor outlook. Its role in stomach cancer had been unknown. Tests in cells and mice probed what it does.

Raising the protein sped cell growth, spread, and invasion. It lifted a fat-burning gate protein, which in turn switched on a growth signal path. That switch raised fat burning inside the cancer cells. Blocking the chain cut the effect. The authors pitch the lead protein as a drug target for stomach cancer care.
pmc-12798678:
Abubakar Gapizov and co-authors review drug plans for patients who have both an irregular heartbeat and a stent in a heart artery in two thousand twenty-five. Such patients need drugs that stop clots, but more drugs also raise the risk of bleeding. The review weighs a two-drug plan against a three-drug plan.

Four trials were found that compare the two plans head-on. The two-drug plan, which pairs a newer blood thinner with one anti-platelet drug, cut bleeding in all of them. It did so without raising the rate of heart attack, stroke, or stent clots. The authors favor the two-drug plan for most patients, with short three-drug use kept for those at high clot risk.
pmc-12800078:
Giacomo Fais and co-authors grow a green alga under fake Moon gravity to test it as space food. The alga, Chlorella vulgaris, could give crews food, oxygen, and recycled resources inside closed habitats on long missions. Their 2025 study used a spinning device that mimics low gravity, comparing full Earth gravity, Moon gravity, and near weightlessness.

The low-gravity cultures grew more biomass and made far more of the pigments that drive photosynthesis. They also held up to 160 percent more polyphenols and antioxidant power than Earth-gravity cultures. Fat profiles shifted too, toward forms that store energy and keep cell walls working. The authors say the alga bends well to odd gravity, but tests under real partial gravity on the Moon are still needed.
pmc-12800278:
Neelam Sharma and five colleagues set out a new model for predicting software reliability growth, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Such models gauge the faults left in a piece of code and the best time to release it. The facts of test work make that hard. Fault finds shift in pace when strategies change, and fixes can bring in new faults of their own.

Debugging is imperfect for human reasons, from plain error to code complexity. That flaw gives rise to epistemic uncertainty, which probability on its own deals with in an awkward way. The team builds its model on uncertain differential equations and belief reliability theory. It takes in both change points and imperfect debugging at once. The goal is reliability estimates that are more frank, to back release decisions. Test teams gain a model that owns up to what it does not know.
pmc-12801478:
Ishbel Whitehead and co-authors ask why spiritual health rarely comes up in social prescribing in a 2025 study. Social prescribers connect patients to community support beyond medicine, and their holistic brief includes spiritual needs. Twelve prescribers were interviewed for an hour each.

Faith groups were used mainly as venues for practical help, not spiritual care. Prescribers blurred spiritual and mental health together and worried that raising faith could offend or harm vulnerable patients, so they waited for patients to bring it up. When patients did, prescribers felt open to helping. Comfort, confidence, and fear of deep conversations decided whether the topic surfaced at all.
pmc-12801978:
Fahad Alshehri surveys community pharmacists in Saudi Arabia on drug help to quit smoking in a 2025 study. Drug aids are a core part of sound quit care. How ready counter pharmacists are to give that aid, though, had not been well mapped in the kingdom.

The survey ran from January to August 2024 and drew 213 licensed pharmacists. Mean scores for know-how, outlook, and day-to-day practice each sat at a mid level. Less than a fifth asked patients as a rule if they smoked, while near a third always sent patients to state quit programs. Know-how rose with practice but fell with outlook scores. Prior training lifted practice scores.
pmc-12802278:
Xue-hui Sun and Chun-Ye Wu reported in 2025 a patient carrying two uncommon inflammatory diseases at once: a spine-attacking arthritis and Takayasu's arteritis, which narrows the great arteries. Each disease appears alone often enough, but together they are rare and easy to miss, since their aches and fevers overlap.

The report follows the patient's course and treatments, then reviews similar published cases. Its warning is practical: when spine patients show stubborn inflammation, low fevers, or poor response to standard drugs, doctors should check the arteries. Catching the second disease early prevents years of mistargeted therapy.
pmc-12804578:
Tao Li and co-authors review, in twenty twenty-five, bionic therapies for spinal cord injury that aim to rebuild and reconnect neural circuits. Spinal injury can cause loss of movement, sensation, and autonomic control, up to paralysis or death. No current treatment is fully satisfactory. Beyond drugs, surgery, and rehabilitation, bionic approaches draw attention for their promise. They split into two families: engineered biomaterials that reconstruct circuits inside the cord, and brain-machine interfaces that link external control to the body's own circuits.

The review surveys the injury field and both therapy families in depth. It focuses on how reconstruction and integration might combine. The authors aim to give clinicians and researchers promising directions for future treatment design.
pmc-12804678:
Hakan Celik and co-authors published a study in 2025 on colon cancer and age. Most care for this cancer does not take the age of the patient into account. Yet genes may act in distinct ways in younger and older patients. The team used machine learning to look for gene patterns split by age.

They studied genes tied to treatment, defense against disease, and sugar coating on cells. Patients were split at age seventy into younger and older groups. Small sets of ten genes sorted tumor tissue from normal tissue with high scores. Sets of just three genes still worked well. The results held up in a second data set from other patients. The authors say age should shape how gene tests for this cancer are built.
pmc-12804878:
Amit Patel and three co-authors build FL-MalDrift, a joint learn frame that spots phone malware as its ways drift. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Phone bad ware shifts fast, and split learn sets make drift worse while they guard folk data. Each phone in the frame first checks its own drift with light tools, then sends just sound updates to the hub. A hub hand smooths drift scores and picks which updates join the pool.

Marks hit near ninety-five to ninety-seven percent on two known phone ware sets and past ninety on a time-split set, with low cost. The team pitch it as a wide, data-safe base.
pmc-12805478:
Zeynep Tekin-Taş and co-authors check whether fast virus testing changes how often doctors prescribe antibiotics, in a 2025 paper. A multiplex PCR test can name several respiratory viruses from one sample within hours. In theory, proof of a virus should cut needless antibiotic use, since antibiotics do not treat viruses. The team reviewed records of patients who had the test at their hospital.

Patients were sorted into flu-like illness, viral pneumonia, bacterial pneumonia, and mixed infection groups. The authors then compared how often antibiotics were given in each group. Even when the test confirmed a virus, antibiotic use stayed high, most of all in viral pneumonia cases. The team argues that testing alone is not enough. They call for stewardship work, staff training, and decision support built into daily care.
pmc-12808178:
Laura Cota Ortega, Eduardo Quiroz-Guzmán, and José Balcázar review ecological drivers of plasmid-mediated drug resistance in aquaculture. Their 2025 mini-review covers resistance spread on fish farms. Heavy, often careless antibiotic use marks the sector. Resistant bacteria persist and multiply under that pressure. Plasmids ferry resistance genes between bacteria readily.

The review explains the ecology behind that gene traffic. Horizontal transfer lets resistance jump species lines. Risks extend to farm workers and consumers alike. Wild ecosystems receive farm effluents carrying resistant strains. Better surveillance and sustainable management are urged. Coordinated international policy is part of the remedy. Food security itself is at stake, the authors argue.
pmc-12808278:
Adrian Wolfgang, Nora Temme, Ralf Tilcher, Mario Schumann, and Gabriele Berg mapped the microbes living on and around wireworms, the beetle larvae that chew through crops in the soil. Killer fungi are used against them, but field results swing widely. The team studied four wireworm species to see how the insects, their microbes, and the soil interact.

Each species carried its own microbe mix, drawn mostly from the soil. The bacterial film on the cuticle stayed steady over time in healthy larvae, and keeping that film stable tracked with long survival. Killer fungi were present but rare. Larvae pre-exposed to the fungi died less and molted more, signs of primed immunity. The authors say control methods should respect these microbe balances.
pmc-12808378:
Xinhui Zheng and co-authors compared two antibody drugs for graft-versus-host disease that no longer answers to steroids in a 2025 study. After a donor stem cell transplant, donor immune cells can attack the patient's body. When steroids fail, this complication often kills. Both drugs block CD25, a marker on the attacking T cells.

One is a chimeric mouse-human antibody and the other fully humanized, a design difference that can affect reactions and durability. Comparing them head-to-head in real patients tells transplant teams which to reach for first. The study adds rare comparative evidence in a corner of medicine where randomized trials are hard to run and choices are often made by habit.
pmc-12808478:
Peifei Shi, Chao Ren, and Hongjie Tong review work on stem cells for a disease of clogged arteries. Their review was published in two thousand twenty-five. Fat builds up in artery walls, the walls swell, and heart attacks or strokes can follow. Drugs and surgery can slow the harm but cannot undo it.

The review covers three main cell types and how they may calm swelling, fix the artery lining, and keep plaques stable. It sums up animal tests and human trials from recent years. It also notes weak points, such as cells reaching the right spot, and ideas to improve care.
pmc-12809678:
Xing Zhang and co-authors study a long RNA strand that helps a fast lung cancer grow and spread. The study appeared in 2025. This cancer makes up about fifteen percent of lung cancers and has poor outcomes. The strand rides in tiny cell packets that move between blood tube cells and tumor cells.

Blood levels of the strand were higher in patients than in healthy peers. In lab tests the strand made tumor cells move, invade, and form groups. It also made tube cells form new paths for blood flow. The strand works by soaking up a small RNA that would rein in three growth paths. The team sees it as a target for new care.
pmc-12810178:
Avneet Kaur and co-authors measure how antibiotic pastes stain teeth and whether bleaching can undo the stain, in a 2025 lab study. Antibiotic pastes are packed into root canals to clear infection, but some mixes discolor the crown. The team used cut human front teeth and filled them with four paste variants or left them empty as controls. Color was read with a spectrophotometer over four weeks.

The classic triple paste with minocycline stained the most. A clindamycin variant stained the least by a clear margin. After the pastes were removed, an internal bleaching agent was placed for a week. The minocycline group's color bounced back the most from its stained state. The clindamycin group barely changed, since it had barely stained. The authors give dentists a ranked picture of staining risk by paste type.
pmc-12812578:
Cíntia Maria Rodrigues and co-authors measure hormone and inflammation signals that may explain why obesity worsens Covid-19. Their 2026 study compares 142 adults across weight classes, including mild and severe infections plus matched uninfected controls. Blood levels of angiotensin II and four inflammatory messengers were assayed for each group.

Patients with obesity carried higher angiotensin II and higher levels of three inflammatory signals, with the calming signal IL-10 reduced. Angiotensin tracked body mass directly. Severe cases showed more need for breathing support, and every death in the cohort occurred in a patient with obesity.
