The authors blame a double hit: a hormone system tilted toward constriction and inflammation, plus a baseline inflammatory hum. They propose these blood markers as early warnings of decline in heavier patients.
pmc-12812678:
Shuang Zhang and six colleagues review how a protein called HIF-1 drives lung injury during sepsis. Sepsis is a body-wide reaction to infection that can fail several organs. The lungs are the most fragile target, and severe cases turn into acute respiratory distress syndrome.

No drug treats this lung injury directly; care rests on breathing support. HIF-1 switches genes on when oxygen runs low, and during sepsis it surges. The review traces how it links three threads: metabolism, inflammation, and immune control. Faulty mitochondria and oxidative stress feed into the same web. The authors argue that tuning HIF-1 activity could attack all three threads at once and improve patient outcomes.
pmc-12812878:
A blocked retinal artery is an eye emergency that also warns of stroke, and the neck arteries often hold the cause. In this 2025 study, Zhen Song and co-authors test whether contrast-enhanced ultrasound finds risky neck plaques better than ordinary ultrasound. They compare one hundred ten patients with the eye blockage against matched healthy controls.

The patients carried far more plaques that lit up with contrast, a sign of fragile, vessel-rich plaque. Several ordinary scan measures also separated the groups. A model combining both kinds of measures reached strong accuracy, well above either method alone. The authors suggest adding the contrast scan to routine checks after a retinal blockage. That could sharpen stroke prevention for a group at high risk.
pmc-12812978:
Yingying Wang and four co-authors modeled school bullying in Chinese junior high schools in a study published in 2025. Using the China Education Panel Survey from 2014 and 2015, they applied hierarchical models that separate student-level and school-level effects. At the student level, gender, grades, health, rule-breaking behavior, and parental discipline each predicted bullying involvement.

At the school level, school type mattered. The interplay was the sharper finding: parental discipline linked to less bullying far more strongly in private schools than in public ones. Discipline at home apparently lands differently depending on the school setting around it. The authors offer the two-level picture as a base for prevention that works on families and schools together, rather than on students alone.
pmc-12813078:
Xiaoyu Cao and six co-authors show that the jawbone helps shape growing teeth by shipping tiny parcels between tissues, in this study published in 2025. Teeth form inside the mandible, yet how the bone talks back to the tooth germ was unclear. The team isolated extracellular vesicles from the jaws of forty-day miniature pig embryos.

One small RNA inside the parcels, miR-206, stood out as the key signal. Lab tests showed it switches down a gene regulator called HDAC4, which loosens chemical marks on DNA packaging. Tooth germs dosed with the parcels, then grown under mouse skin, formed and hardened in line with that switch. The authors frame the jaw as an active coach of tooth development.
pmc-12815278:
Antonio Mutti wrote a 2025 editorial that asks whether smart software tools will take jobs away. The question is heard in schools, offices, and clinics as these tools spread fast. Mutti writes from his work as a journal editor and teacher in medicine, fields built on skill and human trust.

He tells how he gave one new tool a classic task: reviewing papers sent to his journal. The tool did far more than fix spelling. It read and judged the science, made slides and speaker notes, and even planned a full online course with tests. Mutti argues that such tools now act less like chat partners and more like agents that can carry out work. The piece asks what this shift means for skilled jobs and how people should adapt.
pmc-12815778:
Zhimin Chen and five co-authors test simple blood based scores as outlook markers after breast cancer surgery in a 2026 paper. Insulin resistance is tied to how breast cancer grows and fares, and four scores built from blood fats, sugar, and body size can stand in for it. The team follow just under three hundred patients who had radical surgery.

Two scores stood out. Higher values on a fat based score and on a sugar fat score each linked to worse overall survival, and the sugar fat score also linked to time without disease return. Forest based ranking put those two scores on top, and both beat the other scores at each time point checked.
pmc-12815878:
When cancer spreads to bone, two drugs — denosumab and zoledronic acid — are the standard shields against fractures and other skeletal events. Li Zhong and co-authors pooled twenty-one studies to compare their benefit, safety, and value for money in solid tumours and multiple myeloma. The review covered trials, cohort studies, and cost analyses published up to September 2025, with the strength of evidence graded.

Denosumab delayed the first skeletal event and later ones better than the older drug, a benefit clear in solid tumours but not in myeloma. Survival was about the same on both. Denosumab may cause fewer side effects overall and less kidney harm. On cost, it looked good value in rich health systems but poor value where budgets are tight, where the older drug stayed the sensible buy. The authors advise weighing tumour type, safety, and local prices when choosing.
pmc-12816178:
Selviana Wulansari and co-authors build a dental pulp-capping material from nano tricalcium phosphate laced with silver nanoparticles, in a study from 2025. Both parts bring something the job needs: the phosphate releases calcium and phosphate ions that help rebuild dentin, while silver fights bacteria without killing the tissue cells.

The team mixed several silver doses and checked the blends with infrared, X-ray, and microscope tools. The base crystal structure stayed intact, and the particles spread evenly with little clumping. Ion release and acidity stayed steady over three weeks of checks. A one percent silver mix performed best in the early tests reported. Antibacterial assays targeted the two main cavity bacteria, Streptococcus mutans and Lactobacillus acidophilus.
pmc-12816478:
Sulemana Ansumah Saaka and Christa Sato use a large Canada survey to link unfair treatment and mental health for people with disabilities during the Covid years, in a study from 2025. Such treatment was old before the pandemic and grew worse within it.

People who faced unfair treatment tied to their disability, looks, or sex were less likely to rate their mental health as high. Those with more than one disability fared worst. Strong social ties, by contrast, linked to better self rated mental health. Age, schooling, and place of home also shaped the scores in the data.
pmc-12816578:
Qinglong Meng and co-authors make the building blocks of RNA drugs with enzymes and cheap inputs in a 2025 paper. RNA drugs need special blocks called nucleoside triphosphates, some with chemical tweaks. Making them the usual way leans on costly ATP and hard clean up steps, which slows large scale supply.

The team reworked three enzymes to build the blocks from plain nucleosides and simple phosphate sources. They made two tweaked blocks that serve as key parts of sold RNA drugs. The crude product fed straight into RNA building with no clean up. The authors frame it as a greener, cheaper supply route.
pmc-12816678:
Feng and co-authors report a 2025 study that predicts outcomes for locally advanced cervical cancer treated with combined chemo and radiation. Knowing who will do well shapes treatment choices for each patient. Their framework pairs a deep learning model that reads MRI scans with protein data from tumor samples. The scan model works on images taken before treatment starts.

The model split patients into high-risk and low-risk groups and beat standard clinical factors at the task. Its scores held up in training and in two test groups, though with lower accuracy outside the home set. Protein profiles showed that high-risk tumors had a suppressed immune setting. The work links scan traits to tumor biology for better risk sorting.
pmc-12817678:
Elizabeth Braithwaite and co-authors test whether a mother's depression history marks a hormone gene and shapes breastfeeding. Women with depression breastfeed less and struggle more, for reasons not yet pinned down. The suspect pathway runs through the oxytocin receptor gene, OXTR, dimmed or lit by DNA methylation. Their 2025 study uses a large Norwegian birth cohort of 3,607 mothers. Depression history was self-reported in pregnancy, and blood methylation read soon after.

Depression history showed no link to OXTR methylation. One methylation site did track with nursing to six months, with higher marks raising the odds. The team reads the biology as subtle: the gene may matter at the margins, not as the main bridge. Social support likely carries more of the load.
pmc-12817878:
Community nurses increasingly assess patients at home through digital sensory tools that lead with sound, add device data, and use video only by consent. Alotaibi interviews 24 registered nurses across three services in Saudi Arabia about how they run such visits and how the tools affect trust, privacy, and family roles.

Nurses described a stepwise visit flow, with camera view agreed before any visual step and live clinical cues trusted over device logs when the two disagreed. Trust was kept by plain narration and recaps after glitches, privacy by renewed consent and pauses, and family help by bounded tasks. The study turns these habits into a safety bundle and teaching material.
pmc-12818378:
Intakhar Ahmad and co-authors present MyeliMetric, a toolbox for measuring myelin health, in this 2025 paper. The g-ratio compares axon width with total fiber width including its myelin sheath. Values outside the healthy range signal disease in brain and nerve tissue. No standard open tool existed for this measure from microscope images.

Their Python toolbox starts from already segmented electron microscopy images. It groups axons into size bands, since healthy ratios stay steady across sizes. That binning exposes size dependent damage that global averages hide. Built in checks guard against common errors like thin sampling and pseudo replication. The tool needs little statistical training to run. Standardized analysis should make myelin studies easier to compare across labs.
pmc-12819178:
Seven authors, led by Jiyun Chen, report a study of vulvar skin disease using high-frequency ultrasound, with the head dating the work to 2025. The patients had lichenoid vulvar dermatoses, a group of skin conditions in that area. The team asked whether a blood-flow measure from ultrasound matches lab measures of tiny blood vessels.

The study included 37 patients with confirmed disease who came to Henan Provincial People's Hospital between December 2021 and May 2024. A control group of 35 healthy women of like age and body mass took part in the same period. The team compared ultrasound measures of the skin between the two groups. Skin samples from patients were stained to count vessel density and vessel area. They then checked how well those counts lined up with the ultrasound flow index.
pmc-12820078:
Xiangduo Kong and colleagues published a muscle research study in 2025 on a common form of muscular dystrophy. The disease, shortened to FSHD, has no effective treatment. It is linked to a fetal gene switch, DUX4, turning on wrongly in adult muscle. How that switch damages muscle function stayed unclear.

The team grew muscle cells from patients and healthy controls. Electric pulses stood in for nerve signals that make muscle contract. Healthy cells answered with stronger contraction genes and activity. Patient cells responded poorly and showed worse internal structure. Engineered mutant cells showed the same failure pattern. The patient cells also failed to release a protective exercise-related signal. One downstream gene alone could reproduce the defect.
pmc-12820178:
David Horner and co-authors link a mother's metabolism to pregnancy problems in a 2025 study. Obesity before pregnancy is rising and raises the odds of complications. Blood chemistry may carry the mechanism, and naming the exact molecules could open prevention paths.

Two large pregnancy cohorts, one Danish and one American, supplied blood samples across gestation. Untargeted chemistry scans measured hundreds of small molecules at three stages. A metabolic pattern tied to body mass was built in the first cohort. That pattern also tracked diabetes in pregnancy and cesarean delivery. Mediation analysis tested which molecules carry the body-mass effect. Matching results across two cohorts strengthen the signature's claim to guide early risk checks.
pmc-12820278:
Mahmood Barani and co-authors pack a ginseng compound into tiny fat bubbles to treat Alzheimer's disease, in work from twenty twenty-five. The compound, called ginsenoside Rg3, can slow the build up of the amyloid protein that marks the disease. Getting it to the brain in useful amounts is the hard part.

The coated bubbles trapped most of the drug and released it slowly over two days. In cell tests, the formula cut stress and death signals after amyloid exposure. In animals, brain tissue and the blood brain barrier looked better preserved, though behavior scores did not shift firmly. Computer models confirmed the bubbles form on their own with the drug inside. The carrier shows promise for brain delivery.
pmc-12820378:
For people living with chronic illness, wearing a mask during the COVID-19 pandemic was more than a public health rule. Aghajari and co-authors interviewed 15 such patients in depth about the physical, emotional, and social sides of masking. Participants described the experience as nothing less than a revolution in lifestyle. One theme covered the survival routines they built, from new habits to constant planning.

The other covered fresh daily challenges that masks created for already difficult lives. The authors urge clinicians and policymakers to answer with tailored guidance, better mask design, and psychosocial support, so protection does not come at the cost of quality of life.
pmc-12821178:
Blood pooled inside the spine can press on nerves and cause swift harm, and surgery is the usual fix. Menglong Jia and co-authors tell a 2025 case where the care team chose rest and close watch instead. Their patient was a man of fifty nine with sharp back pain and weak, numb legs.

Scans showed the pool of blood spread across part of his lower spine. In place of surgery, the team used a full plan of care without an operation. In twenty days his pain and weakness cleared, and the pooled blood had been taken up by the body. The case shows that a few such patients may do well without surgery.
pmc-12821278:
A gut gene set that handles estrogen is eyed in endometriosis by Stefania Saponara and co-authors in work dated 2025. The ill grows womb-like tissue outside the womb, fed by estrogen, and often blocks fertility. The estrobolome is the set of germ genes that work on estrogen. Five studies passed the team's screen of seven bases. Gut imbalance and estrobolome shifts showed across them.

One enzyme that frees estrogen ran high or awry in some work. Flare marks and awake immune cells rode with the shifts. Germ tuning is a care path worth tests.
pmc-12821478:
John Dotis and co-authors report a child whose kidney disease turned out to be genetic in this 2025 case report. The six-year-old had a syndrome where the kidneys leak protein and steroids did not help. A biopsy pointed to a scarring pattern often blamed on other causes.

Targeted gene reading found a new harmful variant in the COL4A3 gene. Fine microscope views of the kidney filter also looked abnormal. Together, the clues gave a diagnosis of a collagen-related kidney disease, the Alport family. The case argues for early gene testing, which can spare children needless immune-suppressing drugs.
pmc-12822178:
Chava Pollak and three colleagues present a 2025 study of a hospital program that supports heart failure patients after they go home. The team reviewed records for 343 adults discharged from a community hospital in Westchester County, New York, during 2023. They asked which patient traits and which program steps predicted a return to hospital within 30 days.

About one in five patients came back within a month. Each added health condition raised the odds of return, while a follow-up visit within a week cut the odds sharply. Patients the care team actually reached had far lower risk than those never contacted. The study argues that steady contact after discharge is what keeps people safely home.
pmc-12822278:
Dickson Mwenitete and co-authors study surgery outcomes for blocked bowels at a hospital in Malawi. A blocked bowel can kill if care comes late, above all where resources are thin. The team read charts for 262 adults treated at Mzuzu Central Hospital over three years. They checked which traits of patient and illness tracked with death or discharge.

About fifteen percent of patients died, and most of the rest went home well. Wound infections hit about sixteen percent of the group. Small bowel blocks were the most common kind, led by scar bands from past surgery. Two traits stood out after full checks: a high risk score before surgery and a swollen belly. The authors urge sharper pre-surgery checks and faster operations.
pmc-12824278:
Fatemeh Doryani and co-authors built a magnetic nanoparticle that delivers two attacks on stomach cancer cells at once. The drug cisplatin often fails because a long non-coding RNA called MALAT1 helps the cells resist it. The team's cobalt ferrite particles, coated with two polymers, carry a safer prodrug form of cisplatin plus DNA cassettes that produce RNA able to silence MALAT1. Lab tests confirmed the particles' size, charge, and magnetic behavior.

About eighty-nine percent of the particles entered the cancer cells, and MALAT1 levels fell ninefold. Treated cells died more, moved less, and showed higher activity of a self-destruct enzyme. The authors present the nanocomplex as a promising dual therapy in the dish: chemotherapy plus gene silencing in one targeted package. They note the work must still be confirmed in animals before any clinical hopes are raised.
pmc-12824978:
João Menino and colleagues tracked pneumonia deaths among diabetic patients in Portugal over twenty-five years. Their 2025 study uses national hospital records. Pneumonia ranks among Portugal's top causes of death. Diabetes raises both pneumonia risk and the odds of a poor outcome. Admissions from 1989 to 2014 were reviewed retrospectively.

Over 1.3 million hospitalizations entered the dataset. Pneumonia accounted for about forty-four thousand of them. One in five pneumonia patients had diabetes. Their share of pneumonia admissions ran far above non-diabetics. Diabetic patients stayed slightly longer in hospital. Women formed a larger share of the diabetic group. Trends in deaths across the decades are charted for both groups.
pmc-12825178:

Reading news and playing games each showed their own positive link, while the way in mattered too: reaching the internet by computer or by phone both beat non-use. Statistical matching, meant to compare like with like, backed the result. Part of the effect ran through social participation: people who go online also take part more in social life, and that activity tracks with a healthier mind.
pmc-12905478:
Wojciech Marlicz and Grażyna Rydzewska reflect on a national gastroenterology congress held in Warsaw in September two thousand twenty-five. More than a thousand clinicians, researchers, and students attended the three-day meeting. The Polish society behind it is among the oldest of its kind in the world, founded in nineteen hundred nine. This year's theme put the patient at the center of care.

The program mixed hands-on workshops and masterclasses with research talks. Clinical practice and science met throughout, the authors say, rather than sitting in separate tracks. Polish and foreign speakers shared the stage under the patronage of health bodies at home and abroad. The piece closes on the meeting's spirit: skill and discovery matter most when they serve the person in the clinic chair.
pmc-12913878:
Patcharawan Kongkasem and co-authors published this poultry feeding study in 2025. Corn dominates broiler chicken feed for its energy and pigment, but wheat and barley offer flexibility when prices shift. The team fed 525 male broilers one of three diets for thirty-five days: corn only, corn with wheat, or corn with barley. All diets matched in energy and protein and carried the same enzyme supplement. Growth, carcass traits, meat quality, and consumer taste scores were measured.

Corn-fed birds gained slightly more weight, though the edge was not statistically firm. Barley clearly raised belly fat, while wheat produced the leanest birds. Corn meat looked yellowest, reflecting its pigments. Tenderness, juiciness measures, and taste panel scores did not differ between diets, and all scored well. The authors conclude that modest wheat or barley inclusion is safe for performance and eating quality. Wheat may even help farms trim unwanted fat.
pmc-12913978:
Nattamol Phetburom and co-authors test, in a 2025 study, a leaf extract from Siam weed against a wide panel of clinical bacteria. Drug resistance is eroding infection control worldwide. This traditional medicinal plant is rich in phenols and flavonoids with reported germ-fighting power.

The team brewed an ethanol extract from dried leaves. They checked 46 bacterial strains, both major types, for growth inhibition. Biofilm breaking, antioxidant action, and cell disruption were measured as well. Microscopy revealed the physical damage the extract inflicts. A weed that grows freely across the tropics could be a cheap source of antibacterial chemistry. The broad panel makes the claim stronger than single-strain tests.
pmc-12926478:
A 2025 review by Irfan Khan and co-authors traces how mpox changed between 2022 and 2024. The outbreak spread well beyond the virus's old African range and was declared a global health emergency. The authors compare the virus's family branches, highlighting a newer branch, clade Ib, that spreads more readily and carries telltale mutation patterns. They explain how the virus copies itself in the cell fluid and dodges interferon defenses.

Transmission now runs mainly person to person, including through sexual contact. The review also covers pregnancy risks, drug options such as tecovirimat, and three generations of vaccines, ending with calls for stronger surveillance.
pmc-12927478:
Jing Tian, Yonggang Li, Yuanlong Zhao, and Xiaoli Tao map research on chikungunya virus in a paper whose head dates it to 2025. The virus spreads by mosquito and has caused outbreaks with millions of cases worldwide. Lasting joint pain is one of its severe effects.

The team analyzed more than thirty-seven hundred papers from 2015 to 2024. The United States, Brazil, and India led output, and French groups stood out as well. Hot topics included family trees of the virus, spread patterns, disease process, drugs, and vaccines. Joint work across countries plays a key role in tracking the virus, they find.
pmc-12929378:
Yaohua Yue and Anbang Zhao teach a drone to map weeds for spot spraying in a study published in 2025. Weeds choke young soybeans, and blanket spraying wastes chemical. Finding each weed's exact outline from the air is the enabling step.

Their improved segmentation model builds on YOLOv11-seg with parts swapped for sharper small-target vision. Attention and shuffling modules help separate small weeds from look-alike seedlings. On a real field data set, detection scored 0.89 and mask quality 0.84 on the standard overlap measure. Both beat two rival YOLO versions at lower computing cost. The masks feed straight into variable-rate spray prescription maps, the authors say.
pmc-12951978:
Ovarian cancer learns to shrug off chemotherapy, and a signaling network with three branches sits near the center of that resistance. Shiwen Wang and co-authors review in a 2025 paper how traditional Chinese herbal ingredients press on that network while standard drugs strike it. The pairing they propose works two ways at once.

Herbal components are reported to restore drug sensitivity, stall cell division, trigger cell death, choke blood supply, and soften side effects. Yet tumors reroute around single blocks through backup pathways, which is why the authors frame the strategy as network remodeling over time rather than one hard strike. They call for computer-guided combination design.
pmc-12962578:
Qi Zhang, Bingqiu Xiu, Shuang Hao, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2025. It surveys how implant-based breast reconstruction is practiced across China, and how the practice is shifting.

The team questioned 215 hospitals in 2022 and got full answers from 198, of which 122 offer the surgery. Hospitals offering it did more breast surgery overall and rebuilt more often. Implants made up over ninety percent of reconstructions at those hospitals. A small set of high-volume centers did most of the cases. One mesh brand was stocked by three-quarters of hospitals. Placing the implant above the muscle made up about a third of cases, and direct-to-implant surgery grew from 2017 to become the most common quick route. Radiation, scar tightening, and infection topped the worry list.
pmc-12977778:
Doctors in Brazil set out a plan for a trial in pregnant women who have long-term high blood pressure. In such women, a grave added condition called preeclampsia can be hard to tell from a plain rise in pressure. A blood marker called PlGF, made by the placenta, may help split the two. The trial will test whether care guided by the marker leads to better outcomes for mother and baby, and at what cost.

The plan enrols 140 women whose pressure worsens after week 20 of pregnancy. Women are assigned by chance to standard care or to care with a fast PlGF test added. Test results reach the care team within 30 minutes. If the marker is in the normal range, the woman can go home for watchful follow-up. Women with signs of severe disease are left out for safety.
pmc-13000478:
Chao Yang writes a 2025 commentary on a cohort study linking daily physical activity with modeled life expectancy in women and men. The study he discusses used device-measured activity and found that more movement, at a steeper intensity, tracked with added years of life. Even a short brisk walk seemed to help inactive adults, by about ten to thirty minutes a day.

Yang praises the clear message but presses two weak points. Volume and intensity are not separate levers, he argues, since volume is built from intensity over time. Treating them as apart can leave hidden bias. He urges sharper methods before the findings guide programs.
pmc-13085378:
Yi-Chen Chang and three co-authors published a 2026 correction to their study of drug prescriptions during the COVID-19 lockdowns in England. The study tracked monthly doses of two drugs, methadone and buprenorphine, used to treat opioid dependence. Data came from 4,273 primary care practices from March 2019 to February 2022.

In the first version, the second figure was printed the same as the first by mistake. The correction shows both the wrong and the right versions of that figure for full clarity. The right figure charts monthly doses and items dispensed for buprenorphine across the study span. The journal states that the article itself has been fixed. The notice keeps the record straight on what the data show.
pmc-13086978:
William Wiradinata and Faqrizal Qhabibi ask whether a jagged heartbeat trace in athletes signals danger or fitness. The notched pattern, called fragmented QRS, marks scarred heart muscle in patients and can foreshadow sudden death. Athletes' hearts remodel, though, and the sign is not in their screening rules. Seven studies made the cut for this scoping review.

The pattern grew commoner with age and showed most in one chest lead. No athlete with the finding suffered a bad event in follow up. The authors judge a lone notch in that lead likely harmless. Notches across neighboring leads still earn a closer look, with longer tracking needed.
pmc-13089378:
Gabriel Dogbanya reviews Nigeria's long, uneven fight against preventable deaths in childbirth. Nigeria still carries an outsized share of the world's maternal deaths, though rates have eased from over 1,000 per 100,000 births. His 2026 viewpoint calls the progress fragile and easily reversed.

He traces national programs from a midwives scheme to the praised Abiye effort in Ondo State. Again and again, political turnover, shaky funding, and weak follow-through broke good programs before they could scale. The piece tests global strategy goals against Nigerian reality. It urges care without barriers, working emergency obstetric services, and stronger oversight through death review systems. Continuity, he argues, is the missing medicine.
pmc-13090078:
Birth patterns in the United States have shifted over the past decade, and Bane and co-authors chart the change inside one large health system. They track more than 700,000 pregnancies from 2012 to 2023, computing pregnancy and live birth rates per thousand people aged 15 to 44, plus outcomes such as miscarriage, stillbirth, and ectopic pregnancy.

Adjusted pregnancy rates fell about ten percent and live birth rates about fourteen percent over the period. Miscarriage, molar, and ectopic rates also eased, stillbirth stayed flat, and induced abortion rose about twenty-seven percent. The authors say the wider drop in births than in pregnancies is largely explained by the rise in abortions.
pmc-13091578:
Wei Shang and Dexian Lu wire up children and grandparents to learn how each generation's brain reads a shared courtyard. Designing public spaces where old and young thrive together is a stated goal of aging, urbanizing societies, yet the evidence usually stops at questionnaires. Their 2026 study records brain waves and eye movements as forty participants, twenty-five elderly and fifteen children, view community spaces.

Computer vision first sorted photographs of the spaces into their elements and types. The synchronized recordings then exposed distinct neuro-behavioral patterns by generation. Community service areas and the leftover, in-between spaces of a neighborhood drew significantly different responses from the two groups, in where the eyes went and what the brain registered beneath awareness. The authors offer the method as a measuring instrument for design: perception differences between generations can now be quantified, not just surveyed.
pmc-13091978:
Mahbub-Ul Alam and co-authors compare, in a 2026 study, two ways of asking what poor urban households in Dhaka, Bangladesh would pay for a sewer link. Planners need such values to set fair fees for sanitation. The team surveyed one thousand households in five low-income areas and checked their toilets in person.

The direct asking method gave a slightly higher average value than the indirect method, which infers value from rents. Over ninety percent said they would pay, weighing family health and neighbors' consent. Richer households would pay more, but willingness dropped fast as the monthly bill rose, above all among tenants. Rooms and roof type drove the rent-based values.
pmc-13113978:
The authors test whether a plant compound, quercetin, protects the gut in a rat model of cerebral palsy. The condition harms the brain and also the gut lining through the gut-brain axis. Young rats with the condition, and healthy ones, got quercetin or a plain vehicle in the first days of life.

The condition thinned parts of the gut and raised oxidative damage, mostly in the jejunum. Quercetin eased the oxidative stress and switched on genes that seal the gut wall in both groups. It did not fully undo the shape changes. The authors see it as a possible add-on guard for the gut.
pmc-13123378:
Cai and co-authors review composite microgels, tiny gel particles built for medical uses, in a 2026 paper. A microgel is a hydrogel speck about the size of a cell. Mixing polymers, nanomaterials, and active agents into one particle lets designers tune its behavior. The review links how these particles are built to how they steer cells, and then to real applications.

Material traits such as stiffness and surface chemistry guide cells, as do dynamic tricks like responding to a trigger on demand. The authors show the design rules at work in cancer therapy, tissue engineering, and regenerative medicine. Open problems include making the particles at scale, proving safety, and fitting them into clinical routines. AI-driven design is named as a coming direction.
pmc-13128578:
Genhua Mu and co-authors build a warning chart in 2026 for COVID-19 patients sliding toward lung failure. The failure state, called ARDS, often forces a breathing tube, and early flags are prized. The team asked whether a blood level of a tissue sugar, drawn in the first day, could flag risk alone or with standard severity scores.

Charts of 502 adults admitted in one center from late 2022 into early 2023 were reviewed. Levels drawn within a day fed models for disease presence, severe grade, and tube need, then merged into a paper chart doctors can score by hand. Work like this aims to move high-risk patients to closer watch before the slide, not after.
pmc-13135578:
Mayke ten Hoor and five co-authors examine in 2026 at the molecular level a conditional knockout mouse built to study Cdh12, a gene tied to kidney malformation. The SCON system plants a short artificial intron meant to vanish during splicing until a trigger locks it in and kills the gene. Earlier checks judged the system mostly by visible traits.

Both the resting and triggered forms of the gene unexpectedly skipped a neighboring exon, shifting the reading frame and cutting message levels by about a quarter. The resting allele was therefore not silent as designed. Careful molecular audits like this one matter before phenotype results from fast knockout systems are trusted, since hidden splicing damage can mimic or mask a gene's true role.
pmc-13137678:
Mathieu Denoël and co-authors weigh newts to measure the direct cost of metamorphosis. Many amphibians rebuild their bodies to leave the water, but some species can also breed while staying in larval form, a shortcut called paedomorphosis. Which path wins in evolution depends partly on what the change itself costs. Their 2026 study follows palmate newts through a controlled experiment.

The team varied the conditions that push newts to transform and tracked weight over time. Newts that metamorphosed lost body weight, while those that stayed in larval form did not. Warmth played a smaller role than the change itself. Females paid more than males, and eating less during the change explained much of the loss. The authors say such direct costs belong in any account of why metamorphosis evolves or is lost.
pmc-13138078:
Yong Yin and Chun Ren report a 2026 analysis of genes tied to adiponectin, a hormone made by fat tissue, in melanoma skin cancer. Hormones from fat can sway how tumors grow and how the immune system responds. The team asked whether these genes sort patients into groups with different outlooks.

They merged gene-variant data from a large open database with tumor data from a cancer genome atlas. Five gene variants tied to the hormone also tracked with patient survival. Grouping tumors by gene activity produced four subtypes with clearly different outcomes. One protein, albumin, sat at the center of the gene network and marked the worst group. Lab tests showed raising albumin in melanoma cells also raised several inflammation signals. The work links fat-related genes to immune patterns in melanoma.
pmc-13138278:
Avery Shuei-He Yang and four co-authors wrote a 2026 reply to a letter about their study on lung infection risk in frail patients. The study weighed how a load of certain drugs, called anticholinergic burden, links to pneumonia. Frailty, or weakness that comes with age and illness, may change that risk.

In the reply, the authors take up points about thinking and mental illness. People with those problems face higher pneumonia risk, in part through poor swallowing and weak airway protection. The authors explain that their design compared each patient with themselves over time, which cuts bias. They also ran fresh checks that added stroke, heart failure, and lung disease to the model. The reply aims to show that the first findings hold up under closer tests.
pmc-13139278:
Quirin Donath and a large team study severe post-COVID illness in young people in a 2026 paper. The study ran at a children's hospital in Germany and drew on a registry of patients aged 7 to 25. Early spotting of those at risk of severe illness matters for timely care.

Among 120 participants, severe illness linked to more symptoms during the first infection. Faintness on standing and trouble concentrating during that illness also raised the risk sharply. Girls faced higher risk than boys. The team used standard symptom and fatigue scores to define severe cases, including confirmed chronic fatigue syndrome. The findings aim to guide early follow-up for young patients.
pmc-13142278:
Nazanin Alghasi and co-authors study sleep and night eating among medical students in Iran who carry extra weight, in a 2026 survey. Night eating, a pattern of heavy eating after dinner or during the night, links to poor sleep and lower quality of life. Medical students face high stress and odd hours, which can worsen both problems.

The team surveyed 353 students at a medical school in Kermanshah during 2022 and 2023. Students filled out forms on night eating and sleep quality, and the team weighed the links among those scores and body weight. Clear night eating syndrome was rare, found in under one percent. The paper still probes how milder night eating tracks with poor sleep in this group.
pmc-13143278:
Mark van der Kroeg and co-authors published a 2026 study of a way to grow miniature brain cortex tissue, called organoids, in laboratory wells. Brain tissue grown from stem cells lets researchers study how the cortex forms. Free-floating organoids vary in size and die at the core. The new organoids stick to the floor of the well, which holds their shape steady.

The team seeds the wells with cortex-bound starter cells made from stem cells. In eight weeks the tissue builds itself: a flat cortex of fixed size, with cell layers in their places. The organoids hold nerve cells, star-shaped support cells, and wrapping cells. They can live for ten months or more. Imaging shows mature spines on the nerve cells, wrapped fibers, and strong nerve activity. Set beside the floating organoids, the adherent ones are more uniform from well to well.
pmc-13144178:
Cooling caps can save chemotherapy patients' hair, yet at one center Black women used them about six times less often than White women. Abena Minta and seven co-authors interview Black patients to learn why, in this 2026 study. Hour-long conversations were coded for themes about hair loss, the caps, and better care.

Hair loss itself carried heavy weight. Against the caps stood plain barriers: adverts that never showed women who look like them, and doubt that a cap designed around straight hair works on textured hair. Patients asked for honest counseling on cap use, good camouflage options, and pointers to skin doctors. The authors note the single-center, volunteer design, and frame the fixes as concrete steps clinics can take now.
pmc-13144278:
Rabia Gönül and co-authors published a 2026 review on how scientists watch, measure, and manipulate a family of signaling lipids inside cells. These lipids, phosphoinositides, are scarce but powerful. They steer membrane traffic, cell shape, and even gene activity, each in its own corner of the cell. When their balance breaks, cancer, brain disease, and immune problems can follow. Studying them is hard because they are few and fleeting.

The review gathers the current toolbox. Genetic tricks can silence or edit the enzymes that make and break these lipids. Light-controlled tools switch them on command. Glowing sensors and sharp microscopes reveal where each kind sits in living cells. Lab methods such as thin-layer separation and mass spectrometry count the kinds present. The authors compare the strengths and limits of each approach, and show how combining tools can pin down what each lipid pool does.
pmc-13144878:
Marco Tulio Araujo Pedatella and co-authors listen to stroke patients in Brazil on how life changed after their stroke. Their conference abstract from 2026 uses talks and topic based study of the answers. Stroke brings high death and disability rates, plus fear and doubt for patients and their families.

Forty nine patients at a large hospital took part, most of them men. Fear and regret were common themes in the talks. More than half felt their stroke could have been stopped. Most, close to nine in ten, hoped to get back to normal life. Chief fears were a new stroke and loss of independence. Close to half expected a big hit to their funds.
pmc-13145078:
Piyathida Orantanasan and co-authors track body and mind change over four years after chronic stroke, in a 2026 study. Past proof on such long spans is thin. The group had first joined a study of muscle loss after stroke between 2020 and 2022, and the team now checks them again.

Thirty five people took part, with a mean time since stroke of close to six years. The share who could walk on their own fell, and walking speed dropped in a clear way. Grip strength and a sit to stand test did not change much, and mind test scores held steady. Care plans may need to guard walking skill most as years pass.
pmc-13145178:
Claudia Cuccurullo and nine co-authors report a case series of a rare double emergency: a heart attack and a brain stroke striking the same patient at nearly the same time. Over five years, their center found twenty-two such cases among more than two thousand treated stroke patients, about one percent. Most had blockages in large or medium brain vessels, and three quarters had the heart attack in the same window as the stroke.

Treatment had to serve two organs pulling in opposite directions. Ten patients received clot-dissolving drugs, three had clots pulled from brain vessels, and nine got both. Just over half later had a coronary stent placed, on average three days after the stroke. Two patients bled into the brain without dying, and only about a quarter recovered well by three months. The authors call the condition severe and underdiagnosed.
pmc-13145778:
Kenza Khelfaoui Tredano and co-authors report a 2026 conference study on how the follow-up scan type sways choices about starting clot-preventing drugs after stroke. Bleeding inside the stroke zone can delay the drugs. MRI spots faint bleeds that plain scans miss, which may shift the call.

Four blinded raters judged scans for more than one hundred patients who had both scan types within a day. Raters held the drugs far more often on MRI reads than on plain scan reads. In a dozen cases MRI alone blocked a start the plain scan would have allowed. Raters also agreed with each other more on MRI. The authors urge care in reading faint MRI bleed signs.
pmc-13145978:
Lucio D'Anna and co-authors present a 2026 conference study on when to restart thinning pills after a stroke that broke through while on them. Trials back early starts after heartbeat-linked stroke, but breakthrough cases were largely left out. The ASPERA-R data let the team mimic a trial with timing rules set by stroke weight.

More than eight hundred patients fed the checks, split between early and late restarts. Early restarts tied to fewer new blocked-vessel events at ninety days. Mid to heavy bleeding also ran lower with early starts. Death from all causes and from vessel causes both leaned lower. The authors back early restarts in this group while trials are built.
pmc-13146078:
Lucio D'Anna and ten co-authors compare two ambulance routes for stroke patients who need a clot pulled out, in a conference abstract from 2026. In the mothership model, patients go straight to a full stroke center. In drip-and-ship, they get clot-busting drugs at a local hospital first, then transfer.

The analysis pools nineteen studies with more than sixteen thousand patients. Extra delay in the drip-and-ship route steadily cut the odds of living independently at ninety days. Beyond about forty-three minutes of delay, going direct won out. Other outcomes, including bleeding and death, did not differ clearly. The authors advise direct transport when transfer would add a long delay.
pmc-13146378:
Richard Leigh and co-authors presented a conference abstract in 2026 on a brain barrier leak measure and outcome after stroke. The patients had a blocked large brain vessel and were moved from a first stroke center to a full center for clot removal. Data on how leaky the barrier is in this group were limited. Imaging at the first center supplied the leak measure.

Just under three hundred patients were included, with a median age in the mid-seventies. More leakage in the core injured zone linked to lower odds of a good functional outcome three months later. It also linked to higher risk of death. The authors say pre-transfer imaging of the barrier holds useful signs about later outcome.
pmc-13146478:
Seven doctors in China report a registry study on gene guided drug choice after stroke in a 2026 conference abstract. A common anti clot drug works poorly in people whose genes slow its activation. The team asked how common that resistance is and how it tracks with patient outcomes.

The study held 572 stroke patients who had gene tests at one hospital from 2019 to 2024. More than six in ten counted as resistant, most of them mid or poor drug processors. About one in ten got a drug that clashed with their gene type. Age, diabetes, and stroke severity at arrival were among the factors tied to poor outcomes at ninety days.
pmc-13146578:
Huiya Li and co-authors trace post-stroke brain inflammation to a feeding failure inside microglia, the brain's resident immune cells. Their 2026 conference study builds on maps that found two microglial groups after stroke: one in the dead core and one in the salvageable rim. The core group had shut down its breakdown of branched-chain amino acids, which then piled up.

Boosting that breakdown in mice calmed inflammation, shrank the core group, and lessened injury. A gene regulator called Arid3a emerged as the upstream switch for the whole pathway. Silencing it worsened strokes; raising it protected the brain in the acute phase. Drug treatment that pushed the same pathway also shifted cell metabolism. The authors name Arid3a a promising target for limiting stroke damage.
pmc-13146678:
Markus Klammer and co-authors present a 2026 conference abstract comparing kinds of atrial fibrillation found around stroke. Some fibrillation is known before the stroke, some shows on the admission tracing, and some appears only during long monitoring afterward. The team hypothesized the middle group sits between the other two on the disease continuum. They compared hundreds of stroke patients with confirmed brain injury on scans.

Across the three groups, orderly trends appeared. Diabetes, prior stroke, risk scores, and fibrillation burden rose step by step from monitoring found to known cases. Stroke lesion size, island involvement, heart rate, and one cholesterol measure fell along the same order. The admission tracing group held the middle position throughout. The authors read this as support for a staged disease progression.
pmc-13146878:
Monica Serrano and co-authors study sex life after stroke in a 2026 report. Sex harm after stroke is common yet missed in care. It touches want, acts, and self-image for patients and mates alike. The team called 35 patients six months after stroke and sent forms by email. Forms graded sex acts and scores, body image, mood, and life quality. Most strokes were of the clot kind, and most harm was mild.

Nine in ten had a good sex life before the stroke. Seven in ten took up sex acts again. Men kept near sound scores, while women scored low on the main scale. A mate and an active sex life tied to high scores. Poor body image sat with job loss and bladder leaks. The authors urge teams to ask about sex health in stroke care as a set step.
pmc-13146978:
Noelle Audrey Moko Tatuene and co-authors report a 2026 conference study on how stroke patients view shared choices in rehab planning. Shared choice joins the care team, the patient, and family around the patient's own values. Most past work sat in family practice or surgery, not rehab.

Twenty-five patients filled in standard scales on involvement, roles, and content with choices. About seven in ten felt actively involved in making their rehab plan. About three quarters said choices were made jointly with their team. Content with choices ran high across the group. Nine in ten reported no conflict over the choice and stood by their plan, backing wider use of shared choice in rehab.
pmc-13150778:
Lucas Silva, Jorge Coelho, and Valfrido de-Melo-Neto wrote this 2026 study asking whether the COVID-19 pandemic bent Brazil's suicide trend. Brazil suffered heavily in the pandemic, and fears of a suicide surge were widespread. Hard national evidence was missing.

The authors ran an interrupted time series on official death records, adjusting for seasons and splitting by sex and region. Suicide rates were already climbing significantly before 2020. At the national level, the pandemic's arrival did not significantly change that slope. Among men, though, the post-onset climb steepened significantly, while women's trend stayed flat. One region, the Central-West, also showed a shift. The paper's title question gets a qualified answer: no national turning point, but a male one.
pmc-13150978:
Md Sadikuj Jaman and co-authors review the molecular subtypes of breast cancer in this 2026 article. Breast cancer is the most common cancer in women, and its course varies sharply by subtype. The review searched six databases for work through mid 2025 and sorts what is known about each gene class as a drug target. Standard drugs such as tamoxifen and paclitaxel already act on these paths. Natural compounds, including baicalin and ursolic acid, show early promise in lab work. The authors argue that sharper subtype testing can guide personal treatment and help beat relapse and drug resistance.
pmc-13152878:
Veillard, Watkinson, and Poesch track a threatened bottom-dwelling fish to learn what makes it move. The Rocky Mountain sculpin barely spreads, so they tag and recapture fish along a 400-meter stretch of an Alberta creek over four months. They then model movement against living and non-living factors on both ends of each trip.

Neighbors matter most: the presence of kin and competitors at the start and the destination drives the choices, with rocky cobble cover also counting for fish that do move. Living and habitat factors interact strongly. The authors warn that habitat-only restoration work may fall short unless it also reckons with competition.
pmc-13153178:
Christina Granéli led a team testing ultrasound during bowel surgery in children in a 2026 paper. The surgery treats a condition where part of the bowel lacks nerve cells and must be removed. Telling healthy from affected bowel during the operation is the crux. Their idea was that ultra-high-frequency ultrasound, used live in the operating room, could separate the two by wall structure.

In over twenty patients, one muscle layer was much thicker in healthy bowel than in affected bowel, and a layer ratio differed just as clearly. Brightness of another layer also split the groups. The authors call the method promising for guiding how much bowel to remove.
pmc-13153478:
Baye Maru Derso and co-authors test germs in the dirty water that flows out of two hospitals in Addis Ababa, in a paper from two thousand twenty-six. Such water can carry germs into streams and wells and help spread strains that drugs no longer stop. The team took samples from late two thousand twenty-three to early two thousand twenty-four.

They grew 219 germ samples in the lab and tested each one against a range of drugs. Two kinds showed up most often: Klebsiella pneumoniae and Escherichia coli. More than half of the samples could shrug off more than one drug. Klebsiella fought off two drug types most strongly of all. About one in five samples made enzymes that break down key drugs. The team says such water must be cleaned well before it leaves a hospital.
pmc-13154078:
Ibrahim El-Battrawy and co-authors discuss how a heart diagnosis can shift from one condition to another. Their 2026 piece deals with sudden cardiac death, a leading cause of death from heart disease across the world. It claims four to five million lives a year. In older people, blocked arteries dominate. In the young, inherited heart muscle and electrical disorders are major causes.

Muscle disorders show up on heart imaging. Electrical disorders show on heart tracings, at rest or under provocation. Some patients still have no found cause after full checks. Their condition is then called idiopathic ventricular fibrillation, a diagnosis by exclusion. A case in the same issue moves from a presumed electrical disorder to that label. The authors stress repeat checks and long rhythm monitoring.
pmc-13154678:
Behrendt wrote a solo study in twenty twenty-six that tests seven switch-on gene drivers in a germ used to make fuel. The germ, Zymomonas mobilis, is prized for fuel work and for base science. Gene tools for it are old, but a rich set of switch drivers has been lacking.

Four drivers are tried in this germ for the first time, next to three known pairs. All fit a shared gold-gate build frame used by its field. A rare back-bone that holds without drug pick gave high, even out-put in the tests. Two of the new drivers look most fit for broad use, he finds.
pmc-13156078:
