The authors weigh drugs that target the receptor, while noting some evidence comes from other cancers and needs direct proof here.
pmc-13189978:
Hirokazu Ashida and co-authors report a hard case of milky fluid flooding the abdomen after kidney cancer surgery, in a 2026 case report. A seventy-one-year-old woman had her right kidney and a tumor clot in the vena cava removed, then developed chylous ascites, a leak of lymph fluid. Diet-based treatment failed to stop it.

Standard imaging found no leak, and an attempt to plug the main lymph duct from a neck vein failed. A fluid-filled bulge near the liver was sealed through the skin, yet the leak persisted. Finally the team threaded into the liver's own lymph channels, mapped them with dye, and embolized the leak from there. The fluid then resolved. The authors suggest liver-area lymphatics can leak after surgery involving the pancreas head region, and that this transhepatic route is a valuable option before shunt surgery.
pmc-13190378:
Cheng-Han Li and co-authors argue that one kind of self-injury has been misread by the field's standard theory. The usual model treats nonsuicidal self-injury as a pressure valve, a way to drain overwhelming negative feeling. Their 2026 perspective says that story fails a large, treatment-resistant group of adolescents whose core problem is anhedonia, an inability to feel pleasure, with a quieted reward system in the brain.

For this group, network studies put emptiness at the center of the symptom web. The authors propose that injury here works as forced activation, a jolt to feel something, not sedation. They sketch a diagnostic frame that separates this anhedonic subtype from defensive dissociation, and urge a therapy shift from calming distress to building positive feeling. The proposal, named Positive Affect Treatment, awaits real trials, which the authors plainly say still need to come.
pmc-13190578:
Lasting low back pain can shrink a life, from work to family time. Fei Li, Yanjun Cao, and Wei Feng set out a 2026 trial plan that pairs two exercise schools. One, a Western method, uses posture and moves to ease pain and free the spine. The other is a simplified form of a classic Chinese animal-play exercise that trains body and mind at once.

Seventy-four patients will be split at random into two groups. One group does both methods, and the other does the Chinese exercise alone. The team will track how far the lower spine can bend and how good life feels day to day. They also probe the forces at work in the spine. The aim is a simple, sound routine that patients can keep.
pmc-13190778:
Christoph H Saely and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-six update of Austrian guidelines on blood pressure treatment in diabetes. High blood pressure is a leading partner problem in diabetes. It drives both large and small vessel complications and raises deaths.

The guideline tailors pressure targets to each patient's situation. A range in the one twenties over seventies is tied to the best outcomes. Most patients should at least stay below the standard higher threshold. Most also need drug combinations, preferably in single pills. Agents proven to cut heart risk are favoured, and treatment continues once targets are met.
pmc-13194178:
Paul Brown reviews the search for the cause of early atherosclerosis. His review deals with the early steps that form fatty streaks in larger vessels.

Early steps include lining activation, lipoprotein crossing and change, monocyte inflow, and foam cell formation. Many agents mediate these steps and could serve as targets for testing or treatment. Risk factors range from age, sex, and family history to lipids, habits, microbes, dirty air, and uneven blood flow. Despite growing knowledge, Brown argues, the cause remains unsettled. The review sets out the steps and then weighs possible causes.
pmc-13194478:
Yue Chen and co-authors test three simple index scores for spotting fatty liver disease in people with type 2 diabetes. Their 2026 study covers a liver condition tied to metabolic problems, now a major companion illness for diabetes patients. Each index is built from routine measures like blood fats, sugar, body mass, and inflammation.

The team studied close to eight hundred hospital patients with diabetes, about a third of whom had the liver disease. They tested each index alone and in combination, using standard accuracy curves. They also checked whether adding an index truly improved sorting beyond other factors. Cheap, lab-based screening matters because imaging every diabetes patient is costly. The study offers a way to flag which patients most need liver checks.
pmc-13194978:
Okra breeders cross parent lines to find hybrids that outyield both parents, and a line-by-tester design sorts the winners efficiently. Abed and El-Shoura crossed ten female lines with two male testers at an Egyptian research station, producing twenty hybrids. Five crosses clearly outyielded the rest in pods per plant.

The best cross beat its mid-parent by about twenty-four percent and its better parent by seventeen percent. Genetic analysis showed non-additive effects, the kind that hybrids exploit, dominating over additive ones for these traits. Four female lines combined well across partners. The authors name the promising parents and crosses for Egypt's okra hybrid seed programs.
pmc-13195278:
Caspi and seven co-authors studied health effects after a minimum wage rise in Minneapolis in twenty twenty-six. The city raised its wage floor to fifteen dollars an hour. The team tracked whether food and health outcomes changed for low-wage workers compared with a city without a rise, Raleigh.

They followed four hundred ninety workers in Minneapolis and four hundred seventy-nine in Raleigh from twenty eighteen to twenty twenty-two. Body mass index did not change in either city. Neither did the share of grocery spending on fruits and vegetables or sugary foods. Food insecurity fell in both cities, more in Raleigh. The authors found no clear wage effect from the policy, and note pandemic disruption may have clouded the results.
pmc-13195378:
Emily Janio and co-authors study social networks and weight loss in breast cancer survivors in a 2026 paper. Survivors face higher obesity risk, and mobile health tools can help with weight control. Less is known about how social ties help or hinder those efforts. Latina and non Hispanic White survivors used one of two health apps for twelve weeks in a pilot study.

Both groups lost some body mass over the period, with no gap by ethnicity. Changes in social support alone did not track weight change overall. But the link between support change and weight change differed by group, reaching significance only for non Hispanic White participants. Persuasion from others showed no link, while pressure patterns were also examined. Readers see social context may not work the same for all survivors.
pmc-13195578:
Angel Viteri and nine co-authors shared a study in twenty twenty-six. They stimulated heart cells without wires, through a magnetic gel. Electrodes can pace and train cardiac tissue. But they are invasive and imprecise. The team's hydrogel embeds magnetoelectric nanoparticles. Each one has a cobalt ferrite core in a bismuth ferrite shell. They sit in a soft gelatin network that mimics heart tissue.

An external magnetic field makes the particles act. They give off local electric cues, with no wires attached. Microscopy and tomography showed porous, well-mixed gels. The particles stiffened crosslinking by a small amount. They trimmed swelling too. The gels stayed in the soft range that heart tissue prefers. The platform aims at cardiac patches. Clinicians could switch them on from outside the body. They could tune the dose by field, not by surgery.
pmc-13195778:
Five authors trace the source of inflammation from cinnamon e-cigarettes in this 2026 study. Flavor chemicals can add to the harm of e-cigarette aerosols, and the team's earlier work showed that heated cinnamon aerosol strongly inflamed human aortic smooth muscle cells.

Chemical screening of the heated liquid found two aromatic aldehydes, benzaldehyde and phenylacetaldehyde, that appear only after heating. Adding benzaldehyde to unheated liquid reproduced much of the inflammation signal seen with the full aerosol, without killing the cells. The result pins much of the effect on heat made breakdown products, not on the flavor itself. That points regulators and makers at vaping temperatures and flavor chemistry.
pmc-13196478:
Yating Huang and colleagues followed young adolescents' brains over four years in 2026 to watch reward circuits develop along different risk paths. Anticipating a reward engages frontostriatal and related circuits, and that response is relevant to both depression and psychosis. Early adolescence is when these circuits change fast, yet longitudinal comparisons across risk types were scarce. The team used data from the large ABCD study of child brain development.

Brain scans during a monetary incentive task were collected at three time points from more than eighteen hundred adolescents. Groups included healthy controls and youths at high risk for depression, for psychosis, or for both. The title signals the finding: reward anticipation develops divergently across these groups. Divergent trajectories could eventually help identify which at-risk children need watching for which illness, years before symptoms declare themselves.
pmc-13196578:
Yunong Tian and co-authors turned camellia fruit shells into a protein-catching nanomaterial in a 2026 paper. Histidine-rich proteins can fill a dietary gap linked to stress and illness. They are scarce in foods, so enrichment tools are needed. The shells are farm waste, which makes the source cheap.

Oxidized cellulose from the shells was chemically tuned. It was frozen into a sponge with metal oxide particles. The material selectively grabs histidine-rich proteins from food mixes. Structure and strength were checked in detail. Waste shells thus gain a high-value second life in food science.
pmc-13196678:
Katerina Bernardi and co-authors describe a single case from 2026 involving a 15-year-old girl with a rare early form of Parkinson disease linked to the DNAJC6 gene. She had growing tremor, slow movement, and poor balance, and she carried a gene variant not reported before. A standard drug helped at first, but later caused severe swings in movement that other drugs could not control.

Surgeons placed deep brain stimulation leads in a small inner brain area on both sides. The treatment brought marked and lasting relief from the tremor. The case adds rare treatment evidence for this condition and suggests the surgery can help when drugs fail and tremor becomes disabling.
pmc-13196978:
Corine Oldhoff-Nuijsink and colleagues published a 2026 interview study on digital health research panels. People in vulnerable positions often miss out on digital health tools and on the research behind them. A standing panel could give them a voice, so the team explored what draws people in.

They held 23 in-depth interviews, mostly with people in vulnerable positions. Most were keen to join a panel. They wanted to make digital health easier to use for themselves and their peers. Outreach at community centers and clear flyers seemed the best way to recruit. Clear updates and prompt sharing of results kept people engaged. Dutch setting limits how far the lessons travel.
pmc-13197078:
Toshiko Furukawa and Takuya Iimura present a 2026 model of trade between legumes and root bacteria. Legume plants house Rhizobium bacteria in root lumps, trading plant carbon for bacterial nitrogen. The model adds energy budgets, since each side spends ATP, the cell's energy unit, to take in its share.

Trade balance is kept by shifts in bacterial mass when one side gives more. The model makes three forecasts, and the authors show each fits past data. Conditions for the partnership to form match measured energy costs. At balance, plants give modest carbon while bacteria give rich nitrogen. The plant's carbon share falls as its own carbon-to-nitrogen ratio rises.
pmc-13197278:
Catarina Leitão and colleagues describe expert review of a new prostate cancer questionnaire in 2026. Prostate cancer is among the most common cancers in men. Habits such as diet and activity may sway its course, so the team built a form that joins lifestyle and clinical data.

The form grew from literature reviews and talks with clinic staff. It spans four parts: personal background, diet, lifestyle, and clinical data. Twenty-five experts in urology, family medicine, and public health rated it, with input from language and mind-health experts too. Scores were high for fit and accuracy. The lifestyle part scored a bit lower on completeness. Small fixes followed, and the form is now ready for larger studies.
pmc-13197378:
Francesca Calà Campana and co-authors design drug plans that fight bacteria while slowing drug resistance, in a 2026 study. Bacteria can gain resistance by mutation or by swapping genes with each other, so a fixed drug plan often fails over time. The team build a model that tracks the host immune system plus bacteria that are drug-sensitive and drug-resistant.

On that model they pose a planning problem: shrink the total bacteria while using as little drug as possible. They prove a best plan exists, work out the rules it must obey, and add a second method that replans as new readings come in. Computer trials with realistic values show the best plan shifts with the starting mix of bacteria and with how much weight cost is given. The frame gives doctors a principled way to mix several drugs against resistant infections.
pmc-13197478: Silvia Pietrobono and colleagues issued a 2026 author correction to a study on pancreatic cancer response. A reader flagged errors in the work, which links the signal CCL3 to strong response to a TGF-beta blocking therapy. Source data for three figure panels were wrong. One figure legend lacked a needed citation. Staining panels in another figure were pasted in error, and two supplement scratch assay panels were also wrong. The original article has been corrected.
pmc-13198478:
Valentina Ponchio and co-authors review the link between brain vessel malformations and heart disease in children in a paper from 2026. Both conditions are rare and hard to treat. When they occur together, they raise questions about shared roots in early development.

The team pooled one hundred thirty-nine studies published between 1971 and 2023. Together the studies covered more than a thousand patients. A meta-analysis weighed how often the two conditions coincide. The work also looks at what the pairing means for long-term health. Early recognition could help doctors tailor care for these children. The review gives clinics a single map of a scattered literature.
pmc-13198678:
A healed elbow can still feel unsafe to an athlete whose mind lags the joint. Pavel Kadantsev and co-authors build a readiness scale for that gap in a 2026 study. The scale adapts knee and shoulder tools to elbow instability.

Ten patients helped shape the questions after ligament rebuilds. Forty-seven patients then tested the scale over long follow-up. Scores tracked elbow function scores in the expected directions. Repeat takes matched with near-perfect steadiness. Return to sport was logged beside the scale. The tool gives surgeons a mind-side read to pair with strength tests.
pmc-13199778:
Aidan Kincaid, Alex Hewitt, and Rajendra KC review fourth-generation gene editors that insert DNA without cutting both strands. Their 2026 review explains why the field is moving past early CRISPR tools: double-strand breaks can destabilize the genome and cause off-target harm. Integration-based systems promise cleaner placement of new genetic material.

The review tours several enzyme families. Recombinases from microbes rearrange DNA at set sites, transposons move code by cut and paste, and some CRISPR-linked systems guide insertion by RNA. Viral integrases and mobile introns add more options, each with its own strengths in delivery. The authors close on the hurdles that remain: efficiency, specificity, and getting the tools into patients.
pmc-13199878:
Jennie Han, Eva Masmanian, Timothy Wang, and Tuan Peng Chua review cholesterol treatment beyond statins in a 2026 article. Coronary artery disease causes much illness and death worldwide. After a heart event, tight control of blood lipids is a core part of care. Yet fewer than thirty percent of patients reach their LDL target on statins alone.

The review covers oral options such as ezetimibe and bempedoic acid. It also covers injected drugs, inclisiran and PCSK9 inhibitors, and a fish oil drug for high triglycerides. New ideas in trials include gene editing, the authors note. Knowing when to refer to a lipid clinic matters too.
pmc-13199978:
Pengcheng Fan and co-authors build a test that can tell vaccine strains of a poultry germ apart from wild ones. Mycoplasma gallisepticum causes major losses in chicken farming, and live vaccines are a main defence, but after vaccination farmers need to know whether birds carry the vaccine strain or a wild infection. The team compared whole genomes of wild and vaccine strains to find sites that differ between them, then designed primers and probes aimed at those sites.

The result is three duplex PCR assays, one for each approved vaccine strain, each detecting its vaccine strain and the wild type in a single run. Checks confirmed the assays are specific, sensitive, and repeatable. Applied to throat swabs from real flocks, the tests cleanly separated wild infections from vaccine exposure. The authors offer the method for surveillance, eradication programs, and checking vaccine performance.
pmc-13200078:
Shiori Yoshida and co-authors pilot a remote nursing system for cancer pain in a 2026 trial. The system, CAPAMOS, lets nurses follow pain in patients with advanced cancer who live at home. Forty-eight outpatients at a university hospital in Japan were split at random between the system and usual care. All had daily pain of at least three on a ten-point scale.

Pain, self-care, and quality of life were checked at the start and at two and four weeks. No clear group-by-time edge appeared on any measure. Still, within the system group, average pain fell from 4.0 to 3.0 and stayed there, while the control group showed no such gain. Pain's drag on enjoying life also eased in the system group. As a pilot, the trial mainly tests whether a bigger trial is worth running.
pmc-13200678:
Antonio Palermo, Monica Bianchi, Shaila Cavatorti, and Loris Bonetti map what a program to grow nurse leaders should contain in work dated two thousand twenty-six. Specialist clinical nurses hold a new, key role as care needs shift with aging populations. How they see their own leadership, and what blocks or boosts it, was the study's start point.

Seven nurses at a multi-site hospital were interviewed in depth, with the questions shaped by past literature. Themes were drawn out and merged with published work on clinical leadership. A joint meeting of the nurses and their managers then fixed the program's parts. The plan follows a standard frame for building complex health programs, phase by phase.
pmc-13202278:
Win Myat Phyo and colleagues systematically review oral health-related quality of life among sexual and gender minority people. Their 2026 review uses the expanded population label given in the title and examines validated measurement tools.

Searches across several databases in twenty twenty-six found six eligible observational studies. Three came from Brazil, with others from India, Malaysia, and Australia, published between twenty eighteen and twenty twenty-five. Half used a common oral health impact profile instrument. Background evidence links higher oral disease burdens in this population to financial barriers, lower income, and discrimination in care settings. The review aims to guide inclusive, culturally sensitive oral health policy.
pmc-13202478: Akane Togo and co-authors (2026) report a clean way to brominate diarylacetylenes, plus a simple trick for splitting the products. With N-bromosuccinimide and iron bromide in dichloromethane, they brominated diphenylacetylene E-selectively, the bromine adding across the triple bond in the E form. The split exploits how the two forms dissolve: heptane makes the E isomer drop out as a solid, while the Z isomer stays dissolved and is removed by filtration. No column work is needed — the practical point of the study.
pmc-13202678:
Tiny membrane parcels shuttle signals between cells in the mouth, and a 2026 review headed by Abdelhabib Semlali surveys their roles in oral health and disease. The article reviews what is known about extracellular vesicles in saliva and gum fluid, including exosomes, microvesicles, and apoptotic bodies.

Vesicles from host cells and oral microbes help regulate inflammation, biofilm behavior, tissue repair, and microbe colonization, the review finds. When that traffic goes wrong, it contributes to gum disease, oral thrush, and oral cancer progression in the evidence surveyed. Salivary vesicles also look hopeful as test markers, though isolation and testing methods still lack shared standards.
pmc-13202778:
Dilkhosh Shamal Ramadhan and Ibrahim Hasan Mustafa test a food education program plus omega-3 pills in fatty liver disease in a 2026 trial. The disease, not tied to drink, is a growing load on liver and metabolic health in the world, most of all in poor and mid-income lands.

The trial ran at a teaching hospital clinic in Erbil City, in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq. Patients with the disease were split at random, in a set design. Surveys logged their social and health traits. The team then read body weight, liver enzymes, and blood fats, to judge the joint plan.
pmc-13202978:
Somalia's health system leans on community health workers, and a 2026 article authored by Liibaan Abdulahi Sudi argues they are central to its resilience. Written as a letter drawing on Somali and global evidence, the piece examines how these workers support care amid conflict, outbreaks, displacement, and severe staff shortages.

During the COVID-19 response, community workers identified about a third of suspected cases and found higher positivity than facility surveillance, the authors note. They also raised use of maternal health services in underserved areas. Weak integration, uneven supervision, and fragmented donor funding limit the programs, so the authors urge formal recognition, stable financing, and standardized training.
pmc-13203478:
Chang Hu, Wen Zhang, and Joston Gary link exercise and mental resilience to lower self-injury among Chinese teens. Non-suicidal self-injury is a public health worry in adolescence. The survey covered 2,257 junior high students aged 12 to 17 in central China. Both variable-level and person-level analyses were run on activity, resilience, and self-injury scores.

More activity and more resilience each tied to less self-injury, and resilience carried part of the activity effect. Profile analysis found low, moderate, and high groups across the two traits. The low group reported the highest self-injury risk and the high group the lowest. Programs that build both may cut risk.
pmc-13203878:
Shan Zheng and co-authors present a 2026 study of a hospital-wide program to curb drug-resistant infections acquired in hospital. Such infections are a major safety threat, fed by heavy antibiotic use. Whether a joined-up stewardship program can cut their rate over years, across a whole hospital, had little long-term proof.

The program, mixing better diagnosis with tighter prescribing, began in late 2021 at a large multi-campus teaching hospital in China. The team tracked monthly data from 2018 to 2024, covering more than two million hospital stays. An interrupted time-series design lets the trend before and after launch speak for the program's effect.
pmc-13204278:
Tuan Bach and co-authors present a 2026 study hunting prognosis genes in Vietnamese patients with the common form of lung cancer. Gene activity data from thirty patients at one hospital were crossed with a public data set to find shared changes. Most shared genes sat in cancer linked pathways.

A network build pulled out dozens of hub genes. Survival checks then flagged six: two whose high activity spelled worse survival, and four whose low activity did. The authors offer these as candidate markers for judging outlook in Vietnamese patients, a group little covered by the big atlases. Clinical use would need far more testing.
pmc-13204978:
An antimalarial's chemical child may have a second career against liver cancer. Aina Xiao and co-authors study dihydroartemisinin, a derivative of artemisinin, and pin its anti-tumor punch on a motor protein called KIF11. Data mining showed KIF11 runs high in liver tumors and marks poor prognosis, acting through the PI3K/Akt growth pathway. In cell studies the drug slowed tumor growth, movement, and invasion while triggering cell death, and it shrank tumors in mice.

Forcing cells to overproduce KIF11 blunted the drug, and blocking the pathway restored its bite. The authors propose the drug-protein pair as a treatment strategy worth developing for a cancer short on options.
pmc-13206678:
Ann Thong Lee and co-authors present a 2026 study on whether emergency department staff accept new technology. Hospitals adopt new tools slowly, partly from safety worries. Most acceptance research treats all departments as one, yet emergency care has its own pressures, so the authors focused on Malaysian emergency departments.

They built on a standard acceptance model with two extra factors: organizational support and training. Surveys reached emergency staff aged 25 to 60, and 140 valid replies were analyzed. Perceived usefulness and training both shaped attitudes toward new tools. That stance, in turn, was the only direct driver of the intent to use them. The results tell managers that training and clear usefulness sell new tools better than mandates.
pmc-13206978:
Paulina Kober and co-authors study a small RNA that runs high in aggressive meningiomas, the most common tumors inside the skull. Methyl marks on its gene, MIR21, thin out in the atypical and anaplastic grades, and the RNA, named miR-21-5p, rises with them. Their 2026 study traces what that RNA then does.

Gene activity scans found many predicted targets of the RNA among the genes that shift by tumor grade, mostly in cell signaling paths. Cell talk checks found grade linked shifts in the tumor's surroundings. One target pair, tied to interleukin 6 signals, fell in aggressive tumors. In lab cells, the RNA boosted growth and survival and tugged its targets down.
pmc-13207778:
Nina Labedź and co-authors report a man with a rare skin disease spread over his body and a rare gene change, in work published in 2026. The skin disease leaves itchy, thick patches from protein deposits in the skin. It sometimes appears with an inherited syndrome that causes tumours in hormone glands.

In that syndrome, the skin disease is usually confined to the back and linked to one common gene site. This patient's disease was widespread and came before his gland problems were found. Gene tests found a very rare change in the RET gene, not previously linked to the syndrome. The authors suggest wide skin disease of this kind should prompt gene testing. The case may help map how gene changes shape this syndrome.
pmc-13207878:
Early liver cancer can hide aggressive traits, and a 2026 study authored by Huiying Li builds an MRI score to flag them before surgery. The multicenter retrospective study covers 994 patients with very early or early hepatocellular carcinoma who had contrast MRI and then curative resection at three institutions.

The score combines irregular tumor shape, a washout pattern, blood products inside the tumor, and a blood marker threshold. It predicted vessel invasion or high tumor grade with fair accuracy in training and validation groups in the authors' testing. Patients scoring positive relapsed sooner, and extra therapy after surgery appeared to help only that high-risk group.
pmc-13207978:
Fukang Gao and co-authors review ferritin, the body's iron-storage cage, as a ready-made vehicle for medicine, in a 2026 paper. Ferritin is a hollow sphere built from twenty-four protein pieces. It keeps iron dissolved and harmless inside cells, sitting in the cytoplasm and in mitochondria. The cage assembles itself and can be taken apart and rebuilt in the lab, under control.

That trick makes it a versatile carrier: drugs, imaging agents, or vaccine parts can ride inside or on its surface. The review covers the cage's structure and natural roles, the chemistry of its self-assembly, and ways engineers retune it. Applications span drug delivery, diagnosis, and vaccines. The authors weigh what must improve before these cages move from papers to clinics, including targeting accuracy and large-scale production.
pmc-13208378:
Lucio Giuseppe Granata and co-authors back tests based on how the disease works, in patients with angina or ischaemia but no block in the coronary artery. Their 2026 piece covers the states known as ANOCA and INOCA.

These syndromes rest on poor work by the heart vessels. That spans problems in the small vessels, spasm in the epicardial vessels, spasm in the small vessels, and mixed forms. The team backs imaging with more than one method, set out in a firm order, in place of tests added one by one. Imaging of the build of the vessels, imaging that counts blood flow, and invasive coronary function testing each add their own data. The function tests take in flow reserve, indices of resistance, and provocation with acetylcholine. The goal is to set out the endotype beneath the signs, so care can match how the disease works.
pmc-13208978:
Ivana Pavlinac Dodig and co-authors compare two sleep apnea screening questionnaires in a 2026 study across three Mediterranean countries. The STOP and STOP-BANG checklists flag people at risk of obstructive sleep apnea, but their accuracy shifts with body shape and demographics, so one cut-off may not fit every population.

More than nine thousand patients in Croatia, Türkiye, and Greece completed the questionnaires before overnight sleep testing. The team measured sensitivity and specificity in each country. They also tuned the body mass index and neck circumference thresholds per population. The goal is screening that catches more true cases without flooding sleep clinics.
pmc-13209178:
Drugs that restore the missing SMN protein have transformed spinal muscular atrophy, yet many patients still lose ground at the far end of the motor unit. Almir Fajkić and co-authors propose a companion idea: place nanotube-based interfaces at or near the junction between nerve and muscle to steady signal transmission in the motor units that survive.

Their hypothesis predicts a chain of gains, from more reliable junction firing to steadier output over repeated use and, finally, better endurance. The patients most likely to benefit, they argue, are those with some motor units left but measurably unstable junctions. Drawing on related diseases, the paper weighs mechanism, safety, regulation, and ethics, and frames a research path rather than reporting a tested treatment.
pmc-13210178:
Engineering students support blood donation in principle yet rarely roll up a sleeve, and a 2026 survey led by Bhola Teli documents that gap in Nepal. The cross-sectional study questioned 191 first-year students at Pulchowk Engineering Campus between April and June 2022 about what they know, feel, and do regarding donation.

Attitudes were strongly favorable across the group, but fewer than one in five students had actually donated blood at the time of the survey. Women scored higher on knowledge while men were considerably more likely to have donated in practice. The commonest barriers were having no particular reason and lacking the opportunity, prompting calls for campus drives.
pmc-13210378:
Mothers who use substances face stacked risks, and a 2026 cohort profile by Lindsay A Wilson describes the British Columbia resource built to study them. The article introduces a population cohort linking health records for mothers with substance use indications around pregnancy and for their children, drawn from ten provincial databases.

The cohort holds 38,670 mothers and 45,823 children from deliveries between 2000 and 2022, with a median of nine years of follow-up available. Records span care use, prescriptions, housing and income support, incarceration, and deaths for both generations in the linked files. Three planned studies will judge specialized pregnancy care, compare opioid treatment regimens, and trace child outcomes.
pmc-13211278:
Shunming Yao and co-authors report a 2026 study on making carbon fiber parts with uneven thickness and fewer hidden air pockets. Such parts harden in a curing step, but pressure spreads poorly where thickness jumps. Trapped gas then leaves voids that weaken the part.

The team paired shaking during curing with a double vacuum bag method. Shaking helped gas escape and resin flow, while the bag setup cut the path for gas early on. Tuned together, the two steps cut the void share in thick zones from 8.34 percent to 0.43 percent. Tests on the finished parts backed the gain. The method offers a cleaner way to cure thick, high-value composite parts.
pmc-13212578:
Soheil Yousefzadeh-Valendeh and three co-authors are the subject of a 2026 retraction notice from the editors of Scientific Reports. Their 2023 paper claimed silver nanoparticles made with dandelion flowers outperformed synthetic ones across several laboratory tests.

Editors withdrew the paper after questions arose about microscope images in a key figure. Two images appeared to match pictures published elsewhere for different nanoparticle types, and the authors could not supply the raw data behind the figure. The editors therefore lost confidence in the reported results. One author disagreed with the withdrawal, while the other three did not reply to the editors.
pmc-13213078:
Katherine S. Klamer and co-authors test in 2026 how well eleven drugs kill a hard-to-treat yeast in the lab. The yeast came from Michigan hospitals. It spreads in wards and kills many of the sick people it infects, so labs need to know which drugs still work.

They grew 84 yeast samples from Michigan and 27 from stock collections, then found the lowest drug dose that stopped each one. A new drug, manogepix, worked at the lowest dose of all. A drug class called echinocandins came next, and nearly all samples stayed weak against it. One sample had a gene change that made it resist that class. The old drug fluconazole worked poorly, as past reports found.
pmc-13213378:
A 52-year-old woman lived with two clashing risks: a stubborn faulty heart rhythm that invites stroke, and heavy menstrual bleeding made worse by blood thinners. Sophia Alexiou and co-authors report her care in a 2026 case study. She had persistent atrial fibrillation, a recent heart stent, and adenomyosis behind the bleeding.

In one session the team ran pulsed field ablation to steady the rhythm and closed the heart's left atrial appendage, the pouch where clots form. The session went smoothly, and scans at three months showed the closure device seated well. Blood thinners stopped at three months, and a year on she stayed symptom-free on a single antiplatelet drug. The authors present the paired approach as safe and feasible for high-risk patients, while calling for larger studies.
pmc-13213778:
Shanbo Zhang and eight co-authors improve how chemists measure the active compounds in black tea. Their study is from two thousand twenty-six. As fresh leaves are processed, their chemistry grows more complex, and standard liquid separation methods start to blur compounds together. Blurred peaks can badly skew the amounts reported.

The team ran a two-stage separation method against the standard one across four stages of tea making. The standard method overcounted one group of compounds by up to four-fold. It undercounted another group by about two thirds. The two-stage method cut those errors sharply by pulling overlapping peaks apart. It also shrank the skew caused by the sample background. The work matters for tea quality research and for other complex foods.
pmc-13214778:
Eli Magen and co-authors ask whether fibromyalgia and Alzheimer's-type dementia travel together, and in which direction. They ran a nationwide case-control study in Israel with more than nine thousand fibromyalgia patients and forty-six thousand matched controls. Looking twenty years before the pain diagnosis and ten years after let them test the order of events.

Before diagnosis, dementia was no more common in the fibromyalgia group, and the Alzheimer's form was actually less common. After diagnosis, the picture flipped: Alzheimer's-type dementia appeared more often in patients than in controls over the following decade. Other dementia forms showed no consistent link, though cases were few. The authors read the pattern as a possible late rise in risk after fibromyalgia appears. They caution that the design shows association, not proof of cause.
pmc-13215378:
Emma Zattarin, an oncologist, reflected in a 2026 essay on the books her patients keep by their beds. Novels taught her, long before medicine, how to sit with complexity and pain. During residency she had less time to read, but she began noticing patients' bedside books. Asking how a book was going became a small ritual after the talk of symptoms and doses, quietly shifting the room's mood.

One story stayed with her. A dying patient accepted a home care plan but asked a favor in return: she wanted her doctor to read the novel she had brought, a book by José Saramago. At the edge of death, sharing a beloved story was the request. Now working in outpatient care, Zattarin has no bedside tables, and she closes on what was lost with them.
pmc-13216078:
Anali Elsa Bello-Velázquez and co-authors present a 2026 survey of ticks on cattle and wild animals around two lagoons in northern Veracruz, Mexico. Tick burdens shape livestock health and the spread of disease between wildlife and herds.

Between July 2022 and July 2023 the team inspected 440 animals at 35 cattle units and collected 7,026 ticks. Eight species from three genera were identified. Nearly all cattle carried ticks, against about half of wild animals, and wild hosts held the richer species mix. One species, Amblyomma mixtum, linked to the most host species, including cattle and opossums. The authors call for pairing species counts with pathogen testing to judge real transmission risk.
pmc-13219378:
Sumeyye Kizilisik and co-authors compare brain responses to food and alcohol images in this 2026 paper. Both cue types drive reward and approach behavior. Most prior work used brief brain responses to single flashes of images. This study used longer viewing and tracked sustained brain rhythms instead.

Healthy adults viewed food, alcohol, and neutral images while EEG was recorded. Power in standard rhythm bands was compared across image types. Food images raised slow delta power over the back and center of the head. Alcohol images lowered delta power and raised alpha activity in other areas. Alcohol use scores, mood, anxiety, and eating measures were also collected. Distinct rhythm patterns may one day mark cue reactivity in addiction studies.
pmc-13219878:
Alexa Moschella and co-authors report a pregnancy rash cleared by the antibody dupilumab after childbirth in a 2026 case report. Polymorphic eruption of pregnancy, an itchy rash of papules and plaques, strikes one in two hundred pregnancies, in the final month or after delivery. It fades within weeks, but the itch can be severe, and the rescue, oral steroids, was off the table for the patient.

The thirty-four-year-old mother developed the eruption two days after a caesarean delivery, with plaques across her abdomen, arms, legs, and feet. A biopsy excluded gestational pemphigoid. Because her gestational diabetes and hypertension ruled out prednisone, the team gave dupilumab, an antibody used in pregnancy and breastfeeding for other conditions, alongside a topical steroid and a roflumilast cream. By six weeks skin had cleared. The authors offer the case as evidence for a steroid-sparing option in severe disease.
pmc-13220578:
Quan Wang and colleagues build an explainable machine learning system for death risk in home dialysis patients in a 2026 study. People on peritoneal dialysis carry a high risk of dying, from cardiovascular causes, and their measurements change month to month. A warning system that updates with each result could flag the six-month danger window while action is still possible.

Working retrospectively with 1,484 patients from one dialysis centre, the team trained eight machine learning models on demographics, features, and laboratory values refreshed over time. The winners were validated internally and again on a later, separate group of patients. A gradient boosting model performed best, with accuracy of 0.888 internally and 0.850 in the temporal check. An explanation method, SHAP, opened the model up, naming the features that drove its warnings so clinicians can sanity-check them. The authors present the system as decision support for personalized treatment, not a black-box verdict.
pmc-13221678:
Hong Chen and colleagues test apigenin, a plant flavonoid, as a way to calm immune imbalance, in a 2026 study spanning arthritis and sepsis models. Regulatory B cells release calming signals, while other B cells switch antibody types and fuel inflammation. Apigenin was examined on mouse and human B cells, then in arthritic and septic mice.

Treated B cells produced roughly twice as many regulatory cells and far less of a key switching enzyme. Arthritis scores fell by about forty-five percent in mice. Survival after sepsis induction rose sharply, with less lung injury and lower inflammatory signals. Effects depended on the p38 MAPK pathway, pointing to a defined mechanism.
pmc-13222478:
Muthu Sudarshna and co-authors report a rare sarcoma beside the knee joint in a woman with rheumatoid arthritis, a setting that made diagnosis tricky. Spindle cell tumors range from harmless to high-grade cancers and can mimic inflammation. Her swelling grew for months and first looked like a blood collection with cysts on imaging.

A deeper scan raised suspicion of cancer, and wide removal surgery followed. Tissue study showed a high-grade spindle cell cancer with muscle-like features, rapid cell division, and some dead tissue. She received radiation, and a later new lesion was removed as well. The authors warn that odd or lasting swellings in patients with chronic inflammation deserve a cancer check.
pmc-13222578:
Sharif Kullab and co-authors review management of HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer in Saudi Arabia, with an expert survey, in a 2026 article. Twelve breast cancer specialists from tertiary centers answered an eighteen-item survey, set against international guidance gathered from published work. Brain spread receives special attention throughout the review.

Experts estimated that a large minority of metastatic patients have HER2-positive disease, with a wide range developing brain metastases. Local practice largely matched international guidance, though access to three targeted drugs can be limited and force swaps. Few physicians scanned the brains of symptom-free patients, an area of open debate. Tucatinib combinations were favored for later treatment lines.
pmc-13222678:
Safwan Alghwail and co-authors pooled the best recent trials on treating a common wrist bone fracture with a cast versus early surgery, in a review published in 2026. The scaphoid's waist breaks often, and barely shifted breaks sit in a gray zone: casts work but lock the wrist for weeks, while surgery speeds recovery at higher cost and risk.

Following standard review methods, the team searched five databases for randomized trials and strong comparison studies since 2013. Four trial cohorts with five hundred fifty-nine patients qualified. Outcomes tracked whether the bone failed to unite, healing time, function scores, complications, and return to work. Quality and certainty of the evidence were graded with standard tools. The pooled work aims to settle a routine but nagging choice in hand care.
pmc-13223978:
N. Prieur-Blanc and co-authors describe a 2026 refinement of a pig model for spinal cord injury research. Pigs resemble humans in spinal anatomy, yet most pig injury models target the chest-level cord and create difficult aftercare, especially around bladder control. The team instead produced a contusion injury at the third lumbar vertebra, guided by live X-ray imaging.

All animals showed complete paralysis two days after injury, followed by severe but partial recovery by day fourteen. Every animal developed lasting urinary incontinence, so catheter care was unnecessary. Scans and tissue examination three weeks later confirmed consistent lesions in white and grey matter, supporting the model as a practical platform for testing recovery treatments.
pmc-13224878:
Rahul Kurapati and co-workers review hospital readmissions within thirty days at a large New York medical center, in a 2026 paper. Readmissions cost money and signal gaps in care. The team asked how many returns within a month could have been prevented.

Doctors reviewed nearly five hundred readmissions from one year using a structured method. About twenty-eight percent were judged preventable. The top causes were problems in medical management and drug checks, goals of care that did not match patient needs, and late follow-up after discharge. The authors back proven review methods and targeted fixes in these areas.
pmc-13226678:
Joakim Lehrstrand and co-authors present a 2026 imaging method that maps pancreatic cancer tissue in three dimensions without any stains or labels. Pancreatic tumours grow inside dense scar-like tissue that blocks the antibodies normally used to tag structures, defeating standard imaging. Their approach instead reads the tissue's own faint glow under light-sheet microscopy, then lets machine learning sort the structures.

Surgical samples from five patients, plus normal pancreas, were scanned as centimetre-scale discs at micrometre resolution. The resulting volumes separated blood vessels, cancerous lining, hormone-producing islets, and supporting tissue for measurement. Because nothing was added or cut away, the same specimen could still undergo conventional staining afterwards, preserving precious clinical material.
pmc-13226778:
Fuad Al Mutairi and a Saudi team chart a 2026 case series of disorders caused by faults in POLG, a gene that copies and repairs mitochondrial DNA. These conditions range from devastating infant illness to milder adult syndromes, all rooted in failing cellular energy production. Records covered nineteen confirmed patients from sixteen families seen at six referral centres.

Four fifths developed neurological symptoms before age twelve, most often developmental delay and brain dysfunction, with seizures in over half. Genetic testing found eight different disease variants, one of them never previously reported and likely to disturb the protein's folding. Care remains mostly supportive, so the authors emphasise deeper mechanistic research as the route toward treatments that stabilise mitochondrial function.
pmc-13226878:
Hannah Wavering-Walters, Quetzal Class, and Lopa Pandya study operating room waste in this 2026 paper. Operating rooms make most of a hospital's solid waste, and much of it lands in the wrong bin. Hazardous streams often hold mostly harmless waste, which hints at staff knowledge gaps.

The team weighed waste from twenty-seven scope procedures and gathered case details. Average waste ran near eight kilos per case, almost all of it non-hazardous. Only three cases used the hazardous bin at all. The study pairs bin watching with staff knowledge checks to see if practice matches the rules. The authors frame sorting as the biggest lever for cuts.
pmc-13227878:
Andrew Teoh, Mishra Arinjay, Dwaipayan Giri, and Siew Cheng Phua propose a 2026 reframing of primary cilia, the tiny antenna-like projections on brain cells, as computing devices rather than passive sensors. Disorders of cilia often involve abnormal brain development and thinking difficulties, and cilia genes keep surfacing in autism research. The authors define neural computation as integrating inputs, setting thresholds, and routing outputs, then test cilia against that definition.

Inside a cilium, gated transport admits selected molecules, and signalling cascades filter, amplify, and transform them into context-dependent outputs. During development those computations steer neuron production, identity, and wiring. In the adult brain, ciliary receptors tune excitability and balance, and one hypothalamic receptor acts like a thermostat for body-state signalling. Memory effects are also discussed.
pmc-13228178:
Enass Elsayed and colleagues examine a 2026 Egyptian dialysis study asking whether blood-pressure medicines change flow through the surgically created artery-vein fistula that haemodialysis depends on. Calcium channel blockers were the prime suspects because they remodel vessel walls. Seventy-nine patients on maintenance dialysis had fistula flow measured by Doppler ultrasound, then were grouped by the medicines they took.

Median flow looked similar between calcium-channel-blocker users and beta-blocker users, and adjusted analysis tied neither drug class to flow rate. Age pulled flow down measurably with each year. Diabetes hinted at higher flow without reaching significance. The authors note a possible protective hint against fistula failure with calcium channel blockers, but call for prospective studies to confirm it.
pmc-13229678:
Inês Noronha Cipriano and co-authors map past studies on exercise and the match between heart pump and artery load in men, in a review from 2026. That match, called ventricular arterial coupling, marks how well the heart and vessels work as one unit.

Only eleven studies with just over two thousand men met the bar. Methods to gauge the match varied a great deal across studies. Active men and endurance trained men tended to keep a sound match. Steady aerobic exercise linked to better heart efficiency and lower artery load. The authors stress how mixed the proof base still is.
pmc-13230178:
Samantha Stauffer and co-authors studied exercise capacity after lower-limb loss in 2026. People who lose part of a leg often cannot exercise as much. A weak heart rate response to effort is known to limit capacity in other groups, but its role here was unclear.

The study held one hundred thirty adults living in the community with a loss below or above the knee. Heart measures were taken at rest and after a six-minute walk test. Those with above-knee loss used a larger share of their heart rate reserve yet walked shorter distances. A mediation test asked whether that heart response carries the link between loss level and walk distance, as the title states.
pmc-13230278:
Davide Palombi and colleagues ask in 2026 which surgical route works best for tumors in the pineal region deep inside the brain. Their review covered twenty-seven studies with more than seventeen hundred patients. Lab dissections with simulated tumors compared what each route lets a surgeon see.

Two routes dominated, one passing under the back of the brain and one coming from above between the hemispheres. The lower route was linked more often to fluid leaks, meningitis, and fluid balance problems in the review. The upper route carried a higher risk of losing side vision on one side. Each route exposed different corners of the tumor area best. Choice should follow tumor position, nearby veins, and the slope of a membrane inside the skull.
pmc-13231078:
Hai Du and colleagues review in 2026 pairing spun fiber mats with stem cells to heal diabetic foot ulcers. These wounds close slowly, infect easily, and too often end in amputation. Spun fibers copy the weave of natural tissue support, and they can be loaded with germ-fighting or healing factors.

Mesenchymal stem cells add healing signals, calm harmful inflammation, and can turn into several tissue types. Together the mat gives cells a home while the cells release factors that rebuild vessels and skin. The review covers how the ulcers form, what each tool does alone, and where joint studies now stand. Safer large-scale making and dose control remain hurdles before routine clinic use.
pmc-13233278:
Gliomas, tumors of the brain's support cells, vary enormously in how they behave. Huaichao Zhang and co-authors build a risk score from genes tied to two ways cells die: quiet self-destruction and fiery bursting. They fit the score on a large public cancer dataset and check it on outside groups. The score splits patients into high-risk and low-risk groups with clearly different survival.

High-risk tumors carried more mutations and showed busier cell-division and inflammation signals. Single-cell data placed the risky pattern in aggressive tumor cell states that talk heavily to immune and support cells. Those tumors drew in many immune cells yet showed signs the immune attack was worn out. In dish tests, chemotherapy triggered both death styles at once. The authors propose the score as a guide for prognosis and treatment choices.
pmc-13233478:
Ayodamola Bakare and co-authors survey pregnant women in Nigeria about contraceptive use, in a 2026 study. Clinics in three states with unlike cultures took part in late 2023. Modern method use in Nigeria sits near twelve percent, far below the world average, and slow progress keeps maternal deaths high. Nurses asked about past use, barriers, and health reading skill.

About half the women had ever used a method once shown pictures, with big state gaps: two thirds in Lagos against a third in Jigawa. Nearly a third of the pregnancies were unplanned. Health literacy ran lowest in Jigawa. The authors tie uptake to literacy and local context.
pmc-13233678:
Haoquan Kong and co-authors built a new way to track nitrogen in corn leaves from light data in 2026. Good nitrogen checks help farms raise yields while using less feed for the soil. The team worked with a corn type grown in Heilongjiang Province, China, and gathered rich light scans from the crop canopy.

They compared ways to pick the best light bands and built new index scores from the scans. A stacked model that blends three base learners and one top learner gave the best fit for leaf nitrogen. Bands near the red edge and the near infrared range mattered most, which fits what is known about how plants use nitrogen.
pmc-13233778:
Siran Tian, Hyosik Kim, Harrison A. Curnutte, and Tatjana Trcek published a 2026 cell biology study of germ granules, droplets inside egg cells that store the proteins and RNA messages needed to start development. The RNA helicase Vasa, an enzyme that unwinds RNA, is a core granule component across animals, but its job inside the droplets was unclear. The team used fruit fly eggs and human cells to test what happens without it.

Granules still formed without Vasa, driven by a nucleator protein called Oskar. In late eggs lacking Vasa, though, granules clumped into aggregates and exchanged material with their surroundings far more slowly. RNA messages also failed to stay parked in the granules. Adding Vasa restored the fluid exchange. The study casts Vasa as the granules' caretaker of movement and message storage.
pmc-13233878:
Arif Badrou, Crystal A. Mariano, Talyah M. Nelson, and Mona Eskandari published a 2026 biomechanics study measuring how human airway tissue stretches. Blocked central airways, often from lung cancer, are held open with stents, yet poor knowledge of airway stiffness causes mismatches that irritate tissue or let stents migrate. The team stretched samples of trachea and both bronchi in two directions to capture their directional behavior.

Those measurements calibrated a standard tissue model through inverse finite element analysis, a process that works backward from observed deformation to material constants. A neural network stand-in then reproduced the calibration, cutting computation from weeks to minutes. The authors share the tissue values, the framework, and a MATLAB application so stent designers can plan around real airway mechanics.
pmc-13234178:
T Mariprasath and co-authors are named on a 2026 retraction note in Scientific Reports. The note withdraws their article on a high step-up boost converter proposed for electric vehicles and solar power systems. Post-publication review by the journal's editors examined the authors' methods, figures, and equations, and concluded that the circuit work was not reliable.

The listed problems are fundamental. The device was not a boost converter at all, but a push-pull design. Several diodes in the diagrams faced the wrong way. A voltage regulator sat in series with the solar panels. One control chip pin lacked its power link. A figure showed waveforms the circuit could not produce, and a key equation ignored inductance effects. Three authors agreed with the retraction, one gave no explicit position, and four did not respond.
pmc-13234478:
Priscila Espinosa, Josep Lledó, and David Atance described in 2026 a detailed dataset of motor insurance policies from a Spanish company. Records span the years 2022 through 2024 and were anonymised before release. Each policy-year row carries forty-seven variables about the policy, the insured person, the driver, and the vehicle. Financial fields include premiums, exposure, claim counts, and amounts paid out.

Cleaning steps removed duplicate rows, standardized categories, and checked that numeric values fell in valid ranges. A distinctive feature is the split of money and claims by type of coverage, such as liability, theft, fire, and glass. Few insurers share data at this level because of privacy and competition concerns. The dataset supports research on pricing, risk modelling, and claims behaviour. It is deposited in a public repository for reuse.
pmc-13235178:
Ann Zalucky and co-authors retest a landmark trial to see if lung stiffness decides who benefits from lying face down. Prone positioning saves lives in severe lung failure, yet clinics apply it broadly for lack of a selector. The team reanalyzed the PROSEVA trial with Bayesian models, asking whether baseline stiffness changed the survival gain.

It did not, in any meaningful way. Stiffer lungs did gain more pressure relief from the first session, but that relief did not translate into living longer. The authors conclude stiffness should not gate the maneuver. The null result itself guides practice: keep proning eligible patients alike.
pmc-13236178:
Amine Chaabouni and colleagues reported in 2026 a single fluid-filled liver mass that proved to be spread of a hidden throat-area cancer. A 42-year-old man carried a solitary cystic lesion in his liver that first suggested benign or infectious causes. Extensive imaging workup failed to settle what the lesion was. Liver cysts from squamous cell cancer are exceedingly rare, the authors note.

A needle biopsy through the skin finally revealed metastatic squamous cell carcinoma of a non-keratinizing type. Searching afterward located the primary tumour in a deep facial space behind the palate. Magnetic resonance imaging helped characterize the lesion yet could not replace tissue diagnosis here. The authors urge clinicians to keep rare cancers in mind for unexplained cystic liver lesions. Early suspicion may speed the biopsy that gives a definitive answer.
pmc-13236278:
Doctors report the case of a 19-year-old man whose hip joint failed a year after a crash injury. His hip socket had cracked and the joint had slipped out of place. Surgeons had fixed the break with plates and screws at the time. A year on, he had growing pain in the left hip and could barely move the joint. Scans showed the ball of the thigh bone had died from lost blood flow and the joint had worn out.

With the joint too far gone to save, the team replaced the whole hip with an artificial one. They used a cement-free ceramic joint through a side approach. His course after surgery was smooth, with no setbacks. At the 90-day check he had no pain, full hip movement, and was back to daily life. The report weighs why joint loss can strike so young after this injury.
pmc-13237678:
Qiong Xian and co-authors test a CT-guided nerve root procedure for stubborn neck disc symptoms in a 2026 study. The target symptoms are atypical ones, dizziness and ringing ears, in patients whose cervical disc herniation had resisted three months of standard care. The procedure frees the trapped nerve root with injections of ozone-oxygen gas, saline, and steroids.

The cohort held 256 patients, and most had both neck pain and the atypical symptoms. At one year, dizziness eased in about eighty percent of those who had it, and ringing in about seventy-six percent. Scores for dizziness handicap, ringing handicap, pain, and neck disability all fell sharply. No serious side effects appeared. Subgroup checks showed the relief did not depend on neck pain improving.
pmc-13237878:
Daniel F Hanley and a large team describe a support service for multi site trials in a 2026 paper. Running a trial at many sites at once is hard, and weak plans often fail to win funds. The Trial Innovation Network set up a full consult service that links experts across more than sixty research centers.

The service works in three phases that weigh a plan, shape its design, and then draft the grant text. The team reports on seventy five trial plans that went through the process from 2016 to 2024. Two of every three grants sent in won funding. The authors offer the model as one that other trial networks could copy.
pmc-13238878:
Lea Friedrich and colleagues asked in 2026 whether high-pressure processing changes the flavor of pea protein isolates, ingredients central to plant-based foods. Two methods were tested: static high hydrostatic pressure and high-pressure homogenization. Trained tasters profiled the isolates before and after treatment, and instruments sniffed out the aroma chemicals behind the notes.

Tasters described the isolates mainly as pea-like and bean-like, floury, bitter, fatty, and sour, and those profiles barely moved with treatment. The aroma chemistry told the same story: fatty, green notes from oxidized fat compounds stayed essentially unchanged. The authors conclude both pressure methods can process or preserve pea protein without flavor damage. That finding clears a practical worry for makers of meat and dairy alternatives.
pmc-13239178:
Federica Valeri and colleagues described in 2026 how ultrasound during pregnancy spotted blood clots inside the hearts of unborn puppies. A five-year-old pregnant Newfoundland was monitored for fetal viability. Scans showed a bright mass in one fetus's right ventricle beside an abnormal tricuspid valve, and a similar mass in another fetus's right atrium. She delivered eleven puppies, four of which died.

Post-mortem checks found tricuspid valve narrowing in every puppy, with one also showing pulmonary narrowing, and the predicted clots confirmed in two puppies. Detailed fetal heart scanning is uncommon in veterinary obstetrics, where heartbeat checks are the norm. The authors present the series as proof that prenatal detection of such clots is feasible. Early warning, they argue, can flag congenital heart defects before birth.
pmc-13239278:
Alfonso Rodríguez and colleagues fed purple sea urchins a plant-meal diet in 2026, testing whether Bacillus probiotics could turn a kelp-saving ranching idea into good gonad growth. Sea urchin roe is the saleable product, and plant feeds alone often underperform. Four diets ran for eight weeks: the plant diet alone, or with one of three Bacillus species added.

Probiotic groups roughly doubled the gonad index of the plain-diet group and gained far more gonad weight, with the best group up over sixfold. Survival also jumped, from forty-five percent on the plain diet to over ninety percent in the best probiotic group. Chemical analysis suggested the probiotics raised a prized orange pigment in the roe. The authors credit the bacteria with breaking down anti-nutritional factors and improving nutrient uptake.
pmc-13239378:
Divine Darlington Logo and colleagues analyse tobacco use in Ghana in a 2026 study drawn from the 2022 Ghana Demographic and Health Survey. The nationally representative data cover more than twenty-two thousand adults and distinguish smoking, smokeless tobacco, and using both forms.

Smoking was far more common in men than women, and smokeless use stayed low in both groups. Older age raised smoking odds for men, while more schooling lowered odds for everyone. Region, faith, and ethnic background also shaped patterns in differing ways for each sex. The authors call for control efforts that reflect these gender and cultural differences rather than a single national message.
pmc-13239778:
Nischal Shrestha, Abdirahman Hassan, and Jennifer Ann Evans describe a 2026 case of muscle disease triggered by a cholesterol drug. A 78-year-old woman taking atorvastatin developed steadily worsening weakness in her shoulders and hips, strongest in the legs, alongside a history of strokes and metabolic syndrome.

Blood tests showed greatly raised muscle enzymes and antibodies against HMG-CoA reductase, the enzyme statins block. Magnetic resonance imaging supported an autoimmune process that kills muscle fibres. Stopping the statin and giving immune-suppressing treatment did not restore her strength, and she remained bedbound at long-term follow-up. The authors stress early recognition, since delay can leave permanent disability.
pmc-13240178:
Benjamin Vögeli and co-authors untangle two look-alike heart conditions in a 2026 case report. Takotsubo syndrome, a stress-triggered weakening that balloons the tip of the heart, usually heals fully, while apical hypertrophic cardiomyopathy permanently thickens that same region and fills in its cavity.

A 66-year-old woman with high blood pressure arrived with chest pain and weakness lasting a few hours. Her first picture fitted takotsubo syndrome neatly, yet later evaluation raised real suspicion of the thickening condition hiding underneath. The authors walk through the overlap, since early appearances can point both ways, and explain why follow-up imaging matters before settling on a single diagnosis and long-term plan.
pmc-13240378:
Rameshwar Prasad and co-authors describe a newborn with fluid overload, heart defects, and a newly found gene change in a 2026 case report. Nonimmune hydrops fetalis, dangerous swelling in an unborn baby, has many causes, and genetic disorders are recognised more often as testing spreads.

The baby girl, born at thirty-five weeks, had a blocked heart vessel pattern with an underdeveloped left heart, a hernia through the diaphragm, a curved spine, and distinctive features. She needed breathing support, circulation drugs, and a medicine to keep a fetal vessel open. Sequencing found a previously unreported truncating change in the KMT2D gene, confirming Kabuki syndrome and widening its known presentation.
pmc-13240478:
Yoshihiro Nakagami and colleagues describe prostate cancer changing character under hormone treatment in a 2026 case report. An 86-year-old man with severe kidney failure had a very high prostate-specific antigen level and a high-grade tumour that had already spread to lung, bone, and lymph nodes.

He began a powerful hormone-blocking drug at once, and his antigen stayed stable for nineteen months. Scans then revealed multiple new liver deposits despite the quiet blood marker. He died four months later, and autopsy showed every deposit had transformed into neuroendocrine prostate cancer, a rare aggressive variant that sheds little antigen. The authors warn that antigen monitoring alone can miss such transformation.
pmc-13240578:
In severe pneumonia the lung's zones are not sealed off from each other, and immune cells seem to commute between them. Yuean Zhao and co-authors profiled over 275,000 single cells in 2026 from matched lung tissue, airway washings, and blood of twelve patients and five donors. They looked for activated cells shared between the tissue and the air spaces.

One sharing pattern stood out, joining three activated groups: memory-style killer T cells, antibody-making cells, and inflammatory macrophages. The T cells traced back to a blood population that switched on homing markers as it entered the lung, and a shared signal axis linked the macrophages to the other two. The authors offer the pattern as a working hypothesis for treatment research.
pmc-13240878:
Qu and co-authors in Yantai blended physics with machine learning to design concrete mixes that reliably hit strength targets. Their surrogate starts from a physical baseline built on the effective water-to-binder ratio and curing age. A small neural network then learns only the leftover nonlinear patterns. Calibrated uncertainty estimates accompany every prediction.

On a public set of one thousand thirty mixtures, the hybrid reached a test R² above 0.92 on held-out mixes. Accuracy held even when training shrank to forty percent of the data. Prediction intervals landed close to their nominal ninety-five percent coverage. The team turned the model into reliability maps that recommend mixes for a forty-megapascal target.
pmc-13240978:
Authier and colleagues at Aarhus University built a mouse model of OGT congenital disorder, an intellectual disability syndrome. Faulty O-GlcNAc transferase unbalances a sugar tag placed on brain proteins. Their male mice showed small heads and motor problems mirroring patients. Blood and brain both carried the biochemical imbalance.

The team crossed the model with mice whose tag-removing enzyme was disabled. That genetic rescue partly restored balance in brain and blood alike. A simple messenger RNA ratio tracked the correction in both tissues. The result supports blocking the remover enzyme as a treatment strategy.
pmc-13241078:
Lin Wang and a team of co-authors report in 2026 on links between blood markers of inflammation and the makeup of fatty plaques in the neck arteries. Inflammation is thought to play a key role in how these plaques grow, and some plaque traits make a stroke more likely.

In this forward-looking study, patients with carotid plaque gave blood samples, and the team measured high-sensitivity CRP, homocysteine, and a ratio based on white blood cell counts. Detailed three-dimensional scans of the vessel wall then showed traits such as bleeding inside the plaque and soft fatty cores. The study ties simple blood tests to scan findings that doctors watch closely.
pmc-13241378:
Néill and colleagues at Trinity College Dublin compared two cell sources for repairing degenerated spinal discs with microRNA therapy. Their treatment pairs a microRNA mimic with an inhibitor to calm matrix breakdown. Goat cells and whole disc organ cultures modeled the human condition. Native disc cells faced off against bone marrow stem cells.

Both cell types quieted the matrix-chewing enzymes and inflammatory signals. Only native disc cells, though, ramped up fresh matrix markers inside cultured discs. Marrow stem cells delivered to the same organs showed no such response. Néill backs the disc's own cells as the delivery vehicle.
pmc-13241678:
Wei-Hung Hsu and co-authors report a 2026 case of hydrogen therapy in stubborn lung disease linked to Sjögren syndrome. A 72-year-old woman had worsening breathlessness and lung scarring despite steroids, standard immune drugs, and a biologic therapy. She began taking oral molecular hydrogen capsules as an add-on.

Follow-up testing showed better gas exchange and stable scans, with no further scarring advance. A key antibody level fell. Blood cell profiling showed immune patterns shifting toward those of healthy people, including changes in T cell exhaustion markers. No side effects appeared. The authors urge caution, since earlier treatments might explain part of the change. They call for formal trials of hydrogen as an add-on therapy.
pmc-13241778:
David Ruiz-Londoño, Pablo Pérez-Mesa, and Harold Suárez-Baron publish the first full transcriptome dataset for a notorious invader vine and its harmless relative. Thunbergia alata, native to east Africa, now overruns tropical habitats and smothers native plants. Its cousin Thunbergia grandiflora does not invade. pmc-13259278:

pmc-13259578:

pmc-13259678:

pmc-13259878:

pmc-13260178:

pmc-13260278:

pmc-13260478:

pmc-13261078:

pmc-13261178:

pmc-13261778:

pmc-13262578:

pmc-13262678:

pmc-13263278:

pmc-13263478:

pmc-13263578:

pmc-13264178:

pmc-13264278:

pmc-13264378:

pmc-13264878:

pmc-13264978:

pmc-13265678:

pmc-13266178:

pmc-13266578:

pmc-13266778:

pmc-13267978:

pmc-13269178:

pmc-13272278:

pmc-13272478:

pmc-13273878:

pmc-13274678:

pmc-13275478:

pmc-13275578:

pmc-13276278:

pmc-13276578:

pmc-13276778:

pmc-13277078:

pmc-13277278:

pmc-13278778:

pmc-13278878:

pmc-13279178:

pmc-13279378:

pmc-13279478:

pmc-13280878:

pmc-13281478:

pmc-13281578:

pmc-13281878:

pmc-13282378:

pmc-13282478:

pmc-13282778:

pmc-13282978:

pmc-13283178:

pmc-13283378:

pmc-13283678:

pmc-13283978:

pmc-13284978:

pmc-13285278:

pmc-13285678:

pmc-13286078:

pmc-13287178:

pmc-13287878:

pmc-13287978:

pmc-13288478:

pmc-13288678:

pmc-13288778:

pmc-13289978:
Omar Asdrúbal Vilca Mejia and colleagues argue a 2026 editorial case for recognizing coronary bypass surgery as a formal superspecialty in Brazil. pmc-13290678:

pmc-13290778:

pmc-13290978:
Austrian guidance for opening the chest to restart the heart after severe injury is set out in a 2026 consensus study led by Martin W Dünser. pmc-13291078:

pmc-13291878:

pmc-13292578:

pmc-13292678:

pmc-13292778:

pmc-13293278:

pmc-13293378:
Richard Kronick and co-authors weigh, in a 2026 study, the money effects when sicker members leave Medicare Advantage plans for traditional Medicare. Prior work shows high-need members leave more often, but the cost to plans had not been counted.

pmc-13293478:
Mirijana Irnich and colleagues build, in a 2026 study, a classification system for video-based artificial intelligence that watches for epileptic seizures. Tools vary widely in cameras, methods, and aims, and no shared scheme existed to compare them.

Gaps in the evidence base were also mapped for future work.
pmc-13293678:
Cal Robinson and Rulan Parekh replied in 2026 to a letter about metal levels in children's toenails. pmc-13293978:
Sachith Gallolu Kankanamalage and colleagues detail a 2026 protocol for finding transgene RNA and protein in the same mouse spleen cells. pmc-13294178:

pmc-13294378:

pmc-13294678:

pmc-13294878:

pmc-13294978:

pmc-13295378:

pmc-13295778:

pmc-13295978:

pmc-13297278:

pmc-13297778:

pmc-13297878:

pmc-13298978:

pmc-13299878:

pmc-13299978:

pmc-13300178:

pmc-13300278:

pmc-13300978:

pmc-13301778:

pmc-13302278:

pmc-13302778:

pmc-13303278:

pmc-13303878: Wenqi Chen and colleagues issue a 2026 author correction to a study on epigenetic control of thymus homing and T cell development in embryos. pmc-13305278:

pmc-13305578:

pmc-13305778:

pmc-13306378:

pmc-13307578:

Humate and Yucca schidigera extract were fed alone and together to 240 Ross 308 birds over 42 days, with a plain feed control group for comparison. Outcomes covered growth, carcass traits, gut shape, nutrient uptake, and antioxidant defences.

Birds on the combined diet reached the highest slaughter weight and the best carcass, breast, and thigh yields. Gut villi grew taller and wider in all supplemented groups, with the combined group strongest, and protein uptake peaked there too at day 21. Antioxidant enzymes rose in yucca fed groups. The pairing looks useful for meat bird production.
pmc-13323378:
Mohammad Nofalah and four co-authors test in 2026 a greener cement that swaps one form of limestone for another. Calcined clay cements already cut the carbon cost of concrete by replacing much of the clinker. The standard recipe uses calcite; this one uses vaterite, a less stable form of calcium carbonate with rounder grains and livelier chemistry.

The team mixed eight mortars with vaterite shares from none to fifteen percent and tracked how each set, hardened, and built its inner structure. Early work hinted at benefits, but hydration speed, fresh behavior, and long-term strength were unmapped. Their results show what the swap really buys.
pmc-13323478:
Zhibo Dai and co-authors test combined PET and MRI scanning for prostate cancer diagnosis and grading, in work published in 2026. The scan uses a tracer that homes to a prostate cancer marker, paired with magnetic resonance detail. The team reviewed patients scanned over three years who all had tissue confirmation of their diagnosis.

Of 74 patients, 52 had cancer and 22 had benign lesions. Tracer uptake measures and MRI water-motion values differed clearly between the groups. One uptake cut-off separated the groups with high accuracy. Combined models improved diagnosis in the hard low-PSA subgroup, where blood tests give little guidance, and helped sort cancers into grade groups. Checks with resampling and decision analysis supported the models. The authors see the combined scan as a sharper tool for early decisions.
pmc-13323578:
Aria Appoo and co-authors studied serious adverse events in stroke patients treated with clot-busting drugs, comparing tenecteplase with the older drug alteplase. Their 2026 paper is a prespecified secondary analysis of the AcT trial, a phase 3 multicenter randomized trial that enrolled 1,577 ischemic stroke patients within 4.5 hours of onset between 2019 and 2022. Adverse events were recorded within 24 hours of treatment and grouped by organ system.

Serious events touched 219 patients, or 13.9% of the group, and those patients had poorer function at 90 days. Baseline stroke severity, large-vessel blockage, a lower early CT score, and cerebral atrophy each predicted events on their own. Rates and types of events did not differ between the two drugs. The findings give clinicians a risk profile for the first day after thrombolysis, while offering reassurance that tenecteplase looks no less safe than alteplase.
pmc-13323678:
Jan Domaradzki leads a four-country survey of nursing students on patient blood management, published in 2026, testing whether global policy reaches the classroom. Replies came from 645 master's students in Poland, Germany, Kazakhstan and Iran between October 2023 and April 2024.

Self-rated awareness sat at moderate levels, while tested knowledge ran consistently low across all countries and topics. Gaps covered alternatives to transfusion, drug-based strategies and risks of blood management itself, with some variation by country. Regression checks linked scores to background and work factors. The authors call the awareness-knowledge gap a curriculum failure and press for structured teaching of blood management in nursing degrees.
pmc-13323878:
Xiang Li and co-authors review how ginseng reshapes gut germs and, through them, health across body systems, in a paper from two thousand twenty-six. The herb is poorly absorbed, so gut germ work may carry much of its effect. Ginseng use tied to richer helpful germ types, fewer pathogens, and a stronger gut wall.
