Calmer swelling and steadier germ products link to gains along gut paths to brain, liver, lung, heart, and kidney. Human data tie ginseng to better metabolic and thinking marks that track germ shifts. How far each organ gain truly rests on germs varies, the authors stress. Cause-proof studies are still owed. Readers get a germ-first view of a classic herb.
pmc-13324178:
Doctors and nurses both give health advice and judge the officials who issue it, so their trust matters in a crisis. Idan-Chaim Cohen and co-authors measured that trust through social media instead of surveys. They gathered more than fifty thousand tweets from over nine thousand health workers, spanning 2019 to early 2023, and scored trust with language models.

The World Health Organization earned the highest average trust of the three agencies tracked. Its trust dipped early in the pandemic, then recovered. Trust in the CDC eroded steadily through 2022 and 2023, while the FDA held fairly stable. Complaints about honesty dominated the low-trust posts for all three, the 2026 study found.
pmc-13324578:
Ekaterina Varkentin and colleagues test how sudden stress affects picture story understanding in younger and older adults, in a 2026 study. Modern life leans on images and visual stories, yet the role of stress in reading them was little explored.

Two online experiments covered 203 younger adults and 212 older adults. Timed math and logic tasks with social pressure created stress before a three-panel story task with the middle panel missing. Stress hurt younger adults, who judged the missing event worse and felt less sure of their answers. Older adults scored the same with or without stress. The authors suggest richer life-built story schemas may shield older readers.
pmc-13325578:
Kawtar Chadli and five co-authors weigh whether dental X-rays raise cancer risk, in a 2026 review and meta-analysis. Dental scans use low doses of radiation, yet they are very common, so even a tiny risk would matter. The team searched three databases for studies of cancer after dental imaging and kept twenty-four. Nineteen of them, with over four hundred thousand people, fed the pooled sums.

Thyroid cancer showed a clear link with dental imaging in case-control studies, and a small link in cohort studies. Brain and nerve tumor results were mixed and less firm. The team rated the proof as low or very low in quality for all cancers checked. They conclude that current proof cannot confirm a causal risk. Better forward-looking studies are needed, they say, before guidance can harden.
pmc-13326178:
Giulia Passaniti, Roosha Parikh, George Petrossian, and a team of co-authors report a case that doubles as a resource argument. A man of seventy-nine with a narrowed aortic valve needed the detailed heart scan that plans a catheter-based valve replacement. With ordinary CT scanners under growing strain, his planning scan was instead done on a combined PET and CT machine.

The images proved good enough to plan the procedure, and his new valve went in successfully, with no leak on checks a day and a month later. The authors note that demand for valve replacements keeps climbing while scanner time stays scarce. Their point is simple: idle capacity on hybrid scanners can safely absorb some of this planning work.
pmc-13326478:
Şirin Özkan and co-authors measure skipped nursing care in Turkish care homes in this 2026 study. When staff lack time or hands, needed care gets delayed or dropped, a pattern called implicit rationing. It is tied to worse outcomes for residents and burnout for workers.

Two hundred eighty staff in six public homes and rehab centers answered a standard survey. Skipped care ranged from under a tenth to over half, depending on the task. Help with eating was protected most, while social activities with outside contact were dropped most. Rationing tracked with experience, time at the home, and training level. Staff blamed overload, thin staffing, and tasks outside their role. The authors suggest clearer roles and in-service training.
pmc-13326778:
Darlene Heinen-Stach and co-authors systematically review randomised trials of nature-based interventions for mental health, from gardening therapy to green exercise and nature walks. Their 2026 review follows standard reporting guidance and requires a non-nature comparison group and at least one mental health outcome.

Of more than ten thousand records, forty-seven trials qualified. Seventeen reported significantly greater improvements with nature interventions than controls, particularly for depression, anxiety, and stress. No trial found nature interventions worse than established treatments such as cognitive behavioural therapy or art therapy. Studies, however, varied widely in design, duration, and outcomes, and many carried moderate to high risk of bias. The authors call the early evidence supportive but ask for longer, higher-quality studies, subgroup analyses to find who benefits most, and tests of combining nature interventions with standard treatments.
pmc-13327778:
Two kinds of PET scan can tell different stories about how a cancer is responding to treatment. Rangat Bagasariya, Sunita Sonavane, and Sandip Basu reported a case in 2026 of a 60-year-old man with thyroid cancer that no longer responded to radioactive iodine. One scan tracks sugar use in tumors, while the other tracks a protein linked to the tissue around them.

After ten months on the drug lenvatinib, the sugar scan showed stable disease, but the second scan showed a marked drop in the stromal signal in chest nodes and lung spots. A blood marker also fell. The team judged the case as stable disease and argue that reading both scans together gives a fuller picture.
pmc-13328378:
Ridha Horchani critically reviews modern active learning for trustworthy AI in a 2026 article. Active learning fights the labeling bottleneck by asking humans to tag only the most useful examples. But the field has splintered across strategies, supervision levels, and test setups, making gains hard to compare. Horchani covers uses from medical imaging to recommender systems.

A four-axis sorting scheme organizes the field by query logic, supervision grain, operating regime, and how realistic the evaluation is. Families from uncertainty sampling to cost-aware and shift-aware methods are weighed for hidden assumptions and failure modes. The core challenge has moved, Horchani argues, from finding informative samples to building labeling pipelines that stay fair and robust in real work.
pmc-13328578:
Deva and four co-authors present a 2026 math study on choosing green energy plans when the data is vague. Picking the best mix of solar, wind, and hybrid systems is hard when demand swings and expert scores are rough or split. The team uses a fuzzy set frame that records, for each trait, how much it counts as good, neutral, or bad at once.

Two new rules for merging such scores are proposed, both built on a classic fuzzy merging idea. A worked case ranks solar, wind, and hybrid options from a fuzzy score table. In checks that vary the settings, the new rules kept their rankings steady more than ninety-five percent of the time. They also matched expert judgment better than older rules. The authors offer the frame as a firmer base for energy planning under doubt.
pmc-13329378:
Marc Perlman and two co-authors put a gene-based risk score for heart artery disease in context in a 2026 commentary. Coronary disease still kills more Americans than anything else, and repeat events strike many patients despite full standard prevention. A polygenic risk score sums millions of small gene variants into one measure of inborn susceptibility. It captures risk that standard factors miss.

A large health system study in the same issue found that high gene risk added about six percent to repeat event rates. It also sharpened prediction by roughly four percent beyond clinical factors. Patients judged low risk by standard measures sometimes carried high gene risk. The commentary weighs how such scores might reclassify patients in secondary prevention.
pmc-13329478:
William Wanzor and Aakriti Bhargava present a 2026 case of fast-spreading skin death in a toddler from West Texas. The boy was 15 months old and had been healthy. Carers found a dusky patch on his buttock that grew within two days, blistered, and turned black in the centre. No bite or injury had been seen.

Doctors cut away dead tissue, placed a temporary skin matrix, and later applied a skin graft. At 60 days a small open area remained and was treated with silver nitrate. The team judged the cause to be presumed brown recluse spider bite damage, based on the look of the wound and the region. Care rests on wound support, with surgery for severe cases.
pmc-13329578:
Henrietta Bánfai-Csonka and colleagues describe a university first aid responder scheme in a 2026 letter. The University of Pécs holds about 25,000 students plus several thousand staff, yet readiness for cardiac arrest varies across workplaces. A campus-wide programme began in 2022 to train staff as first responders.

Since launch, 266 employees finished the first 10-hour course, and yearly refreshers drew 390 attendances in total, as reported in the letter. Training stresses hands-on resuscitation and defibrillator use, taught by paramedics, with yearly 4-hour scenario refreshers. An online group shares updates and case talk between courses. Defibrillator coverage also grew, reaching 15 devices across the university in the account given.
pmc-13330078:
Oziri leads a team testing the safety of silica-coated iron oxide nanoparticles used to rewarm frozen organs in a 2026 paper. Nanowarming has already revived cryopreserved rat kidneys for transplant. Leftover particles in a graft are the safety question.

Rats received doses far above expected leftover exposure, up to a worst case of a fully loaded organ with no washout. Blood tests, tissue distribution, and organ slides were tracked for up to a month. Lower doses showed no clear harm. Some adverse effects appeared only at the highest dose. The authors say the results support moving nanowarming toward clinical scale. The particles are perfused through organs with protective agents, then washed out.
pmc-13330178:
Rong Zhao and colleagues study how the water fern Azolla changes soil life in rice fields, in work published in 2026. Azolla fixes nitrogen with a partner microbe and is used as green manure. Its full effect on soil quality and nutrient cycling in paddy systems was still unclear.

The team compared rice alone with rice grown alongside Azolla. Soil tests, enzyme assays, and bacterial profiles tracked how the two systems differed. The mixed system raised carbon and nitrogen cycle enzyme activity, while phosphorus cycle activity fell. Azolla also shifted bacterial groups and drew in specific helpful taxa. The findings support Azolla as a way to lift soil nutrients and drive microbe led recycling in place of some added fertilizer.
pmc-13330278:
Giovanni Franzo and Joaquim Segalés argue in a 2026 study that a pig virus is being split into named genotypes the data do not support. Porcine circovirus 3 turns up worldwide in healthy and sick pigs alike. Several naming schemes exist, most built on arbitrary cutoffs that disagree with each other.

They reanalyzed every good public sequence of the virus's key gene. Family trees built by different methods clashed, deep branches lacked support, and genetic distances within and between the named groups overlapped fully. With so little variation and no proven difference in harm, formal genotypes are premature, they conclude.
pmc-13330378:
Sameeksha Chopra, Naomi Madokoro, Mya Bal, and Kelly McNagny argue that chronic immune disease is partly programmed before birth in a 2026 review. Immune cells colonize tissues in waves that start in the womb. Signals from the mother, infection, or molecules from her microbes train those early settlers. The trained cells can persist for life, acting as dials that set how strongly each tissue inflames later.

The review gathers the developmental evidence and warns about translation: animal timelines differ from human ones, so mouse milestones mislead if mapped carelessly. Framing the womb as a training ground shifts prevention thinking toward pregnancy, long before symptoms could ever appear.
pmc-13330678:
Jennifer Macdonald-Obermann and team showed that ErbB dimerization shapes how EGF receptor ligands control metabolic flux. Their 2026 study studied seven EGF receptor ligands plus neuregulin 2-beta in two cell lines, tracking labeled glucose or glutamine. The EGF receptor drives MCF-7 proliferation while epigen and EPR drive differentiation, a split from ligand bias, where two agonists on one receptor differ in response.

EGF drove flux through glycolysis, the pentose phosphate pathway, and the tricarboxylic acid cycle in both. MCF-7 cells sent pentose phosphate ribose into nucleotide biosynthesis while MDA-MB-468 cells returned riboses to glycolysis. In MDA-MB-468 cells, all ligands induced similar flux and neuregulin 2-beta did nothing. In MCF-7 cells, neuregulin 2-beta, betacellulin, EPR, and epigen worked better than other ligands, so bias appeared in MCF-7 only. The team thinks that varied ErbB complements drive dimer pairings, urging care with system bias in reading ligand bias.
pmc-13330978:
Hui Wang and colleagues scan United States harm reports for dual-target antibodies in blood cancer care in a 2026 study. Reports tied to CD3 by CD20 bispecific drugs were drawn from the FDA system from late 2022 to early 2025. In total, 2,237 reports covered three drugs: epcoritamab, glofitamab, and mosunetuzumab.

Signal counts came to 93 for the first drug, 65 for the second, and 41 for the third in the reported analysis, with methods agreeing closely. Some signals are absent from current labels, including a brain white matter disease and a severe immune overreaction for one drug. Fatal outcome and timing patterns were also charted. The authors urge closer watch and further study of fresh signals.
pmc-13332078:
Jie Ding and co-authors study stiripentol, a drug that induces ER stress and pyroptosis in pancreatic cancer cells under metabolic stress. Their paper deals with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, a highly lethal cancer that resists drugs.

Stiripentol had shown anti-tumor activity in glioblastoma, but how it works was unclear and its value in this cancer untested. The team joined gene and chemical analyses with lab and animal tests. Standard assays showed the drug held back cell growth. Staining and protein tests showed cell death pathways. The drug acts by tipping the balance between saturated and unsaturated fatty acids in the cells.
pmc-13332178:
Takahiro Kamihara and colleagues test a 2026 pilot question: can heart doctors safely start a triple inhaler for lung disease in heart failure patients? Chronic obstructive lung disease often travels with heart failure and worsens outlook. The single inhaler combines budesonide, glycopyrronium, and formoterol, yet its start by cardiologists, who often spot hidden lung disease, has been little studied. The team compared cardiology-led and lung-specialist-led starts in 22 outpatients treated between April 2024 and March 2025.

No clear gaps appeared in deaths, hospital stays, or flare rates between the two departments. Survival curves and risk models were used to compare outcomes and to hunt for factors tied to flares. The pilot is small, so its verdict is tentative rather than firm. Still, it supports letting heart teams start this inhaler with proper follow-up, while larger studies test safety and flare predictors more fully.
pmc-13332478:
Myles N. Arrington and co-authors linked brain responses to faces with teenagers' social lives in a 2026 analysis of the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study. Social health means having enough good relationships, and early adolescence is when peer bonds take center stage, yet brain studies usually examine single social measures at a time.

They paired brain scans at ages 8 to 11 with social data at ages 10 to 13. The data covered 5,832 adolescents, grouping peer measures such as friend counts, bullying experiences, and peer support into profiles. Three profiles emerged: concerning at 12.96 percent, robust at 33.95 percent, and selective at 53.09 percent. Amygdala reactivity to emotional faces interacted with sex in predicting profile membership, while other regions mattered only for single outcomes. The authors read this as evidence of divergent paths between brain function and social health.
pmc-13332978:
Satoshi Kikuchi and co-authors present early family-tree results for Japan's willows in a 2026 phylogenetics study, with special care for species found nowhere else. Willows are notoriously hard to classify because they hybridize freely and vary widely in form.

The team used multi-locus data from low-copy nuclear genes plus chloroplast sequences for all available native species. They found three major lineages inside the Japanese subgenus Vetrix and showed that subgenus Chamaetia is not a single natural group. Two species, S. hukaoana and S. futura, look like survivors of ancient lines splitting in the mid to late Miocene, while the Hastatae section species appear to be fresh offshoots of S. vulpina. Signs of past hybridization turned up in S. miyabeana and S. nakamurana. The authors note tangled gene trees and old cross-breeding mean genome-scale work is still needed.
pmc-13333078:
Two fiber highways link the brain's temporal lobe to its frontal lobe along the underside, and Kep Kee Loh and co-authors redraw their map in a 2026 paper. Conflicting reconstructions had muddled what each highway does. The team starts from monkey tracer studies, the ground truth, and writes a scanning protocol that rebuilds both bundles in living humans by their true endpoints.

One bundle ties the frontal underside to the front temporal lobe, serving emotion and memory blending. The other splits into strands for monitoring working memory and for fetching well-processed sights and sounds on demand. Clean anatomy, they argue, must precede claims about function.
pmc-13333378:
Stephan Neidhart and colleagues charted the brain-wave fingerprint of epilepsy that follows autoimmune encephalitis in a 2026 study, comparing it with ordinary temporal lobe epilepsy. After the immune attack settles, doctors often struggle to tell whether ongoing seizures stem from that earlier inflammation or from a separate cause.

The team studied 72-hour EEG recordings, scans, and spinal fluid results from 25 patients with post-encephalitis epilepsy and 30 with temporal lobe epilepsy. The autoimmune group showed far more slowing and epileptic discharges arising independently on both sides of the brain, the two patterns often appearing together. It also showed a wider spread in the EEG spectrum across wake and sleep, most over the temporal regions. A combined score built from EEG, imaging, fluid, and clinical features separated the groups sharply. The authors propose the patterns and score as biomarkers to guide immune testing, seizure drug choices, and surgery decisions.
pmc-13336378:
Lingzhi Chen and co-authors built a sensing facemask that screens for tuberculosis from breath droplets or sputum in a 2026 diagnostics study. Conventional TB testing is invasive and slow, which delays control of a disease that spreads through the air.

The mask carries an array of silver-gold nanoflowers. A second sensor uses urchin-shaped gold-silver particles in a covalent organic framework. Together they detect the TB antigen pair ESAT-6/CFP-10 by surface-enhanced Raman scattering. On clinical samples the assay sorted 12 negative and 17 positive patients with 100 percent specificity and 76.5 percent sensitivity in the study, and sputum testing caught two cases droplets missed. It also flagged two of six close contacts with suspiciously high antigen, hinting at hidden infection.
pmc-13336878:
Yan Zu and colleagues identify a protein-tagging enzyme that drives harmful heart enlargement in a 2026 study. RNF115 was high in failing human hearts, in mouse hearts squeezed by a narrowed aorta, and in heart cells dosed with angiotensin II. Quieting it eased cell enlargement in the lab, and removing it only in heart cells protected mice from pressure-induced damage.

RNF115 tags a scaffold protein, SPTBN1, for destruction, which unravels actin fibers, switches off the Hippo-YAP pathway, and turns on growth genes. A compound called DTD blocks RNF115, spares SPTBN1, and protects the heart in models. Blocking this enzyme could become a therapy for heart failure.
pmc-13336978:
Shirui Huang and colleagues hunted for a driver of aggressive basal bladder cancer that spreads to the lung, in a 2026 study. They combined patient cohort data with mouse models of bladder cancer to single out the protein KRT14. The work then mapped how KRT14 teams up with the RNA-binding protein IGF2BP1 to push tumors forward.

Two matching patches on the proteins lock together, letting IGF2BP1 move into the cell fluid and stabilize its own messenger RNA. That loop raises genes that help cancer cells invade, and breaking the link slowed both primary tumors and lung spread in the models. The KRT14-IGF2BP1 link thus looks like a fresh drug target for a cancer type that now lacks one.
pmc-13337078:
Shijie Qian and colleagues unmask a non-enzyme trick behind kidney cancer drug resistance in a 2026 study. Sunitinib blocks tumor blood supply and growth, yet resistance always emerges. Using patient-derived grafts sorted into resistant and sensitive models, protein profiling fingered DHODH, a metabolic enzyme, as a key driver.

DHODH shields the protein TRIM28 from tagging and destruction by competing for its binding partner. Stable TRIM28 switches on VEGFA, restoring the growth signal the drug tries to cut. A small molecule, lisaftoclax, breaks the DHODH-TRIM28 grip and restored sunitinib's power with a synergistic effect in models. Targeting a protein's side job, not its enzyme work, opens a fresh resistance strategy.
pmc-13337678:
Renata Matheus Faccioli and co-authors build a risk score for death after lung surgery in a 2026 paper. Removing lung tissue is the top cure for early lung cancer, yet some patients die within months. Data came from a Brazilian registry of near three thousand operations. Two thousand patients with full records fed model building and tests.

About four percent died within ninety days of surgery. The winning model mixes age, sex, lung power, and heart and brain history. Surgery type and extent also count in the score. Accuracy and calibration both tested strong against older models. The score can sharpen talks and planning before surgery, the authors argue.
pmc-13337878:
Can Cui and co-authors study allergy to hair products in scalp seborrheic dermatitis in a 2026 clinic study. The scaly, inflamed scalp condition weakens the skin barrier and makes topical products hard to tolerate. Links between product allergy and scalp microbes were unclear.

Sixty-three people had patch tests with 62 allergens and were grouped by scalp involvement. Severity, water loss, and moisture were measured, and 36 patients with scalp disease gave samples for bacterial and fungal sequencing. Cobalt, nickel, and several product ingredients were common triggers. Certain allergens tracked with water loss and with microbes such as Malassezia and Candida in the reported links.
pmc-13338178:
Jie Chen and co-authors teach models trained on simulated data to read real experiments, and to say when they are unsure. Their 2026 paper tackles a bottleneck in fast materials screening: simulations are plentiful and labeled, while real measurements are scarce and unlabeled. Their method, called USEM, adapts a model across that gap.

An adversarial step aligns the model's internal representation of simulated and real X-ray diffraction patterns. A special network design then attaches honest uncertainty estimates to each prediction. On synthetic and real diffraction data the adapted model read patterns more accurately than unadapted rivals. It also flagged samples unlike anything in training, the cases where a wrong answer would be most dangerous. For discovery pipelines that screen thousands of candidates, knowing when the machine is guessing may matter as much as the guesses.
pmc-13338278:
Nitin Chauhan and co-authors teach two famous image networks to read Pap smears together. Cervical cancer screening from whole slide images is slow by eye, and hand-built features limit older software. Their hybrid model fuses features from VGG-16 and ResNet-152, both fine-tuned, and feeds the blend to a classifier.

Training images were resized in stages, growing sharper across rounds, with augmentation swelling the data. The system sorted slides into five classes with accuracy above ninety-seven percent, and into cancer versus not at above ninety-eight percent. The authors present the hybrid as a fast second reader for cytology labs, especially where expert screeners are scarce.
pmc-13338678:
Sarah Vollam and a large team review wearable monitoring of hospital patients with COVID-19 in a 2026 data study. Wrist or patch systems track heart rate, breathing rate, and oxygen nonstop. Evidence on real ward use and on how often nurses still take manual readings was thin.

Three isolation wards in a large United Kingdom hospital displayed live readings on a central dashboard. Records were reviewed to describe vital sign patterns outside intensive care. A later exploratory check asked whether showing the data changed manual measurement frequency. Findings help wards judge what continuous monitoring adds beyond standard spot checks.
pmc-13339378:
Yu Dan Zhang and co-authors report research from two thousand twenty-six on collagen from local pig breeds in Guizhou, China. Collagen gives skin and meat their structure, and these breeds are prized for elastic skin and tender meat. Pig skin is rich in collagen but is often wasted after slaughter, so better use of it has real value.

The team tested skin and loin muscle from six local breeds and tuned the extraction method, settling on set acidity, enzyme dose, and time. They compared collagen amount, type, and structure across breeds. Breeds with the largest contrasts then went through genome resequencing to find differing genes and variant sites tied to collagen traits.
pmc-13339578:
Aisling Murray, Imogen Hensler, Eleanor Keiller and colleagues used body mapping to learn how Muslim children in East London understand resilience in 2026. Twelve children aged seven to twelve drew and annotated full-body outlines during a workshop at a community centre.

The children pictured resilience as personal strength, and tied it to nature, sports and physical health. They also named outside supports: family, friends, teachers and role models. This group faces higher deprivation and discrimination yet is rarely asked directly about coping. The authors say body mapping engaged the children creatively without relying on words alone, and the results favour support programmes that build on the resources children already name.
pmc-13339678:
Joud Hajjar and Mark A. Lewis reflected in 2026 on social media in oncology care, responding to a review of its benefits and risks. Social media shapes how patients seek information, how clinicians communicate, and how institutions present themselves. For cancer patients and families, digital platforms often become a first source of support and trial news.

The authors note clear value in wider access, peer support, and scientist communication beyond academic walls, alongside risks of misinformation and misinterpretation. Oncology teams need guidance for engaging online responsibly. The reflection offers a balanced stance for clinicians navigating digital spaces with patients.
pmc-13339978:
Wenjun Chen and six co-authors traced a brain pathway that links high blood pressure to anxiety in mice, and showed a way to calm it, in this 2026 study. High blood pressure affects over a billion people and raises the risk of anxiety, but the wiring between the two was unclear. The team gave mice a hormone that lifts blood pressure.

Treated mice grew anxious, and a brain area called the ventral CA1 became overactive and extra responsive to anxiety triggers. Quieting those neurons eased the anxious behavior. The team also found that a serotonin receptor in that area had faded under high blood pressure. A drug that activates that receptor restored calmer behavior. The work names targets for treating pressure-linked anxiety.
pmc-13340578:
Eleven authors report a case where a gut disorder caused immune deficiency in a child in this 2026 paper. The disorder, primary intestinal lymphangiectasia, widens the gut's lymph vessels so lymph, and the immune cells and antibodies it carries, leak away.

The patient was an eleven year old boy referred after repeated Cryptosporidium infections. Tests confirmed the gut disorder, and immune profiling showed very low antibody levels and low T cell counts. Antibody infusions and preventive antibiotics helped only partly, but diet changes then raised his antibody level fivefold, though T cells stayed low. The authors review the literature and urge doctors to consider this cause when no other explains a combined deficiency.
pmc-13340678:
Breast inflammation in pregnancy caused by an unusual germ is reported by Hassan Alyami's team in a 2026 case report. The 42-year-old woman, early in pregnancy, got pain, swelling, and redness in her left breast that kept returning despite several rounds of antibiotics and repeated drainage work.

Tissue showed non-caseating granulomatous inflammation, and culture in the third trimester grew Mycobacterium avium complex, never before seen in an immunocompetent pregnant patient. Steroids and anti-mycobacterial drugs were held back until after delivery. Eighteen months of rifampin, ethambutol, and azithromycin after delivery then cleared the disease fully, on examination and imaging alike.
pmc-13340978:
Yixin Ye and co-authors wrote a review from 2026 on tea tree oil as a treatment for acne. Acne is a common, long-term skin disease that starts in the teen years and can scar both skin and mood. The oil, from an Australian tree, is sold widely for spots, but trial proof of its worth and safety has been patchy. The team pooled the clinical studies they could find.

Seven studies with 445 patients met their bar. Pooled results tied the oil to a modest drop in acne severity. Side effects were mostly mild and local, such as itch and dryness. Mild itch was in fact less common with the oil than with rival care. Bias checks came out clean. The team calls for larger, longer trials with set formulas.
pmc-13341078:
Predicting where microRNAs bind their targets is the job of miRNAProtPred, a 2026 software paper by Somenath Dutta and colleagues. The Python package merges seed matching with thermodynamic stability checks from ViennaRNA into one workflow needing little manual setup.

It draws on 2,656 curated human miRNAs and accepts DNA, RNA, or protein inputs, scoring candidates by seed fit, free energy, flanking AU content, and match type. A strict mode demands exact seed pairing, while a relaxed mode allows G:U wobble. Tests recovered all 16 known antiviral miRNAs for SARS-CoV-2, with 75% rated high confidence, and benchmarking used 62,215 miRNA-target pairs from miRAW.
pmc-13341178:
Heart safety questions around the osteoporosis drug romosozumab are weighed by Beom-Jun Kim in a 2026 review. The antibody blocks sclerostin, building bone while slowing its breakdown, and produces fast density gains and fewer fractures in severe postmenopausal osteoporosis.

Trial results conflict: FRAME against placebo looked reassuring, while ARCH against alendronate showed more major cardiovascular events in the first year, prompting boxed warnings. Kim asks whether the signal reflects true heart toxicity or a protective effect of the comparator drug. Lab and tissue studies have not found a convincing mechanism for harm, leaving real-world evidence to help settle the question.
pmc-13341378:
Chuyan Yu and colleagues reviewed spit biomarkers in 2026 for hormone and body chemistry checks, a pain free, repeatable swap for blood sampling. Spit carries a broad range of biomarkers, yet clinical use needs a critical read of diagnostic trust and potential. The team searched PubMed, Web of Science, and ScienceDirect for English papers to July 2025, with focus on studies from 2020 to 2025.

Studies on how biomarkers are made and moved in spit, plus clinical use for hormone and body chemistry disorders, were pulled together. Spit tests could ease repeated checks for hormone and metabolic conditions if trust holds. The review maps which spit markers are ready for clinic and which need stronger proof.
pmc-13342278:
Manuchehr Rahimi, Zahra Lasemi, and Mohsen Zeeb present a 2026 chemistry study on a greener way to make a class of compounds. The compounds, dihydropyridines, are building blocks for drugs. The team made a catalyst from natural phosphate rock, made it magnetic, and coated it with an amino acid. Tests confirmed the coating and the magnetic trait.

The catalyst drove the reaction in ethanol at room temperature. Many variants of the product formed in high yield, from 86 to 98 percent, in ten to twenty minutes. Only a small amount of catalyst was needed. A magnet pulled it back out for reuse, and it stayed active for nine rounds. The method cuts waste and cost.
pmc-13342978:
Xiaoman Wang and colleagues present a 2026 genomic dataset for Aristida triseta, a protected wild grass in China. The team sequenced its full chloroplast genome from dried leaf material and then built richer DNA barcode sets for the whole Aristida genus by merging new reads with public sequences.

The circular chloroplast genome runs 138,428 base pairs with the typical four-part layout and 133 annotated genes. Six core barcode regions were pulled from the data and combined with database sequences for relatives. Matching and tree analyses showed each barcode tied the species to its genus while carrying differing signals. The sets support species identification, breeding work, and diversity studies for this protected plant.
pmc-13344378:
Marie-Julie Trahan and thirteen co-authors hunted risk factors for emergency cesarean birth in pregnancies with diabetes in a 2026 paper. Diabetes raises the risk of such a birth, but which patients planning a vaginal birth will end in an unplanned operation was unclear. The team reanalyzed a trial of people with type 2 diabetes, or diabetes found early, who tried labor.

Of 405 people who could take part, 144, about 36 percent, had one, while 261 gave birth vaginally. The analysis compares traits at the start and in pregnancy between the two groups, adjusting for confounders, and lists the reasons these births were called, led by failed induction. The authors aim to sharpen counseling and planning for a high-risk group where surgery carries extra danger.
pmc-13347078:
Asma Ali and co-authors set out a protocol for a qualitative study. The protocol was issued in 2026. It covers metabolic syndrome care in two countries. One site sits in Memphis, in the United States. The other sits at a health sciences university in Saudi Arabia. Each site will recruit 20 to 30 adults. Clinic partners will help with recruiting. Sampling will vary on purpose.

Each person will join a one-hour guided interview. Daily self-care is one topic. Barriers and supports are others. Views on digital health tools will be asked too. Themes will be drawn out with mixed coding. Enrolment was set to begin in August 2026. The value lies in the comparison plan, not in findings.
pmc-13347178:
Utkarsh Tripathi and co-authors weighed in 2026 two grading systems for needle samples from breast lumps in India. Breast cancer has passed cervical cancer as the top women's cancer there. Needle aspiration, plus exam and mammography, guides treatment. Yet overlapping cell traits can mislead diagnosis.

Cases sent for aspiration were looked back at from early 2023 to mid-2024. Two cytopathologists scored slides on their own. They used both the IAC Yokohama system and the Modified Masood index. They were blind to each other's calls. The test asks which system sorts benign from malignant lumps more truly in daily work. It helps pathologists pick a frame that cuts errors and speeds treatment choices.
pmc-13347378:
Satheesh G and colleagues reported in 2026 a case series on injectable platelet-rich fibrin for internal derangement of the jaw joint. The condition, in which the disc slips from its normal place against the jaw condyle, causes pain, clicking, and limited mouth opening, and its causes span mechanical, functional, and biological factors.

After conservative care, many patients face a choice between joint washing by arthrocentesis, which clears inflammatory mediators and frees adhesions, and more invasive surgery. Injectable fibrin, rich in growth factors from the patient's own blood, offers a minimally invasive regenerative option. The series tracks pain, opening, and function after injection, testing whether this approach can restore smoother, less painful jaw movement without an operation.
pmc-13347778:
Dineo Monaheng and colleagues check lasting hepatitis B protection in South African health students, in a study from 2026. Infant vaccination entered the national program in 1995, so 122 students born after that start gave blood at entry and after booster doses at set months. Antibody levels marked whether protection still held.

At entry only 43 percent held antibody levels counted as protective, a gap that matters for ward work where exposure risk is real. One booster lifted the protected share to 92 percent, and three doses brought it to 100 percent in the reported counts. No split appeared by race or sex. Immune memory survives even when blood levels fade.
pmc-13347978:
Xin Wang and seven co-authors lay out a trial plan for colon screening in a 2026 protocol paper. Colon cancer screening saves lives, but high risk people in China often skip the scope test. The trial tests whether AI assisted team care lifts uptake. Specialists alone form the comparison arm.

Four hundred high risk residents aged forty to sixty four will join. They come from forty communities in one city district and two rural counties. Whole communities are assigned to one arm by chance. The AI arm adds tailored health teaching to linked specialist and local doctor care. Uptake at three and six months is the main measure. Time until the scope test also counts. Results should guide national screening programs.
pmc-13348378:
Kiersten R. Fullem and colleagues present draft genomes for two peanut fungi. Their announcement came out in 2026. The fungi cause early and late leaf spots. Spores came from spotted leaves in Florida. A trial field supplied the leaves in 2016. Treated agar cleaned the spores. Long-read sequencing then read their DNA. Few public genomes exist for either culprit. Yet both diseases rank among the widest peanut threats.

Assemblies differed in size and piece count. The early spot fungus reached about 37.75 million bases. Its draft holds 194 pieces. The late spot fungus reached about 49.04 million bases. Its draft holds 571 pieces. Open genomes should speed several lines of work. Fungal variation is one line. Spray resistance is another. Tougher peanut lines are the goal.
pmc-13348778:
José Rodrigues and co-authors told in 2026 of a Lord femoral stem still stable 32 years after revision hip replacement. This is a rare long-term follow-up for a prosthesis dropped over failures of its threaded cup and bone loss from stress shielding. Long-term implant tales rarely span three decades.

In 1994, a 37-year-old tailor got a left revision hip replacement with the Lord system. Fifteen years later, pain and loss of function led to scans showing cup loosening with massive bone loss. Revision used impacted bone graft plus an anti-protrusio cage. The femoral stem, by contrast, stayed solid. The case shows that even in a troubled system, single parts can endure. It informs revision plans for ageing implants.
pmc-13348878:
Mubarak S Aldosari weighed in 2026 how stakeholders view educational rehabilitation for pupils with intellectual disabilities in Saudi Arabia. He also asked what blocks innovation. Programmes for these pupils hinge on shared insight among teachers, managers, pupils, and rehab staff. Yet views often diverge.

A structured 30-item form reached 298 people across three domains: awareness and views, blocks to good rehab, and innovations and future paths. Reliability was strong in each domain. Replies varied markedly by stakeholder group, signalling gaps in insight and confidence. The findings point to focused training, clearer roles, and pilot innovations that can align groups round better classroom support.
pmc-13349078:
Yan Li and co-authors set out a trial plan for delirium after surgery in a 2026 paper. Patients with sleep apnea face high risk of muddled thought after an operation. A calming drug used in surgery may cut that risk, but proof in apnea patients is thin.

Patients bound for planned belly surgery are screened for apnea risk with a short survey. Those at mid to high risk get a sleep test to confirm the state. They then draw lots for high dose drug, low dose drug, or none. Thought state is checked after surgery in a set way. The plan is laid out ahead, so results can be trusted.
pmc-13349778:
Xiaoou Wang and co-authors published a review in 2026 comparing psoriasis and Crohn's disease, two long-term immune-driven illnesses of the skin and gut. They ask how far the two conditions truly overlap and where their biology parts ways.

Shared upstream signals, chiefly TNF and IL-23 driven type 17 immunity, sit at the centre of the argument, while later IL-17 responses behave differently in skin and bowel. Gut-skin links through barrier damage, microbes, and moving immune cells are weighed with care, since direct proof in people is still thin. Treatments that can suit both diseases are set against those that help one organ and harm the other, guiding patient grouping by signs, markers, and past therapy.
pmc-13349978:
Hua Zhong and co-authors used an image-generating AI in 2026 to map lung blood vessels from scans taken without dye. Planning partial lung removal needs a clear three-dimensional picture of arteries and veins near a nodule, but some patients cannot receive contrast dye.

Their generative model learned from paired spectral scans in 130 patients to fake contrast-style images from plain ones, using attention and a mixed slice approach to handle breathing shifts. It was then tested on 82 patients scanned on machines from two makers. Vessel rebuilding within a zone around each nodule was checked. Success could widen safe surgical planning to dye-free patients.
pmc-13350178:
Cassandra A. Omane and Sarah Forberger reviewed in 2026 how young adults judge online nutrition information. Young people search the internet daily for diet advice, while traditional health gatekeepers matter less and misinformation spreads fast.

Screening five databases and grey literature through late 2024 yielded 48 papers and 82 separate factors shaping trust. Clear writing was named most often, followed by the reader's own prior knowledge and education. Far fewer studies covered the channel, setting, or design of the information. Knowing what earns trust helps health communicators present sound diet advice in forms young adults will actually believe and use.
pmc-13350678:
Qiao-Lin Li and co-authors tested in 2026 deep learning-based MRI rebuild for diffusion imaging in patients with brain tumours. They asked whether faster, cleaner images keep quantitative accuracy. Deep learning rebuild promises better quality and shorter scans. Yet its effect on apparent diffusion coefficient measures, used to chart tumours, was unclear.

Fifty-eight consecutive adults with intracranial space-occupying lesions took part in a single-centre prospective intra-individual study. Diffusion imaging was rebuilt with and with no deep learning. Image quality, lesion ADC values, and consistency of quantitative work were weighed in each patient. Keeping ADC accuracy while lifting quality would let radiologists adopt faster protocols with no harm to the numbers that guide tumour checks.
pmc-13350978:
Benjamin J. Tombling and co-authors built in 2026 small peptides that bind LRRC15, a protein found only on cancer support cells, for PET imaging of the tumour microenvironment. Support cells that aid tumours are hard to image directly. Yet their presence shapes treatment response and outlook.

Using a joined library aided by machine learning, the team made locked peptides, notably ML-YSD-07 and ML-PD-03. These bound murine LRRC15 with subnanomolar strength and homed to LRRC15-expressing support cells. PET imaging with fluorine-18-labelled ML-YSD-07 showed specific tumour build-up in a mouse pancreas cancer model rich in LRRC15 support cells. The peptides give a targeted imaging tool for tumours driven by their stromal backing.
pmc-13351378:
Yuxin Jiang and colleagues proposed a framework in 2026 for reading kidney harm from antibody-drug conjugates, cancer drugs that carry a toxic payload to tumour cells. Kidney injury and salt disturbances appear with these drugs but are recorded unevenly across trials and often lack any shared explanation.

Their review links each drug's construction and inner cell processing to how much free payload reaches the kidney, then matches those patterns against the well-known kidney effects of ordinary chemotherapy. Evidence is layered by source quality rather than pooled. A mechanism-first map could help oncologists anticipate which patients will develop which kidney problem.
pmc-13351578:
Lydia Viviana Falsitta leads a 2026 scoping review of brain scan changes around seizures in children. Such changes are seen more often now, but their timing and meaning in childhood stay poorly mapped. The review searched PubMed and MEDLINE for work from January 2000 to September 2025 on focal seizures, long febrile seizures, and status epilepticus.

Twenty-seven studies met the criteria, most on long febrile seizures and status epilepticus. Early scans often showed swelling and bright signals in the hippocampus, while later scans showed shrinkage and scarring in some children. Blood-flow scans showed early high flow at the seizure site. The authors stress uneven evidence and call for larger studies split by seizure type.
pmc-13351778:
Quinton E. A. Sirianni and co-authors set out in 2026 Dexime, a selectively enzyme-degradable gel for protein drug release. Gels guard protein drugs from denaturing shear and solvents. Dextrin, a starch-derived polysaccharide, has been largely skipped for gel design despite being biodegradable.

Dextrin tweaked with ketone or aldehyde groups was click-crosslinked with PEG tetraoxyamine to form dexime gels, whose stiffness and mechanics tune with dextrin share and pH. The gels jab through a 30-gauge needle, degrade selectively via alpha-amylase, yet stay stable and barely swell with other enzymes. Dexime gives an injectable, enzyme-triggered depot for sustained protein delivery that releases only where amylase is present.
pmc-13351878:
Toru Morikawa and a large team of co-authors report in 2026 a careful reuse of cisplatin after a patient's kidneys recovered from platinum damage. The 57-year-old man's lung cancer had transformed to squamous type after targeted drug resistance. A first chemo-immunotherapy cycle with carboplatin caused biopsy-proven acute tubular necrosis, a severe kidney injury that usually bars further platinum treatment.

His kidney function fell sharply, then recovered. With few options left, the team re-challenged with cisplatin. Evidence for safety after such injury is extremely scarce, they note. The case offers practical guidance for a hard therapeutic dilemma.
pmc-13351978:
Fawen Dai and co-authors test finely ground bamboo powder in layer hen feed in 2026. Bamboo powder is rich in insoluble fibre, but its value and best dose in hen diets were unclear. A total of 480 Hy-Line Brown hens aged 42 weeks were split into four groups for 28 days after a 7-day settling period.

Groups ate a plain diet or diets with 2, 3, or 4 percent bamboo powder added. The 4 percent group laid fewer eggs and had lower egg mass in the second half and overall. Blood fat, protein, and sugar levels did not differ clearly. Nutrient uptake fell in the highest dose group. Gut structure and gut microbes in droppings were also checked to guide a sensible dose.
pmc-13352278:
Aguilar-Del-Valle and seven co-authors make transparent n-type copper oxide films by low-power sputtering plus annealing, in a study from twenty twenty-six. Stable copper transparent semiconductors are hard to make by scalable routes. Tuning absorption, resistance, and carrier type is equally challenging. Ultrathin copper layers are sputtered in air for seconds, then annealed briefly.

Annealing converts layers to single-phase cuprous oxide with tunable thickness. Best films transmit about seventy percent of visible light. Resistivity, band gap, and electron concentration suit prototype devices. Surface analysis confirms copper one dominance with defective oxygen environments. Paired with prior p-type films, copper p-n junctions become plausible.
pmc-13352678:
Wei Wang and three co-authors report a prenatal genetics case from China in this two thousand twenty-six paper. A thirty-five-year-old woman had amniocentesis at eighteen weeks due to her age. Testing found a small duplicated stretch on chromosome five in the fetus. Such findings are hard to interpret, since this exact duplication is rarely reported. The team ran chromosome checks, a microarray, and gene sequencing on the whole family.

The father carried the same duplication and was healthy. The fetus shared his normal picture. Inheriting the variant from a healthy parent argues that it is likely harmless. Still, the authors walk through how they counseled the family. The case gives other genetics teams a reference point for a rare finding.
pmc-13355578:
Wenlong Li and Weikai Dong wrote a 2026 letter urging stronger causal interpretation of a study linking home blood pressure patterns to heart shifts in haemodialysis people. The first work offered useful reference points for home monitoring and showed how dialysis-unit readings can misclassify people. Its snapshot design, however, limits what can be claimed about cause.

The letter notes that blood pressure load and vascular status across the dialysis interval were not fully captured, leaving other explanations open. Readers are warned against reading an link as proof that a blood pressure phenotype causes shifts. The letter helps doctors use home monitoring wisely while respecting the limits of watched evidence.
pmc-13356478:
Eric Jauniaux led a 2026 full scoping review of placenta basal plate myofibers and adverse pregnancy results. Finding myometrial fibres attached to the delivered placenta has been linked to many pregnancy and hand-off harm, but the medical value of this tissue sign was unclear. A structured making was needed to judge its usefulness.

Searching PubMed, Google Scholar, and Embase for studies from March 1996 to December 2025, two reviewers independently tested studies linking basal plate fibres to birth harm, following scoping review guidance. The review maps which harm show consistent links and which do not. Obstetricians gain a clearer sense of when this placenta finding should change advice or follow-up.
pmc-13356778:
Paula Diaz and co-authors studied in 2026 why sensory nerves fail to regrow in skin affected by recessive dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa, a severe blistering disease from a faulty collagen gene. Patients live with chronic wounds, pain, and itch, and often lose small nerve fibers. The team compared wounded skin and skin cells from patients with healthy responses.

Patient skin barely switched on the genes needed for repair, inflammation control, and nerve guidance after injury, yet it kept pouring out inflammatory signals. Fluid from patient blisters made sensory nerve tips collapse and blocked new growth in lab tests. The authors say this hostile mix both blocks regrowth and fuels nerve pain.
pmc-13359878:
Leilei Zhang and co-authors forecast good fishing spots for chub mackerel in a 2026 study. This Northwest Pacific fish shifts its grounds with the seasons and ocean state, so fishers waste fuel hunting for it. The team built a prediction model from ocean data and asked which time spans of data matter most: the moment, the recent week, or the long background.

Blending time scales helped in different ways: a week of recent ocean data sharpened overall sorting, while mixing short and long views caught more of the truly rich grounds. An explanation method showed which ocean factors drove each call. Better forecasts can raise catches while easing pressure on the stock.
pmc-13359978:
Atsushi Ogura and co-authors test tailor-made treatment for advanced rectal cancer in a 2026 study. Standard care gives radiation before surgery to nearly everyone, yet radiation can cause lasting harm and some patients may not need it. The team instead shaped each plan to the tumor's traits and to how it answered an opening round of chemotherapy.

Nearly a third of patients safely skipped radiation altogether, with no loss in complete cancer removal at surgery. A subset responded strongly enough to skip surgery altogether. The early outcomes suggest that customizing care can prevent overtreatment, preserve organs, and protect quality of life while keeping cure rates strong.
pmc-13360878:
Maham Akhlaq and others surveyed inorganic hole transport items for regular perovskite solar cells, in 2026. Perovskite cells promise high speed at low fabrication cost, and the regular n-i-p layout remains a benchmark for inorganic hole transport layers, despite growing notice in inverted designs. The hole transport layer extracts photogenerated holes while minimising recombination and energy loss.

Organic items such as spiro-OMeTAD have dominated hole transport research, but inorganic alternatives may offer firmness and cost advantages. The review matches inorganic candidates, their interfacial energy levels, and device work. Solar teams gain a consolidated guide to replacing fragile organic layers with durable inorganic ones.
pmc-13361678:
Kaltrina Veseli and co-authors surveyed tooth care habits and bite alignment in young children in a 2026 study. Good habits in childhood prevent oral disease and may shape how the jaws and teeth develop. The team studied 90 children aged six to nine in the Pristina region of Kosovo. They used the World Health Organization's standard oral health questionnaire for children.

The survey covered brushing habits, fluoride awareness, dental visits, diet, mouth symptoms, and quality of life. Each child's bite was also classed by the Angle system, which sorts how the upper and lower teeth meet. The team then looked for links between habits and bite class. Such links can guide school and family programs that build good habits before crooked bites set in.
pmc-13362478:
Ryang Soon Lim and colleagues report a 2026 before-and-after study of a smart drug cabinet in a Korean hospital emergency department. The cabinet links to the hospital record system and controls how drugs are stored and handed out. The team compared drug use, errors, and costs in the months before and after the cabinet arrived, then checked again three years later.

Drug errors fell from 41 in the first window to 14 in the next, with the biggest drop in delivery mistakes. Stored drug items in the department shrank by more than nine tenths, and upkeep costs fell sharply too. Nurses rated drug safety high, and the gains held at three years, which supports wider use of linked cabinets.
pmc-13364378:
Yakubu Zakaria and co-workers build a 2026 low cost soil wetness node that runs on sun power for farms in Ghana. Cheap probes drift by soil type, so the team first tuned three probes in loam sand in the lab. They then set the node in a drip fed onion field.

Lab tuned reads matched the hand weigh method well, with small error. The node sent field data by long range radio to a small local server and a cloud store. With wider field proof, such nodes could time watering by real soil need and save scarce water.
pmc-13364778:
Scar tissue inside the belly can obstruct the bowel, cause lasting pain, and block fertility, yet patients have no standard questionnaire for reporting how it feels. Reid Christensen led a team that scoured the literature for such patient-reported tools. From over three thousand papers they found ten questionnaires touching the disease's ground: pain, bowel function, and life quality.

None was built for this disease alone. One, a small bowel obstruction questionnaire, covered the most ground, nine of ten domains, and had passed reliability and validity tests. A bowel function tool from a cancer center covered the least. The team urges testing the leading questionnaire in these patients and, later, shaping one made for the disease itself.
pmc-13366178:
Theyazn Aldhyani builds in 2026 a deep learn frame to spot Parkinson ill from hand draws and hand write bits. Folks with the ill gain most from early care. Hand tasks show its marks in a cheap, safe way. The frame pairs a known image net with a sight form net.

Its test set holds spiral, wave, and round draws, plus two words in Arabic script, from ill and well folks. The form net scores full marks on the draw sets and on one word set. With more data, such hand checks could back fast, low cost calls in clinic.
pmc-13367078:
Carolina Schinke and co-workers give in 2026 a plain words sum of how a bone marrow cancer drug, talquetamab, shapes how patients feel and act day to day. The sum rests on a trial of folks whose ill came back or shrugs off past care. Folks fill three forms on health and acts at set rounds.

First rounds feel worse, the sum says. Past round three, body, mood, and mate acts hold or rise, with less tire, pain, and breath short. Gains hold to round twenty one. The plain sum helps patients weigh care by life feel, not just lab marks.
pmc-13369278:
Jingyu Xing and co-authors share their center's experience treating a rare, poorly differentiated bone tumor called chordoma, in a 2026 paper. The tumor is aggressive and returns early. Evidence on how chemotherapy fits into care is limited, so the team combine their cases with a pooled review.

Five patients with spinal tumors were treated from 2021 to 2025 with surgery plus a two-drug chemotherapy regimen. Response before surgery and survival were assessed. The authors also review published cases with treatment and outcome data, comparing survival by chemotherapy exposure and other factors. Their series patients were young on average, with a mean age near twenty-one.
pmc-13369978:
Libera Siciliano and co-authors use virtual reality to watch social prediction grow with age in a 2026 study. People build inner models of others' likely moves from repeated patterns. How fast those models form in youth was unclear.

Early teens, young adults, and adults wore headsets for two scenarios. In each, four avatars reached for a favored object among three, and players learned the pattern without being told. All groups improved from the first scenario to the second. Early teens learned more slowly and scored lower, while the two adult groups matched. Standard social tests and headset comfort checks backed the task as a valid measure.
pmc-13370078:
Hinata Niimi and eight co-authors study skin sarcomas in pet rabbits in work from twenty twenty-six. Such tumors are common in rabbits, but many get a vague label that says the cell type is unknown. That label gives no clue to how the tumor will behave.

The team retested forty-eight skin masses that had carried the vague label. They used standard tissue views, special stains, and marker tests. The tumors were made of spindle cells with wide shape variation and often had giant cells with many nuclei. The tests aimed to show whether the cells act like fibroblasts, muscle like cells, or both. A clearer cell type could guide treatment and prognosis.
pmc-13371278:
Changmeng Wu and colleagues give the newly coded AC-30 antinuclear antibody pattern a quantitative profile in a 2026 study. The pattern shows fine speckled staining in cell nuclei and staining of metaphase chromatin, but its clinical meaning was unclear. Archived HEp-2 test images were scored by three blinded experts, with AC-1 and AC-2 patterns as comparators.

The AC-30 set held 183 images. Over half had no autoimmune diagnosis or an unknown one, about one quarter had another autoimmune disease, and about one sixth had an ANA-linked rheumatic disease. Rheumatoid arthritis accounted for about one sixth of AC-30 cases. Image measures showed lower per-nucleus intensity than comparators. The work gives labs an objective anchor for a pattern that was previously judged by eye alone.
pmc-13371878:
Andrea Navalón Calzada and co-authors report a rare gut tear in a 2026 case report. A man aged 74, who had a kidney swap and took drugs to calm his immune system, came in with belly pain, fever, and loose stool. Small pouches in his small gut had grown sore.

Scans showed a pouch with air in the gut wall and a small leak held in by nearby tissue. At surgery the team found the tear and cut out the bad gut part, then joined the ends. He did well after the work. The case shows why fast scans and surgery count in patients with weak immune defenses.
pmc-13372378:
Arman Athwal and co-authors tested how scan settings shape eye response reads in a 2026 study. The method watches the light cells at the back of the eye shrink and stretch when light hits them. It uses a common type of eye scanner, set up as clinics might use it.

Seven healthy eyes were scanned while beam width, scan speed, and image blends changed. The two-step response showed each time. A wider beam showed cells more clearly but did not lift the response much. More blends of shots cut noise a lot. The work gives plain rules for clinics that want to add this test on standard gear.
pmc-13372678:
Nancy Morrow-Howell and co-authors asked older adults about age bias in a 2026 study. They ran nine group talks with 58 people aged 60 and up. Most were women, and the most common age band was 75 to 79.

Some had not heard the term for age bias, and some said they had not felt it. Once the idea was clear, most named slights at work, in clinics, in shops, and in the home. Bias turned inward was less known but came up in talk. The team says anti-bias work should speak to older adults first, not just to the young or to staff.
pmc-13374178:
Lin, Lin and their co-authors test an added bone procedure for diabetic foot ulcers with poor blood flow, in work listed for 2026. Even after a vessel-opening procedure, some wounds heal slowly because local blood supply stays low.

The study compared patients who got the added tibial procedure within days with those who got vessel opening alone. The added group healed fully in less time, and more had healed at the early check. Limb survival at one year was higher in the added group but not by a clear margin. Wound size and blood flow measures also moved in a better direction over time.
pmc-13374378:
Jon Azpeitia and co-authors watched a small molecule land on a prized sheet stuff in a 2026 study. The sheet is a two-part crystal used in chips and sensors. Dressing its face with molecules can tune its traits, but the type of bond has long been in doubt.

The molecule was laid down in a vacuum on sheets with few and with many face gaps. Fine scope views showed it lay flat and kept its sulfur tip whole. It roamed the face with ease and gripped gaps hard. The clear bond tale helps chip staff dress the sheet with more trust and less waste.
pmc-13375178:
Rui Lin Li and co-authors build models that flag nursing students at risk of failing a core course. The course, Fundamentals of Nursing, feeds both book knowledge and hands-on skill. Their 2026 study uses records from 527 students in two entry cohorts. Behavior and background data were split into training and test sets.

Five machine learning methods were tried, from logistic regression to neural networks. About one in nine students failed the theory exam. About one in five failed the practical exam. Scores on practice runs and course tests were strong flags for the practical side. Sex and research activity flagged the theory side. The team hopes such models can trigger early help and sharper teaching.
pmc-13376078:
Ming Li and colleagues split high PD-L1 lung cancers into subtypes using two extra markers. Their study from twenty twenty-six examines surgically removed tumours. High PD-L1 marks patients for immune therapy. Yet patients inside that group still behave very differently.

Sixty-nine tumours with top-level PD-L1 scores were tested further. Protein stains measured p53 and an interferon signal. Killer T-cell density inside tumours was also counted. Gene tests covered common driver mutations for context. Higher PD-L1 intensity linked with age and spread patterns. Marker combinations separated clinically distinct subgroups. Finer splitting could sharpen who gets which immune treatment.
pmc-13376778:
Ismail Hossain and co-authors design a blockchain-secured 6G smart grid framework, in this 2026 Europe PMC paper. Renewable energy is intermittent, and feeding it into grids raises security, transparency and resilience problems. Their architecture combines next-generation wireless slicing, a permissioned blockchain with verified smart contracts, and an ensemble of machine learning models for anomaly detection.

Different network slices serve energy trading, grid control and security monitoring with very low latency. On a synthetic dataset of five thousand hourly records, blockchain transactions succeeded about ninety-five percent of the time and latency stayed low even under simulated cyberattack. The anomaly detector scored high recall on both normal and attack traffic.
pmc-13377178:
Lijin Liu and co-authors present a 2026 system for spotting tiny cracks in dams from drone photos. Small cracks are an early sign of trouble in a dam, yet they are hard to catch in the very large images drones collect. Older detectors either miss the fine cracks or run too slowly on such large frames.

The team's system builds on a current detection model and adds three new parts. One part sharpens how the model reads fine detail, one weighs context at several scales, and one handles full-size images by slicing them with guidance from likely crack regions. On a dam photo set the team gathered itself, the system beat rival methods on precision and recall while staying fast. The code is public, and the authors aim the tool at routine dam safety checks.
pmc-13377278:
Feriz and co-authors test in 2026 how exact trial tooth veneers are when made by two smile design programs and two build methods. Veneers for front teeth are first tried in trial form to check fit and look. Designs were made for 25 patients for the upper front teeth.

Each design was built by printing and by milling, for 600 trial pieces in total. Set photo and scan rules kept measures steady across cases. Length measures from designs and built pieces were compared for gaps. Both program and build method shaped the gaps found. The work helps labs pick tools that keep trial veneers true to plan.
pmc-13378178:
Jessica C Costa-Pinto and co-authors set out a 2026 trial protocol called ARROW, on preventing repeat hospital stays for preschool wheeze. Wheezing illness is one of the most common reasons young children are admitted to hospital. Many are readmitted, and few preventive options exist.

Children in the trial receive either OM-85, a product made from killed bacteria that is taken by mouth, or a dummy treatment, with neither families nor staff knowing which. The main question is whether OM-85 cuts admissions for wheeze over twelve months of treatment. The trial also counts wheeze episodes and their length, and weighs the cost of treatment against any savings from fewer admissions.
pmc-13378378:
Xinyu Wang and colleagues present a 2026 review of a family of enzymes in heart failure, where the heart cannot pump well enough. These enzymes, called ADAM and ADAMTS proteases, cut other proteins and thereby shape inflammation, scarring, and heart muscle growth. Earlier accounts often treated them one by one.

The review joins the picture in two directions: members of the family meet within each disease process, and single enzymes such as ADAM17 act across several processes at once. Some actions harm the heart while others protect it. That fuller view may guide drugs that block only the harmful members, and it supports using some members as blood markers for diagnosis.
pmc-13382578:
Julie den Hartog's team tracked blood toxicity from pelvic and para-aortic radiation in prostate cancer, in a 2026 study. Whole pelvic radiation plus hormone therapy improves prostate cancer survival in node-positive disease, and adding para-aortic radiation is under trial. The team analyzed the first 75 Leuven patients in the PART trial, all on 24 months of hormone therapy.

At a median 57 months of follow-up, no blood toxicity forced a treatment break. All blood counts fell after radiation, but grade 4 toxicity was limited to lymphopenia, and no severe anemia or platelet toxicity appeared. Larger low-dose volumes to pelvic marrow tracked with greater late lymphocyte decline, giving planners dose limits to protect blood counts.
pmc-13383178:
Lokeswara Rao Potnuru's team found water-linked phosphate wires holding diseased tau fibrils together, in a 2026 study. Heavy phosphorylation of tau marks tau diseases, yet how phosphate groups drive clumping was unclear, since packed negative charges should repel. The team tested the opposite idea: phosphates line up into a stabilizing wire inside the fibril core.

Using seeding-ready tau peptide fibrils, phosphorus NMR counted at least six phosphate signals arranged in a line in an early fibril. Computer models showed water bridging the phosphate groups at sites S305p and Y310p, easing pushback. The wire model reframes tau phosphorylation from a mere marker to a structural glue that drug designers might target.
pmc-13383978:
Gioele Pecin and co-authors uncover a new cell-killing compound from a little-studied fungus in 2026 work. The fungus, gathered from a rare Spanish plant, was grown under 78 conditions to wake up its chemistry. Screening and molecular networking mapped a wide set of toxins and active compounds it can make.

Among them sat spectabilide A, a ring-shaped molecule built from three amino acids and a fatty side chain. It killed breast cancer cells strongly in lab tests, the team reports. Gene and chemistry evidence also moved the fungus into a new genus placement, which the authors formalize with a new name combination.
pmc-13384778:
Watanabe and Inaba reviewed in 2026 how zinc ions steer two quality-control proteins that cycle between the endoplasmic reticulum and the Golgi, the cell's folding and shipping stations. Zinc is the second most common trace metal in cells and serves as enzyme helper, structural brace, and signal. Two transporter families keep its levels tight, feeding it into or out of the cell's compartments.

Recent structural work shows zinc binding reshapes the chaperone ERp44, which retrieves stray proteins. The cargo receptor ERGIC-53, which ferries select proteins onward, switching their grip and release in step with zinc and acidity changes along the route. These findings cast zinc as an active regulator of the early secretory pathway, not just a nutrient. The authors say the mechanism helps explain how metal balance supports proteostasis, the upkeep of a healthy protein set, and may inform disease linked to these proteins.
pmc-13385078:
Wei Zhao and co-authors organize cancer drug design around the pyridine ring in a 2026 medicinal chemistry review. Pyridine appears in many approved cancer drugs, yet its value depends heavily on context, the authors stress. Sections sort compounds by what the ring actually does, from target binding to property tuning.

Examples span classic drugs, antibody-drug conjugate payloads, targeted degraders, and metal complexes with several pyridine units. Each case is weighed for structure-activity patterns and for body handling and safety liabilities. The closing message treats pyridine as a design module to validate case by case, not a magic scaffold.
pmc-13385378:
Ranee Harrison and colleagues show that the immune system's peacekeepers need their internal recycling service to keep the peace, in this study from twenty twenty-six. Regulatory T cells suppress immune responses, and they rely on a selective cleanup pathway, chaperone-mediated autophagy, that feeds worn proteins into lysosomes one by one. That pathway fades with age.

Peacekeeper cells lacking the pathway, in mice engineered so only their regulatory T cells were deficient, failed at their job. The mice developed chronic inflammation and died earlier as they aged. In two tests, a gut inflammation model and a tumor model, the deficient cells suppressed poorly. Protein-level analysis mapped which proteins the pathway normally destroys in these cells, and so which cellular programs it tunes. The authors establish the cleanup route as a working part of immune tolerance.
pmc-13386678:
Ellen Gabrielsen Hjelle and a large team test a coordinator-led support program for Parkinson's patients and family carers in 2026 work. OPTIM-PARK ran across Denmark, Norway, Spain, and the United Kingdom in community settings. A named coordinator assessed personal needs, gave support, and linked health, social, and voluntary services over three months.

The program enrolled 130 people, 72 with Parkinson's and 58 family carers, typically across three consultations. Active listening and tailored information anchored the coordinator's work, the team reports from logs and interviews. The mixed-methods study weighs feasibility and acceptability to guide wider rollout of multisector care.
pmc-13387678:
Koichiro Matsumura and co-authors measure mental distress among family caregivers of heart and vessel disease patients in Japan, in a 2026 study. Data came from a nationwide living conditions survey run by the health ministry, covering patients who needed care and the relatives living with them. Distress was scored on the six-item Kessler scale.

About thirteen percent of caregivers crossed the distress threshold. Risk ran higher when the patient was also distressed, when caregivers were younger, female, not working, or living alone with the patient, and when the patient also had dementia. The authors urge care teams to watch the mental health of the family, not only the patient, and to build support for both.
pmc-13387878:
The journal issued a fix to a 2021 paper by Ding's team. It concerns how the protein FtBPM3 shapes flavonoid making in Tartary buckwheat, a grain crop valued for its health-linked compounds. The notice fixes a set of figure errors: one pull-down assay image had been taken from the wrong panel, and several figure labels named the wrong protein tags.

A passage about one figure also named the wrong tag, and the fixed wording and image are supplied with the notice. The authors state that none of these errors change the paper's results, so readers can use the fixed figures with the original findings intact.
pmc-13388478:
Tuck Wah Siew and co-authors describe a new filler technique for hollows under the eyes in a 2026 report covering three patients. The area is hard to treat because the skin is thin and fat is sparse, and standard filler placed deep in the muscle can still cause swelling or a bluish tint.

Called BB8, the method dilutes a cohesive hyaluronic acid gel with saline and places it just under the skin through a cannula. Photos were taken before care and again afterwards. Follow-up ran for six to nine months, with hollow severity scored on a standard scale. Clinicians interested in facial aesthetics get a detailed early account of the approach, its steps, and its safety record in this small group.
pmc-13389078:
L Caeiro's team tracked muscle and quality of life in prostate cancer patients across six months of androgen deprivation therapy, which worsens the muscle loss the cancer itself causes. Mitochondria, the cell's energy units, were suspected players, but their role during this therapy was unclear.

Before treatment, stronger energy-unit function and endurance went with better patient-found results, while greater lean mass oddly went with worse ones. Higher baseline fitness and energy-unit function model smaller declines, and protein analysis showed energy-unit trouble plus inflammation and clotting pathways rising on therapy. Targeting energy units might one day protect function, but that idea still needs a trial.
pmc-13390078:
Asato Maeda's team developed a proteome-wide way to spot protein shape changes by using a kinase as a labelling tool. Their method pairs residue-specific phosphate labelling, which depends on kinase recognition of exposed sites, with quantitative phosphoproteomics after enrichment.

Tests on myoglobin with and without heat denaturation and on cell extracts with and without protease treatment showed labelling efficiency tracking structural state. Comparing extracts before and after RNA digestion then showed proteome-wide shape changes in intact cell material, giving teams a site-resolved readout of protein dynamics inside cells.
pmc-13390378:
Jonghoon Kang writes, in 2026, a letter offering a fresh thermodynamic reading of how a heat-loving bacterium gathers plant sugars. The letter responds to work by Tjo and colleagues on an uptake system in Anaerocellum bescii, a microbe that breaks down tough plant material at very high temperatures.

Because the original work reported full heat, disorder, and energy values for sugar binding to two carrier proteins, Kang argues that an extra layer of analysis is possible. The letter contrasts the distinct strategies the two proteins use to bind chains of sugar units. Biochemists gain a compact reinterpretation showing how complete thermodynamic reporting lets other scientists extract new meaning without new experiments.
pmc-13392078:
Xiaoyu Su's team built a self-powered, machine-learning ear tag that tracks farm-animal energy-use-linked welfare through between-cell fluid ions. Heavy farming diets often disturb energy use, yet spotting off animals at scale is hard.

A friction-plus-solar gatherer with on-off operation powers micro-needle sensors tracking pH, potassium, and calcium over time. A machine-learning chain reading joint ion dynamics told apart five welfare-related states at over ninety-five percent average hit rate, checked across 5,399 sample windows from three animals, establishing a large-scale precision-farm-animal model. The tag tracked pH, potassium, and calcium over time.
pmc-13393278:
Keunho Soh and seven colleagues put two kinds of memristor into a single probabilistic computing chip. A memristor is an electrical part whose resistance remembers current history. Hard pairing problems can be cast as energy landscapes stored in a grid of such devices, while flickering probabilistic bits explore the landscape.
