Hitting hormone and chemokine paths together blunted the macrophage shift in dishes.
pmc-13472978:
Mariah F. Calubag and colleagues report in 2026 that cutting one amino acid, valine, from the diet helped mice stay healthier for longer. Valine is one of three branched-chain amino acids found in protein foods. Mice fed low valine stayed leaner and handled blood sugar better at many ages. Both male and female mice showed less frailty and fewer cancers with age.

Male mice on the low valine diet also lived notably longer at the median point. Gene checks pointed to liver pathways tied to cell power plants working harder in males. Readers learn that a single food part, not protein as a whole, may drive many gains seen with low protein diets. The team sees promise for future care aimed at aging.
pmc-13473378:
Debertshaeuser and colleagues tested in 2026 whether brain imaging can be combined with fixed-bike cycling to study exercise and thinking. Nine young healthy adults cycled for twenty minutes at low, mid, and high intensity in a randomised crossover design. Forehead sensors using near-infrared light tracked prefrontal activity during number memory tasks before and after exercise.

The team checked practicality: dropout, timing, sensor reliability, and how well target loads were hit. The two ways of computing blood-oxygen signals agreed closely, showing good data from the moving setup. Memory task performance and brain responses varied with task load as expected. The authors conclude the joint protocol is feasible. They suggest minor design changes and better fitness testing to cut dropout and improve load targeting in future studies.
pmc-13473678:
Xi Chen and three colleagues modelled in 2026 how shield tunnel segments behave in soft ground, using the Liuyang River crossing of Changsha Metro Line 3. Lining segments in such strata face severe stress from groundwater swings and fluid-solid coupling, yet their responses under varying water levels were poorly quantified. The team built a finite element model in ANSYS, testing four water levels, then ran a sensitivity analysis with 10,000 Monte Carlo samples across nine variables.

Groundwater level dominated segment behaviour, with pore water pressure, stress, and horizontal convergence rising with it, while vertical deformation fell. The outer ring proved most likely to fail in tension, with crown and haunches as key control points. Stiffer segments carried higher forces while stronger rock eased them. Sensitivity analysis found rock density dominating axial force and lining thickness dominating bending moment. The study gives designers a ranked list of parameters for similar tunnels.
pmc-13474178:
Wenze Ding presents a framework designing peptide binders from sequence alone, in a 2026 paper. Peptides can modulate protein targets that small molecules handle badly, but finding binders usually takes heavy screening or known structures. Sequence design scales better for targets without a stable structure, though target control often slips and language model habits learned on full proteins transfer poorly to short chains.

The framework, BOND-PEP, retrieves known peptides relevant to the target. It aligns those examples with the protein through message passing, building a protein-centred representation. That representation then guides decoding of new sequences. On a benchmark of unrelated targets, judged by a structure prediction tool, it beat three rivals at producing winning designs. It also transferred to an outside panel of targets with lab-backed binders. The author offers this decoding as a practical route to controllable design.
pmc-13474478:
Rounak Mukherjee, Tripthi P. Shetty, and Padmaraj J. Hegde compare two ways to fix cheekbone fractures in 2026. Breaks of the cheek and jaw joint area are among the most common mid-face injuries. The standard fix opens the site and holds bones with plates, which adds surgical strain. The newer way lifts the bone from inside with a small balloon catheter, plus glue in place of hardware.

Forty-two patients were split evenly between the two methods. The balloon method took far less time in surgery. Scores for ease, stability, and scan results all favored the balloon group. Pain and side issues after surgery were also lower there. A gentler fix may suit many cheek fractures.
pmc-13474778:
Ecehan Kaplan and four colleagues tested in 2026 whether combining a dental laser with nano-hydroxyapatite better repairs early enamel lesions. They created artificial white spots on 100 cow incisors and split them into five groups: a standard paste, nano-hydroxyapatite alone, laser alone, laser then nano-hydroxyapatite, and the reverse order.

Laser groups gained significantly more hardness than the other groups at every stage, and laser-first preserved hardness best after acid cycling. Laser roughened surfaces, but nano-hydroxyapatite partly smoothed the irregularities, and microscopy showed the laser-first group formed the most compact mineral layer. Laser-first combination offers a promising route for lasting early caries care.
pmc-13474878:
Yoko Azuma and six colleagues reported in 2026 a rare case of phlegmonous esophagitis that mimicked descending necrotizing mediastinitis, a fatal chest infection. A 61-year-old man with deep neck infection was first diagnosed with chest infection on scans and underwent emergency neck drainage, airway surgery, and chest surgery.

During surgery the whole throat tube was swollen, and a scope exam after surgery confirmed throat-tube infection rather than the presumed diagnosis. He recovered well on antibiotics and fasting. The case shows that scan and surgery findings inside the chest matter for telling this rare throat-tube infection apart from its deadly mimic.
pmc-13474978:
Piccolo and colleagues piloted a rural palliative care program for heart failure patients in Maine in 2026, testing whether the model could work at all before any larger trial. A primary care complex care team, trained in comfort-focused care, met weekly with city-based specialists by video for coaching on their cases. Patients joined from one rural clinic, and the team tracked recruitment, completion, and how the experience felt to everyone involved.

Of 31 patients approached, 13 enrolled, and 12 of them, or 92.3 percent, completed every part of the program offered. All 12 finished a serious illness conversation and an advance directive, and 11 also spoke directly with the specialist physician by telehealth. Care team members attended at least 90 percent of the weekly meetings and reported stronger skills and confidence, and patients said the goal-setting talks felt manageable, not overwhelming.
pmc-13475178:
Yutaro Kaneko and co-authors compare two add-on ablation styles in 2026 for persistent atrial fibrillation. Standard vein isolation alone often fails in this lasting form of the rhythm fault. One group got extra burns guided by scattered signal zones, while a past group got burns guided by low-voltage zones. A total of 107 patients were tracked for two years.

Freedom from rhythm return at two years ran higher with signal-guided care, near seventy-six percent versus fifty-eight percent. The signal group also received more extra burns overall. Longer disease duration and larger left heart chamber size predicted return on their own. Signal mapping may refine who gains from extra ablation.
pmc-13475378:
Kanagavel and colleagues report a 2026 case of a giant neurofibroma, a benign nerve sheath tumor, in the abdomen and pelvis of a 29-year-old man. Such tumors in this location are very uncommon, with only about 60 cases reported. He had six months of growing abdominal swelling, frequent urination, and constipation.

Scans showed a large pelvic mass pressing on his rectum and bladder, which had backed urine up into both kidneys. Surgeons removed the mass completely through an open abdominal operation. Tissue testing confirmed a neurofibroma, and his recovery was smooth, with no return of the tumor at six months. The authors stress careful imaging and tissue diagnosis, since these rare masses can mimic other pelvic diseases.
pmc-13476378:
Zhiqian Luo and co-authors asked what drives the pelvis to tilt back to normal after spine surgery, in this 2026 study. In worn lower backs, the pelvis tips back to make up for a lost curve. Fixing the curve at surgery should let the tilt ease. The team read X-rays taken both standing and sitting before surgery to hunt for clues.

One hundred sixty-one patients who had surgery for worn lower backs took part. The bend of the lower back gained at surgery and the tilt held before it both tracked how much tilt came back. So did how much the tilt moved between standing and sitting. The team built a short math rule from those three to foretell the gain. Back pain after surgery also tracked the tilt that stayed. Sitting films, they say, earn a place in surgery plans.
pmc-13476778:
Tanzina Tanu and co-authors find in 2026 that faults in an RNA cleanup factor fuel cancers by freeing ancient viral RNA. The factor, ZC3H18, is cut short by mutations in about thirty percent of cancers. In zebrafish, the cut form sped melanoma onset and raised viral RNA levels. Human tumors and cell lines with the fault showed the same viral RNA rise.

The cut factor gripped viral RNA and moved it out of the nucleus instead of destroying it. Melanoma growth in fish needed that viral RNA to proceed. Human melanoma cells likewise depended on the freed RNA to grow. An old viral echo becomes a drug target.
pmc-13476878:
Mairim Alexandra Solis and co-authors warn in 2026 about unproven stem cell treatments marketed in Panama. Clinics have sold such treatments for over a decade for many diseases without solid proof of safety or benefit. The authors track online marketing and count new businesses entering the market. Harms reported worldwide span clots, tumors, vision loss, and death.

Panama first drew notice in 2013 when a clinic chain moved there from other countries. Ads used celebrity praise in papers, travel magazines, and social media. Weak enforcement let the market grow, the authors argue. Urgent action is urged to protect patients and steer funds to proven care.
pmc-13477078:
Fatemehsadat Pezeshkian and eleven colleagues built in 2026 a risk tool for recurrence after surgery meant to cure early-stage lung cancer without node spread. They followed 497 patients with tumours under 4 cm, clean nodes, and complete resection, tracking which surgical and pathology features predicted return of disease.

One in ten patients recurred over a median 30 months. Vessel invasion, pleural invasion, poor cell maturity, narrow margins, and incomplete lymph node removal each raised recurrence risk, with vessel invasion strongest. A combined risk chart scored well. The authors argue that combined burden, not any single feature, should guide follow-up and future risk-adapted treatment.
pmc-13477478:
The mountain plant Arnica montana is declining across Europe, and tracing how its populations relate has been hard because its chloroplast DNA varies so little. Siddharth Annaldasula and co-authors built a software pipeline in 2026 that assembles whole chloroplast genomes in a standard, repeatable way from short reads. They ran it on public data for eight accessions of the species across Europe, plus relatives.

All the plant's chloroplast genomes grouped into one family tree branch, splitting into an Iberian group and a central and northern European group. Signs of mixed chloroplast types within samples linked the groups. The authors recommend reading that within-sample variation and standardizing new genomes the same way.
pmc-13478378:
Carina Karner and Emanuela Bianchi showed in 2026 how planned partial bonding can steer colloidal crystals rather than spoil them. Partial bonding is usually seen as an obstacle to order, but by varying patch layout on diamond-shaped platelets they tuned frustration to select crystal forms.

Limiting bonds, rather than maximising them, directed crystal choice, tuned pore levels, and improved crystal yield in porous single layers. The strategy programs function into colloidal materials, with relevance for molecule design, DNA nanomaterials, and responsive assemblies. Frustration emerges as a design tool, not just a defect.
pmc-13478678:
Fei Li and co-authors tracked a blood ratio over time in 2026 for patients whose kidneys fail during sepsis, the body's extreme response to infection. A single reading of the ratio, lactate over albumin, already hints at risk, but its movement over the first days might say more.

The team mined a large United States intensive care database for patients with at least three paired readings in the first seventy-two hours. Pattern modeling sorted patients into distinct paths for the ratio. Those paths tied to death at twenty-eight and ninety days and to the need for dialysis machines. A scoring chart built on the paths was checked in patients from five Beijing hospitals. The authors propose it for early triage.
pmc-13479578:
Anqi Huang and colleagues present a 2026 feasibility study of a culturally adapted dialectical behavior therapy coaching program for Chinese parents of adolescents with mental disorders. These parents carry heavy distress, and structured caregiver support is scarce in China. Forty-two parents joined a ten-week program of weekly online group sessions plus home practice.

The mixed-methods design tracked numbers at baseline, program end, and three months, alongside parents' own accounts of the experience. Dialectical behavior therapy teaches emotion regulation and relationship skills, and the adaptation reshaped examples and delivery for Chinese family culture. Feasibility questions came first: would parents enroll, stay, and practice? Preliminary effectiveness signals on distress and family functioning were secondary, guiding whether a full trial is justified.
pmc-13479978:
Jin Zhou and coauthors published a 2026 multi-omics study of gestation length in Large White pigs, a trait that directly affects litter size and piglet survival. The dataset was large: 22,783 reproductive records from 9,057 pigs across five populations. Genome scans and a combined meta-analysis searched for DNA regions tied to how long pregnancies last.

New associated regions appeared on four chromosomes. Statistical fine-mapping narrowed the credible causal variants, and studies linking genes to traits and traits to health outcomes added functional evidence, alongside chemical mark profiling of the genome. Two genes, GNAZ and SLC5A4, emerged as critical regulators in the combined analysis. Breeders gain markers for selecting sows whose gestation length supports larger, hardier litters.
pmc-13480078:
Taiqing Luo and colleagues report a 2026 survey of doctors and their plans to work through internet hospitals in China. These online platforms let doctors treat patients at a distance. The team polled 233 doctors at eight public hospitals in Shanghai in late 2022 and modelled how support at work, felt risk, and expected gains shape plans to join.

Good support at work linked directly to stronger plans to use the platforms. Support also worked through two middle paths, by lowering felt risk and by raising expected gains, and those paths chained together as well. Together the indirect paths made up close to forty-five percent of the total effect. Junior doctors leaned more on workplace support, while senior doctors weighed risk more heavily. Hospitals that want uptake should build support systems, show clear gains, and ease risk worries.
pmc-13480278:
Boldizsar Kovacs and co-authors review racing-heart relapse after ablation in a 2026 paper. Patients with a non-ischemic heart muscle disease face sustained fast rhythms. Defibrillator implants are standard after such events, yet ablation may change that need. The review asks how often the rhythm returns when pumping strength is near normal.

Three databases were searched through June 2025 under standard review rules. Eleven studies covering over fourteen hundred patients qualified. About two-thirds of patients had full data for synthesis. Relapse rates ranged widely, from low to two-thirds of patients. Non-inducibility at the procedure consistently predicted lower relapse. Inducible patients relapsed at much higher rates in the studies. Scan patterns of scarring also carried prognostic clues. The authors weigh whether implants can be safely deferred in selected cases. Evidence stays too mixed for a blanket rule.
pmc-13480678:
Pham and colleagues surveyed neonatal clinicians in 2026 about sending babies with bronchopulmonary dysplasia home on oxygen, the lung disease that ranks as the commonest complication of preterm birth. The anonymous online survey, offered in four languages, drew 610 responses from 44 countries between December 2022 and August 2023. Three quarters of respondents worked in richer countries, and one quarter in low and lower-middle income settings.

Most clinicians, 84 percent, would discharge these infants on home oxygen, but in poorer countries only 65 percent could do so, against 91 percent in richer ones. Clinicians credited home oxygen with better growth and brain development, and home oxygen monitoring was also commoner in richer settings, at 78 versus 67 percent of respondents. Saturation targets and weaning rules varied widely, and over three quarters called wearable monitors with parent-led control important for fixing the gaps.
pmc-13481078:
Sudakou and colleagues worked out in 2026 new maths for diffuse optics, a method that reads tissue by watching how light spreads through it. Time-based versions record how long light takes to cross tissue. Analysts then turn shifts in that timing into shifts in how much light the tissue soaks up or scatters. Standard formulas assume tiny shifts, so large ones break their accuracy.

Sudakou extended the maths from tiny shifts to large ones, in uptake, scattering, and the gap between light source and sensor. Their formulas cover both deep tissue and surface tissue models, with no added guesses. They include a fixed form of a known light law used in steady-light tools. They also tested how wrong starting values skew the results, and how scattering shifts can fake uptake shifts. The work aims to sharpen light-based tissue readings in medicine.
pmc-13481978:
When HIV resists nearly every drug class, two newer entry blocking medicines offer a last line, and real world evidence on them is thin. Karl Stefic and co-authors survey France in 2026, following seventy people starting fostemsavir and eleven starting ibalizumab, all carrying multiresistant virus. Many arrived with virus already suppressed; others were failing openly.

Among those failing, about sixty-three percent on the first drug and thirty-six percent on the second reached success, and suppression held in ninety-one percent of those who started suppressed on fostemsavir. Failures sometimes traced to low drug levels rather than new resistance. The authors say the pair works in the hardest cases, with adherence the weak point. Their observatory will keep watching.
pmc-13482278:
Behrens and colleagues measure how laboratory embryo production alters the earliest tissues of cattle embryos. Their 2026 paper compares day-15 bovine conceptuses made in vitro with counterparts conceived by artificial insemination, examining the embryonic disc, which forms the calf, and the extra-embryonic membranes. Both DNA methylation, a chemical control layer, and gene activity were sequenced, then integrated with machine learning.

In the embryonic disc, one gene set stood out. It covered body segment formation, mesoderm development, and gastrulation. Those genes were enriched among ones over-methylated and switched down in lab-made embryos. In the membranes, the affected genes clustered around epigenetic regulation itself. Effects persisted even though lab embryos spent a week developing inside the mother after transfer. The authors conclude in vitro procedures leave marks on both main lineages before implantation.
pmc-13482578:
Pezeshki and colleagues test a belief-based teaching program in 2026 for a neglected pairing, mouth care in people with type 2 diabetes at the Fasa Diabetes Center in Iran. Diabetes multiplies gum and tooth disease rates, yet oral self-care rarely features in routine diabetes education. The experimental study randomized 220 patients into two equal groups, one receiving six teaching sessions built on the Health Belief Model and one receiving routine care.

Sessions ran 50 to 55 minutes each, mixing group discussion, questions, demonstrations, and printed material on why mouth care matters for diabetes control. Six months later the taught group scored significantly higher than controls on every measure tracked, knowledge, perceived risk, severity, benefits, barriers, confidence, and prompts to act. Their actual oral and dental health behaviors improved significantly too, and the authors recommend weaving belief-based oral health teaching into standard diabetes center programs.
pmc-13483578:
Jia and team traced a chain of brain inflammation that may explain memory loss after severe body-wide infection. Their 2026 mouse study modeled sepsis-associated brain dysfunction, a condition striking most sepsis patients and often leaving lasting cognitive damage. The team focused on microglia, the brain's immune cells, and one of their proteins, the protein-3, in the hippocampus, the region central to forming memories.

Infection signals drove the protein-3 sharply upward, which switched on further immune machinery inside microglia. The resulting stress selectively harmed parvalbumin interneurons, fast-signaling cells that keep brain rhythms coordinated. With those cells damaged, the memory-area rhythms that support memory fell out of sync. Blocking the protein-3 eased the cascade in the experiments described. Jia names the protein a candidate drug target for protecting sepsis survivors' thinking.
pmc-13484478:
Rasheed and team crossed maize lines to learn which genetic patterns help seedlings survive drought, a growing threat to Pakistan's third-largest crop. Their 2026 study grew seven commercial genotypes and their crosses under full watering and half watering, measuring roots, shoots, and leaves at the seedling stage. Stress chemistry, including damage markers and protective enzyme activity, was assayed in parallel.

Genotypes differed strongly on every trait measured, giving breeders real variation to work with. Some traits, like the root-to-shoot length ratio, were governed mainly by additive gene effects, which respond well to straightforward selection. Root length and leaf area leaned on dominant gene effects under drought instead. One genotype, E-322, combined high heritability for key traits with stable drought performance. Rasheed cautions that environment swayed several traits, so multi-site trials must confirm the winners.
pmc-13486478:
Durgadevi and co-authors paired two artificial intelligence methods to keep voltage steady in power grids crowded with solar and wind farms. Renewable output swings with weather, which makes voltage drift and wastes energy as losses. Their 2026 framework uses ant colony optimization, a search method modeled on ant trails, to plan voltage profiles, while a reinforcement-learning controller adjusts reactive power moment by moment.

The combined controller settled on good settings within about 45 to 50 search rounds across the scenarios tested. Voltage stability improved and system losses fell compared with the baseline strategies in their simulations. The learning controller trained on historical and simulated data, so it reacts without waiting for a fresh optimization run. Durgadevi presents the hybrid as a scalable option for grid operators facing rising shares of variable renewable generation.
pmc-13486778:
Pengli Song and others find a eater cell subtype that drives regeneration of the pancreas after acute pancreatitis. In 2026, the study uses single-cell reading, lineage tracing, and mice lacking the dock TREM2 in myeloid cells, plus samples from patients. These monocyte-derived eater cells gather around areas where pancreas cells change self during injury.

Removing TREM2 blocked the shift toward a repair-oriented eater cell state, left swelling and scarring unresolved, and impaired regrowth of enzyme-producing cells. The defect involved blood fat fuel use and reduced release of Desert Hedgehog, a signal that activates repair in progenitor-like cells, and drug switching on of that pathway rescued regeneration. Patient blood levels of soluble TREM2 fell as disease gravity rose, backing medical relevance.
pmc-13488178:
Shengze He and colleagues measure delirium after shoulder rotator cuff surgery in United States hospital data in a 2026 retrospective study. Delirium is sudden confusion after an operation, and national figures for this common shoulder procedure were lacking. The team used a large inpatient database covering 7,216 patients treated from 2016 to 2019, comparing those coded with delirium against those without on age, other illnesses, complications, stay length, and cost.

Delirium was coded in about seven to eight percent of inpatients, a share the authors call far from trivial. Affected patients were older, sicker, stayed longer, cost more, and suffered more medical and surgical complications during admission. Older age, substance misuse, anemia, and brain or mental disorders raised risk, while elective admission lowered it.
pmc-13488678:
Henny Suzana Mediani and co-authors analyze in 2026 the concept of virtual reality for managing pain during medical procedures in children. Such pain and anxiety are common, and drugs or simple behavior methods may not fully help young children. Twenty eight studies from 2005 to 2025 were synthesized. Three defining traits emerged: a sense of being inside a three dimensional world, distraction that engages the mind away from pain, and control of feelings. The analysis also sets out what must come before use, what follows from it, and how it can be measured in practice.
pmc-13488778:
Anna Carolina Faria Moreira Gomes Tavares and co-authors compare telomere length in lupus patients and healthy peers. Telomeres cap the ends of chromosomes and shorten as cells age. Lupus is linked to early cell aging, but the clinical meaning of short telomeres is unclear.

The team measured telomeres in adults with lupus and matched healthy controls. They also recorded disease activity, damage, fatigue, mood, stress, and activity levels. Lab tests used a standard DNA copying method to size the telomeres. Their analysis tests if shorter telomeres track with worse disease burden. It also tests links with anxiety and stress. The study adds data on aging marks in a complex immune disease.
pmc-13489078:
Nafas Rafiyan, Farnaz Malekifard, and Bijan Esmaeilnejad survey external parasites on dogs in Isfahan, Iran, in a 2026 paper. Ticks, mites, fleas, and lice on dogs can carry agents that harm animals and people. The team examined 138 dogs between mid 2023 and mid 2024: strays, herd dogs, and owned dogs.

Close to four in ten dogs hosted at least one parasite. Ticks were the most common, then mites, fleas, and lice. Rates differed in a clear way by sex and age, and spring was the peak season. Since several of these parasites can pass disease to people, the authors call for stronger veterinary and public health steps in the county.
pmc-13490478:
Nicholas Bartelo and others search for energy markers of drug resistance in two major gut germs. In 2026, the study looks at 512 listed breakdown products from 297 germ samples across eight germ types, with a focus on Klebsiella pneumoniae and Escherichia coli. These drugs are last-line treatment for tough Gram-negative germ ills, so reliable drug markers matter.

Because breakdown products varied more between species than between tough and weak strains, the team modeled each germ type on its own. Models predicted well for the first germ and fairly for E. coli, yielding four possible markers in the former and seven in the latter. These germ-specific signs offer a base for faster tests and for probing how germs turn drug-proof.
pmc-13490578:
Kollapudi and Singh simulated a switch device-based sensor that detects targets by how they change the electrical behavior of a tiny cavity near the device's passage junction. Label-free sensors skip the dyes and tags of lab assays, promising bedside speed. Their 2026 design uses a gate overlapping the source channel on an insulated silicon platform, modeled with realistic imperfections like uneven probe placement and targets crowding each other.

Response depended strongly on where captured targets sit, peaking when they lodge right at the passage junction. For gelatin samples the device's current response reached a figure on the order of hundreds of millions relative to baseline in the model run. Charged and neutral targets both registered, through varied mixes of the modeled passage mechanisms. Kollapudi presents the asymmetric gate and cavity placement as the keys to the extreme response claimed.
pmc-13491078:
Sathish K OV and co-authors present a 2026 study of the hearts of children who recovered from multisystem inflammatory syndrome, a post-viral illness linked to COVID-19. The syndrome often weakens the heart muscle at its peak, and children seem to recover fast. Whether quiet changes linger in the heart muscle long after was unclear.

The team used cardiac magnetic resonance scans, which can spot swelling and scarring that ordinary checks miss. They also measured galectin-3, a blood marker tied to inflammation and scar formation. Finding lasting silent changes would argue for long-term heart follow-up in these children, even when they feel fully well.
pmc-13491778:
Manlin Yan and three colleagues work in 2026 with a yellow mutant of the green alga Chlorella that barely makes chlorophyll, a trait that could simplify production of the eye-health pigment lutein. Less green pigment means a purer lutein extract at the end of processing. The team grew the original strain and the mutant under three feeding modes and compared pigments and gene activity.

The mutant's chlorophyll a fell to about a ninth of the original strain's level, and its chlorophyll b nearly vanished. The original strain made lutein fastest when fed both light and carbon, while the mutant did best growing on sugar in the dark. Glucose suited the mutant better than acetic acid. Gene comparisons between the strains traced how the two pigment pathways are regulated together.
pmc-13492078:
Alisa Dewald and four colleagues audit in 2026 how many of America's two hundred largest health systems run programs that tackle homelessness among their patients. The year 2024 set a national record for people without housing, and hospitals absorb much of the fallout. The team mined each system's website for mitigation programs and tested which state and system traits predicted having one.

Just over half, fifty-six percent, advertised a homeless mitigation program. Affordable and permanent supportive housing led the list, followed by outreach teams and shelter-based medicine. Systems in states that had expanded Medicaid had more than double the adjusted odds of running a program. Richer shelter capacity in a state also nudged the odds upward. With federal safety-net spending shrinking, the authors expect these programs to matter more.
pmc-13492578:
Heslop and co-authors show how plant breeders can tap wild gene bank stock to harden red clover against a changing climate. Red clover is a pasture legume that pulls nitrogen from the air with help from soil bacteria. Local varieties lack traits needed as drought and heat grow.

The team crossed exotic stock into local varieties and tracked the inherited DNA with gene sequencing. Field trials across sites and years tested the second generation against standard varieties. Several new lines matched or beat the standards, and most traits passed to offspring at solid rates. The search found seventy-seven DNA markers tied to climate conditions, with a subset linked to plant traits. Prediction models trained on the stock forecast growth and density well in the derived lines. The authors offer this as a working route from gene bank shelves to climate-ready pasture seed.
pmc-13493478:
Filipe R Valeriano leads a ten-author team comparing in 2026 how three Brazilian blackberry varieties withstand a rust fungus that invades their leaves. Blackberry growing supports family farms in Brazil, and the fungus Kuehneola uredinis colonizes the leaf's middle layer, swelling cells before bursting through the surface to release spores. Microscopy and chemical staining compared healthy and infected tissue across the cultivars.

Guarani answered invasion with vigorous tissue expansion, thickening its leaf blade and upper skin. BRS Xavante suffered the worst structural losses, losing nearly half the thickness of its light-catching cell layer. BRS Tupy held its anatomy steadiest, looking the most tolerant. Infected zones everywhere accumulated defensive phenolics, proteins, and oils, although the weakest cultivar made fewer protective oils. Breeders, the authors say, now know which parent stock to favor.
pmc-13493778:
Zhang and a large team examine how neuroticism, the personality trait of reacting strongly to stress and negative feelings, affects visual attention. In their 2026 experiment, 31 young adults scoring high on neuroticism and 31 scoring low searched displays for targets while the researchers recorded brain waves. Those recordings capture tiny voltage changes that reveal each stage of attention, from spotting a target to holding it in short-term memory.

The high group answered less accurately than the low group, despite their brains working harder at several stages. Signals linked to selecting a target and storing it in visual memory ran larger, suggesting extra effort that still fell short of the task's demands. Another signal, tied to noticing new distracting items, was also bigger, which the authors link to trouble letting go of distractions. They read the pattern as inefficient use of attention resources rather than a simple lack of effort.
pmc-13493978:
A liver disorder of pregnancy, intrahepatic cholestasis, is often tied to variants in the gene ABCB4, but most rare variants found in patients are hard to judge. Bracanovic and co-authors took nine rare variants from women with the disorder. They ran them through five computer prediction tools, including one built for this gene and a recent learning-based tool. They checked the calls against published lab studies of the same variants.

The tools agreed on only four of the nine variants. Lab results often contradicted the predictions. One variant that did nothing in cell tests was called likely harmful by the gene-specific tool and harmless by the learning-based one. A second variant flipped the other way. The authors conclude that computer calls alone cannot settle these variants. Functional tests or family data are needed before a variant can be classed with confidence.
pmc-13494078:
Eigbefoh-Addeh and colleagues examine whether folate, a B vitamin needed to build DNA, affects sperm quality in healthy men, an angle far less studied than folate in pregnancy. Their 2026 study recruited 197 men aged 18 to 40 in Spain. It measured folate in blood plasma and red cells plus related vitamins, checked gene variants in the folate pathway, and graded semen by World Health Organization criteria.

Outright deficiency was uncommon, affecting only a small share of the men, but gradations mattered. Those in the lowest third for plasma folate had clearly lower sperm counts than those in the highest third, and red-cell folate showed the same pattern. One gene variant, the AA form of a gene called MTHFD1, was likewise tied to worse semen measures. The authors say even sub-deficiency folate levels may quietly undermine male fertility.
pmc-13495078:
Chen and colleagues measured in 2026 how the brain responds to astringency, the dry puckering feel of tannin-rich drinks. They used near-infrared light sensors on the forehead to track blood flow in the front of the brain. Volunteers tasted proanthocyanidin, the compound behind astringency, in water, in ethanol, and in red wine, at several strengths. Responses were split into the tasting phase and the aftertaste phase.

Perceived intensity rose with concentration, but its size and time course differed by drink base. During tasting, frontal blood-flow responses were limited and inconsistent. During aftertaste, responses became broader and stronger across the prefrontal area. Different channels over regions for reward, planning, and control showed distinct drink-related patterns. The authors argue that the lingering feel involves spread-out judging, not a simple readout of intensity.
pmc-13495978:
Kailin Weitkämper and co-authors show how Pearl's causal method can join separate ecological datasets into one clear picture. Published in 2026, their case study follows Myricaria germanica, a shrub of river banks, in northern Italy. The team argues that field ecology shapes policy, so its methods should be open and repeatable.

River channel width and bank protections stood out as the top factors for the survival of young plants. Height above sea level and other human acts mattered mostly by way of channel width. The authors offer the diagrams as a shared language for work across fields.
pmc-13499478:

pmc-13500678:

pmc-13501278:
Lindgren and colleagues tested whether patterns of co-occurring gut bacteria can forecast health, in a 2026 study of Finland's FINRISK cohort followed for twenty years. pmc-13501378:
Santana and three co-authors review ways to turn cassava processing waste into useful products, in work published in 2026. Gentler biological routes were clean but slow. Combined biorefinery routes won on energy and impact, yielding fuels and acids.
pmc-13501778:

pmc-13502378:

pmc-13502578:

The authors offer sequence and selective solvation as dials for vat photopolymerization design.
pmc-13503278:

Bowel rupture in this disorder is rarely described and poorly understood.

The authors suggest gut manifestations here may differ from vessel Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and warrant further case accumulation.
pmc-13503778:
Mason L. Hatwan and three colleagues track how daily movement and stress relate to drinking signs among college students, in a 2026 study. Young adults move through many settings each day, and those settings can raise or lower stress and drinking risk. Phone-based daily reports let the team watch both patterns shift together.

The study followed 185 undergraduates, most of them women with a mean age near 18. Each day they logged places visited and stress felt. Stress tended to carry over from one day to the next, while movement did not. Later checks found stress and movement feeding each other across days. Students with higher drinking scores at the start moved more on average, though their stress was no higher.
pmc-13503978:
Eight authors pool trials of a cough aid tool in vented ICU adults in a 2026 review and meta check. Harm marks were read with the same care.

pmc-13504578:

Gene and stain tests tied the markers to clear tissue states, such as areas that shut immune cells out.
pmc-13504978:
Al-Jobur and colleagues measured Yemeni adults' dental arches to check whether the ready-made wires orthodontists bend teeth with actually fit local mouths. Ovoid was the commonest natural arch form, and men's arches ran wider than women's across the measurements. Most preformed wires were too wide at the canine level, overshooting the natural upper arch by a few millimetres on average. The lower arch was overshot by even more, with smaller excesses at the molars. No single product matched the sample on every measure.
pmc-13505478:
Xiuli Wu and Aimei Kang rank what heart patients want from nursing robots, in a survey from 2026. China ages fast, heart disease climbs, and wards are short of hands. Robots could ease the load, but what patients want from them was unmapped.

The study ran at a Wuhan heart hospital across a year, with 156 patients. A Kano-style form grades fifteen robot jobs: which thrill, which are mere musts, which leave users cold. Company and chat, health talks, and record care drew strong want in the part of the head shown here. The team scores each job with gain-loss weights and a four-box map. Builders, they say, should fund the jobs patients rank as gains, not the jobs that merely look new.
pmc-13506178:
Julio César López-Valdés and four co-authors weigh the ethics of brain surgery for severe mental illness. Modern psychosurgery has moved from crude lesions to precise targets and implanted stimulators, with better safety and oversight. At the same time, brain research has mapped the networks behind theory of mind: how we grasp others' thoughts, feel empathy, and judge right from wrong. Their 2026 article links the two stories. Surgery near these networks could touch a patient's agency and sense of self.

The authors propose an ethical frame for work with suffering patients who have failed other care. History warns against haste, while present need argues against blanket refusal. Their aim is a path where consent, identity, and oversight guard every step.
pmc-13506578:
Cristina Vecchio and colleagues survey, in a 2026 review, how lasting inflammation pushes fatty liver disease toward a more harmful stage. The mild form, called MASLD, involves fat buildup in the liver tied to body weight and blood sugar problems. The advanced form, called MASH, adds liver cell injury, scarring, and a higher risk of liver cancer.

The review traces roles for insulin resistance, harmful fats, cell stress, and gut imbalance in keeping inflammation active. Immune cells and liver support cells turn that signal into scar tissue over time. Treatment choices remain limited for advanced disease. The authors map open questions that new drugs will need to answer.
pmc-13507078:
Adam G Bainbridge and colleagues characterize, in 2026 work, a DNA repair enzyme from Aspergillus fumigatus, a fungus that causes severe lung infections in people with weak immunity. Since the fungal pathway diverges from the human one, it may offer a selective target for new antifungal drugs.
pmc-13507178:
Riccardo Lanari and colleagues run 2026 bench models that couple magma pushing upward with rain-driven surface erosion, to probe volcanic risk under a changing climate. Heavier rain is expected as the world warms, and erosion unloads rock above magma chambers. Their box models injected a magma-like fluid at varied rates while artificial rain fell at varied strengths.

The team suggests that unloading could raise chamber pressure and push the system closer to eruption. Results are early and call for field checks.
pmc-13508278:
Hilda Pena leads a ten-author team studying a widespread parasite in rescued birds of prey near São Paulo, Brazil, in 2026 work. Live parasites were recovered from 27 of the mouse tests, across nine bird species. The strain mix showed the wide genetic variety typical of this parasite in Brazil. pmc-13508378:

Salmonella turned up only in the wild goat enclosures, which pointed away from those outside sources. The report gives wildlife managers a rare full picture of a wild goat outbreak with food safety stakes.
pmc-13508578:

Models then sorted which factors independently track with pressure problems and poor quality of life. pmc-13509378:

pmc-13511678:

pmc-13512278:

pmc-13512478:

pmc-13514978:

pmc-13515778:

pmc-13517078:

pmc-13517478:

pmc-13517578:

pmc-13517678:

pmc-13518278:

pmc-13518478:

pmc-13518878:

pmc-13518978:

pmc-13519278:

pmc-13519478:

pmc-13519978:

pmc-13520178:

pmc-13521778:

pmc-13522378:

pmc-13522478:

pmc-13522578:

pmc-13523278:

pmc-13523378:

pmc-13523478:

pmc-13523578:

Mehmet Cetiz and co-authors test how the fluid used to pull chemicals from a wild herb shifts what the extract can do, in a study from 2026. pmc-13523878:

pmc-13524678:

pmc-13524878:
Angela Yee-Moon Wang leads an international expert group in a 2026 consensus statement on putting nutritional supplementation into practice for patients on dialysis. pmc-13525078:

pmc-13525678:
Matthew Luzentales-Simpson and co-authors build a patient board to steer person-first care marks in Alberta front-line care. pmc-13525778:
Dandan Chi and Yuntao Guan wrote a 2026 letter on a study of distress and disordered eating in adults with obesity. The study, by Cyranka and co-authors, surveyed patients at an obesity clinic. Reporting choices, the fit of screening tools, adjustment for other factors, and repeated testing all need care. pmc-13525878:
Muhammad Umar Farooq and others set out, in a 2026 paper, a protocol for rebuilding complex defects at the side of the skull base. This region packs fine nerves and vessels between the cranium and face, so tumors there challenge both removal and reconstruction.

Planning, choices during surgery, care around it, and long-term rehabilitation are shown as one pathway. pmc-13526478:
Baayoud and colleagues report a 2026 case, with a review of past reports, of a 30-year-old man whose bulging left eye revealed IgG4-related disease. He had nine months of painless eye protrusion and eyelid swelling, and scans showed an orbital growth reaching back into the skull.

pmc-13527478:
Wu and colleagues present a 2026 case report linking an outbreak of gouty panniculitis, urate crystals inflaming the fat under the skin, with a rare immune disorder. pmc-13527678:
Colette SA Wesonga and Benard W Kulohoma wrote a 2026 article on health funding in Kenya. Kenya must fill the gap with its own money while care needs stay high. A United States order in January 2025 paused aid and hit clinics and health workers fast. The authors weigh how Kenya can raise funds at home, keep drug supply chains running, and build local vaccine and drug plants.
pmc-13527978:
Yi Gao and four colleagues investigate a gene called FBXW7 in intervertebral disc degeneration, a common cause of back pain. Lab checks on patient tissue confirmed higher levels of both FBXW7 and a signaling protein named JNK.

In cell experiments, silencing FBXW7 reduced the death of nucleus pulposus cells, the cells that cushion the disc center. Forcing extra FBXW7 raised JNK and pushed cells toward death. pmc-13528078:
Suprapto and seven colleagues explore how to lift health service quality in Indonesia in a 2026 qualitative study. Transcripts were coded for themes, with peer checks and member feedback for rigor.

Workforce strain stood at the center. Staff faced scarce ongoing training, heavy loads, and mixed clinical and management skills. Digital tools varied wildly between sites. Weak internet, low digital skill, and unlinked systems blocked progress. Policies often stalled at facility level under red tape. Community input channels were rare and thin. pmc-13528278:
Gizem Erdem, Nilüfer Kafescioğlu, and Gökçenay Başer put a chatbot therapist on trial in a 2026 study. A model tuned for family therapy methods held a session with a volunteer client. The client raised a relationship concern. Twelve seasoned supervisors then graded the transcript with standard scales. They did not know the therapist was an AI.

Ratings landed at moderate competence for systemic thinking and technique. Weak spots included pacing, joining with the client, and culture and context. Supervisors guessed the therapist was a beginner with under five hundred hours of practice. Erdem and colleagues say the gaps show what human therapists add. pmc-13528978:
Liver chemosaturation floods the liver with chemotherapy while filters scrub the blood leaving it, and the procedure swings patients' blood pressure wildly. Jan Turra and co-authors measured what the charcoal filter itself removes in 2026, across fifteen procedures.

Blood drawn before and after the filter told a sharp story. Noradrenaline, the body's own pressure-raising hormone and also a drug given during the procedure, rose steeply as the circuit ran. The charcoal filter then stripped about 95.5 percent of it in a single pass, even while infusions kept the dose high. Adrenaline and dopamine behaved differently. The authors warn that teams must plan around the filter eating the very drug that steadies the patient.
pmc-13529578: Peter and colleagues published a correction in 2026 in the European Stroke Journal to their article on calibrated non-inferiority margins. That method sets fair comparison thresholds in stroke trials when patient populations shift. The correction fixes panel B of Figure 3, whose graph did not match the data in Table 1. It supplies the corrected figure caption describing how prognostic factors were distributed across the historical meta-analysis and the new trial datasets.
pmc-13529778:
Shilin Yin and five colleagues tie a body clock gene to cholesterol making in mouth cancer in a 2026 study. The gene, PER2, runs daily rhythms. It was scarce in oral squamous cancers. pmc-13529878:
Sun and five co-authors test whether a blood protein called sLRP-1 relates to obstructive sleep apnea in people who snore. The study enrolled 180 adults who had overnight sleep recordings. One hundred had sleep apnea and 80 did not. The team measured the protein with a standard lab test.

Machine learning models separated the two groups well, and the protein ranked among the top signals. The authors say outside validation is needed before any clinical use.
pmc-13531378:

pmc-13532678:

pmc-13532778:

pmc-13533878:

pmc-13534378:

pmc-13534878:

pmc-13535378:

pmc-13536578:

pmc-13536678:

pmc-13536778:

pmc-13536878:

pmc-13537378:

pmc-13537478:

pmc-13538378:

pmc-13538478:

pmc-13538578:

pmc-13539278:

pmc-13539778:

pmc-13539878:

pmc-13539978:

pmc-13540078:

pmc-13540578:

pmc-13540878:

pmc-13541578:

pmc-13541778:

pmc-13541878:
Yuxuan Zhao and co-authors model how patterns form when cooperators and free-riders share a space and a common good, in a 2026 paper. pmc-13542578:

pmc-13543378:
